The cool climate is a relief if you dislike tropical heat, and the coffee and food scenes are strong. The city feels calm and orderly. On the downside, that same cool, grey winter weather disappoints anyone expecting beaches and constant sun, and Curitiba has no coastline. The nomad and expat community is smaller than in Florianopolis, Rio, or Sao Paulo, so social life takes more initiative. Portuguese is essential, since English is not widely spoken. Some visitors find the city a touch quiet or lacking the vibrant energy of Brazil's more famous destinations. If you crave nightlife, warmth, and a big international crowd, Curitiba may feel understated compared with its flashier Brazilian rivals.
curitiba.whoFor: Livability rather than spectacle is the trade being made here: someone who wants a safe, clean, well-run city with reliable internet, great parks, and a temperate climate rather than beaches and heat. It is ideal for focused remote workers, digital professionals, and anyone who finds tropical humidity draining and appreciates cool evenings and four real seasons. Coffee lovers and park-and-cycle types will feel at home. It rewards those willing to learn some Portuguese and build their own social circle, since the international community is modest. It is a weaker choice for beach seekers, party-focused travelers, or anyone wanting a large ready-made nomad scene, who would be happier in Florianopolis or Rio. Choose Curitiba if you value calm, order, green space, and a comfortable base for exploring southern Brazil, and if a mild, sometimes chilly climate sounds like a feature rather than a drawback.

fortaleza.costOfLiving: Fortaleza, a large coastal city in Brazil's northeast, offers beach living at a lower cost than the south, and a solo remote worker manages well on around $1,300 per month (editorial estimates in USD). A one-bedroom apartment near the beach in Meireles or Aldeota runs roughly $300 to $500, while further from the coast you find places for $200 to $320. Groceries cost about $180 to $260 monthly, with cheap tropical fruit, fish, and produce widely available. Eating out is inexpensive: a set lunch runs $4 to $7, and fresh seafood or a beachside meal stays affordable. Local buses cost around $1, keeping monthly transport near $30 to $50 if you mix in ride-hailing. Coworking memberships run $80 to $150. Air conditioning and its electricity bill are a real line item here given the year-round heat, so budget a bit extra for cooling and utilities.
fortaleza.whereToWork: Fortaleza has a growing coworking scene concentrated in the Meireles, Aldeota, and Praia de Iracema areas near the beach, offering desks, meeting rooms, and a local startup community. As a major Brazilian city, its internet is generally good, with fiber home connections common and reliable, though quality can vary more by building than in the wealthier south. A prepaid SIM from Vivo, Claro, or TIM provides solid urban 4G and 5G as a dependable backup. Cafe-work culture exists along the beachfront and in Aldeota, with air-conditioned cafes being especially welcome given the heat. Many nomads value a coworking space here not just for the wifi but for the reliable air conditioning during long working days. Connectivity in central and beachfront neighborhoods is dependable enough for video calls, though it is wise to test your specific apartment's connection before committing to a longer lease. More submarine internet cables come ashore here than anywhere else in the southern half of the world, which is why a city this far from the wealthy south has latency to Europe and North America that the bigger cities cannot match. That is not a detail: it is the strongest technical argument there is for working from this coast rather than another one.
fortaleza.gettingAround: Fortaleza is a sprawling city, and while the beachfront districts of Meireles and Iracema are pleasantly walkable with a long seaside promenade, getting across town requires transport. There is a limited metro and an extensive bus network, with fares around $1, though buses can be crowded and slow. Most nomads lean on ride-hailing, with Uber and 99 both cheap and widely available; typical trips cost $3 to $8. You do not strictly need a car if you base yourself near the beach and use apps, though a car helps for exploring the famous dune beaches and coastline beyond the city. Pinto Martins International Airport connects Fortaleza to the rest of Brazil and increasingly to Europe, making it a convenient Atlantic gateway. For day trips to spots like Cumbuco or Jericoacoara, arrange a transfer or rental, since public options thin out fast. The road west along the coast is the one that matters, running past a string of kite beaches to the dune village most people come for, and the final stretch of it is sand crossed by buggy rather than by car. A full day goes each way. Long-distance coaches leave from a station well inland of the beach districts, and reaching it is itself a trip across town.
fortaleza.visas: Brazil's Digital Nomad Visa applies here just as anywhere in the country: it grants a one-year, renewable stay for remote workers employed by foreign companies, requiring proof of income around $1,500 per month or equivalent savings, plus valid health insurance. You apply through a Brazilian consulate abroad, and it is the cleanest legal route for a longer Fortaleza stay. For shorter visits, many nationalities including most Europeans enter visa-free as tourists for 90 days, frequently extendable to 180 days within a year. However, visa requirements for some countries, including recently the US, Canada, and Australia, have been in flux, so do not assume. Because these thresholds and reciprocity rules change, always verify the current income requirement, document checklist, and your own passport's status directly with an official Brazilian consulate or the immigration authority before you travel or commit to a rental. A national tax number is the document that unlocks ordinary life here: no phone contract, no bank account and no great many online purchases without it, and a foreigner can obtain one at a consulate before arrival or at a federal revenue office afterwards. Getting it early saves a fortnight of being unable to pay for things the way everybody around you does.
fortaleza.bestTime: Fortaleza sits close to the equator and is hot and sunny essentially year-round, with temperatures typically in the high 20s to low 30s Celsius every month, tempered by a near-constant sea breeze. Unlike southern Brazil, there is no cool season, so if you dislike heat, be prepared for it all the time. The year splits into a wet season and a dry season rather than hot and cold. The rainy months run roughly from February through May, when heavy showers are common, though they often pass quickly. The best time to visit is the dry season from around July to December, when you get reliable sunshine, lower humidity, and ideal beach and dune conditions. September through November are especially good. Wind sports enthusiasts favor the windy second half of the year. Whenever you come, plan for strong sun and pack accordingly.
fortaleza.prosCons: Fortaleza's appeal is straightforward: warm weather every single day, long urban beaches, a lively seaside promenade, fresh seafood, low costs, and easy access to spectacular dune-lined coastline like Jericoacoara. The constant sea breeze takes the edge off the heat, and flights to Europe are handy. On the downside, the relentless heat and, in season, heavy rains can wear on some people, and there is no escape into cool weather. Safety is a genuine consideration, as Fortaleza has higher crime rates than the calmer southern cities, so you must be street-smart about neighborhoods and nighttime movement. The city sprawls, English is limited, and the nomad community is smaller and less established than in Florianopolis or Rio. Air conditioning is close to a necessity, adding to costs. It is a trade-off of beach lifestyle and value against heat, sprawl, and safety caution.
fortaleza.whoFor: Sun-loving, beach-focused arrivals are the obvious fit here: warm weather guaranteed year-round, affordable coastal living, and a base for exploring the stunning dunes and lagoons of northeastern Brazil. It is a natural fit for kitesurfers and windsurfers, who flock to the region for its steady winds, and for anyone happy trading cooler climates for permanent summer. Budget-conscious remote workers get real value here compared with southern or international beach hubs. It rewards those who speak some Portuguese and are comfortable staying alert about safety in a big northeastern city. It is a weaker choice for anyone sensitive to heat, wanting a large polished expat scene, or prioritizing safety and walkable compactness above all, who might prefer Florianopolis. Come to Fortaleza if endless sun, beaches, seafood, and low costs outweigh the heat, sprawl, and need for everyday street awareness.

belohorizonte.costOfLiving: Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, is a large inland city offering strong value, and a solo remote worker lives comfortably on about $1,300 per month (editorial estimates in USD). A one-bedroom apartment in sought-after central areas like Savassi or Funcionarios runs roughly $300 to $480, while neighborhoods further out drop to $200 to $320. Groceries cost around $180 to $260 monthly, with the region's famous produce and markets keeping quality high and prices low. Eating out is a highlight and a bargain: a generous prato feito or per-kilo lunch runs $5 to $9, and the city's legendary bar food, or comida de boteco, is cheap and plentiful. Buses and the limited metro keep transport near $30 to $50 monthly, supplemented by ride-hailing. Coworking memberships run $80 to $150. Minas food culture means eating out often is both a pleasure and easy on the budget here.
belohorizonte.whereToWork: Belo Horizonte has a solid coworking ecosystem, much of it clustered in and around Savassi, the city's hip commercial and nightlife hub, alongside spaces in the central business districts. As one of Brazil's largest metros, its internet is generally reliable, with fiber home connections widely available and cafe wifi usually dependable in the better neighborhoods. A prepaid SIM from Vivo, Claro, or TIM delivers good urban 4G and 5G coverage as a solid backup for calls. Cafe-work culture thrives, helped by Minas Gerais's serious coffee heritage and a dense scene of bakeries and cafes where lingering with a laptop is normal. Savassi in particular has plenty of laptop-friendly spots that transition from daytime workspace to evening bar. For longer focus sessions and meeting local founders, a coworking membership is worthwhile, plugging you into the city's genuine startup and tech community, one of the more active in Brazil. Iron ore is what this state actually runs on, and the two tailings dam collapses at Mariana and Brumadinho, which killed hundreds of people and poisoned two river systems, are still live in the courts and in local politics. The mining companies are headquartered here, which is why the engineering and legal sectors are as large as they are.
belohorizonte.gettingAround: Belo Horizonte is a big, hilly city, and while central neighborhoods like Savassi and Funcionarios are walkable and lively, the terrain and sprawl mean you will use transport for longer trips. There is a single metro line of limited reach plus an extensive bus network with fares around $1, though buses can be slow and crowded. Ride-hailing through Uber and 99 is the go-to for most nomads, being cheap, quick, and safe for night moves, with typical trips costing $3 to $8. You do not need a car to live centrally, though one helps for weekend trips into the beautiful Minas countryside and historic towns like Ouro Preto. Tancredo Neves International Airport, at Confins about 40 minutes out, connects the city domestically and with some international routes. Between walkable central districts and cheap ride-hailing, daily mobility is manageable without owning a vehicle. A second, older airport much closer to the centre handles regional flights, and checking which one a ticket uses saves an hour in each direction. The colonial road that carried gold down to the coast passes through the hills south of the city and is now walked and ridden in stages, which is the best way into that country.
belohorizonte.visas: As with anywhere in Brazil, Belo Horizonte falls under the country's national Digital Nomad Visa, which allows remote workers employed by foreign companies to stay for one year, renewable for a second. You will need to show income of roughly $1,500 per month or sufficient savings, plus health insurance, and apply through a Brazilian consulate abroad. This is the most straightforward legal path for a longer stay. For shorter visits, many nationalities including most Europeans enter visa-free for 90 days as tourists, often extendable to 180 days within a twelve-month period. Be aware that visa reciprocity rules have recently shifted for some countries, including the US, Canada, and Australia, so your situation depends on your passport. Because income thresholds and entry rules change, always verify the current requirements and document list directly with an official Brazilian consulate or immigration authority before booking or signing a lease.
belohorizonte.bestTime: Belo Horizonte enjoys a pleasant highland tropical climate, sitting at around 850 meters elevation, which keeps temperatures milder and more comfortable than Brazil's steamy coastal cities. The year divides into a wet season and a dry season rather than hot and cold extremes. The rainy season runs from roughly October to March, bringing warm days and frequent, sometimes heavy afternoon showers along with higher humidity. The dry season, from about April to September, is the sweet spot: warm, sunny days, low humidity, cooler and very pleasant evenings, and little rain. Those dry-season months are the best time to base yourself here, with June and July occasionally cool at night, so pack a light jacket. Summers are warm but rarely oppressive thanks to the altitude. If you want to avoid the wettest, most humid stretch, steer clear of the peak of the rainy season around December and January. The street carnival here grew from almost nothing over the last decade into one of the largest in the country, with blocks parading through the central neighbourhoods for a week and the whole city out on the street. It is worth arranging a room around, in one direction or the other, because nothing else happens that week.
belohorizonte.prosCons: Belo Horizonte's strengths are its famous food and bar culture, genuinely warm and welcoming locals, a pleasant highland climate, strong value for money, a real tech and startup scene, and easy access to the stunning colonial towns and mountains of Minas Gerais. It feels authentically Brazilian rather than touristy. On the downside, it is a large, sprawling, hilly city with limited metro coverage, so you depend on buses and ride-hailing. There is no beach and fewer marquee sights than Rio, so its appeal is more about lifestyle and food than postcard attractions. The nomad and international community is smaller than in coastal hotspots, and English is not widely spoken, making Portuguese important. As in any big Brazilian city, you should stay aware of safety in certain areas and at night. It rewards those who value substance, cuisine, and local life over obvious tourist glamour.
belohorizonte.whoFor: Anyone who wants a food-obsessed Brazilian city rather than a beach resort or a heavily touristed one will do well here. It is perfect for anyone who loves eating and drinking out, since the boteco bar culture and Minas cuisine are among the best in the country and remarkably affordable. It fits sociable travelers happy to learn some Portuguese and connect with warm locals and an active startup community rather than lean on a big expat bubble. The mild highland climate appeals to those who find coastal heat and humidity tiring. It is a launchpad for exploring historic colonial towns and mountain scenery. It is a weaker pick for beach lovers, first-time visitors wanting famous landmarks, or anyone needing a large ready-made international nomad crowd. Choose Belo Horizonte if great food, genuine local culture, good value, and a comfortable climate matter more to you than beaches and tourist fame.

kolkata.costOfLiving: Kolkata is one of India's most affordable major cities, and a solo remote worker can live well on around $700 per month (editorial estimates in USD). A one-bedroom apartment in a central area like Park Street, Ballygunge, or Salt Lake runs roughly $150 to $280, while outside the core you find places for $90 to $160. Groceries are very cheap at around $80 to $130 monthly, helped by abundant local markets. Eating out is where Kolkata shines: legendary street food like kathi rolls and puchka costs under $1, and a full restaurant meal rarely exceeds $5 to $8. Public transport, including the metro, buses, and iconic trams, costs mere cents per ride, keeping monthly transit under $25 even with regular ride-hailing. Coworking desks run a modest $60 to $110 monthly. The low rent and dirt-cheap, extraordinary food make Kolkata one of the best-value nomad bases anywhere in Asia.
kolkata.whereToWork: Kolkata has a developing coworking scene, with spaces concentrated around Salt Lake Sector V, the city's IT hub, plus options near Park Street and the central business district offering desks and meeting rooms. The important caveat is that internet reliability in India is variable: a good fiber connection at home or in a coworking space is fine, but power cuts and inconsistent building wiring happen, so carry a backup. A prepaid 4G SIM from Jio or Airtel is cheap, delivers strong data across the city, and is essential insurance for keeping video calls alive when the wifi falters. Buy one on arrival with your passport. Cafe-work culture exists in the more modern coffee chains and Park Street cafes, though it is less entrenched than in Bengaluru. For dependable connectivity and air conditioning during the intense heat, a coworking membership is the safest bet for serious remote work here. College Street is the largest second-hand book market anywhere, a kilometre of stalls that has supplied this city's students for a century and a half, and the publishing trade standing behind it still employs people in a way that has died out everywhere else in the country.
kolkata.gettingAround: Kolkata has India's oldest metro, now expanding, which is cheap, fast, and a lifesaver for crossing the congested city, with fares of just a few cents. The city also runs an extensive bus network and the historic tram, a charming if slow relic. Central areas around Park Street are walkable, though pavements are crowded and traffic is chaotic, so walking is more sightseeing than efficient transport. Ride-hailing via Uber and Ola is cheap and widely used, alongside the ubiquitous yellow Ambassador taxis and auto-rickshaws for short hops; app trips often cost just $1 to $4. You absolutely do not need a car, and driving yourself here would be stressful and unnecessary. Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport connects Kolkata across India and to regional international destinations. Between the metro, cheap ride-hailing, and rickshaws, getting around is inexpensive, if best approached with patience for the traffic. This is the last city anywhere still using hand-pulled rickshaws, repeatedly banned and never actually removed, and the argument about them is as much about the pullers' livelihoods as about dignity. Ferries cross the river constantly and beat the bridges at rush hour.
kolkata.visas: India makes short stays easy through its e-Tourist Visa, applied for entirely online in advance, with options ranging from 30 days up to multi-year multiple-entry validity depending on your nationality. It is quick, affordable, and the standard route for most visitors. Crucially, India has no dedicated digital nomad visa, and working remotely while on a tourist visa sits in a legal grey area: the tourist visa is officially for tourism and recreation, not employment, even if your employer and income are entirely outside India. Many nomads do work quietly on tourist visas, but understand it is not formally sanctioned, so keep a low profile and do not seek local income. For anything longer term or for actual India-based work, you would need an appropriate business or employment visa. Because visa categories and e-Visa eligibility change, always verify the current rules and your nationality's options on the official Indian government e-Visa portal before applying.
kolkata.bestTime: Kolkata has a tropical climate with a punishing hot and humid season, so timing your stay matters more here than in many cities. The clearly best months are the cool, dry winter from November to February, when daytime temperatures are pleasant, humidity drops, and the city is at its most livable and festive. This is the ideal window for a longer base. Avoid the pre-monsoon stretch from March to May, when heat and humidity become oppressive, with temperatures pushing into the high 30s Celsius and sticky, draining conditions. The monsoon, from June to September, brings heavy rain, flooding in parts of the low-lying city, and relentless humidity, making it the least comfortable and most disruptive time. October offers a pleasant, celebratory shoulder period around Durga Puja. In short, come in winter for comfort, and steer well clear of the hot, humid monsoon months if you can. The pre-monsoon storms that come out of the northwest in the hottest weeks are violent and short, dropping the temperature ten degrees within the hour and taking down trees and power lines as they go. They have a local name, and everybody watches for the sky turning that particular colour.
kolkata.prosCons: Kolkata's strengths are its remarkable affordability, extraordinary street food, deep cultural and intellectual heritage, grand colonial architecture, and warm, famously welcoming, literary-minded locals. It offers an authentic, un-sanitized Indian experience at rock-bottom prices, with a metro and cheap transport that make it navigable. On the downside, the summer heat and monsoon humidity are genuinely brutal, air pollution and congestion are real issues, and the infrastructure feels older and more worn than in Bengaluru or Delhi. Internet and power can be inconsistent, so backups are essential. The nomad and international community is small and the coworking scene modest, so you will not find a big ready-made expat crowd. The pace, noise, and crowds can overwhelm newcomers to India. It is a city that rewards curiosity and patience, trading polish and convenience for culture, character, and value that are hard to match anywhere else.
kolkata.whoFor: The culturally curious and budget-minded, who want India at close quarters rather than a comfortable, ready-made expat hub, are who this is for. It is ideal for lovers of food, history, literature, art, and street life, since the city rewards wandering, conversation, and exploration at every turn. Extreme value seekers will stretch their money remarkably far here. It works best for experienced travelers, ideally with some prior India exposure, who can handle heat, crowds, noise, and variable infrastructure with patience and good humor. Slick amenities, guaranteed bandwidth and a sizeable nomad scene are none of them on offer, and as a first encounter with India this city asks a great deal too much: Bengaluru or Goa introduce the country far more gently. Come to Kolkata if you value soul, culture, incredible cheap food, and genuine human warmth over convenience, and if you visit during the cooler, comfortable winter months.

chennai.costOfLiving: Chennai runs around $750 per month for a comfortable single nomad. A furnished one-bedroom in a central area like Nungambakkam or T. Nagar costs roughly $250 to $400, with cheaper options further out. Eating local is very affordable, and a filling South Indian meal can run $2 to $4, so budget $180 to $250 for food if you mix home cooking, cafes, and the odd restaurant. A prepaid SIM with generous data is about $3 to $5 monthly. Add $40 to $70 for a coworking hot desk, plus transport, utilities, and air conditioning during the hot months. Air conditioning pushes electricity bills up noticeably from March through June. Domestic help and laundry are cheap. You can live on less by choosing a shared flat and eating at local messes, or spend more for a sea-facing apartment and frequent cabs.
chennai.whereToWork: Chennai has a solid coworking scene concentrated around Guindy, Nungambakkam, and the OMR tech corridor, with day passes and monthly hot desks widely available. Home wifi is generally decent in the city but can be inconsistent during monsoon and outages, so keep a backup 4G or 5G SIM topped up with data as a reliable fallback. Mobile coverage is strong and cheap, which matters when fixed lines wobble. Cafe culture leans toward filter coffee spots and modern cafes in Besant Nagar and Alwarpet where you can plug in for a few hours, though not every place welcomes long laptop sessions. Power cuts still happen occasionally, so a coworking space with backup power is the safest bet for calls. Working from your apartment is fine most days, but treat unmetered fixed broadband as a bonus rather than a guarantee. This is the country's car manufacturing centre, with assembly plants and a deep supplier network south of the city that together account for a large share of national vehicle exports. Medical treatment is the other export, and the hospitals here draw patients from across the region, which is why a good many of the flights arriving are not carrying tourists at all.
chennai.gettingAround: Chennai is spread out and fairly flat, but heat and traffic make walking long distances tiring outside cooler months. The metro is clean, cheap, and expanding, though it does not yet cover every neighborhood, so many nomads rely on ride-hailing. Ola and Uber both operate widely, and autorickshaws are everywhere, though metered fares are inconsistent, so agree a price or use the app. Suburban trains and city buses are extremely cheap but crowded and less intuitive for newcomers. Chennai International Airport is well connected domestically and to Southeast Asia and the Gulf, roughly 30 to 45 minutes from the center depending on traffic, and reachable by metro. Owning or renting a two-wheeler is common among longer-stay residents but traffic is chaotic. For most short-term nomads, a mix of metro plus app cabs and autos covers daily life comfortably. The coast road south is the drive that opens the region up, running past the shore temples to a former French territory a couple of hours down, and it is the standard weekend out. In the city, the beach fronting the centre is one of the longest urban stretches of sand anywhere, and the evening crowd on it is a fixture rather than an event.
chennai.visas: India has no dedicated digital nomad visa. Most visitors enter on the e-Tourist Visa, applied for online before travel, available in 30-day, one-year, and five-year variants depending on nationality. It is straightforward to obtain and is the standard route for nomads staying a few weeks to months. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a tourist visa sits in a legal grey area that Indian rules do not clearly address, so understand you are not formally authorized to work and weigh that risk yourself. For any local employment or paid activity inside India you would need a proper employment or business visa. Rules, permitted stay lengths, and registration requirements change, and some longer stays trigger FRRO registration, so always verify the current requirements on the official Indian government visa portal before booking and again close to travel. Anybody with Indian ancestry or an Indian spouse can hold an overseas citizen card, which removes the visa question permanently and allows an indefinite stay, so eligibility is worth checking before assuming a tourist route. The longer electronic visas run from the date they are granted rather than the date of arrival, so applying too early quietly shortens the time actually available.
chennai.bestTime: The most comfortable window in Chennai is November through February, when temperatures ease and humidity drops to bearable levels, making this the clear peak for visitors. March through June is hot and very humid, with pre-monsoon heat that can feel punishing, so avoid this stretch if you are heat-sensitive. Chennai gets most of its rain from the northeast monsoon between October and December, and heavy downpours can cause flooding and disrupt travel, so factor that in if you visit late in the year. Coastal humidity is a constant, meaning even pleasant months feel sticky compared to inland India. If you want festivals, the Margazhi music and dance season peaks in December and January, coinciding with the best weather. For remote work with reliable power and comfortable evenings, aim for the December to February sweet spot and treat everything else as a compromise.
chennai.prosCons: Chennai's strengths are low costs, excellent and cheap South Indian food, a genuine tech industry with real coworking options, warm and orderly local culture, and good air links to Southeast Asia and the Gulf. The beaches and the nearby heritage sites of Mahabalipuram add appeal. On the downside, the heat and humidity are relentless for much of the year, traffic is heavy, and the city is more conservative and less overtly nomad-oriented than places like Goa or Bangalore. English is widely spoken, but Tamil dominates daily life. Wifi can be patchy, power cuts still occur, and monsoon flooding is a real risk. Nightlife is limited compared to other metros. It is a practical, affordable base with authentic culture rather than a polished nomad hub, rewarding travelers who value substance and value over scene and convenience.
chennai.whoFor: Budget-conscious arrivals who want a working South Indian city rather than a curated nomad bubble are the right audience. Tech people who want to be near an actual industry rather than a coworking desk get exactly that here. So do food lovers, between the filter coffee, the vegetarian cooking and Chettinad, and so does anybody who came for the temples and the classical arts. If you tolerate heat and humidity well and can handle occasional infrastructure hiccups with a backup SIM, you will find great value here. It is a strong pick for longer stays where low costs compound. It is less ideal for those who need a buzzing party scene, cool weather, or a large ready-made international community. Solo travelers and couples who like calm, orderly cities will feel comfortable, and the strong English usage lowers the language barrier for getting set up and finding services quickly.

hyderabad.costOfLiving: Hyderabad sits around $800 per month for a single nomad living comfortably. A furnished one-bedroom in a good area like Gachibowli, Madhapur, or Banjara Hills runs roughly $280 to $450, with more affordable flats a little further from the tech hubs. Food is a highlight and a bargain, and you can eat well on $180 to $260 a month, whether that means famous biryani, local tiffin, or the many mid-range restaurants. A data-heavy SIM is around $3 to $5 monthly. Budget $45 to $75 for a coworking hot desk, plus utilities, air conditioning in summer, and transport. Electricity bills climb during the hot April to June stretch when air conditioning runs constantly. Groceries, domestic help, and laundry are inexpensive. You can trim costs with a shared flat and local eateries, or spend more for a modern apartment near the IT corridor with easy access to malls and cafes.
hyderabad.whereToWork: Hyderabad has one of India's better coworking ecosystems, clustered around HITEC City, Madhapur, and Gachibowli where the IT industry concentrates, so hot desks and day passes are plentiful and professional. Fixed broadband in these tech areas is generally reliable, but service can still drop during outages or storms, so keep a backup 4G or 5G SIM loaded with data as insurance for important calls. Mobile coverage is strong and cheap across the city. Cafe culture is growing, with plenty of modern cafes near the tech corridor and in Jubilee Hills that tolerate laptop work, alongside traditional Irani cafes better suited to a chai break than a long session. Many coworking spaces run backup power, which matters during occasional cuts. For remote workers, basing yourself near HITEC City gives the best combination of connectivity, backup infrastructure, and workspace choice. The pharmaceutical industry here is as large as the software one and rather more consequential: a substantial share of the world's vaccines is manufactured in this city, and the research campuses north of it employ tens of thousands of scientists. None of that is visible from the technology corridor, but it explains the cargo the airport handles.
hyderabad.gettingAround: Hyderabad is large and car-oriented, and the tech districts sit well outside the historic center, so distances are significant. The metro is modern, clean, and covers key corridors including parts of the IT belt, making it a good backbone for daily travel, though it does not reach everywhere. Ride-hailing through Ola and Uber is widespread and affordable, and autorickshaws fill the gaps, though you should use the app meter or agree fares. Traffic is heavy during peak hours, especially around HITEC City. Rajiv Gandhi International Airport is one of India's better airports, well connected domestically and internationally, but it sits far south of the city, so allow 45 to 75 minutes by cab depending on traffic. Two-wheelers are popular with longer-stay residents. For most nomads, combining the metro with app cabs and the occasional auto covers daily life without needing your own vehicle. A complete orbital motorway rings the city at a radius of around twenty kilometres, which is unusual in this country and is why the airport run is quick in spite of the distance, provided you join it rather than cutting through town. The metro was built as one of the largest public-private rail projects anywhere, and it shows in how it is run.
hyderabad.visas: India has no digital nomad visa, so Hyderabad visitors use the e-Tourist Visa, applied for online before arrival in 30-day, one-year, or five-year forms depending on nationality. It is easy to obtain and is the usual route for stays ranging from a few weeks to several months. Working remotely for an overseas employer while holding a tourist visa falls into a legal grey area that Indian regulations do not clearly resolve, so recognize you are not formally permitted to work and decide how comfortable you are with that ambiguity. Local employment or any India-based paid activity requires a proper employment or business visa instead. Permitted stay lengths, entry conditions, and any registration duties can change, and some extended stays require FRRO registration, so confirm the current rules on the official Indian government visa portal before you book and again shortly before you travel.
hyderabad.bestTime: The best time to be in Hyderabad is roughly October through February, when the weather is mild, dry, and pleasant for both work and sightseeing, marking the clear peak season. Hyderabad sits on the Deccan plateau, so it is generally a touch less humid than coastal Chennai, which makes the cool season especially comfortable. Avoid the peak heat of April through June, when temperatures climb high and air conditioning becomes essential all day. The southwest monsoon brings rain mainly from June to September, which cools things down but can cause waterlogging and traffic snarls, so it is a mixed period. Winter nights can feel genuinely cool by Indian standards, a welcome change. For the most productive remote-work stint with comfortable evenings and minimal weather disruption, target November to February, and treat the pre-monsoon summer as the stretch to plan around rather than through. Bonalu, the city's own festival, fills the old quarter with processions to the goddess temples over several weeks in the wet months, and it is entirely local rather than something put on for visitors. The lakes ringing the city fill during the same weeks, and the evenings out on the bunds are the best the year offers.
hyderabad.prosCons: Hyderabad's pluses include a strong and modern tech economy with excellent coworking, relatively good infrastructure in the IT districts, legendary and affordable food, a plateau climate that is milder than the coast, and a clean, expanding metro. The historic Charminar area, forts, and lakes give it real character beyond the office parks. Costs stay low for the quality on offer. Drawbacks include a sprawling layout with long distances between the old city and the tech belt, heavy peak-hour traffic, and summer heat that demands constant air conditioning. It is more of a business and IT city than a leisure nomad hotspot, so the ready-made international scene is smaller than in Goa or Bangalore. English is widely used alongside Telugu and Urdu. Occasional power cuts and monsoon waterlogging remain nuisances. Overall it balances practicality, value, and culture well for a working base.
hyderabad.whoFor: Hyderabad fits nomads who want a well-run, affordable Indian city with a genuine tech backbone and solid coworking rather than a beach-party crowd. It suits remote workers in software who value proximity to a real industry and reliable-enough infrastructure near HITEC City, plus food lovers eager to work through the city's famous biryani and rich culinary mix. History and culture fans get the Charminar, Golconda Fort, and lakeside evenings. The milder plateau climate appeals to those who find coastal humidity draining. It is a good long-stay value base where low costs add up over months. It suits solo travelers and couples comfortable navigating a large, car-oriented city with cabs and the metro. It is less suited to people seeking a compact walkable town, cool mountain weather, or a large established international nomad community, since Hyderabad is more workmanlike than scene-driven.

ahmedabad.costOfLiving: Ahmedabad is among India's better-value cities, running around $650 per month for a comfortable single nomad. A furnished one-bedroom in a decent area such as Navrangpura, Satellite, or near the riverfront costs roughly $200 to $350, with cheaper options further out. Food is very affordable, and Gujarati thalis, street snacks, and local eateries let you eat well on $150 to $220 a month, though note this is a largely vegetarian city so meat and especially alcohol are hard to find. A generous data SIM is about $3 to $5 monthly. Budget $35 to $65 for a coworking hot desk, plus utilities and heavy air conditioning use in the intense summer. Electricity bills spike badly from March through June. Groceries and domestic help are cheap. You can live comfortably on modest spending here, and the low rents make Ahmedabad one of the most economical metro bases in the country.
ahmedabad.whereToWork: Ahmedabad has a growing but smaller coworking scene than the big tech metros, with spaces concentrated around Navrangpura, C.G. Road, Prahlad Nagar, and the SG Highway corridor offering hot desks and day passes. Fixed broadband in the city is reasonable, but reliability can dip during outages and the hot season, so keep a backup 4G or 5G SIM loaded with data for critical calls, which is wise across India. Mobile coverage is strong and cheap. Cafe culture is developing, with modern cafes along C.G. Road and in newer commercial areas where laptop work is tolerated, though the city is more business-driven than cafe-lounging in character. Being a dry state, do not expect cafe-bar hybrids for evening work sessions. Coworking spaces with backup power are the safest choice during occasional cuts. Basing near Prahlad Nagar or SG Highway gives good access to workspaces and amenities. The management institute here occupies a campus designed by Louis Kahn in brick, and the national design school sits a few kilometres away, which between them make this the country's centre for design and management education rather than for software. Architects travel specifically to see those buildings, and the city holds more of that kind of thing than its reputation carries.
ahmedabad.gettingAround: Ahmedabad is relatively flat and has invested in transport, including a growing metro and the BRTS bus rapid transit system that runs on dedicated lanes and is cheap and reasonably efficient. Still, the city is spread out and summer heat makes long walks unpleasant much of the year. Ride-hailing via Ola and Uber works well and is affordable, and autorickshaws are plentiful, though you should use app meters or agree fares in advance. The metro is clean and expanding but does not yet reach every area. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport sits close to the city, typically 20 to 40 minutes from central areas, with good domestic links and some international routes to the Gulf. Two-wheelers are common among residents. For most nomads, a combination of app cabs, autos, and the BRTS or metro covers daily needs comfortably without owning a vehicle. A high-speed line to the country's financial capital has been under construction here for years and its viaducts are now visible across the outskirts, though the opening date has moved more than once and is best treated as a plan. For now the overnight trains and a short flight are the two ways to cover that distance.
ahmedabad.visas: India offers no digital nomad visa, so visitors to Ahmedabad rely on the e-Tourist Visa, applied for online ahead of travel in 30-day, one-year, or five-year versions depending on nationality. It is simple to obtain and is the standard path for stays from a few weeks to several months. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a tourist visa occupies a legal grey area that Indian rules do not clearly address, so understand you are not formally authorized to work and judge that risk for yourself. Any local employment or India-based paid work requires a proper employment or business visa instead. Allowed stay durations, entry rules, and possible registration steps can change over time, and certain longer stays require FRRO registration, so always check the current requirements on the official Indian government visa portal before booking and again just before you travel.
ahmedabad.bestTime: The comfortable season in Ahmedabad is November through February, when the weather turns mild and dry, making it the clear best window for visiting and working. Gujarat is a hot, dry state, and the pre-monsoon stretch from March through June is genuinely punishing, with high temperatures that make air conditioning essential and outdoor activity difficult, so avoid this period if you can. The southwest monsoon arrives around late June and runs through September, bringing relief and some rain, though the city stays drier than coastal India. Winter is the highlight for events too, with the famous Uttarayan kite festival in January and Navratri in autumn drawing crowds. The dry heat is intense but at least less sticky than coastal humidity. For a productive remote-work stay with tolerable evenings and cultural festivals, aim squarely at the November to February window and plan around the brutal summer. The salt flats several hours west turn into a white plain once the monsoon water dries off, and a season of tented camps runs out on them through the cool months, which is the one trip out of this city that more or less everybody makes. Full moon nights there are the point, and they book out well ahead.
ahmedabad.prosCons: Ahmedabad's strengths are very low costs, some of India's best vegetarian food, strong and improving public transport with the BRTS and metro, a nearby and convenient airport, and a rich heritage as a UNESCO-recognized historic city with the Sabarmati riverfront and Gandhi's ashram. It is safe, orderly, and business-friendly. The main drawbacks are extreme dry-season heat, a smaller coworking and international nomad scene than the tech metros, and the practical realities of a dry, largely vegetarian state, meaning no easy access to alcohol and limited meat options, which some travelers find restrictive. Nightlife is minimal by design. English is widely used in business alongside Gujarati and Hindi. The city is more industrious than glamorous, appealing to those who value substance and value over scene. Overall it rewards budget-focused, culturally curious nomads who do not need a party lifestyle.
ahmedabad.whoFor: An affordable, safe Indian city with strong food and deep heritage, and not a party hub of any kind, is what is on offer to the budget-minded. It is a natural fit for vegetarians, who will find some of the best plant-based food in the country, and for travelers happy in a dry state where alcohol is not part of the routine. It works for people drawn to history, textiles, architecture, and festivals like Uttarayan and Navratri, and for those who appreciate genuinely good public transport in an Indian metro. The very low rents make it excellent for cost-focused long stays. It is less ideal for anyone who needs nightlife, a large established international community, meat-heavy dining, or cool weather, since summers are severe. Solo travelers and couples who value calm, order, and value over buzz will feel at home here quickly.

tashkent.costOfLiving: Tashkent runs around $900 per month for a comfortable single nomad, higher than Indian metros but still good value for a capital. A furnished one-bedroom in a central district costs roughly $350 to $600, with Soviet-era apartments cheaper and modern builds pricier. Food is affordable, and hearty local meals of plov, shashlik, and fresh bread and produce let you eat well on $200 to $300 a month, especially if you shop the bustling bazaars like Chorsu. A local SIM with generous data is inexpensive, around $5 to $10 monthly. Budget $60 to $120 for a coworking hot desk where available, plus utilities, which climb in the cold winter for heating. The metro and taxis are cheap. English is limited, so learning some Russian or Uzbek helps with markets and services. Overall, Tashkent offers solid value with a comfortable, spacious feel and low daily costs outside rent. The currency was floated in 2017 and the parallel exchange market that had run for decades disappeared with it, so the rate a bank gives is now the rate, which was emphatically not the case before. Cards work across the capital, cash still rules outside it, and the notes come in denominations that fill a pocket.
tashkent.whereToWork: Tashkent's coworking scene is small but emerging, with a handful of spaces in central business districts offering hot desks, though options are far fewer than in established nomad hubs, so research availability before arriving. Home internet has improved substantially and fixed broadband in the capital is generally workable, but speeds and reliability still lag behind top nomad destinations, so keep a data-loaded mobile SIM as a backup for calls. Mobile coverage in the city is decent and cheap. Cafe culture is growing, with modern coffee shops in central areas where you can work for a few hours, alongside traditional teahouses better suited to relaxing than long laptop sessions. English is limited among staff, so a translation app smooths ordering and asking about wifi. For reliable video calls, a central apartment with a tested connection plus a backup SIM is the pragmatic setup, since dedicated coworking coverage is thinner than you may be used to.
tashkent.gettingAround: Tashkent is a spacious, orderly capital with wide boulevards and one of the region's highlights, an inexpensive and famously ornate metro system that is clean, safe, and easy to use once you learn the lines. Buses and marshrutka minibuses fill the gaps cheaply. The city is fairly walkable in central districts, though it is spread out overall. Yandex Go is the dominant ride-hailing app and is cheap and reliable, making taxis an easy default, while informal street taxis also operate but require haggling and some Russian. Tashkent International Airport sits close to the center, usually 20 to 40 minutes away, with growing connections across Central Asia, Russia, the Gulf, and some European and Asian cities. High-speed trains link Tashkent to Samarkand and Bukhara, making domestic travel comfortable. For daily life, the metro plus Yandex Go covers almost everything affordably and without stress. Photographing the metro was forbidden for decades because the stations doubled as bomb shelters, and the ban lifted only a few years ago, which is why those ornate platforms are suddenly all over the internet. It was the first system of its kind anywhere in the region and is still the only one built at that scale.
tashkent.visas: Uzbekistan has made entry easy for many travelers, offering 30-day visa-free stays for a long list of nationalities, which covers most short to medium nomad trips without paperwork. Those not eligible for visa-free entry can typically apply for an e-visa online in advance, which is straightforward. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa, so remote work is done on tourist entry, and as with most countries that means you are not formally authorized to work locally, so weigh that as you would elsewhere. For stays beyond the visa-free or e-visa window you would need to look into extensions or other permit categories, which are more involved. Registration requirements historically applied to visitors, often handled automatically by hotels, so if you rent privately confirm whether you must register your stay. Visa-free lists, durations, and registration rules change, so verify the current terms on official Uzbek government sources before you travel. Keep every registration slip a hotel hands over, because they used to be collected and counted on the way out and the habit has not entirely gone away. A private landlord will not produce one, which is the gap that catches people renting an apartment rather than staying in hotels.
tashkent.bestTime: Tashkent has a continental climate with hot summers and cold winters, so the shoulder seasons of spring and autumn are clearly the best times to visit. Spring, roughly April into early June, brings mild temperatures, green landscapes, and blooming surroundings, making it ideal for both work and exploring the wider country. Autumn, around September into November, is similarly pleasant, with comfortable temperatures and the bonus of fresh harvest produce and fruit filling the bazaars. Summers from June through August get hot and dry, with temperatures that can climb high and make midday activity draining, though evenings cool off. Winters from December through February are genuinely cold, with freezing temperatures and some snow, so heating costs rise and outdoor time shrinks. For the most comfortable stay and easy day trips to Samarkand and Bukhara, target the April to June or September to November windows and avoid the extremes of deep summer and winter.
tashkent.prosCons: Tashkent's appeal lies in strong value, a spacious and safe capital, a superb and cheap metro, excellent and affordable food, warm local hospitality, and easy rail access to the Silk Road cities of Samarkand and Bukhara. Visa-free entry for many nationalities lowers the friction of arriving. Costs outside rent are low and the pace is relaxed. On the downside, the coworking and international nomad scene is small and still developing, English is limited so you will lean on Russian, Uzbek, or translation apps, and internet reliability, while improved, still trails top destinations. Winters are cold and summers are hot, narrowing the ideal window. Some bureaucratic quirks like stay registration linger. It is an off-the-beaten-path base rather than a polished hub, rewarding independent travelers who value authenticity, culture, and value over a ready-made community and seamless infrastructure.
tashkent.whoFor: Anyone drawn to Central Asia and the Silk Road who wants an affordable, safe and culturally rich base, rather than another stop on a well-worn circuit, has come to the right place. It fits people comfortable navigating limited English with some Russian or a translation app, and travelers who value authentic food, ornate architecture, and easy rail trips to Samarkand and Bukhara. It works for those who can arrange a reliable connection and carry a backup SIM, since coworking density is thin. The relaxed pace and spacious, orderly city appeal to solo travelers and couples seeking somewhere genuinely different. It is less ideal for anyone who needs a large established international community, abundant coworking, or seamless top-tier internet, and the cold winters and hot summers mean timing matters. Choose Tashkent for exploration and value, and time your stay for spring or autumn.

sendai.costOfLiving: Sendai runs around $1600 per month for a single nomad, cheaper than Tokyo while still being a comfortable Japanese city. A furnished apartment or monthly rental in a central area typically costs $600 to $950, with short-term furnished options at the higher end and standard leases cheaper but harder to arrange short-term. Food is reasonable for Japan, and you can eat well on $350 to $500 a month by mixing supermarkets, convenience stores, and affordable local spots serving the region's specialties like gyutan grilled beef tongue. A tourist or local SIM with data runs $20 to $40 monthly. Budget $100 to $200 for a coworking membership, plus utilities, which rise in the cold winter for heating. Transport is efficient but not free, so factor in metro and train fares. Overall Sendai offers Japan's famed reliability and cleanliness at a noticeably gentler cost than the biggest cities, making it strong value by Japanese standards.
sendai.whereToWork: Sendai offers the excellent connectivity Japan is known for, with fast, reliable fixed broadband and strong mobile coverage, so you will not need a backup SIM for reliability the way you would in India, though a data SIM is still handy for getting around. Coworking spaces exist downtown around the station and central business districts, offering day passes and monthly memberships, and the quality and etiquette are high. Cafe culture is strong, with plenty of quiet, comfortable cafes and chains like the ubiquitous coffee shops where laptop work is common and outlets are often available, making cafe-based work easy and pleasant. Public wifi is available but a personal connection or SIM is more dependable. As a university city home to Tohoku University, Sendai has a studious, relaxed atmosphere well suited to focused work. For remote workers, the combination of rock-solid internet, good cafes, and central coworking makes daily productivity effortless. The university runs an international research institute on disaster science, set up after the tsunami of 2011, and the reconstruction of the coast east of the city has made this a centre for that field worldwide. It is the most distinctive professional thing about the place.
sendai.gettingAround: Sendai is compact, clean, and very walkable in its center, with a grid of covered shopping arcades that make getting around pleasant in any weather. The city has two subway lines plus an extensive bus network, all punctual and easy to use with an IC card, and the loop bus is handy for sightseeing. Trains connect the center efficiently. Sendai sits on the Tohoku Shinkansen line, so Tokyo is only about 90 minutes away by bullet train, making weekend trips simple, and regional rail reaches the coast and mountains. Sendai Airport connects by a direct rail line to the city center in around 25 minutes and offers domestic flights plus some international routes. Ride-hailing exists but taxis are the usual on-demand option and are reliable if pricier than public transit. For most nomads, walking plus the subway, buses, and the occasional Shinkansen covers everything smoothly and dependably. The airport and the rail line serving it were both under water in 2011 and have since been rebuilt, and the coast road out that way runs past embankments and memorial parks that were rice fields before. It is an ordinary commute through a landscape remade inside a decade.
sendai.visas: Japan launched a digital nomad activity status in 2024, allowing eligible nationals to stay for up to six months for remote work, but it comes with conditions, notably an annual income requirement of roughly $67,000 and eligibility limited to certain countries with the right agreements, plus private health insurance coverage. It is a designated activity status rather than a long residence visa, and the six-month stay is not straightforwardly renewable, so read the criteria carefully. Many nationalities can alternatively enter Japan visa-free as tourists for stays of around 90 days, which suits shorter trips, though tourist entry is not intended for work. There is no traditional long-term nomad residence route beyond this. Because income thresholds, eligible nationalities, insurance rules, and the exact terms of the nomad status can change and are still relatively new, verify the current requirements on official Japanese immigration and embassy sources before making plans. Anybody staying long enough to be issued a residence card gets a personal number alongside it, and that number rather than the passport is what banks, employers and the tax office work from. A visitor without one finds a great deal of ordinary administration simply closed off.
sendai.bestTime: Sendai enjoys four distinct seasons, and spring and autumn are the standout times to visit. Spring, particularly April, brings cherry blossoms and mild, pleasant weather ideal for exploring, while autumn from September into November offers crisp air and beautiful foliage. Summer, June through August, is warm and more humid, with a rainy season in early summer, though Sendai stays cooler and more comfortable than Tokyo or the south thanks to its northern location and coastal breezes. The city is famous for its Tanabata star festival in early August, a major draw. Winters from December through February are cold with some snow, colder than much of Japan's main population belt, so heating matters and it appeals if you like a proper winter. For the most comfortable stay with the best scenery and events, aim for spring or autumn, and consider early August if you want to experience the celebrated Tanabata festival.
sendai.prosCons: Sendai's strengths are Japan's hallmark reliability, safety, cleanliness, and excellent internet, all at a meaningfully lower cost than Tokyo, plus a compact walkable center, great food, strong public transport, and a quick 90-minute Shinkansen link to Tokyo. The new digital nomad status gives eligible high earners a legitimate route to stay six months. It is a relaxed university city with easy access to nature. The drawbacks are that it is still pricier than Asian nomad hubs, the international nomad community is small, and English can be limited outside tourist and academic circles, so a translation app helps. Winters are genuinely cold and snowy, and the six-month nomad status carries a high income bar and is not easily renewed. It is less lively than Tokyo or Osaka. Overall it is a calm, high-quality, well-run base for those who prioritize comfort, safety, and infrastructure.
sendai.whoFor: The safety, reliability and infrastructure of Japan, without the crowds and prices of Tokyo, is the proposition here, for anyone who values a calm, walkable city with quick bullet-train access to the capital. The income requirement on Japan's digital nomad status means higher earners qualify for it and others do not, which leaves shorter tourist-length stays as the practical alternative. It appeals to people who love four-season climates, nature and hot springs nearby, and refined food culture including the local gyutan specialty. The university atmosphere and quiet cafes make it ideal for focused, heads-down work. It fits solo travelers and couples who prioritize comfort and quality over a big party scene or a ready-made international community. It is less suited to budget-focused nomads chasing the lowest costs, those who need a large English-speaking crowd, or anyone who dislikes cold, snowy winters, since Sendai's north climate is real.

beijing.costOfLiving: A single nomad in Beijing lands close to $1500 per month without much strain. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease inside the Third Ring, in Dongcheng, Sanlitun or Wudaokou, runs $600 to $950; shared flats and serviced studios in Chaoyang start nearer $400. Eating mostly local, at jianbing stalls, noodle shops and canteen-style Sichuan places, costs $200 to $320 a month, though a Western brunch habit adds $150 fast. A China Unicom or China Mobile SIM with 30GB to 60GB is $10 to $18. Hot-desking at a coworking space is $130 to $220; cafes are cheaper and widely tolerated. Utilities including heating, electricity and water average $40 to $80, spiking in winter. Transport is trivial: $20 to $35 covers a month of metro and buses. Value verdict: Beijing delivers a genuine world capital, superb food and near-flawless infrastructure at roughly half the cost of Tokyo or Seoul, with rent the only real pressure point.
beijing.whereToWork: Base yourself in Dongcheng near the Lama Temple and Gulou for hutong quiet with metro access, in Sanlitun or Chaoyangmen for a more international feel, or in Wudaokou if a young student-heavy scene appeals. WeWork operates several Beijing locations including Sanlitun and the CBD, and Kr Space and Ucommune run domestic-brand alternatives at lower rates. Cafe work is normal in the hutong belt around Beiluoguxiang and Wudaoying, where independent roasters keep long tables and reliable wifi; the Metal Hands and Voyage Coffee groups are dependable fixtures. Fixed broadband commonly delivers 100 to 300 Mbps and mobile 5G is fast and near-ubiquitous. The critical caveat is the Great Firewall: Google, Gmail, WhatsApp, Instagram, Slack in places, and most Western SaaS require a working VPN, and consumer VPNs degrade during political meetings. Power is stable. Cafes get loud after 2pm and rarely have plentiful sockets. The city has been under an explicit population cap for a decade and has cleared a great deal of informal housing and small shopfront frontage to enforce it, which is why parts of the hutong belt look tidier and emptier than photographs from ten years ago show them. The effect on rents has been to push the cheap end further out year by year.
beijing.gettingAround: Beijing's metro is the workhorse: over twenty lines, signage in English, trains every two to four minutes, and fares of roughly $0.40 to $1.20 depending on distance. Buses cost about $0.15 with a transit card but are slower and less foreigner-friendly. Didi is the dominant ride-hailing app and works in English; a typical crosstown ride is $4 to $10, though rush hour traffic inside the Fourth Ring is genuinely bad. Shared bikes from Meituan and Hellobike blanket the city at around $0.20 for thirty minutes and are often the fastest option for short hops. Payment runs through Alipay or WeChat Pay, both of which now accept foreign cards. Capital Airport connects by the Airport Express for about $3.50; Daxing is further out but linked by its own express line. The city is flat and walkable block by block, but the blocks are enormous. No scooter or car is needed. Private cars are kept off the roads one weekday a week according to the last digit of the plate, a permanent measure rather than an emergency one, and it is part of why the ride-hailing fleet here is as enormous as it is.
beijing.visas: China does not offer a digital nomad visa, and remote work on a tourist entry is technically outside the visa's purpose. As of 2026, citizens of a long list of countries including most of the EU, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea can enter visa-free for up to 30 days for tourism, business and family visits, a scheme repeatedly extended and expanded since 2024. United States and Canadian passport holders are not on that list and still need a visa: the standard L tourist visa is usually issued for 30 or 60 days per entry, often with ten-year multiple-entry validity for Americans. Separately, the 240-hour visa-free transit policy allows stays of up to ten days for travellers continuing to a third country through Beijing and most major ports. Extensions of 30 days are possible at the Public Security Bureau exit-entry office but are discretionary. Register your address with local police within 24 hours of arrival.
beijing.bestTime: Beijing has a sharply continental climate with four unmistakable seasons. September and October are the clear best window: dry, blue, with highs around 22C to 26C and the golden light that makes the Fragrant Hills and the Great Wall worth the trip. April and May are the second choice, pleasant but punctuated by spring dust storms blowing in from the north. June through August are hot and humid, peaking near 35C, with the bulk of the annual rain arriving in July and August as short violent downpours. Winter, from December to February, is dry, bright and bitterly cold, with lows near minus 10C and the worst air-quality episodes when coal heating and still air combine, though pollution has improved markedly since the 2010s. Chinese New Year, falling in late January or February, shuts much of the city and makes domestic travel chaotic. Mid-Autumn Festival and the October National Day week also crowd every attraction.
beijing.prosCons: The strengths are substantial. Beijing is one of the great historical capitals, with the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Great Wall within reach, backed by an art scene at 798 and a hutong bar and coffee culture that rewards long stays. Infrastructure is exceptional: a vast cheap metro, fast trains to Shanghai and Xi'an, sub-second mobile payments, delivery of anything within an hour, and personal safety at a level few world cities match. Food, from imperial to Uyghur to Sichuan, is world class and cheap. The internet is what rules Beijing out for many people: the Great Firewall makes routine Western tools dependent on a VPN that can and does fail at politically sensitive moments. Winter air quality still has bad days, winters are punishing, and the language barrier is real, since English is far less widespread than in Southeast Asia. The nomad community is thin and bureaucracy for foreigners is heavy.
beijing.whoFor: Depth rather than convenience is the bargain being offered here: someone with an interest in Chinese history, language or business, a tolerance for bureaucracy, and work that survives a VPN-mediated internet connection. It rewards long stays, learners of Mandarin, and people whose income is high enough that a $700 flat and $3 metro days feel like an obvious bargain against Tokyo or Singapore. Journalists, researchers, supply-chain and manufacturing consultants, and anyone building China-facing product will find the city indispensable. It fits poorly for those who need Google Workspace, Slack and Zoom to work without friction every single hour, for social nomads seeking a ready-made expat coworking scene of the Chiang Mai or Lisbon variety, and for anyone chasing beaches, warmth or year-round outdoor living. Travellers who dislike cold winters, heavy air-pollution days, or navigating daily life in a language they cannot read should look elsewhere in Asia.

shanghai.costOfLiving: Shanghai is China's most expensive city and $1800 per month is a realistic single-person figure rather than a generous one. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in the former French Concession, Jing'an or Xuhui costs $750 to $1200; move out to Hongkou, Yangpu or beyond the Inner Ring and $500 to $700 buys the same space. Food splits sharply: local noodle shops, dumpling joints and canteens keep monthly spend near $250, while the international restaurant scene that makes Shanghai famous can double it. A data SIM with 30GB or more runs $10 to $18. Coworking hot desks are $150 to $280, the highest in mainland China. Utilities average $45 to $90, with summer air-conditioning and winter heating the swing factors. Metro and Didi together come to $30 to $50. Value verdict: costs are high by Chinese standards and modest by global ones, and Shanghai buys more genuine urban quality per dollar than any comparable city in East Asia.
shanghai.whereToWork: The former French Concession is the default base, walkable and plane-tree shaded, with Jing'an offering a more polished version and Xuhui a quieter one. Coworking is mature here: WeWork holds numerous Shanghai buildings, Distrii and Kr Space run large domestic networks, and Naked Hub sites were absorbed into WeWork's portfolio. Independent cafe work is easy and accepted; the Seesaw and Manner chains are ubiquitous, and specialty roasters cluster around Anfu Lu, Yongkang Lu and Wukang Lu. Fibre broadband typically runs 200 to 500 Mbps and 5G coverage is excellent throughout the inner districts. The Great Firewall applies as it does nationwide, so a functioning VPN is a prerequisite for Google, Slack, WhatsApp and most Western SaaS, and reliability dips during major political events. Power supply is stable. The practical caveats are noise and seating: popular cafes are packed on weekends and sockets are scarce, so arrive before eleven.
shanghai.gettingAround: Shanghai's metro is among the world's largest, with twenty-plus lines, bilingual signage and fares of about $0.40 to $1.30. Buses cost around $0.30 but are slower. Didi handles ride-hailing; a typical inner-city trip is $4 to $12 and the app works in English with foreign cards linked through Alipay or WeChat Pay. Shared bikes from Meituan and Hellobike cost roughly $0.20 per half hour and suit the flat, dense inner districts perfectly. Shanghai is the most genuinely walkable major city in China, especially the French Concession, where the street grid is human-scaled. Pudong Airport connects by metro Line 2 for about $1 or by the Maglev in eight minutes for around $7; Hongqiao is on Lines 2 and 10 and doubles as the high-speed rail hub, putting Hangzhou within 50 minutes and Beijing within four and a half hours. No scooter or car is required. The maglev out to the eastern airport is the only commercial line of its kind running anywhere, reaching four hundred and thirty kilometres an hour for about a minute, and it is worth doing once even though the metro costs less and puts you closer to where you are going.
shanghai.visas: China has no digital nomad visa and none is planned as of 2026, so remote work here happens on tourist or business entries. Passport holders from most EU states, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea can enter visa-free for up to 30 days under the unilateral scheme China expanded through 2024 and 2025. American and Canadian citizens remain excluded and need a standard L tourist visa, typically valid for 30 or 60 day stays, often on a ten-year multiple-entry sticker for US applicants. Shanghai is also a designated port for the 240-hour visa-free transit policy, which permits stays of up to ten days when continuing to a third country, a route many use to add a Shanghai leg between two other destinations. A single 30-day extension can be requested at the municipal exit-entry administration but approval is discretionary. Hotels register guests automatically; anyone in private accommodation must register at the local police station within 24 hours.
shanghai.bestTime: Shanghai is humid subtropical, and the shoulder seasons are the reason to come. October and early November are the standout window: dry, clear, highs near 22C, low humidity. Late March through May is nearly as good, though April and early June bring persistent drizzle. June and July deliver the meiyu plum rains, weeks of grey, sticky, near-constant humidity that locals dread more than the heat. July and August are the peak of summer, with highs above 35C, high humidity and typhoon risk that runs from July into September, occasionally closing the airport and flooding low streets. Winter, December to February, is not freezing but is damp, grey and poorly heated indoors, and feels colder than the 4C to 8C readings suggest. Chinese New Year empties the city for about a week and reopens it slowly. The Shanghai International Film Festival in June and the November import expo crowd hotels. The national holiday week at the start of October and the new year fortnight are when the entire country travels at once, and every train, flight and attraction books solid. The best weather of the year falls in the same week as the worst of the crowds, which is the trade to plan around. Booking either week a month ahead is already late.
shanghai.prosCons: Shanghai is the most livable large city in mainland China for a foreigner. The former French Concession offers tree-lined walkability that almost nowhere in Asia matches, the food scene spans street dumplings to genuinely world-class restaurants, the metro is vast and cheap, and personal safety is excellent at any hour. English is more widely spoken here than anywhere else in China, the international community is large and long-established, high-speed rail puts half the country within a day, and infrastructure from mobile payments to same-hour delivery simply works. The drawbacks are equally clear. Costs are the highest in the country and rents in the desirable inner districts have risen steadily. The Great Firewall still gates every Western work tool behind a VPN that can fail without warning. Summer is oppressively humid with typhoon disruption, winter is damp and badly heated, air quality has bad days, and the visa framework caps most visits at 30 to 60 days.
shanghai.whoFor: Shanghai fits the nomad who wants a serious, fully functioning global city rather than a cheap one: high earners, consultants and founders with China-facing business, finance and design professionals, and anyone who values walkable streets, restaurant depth and an international social scene over a low burn rate. It is also the softest landing in China for a first visit, since English goes further and the expat infrastructure is decades old. Mandarin learners get a diverse, tolerant environment, though Beijing offers cleaner standard pronunciation. It suits poorly the budget nomad, since $1800 buys markedly more in Chiang Mai, Hanoi or Tbilisi, and anyone whose workflow depends on uninterrupted access to Google, Slack or Zoom without a VPN should think hard. Nomads chasing long visa runways, tropical weather, beaches or an outdoor lifestyle will find the 30-day tourist cap and the muggy summers frustrating.

xiamen.costOfLiving: Xiamen supports a comfortable single-person month at about $1200. Furnished monthly rentals on Xiamen Island, in Siming district near Zhongshan Road or the university, run $350 to $600 for a one-bedroom, and sea-view apartments in the newer Huli towers sit at the top of that band; mainland-side Jimei and Haicang drop to $250 to $350. Food is a highlight and a bargain: local seafood, satay noodles and Hokkien snacks keep monthly eating near $180 to $280. A 30GB SIM costs $10 to $18. Coworking desks are $90 to $170, well below the tier-one cities. Utilities average $35 to $70, driven mainly by summer air-conditioning. Metro, bus and BRT together cost $15 to $25 a month. Value verdict: Xiamen is one of the best cost-to-quality trades in coastal China, offering clean air, a subtropical waterfront and tier-one infrastructure at roughly two-thirds of Shanghai's price. Property here is priced like a first-tier city even though the salaries are not, which gives this island one of the worst ratios of purchase price to income anywhere in the country and is why so many people who work on it live across the water. Rents have not followed those purchase prices up, which is the arbitrage for anybody renting rather than buying.
xiamen.whereToWork: Base on Xiamen Island. Siming district puts you near the seafront ring road, Zhongshan Road's old shophouses and Xiamen University; the Shapowei and Zengcuoan areas draw a younger, creative crowd with a dense cluster of independent cafes. Huli is newer, more corporate and closer to the airport. The city's coffee culture is unusually strong for a second-tier Chinese city, and cafe work in Shapowei or around Baicheng Beach is straightforward, though most independents are small and seating is limited. Coworking exists through domestic operators and the Software Park II and III campuses in Siming, which host a real tech workforce and serviced offices at reasonable rates. Broadband commonly delivers 100 to 300 Mbps and 5G coverage is comprehensive across the island. The nationwide firewall applies, so a VPN is essential for Western tools. Power is reliable. Typhoon season can bring occasional outages and closures in late summer.
xiamen.gettingAround: Xiamen has a growing metro network, with Lines 1, 2 and 3 covering the island and the mainland districts and fares of about $0.30 to $1. Line 1 crosses the sea on a causeway, which is a genuinely scenic commute. Buses cost around $0.15 and the BRT elevated busway is fast across the island. Didi is the ride-hailing standard, with typical island trips at $3 to $8. Shared bikes are everywhere at roughly $0.20 per half hour, and Xiamen is one of the better Chinese cities for cycling thanks to the seafront path and a dedicated elevated bike skyway. The island core is genuinely walkable and pleasant on foot. Gaoqi International Airport sits on the island itself, only fifteen minutes from Siming by taxi at around $6. High-speed rail links Fuzhou in about ninety minutes and Shenzhen in three and a half hours. No scooter or car is needed; electric scooters are in fact restricted on the island.
xiamen.visas: The rules are national, so Xiamen follows the same framework as Beijing and Shanghai. There is no Chinese digital nomad visa. Citizens of most EU countries, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea can enter visa-free for stays of up to 30 days under the scheme China has progressively widened since late 2023. US and Canadian passport holders are not covered and must obtain an L tourist visa in advance, generally permitting 30 or 60 days per entry, with long multiple-entry validity common for Americans. Xiamen Gaoqi is a designated port for the 240-hour visa-free transit policy, allowing up to ten days when travelling onward to a third country, which suits a short island stopover well. A 30-day extension may be requested from the Xiamen exit-entry bureau but is granted at the officer's discretion. Police registration within 24 hours applies to anyone not staying in a hotel.
xiamen.bestTime: Xiamen is subtropical and mild, with a comfortable stretch that is longer than most of China's. October to December is the best window: dry, sunny, highs of 22C to 28C and low humidity, ideal for the seafront and for day trips to the Fujian tulou earth buildings. March to May is warm and pleasant but increasingly humid, with spring sea fog common. June through September is hot and sticky, regularly above 32C with high humidity, and this is also typhoon season; Fujian takes direct hits most years, and a serious storm can close the airport and shut the city for a day or two.
