Rainfall peaks between May and August. January and February are the coolest months, around 12C to 18C, damp but rarely cold. Chinese New Year fills Gulangyu island and the seafront with domestic tourists, as do the May and October national holiday weeks. The marathon in early January runs the seafront ring road and is one of the larger races in the country, filling every hotel on the island for that weekend. It is also about the coldest the place ever gets, which is precisely why the date works. Sea fog in spring can close the airport for a morning.
xiamen.prosCons: Xiamen is widely rated one of China's most liveable cities and the reasons hold up. The air is clean by mainland standards, the island is compact, green and edged by a continuous seafront promenade and bike skyway, and the climate is mild for most of the year. Seafood and Hokkien cuisine are excellent and cheap, the metro and airport are modern, Gulangyu island and the Fujian tulou are on the doorstep, and the pace is markedly calmer than Shanghai or Shenzhen while the infrastructure is barely worse. Costs sit around two-thirds of tier-one levels. The drawbacks start with isolation: the foreign community is small, English is much less common than in Shanghai, and there is no established nomad scene, so a Mandarin base or high tolerance for solitude matters. The firewall applies in full, coworking options are limited compared with tier-one cities, typhoons disrupt late summer, and domestic tourist crowds swamp the main sights during national holidays.
xiamen.whoFor: This is for the self-sufficient, who want a coastal Chinese city with real quality of life and do not need a ready-made expat network: solo workers with steady clients, Mandarin learners looking for a calmer environment than Beijing, cyclists and runners drawn to the seafront, and anyone burnt out on megacity density but unwilling to give up fast trains, cheap metro and same-day delivery. It is a strong second or third China destination for someone who has already learned how the country works. Beginners who need English signage and some hand-holding will struggle, social nomads who want coworking friends and meetups on tap will not find them, and any job that cannot tolerate VPN-dependent access to Western tools will break here rather than bend around it. Those needing long visa runways will also find the 30-day ceiling restrictive, and travellers sensitive to humidity should avoid the June to September window entirely.

guilin.costOfLiving: Guilin is genuinely cheap and $900 per month buys a comfortable single life. Furnished monthly rentals in the city centre near Zhengyang pedestrian street or the Two Rivers and Four Lakes area run $200 to $380 for a one-bedroom; Yangshuo, an hour south and the more scenic base, sits at $250 to $450 for a guesthouse room or small flat with a karst view. Food is inexpensive, with Guilin rice noodles at under $2 a bowl keeping monthly eating to $150 to $230. A data SIM is $10 to $18. Formal coworking barely exists here, so budget $0 to $80 for cafe spend or a desk in a Yangshuo guesthouse. Utilities average $30 to $60. Local transport is $10 to $20 a month. Value verdict: among the lowest costs available in a Chinese city with modern infrastructure, and the landscape is the compensation for the thinner urban amenities. Guangxi is among the poorer provinces and local wages reflect it, which is why the gap between what a visitor pays on West Street and what the same thing costs two streets back is so wide. Asking the price before ordering is ordinary practice rather than suspicion, and it saves an argument later.
guilin.whereToWork: Guilin city is the practical base for infrastructure, with the area around the Lijiang riverbank and Zhengyang Road offering hotels, apartments and a reasonable cafe scene. Many long-stayers prefer Yangshuo, an hour away by high-speed rail, where West Street has decades of backpacker infrastructure and the surrounding villages of Jima and Gaotian offer riverside guesthouses with desks and terraces. Dedicated coworking is essentially absent in both; work happens in cafes, guesthouse lobbies and hotel business centres. Broadband is generally solid at 50 to 200 Mbps in the city and more variable in rural Yangshuo, where a good 5G plan and a mobile hotspot are the sensible backup. Coverage across the karst valleys is better than expected but has dead spots. The national firewall applies, so a working VPN is mandatory. Power is generally reliable but rural outages happen during heavy summer storms. Cafes are quiet outside tourist peaks. The city's name means a forest of sweet osmanthus, and the tree is planted everywhere, which in early autumn makes the whole place smell of it for a fortnight. The local economy beyond tourism is farming and the fruit trade, and neither has any use for an outsider with a laptop. What passes for a professional network here is other people who came for the scenery.
guilin.gettingAround: Guilin has no metro. City buses cover the centre at roughly $0.15 to $0.30 a ride and are the local default. Didi works throughout and is the practical choice for most trips, with typical city fares of $2 to $6; taxis are similarly cheap. Shared bikes and shared e-bikes are available in the city, and in Yangshuo renting an electric scooter for around $8 to $12 a day is the standard way to reach the villages, rice terraces and climbing crags, since the countryside is spread out and buses are infrequent. Guilin is flat and walkable in its centre, and the lakeside paths are pleasant. High-speed rail is the strong point: Yangshuo is under 30 minutes and Guangzhou around two and a half hours from Guilin West. Liangjiang International Airport lies 30 kilometres out, connected by an airport bus for about $3 or a $15 taxi. A scooter is genuinely useful in Yangshuo, unnecessary in the city.
guilin.visas: National Chinese rules apply, and there is no digital nomad visa. Most EU, UK, Australian, New Zealand, Japanese and Korean passport holders can enter mainland China visa-free for up to 30 days under the expanded unilateral scheme; US and Canadian citizens still need an L tourist visa, usually issued for 30 or 60 day stays. Guangxi province has an additional regional feature worth knowing: a visa-free arrangement exists for ASEAN tour groups entering Guilin, but it applies to organised groups, not independent Western travellers, so it is not a workaround. The 240-hour visa-free transit policy covers designated ports, and travellers commonly enter through Guangzhou, Shenzhen or Shanghai and reach Guilin by high-speed rail within that window. Extensions of 30 days can be applied for at the Guilin exit-entry bureau, though smaller-city offices tend to be slower. Police registration within 24 hours is required for anyone not in a hotel.
guilin.bestTime: Guilin is subtropical with a long humid summer. April to June is when the karst landscape looks best, green and misty, but it is also the wettest stretch, with May the peak rainfall month and occasional flooding along the Li River. The most comfortable window is late September to November: warm days around 22C to 28C, far less rain, clear enough for the Longji rice terraces, which are golden in late September and October before harvest. July and August are hot at 33C to 35C, humid, stormy and crowded with domestic tourists on school holidays. December to February is cool, damp and often grey, with temperatures of 8C to 14C, misty in a way that photographers love and everyone else finds bleak; the Li River cruise still runs but views can vanish. Chinese New Year and the May and October golden weeks bring heavy domestic crowds to Yangshuo and the terraces.
guilin.prosCons: The landscape is the whole argument and it is a strong one. The karst hills along the Li River and around Yangshuo are among the most striking scenery in Asia, with world-class rock climbing, cycling through rice fields, bamboo rafting and the Longji terraces a few hours north. Costs are very low even by Chinese standards, food is cheap and distinctive, high-speed rail links the region efficiently, and Yangshuo has a decades-old backpacker infrastructure that means more English and more foreigner-friendly guesthouses than a city of this size would normally offer. The drawbacks are structural. There is no real coworking, no professional community and no nomad scene beyond climbers and travellers passing through. Guilin city itself is unremarkable and heavily geared to domestic tour groups, whose crowds and hard selling can wear thin. Summers are hot, wet and stormy, winters grey. The firewall applies, medical and international services are limited, and the 30-day visa ceiling caps any real settling in.
guilin.whoFor: Guilin and Yangshuo fit the outdoor-minded nomad on a modest budget: rock climbers above all, since Yangshuo is one of the world's great sport-climbing destinations, plus cyclists, runners, photographers and writers who want low costs and dramatic scenery over urban amenities. It rewards short, focused stays of a few weeks where the work is solitary and the reward is the countryside, and it suits travellers already comfortable in China who can handle limited English outside the tourist strip. It is wrong for anyone who needs coworking, a professional network or reliable in-person meetings, for nomads who want nightlife, restaurant variety or a large international community, and for anyone with heavy bandwidth demands in rural accommodation. Those who dislike heat, humidity, heavy rain or tour-group crowds should avoid the summer entirely, and anyone seeking a long-term base will run into the visa limits quickly.

newdelhi.costOfLiving: New Delhi runs comfortably at $900 per month for a single nomad, and can be done for far less. A furnished monthly rental in a good central-south neighbourhood such as Hauz Khas, Safdarjung Enclave, Saket or Greater Kailash costs $300 to $550 for a one-bedroom; barsati rooftop rooms and serviced studios start nearer $200, while Lutyens' Delhi and Vasant Vihar climb well past $800. Food is very cheap: local thalis, street food and home delivery keep monthly eating at $120 to $220, with restaurant meals in Khan Market or Aerocity at $12 to $25 pushing that higher. A Jio or Airtel SIM with generous data is $5 to $10, among the cheapest in the world. Coworking hot desks run $70 to $160. Utilities are $40 to $90, with summer air-conditioning the dominant cost. Metro and cabs total $25 to $50. Value verdict: exceptional purchasing power, with air quality rather than money the real tax on living here.
newdelhi.whereToWork: South Delhi is the sensible base. Hauz Khas and its village, Saket, Greater Kailash and Shahpur Jat combine cafes, metro access and residential calm; Gurugram, technically in Haryana, holds the densest concentration of corporate coworking. WeWork, Awfis, 91springboard, Innov8 and IndiQube all operate multiple Delhi and Gurugram locations, with Awfis and 91springboard the best value. Cafe work is well established at Blue Tokai Coffee Roasters, which has numerous Delhi outlets and reliable wifi, and at the cafes around Hauz Khas Village and Champa Gali in Saidulajab, a converted lane of studios and coffee shops built for exactly this. Fibre broadband from Jio or Airtel delivers 100 to 300 Mbps cheaply and 4G and 5G are fast and inexpensive, so a hotspot is a viable primary connection. No VPN is needed. Power cuts are shorter than they once were but inverters or backup are worth confirming with any landlord, especially in summer. Electricity supply here is far steadier than elsewhere in the country because distribution was privatised two decades ago, and long cuts are now unusual rather than expected, which removes the single biggest practical obstacle to working from an apartment in India.
newdelhi.gettingAround: The Delhi Metro is the best in India: clean, air-conditioned, extensive, with fares of about $0.15 to $0.75 and a contactless card or the DMRC app for entry. It is the fastest way across a city where road traffic is severe. Uber and Ola both operate, and Rapido offers cheap motorbike taxis; a typical car ride across South Delhi is $2 to $6, an auto-rickshaw the same trip $1.50 to $4, best booked through an app to avoid meter arguments. Walkability is poor in most areas: footpaths are broken or absent, distances are large and summer heat and winter smog discourage it, though Lodhi Gardens, Khan Market and Hauz Khas are pleasant on foot. Indira Gandhi International Airport connects via the Airport Express in about twenty minutes to New Delhi station for roughly $0.70. Rail from Nizamuddin and New Delhi stations reaches Jaipur and Agra in a few hours. No scooter or car is necessary.
newdelhi.visas: India offers no digital nomad visa as of 2026, and remote work is done on a tourist entry. The e-Tourist visa is the standard route and is granted online to citizens of most Western countries, typically in 30-day, one-year and five-year variants; the one-year and five-year versions allow multiple entries with a maximum continuous stay of 90 days for most nationalities, extended to 180 days per visit for US, UK, Canadian and Japanese passport holders. Apply only through the official indianvisaonline government portal, since numerous lookalike sites charge inflated fees. Tourist visas cannot generally be extended inside India; the expected pattern is to exit and re-enter, and while the old 60-day re-entry gap was removed years ago, immigration officers still scrutinise back-to-back tourist stays. Employment in India requires a separate business or employment visa. Protected Area Permits apply to parts of the northeast, Ladakh and the Andamans, none of which affect Delhi itself. Anybody on a long-stay visa has to report a change of address through the immigration portal, and the office here is the busiest in the country with appointments released online in batches. Leaving it late is the usual cause of trouble on the way out.
newdelhi.bestTime: Delhi's year has one clearly good stretch and several difficult ones. October to March is the season, with the sweet spot from late October to early December and again in February and March: dry, sunny, highs of 20C to 28C. Deep winter, late December and January, is cool at 5C to 18C and afflicted by dense fog that delays flights and trains, compounded by the city's worst air pollution, which peaks after Diwali as crop stubble burning coincides with cold stagnant air. April and May are punishingly hot, regularly above 40C and touching 45C, with hot loo winds. The southwest monsoon arrives around late June and runs through September, breaking the heat but bringing humidity, flooding and waterlogged roads. Holi falls in March, Diwali in October or November, and Durga Puja and Dussehra in the autumn; all are worth planning around, and the air after Diwali is the single biggest reason to avoid November.
newdelhi.prosCons: Delhi delivers enormous value and depth. The cost of living is extremely low relative to the quality of housing, food and coworking available, mobile data is world-beating in price and speed, no firewall or VPN complicates work, and English is widely spoken in professional and urban settings, making daily life far easier than in China. The metro is excellent, the coworking sector is mature and competitive, and the historical layers, from Mughal tombs to Lutyens' avenues, are extraordinary. Rail and cheap flights open the whole subcontinent. The overwhelming drawback is air quality: winter pollution in Delhi routinely reaches hazardous levels and represents a genuine health cost, not an inconvenience. Summer heat above 45C is dangerous, monsoon flooding disrupts the city, traffic and noise are relentless, and walkability is poor. Women travellers consistently report Delhi as less comfortable than southern Indian cities. Bureaucracy, scams targeting new arrivals, and inconsistent power and water in cheaper housing add friction.
newdelhi.whoFor: New Delhi fits the nomad who wants maximum purchasing power in a large, English-functional city with real professional infrastructure: founders and freelancers working with Indian teams, journalists and researchers, consultants in tech or development, and long-haul travellers using the capital as a base for the subcontinent. It rewards those who plan around the calendar, arriving in October or February and leaving before the November smog and the May heat. Budget-conscious workers who want a $400 flat, $8 monthly data and $100 coworking will find few equivalents anywhere. Asthma, allergies or any respiratory sensitivity rule this out entirely, because the winter air is disqualifying rather than merely unpleasant. Walkability, quiet and outdoor exercise are also in short supply for anyone who ranks them near the top. Those seeking a gentler Indian introduction should consider Bengaluru, Goa or Pondicherry; those wanting a beach or mountain lifestyle will be happier in Rishikesh, Dharamshala or the coast.

dhaka.costOfLiving: A single nomad can live in Dhaka on roughly $700 per month, and that figure buys a comfortable rather than a bare existence. A furnished one-bedroom flat on a monthly basis in Gulshan, Banani or Dhanmondi runs $300 to $500, while comparable space in Mohammadpur or Uttara drops to $180 to $300. Local meals cost $1 to $3, a plate of biryani at a neighbourhood institution is around $2.50, and restaurant dining in the diplomatic zone climbs to $10 to $20 per head. A Grameenphone or Robi SIM with 30GB to 50GB costs $4 to $8 monthly. Coworking desks run $60 to $120. Utilities including electricity, an inverter or generator share and a fibre line total $40 to $80, higher in summer when air conditioning runs constantly. Transport rarely exceeds $40. The value is genuine, though comfort here is bought in air conditioning, filtered air and backup power rather than in square metres.
dhaka.whereToWork: Base yourself in Gulshan, Banani or Dhanmondi; these hold the embassies, the reliable fibre and most of the cafe culture. Moar and North End Coffee Roasters have branches across Gulshan and Dhanmondi and are the default laptop cafes, with Crimson Cup and Cafe Mango also tolerating long sessions. For dedicated space, Impact Hub Dhaka and Hubdhaka in Gulshan offer day passes and monthly desks, and Bangladesh has a growing cluster of startup incubators around Gulshan Avenue that rent desks. Fibre to residential and office buildings commonly delivers 30 Mbps to 100 Mbps and is decent by regional standards, but load shedding remains a real constraint, so confirm any building has an IPS, inverter or generator before signing. Mobile 4G is widely usable as backup. Cafes get loud in the evening, power sockets are scarce in older venues, and the government has previously throttled mobile internet during unrest, so a VPN and a data buffer are sensible.
dhaka.gettingAround: Dhaka has no comprehensive metro, but Line 6 of the Dhaka Metro Rail now runs elevated from Uttara North through Mirpur, Farmgate and Motijheel, and it is transformative for that corridor; fares are roughly $0.20 to $1.00. Everything else is road, and Dhaka has some of the worst congestion on earth, with average speeds in the single digits during peak hours. Pathao and Uber are the workhorses: a Pathao motorcycle ride across town costs $1 to $3 and is far faster than a car, while a car booking is $3 to $8. CNG auto-rickshaws cost $1.50 to $4 after the inevitable haggling. Local buses are cheap at under $0.30 but crowded and hard to parse without Bangla. Walkability is poor because footpaths are broken, occupied or missing. Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport sits north of the city; allow ninety minutes from Gulshan by car despite the short distance. No scooter or car ownership is needed. More cycle rickshaws work these streets than in any other city on earth, several hundred thousand of them, and they are periodically banned from the main roads and then quietly return. For short distances in traffic already moving at walking pace they beat everything else, which is the whole argument for their survival.
dhaka.visas: Bangladesh has no digital nomad visa and none is under serious discussion. Most Western nationals, including US, UK, EU, Canadian and Australian passport holders, are eligible for visa on arrival at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport for up to 30 days at a fee of around $51, but this is discretionary rather than guaranteed: immigration officers can and do refuse it, and they typically expect proof of onward travel, a hotel booking and sufficient cash. The safer route is applying in advance at a Bangladeshi mission for a tourist visa, which is commonly issued for 30 to 90 days and sometimes with multiple entries and validity up to a year. Extensions are handled by the Department of Immigration and Passports in Agargaon, are bureaucratic and are usually granted only for short periods. Overstays attract fines and departure delays. Working remotely on a tourist visa is not formally provided for; the on-the-ground reality is that laptop work goes unremarked.
dhaka.bestTime: The comfortable window is November to February, when daytime highs settle around 25C to 29C, humidity drops and evenings turn genuinely cool in December and January. That is the season for travel and for the winter wedding and cultural calendar. March and April heat up quickly, and by April and May temperatures reach the high thirties with brutal humidity and pre-monsoon nor'wester storms. The southwest monsoon runs roughly June to September, delivering heavy, sustained rain, waterlogged streets and serious traffic paralysis, though it is also the greenest and cheapest stretch. October is a transitional month and increasingly pleasant late on. The offsetting problem with the cool season is air quality: Dhaka regularly ranks among the world's most polluted cities from December through March, with brick kiln smoke and dust pushing AQI past 200. Key dates include Pohela Boishakh in mid-April, Durga Puja in autumn and the two Eid holidays, which empty the city. The Bengali new year in the middle of April fills the parks with crowds dressed in red and white from before dawn, and it is the one occasion when the city looks like a single thing rather than twenty million separate errands.
dhaka.prosCons: Cost, energy and access are what bring people to Dhaka. Very few capitals let a remote worker live centrally, eat well and hire help on $700 a month, and the country is genuinely cheap once rent is settled. English is widely spoken in the professional and educated classes, hospitality toward foreigners is warm and often disarming, the food culture is underrated, and Dhaka is a serious base for exploring Sylhet's tea hills, the Sundarbans and Cox's Bazar. The startup and NGO scene means there are actual peers. The traffic is genuinely among the world's worst and eats hours daily, the air quality in winter is a real health cost rather than a passing inconvenience, footpaths and public space are poor, and load shedding still interrupts the working day. Political unrest and hartals can shut the city and disrupt internet. Solo women face persistent staring and harassment, alcohol is restricted, serious medical care means flying to Bangkok, and there is close to no nomad infrastructure.
dhaka.whoFor: Everyone who comes here has a purpose beyond arbitrage: development sector workers, researchers, journalists, textile and supply chain people, and anyone with family, business or a genuine curiosity about South Asia at full volume. It rewards travellers who have already done India or Pakistan, who are comfortable negotiating chaos, and who value cost and human warmth over infrastructure. Founders on a tight runway can extend it dramatically here. A first-time nomad should not start here. Asthma, allergies or a cardiovascular condition make the winter air a genuine health question rather than a comfort one, and walkable streets, dependable power, an established coworking scene and a ready supply of other remote workers are all things this city has no way to provide. Anyone whose priority list includes nightlife, beaches within reach, or predictable calendars will be frustrated. Solo women should weigh the harassment reality honestly. Those wanting cheap Asia without the friction should look at Chiang Mai, Da Nang or Kathmandu instead.

islamabad.costOfLiving: Islamabad is Pakistan's most expensive city and also its most liveable, and $800 a month covers a single nomad comfortably. A furnished one-bedroom or studio on a monthly lease in F-6, F-7, F-8 or E-11 runs $250 to $450, with G-sectors and Bahria Town cheaper at $150 to $280; serviced apartments aimed at expats climb past $600. Local food is very cheap, with a plate of nihari or karahi at $2 to $4 and street food under $1, while Western style restaurants in the F-6 Super Market or Kohsar Market area cost $8 to $18. A Jazz or Zong SIM with a generous monthly data bundle costs $5 to $10. Coworking desks are $70 to $130. Utilities including electricity, gas and a fibre line run $50 to $100, spiking in summer with air conditioning. Transport is $30 to $60 on ride-hailing. The value is strong: clean air, greenery and space for far less than comparable Asian capitals.
islamabad.whereToWork: Base yourself in the F-6, F-7, F-8, F-11 or E-11 sectors; they are leafy, low-rise and close to the markets and cafes. Kohsar Market and F-6 Super Market are the cafe cores, with Chai Khana, Burning Brownie, Mocca Coffee and the various branches of Gloria Jean's and Second Cup all workable, and Monal and the Pir Sohawa road offering views rather than productivity. For dedicated space, the National Incubation Center at NUST, Daftarkhwan and Colabs have Islamabad operations, and Blue Area holds most of the serious office coworking stock. Fibre from Nayatel or StormFiber commonly delivers 50 Mbps to 200 Mbps and is genuinely reliable, which is the city's quiet advantage. The caveats: load shedding is milder here than in Karachi or Lahore but still occurs, so verify a UPS or generator; mobile internet is periodically throttled or suspended during protests, so a paid VPN is effectively mandatory; and cafes close early. This country has one of the largest populations of freelancers on the international platforms anywhere, and a good share of them work out of this city, which means the coworking spaces and the coffee shops are full of people doing more or less what you are doing.
islamabad.gettingAround: There is no metro in the underground sense, but the Islamabad-Rawalpindi Metrobus runs a dedicated corridor from Saddar in Rawalpindi to Pak Secretariat, with a separate line out to the airport, and fares are about $0.10 to $0.15. Beyond that, ride-hailing dominates: Careem, InDrive and Yango cover the city, with a typical cross-sector car ride at $1.50 to $4 and a bike ride at $0.60 to $1.50. Traditional taxis and Suzuki vans exist but are not worth the negotiation. Islamabad is unusually spacious, laid out on a numbered sector grid with wide roads and good greenery, but the sectors are large and distances long, so it is pleasant to walk within a sector and impractical between them. Islamabad International Airport is roughly 25km southwest; expect $8 to $15 by Careem or 45 minutes on the airport Metrobus. A car is not needed, though it helps for weekend trips toward Murree, Swat and the north. The airport is shared with the older city next door and sits well out to the west of both, which makes the run there longer than the map suggests at any hour of the day. The two cities run into one another and feel nothing alike.
islamabad.visas: Pakistan runs an online e-visa system through the NADRA portal, and it is the standard route for Western nationals. Tourist e-visas are commonly granted for 30 to 90 days, and citizens of a long list of countries including the US, UK, most of the EU, Canada and Australia can apply fully online without a sponsor or letter of invitation; processing typically takes days to a few weeks and fees vary by nationality, often $30 to $60. Pakistan does not have a digital nomad visa despite periodic press speculation, so do not plan around one. Extensions are applied for through the same online portal and are sometimes granted, though outcomes are inconsistent and best started well before expiry. Business visas are available with an invitation from a registered Pakistani company. The important gotchas are regional rather than bureaucratic: some areas require a No Objection Certificate for travel, notably parts of Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's border districts and Azad Kashmir. Overstaying is treated seriously.
islamabad.bestTime: Islamabad's climate is one of its best arguments, with four real seasons rather than a wet and dry binary. March and April are the peak, with highs in the low twenties, blossom across the sectors and hiking weather on the Margalla Hills trails. May and June are hot and dry, regularly hitting 38C to 40C, and this is the window when the Margallas become unpleasant by midday. The monsoon lands roughly July through mid-September, bringing violent thunderstorms, spectacular skies, humidity and occasional flash flooding on the nullahs, though it also greens the hills. Late September through November is the second excellent window: dry, mild and clear, and the season for heading north to Hunza and Skardu before the passes close. December to February is genuinely cold, dropping near freezing at night, with fog and a smog season that is real though far milder than Lahore's. Pakistan Day in March and both Eids anchor the calendar.
islamabad.prosCons: Islamabad is the anomaly in South Asia: a planned, green, low-density capital backed onto the forested Margalla Hills, with clean air by regional standards, wide roads, functional fibre, cheap ride-hailing and almost none of the density or noise of Karachi, Lahore or Delhi. Food is excellent and very cheap, the people are famously hospitable, and the city is the gateway to the Karakoram, arguably the best mountain trekking on the planet, with Hunza and Skardu a short flight or long drive away. The costs are considerable. It is quiet to the point of dullness, with an early-closing, largely alcohol-free social life and no nomad scene to speak of. Internet shutdowns and platform blocks during political tension are routine and can genuinely disrupt work. Security requires ongoing attention, with periodic incidents in the wider region and hard restrictions on travel to some provinces. Bureaucracy is heavy, distances are car-dependent, and solo women face real cultural friction.
islamabad.whoFor: Islamabad fits the self-directed remote worker who wants mountains within reach, a low burn rate and clean air, and who does not need a scene to be productive. Trekkers, climbers, motorcyclists and photographers get outsized value because the city is a comfortable, well-connected base camp for the Karakoram and Hindu Kush. It also suits people with Pakistani family or business ties, and those already working with the country's fast-growing outsourcing and startup sector. Long-stay travellers who value order and greenery over stimulation will be surprised at how well it works. Skip it if a bar culture, an existing nomad community or a dense walkable core matters, if your work cannot tolerate occasional internet suspensions, or if you want a low-friction visa reset ecosystem. Solo women, LGBT nomads and anyone who needs to be visibly unconventional should weigh the social conservatism seriously. Party-oriented or first-time nomads will be much happier in Southeast Asia.

male.costOfLiving: Malé is expensive, small and imports nearly everything, and $2,200 a month is a realistic single-person figure that still requires care. A furnished studio or one-bedroom in Malé proper or Hulhumalé runs $700 to $1,300, with Hulhumalé Phase 2 the value option and central Malé the cramped premium. Food is the other big line: local hotaa cafes serve mas huni, roshi and short eats for $2 to $5, but a normal restaurant meal is $12 to $25 and groceries are heavily marked up, with a typical monthly food spend of $400 to $700. A Dhiraagu or Ooredoo SIM with data costs $20 to $40, notably pricier than elsewhere in Asia. Coworking is scarce; expect $150 to $250 where it exists. Utilities and water run $60 to $150, with air conditioning dominating. Transport is cheap at $30 to $80 including ferries. The verdict: island-life value is real, but Malé itself is dense urban living at resort-country prices.
male.whereToWork: Malé is one of the most densely populated islands on earth and has almost no dedicated coworking stock, so most remote workers base in Hulhumalé, the reclaimed island beside the airport, which has wider streets, newer apartments and a beach. Practical work happens in cafes and apartments: Seagull Cafe' House and the cluster of cafes around Chaandhanee Magu and Boduthakurufaanu Magu in Malé, and the newer cafes along the Hulhumalé beach road, are all usable, and hotel lobbies in Hulhumalé are quietly the most reliable option. Fibre from Dhiraagu and Ooredoo is genuinely good, commonly 50 Mbps to 200 Mbps, and the Maldives has strong undersea cable connectivity, though international latency to Europe and the US is noticeable. Caveats matter: VoIP calling over Skype, WhatsApp and Viber has historically been restricted by the operators, so test your calling stack before committing; cafes are small, hot and rarely have sockets; and construction noise in Hulhumalé is constant.
male.gettingAround: Malé is walkable end to end in about twenty minutes because the island is barely two square kilometres, and that is genuinely the main mode of transport. Beyond walking, the system is ferries and bridges. The Sinamalé Bridge links Malé to Hulhulé, the airport island, and on to Hulhumalé, served by frequent buses at roughly $0.65 to $1.30. MTCC ferries connect Malé to Villingili and other nearby islands for about $0.20 to $0.70, and public speedboat and ferry networks reach the wider atolls at $3 to $30 depending on distance. Taxis within Malé are a flat fare of around $1.60 to $3.20, and across the bridge around $5. Ride-hailing apps such as Ryde and Avas Ride operate locally. The airport is on its own island, so the connection is a bridge taxi or the free-standing airport ferry to Malé at about $0.65. No car is needed; owning one is impractical and parking is a serious problem.
male.visas: The Maldives grants a free 30-day visa on arrival to every nationality, with no advance application, which is one of the most open policies in the world. Requirements are a passport valid six months, proof of onward travel, a confirmed booking for accommodation registered with the tourism ministry and sufficient funds, and immigration does check the accommodation line. Extensions are possible through Maldives Immigration up to a total of 90 days, applied for before expiry with a local sponsor and a fee. The Maldives does not have a digital nomad visa. A widely publicised long-stay programme was floated years ago and never launched, so plan around the 30-day plus extension reality, not around a nomad permit. Working remotely for a foreign employer on a tourist visa occupies the usual grey zone: it is not explicitly permitted and any local employment absolutely requires a work permit and sponsor. Do not attempt to work for Maldivian entities without one; enforcement on local labour is strict.
male.bestTime: The Maldives runs on two monsoons rather than four seasons, and temperatures barely move, sitting between 25C and 31C year round. The dry northeast monsoon, locally the iruvai, runs roughly December to April and is the high season: sunny, low humidity, calm seas and the best visibility for diving and snorkelling. January to March is the peak of that window and also the peak of prices. The wet southwest monsoon, the hulhangu, runs roughly May to November, bringing squalls, higher humidity, choppier seas and shorter but heavier rain; it rarely rains all day and accommodation drops noticeably, so it is the value window for long stays. June and July can be genuinely blowy, which affects ferry schedules between islands. Manta and whale shark season peaks around Hanifaru Bay from May to November. Ramadan, whose dates shift each year, changes daytime opening hours in Malé considerably, and Eid brings a national holiday exodus. The mantas and whale sharks move between the eastern and western sides of the atolls with the monsoon rather than appearing on any fixed date, so the month decides which side of the country the diving is on. A trip planned around them needs the atoll chosen as carefully as the dates. Domestic flights and speedboat transfers between atolls often cost more than the diving does.
male.prosCons: The appeal is obvious and real: the Maldives is a genuinely beautiful, safe, low-crime country with excellent internet, a free 30-day entry for every passport, and world-class diving, snorkelling and surfing a ferry ride away. Hulhumalé offers a modern, orderly base with a public beach, and the guesthouse economy on local islands such as Maafushi, Dhigurah, Thulusdhoo and Fulidhoo makes long stays affordable in a way the resort marketing hides. The drawbacks are equally real. Malé itself is a crowded, concrete, hot and largely charmless city with little green space and constant construction. It is a conservative Muslim country: alcohol is banned outside resorts and airport hotels, pork is unavailable, bikinis are restricted to designated beaches and public behaviour is regulated. Costs are high for what you get, imported goods are expensive, medical care for anything serious means evacuation to Colombo or Bangkok, VoIP restrictions frustrate remote work, and 30-day visa limits make long basing awkward.
male.whoFor: Divers, surfers, freedivers and anyone whose non-work life is genuinely built around the ocean are the natural audience, plus remote workers on strong Western salaries who want an unusual, safe, sunny base for a month or two. An asynchronous, low-call workload is close to a requirement. So is a tolerance for sitting a long way from everybody else's time zone, and a budget that can meet the cost floor without argument. Couples and solo travellers who want quiet, safety and daily sea time over nightlife will get real value, particularly if they base in Hulhumalé or a guesthouse island rather than central Malé. Skip it if the budget is the priority, since the same money buys far more in Sri Lanka, Bali or Thailand. Skip it too if alcohol, nightlife, a large nomad community, a walkable historic city or a long visa runway matter, or if you need heavy real-time video calling given the VoIP restrictions. Anyone who needs seasons or urban stimulation will go stir crazy fast.

yangon.costOfLiving: Yangon is very cheap in dollar terms and $800 a month buys a good standard of living, though the currency situation complicates everything. A furnished one-bedroom apartment on a monthly basis in Bahan, Golden Valley or the Inya Lake area runs $250 to $500; older walk-up flats downtown or in Sanchaung go for $120 to $250. Street food is the great bargain, with mohinga, shan noodles and a tea shop breakfast at $0.50 to $2, while a mid-range restaurant meal is $5 to $12. A Mytel, Ooredoo or ATOM SIM with data costs $5 to $12. Formal coworking is thin, roughly $60 to $120 where it operates. Utilities run $40 to $90, with generator fuel a real line item because power cuts are frequent and long. Transport is under $40. The kyat has an official rate and a much weaker parallel rate, so bring clean US dollar notes; costs are low but banking friction is severe. Rent is asked in dollars from a foreigner and in kyat from a neighbour, and the two numbers are not converted from one another, so what the flat next door costs tells you nothing about what you will be quoted. Six months up front is a normal opening request and is negotiable downwards.
yangon.whereToWork: Base yourself in Bahan, Golden Valley, Sanchaung or around Inya Lake; downtown near Sule Pagoda and Pansodan is atmospheric but noisy and heavily policed. Yangon's tea shop culture is the informal office, and the modern cafe scene around Dhammazedi Road, Yaw Min Gyi Street and Kabar Aye Pagoda Road, including long-running spots like Rangoon Tea House and various independent roasters, tolerates laptop sessions. Formal coworking, once represented by Phandeeyar and a handful of startup hubs, has been badly reduced since 2021, so verify anything is still operating before relying on it. Fibre from Ooredoo, MPT or 5BB delivers 20 Mbps to 100 Mbps in good buildings, but this is the hardest connectivity environment in the region: the military authorities operate extensive blocking of Facebook, most social platforms and news sites, and have criminalised unauthorised VPN use, while running periodic shutdowns. Assume a VPN is needed and may still be blocked, and verify generator or inverter backup. Foreign currency entering the banking system has been subject to forced conversion at a rate well below the street one, which is the single most consequential financial fact for anybody earning abroad and the reason nobody here receives money into a local account if they can avoid it. Cash brought in and changed informally is the working arrangement.
yangon.gettingAround: Yangon has no metro. The Yangon Circular Railway loops the city on a slow, three-hour, deeply local circuit for about $0.10 and is more of an experience than transport. Day to day, the YBS bus network covers the city at $0.10 to $0.20 a ride but requires some Burmese to navigate confidently. Ride-hailing is the practical answer: Grab operates in Yangon and a typical cross-city car ride costs $2 to $6, with app pricing sparing the haggling. Taxis flagged on the street cost similar but require negotiation upfront. Motorcycles are banned within most of central Yangon, so there are no motorbike taxis and no scooter option, which is unusual for Southeast Asia and means a car is the only fast mode. Walking downtown along the colonial grid is genuinely pleasant, but footpaths elsewhere are broken and the heat is punishing. Yangon International Airport is around 15km north; expect $4 to $10 and 30 to 60 minutes by Grab.
yangon.visas: Myanmar remains under military rule following the 2021 coup, and a civil war continues across much of the country; this dominates any visa discussion. The eVisa system does operate, and tourist eVisas are issued for 28 days, single entry, valid for entry within 90 days of approval, at a fee of around $50; business eVisas run 70 days. There is no digital nomad visa and none is contemplated. Tourist visa extensions are generally not granted; overstaying is instead handled by paying a fine of around $3 per day at the airport on departure, which is common practice but should not be relied on. The serious gotchas are non-bureaucratic. Many Western governments advise against all travel to Myanmar, which can void travel insurance entirely. Large parts of the country including Rakhine, Chin, Kachin, Karen, Sagaing and parts of Shan are effectively off limits, banking and card networks barely function, and there are legitimate ethical questions about spending that reaches the junta.
yangon.bestTime: The clear window is November to February, the cool dry season, when Yangon sits around 30C to 33C by day with low humidity and comfortable nights near 18C to 20C. That is also when the pagoda festivals and the Buddhist calendar are at their richest, including Tazaungdaing, the festival of lights, in November. March to May is the hot season and it is genuinely severe, with April routinely exceeding 38C and humidity making outdoor movement unpleasant; this is also when Thingyan, the Burmese water festival new year, effectively closes the country for a week in mid-April. The southwest monsoon runs roughly late May to October and Yangon is one of the wettest cities in Southeast Asia, receiving well over 2,500mm, most of it between June and August, with flooded streets and grey skies for weeks. October is transitional and often pleasant late in the month. Cyclone risk in the Bay of Bengal peaks in April, May and October.
yangon.prosCons: Yangon is extraordinary, and the word is not decoration: a decaying colonial downtown that is architecturally unlike anywhere else in Asia, the Shwedagon Pagoda, an outstanding and largely undiscovered food culture, tea shop life, and warm, curious people. It is genuinely cheap, essentially untouristed since 2021, and offers an experience no other Southeast Asian city can. The drawbacks are severe and honest assessment is required. The country is under military rule with an active civil war, most Western governments advise against travel, and travel insurance is frequently void as a result. Internet censorship is heavy, VPN use has been criminalised, and outages and shutdowns are routine and can stop work entirely. Power cuts are long and daily. The banking system barely functions for foreigners, so cash dollars are essential and ATMs are unreliable. Conscription has been reintroduced, checkpoints are common, and photographing the wrong thing carries real legal risk. Medical care is inadequate for anything serious.
yangon.whoFor: Yangon is not a general-purpose nomad base and should not be treated as one in 2026. It fits a narrow group: journalists, researchers, humanitarian and development workers, people with family or long business ties to Myanmar, and highly experienced travellers who have already lived through difficult environments and are making an informed, ethically considered choice. Those people will find a fascinating, cheap and moving city with almost no other foreigners in it. Anyone else should skip it. That includes first-time nomads, anyone whose income depends on uninterrupted connectivity or reliable video calls, anyone who needs functioning banking or travel insurance, and anyone uncomfortable with the reality that tourist spending in a junta-controlled economy is politically loaded. Digital nomads seeking cheap Southeast Asia with community and infrastructure are far better served by Chiang Mai, Hanoi, Da Nang or Phnom Penh, all of which deliver similar costs without the political risk or the censorship.

ulaanbaatar.costOfLiving: Ulaanbaatar runs around $900 a month for a single nomad, which covers a modern apartment and an unremarkable but comfortable life. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Sukhbaatar district, near the State Department Store or around Seoul Street costs $300 to $550; further out in Bayanzurkh or Songinokhairkhan drops to $200 to $350. Food is moderately priced: a bowl of guriltai shul or a plate of buuz at a local canteen is $2 to $4, a mid-range restaurant meal is $8 to $15, and imported groceries carry a noticeable markup. A Mobicom or Unitel SIM with a monthly data bundle costs $8 to $15. Coworking desks run $80 to $150. Utilities are the seasonal variable: $40 in summer, $80 to $130 in winter when heating and electricity peak, though district heating is often bundled into rent. Transport is under $30. The verdict: fair rather than exceptional value, bought with a very hard winter. Heating in the apartment blocks comes from the power stations and runs from the middle of September to the middle of May whether anybody wants it or not, billed through the building charge, so a flat is warm and the cost is not a variable to manage.
ulaanbaatar.whereToWork: Base yourself in Sukhbaatar district, ideally within walking distance of Sukhbaatar Square, Seoul Street or the State Department Store, since these hold the best apartment stock, the cafes and most services. Ulaanbaatar has a real cafe culture for its size: Tom N Toms, Caffe Bene and Coffee Bean cover the reliable Korean-style chains with sockets and long-stay tolerance, while independents around Seoul Street and the Blue Sky area are quieter. For dedicated space, look at the coworking and startup hubs around Sukhbaatar Square and the Shangri-La and Blue Sky towers; Mongolia's startup scene is small but the incubator space around the National University and the tech park rents desks. Fibre is genuinely good, with 50 Mbps to 200 Mbps common and Mongolia performing well on connectivity relative to its GDP, and 4G coverage is strong in the city. The main caveats are winter power and heating load, minimal English outside the centre, and cafes that close early.
ulaanbaatar.gettingAround: There is no metro. Public transport is a dense city bus and trolleybus network with a U Money smart card, and fares are about $0.15 to $0.25, though buses are crowded and the routes are signed largely in Cyrillic. Ride-hailing dominates for foreigners: UBCab and local apps operate, and a cross-city car ride costs $2 to $5, while informal taxis, essentially any private car flagged down, charge a per-kilometre rate around $0.50. Traffic in Ulaanbaatar is genuinely bad for a city of 1.6 million, with license plate restrictions by day of week in place to manage it. The core around Sukhbaatar Square is walkable, but winter ice and sub-freezing temperatures from November to March limit walking for much of the year. Chinggis Khaan International Airport is 50km south, roughly 60 to 90 minutes, at $15 to $25 by taxi. No car needed in town; a hired 4x4 with driver is the norm for countryside trips.
ulaanbaatar.visas: Mongolia liberalised its entry rules substantially, and citizens of the US, UK, EU member states, Canada, Australia, Japan and many others can now enter visa free for 30 days for tourism, a policy extended through at least the end of 2025 and repeatedly renewed, so verify the current expiry date before booking. US citizens have long held a separate 90-day visa free arrangement. Where a visa is required, Mongolia operates an e-visa system for tourist and business categories. There is no digital nomad visa. Extensions of a visa free or tourist stay are possible through the Immigration Agency of Mongolia in Ulaanbaatar, typically adding up to 30 days, and must be applied for before the current stay expires; the office is on the road toward the airport. Anyone staying beyond 30 days on a longer visa must register with the immigration agency within one week of arrival, and failure to register is the single most common and most expensive mistake foreigners make here.
ulaanbaatar.bestTime: Ulaanbaatar is the coldest capital city in the world and the climate dictates everything. The good window is short: mid-June to early September, when days reach 20C to 25C, the steppe is green, and the countryside is genuinely accessible. Naadam, the national wrestling, archery and horse racing festival, falls on 11 to 13 July and is the single best reason to be in the country. May and September are shoulder months, cool, dry and pleasant, with September particularly good for travel as the crowds thin. From late October the temperature collapses, and December through February routinely sit between minus 20C and minus 35C, with January averaging around minus 25C. Winter also brings the city's worst problem: ger district coal burning creates particulate pollution among the worst on earth. Tsagaan Sar, the lunar new year, falls in February. March and April are windy, dusty and unpredictable. The winter air here is among the worst measured anywhere, because the districts on the hillsides burn coal for heat and on a still freezing night the smoke sinks and sits over the whole basin. It is a serious health matter rather than an inconvenience, and masks are ordinary equipment.
ulaanbaatar.prosCons: Ulaanbaatar offers something scarce: a genuinely different, low-tourism capital with surprisingly good internet, an easy visa position for most Western passports, a compact walkable core, decent coffee and a young, educated, increasingly English-speaking population. The real draw is outside the city, with the steppe, the Gobi, Terelj and the Khuvsgul region among the most spectacular and least crowded landscapes anywhere, and horse riding and ger stays within a couple of hours. Costs are moderate and crime against foreigners is generally low. The problems are seasonal and structural. Winter is not a figure of speech: five months below freezing, often far below, and coal smoke that makes the city's air among the world's most polluted from November to March, which is a genuine health cost. Infrastructure outside the centre is rough, pickpocketing in crowded areas is common, traffic is heavy, English drops off quickly outside the core, and the nomad community is essentially nonexistent.
ulaanbaatar.whoFor: Ulaanbaatar fits the summer-season nomad and the adventure-oriented traveller: someone arriving in June and leaving in September, using the city as a serviceable, connected base for horseback trips, the Gobi, Naadam and long drives across empty country. It suits photographers, writers and anyone drawn to landscapes and cultures still far off the standard circuit, and it works for remote workers on European or Asian hours who want somewhere genuinely unlike anywhere else without visa hassle. Skip it as a winter base unless there is a specific reason to be there, because the cold and the air quality together are punishing, particularly for anyone with respiratory conditions or young children. Skip it too if a nomad community, year round outdoor life, beaches, cheap tropical costs or a large restaurant and nightlife scene matter, or if the work requires overlap with US time zones. Those wanting a full-year Asian base should look elsewhere.

dunedin.costOfLiving: A budget of $1900 a month covers a single nomad in Dunedin, though it demands discipline by New Zealand standards. A furnished one-bedroom flat near the Octagon or in Roslyn runs roughly $850 to $1200; a room in a shared student-era villa in North Dunedin costs $400 to $650. Groceries at Countdown or the Saturday Otago Farmers Market come to $300 to $420, with cafe brunches around $15 to $22 and pub mains $20 to $30. A prepaid SIM from One NZ, Spark or 2degrees costs $15 to $28 monthly for 10GB to 40GB. Hot-desking at Petridish sits near $150 to $260. Power is the hidden cost: older uninsulated villas push winter bills to $110 to $170, with fibre broadband at $50 to $65. Bus fares are about $2 with a Bee Card. Verdict: cheap for New Zealand, expensive for the world.
dunedin.whereToWork: The compact centre around the Octagon and Vogel Street is the natural base, with Roslyn and Maori Hill quieter and North Dunedin loud during term time. Petridish on Vogel Street is the established coworking space, a converted warehouse popular with startups and researchers spilling out of the University of Otago. Cafe work is the cheaper default: Vanguard Specialty Coffee, Mazagran Espresso Bar, Morning Magpie and the cluster along lower Stuart Street all tolerate laptops outside the brunch rush. Fibre is widespread thanks to New Zealand's ultrafast broadband rollout, with 300 Mbps to 900 Mbps typical in flats and 100 Mbps plus in most cafes. Practical caveats: many venues close by 4pm, Sunday hours are thin, seating vanishes when students return in late February, and heating rather than bandwidth is the real limiting factor between May and September. The country's oldest medical school is here, and the health research attached to it is the largest professional employer in the city after the university itself. The chocolate factory that defined the place for a century closed a few years ago and the site became a hospital, which says plainly enough which way the local economy has moved. Neither of them hires from abroad casually.
dunedin.gettingAround: Dunedin's centre is walkable in about twenty minutes end to end, but the city is famously hilly and Roslyn, Maori Hill or Northeast Valley involve serious climbs. The Orbus network covers the city and the harbour road to Port Chalmers; fares are roughly $2 to $3 with a Bee Card and about double in cash, with day caps keeping costs low. Uber does not operate here, so Dunedin Taxis, Blue Star and Southern Taxis handle late nights at around $10 to $20 for a cross-town trip. Dunedin Airport sits 30km south at Momona; a shuttle costs about $25 to $35 and a taxi $70 to $90, so pre-booking matters. Rail is scenic only, running the Taieri Gorge and coastal excursions rather than commuter services. A car helps for the Otago Peninsula and Central Otago, but a scooter is not essential and the weather discourages it.
dunedin.visas: New Zealand grants visa-waiver entry to most Western passport holders, generally 90 days, with British citizens receiving six months. Travellers must buy an NZeTA online before boarding, valid two years, costing around $10 plus the International Visitor Levy of roughly $60. Since 2023 New Zealand has explicitly permitted visitors to work remotely for an overseas employer while on a visitor visa, provided the work is not for a New Zealand company or the New Zealand market, so nomads no longer occupy a grey zone. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa. Visitor visas can be extended in-country to a maximum of nine months within any eighteen-month period, and immigration officers expect proof of onward travel and funds of about $1000 per month. Longer stays require a work, student or Working Holiday visa, the last available to under-30s or under-35s from selected countries. Any stay that will add up to more than six months triggers a medical requirement, a chest x-ray included, which has to be done by a panel physician rather than an ordinary doctor and takes time to arrange. Biosecurity at the border is the strictest anywhere: boots, tents and food all get declared, and an undeclared apple carries an instant fine.
dunedin.bestTime: Dunedin has a cool oceanic climate with no genuinely hot season. December to February is the peak window, with daytime highs of 18C to 22C, long southern daylight until nearly 10pm, and the beaches at St Clair and Aramoana at their best. March and April are the connoisseur's months: settled, golden, and quieter once summer visitors leave. May through August is the low point, with highs of 9C to 12C, frequent southerly fronts, damp interiors and short days, though snow in the city itself is uncommon. September and October are windy and changeable. Rain is spread evenly rather than concentrated in a monsoon, so a waterproof jacket matters more than a season. Key dates include the Dunedin Fringe Festival in March, iD Dunedin Fashion Week, the Vogel Street Party in spring, Matariki in June or July, and rugby test weekends at Forsyth Barr Stadium. The southern lights are visible from the hills above the harbour on a clear dark night when the activity is up, and this is one of the better places in the country to catch them, which is a compensation for the long winter nights that nobody advertises. Cold fronts arrive from the south with no warm ground between here and the ice.
dunedin.prosCons: Dunedin's strengths are unusual for a city this size: a genuine Victorian and Edwardian streetscape, a serious university that keeps the arts, music and cafe scene alive, wildlife that includes albatrosses, sea lions and yellow-eyed penguins within half an hour of the Octagon, gigabit fibre, safe streets, drinkable tap water and immediate access to the Otago Peninsula and Central Otago. Living costs are the lowest of New Zealand's main centres. The housing stock, though, is cold, damp and poorly insulated, and winter power bills bite; wages and prices are high relative to Asian or Latin American hubs, so $1900 buys modestly; the weather is grey and wind-lashed for months; the city empties and quietens during university breaks; there is no Uber and very limited late-night life; the international nomad community is thin; and long-haul flights out are expensive, indirect and time-consuming from a small regional airport.
dunedin.whoFor: A small, safe, English-speaking Western city with fast internet, a strong academic and creative culture and wilderness at the doorstep is the offer, and cheap living or a large coworking scene is not part of it. It rewards writers, researchers, developers on Northern Hemisphere-friendly schedules who do not mind an early start, outdoor people, wildlife photographers and anyone treating New Zealand's South Island as a base for months of exploration. It also fits those on Working Holiday visas who want an affordable landing pad. Skip it if the budget is the priority, if a warm climate is non-negotiable, if a dense international nomad community and constant networking events matter, or if the work requires overlapping heavily with European business hours. Party travellers and those needing frequent cheap flights to other countries will find the isolation frustrating.

kohtao.costOfLiving: About $1000 a month is realistic on Koh Tao if the accommodation is monthly rather than nightly. A furnished studio or small bungalow with air conditioning in Mae Haad, Sairee or Chalok Baan Kao rents for $250 to $450 monthly off-season, climbing to $500 or more from December to March; long-stay negotiation is standard. Thai food at local shops costs $2 to $4 a plate, while Western restaurants on Sairee run $8 to $15, so a mixed diet lands at $300 to $400. An AIS or True tourist SIM with generous data is $10 to $18 a month. Formal coworking day passes are around $8 to $12, or roughly $90 to $150 monthly where offered. Electricity is the sting: island rates and constant air conditioning produce $50 to $120 bills. Scooter hire is $5 to $8 daily. Verdict: excellent value if diving is the point, otherwise mainland Thailand is cheaper.
kohtao.whereToWork: Base yourself in Mae Haad if ferries, banks and the widest cafe choice matter, Sairee for the social and dive-school density, or Chalok Baan Kao for quiet and better sleep. Reliable laptop-friendly cafes cluster in Mae Haad and along the back road behind Sairee: Zest Coffee Lounge and Cafe del Sol are long-standing fixtures, alongside a rotating set of air-conditioned specialty roasters that come and go each season, so it pays to check current openings rather than trust old lists. Dedicated coworking has never taken firm root here; most remote workers rely on cafes plus a good room connection. Fibre reached the island years ago and 50 Mbps to 200 Mbps is common, but island bandwidth degrades in peak season, power cuts happen during storms, and the November to December monsoon can sever service for hours. A 5G phone plan as backup is close to essential. Almost everybody working on this island is doing so on the wrong paperwork, since a work permit is tied to a registered employer and the dive schools sponsor only a fraction of the people teaching. That is the island's open secret, and worth understanding before accepting anything offered casually over a beer. A remote job billed abroad sidesteps the question entirely.
kohtao.gettingAround: Koh Tao has no airport and no public bus network. Arrival is by ferry into Mae Haad pier: Lomprayah and Seatran catamarans from Chumphon on the mainland cost roughly $18 to $28 and take under two hours, while services from Koh Phangan and Koh Samui run $12 to $22. Combined bus-boat or flight-boat tickets from Bangkok, Surat Thani or Samui airport are sold everywhere. On the island, songthaew pickups charge about $3 per person on shared routes and $8 to $15 for private hires at night, which adds up fast. Sairee and Mae Haad are walkable, but the road between beaches is steep and unlit. A scooter at $5 to $8 a day is effectively essential for anything beyond one beach, though the hills, gravel and rental damage scams make it the single biggest risk on the island. Helmets and photographic evidence at pickup are non-negotiable.
kohtao.visas: Most Western passport holders enter Thailand under the visa exemption scheme, which since mid-2024 grants 60 days on arrival, extendable once at an immigration office for a further 30 days for a fee of about $55. The nearest immigration office for Koh Tao is on Koh Samui, so extensions require a ferry trip. Since 2024 Thailand has offered the Destination Thailand Visa, or DTV, a five-year multiple-entry visa aimed squarely at remote workers and long-stay soft-power visitors such as divers and Muay Thai students. It permits 180 days per entry, extendable once inside Thailand by another 180 days, costs about $290 and requires proof of about $14,000 in savings plus supporting documents such as a remote employment contract. Thailand also requires a digital arrival card. Overstaying carries fines and blacklisting, so it is not worth risking. A long-stay visa carries a standing obligation to report your address to the immigration office four times a year, in person or online, and it continues even when nothing whatever has changed. A landlord is separately supposed to notify them when a foreigner moves in, and an extension can stall if that was never done, so ask whether the place you are renting has ever filed one.
kohtao.bestTime: Koh Tao sits in the Gulf of Thailand and runs on a different calendar from Phuket or Chiang Mai. February to April is the prime window: calm seas, visibility often above 20 metres, hot days near 33C and reliable ferries. May to August stays good, with short afternoon showers, whale shark sightings peaking around March to May and again in September, and fewer crowds. September and October bring increasing rain and choppier crossings. The worst window is late October through December, when the northeast monsoon delivers heavy sustained rain, rough seas, occasional cancelled ferries and power interruptions; some businesses close for a few weeks. January is a transitional month, improving steadily. Festivals worth timing include Songkran in mid-April, Loy Krathong in November, the Koh Tao Festival and the neighbouring Koh Phangan Full Moon parties, which draw the island's crowds every lunar month. Warm-water bleaching has hit these reefs several times over the last decade and the authorities have closed individual sites temporarily to let them recover, so a dive plan made months ahead is worth checking again on arrival. The water is at its warmest in the same weeks the visibility is at its best, which is precisely the problem.
kohtao.prosCons: Koh Tao's strengths are specific and strong: it is one of the cheapest and best places on earth to learn or teach scuba diving, the water is warm year round, the community of divers, instructors and long-stay remote workers is genuinely tight, monthly rents are low, Thai food is excellent and inexpensive, and the island is small enough to feel like a village within a week. Free diving, bouldering and hiking add variety. The drawbacks accumulate, though: the island is tiny and can feel claustrophobic after two months, medical facilities are basic with serious cases evacuated to Koh Samui or Bangkok, scooter accidents are common and roads are steep and poorly surfaced, rental scams and inflated damage claims are a recurring complaint, waste management and water quality lag behind visitor numbers, electricity is expensive, the monsoon can strand people, and formal coworking infrastructure remains thin.
kohtao.whoFor: Koh Tao fits the diver first and the nomad second: instructors, divemaster trainees, underwater photographers and remote workers who want to be in the water every morning before a European-facing afternoon of work. It also suits low-budget solo travellers who value a small, friendly, easy-to-join community, freelancers on the Destination Thailand Visa planning a long soft-power stay, and anyone who prefers a village rhythm to a city. Skip it if the work needs enterprise-grade uptime, if a large formal coworking scene with events and networking matters, or if family-sized apartments, hospitals and international schools are requirements. It is also a poor fit for anyone who dislikes scooters, gets restless on small islands, or needs a varied nightlife and restaurant scene beyond beach bars. Those seeking cheaper city living with the same visa should compare Chiang Mai.

haiphong.costOfLiving: Hai Phong is one of Vietnam's better-value large cities, and $700 a month is comfortable rather than tight. A furnished serviced studio or one-bedroom in Le Chan, Ngo Quyen or central Hong Bang costs $200 to $330, often with cleaning included; older local apartments go for $130 to $200. Street food is the backbone of the budget: banh da cua at $1.50, com binh dan plates at $2, bia hoi under $0.50 a glass, so $150 to $220 covers food with occasional Western meals at $8 to $12. A Viettel or Vinaphone SIM with abundant data runs $4 to $8 monthly. Dedicated coworking is limited, with desks around $60 to $110 where available. Electricity, water and fibre together come to $35 to $70, higher in the humid summer. Grab trips are $1 to $3. Verdict: strong value, with the trade-off being fewer nomad-specific amenities. A foreigner may own an apartment here but only on a fifty-year title rather than outright, and the land itself belongs to the state whoever is living on it, which shapes every conversation about buying. Rent is commonly asked three or six months at a time, and a discount for taking the longer term is normal.
haiphong.whereToWork: Central Hong Bang around the Tam Bac lake and the French colonial theatre district is the most walkable base, with Le Chan and Ngo Quyen offering cheaper apartments and dense local food. The city's cafe culture is deep, and Vietnamese chains do the heavy lifting: Cong Caphe, Highlands Coffee and Trung Nguyen Legend branches all have air conditioning, power outlets and workable wifi, while independent roasters along Dien Bien Phu and Lach Tray streets suit longer sessions. Formal coworking is scarce compared with Hanoi or Da Nang, so most remote workers combine a good apartment fibre line with cafes. Fibre performance is solid at 60 Mbps to 300 Mbps, though Vietnam's reliance on undersea cables means periodic international slowdowns even when domestic speeds look fine. Caveats: cafes get loud and smoky in the evening, seating tightens at lunch, and typhoon season brings genuine power and internet outages.
haiphong.gettingAround: Hai Phong is flat and moderately walkable in the centre, but the city sprawls and the heat and traffic push most people onto two wheels. Grab dominates, alongside the electric Xanh SM fleet: motorbike trips cost $0.60 to $1.50 and car rides $2 to $5 across town. Monthly scooter rental is $45 to $70 and makes life considerably easier, though not strictly essential given app coverage. Cat Bi International Airport lies only about 7km from the centre, roughly a $4 to $7 car ride, with domestic flights nationwide and regional connections. The train to Hanoi is a local favourite: around 2.5 hours for $3 to $6, arriving at Long Bien. Limousine vans to Hanoi cost $7 to $10. Ferries and fast boats from Ben Binh pier and Got connect to Cat Ba island for $5 to $15, the main reason many nomads choose this city. An expressway opened a decade ago reduced the run up to the capital to ninety minutes flat, which is why the limousine vans run as often as they do. The deepwater container port east of the city is the largest in the north, and it is the reason the roads carry the lorry traffic they do at every hour of the day.
haiphong.visas: Vietnam runs one of Asia's easiest entry systems. Since August 2023 the e-visa is available to all nationalities, valid up to 90 days, single or multiple entry, applied for online at the official portal for about $25 single and $50 multiple, usually approved within three to five working days. Separately, citizens of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and several Nordic and Asian countries receive a visa exemption of 45 days, with periodic extensions to that list, so checking the current rules before booking matters. There is no digital nomad visa. Extensions inside Vietnam are possible through agencies but are inconsistent and increasingly discouraged, so most long-stayers simply exit to Cambodia, Thailand or Laos and return on a fresh e-visa, which is legal and routine. Working for a Vietnamese employer requires a work permit and temporary residence card, a separate and much slower process.
haiphong.bestTime: Hai Phong has a northern Vietnamese climate with four distinct seasons, unlike the tropical south. October and November are the best months: dry, clear, with highs of 25C to 29C and low humidity, ideal for Cat Ba and Ha Long Bay trips. April and early May are the second window, warm and green before the heat sets in. December to March is cool and often grey, with temperatures of 14C to 20C and a persistent drizzle known as mua phun that keeps everything damp; heating is rare in apartments. June to August is hot and sticky at 32C to 36C with high humidity and heavy afternoon downpours. The typhoon window runs from July to September, and Hai Phong takes direct hits, as Typhoon Yagi demonstrated in 2024. Local highlights include Tet in January or February, and the red flamboyant flower festival in May. Lychees come in from the province next door for a few weeks at the start of summer and are sold by the branch at every roadside, which is one of the few compensations for the heat arriving. Humidity in the damp months is high enough that clothes left in a wardrobe grow mould, and a dehumidifier is an ordinary purchase.
haiphong.prosCons: Hai Phong offers genuine value: low rents, some of the best street food in Vietnam including banh da cua and nem cua be, a walkable French colonial core, an airport seven kilometres from downtown, cheap trains to Hanoi, and ferries to Cat Ba and Ha Long Bay for weekends. Prices have not been inflated by tourism, locals are welcoming, and the pace is calmer than Hanoi or Saigon. On the other side, this is an industrial port city rather than a nomad hub, so the international community is small, coworking options are thin, and English is less widely spoken than in Da Nang or Hoi An. Air quality is poor in winter, the damp cold season is genuinely unpleasant indoors, traffic is chaotic, typhoons cause real outages between July and September, there is no true beach in the city, and long-stay visa options remain limited.
haiphong.whoFor: Anyone who has already done the obvious stops in Vietnam, and wants low costs, real food and easy access to Ha Long Bay and Cat Ba without paying tourist prices, will find the arithmetic works. It works for solo developers, writers and traders who need little more than a fast apartment line, for people with business or manufacturing interests in the northern industrial belt, and for anyone who enjoys big-city Vietnamese life without a foreigner bubble. Skip it if a ready-made nomad community, frequent meetups and a choice of coworking spaces are what make a base work, if beaches are the priority, or if damp grey winters and poor winter air quality are dealbreakers. Those who want the same country with more infrastructure should compare Da Nang; those who want more culture and nightlife should compare Hanoi, two hours away by train.

vungtau.costOfLiving: At $800 a month a single nomad lives well in Vung Tau, a seaside city that is cheaper than Ho Chi Minh City while offering better air and a coastline. Furnished studios and one-bedroom apartments in Ward 1 near Front Beach or around Back Beach rent for $230 to $400, with sea-view units at the upper end and long-term deals common. Food costs $170 to $250: banh khot at $2 to $3, seafood plates at $4 to $8, and Western or Russian-influenced restaurants at $8 to $14. A Viettel or Mobifone SIM with plentiful data is $4 to $8. Coworking is limited, with desks near $60 to $100 where available, so many work from cafes at the price of a $1.50 coffee. Electricity, water and fibre total $40 to $80, spiking with air conditioning. Grab rides cost $1 to $3. Verdict: excellent coastal value. Power is billed in rising bands, so a flat running its cooling all evening crosses into a dearer tier and the bill jumps rather than climbs. Landlords often quote a foreigner one rate and a neighbour another, and that gap narrows with a longer commitment.
vungtau.whereToWork: Ward 1 around Front Beach, Bai Truoc, is the most convenient base, walkable to the promenade, markets and the ferry pier; Ward 2 and the Back Beach strip, Bai Sau, suit surfers, kitesurfers and those wanting a wider beach but a longer walk to the centre. Cafe culture carries the working day here: Cong Caphe, Highlands Coffee and a dense set of independent sea-view cafes along Ha Long and Thuy Van streets all offer air conditioning, outlets and reliable wifi, and several stay open late. Purpose-built coworking has never established itself, so an apartment with a good fibre line is the sensible core setup. Speeds of 60 Mbps to 250 Mbps are normal, with occasional international slowdowns from undersea cable faults. Caveats: weekend crowds from Ho Chi Minh City fill cafes on Saturdays and Sundays, and coastal wind and beachfront noise make outdoor tables impractical for calls.
vungtau.gettingAround: Vung Tau is compact and largely flat along the coast, so the centre is walkable and a bicycle covers most daily needs. Grab and the electric Xanh SM service dominate for anything longer: motorbike rides cost $0.60 to $1.50 and cars $2 to $5. A monthly scooter rental of $45 to $70 is worth it for the Nghinh Phong cape loop, Ho May cable car area and the beaches south of the city, though it is not strictly essential. The city has no airport; arrival is from Ho Chi Minh City, roughly 100km away. Limousine vans and buses from Saigon cost $6 to $10 and take two to three hours depending on the Long Thanh expressway traffic. The Greenlines DP hydrofoil from Bach Dang pier in District 1 is the more pleasant option at about $12 to $15 for a two-hour crossing, though sailings are weather-dependent. A vast new international airport is being built inland between here and the big city, and when it opens it puts long-haul flights within about an hour of this coast for the first time, which would change the case for basing here considerably.
vungtau.visas: Vietnam's rules apply identically in Vung Tau. The universal e-visa, available to all nationalities since August 2023, grants up to 90 days single or multiple entry, costs roughly $25 or $50 respectively, and is applied for online with approval typically in three to five working days. Citizens of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and several other European and Asian countries also qualify for a 45-day visa exemption, with the eligible list revised periodically. Vietnam has no digital nomad visa, and remote work for a foreign employer while on a tourist entry is a widely practised grey area rather than an explicitly permitted category. In-country extensions exist through agencies but are unreliable and expensive; the standard long-stay pattern is a border run to Cambodia, Thailand or Singapore followed by a fresh e-visa. Local employment requires a work permit and temporary residence card obtained by a Vietnamese sponsor.
vungtau.bestTime: Vung Tau follows southern Vietnam's two-season pattern and sits largely outside the main typhoon corridor, which is a meaningful advantage over central and northern coastal cities. The dry season runs from November to April: sunny, breezy, with highs of 29C to 33C, clean beaches and the best window overall. December to March is peak kitesurfing season at Back Beach thanks to consistent northeast winds.
