The wet season spans May to October, characterised by intense but usually short afternoon downpours rather than all-day rain, with humidity high and skies dramatic; September and October are the wettest and the sea is murkiest. Temperatures stay between 25C and 34C year round, so there is no cold season at all. Tet in January or February shuts many businesses and fills the city with domestic visitors, as do the Whale Worship festival and every Vietnamese public holiday weekend. The wind swings right round between the seasons, which is why one beach works in the dry months and the other in the wet, and why locals will tell you to change sides rather than change towns. Fishing boats work the bay at night under lamps visible from the promenade.
vungtau.prosCons: Vung Tau's strengths are its balance: sea air and a long promenade, cleaner and cooler than Ho Chi Minh City, genuinely cheap rents with sea views, superb seafood and the local banh khot, a walkable and flat centre, decent fibre, a small but established expat presence rooted in the offshore oil industry, and a two-hour hydrofoil to Saigon for anything the city lacks. Kitesurfing from November to March is a real draw. The drawbacks are equally clear: weekends bring heavy domestic crowds and inflated prices, the beaches are pleasant rather than world class and can be littered after busy periods, there is no airport or formal coworking scene, the nomad community is small and transient, English is limited outside tourism, the wet season is humid and grey, and anyone wanting culture, nightlife or a large international network will be commuting to Ho Chi Minh City regularly.
vungtau.whoFor: Vung Tau fits the nomad who wants Vietnamese prices with a coastline and cleaner air, and who is happy to be near Ho Chi Minh City rather than in it. Kitesurfers and swimmers come first. After them it is long-stay budget freelancers who need nothing more than a fast apartment connection, couples and quiet-living remote workers, and people who cycle in and out of Saigon for meetings, flights and whatever social life they want out of it. It is also a sensible soft landing for a first long stay in Vietnam given how manageable the city is. Skip it if the priority is a dense nomad scene with coworking, meetups and constant new arrivals, if a top-tier beach is expected, or if an international airport on the doorstep is required. Those wanting more infrastructure and a bigger community should compare Da Nang; those wanting pure city energy should base in Saigon.

bohol.costOfLiving: Around $800 a month works on Bohol, with the split between Tagbilaran and Panglao mattering more than anything else. In Tagbilaran city a furnished studio or one-bedroom costs $200 to $330; on Panglao near Alona Beach or Dumaluan the same unit runs $280 to $500 because of tourism demand, though monthly rates fall sharply outside December to April. Food is $180 to $260: carinderia meals at $1.50 to $3, fresh fish and rice cheaply at markets, and Alona restaurants at $7 to $14. A Globe or Smart SIM with a data bundle costs $8 to $15 monthly. Coworking is scarce, with day passes around $8 to $12 where offered. Electricity is expensive in the Philippines: $50 to $120 with steady air conditioning, plus $30 to $50 for fibre. Scooter rental is $70 to $110 monthly. Verdict: good value, with power the main budget risk. A foreigner cannot own land here at all, only a unit in a building where the foreign share stays under a set proportion, so a beach house offered for sale to somebody from outside involves a long lease or a local partner, and the arrangement matters a great deal more than the price does. Renting sidesteps the whole question.
bohol.whereToWork: Panglao island is where most remote workers base themselves, either around Alona Beach for restaurants and dive shops or in the quieter Danao, Doljo and Dumaluan areas for lower rents and less noise. Tagbilaran, 20 minutes away over the causeway, is the practical city with banks, hospitals, malls and the Bureau of Immigration office. Dedicated coworking has come and gone on Panglao, so verify what is currently trading rather than relying on old listings; in practice most people work from air-conditioned cafes near Alona and Tawala, from dive-resort common areas, or from home. Converge and PLDT fibre reaches much of Panglao at 50 Mbps to 300 Mbps, and Starlink has become a common backup among villa owners. The real caveats are brownouts, which are frequent and can last hours, plus typhoon-driven outages; a large power bank and a well-loaded mobile data plan are essential rather than optional.
bohol.gettingAround: Bohol runs on tricycles, multicabs and scooters. Tricycle hops within Tagbilaran or around Alona cost $0.40 to $2, and a Tagbilaran to Panglao run is $6 to $10 by private tricycle or van. Ceres buses serve the interior towns, Loboc, Carmen and the Chocolate Hills, for $1 to $4. Ride-hailing coverage is patchy and Grab is not reliably available, so a scooter at $8 to $12 a day or $70 to $110 a month is effectively essential for anyone staying more than a couple of weeks. Panglao Bohol International Airport, opened in 2018, sits about 20 minutes from Alona with domestic flights to Manila, Cebu and Davao plus occasional international charters. Fast ferries are the other lifeline: OceanJet, Lite Ferries and Supercat run Tagbilaran to Cebu in about two hours for $10 to $22, with services to Camiguin, Siquijor and Dumaguete. The road through the interior passes a two-kilometre stretch of mahogany planted in the nineteen sixties, dark enough at midday to drop the temperature noticeably, and it is the part of the inland loop everyone remembers. Roads away from that circuit narrow quickly and are unlit, so the interior is a daytime proposition.
bohol.visas: Most Western passport holders enter the Philippines visa-free for 30 days, provided they hold an onward or return ticket. Extensions are handled at Bureau of Immigration offices, including one in Tagbilaran: the first extension adds 29 days for roughly $60, after which longer six-month blocks become possible, and tourists may ultimately stay up to 36 months. Anyone staying beyond 59 days must obtain an ACR I-Card, costing about $100. There is also a mandatory eTravel registration online before arrival, which is free. The Philippines approved a digital nomad visa framework in 2025 for one-year renewable stays aimed at remote workers with foreign income, but implementation has been slow and application details remain limited, so most nomads still use the tourist extension route, which is straightforward and widely used. Long-term retirement residency via the SRRV is a separate option for those over 35 with capital to deposit.
bohol.bestTime: Bohol's best window is March to May: dry, hot at 30C to 34C, with the calmest seas and the best diving visibility around Balicasag and Pamilacan. February is also excellent and slightly cooler. June to October is the southwest monsoon, with humid days, heavy but often brief showers and greener interiors; prices drop and Panglao empties, which suits budget-focused stays. The riskiest window for the central Visayas is November to January, when tropical cyclones tracking west can hit hard, as Typhoon Odette did in December 2021, causing weeks of power and communication outages. December to early January is simultaneously peak tourist season, with Alona busy and rents highest. Whale shark and dolphin activity around Pamilacan peaks in the dry months. Festival highlights include the Sandugo Festival in Tagbilaran each July and Sinulog spillover from nearby Cebu in January. An earthquake in 2013 brought down several of the island's Spanish-era stone churches and lifted parts of the coastline clear of the water, and the rebuilt facades and the raised reef flats are both still there to see. Seismic risk here is not theoretical, and what has been put up since is noticeably better braced than what failed.
bohol.prosCons: Bohol's appeal is straightforward: white-sand beaches at Alona and Dumaluan, some of the best diving and freediving in the Philippines at Balicasag and Napaling, the Chocolate Hills and Loboc River inland, tarsiers, warm water year round, low rents outside peak season, English spoken almost universally, and an international airport plus fast ferries to Cebu. Food and beer are cheap and the pace is relaxed. The counterweight is infrastructure: brownouts are frequent and can last hours, typhoons are a genuine seasonal risk with slow recovery, fibre coverage is uneven and Starlink is often needed as backup, coworking spaces are scarce and impermanent, medical care beyond basic cases means flying to Cebu, ride-hailing is unreliable so a scooter is mandatory, road quality varies, Alona has become noisy and overbuilt, and the nomad community is small and seasonal.
bohol.whoFor: Divers, freedivers and beach-focused remote workers are the fit: Philippine costs, warm water and island life, with an airport and a hospital on the same island, which is not true of most of them. It works for self-sufficient solo nomads and couples with redundant connectivity, for anyone comfortable riding a scooter daily, and for long-stay travellers using the generous tourist extension system to spend months in the region. It also fits people who value nature, the Chocolate Hills, river trips and empty inland roads, over urban amenities. Skip it if the work cannot tolerate power cuts or a typhoon-season outage, if a structured coworking and meetup scene is what makes a base productive, or if consistent city infrastructure, public transport and healthcare matter. Those wanting the same country with more urban reliability should compare Cebu City; those wanting a larger nomad crowd should compare Siargao or Manila.

havana.costOfLiving: Havana at $800 a month is achievable but the cost structure is unlike anywhere else, and much of it depends on the informal exchange rate rather than the official one. A furnished casa particular room or small apartment on a monthly arrangement in Vedado or Centro Habana runs $250 to $500, with Habana Vieja and Miramar higher. Food is the volatile line: state shops are frequently empty, so groceries come from private markets and hard-currency stores at $150 to $300, while a paladar dinner is $8 to $20 and a peso street pizza under $1. ETECSA is the only mobile operator; a tourist data package with a few gigabytes costs $10 to $35 and is the single biggest working expense. Formal coworking barely exists, so budget $0 to $60 for hotel lobby access. Utilities in a rental usually bundle in at $30 to $80. Transport is $30 to $60. Value verdict: cheap headline, expensive friction.
havana.whereToWork: Havana is the hardest working environment on this list, and expectations should be set accordingly. Vedado is the practical base: leafy, mid-century, close to the Malecón, the university and most of the reliable wifi points. Centro Habana is cheaper and more chaotic; Habana Vieja is beautiful but touristed and noisy; Miramar holds the diplomatic and business infrastructure and the most stable connections. There is essentially no coworking sector. The workable options are hotel lobbies and bars, with the Habana Libre, the Nacional and the larger Miramar hotels offering the steadiest signal, plus ETECSA wifi parks and cafes in Vedado. Mobile data on ETECSA is the main lifeline but speeds are typically a few Mbps, congested in the evening, and video calls often fail outright. Nationwide blackouts and rolling power cuts of several hours are routine, so a power bank and offline-first workflow are essential. Occasional national internet restrictions during unrest are a real risk.
havana.gettingAround: Havana has no metro and no functioning ride-hailing apps in the Western sense; Uber does not operate. The dominant private option is the colectivo, a shared fixed-route almendrón running along arteries such as Línea and Neptuno, costing roughly $0.40 to $1 per person in local pesos. Private taxis negotiate a flat fare: expect $5 to $15 for a crosstown trip, more if you look like a tourist and do not agree the price first. State buses, the guaguas, cost pennies but are overcrowded and unreliable. A local app called La Nave functions in parts of the city but coverage and payment are inconsistent. Vedado, Centro Habana and Habana Vieja are highly walkable and best explored on foot, with broken pavements the main hazard. José Martí airport is 20 km south: a taxi is $25 to $35, fixed by convention. No car needed; renting one is expensive and fuel shortages are chronic. A small ferry crosses the harbour to Regla and Casablanca for a few pesos and is the cheapest way onto the water, running all day from a pier beside the old town. Fuel shortages thin every other service without warning, so a plan that depends on a bus is a plan with a hole in it.
havana.visas: Cuba does not issue a digital nomad visa and there is no remote-work route. Nearly all Western visitors enter on a tourist card, the tarjeta del turista, which is a paper visa bought from an airline, a Cuban consulate or an authorised agency for roughly $25 to $110 depending on source. It grants 30 days for most nationalities and 90 days for Canadians, and can be extended once in country for an equal period at an immigration office, giving a practical maximum of 60 days for most Europeans and 180 for Canadians. Travel medical insurance is mandatory and checked. US citizens face additional constraints: travel must fall under one of the authorised OFAC categories, ordinary tourism is not one of them, and travel to Cuba disqualifies a traveller from later using ESTA visa-waiver entry to the United States, a rule that also applies to Europeans who have visited Cuba since 2021. Working remotely on a tourist card is not formally sanctioned.
havana.bestTime: Havana is tropical and warm all year, with a clear dry and wet split. The dry season, November through April, is the best window: highs of 26C to 29C, lower humidity, sea breezes along the Malecón, and the least rain. December to March is the peak and books out. May through October is hot, humid and wet, with July and August reaching 32C or more and feeling considerably worse in buildings without air conditioning, especially during power cuts. Hurricane season officially runs June to November, with the real risk concentrated in September and October; Cuba is directly in the Atlantic track and major storms cause extended outages and damage. Key dates include the Havana Jazz Festival in January, the Havana Biennial in spring on its irregular cycle, the International Film Festival in December, and Carnaval de La Habana in August. Book anything around Christmas and new year far ahead. Cold fronts in the winter months push the sea straight over the seawall and close the road behind it, which happens several times each season and soaks anything parked along it. Residents watch for it, and the spray reaching the buildings opposite is the standard photograph of this city in January.
havana.prosCons: The appeal is genuine and almost entirely non-practical. Havana is one of the most visually and culturally extraordinary cities in the Americas: mid-century Vedado, crumbling Habana Vieja, live son and jazz most nights, and street life untouched by chains. Accommodation and food can be cheap, violent crime is minimal, and casa particular hosts provide local access hotels never match. The drawbacks are severe and disqualifying for most remote workers. Internet is slow, expensive, ETECSA-monopolised and prone to national outages during unrest; video calls frequently fail. Blackouts of four to twelve hours are routine, not exceptional. Shortages of food, medicine, fuel and cash are chronic, ATMs often fail, and US-issued cards do not work at all, so hard currency must be carried in. Bureaucracy is opaque, the dual exchange rate confuses constantly, heat without air conditioning punishes half the year, and no nomad community exists.
havana.whoFor: This is a place for travellers first and remote workers a distant second. It fits writers, photographers, musicians, researchers and anyone whose work is asynchronous, offline-tolerant and unbothered by a week without a stable connection. It rewards people with genuine curiosity about Cuban history, music and politics, patience for improvisation, and a willingness to carry cash, plan around blackouts and accept that nothing runs on schedule. Spanish is close to essential. Stays of a few weeks between projects work far better than a base. It is emphatically wrong for anyone doing client calls, live collaboration, trading, streaming, or any job that assumes reliable bandwidth and power. Skip it if a stable coworking routine, card payments, food variety, air conditioning or a nomad social scene matter, and skip it entirely if a US ESTA or frequent US travel is part of the plan, since a Cuba stamp forfeits visa-waiver eligibility.

brasilia.costOfLiving: Brasília runs about $1,100 a month for a single nomad, a figure inflated by government-city rents and deflated by cheap food and fuel. A furnished one-bedroom in Asa Sul, Asa Norte or Sudoeste costs $400 to $700 monthly; the Águas Claras and Taguatinga satellite areas drop to $250 to $400 but add commuting. Groceries run $200 to $300, and the prato feito or per-kilo lunch, a Brasília institution, costs $5 to $9. A Vivo, Claro or TIM prepaid SIM with a solid data allowance is $8 to $15. Coworking hot desks are $90 to $180, with plenty of supply thanks to the consulting and government-contractor economy. Utilities are $50 to $90, higher in the hot dry months when air conditioning runs, and fibre internet is $25 to $45. Transport is $40 to $80. Value verdict: solid value for a capital, though weaker than Brazil's cheaper northeastern cities.
brasilia.whereToWork: Base yourself in Asa Sul or Asa Norte along the residential superquadras, or in Sudoeste and Noroeste for newer, quieter stock. These give access to the commercial blocks where the cafes cluster. Coworking is plentiful because the city's economy runs on government contractors and consultancies: national chains such as WeWork have operated in the central business sectors, and local spaces populate the SCS, SCN and Asa Norte commercial areas alongside CLDF-adjacent offices. Specialty coffee has grown steadily around the Asa Norte commercial blocks and in the shopping centres, though Brasília's superblock design means cafes sit in commercial strips rather than on a walkable high street. Fibre is widely available and fast, commonly 200 to 600 Mbps, and Brazil's internet infrastructure is among the best in Latin America. The caveats are architectural: distances between blocks are large, and the city empties on weekends when politicians fly home. Federal salaries give this city the highest average income in the country by a wide margin, which explains both the restaurant prices and the fact that nothing here looks like the Brazil most visitors picture. The economy is the state, and in the recess months it moves at the pace of the state. Consultancies follow the ministries and account for most of the private sector.
brasilia.gettingAround: Brasília was designed for cars, and it shows. The Metrô-DF has two lines running from the central bus station out toward Águas Claras, Taguatinga and Samambaia, with fares around $1; it serves commuters from the satellite cities well but barely touches the residential superquadras. Buses cover the gaps at $0.60 to $1.20 but are slow. Uber and 99 both operate strongly and are the default for most residents and visitors, with typical fares of $3 to $10 across the Plano Piloto and higher out to the satellites. Distances are the real issue: crossing from Asa Norte to Asa Sul is a several-kilometre trip along highway-scale axes. Walkability is poor between sectors and pleasant only within a superquadra. Brasília International is 12 km south of the centre: Uber is $8 to $15. A car is genuinely useful here, more so than in most Brazilian cities. Addresses here are codes rather than names, a sector letter and a block number, and once the logic clicks the whole city can be navigated off a single string of characters, which is either the most rational address system anywhere or entirely alienating depending on the day you are having.
brasilia.visas: Brazil reinstated visa requirements for US, Canadian and Australian citizens in April 2025, and those nationals now need an eVisa obtained online before travel, costing around $81, valid for multiple entries over ten years with stays of up to 90 days. Citizens of the UK, the EU, New Zealand and most other Western countries continue to enter visa free for 90 days. Either way, the 90-day allowance can be extended once at a Polícia Federal office for a further 90 days, giving a maximum of 180 days within any twelve-month period, after which departure is required. Brazil does operate a genuine digital nomad visa, created in 2022, granting one year with the possibility of a one-year renewal. It requires proof of remote employment or contracts with a non-Brazilian entity plus either monthly income of at least $1,500 or available bank funds of at least $18,000, along with health insurance. Applications go through a Brazilian consulate abroad.
brasilia.bestTime: Brasília sits at about 1,100 m on the cerrado plateau, giving a savanna climate of two sharply different halves and daily highs of 26C to 30C most of the year with cool nights. The dry season, May to September, is the best window for comfort and clear skies, with warm days, chilly mornings near 13C and virtually no rain, though humidity crashes to 15 or 20 percent in August and September, causing dry skin, nosebleeds and heavy smoke from cerrado fires. The wet season, October to March, brings dramatic afternoon thunderstorms, greener surroundings and better air, with January and February the wettest. April and May are the sweet spot: rain has eased and the air is still comfortable. There is no hurricane risk. Key dates include Carnival in February or March, though Brasília's version is muted, Independence Day on 7 September with military parades along the Esplanada, and the city's anniversary on 21 April.
brasilia.prosCons: Brasília's strengths are underrated. It is Brazil's most orderly large city, with fast fibre, plentiful coworking, high average incomes, good private healthcare and a UNESCO-listed modernist landscape: Niemeyer's Congress, Cathedral and Itamaraty are world class. Altitude makes the climate more comfortable than coastal Brazil, food is cheap and good, the airport is a national hub, and the central Plano Piloto is safer than most Brazilian metropolises. The drawbacks are structural. The city was built for cars, so walkability is poor, distances are large and street life is nearly absent outside a few commercial blocks; the spontaneous urban texture that makes Rio or Salvador compelling does not exist. Rents are high by Brazilian norms, the population skews civil servant and conservative, and the city empties at weekends. Crime rises sharply in the satellite cities. There is almost no nomad community, English is rare, and dry-season air turns harsh.
brasilia.whoFor: Brazilian value and infrastructure without the chaos, the noise and the crime of the big coastal cities is what this is, and it asks for self-sufficiency in return. It fits people with business in the capital, consultants and anyone working with government or NGOs, plus architecture and design enthusiasts who will get more from the city than casual visitors. It rewards those who will rent or hire a car, speak or want to learn Portuguese, and treat the city as a calm, well-wired base for domestic travel across a country that Brasília connects to better than anywhere else. Families and older nomads often prefer its order and space. Walkable street life, beaches, nightlife and a ready-made foreign social scene are precisely what this city was not built to provide, and that omission is deliberate rather than accidental. Skip it if car-dependence is a dealbreaker, if a lively historic centre matters, or if the appeal of Brazil is specifically coastal and spontaneous.

portoalegre.costOfLiving: Porto Alegre is one of the better value southern Brazilian capitals, and $1,000 a month covers a comfortable single-person life. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Moinhos de Vento, Bom Fim, Cidade Baixa or Petrópolis runs $300 to $600, with cheaper options further out in Menino Deus or Santana. Groceries are $180 to $280, helped by the agricultural south, and a per-kilo or executivo lunch costs $5 to $8, with a churrascaria dinner $15 to $25. A prepaid SIM from Vivo, Claro or TIM with generous data is $8 to $15. Coworking hot desks run $70 to $150, cheaper than São Paulo or Florianópolis. Utilities are $45 to $85, with the notable difference that winter here needs heating rather than cooling, and fibre internet is $25 to $45. Transport is $35 to $70. Value verdict: strong, particularly for a city with real infrastructure and a genuine university culture. The flood of 2024 changed the rental map rather than just the skyline: demand shifted uphill afterwards and prices in the higher neighbourhoods moved with it, so a bargain in a low-lying street now carries a question that did not exist before.
portoalegre.whereToWork: Moinhos de Vento is the polished base: leafy, safe by local standards, dense with specialty coffee, and walkable to the centre. Bom Fim and Cidade Baixa are the bohemian and student districts, cheaper, louder and better for nightlife, while Petrópolis and Auxiliadora suit quieter, longer stays. Coworking is well established thanks to the city's technology sector; the Tecnopuc innovation park at PUCRS and the Distrito Criativo around the Quarto Distrito anchor a startup ecosystem, with independent spaces spread across Moinhos, Independência and the centre. Specialty coffee culture is strong and laptop friendly in Moinhos de Vento and Bom Fim, though tables fill at lunch. Fibre from Vivo, Claro and regional providers commonly delivers 200 to 600 Mbps. The practical caveats are the 2024 flooding, which damaged parts of the low-lying centre and Quarto Distrito, plus street-safety vigilance downtown after dark. The valley north of the city has been the country's shoe manufacturing centre for generations and a petrochemical complex sits beyond it, which together are why the commuter line runs where it does and why this state's economy is industrial at heart rather than agricultural.
portoalegre.gettingAround: Porto Alegre has a single elevated metro line, Trensurb, running north from the Mercado Público to Canoas, Esteio, Sapucaia and São Leopoldo for roughly $1; it is a commuter link rather than an urban network. City buses are extensive and cost about $1 with a rechargeable TEU card, and a lotação minibus network runs faster semi-express routes for slightly more. Uber and 99 dominate for most trips, with typical fares of $2.50 to $8 across the central neighbourhoods, and they are the standard choice at night. The centre, Moinhos de Vento, Bom Fim and Cidade Baixa are walkable and connected, though hilly in places and unsafe downtown after dark. Salgado Filho airport sits about 7 km north and is directly served by Trensurb's Aeroporto station; an Uber is $5 to $10. A car is unnecessary in the city but useful for the Serra Gaúcha wine country. Whether the water the city sits on is a river or a lake is a genuine local argument with geographers on both sides, and either way the sunset over it is a civic ritual, with a boat that runs out each evening to watch it.
portoalegre.visas: Brazil reinstated visa requirements for US, Canadian and Australian citizens in April 2025; those nationals now apply online for an eVisa costing around $81, valid for multiple entries over ten years with stays of up to 90 days each. UK, EU, New Zealand and most other Western passport holders still enter visa free for 90 days. In both cases the 90 days can be extended once at a Polícia Federal office, including the one in Porto Alegre, for another 90 days, capping the stay at 180 days in any twelve-month window before departure is required. Brazil's digital nomad visa, introduced in 2022, offers a legitimate longer route: one year, renewable once, requiring proof of remote work for a non-Brazilian employer or clients plus monthly income of at least $1,500 or bank savings of at least $18,000, together with valid health insurance. It must be applied for at a Brazilian consulate outside the country, not converted from a tourist stamp.
portoalegre.bestTime: Porto Alegre has a humid subtropical climate with four genuine seasons, unusual for Brazil, and no dry season. Summer, December to February, is hot and humid with highs of 30C to 34C and frequent heat spikes, plus afternoon storms. Autumn, March to May, is the best window: warm days around 24C, comfortable nights and manageable rain. Winter, June to August, is cool and grey, with highs of 18C to 20C, lows near 9C, and occasional cold snaps driven by Antarctic air; buildings are poorly insulated and rarely heated, so it feels colder indoors than the numbers suggest. Spring, September to November, is pleasant but windy and wet. Rain falls year round at roughly 100 to 140 mm a month, and the catastrophic floods of May 2024 demonstrated the Guaíba basin's vulnerability. Key dates include Carnival in February, the Semana Farroupilha gaúcho festival in September, and the Feira do Livro in the centre each November.
portoalegre.prosCons: Porto Alegre offers a distinctly un-tropical Brazil that suits some people far better than the beach cities. It is affordable, with a strong food culture built on churrasco and Italian and German immigrant traditions, a serious specialty coffee scene, and an easy chimarrão-drinking social life. Fibre is fast, the technology sector around Tecnopuc gives professional depth, universities keep the city young, and the Serra Gaúcha wine country, Gramado and the Santa Catarina beaches sit within a few hours. Four real seasons appeal to anyone who finds constant heat draining. The drawbacks are not trivial. Crime leads them: robbery rates rank among the higher Brazilian capitals, the centre is unsafe after dark, and phone-snatching shapes daily habits. The May 2024 floods inundated large parts of the city and recovery is uneven. Winters are cold in unheated buildings, English is scarce, and the foreign nomad community is tiny.
portoalegre.whoFor: This is a working Brazilian city and not a nomad hub, which suits people who speak or will learn Portuguese and who prefer four seasons, wine country and a strong food culture to beaches and heat. It fits developers and technology workers who value the Tecnopuc ecosystem and cheap fast fibre, budget-conscious remote workers who want a capital city at small-city prices, and anyone using it as a base for southern Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina, both a short trip away. Students, academics and people who thrive on university-town energy do well in Bom Fim and Cidade Baixa. It is wrong for anyone who wants tropical weather, a ready-made expat social circle, or English-language convenience. Skip it if street-crime vigilance is exhausting rather than manageable, if cold unheated winters are a dealbreaker, or if flood risk in the low-lying districts is a concern worth avoiding.

manaus.costOfLiving: Manaus runs close to $900 a month for a single nomad, though isolation inflates certain lines. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Adrianópolis, Nossa Senhora das Graças or Ponta Negra costs $300 to $550; Centro is cheaper at $200 to $350 but noisier and less safe. Groceries are the weak spot: almost everything arrives by river barge or air, so a supermarket run costs $220 to $330, above the Brazilian norm, while river fish, açaí and tropical fruit at the Mercado Adolpho Lisboa are cheap. A prato feito lunch is $5 to $8. A Vivo, Claro or TIM prepaid SIM with generous data is $8 to $15. Coworking hot desks run $80 to $160. Utilities hit $70 to $130 because air conditioning runs constantly, and fibre internet is $25 to $50. Transport is $35 to $70. Value verdict: reasonable, but the humidity tax on electricity is unavoidable. The free trade zone works in a visitor's favour on exactly one line of the budget: electronics and appliances are cheaper here than they are anywhere south of the river, which is why people fly up to buy them. Everything else that arrives by barge costs more.
manaus.whereToWork: Adrianópolis is the practical base: central, relatively safe, full of restaurants, gyms and serviced apartments, and close to the Ponta Negra corridor. Ponta Negra itself sits on the Rio Negro waterfront and offers newer towers, a promenade and beach-adjacent evenings, at the cost of a longer trip into town. Centro holds the Teatro Amazonas, the Mercado Adolpho Lisboa and the historic port architecture, and is worth visiting daily but rarely worth living in. Coworking exists but is thin compared with southern Brazil; spaces cluster around Adrianópolis and the Vieiralves district, supported by the professional class working in the Manaus Free Trade Zone, the tax-incentive industrial park that anchors the local economy. Fibre commonly delivers 100 to 400 Mbps and is more reliable than the city's isolation suggests. The caveats are heat, near-constant 80 percent humidity, aggressive air conditioning indoors and frequent afternoon storm outages. The national institute for Amazon research has been based here since the nineteen fifties, which makes the city a genuine centre for tropical biology and puts a scientific population alongside the industrial one. Researchers and the visitors they bring are a large share of the foreigners you will meet. Portuguese carries both of those worlds, and arriving without it closes off most of the conversation.
manaus.gettingAround: Manaus has no metro and no rail. City buses cover the sprawl for roughly $1 with a rechargeable card, but routes are slow, crowded and hard to parse without Portuguese. Uber and 99 both operate well and are the default for visitors, with typical fares of $2.50 to $8 within the central and Ponta Negra areas. Traffic on Avenida Djalma Batista and Avenida Torquato Tapajós clogs badly at peak. Walkability is limited to Centro and the Ponta Negra promenade; the heat alone discourages long walks. The defining fact is that Manaus is unreachable by road from the rest of Brazil: there is no highway link south across the Amazon, so arrival is by air or by multi-day riverboat from Belém, Santarém or Tabatinga. Eduardo Gomes International sits about 14 km north, with Uber at $6 to $12. A car is unnecessary but useful for the Ponta Negra commute.
manaus.visas: Brazil reinstated visa requirements for US, Canadian and Australian citizens in April 2025; those nationals must obtain an eVisa online before travel, costing around $81, valid for multiple entries over ten years with stays of up to 90 days. UK, EU, New Zealand and most other Western passport holders still enter visa free for 90 days. In both cases the stay can be extended once at a Polícia Federal office, including the one in Manaus, for a further 90 days, capping the total at 180 days within any twelve-month period before departure is required. Brazil's digital nomad visa, introduced in 2022, grants one year renewable for a second, and requires proof of remote work for a non-Brazilian employer or clients plus monthly income of at least $1,500 or bank savings of at least $18,000, together with valid health insurance. It must be applied for at a Brazilian consulate abroad rather than converted in country.
manaus.bestTime: Manaus is equatorial: highs of 31C to 34C every month, lows around 24C, and humidity that rarely drops below 75 percent. The variation is rainfall, not temperature. The drier season runs June to October and is the best window, with September and October the least wet and the easiest for jungle excursions, though river levels fall and some igarapé routes become impassable. The wet season runs December to May, peaking in March and April, when daily downpours are heavy and prolonged. Peak river levels arrive in June, which is the classic time to see the Meeting of the Waters and to reach flooded forest by boat. There is no hurricane or cyclone risk this close to the equator. Key dates include the Boi Bumbá festival at nearby Parintins in late June, one of Brazil's largest folk celebrations, the opera and classical season at the Teatro Amazonas in April and May, and Carnival in February.
manaus.prosCons: Manaus is unlike anywhere else in Brazil. The Teatro Amazonas, a belle époque opera house built on rubber money and still hosting a genuine festival season, anchors a Centro of extraordinary faded grandeur. The Amazon itself is the draw: jungle lodges, the Meeting of the Waters, river trips and wildlife are all within reach of a working week. Costs are moderate, fibre is faster than expected, the Free Trade Zone gives the city a real professional middle class, and the river-fish and tambaqui food culture is distinctive. The drawbacks are heavy. Humidity and heat are relentless year round with no relief season, and air conditioning becomes a dependency and an expense. The city is isolated, reachable only by air or multi-day boat, so flights are expensive and regional travel is not casual. Crime is a genuine concern in Centro, the port area and outer zones after dark. Almost no English is spoken and the foreign nomad community is negligible.
manaus.whoFor: A real interest in the Amazon is the entry requirement, and what you get is a base rather than a nomad hub, and who will use weekends for river trips, lodges and wildlife rather than city nightlife. It fits biologists, photographers, journalists and researchers whose subject matter is the rainforest, plus anyone working with the Free Trade Zone's industrial and logistics sector. Portuguese is close to essential; the city rewards people who speak it and frustrates those who do not. Nomads who tolerate constant heat well, and who value a genuinely unusual place over comfort and convenience, get the most from it. It is wrong for anyone who wants a walkable temperate city, a social scene of foreigners, cheap onward travel or a break from humidity. Skip it if heat and 80 percent humidity sap productivity, if crime vigilance is draining, or if isolation from the rest of Brazil is a dealbreaker.

monterrey.costOfLiving: A single nomad lands near $1,200 a month in Monterrey, which buys a comfortable rather than bare existence. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in San Pedro Garza Garcia runs $650 to $950, while equivalent space in Colonia Del Valle Oriente, Contry or the streets around Barrio Antiguo sits closer to $450 to $700. Groceries for one come to $180 to $260, and eating out is cheap outside San Pedro: taqueria plates cost $3 to $5, a proper cabrito dinner $15 to $25. A Telcel or AT&T Mexico prepaid SIM with generous data costs $10 to $18 a month. Coworking hot desks at the main business-district operators run $110 to $180. Utilities including electricity, water and fibre total $50 to $110, with summer air conditioning pushing the top of that range hard. Transport, mostly Uber and Metro, adds $60 to $110. The value verdict: strong, provided rent is not paid in San Pedro dollars.
monterrey.whereToWork: Monterrey is a business city first, so infrastructure is genuinely good. Fibre in apartments commonly delivers 200 to 500 Mbps, and coworking spaces advertise similar. The obvious bases are San Pedro Garza Garcia, polished, safe and expensive, with Valle Oriente offering towers, malls and serviced offices; Colonia Del Valle for a slightly cheaper version of the same; and Centro or Barrio Antiguo for character, walkable streets and lower rents at the cost of more noise. WeWork operates in the Valle Oriente towers, and a cluster of independent operators sits along Avenida Vasconcelos and Calzada del Valle. Specialty coffee is a real scene: Cafe Iberico, Rojo Cafe and the third-wave roasters around San Pedro and Centro serve as informal offices. Caveats matter: many Mexican specialty cafes tolerate laptops on weekday mornings but discourage them at weekend brunch, sockets are scarce, and traffic noise on the avenues is constant. Several of the largest industrial groups in the country are headquartered here rather than in the capital, and the private university they founded is the most selective in the country, which between them explain why the business culture reads more like Texas than like the rest of Mexico.
monterrey.gettingAround: Monterrey has a real metro, unusual for a Mexican city of its size. Metrorrey runs three lines with a flat fare around $0.30, useful for the Centro to north axis but weak for San Pedro, which the network barely serves. Ecovia and Transmetro buses fill gaps for similar money. In practice most nomads live on Uber and DiDi, which are cheap and reliable: a typical cross-city ride costs $4 to $9, Centro to San Pedro about $6 to $10. Monterrey International Airport sits roughly 30 to 45 minutes northeast of the centre, and a ride-hail there runs $15 to $25. Walkability is patchy. San Pedro and Centro have pleasant walkable pockets, but the wider metropolitan area is highway-scaled, sidewalks vanish, and summer heat discourages long walks. A car is not mandatory given cheap ride-hailing, but anyone based outside the Centro-San Pedro corridor will want one. The border is two hours north, which makes a day on the other side an ordinary errand rather than a trip and is why so much of the shopping and so many of the flights go that way. Buses to the crossing run more or less constantly.
monterrey.visas: Mexico admits most nationalities, including citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the European Union and Japan, visa-free as tourists. The critical detail as of 2026 is that the old automatic 180 days no longer applies: immigration officers set the permitted stay individually at the border, and durations of 30, 60 or 90 days are now common, with up to 180 days at officer discretion. Stating a clear plan, showing onward travel and proof of funds improves the outcome. The tourist entry does not permit working for a Mexican employer, though remote work for a foreign company on foreign income is widely tolerated in practice. Mexico has no dedicated digital nomad visa. For stays beyond six months, the standard route is a Temporary Resident visa applied for at a Mexican consulate abroad, granted on proof of income or savings, valid one year and renewable up to four.
monterrey.bestTime: Monterrey sits in a mountain bowl that traps heat, and the climate is the single biggest constraint. From late May through mid-September daytime highs routinely reach 95F to 105F, with humidity, and outdoor life largely stops. The best window runs from late October through April: October to November brings warm, dry days in the 75F to 85F range, December to February is mild and pleasant with occasional cold northers dropping temperatures sharply for a day or two, and March to April is close to ideal before the heat builds. Rain is concentrated between June and September, when remnants of Gulf tropical systems can deliver serious flooding; Monterrey has a history of destructive storm flooding down the Santa Catarina riverbed. Worth planning around: the Festival Santa Lucia in September, Fiestas de Guadalupe in December, and Semana Santa in spring, when the city partly empties for the coast. The reservoirs serving the city ran effectively dry in 2022 and the taps were rationed to a few hours a day for months, which is a recent enough memory that every dry winter now gets watched closely. Water rather than heat is the constraint people here actually worry about.
monterrey.prosCons: The strengths are concrete. Monterrey is Mexico's industrial and financial capital, so internet, banking, healthcare and international flights are all better than the tourist-city average, and English is widely spoken in business circles. Costs stay low relative to the quality of infrastructure, the food scene is distinctive, and the Sierra Madre puts serious hiking, climbing and canyon country within an hour, with Chipinque and Huasteca Park nearly in the city. Nightlife is real and unpretentious. The summer heat is brutal and long, and the air quality is among the worst in Mexico, with the mountain bowl trapping industrial and vehicle pollution to unhealthy levels for weeks in winter. The city is sprawling and car-scaled, walkability outside a few pockets is poor, and the nomad community is thin compared with Mexico City or Playa del Carmen. Security is better than its reputation but uneven by neighbourhood, and San Pedro rents approach US levels.
monterrey.whoFor: People come here with a business or industrial reason to be in Mexico: consultants serving manufacturing and logistics clients, engineers, anyone working with nearshoring supply chains, or people who want a Latin American base with dependable infrastructure and a short flight to Texas. It rewards outdoor types, since world-class hiking and climbing begin at the city edge, and it works well for those who prefer a functional real city over a nomad enclave. A ready-made coworking scene, cafe-hopping walkability and beaches are all better found elsewhere, and Mexico City, Oaxaca and the Caribbean coast each do one of them far better than this city manages any of the three. Skip it if heat sensitivity or asthma is an issue, since summer temperatures and winter smog are both genuinely punishing. Also skip it if the intention is to live entirely without a car in an outer neighbourhood.

houston.costOfLiving: Budgeting $2,400 a month works for a single nomad in Houston, which by American standards is decent value for a city of this size. A furnished one-bedroom on a short monthly lease in Montrose, Midtown or the Museum District runs $1,300 to $1,900; unfurnished annual leases go far lower, around $1,100 to $1,500, but rarely suit short stays. Groceries for one cost $350 to $480, and Houston's restaurant scene means eating out well is possible from $12 to $20 a meal. A prepaid SIM with unlimited data on Mint, Visible or T-Mobile costs $25 to $45. Coworking hot desks run $180 to $350 a month, with dedicated desks higher. Utilities are the local trap: electricity for summer air conditioning can hit $150 to $220 in August, with $120 to $180 typical once internet is included. Transport, meaning a car with insurance, fuel and parking, realistically adds $400 to $650. Value verdict: cheap housing, expensive to move around.
houston.whereToWork: Base yourself inside the 610 Loop or the working week becomes commuting. Montrose is the default nomad choice: walkable by Houston standards, dense with independent cafes and bars, and central to everything. The Heights offers a quieter, prettier version; Midtown and EaDo trade charm for proximity to downtown and the rail line. Internet is strong, with Xfinity and AT&T Fiber delivering 300 Mbps to 1 Gbps in most inner-loop apartments and coworking spaces matching that. Coworking options include WeWork and Common Desk locations downtown and in the Heights, plus The Cannon on the west side for a startup-heavy crowd and Impact Hub Houston. Cafes that reliably accommodate laptops include Agora in Montrose, Blacksmith and the Boomtown Coffee locations, and the Siphon Coffee crowd in Montrose. Caveats: peak-hour seating disappears, some independents cut wifi at weekends, and parking at popular cafes is genuinely difficult. The medical centre south of downtown is the largest concentration of hospitals and research institutes anywhere in the world, employing more people than the energy industry does, and the space agency's mission control sits half an hour southeast. Neither is what the city's reputation leads with, and both hire internationally.
houston.gettingAround: Be honest about this: a car is close to mandatory in Houston. The METRORail Red Line usefully links downtown, Midtown, the Museum District, the Texas Medical Center and NRG Stadium, with the Green and Purple lines serving the east side; a fare is $1.25 and a day pass $3. The bus network was redesigned into a frequent grid and is better than its reputation, but the city covers over 600 square miles and most destinations sit off any transit spine. Uber and Lyft are ubiquitous: a typical inner-loop trip costs $12 to $22, and rides to George Bush Intercontinental, roughly 35 to 50 minutes north, run $45 to $70. Hobby Airport is closer and cheaper, around $30 to $45. Walkability is poor outside Montrose, the Heights and downtown, sidewalks are inconsistent, and summer humidity makes even short walks unpleasant. Cycling exists on the bayou greenway trails but is not a practical commute for most.
houston.visas: The United States has no digital nomad visa, and as of 2026 no such category is under active legislation. Citizens of Visa Waiver Program countries, including most of Western Europe, the United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, Australia and Chile, may enter for up to 90 days with an approved ESTA, which now costs $40 and must be obtained before travel. The 90 days cannot be extended and time is not reset by short trips to Mexico, Canada or the Caribbean. Everyone else needs a B-1 or B-2 visitor visa, typically granted for up to six months per entry, with consular interview waits that in some countries still run many months. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a tourist entry occupies a genuine grey area: it is not explicitly authorized, and the deciding factor is whether income sources are foreign and no US labor market participation occurs. Officers hold discretion, and admission is never guaranteed.
houston.bestTime: Houston's climate is defined by heat and humidity rather than cold. The comfortable window runs from late October through April. November and March are close to perfect, with highs from 68F to 78F, low humidity and blue skies; December through February is mild, generally 55F to 68F, with rare short freezes that occasionally cause real disruption given the fragile Texas grid. April brings warmth and thunderstorms. From June through September the city is hot and saturated, with highs near 95F, dewpoints in the 70s and heat indices well past 105F, so life moves indoors entirely. Atlantic hurricane season runs June through November, peaking in August and September, and Houston floods badly: Harvey in 2017 remains the reference point. Events worth timing around include the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo in late February and March, the Art Car Parade in April, and the Bayou City Art Festival in the autumn. Wildflowers come up along the highway verges for a few weeks in spring, planted deliberately decades ago and now a fixture that people drive out of town to photograph. It is the one thing in this climate everybody agrees is worth waiting for. Mosquitoes arrive with the first warm rain and stay until the first cold front.
houston.prosCons: Houston's strengths are underrated. It is the most ethnically diverse large city in the United States, and the food reflects that, with Vietnamese, Nigerian, Mexican, Indian and Gulf seafood cooking all at a serious level and prices far below the coasts. Housing is cheap for a top-five US metro, Texas levies no state income tax, the Texas Medical Center is the largest medical complex in the world, the museum district and Menil Collection are excellent, and two airports give strong international connectivity. Now the drawbacks, which are substantial. Sprawl is extreme and car dependence total, so a car payment, insurance and fuel are unavoidable. Traffic on I-45 and the 610 Loop is severe. Air quality is poor, with ozone alerts common and petrochemical emissions from the ship channel a real concern. Summer is oppressive for a third of the year, flooding risk is not theoretical, the grid is unreliable in extremes, and the city is visually charmless in long stretches.
houston.whoFor: Houston fits nomads who want a large American base with low housing costs and no state income tax, particularly those with ties to energy, aerospace, medicine or international logistics, since all four industries are concentrated here. It suits people who prioritize food, cultural diversity and cheap space over scenery or walkability, and those who already own or are willing to run a car. Long-stay remote workers who want to bank savings while keeping easy flights to Latin America and Europe do well. It is a poor choice for car-free nomads, for anyone with asthma or heat intolerance, and for those who want a compact, strollable European-style city or a visible international nomad community, which Houston does not have in any concentrated form. Anyone whose priority is nature, mountains or a temperate climate should look elsewhere entirely.

tampa.costOfLiving: Tampa at $2,300 a month is workable for a single nomad but tighter than it was five years ago, since Florida rents rose sharply post-2020. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Hyde Park, Seminole Heights or downtown runs $1,400 to $2,000; heading to Ybor City or across to St Petersburg's outer neighbourhoods can shave $200 to $300. Groceries for one come to $350 to $480, and a decent restaurant meal costs $16 to $28, with Cuban sandwiches and taquerias far cheaper. A prepaid unlimited SIM costs $25 to $45. Coworking hot desks run $150 to $300 a month. Utilities including summer air conditioning, water and fibre total $130 to $200, with August electricity bills the worst of it. Transport, realistically a car with insurance, runs $400 to $650; Florida car insurance is among the most expensive in the country. Value verdict: fair rather than cheap, saved by no state income tax.
tampa.whereToWork: The best bases are Hyde Park and SoHo for walkable, expensive charm; Seminole Heights for a cheaper, creative, bungalow-lined alternative; downtown and Channelside for high-rise convenience next to the Riverwalk; and Ybor City for history and nightlife with rougher edges. St Petersburg across the bay is an equally credible base with a stronger arts scene. Internet is good: Spectrum and Frontier Fiber deliver 300 Mbps to 1 Gbps across the urban core, and coworking spaces match it. Options include Industrious and Regus in the downtown towers, plus Tampa's independent operators and the Embarc Collective startup hub near downtown for tech-oriented members. Cafes tolerant of laptops include Buddy Brew Coffee in Hyde Park, Foundation Coffee in Seminole Heights and Kahwa Coffee across the bay in St Petersburg. Caveats: seating is scarce mid-morning, some cafes cap stays at weekends, and summer thunderstorms cut short outdoor patio work most afternoons. Two of the country's major military commands are headquartered at the air base on the peninsula south of downtown, and the defence contracting and intelligence work around them is a large and largely invisible part of the local professional economy.
tampa.gettingAround: Tampa is car-dependent, though slightly less absolutely than Houston or Dallas. HART buses cover the city for $2 a ride and $4 a day, but frequencies are low and routes are slow. The TECO Line Streetcar links downtown, Channelside and Ybor City and is currently free to ride, genuinely useful within that corridor. The Cross-Bay Ferry runs seasonally between downtown Tampa and St Petersburg, around $8 to $12 each way. Uber and Lyft cover the rest: a typical urban trip costs $12 to $22, and Tampa International Airport, only 15 to 20 minutes from downtown and consistently rated one of the best US airports, runs $20 to $30. Walkability is real in Hyde Park, downtown, Ybor and central St Petersburg, and the Riverwalk is a pleasant spine, but anything beyond those pockets requires driving. Cycling is flat and possible, though driver behaviour in Florida makes it riskier than the terrain suggests. Three causeways cross the bay to the western shore and all of them back up at the same hours, which is why anybody commuting that way learns which one fails first. The long bridge over the mouth of the bay to the south is worth driving once for the view alone.
tampa.visas: The United States offers no digital nomad visa, and none is expected in 2026. Nationals of the roughly 40 Visa Waiver Program countries, which include the United Kingdom, most of the European Union, Japan, Australia, South Korea and Taiwan, can enter for up to 90 days with an approved ESTA, now $40, applied for online before departure. That 90-day limit is firm, cannot be extended, and short hops to the Bahamas, Mexico or Canada do not reset it. Applicants outside the programme need a B-1 or B-2 visitor visa, usually issued for six months per entry and often multi-year in validity, with interview waiting times varying enormously by consulate. Working remotely for a non-US employer while on a visitor entry is a grey area rather than a clear permission: what matters is that the income is foreign-sourced and no US employment or client relationship is established. Border officers retain full discretion over admission and stay length.
tampa.bestTime: Tampa's season structure is the inverse of most of the United States. The prime window runs from November through April, when highs sit between 70F and 82F, humidity drops, rain is rare and the outdoor life the region is built for actually functions. January and February are the coolest, occasionally dipping to 45F at night. March brings spring training baseball and heavy snowbird crowds, which push prices up and traffic with them. From June through September the city is hot and humid, with highs near 92F, punishing dewpoints and near-daily afternoon thunderstorms; Tampa sits in one of the most lightning-prone areas in the country. Atlantic hurricane season runs June through November, peaking mid-August to early October, and Tampa Bay's shallow shelf makes it unusually exposed to storm surge, as the 2024 season demonstrated. Gasparilla in late January is the city's signature event. Red tide is the seasonal risk the brochures leave out: an algal bloom that reaches the Gulf beaches in some years, kills fish in numbers and catches at the throat and eyes of anybody standing on the sand. It arrives and clears again without much warning.
tampa.prosCons: Tampa's appeal is straightforward: warmth in winter, water everywhere, no Florida state income tax, an excellent and easily reached airport, and Gulf beaches at Clearwater and St Pete within 40 minutes. The urban core has improved markedly, with the Riverwalk, Armature Works and Water Street adding genuine density and walkable life, and St Petersburg across the bay contributes a real arts and craft-beer culture. Costs undercut Miami substantially. The drawbacks are equally clear. Rents have climbed steeply and no longer feel like a bargain, while Florida home and car insurance costs have risen to punitive levels and are passed through in rents. Summer is oppressively hot and humid for four to five months. Hurricane and storm-surge exposure is real and rising, with evacuation zones covering much of the desirable waterfront. Outside a handful of neighbourhoods the city is sprawling, strip-mall dominated and car-dependent, transit is poor, and the culture skews retiree and transient rather than settled.
tampa.whoFor: Winter warmth in an English-speaking country with strong infrastructure is the draw, particularly for anyone escaping a northern US or European winter between November and April. It works for water-oriented people: boaters, paddlers, divers and beachgoers, and for anyone building US business presence who benefits from Florida's tax treatment and easy flights. It is a reasonable landing pad for first-time US-based remote workers because everything is familiar and functional. It is a bad fit for anyone determined to live without a car outside the small walkable core, for those sensitive to heat and humidity who would be trapped indoors all summer, and for nomads seeking a dense, culturally deep old city; Tampa is young, sprawling and pragmatic. Anyone unwilling to plan around hurricane season, insurance costs and evacuation logistics should choose a different American base.

dallas.costOfLiving: Dallas at $2,400 a month gives a single nomad a comfortable, if car-shaped, standard of living. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in Uptown, Deep Ellum or Bishop Arts runs $1,400 to $2,000, while Oak Cliff, Lower Greenville or the eastern suburbs drop that to $1,100 to $1,500. Groceries for one cost $350 to $480. Restaurants span a wide range: $10 to $15 for excellent Tex-Mex or barbecue, $25 to $40 for the Uptown scene. A prepaid unlimited SIM costs $25 to $45. Coworking hot desks run $180 to $350 a month. Utilities including air conditioning, which dominates the bill from June to September, plus water and gigabit fibre, total $130 to $210. Transport is the honest budget-breaker: a car with insurance, fuel, tolls on the North Dallas Tollway and parking realistically costs $450 to $700. Value verdict: solid space and amenities for the money, undermined by mandatory driving costs. The absence of a state income tax is the headline here, and the property taxes, which are about as steep as any state levies, are not: they fall on the owner and come through in the rent, so the saving is smaller than the comparison usually suggests.
dallas.whereToWork: Location choice determines whether Dallas is pleasant or a commuting sentence. Uptown and the Knox-Henderson corridor offer the most walkable density with cafes and restaurants at street level. Deep Ellum is the creative and music quarter, gritty and loud but central. Bishop Arts in North Oak Cliff is the prettiest low-rise option, and Lower Greenville splits the difference. Internet is excellent: AT&T Fiber and Google Fiber deliver gigabit widely, and coworking spaces run comparable speeds. Coworking includes WeWork and Industrious in the Uptown and Arts District towers, Common Desk locations across Deep Ellum and Oak Cliff, and The Dallas Entrepreneur Center for a startup crowd. Cafes that reliably accept laptops include Ascension Coffee in the Design District, Houndstooth Coffee near Knox-Henderson, Weekend Coffee and the Magnolia-adjacent independents in Oak Cliff. Practical caveats: sockets are limited, weekday afternoons are the reliable window, and paid or valet parking is common in Uptown. A steady stream of large companies has moved its headquarters here from the coasts over the last decade, chasing the tax position and the cheaper space, and the professional population that arrived with them is why the northern suburbs look the way they do. For a freelancer it means corporate clients who are themselves recent arrivals and still assembling their suppliers.
dallas.gettingAround: A car is effectively mandatory in Dallas. DART operates the largest light rail network by mileage in the United States, four lines with a $3 single ride and $6 day pass, and it usefully connects downtown, Uptown via the free M-Line trolley, Deep Ellum, Fair Park and both suburbs and Dallas Love Field via a shuttle link. The problem is that coverage is broad but thin: headways are long, stations sit in parking lots, and journeys that take 20 minutes by car take an hour by rail. The TRE commuter line links Dallas and Fort Worth. Uber and Lyft cost $12 to $25 for typical inner-city trips. DFW International Airport is 30 to 45 minutes northwest and $45 to $70 by ride-hail, though the DART Orange Line reaches Terminal A directly for the standard fare; Love Field is closer and cheaper. Walkability is confined to Uptown, Deep Ellum and Bishop Arts, and summer heat suppresses even that.
dallas.visas: There is no United States digital nomad visa, and nothing resembling one exists in 2026 policy. Visa Waiver Program nationals, covering the United Kingdom, most EU states, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Singapore and others, may enter for a maximum of 90 days with an approved ESTA costing $40, which must be secured before boarding. The 90-day allowance is not extendable, and leaving briefly for Mexico or Canada does not restart the clock. Non-VWP nationals need a B-1 business or B-2 tourist visa, commonly granted for up to six months per entry with long consular interview queues in high-demand countries. Remote work for a foreign employer during a visitor stay sits in an unresolved grey area of US immigration practice: it is generally tolerated where income is foreign-sourced, no US clients are served and no local labour market participation occurs, but it carries no formal authorization. Admission and permitted duration remain entirely at the officer's discretion.
dallas.bestTime: Dallas has four distinct but lopsided seasons. The best months are April, May, October and November, when highs sit between 72F and 85F, skies are clear and the patio culture the city runs on is comfortable. Spring is also severe-weather season: North Texas lies in the southern edge of Tornado Alley, and April through early June brings supercells, hail large enough to damage cars and occasional tornado warnings. From late June through September the heat is relentless, with highs from 95F to 105F, extended stretches above 100F and the electricity grid under visible strain; outdoor life stops between noon and dusk. Winter is mild, generally 45F to 60F, but ice storms rather than snow are the hazard, and they shut the city down when they arrive. Key events include the State Fair of Texas at Fair Park from late September through October and the spring arts festivals in the Arts District.
dallas.prosCons: Dallas offers genuine practical advantages: no state income tax, a huge and diversified job market in finance, telecom and corporate headquarters, gigabit fibre almost everywhere, an enormous restaurant scene, the largest arts district in the country, and DFW International, one of the world's best-connected airports, which makes it an excellent base for a nomad who flies often. Housing gives far more space per dollar than the coasts. The negatives are the familiar Sunbelt list, and they are serious. The metroplex is one of the most sprawling urban regions on earth, so a car is not optional and the true monthly cost of living is inflated by driving. Traffic on the interstates is heavy and the tolled highways add up. Summer heat is extreme and long, air quality suffers with regular ozone action days, and the grid's reliability in both heat and ice is a live concern. Aesthetically, much of the metroplex is highway, parking lot and chain retail.
dallas.whoFor: Dallas fits nomads who fly constantly and want to live next to a major global hub, those working with US corporate clients in finance, telecom, logistics or professional services, and anyone optimizing for disposable income given no state income tax and reasonable rents. A large, modern, comfortable American city with excellent internet and infrastructure is exactly what this is, on the single condition of being entirely at ease with driving everywhere. Long-stay remote workers seeking a stable, unglamorous, high-functioning base do well here. It is the wrong choice for car-free nomads, for anyone drawn to walkable historic urbanism, mountains, coastline or temperate summers, and for those with asthma or heat sensitivity. Nomads looking for an international backpacker or coliving community will not find one; Dallas's remote workers are largely settled Americans, and the social entry point is professional networks rather than hostels or coworking scenes.

saltlakecity.costOfLiving: Salt Lake City at $2,200 a month is manageable but no longer cheap, since demand from Californian transplants pushed rents up sharply. A furnished one-bedroom on a monthly lease in the Central City, 9th and 9th or Sugar House areas runs $1,300 to $1,800; Rose Park, Glendale or South Salt Lake bring that down to $1,000 to $1,400. Groceries for one cost $350 to $480, and restaurant meals run $15 to $28. A prepaid unlimited SIM costs $25 to $45. Coworking hot desks run $150 to $300 a month. Utilities are moderate: winter heating and summer cooling plus gigabit fibre come to $110 to $180. Transport is genuinely cheaper here than in Texas because UTA transit is usable, so $100 to $200 covers passes and occasional ride-hailing, though a ski season adds $300 to $900 in passes and gear. Value verdict: fair, and outstanding if outdoor access is the reason for coming. Spirits and stronger beer are sold only through state stores with restricted hours, and the rules on restaurant service are a subject of their own, which is a genuine adjustment rather than a quirk and shows up in what an evening out actually costs.
saltlakecity.whereToWork: The best bases are the Avenues, a hillside grid of older homes just above downtown; the 9th and 9th district for cafes and independent shops; Sugar House for a more residential, tree-lined feel with its own commercial core; and Central City or the Granary District for downtown proximity and warehouse conversions. Internet is strong: Google Fiber, Xfinity and the municipal-adjacent UTOPIA network deliver gigabit across much of the valley. Coworking includes Kiln in the downtown core, Impact Hub Salt Lake City and a set of independent operators in the Granary District, plus WeWork downtown. Cafe culture is better than outsiders expect: Publik Coffee Roasters, Three Pines Coffee downtown, Blue Copper and La Barba are all working-friendly, with Publik in particular built around long stays. Caveats: many cafes close early by nomad standards, Sunday hours are restricted across the city, and downtown seating fills fast during ski season. The largest genealogical archive in the world sits downtown and is open to anybody at no charge, which is an odd thing for a city of this size to hold and draws researchers from everywhere. The church that built it shapes the working week here more than any employer does.
saltlakecity.gettingAround: Salt Lake City is the most transit-usable city in this group. UTA runs three TRAX light rail lines and the FrontRunner commuter train up and down the Wasatch Front, with a single fare around $2.50 and a day pass about $6.25; the downtown Free Fare Zone covers the core at no charge. TRAX reaches Salt Lake City International Airport directly, roughly 20 minutes from downtown, which is unusual for a US city of this size and makes airport transfers trivial; a ride-hail costs $18 to $28. Uber and Lyft handle everything else at $10 to $20 per trip. The street grid is enormous in block size, which makes walking slower than the map suggests, but downtown, the Avenues and 9th and 9th are genuinely walkable. A car is not strictly necessary in the valley, but reaching the Cottonwood Canyons ski resorts and the national parks to the south effectively requires one, though ski buses run in winter.
saltlakecity.visas: The United States has no digital nomad visa and no proposal close to enactment as of 2026. Citizens of Visa Waiver Program countries, including the United Kingdom, most of the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand, can visit for up to 90 days on an approved ESTA costing $40, which must be obtained online before travel. That period cannot be extended, and a short trip to Canada or Mexico does not reset it. Other nationalities require a B-1 or B-2 visitor visa, typically admitted for up to six months per entry, with consular appointment waits that vary from weeks to over a year depending on the post. Remote work for a foreign employer on a visitor entry is an acknowledged grey area: it is not expressly permitted, and tolerance rests on the income being foreign-sourced with no US employer or local clients. Customs and Border Protection officers decide admission and duration case by case.
saltlakecity.bestTime: Salt Lake City has four real seasons at 4,300 feet. December through March is ski season, and the Wasatch snow that markets itself as the greatest on earth is genuinely exceptional, with Alta, Snowbird, Brighton and Solitude all within an hour. The catch is the winter inversion: cold air pools in the valley for days or weeks, trapping pollution and producing some of the worst air quality in the United States, while the mountains above sit in sun. April and May are unsettled but pleasant, and May through June is excellent for hiking as trails clear. July and August are hot and very dry, often 92F to 100F, tolerable because of low humidity but increasingly marked by wildfire smoke drifting in from the west. September and October are the finest months: warm days, cool nights, brilliant canyon foliage. Sundance Film Festival in nearby Park City in January is the marquee winter event.
saltlakecity.prosCons: Geography is most of what recommends Salt Lake City. Four world-class ski resorts sit within an hour of downtown, five national parks lie within a day's drive, and hiking, climbing and mountain biking start at the valley edge. Transit is unusually good for the American West, the airport is a Delta hub reached directly by light rail, internet is gigabit, the Silicon Slopes tech corridor provides a real professional network, and the city is compact and safe. The winter inversion is the serious health drawback here, producing weeks of hazardous air, and summer wildfire smoke increasingly does much the same at the other end of the year. The Great Salt Lake's shrinking has raised the further prospect of toxic dust from the exposed lakebed. Rents have risen quickly, the alcohol laws remain restrictive by US standards, the cultural scene is modest for the population, and the dominant local religious culture can make the social landscape feel closed to outsiders.
saltlakecity.whoFor: Salt Lake City is built for the outdoor nomad. Anyone who skis or snowboards seriously, climbs, trail runs, or wants national park access will find no better-positioned American city, and the combination of a real airport, gigabit internet and a mountain twenty minutes from a desk is rare. It suits remote tech workers who benefit from the Silicon Slopes network, and people who value a compact, orderly, transit-served city over big-city intensity. It is also a good fit for those who want American infrastructure without Texas-scale car dependence. Skip it if respiratory health is fragile, since the winter inversion and summer wildfire smoke are both genuinely hazardous. Skip it too if the priority is nightlife, a dense international food scene, or a large visible expatriate community; the alcohol regulations and comparatively homogeneous social fabric make Salt Lake City a quiet place for anyone whose life is not organized around the mountains.

abidjan.costOfLiving: A single nomad living carefully lands near $900 a month in Abidjan, though the city is expensive by West African standards and rewards anyone willing to live slightly outside the expatriate core. A furnished studio or one-bedroom in Cocody, Marcory Zone 4 or Plateau typically runs $400 to $700 a month on a monthly rental, with short-term serviced apartments pushing past $900. Groceries and a mix of maquis meals and mid-range restaurants cost $180 to $280; a plate of attieke and grilled fish at a neighbourhood maquis is under $4, while Zone 4 restaurants charge $15 upward. A local SIM from Orange, MTN or Moov with a generous data bundle costs $8 to $20 a month. Coworking desks run $80 to $150. Utilities including electricity and water average $40 to $80, with air conditioning the main variable. Transport is $40 to $90. Value is mediocre: prices resemble Southern Europe while services do not.
abidjan.whereToWork: Base yourself in Cocody, particularly around Riviera and Deux Plateaux, or in Marcory Zone 4, which holds most of the expatriate cafes, restaurants and short-term apartments. Plateau is the business district and works for anyone wanting to be near corporate offices, but it empties in the evening and is not a comfortable residential base. The coworking supply is thin but real: several small operators cluster around Deux Plateaux and Cocody Angre, and incubator-style spaces attached to the local startup and fintech scene rent hot desks by the day or month. Hotel lobbies and the cafes and bakeries of Zone 4 fill the gap for casual work. Fibre in Cocody and Plateau delivers 50 to 200 Mbps and is genuinely usable for video calls, but mobile 4G is the practical fallback and coverage is uneven. Power cuts and voltage dips are frequent enough that a laptop battery and a power bank matter.
abidjan.gettingAround: Abidjan sprawls across a lagoon and is not a walking city outside individual neighbourhoods, so plan on daily rides. Yango is the dominant ride-hailing app and is cheap: most crosstown trips cost $2 to $6, and a long run from Cocody to the airport is $8 to $15. Heetch also operates and is worth having installed as a backup. Orange metered taxis exist and can be flagged anywhere, but the fare is usually negotiated in advance rather than metered, so agree a price first. Woro-woro shared taxis and gbaka minibuses serve fixed routes for under $1 and are how most residents move, though they are crowded and hard to decode without local help. Lagoon boats between Treichville, Plateau and Abobo-Doume are a pleasant shortcut. Felix Houphouet-Boigny airport sits close to Port-Bouet, roughly 30 to 60 minutes from Cocody depending on traffic, which is severe. A private car is unnecessary. The city has been building a metro line for years now, and the works are still part of the traffic problem rather than a solution to it, though the bridges added over the lagoon in the last decade have genuinely helped.
abidjan.visas: Cote d'Ivoire runs a pre-enrolment e-visa system rather than a true visa on arrival. Most Western passport holders, including EU, UK, Canadian and Australian citizens, apply online through the official Snedai portal before flying, pay the fee, and then receive the physical visa sticker at a dedicated counter at Abidjan airport on arrival, where fingerprints and photo are taken. US citizens benefit from a separate arrangement and are generally granted longer multi-entry visas issued through the embassy. The standard tourist entry is up to 90 days, commonly issued as a shorter single-entry validity, and extensions are handled in person through the immigration directorate in Abidjan, a slow and bureaucratic process best avoided by simply applying for the longer validity upfront. There is no digital nomad visa. Yellow fever vaccination is legally required and the certificate is checked. Carry a printed e-visa confirmation and a hotel address. Identification should be on you at all times, because checks on the road and in the street are routine and a photocopy is not always accepted. A passport left behind in a hotel safe is the usual cause of an avoidable and expensive conversation.
abidjan.bestTime: Abidjan has a hot, humid equatorial climate with two rainy seasons and no cool season at all; temperatures sit between 24 and 32 Celsius year round. The best window is December to March, the long dry season, when humidity eases and rain is rare. This period also brings the harmattan, when dust blown south from the Sahara hazes the sky, dulls the light and irritates sinuses, though Abidjan sits far enough south that the effect is milder than in the Sahel. The main rains run May to July and are genuinely heavy, with June the wettest month; streets flood, traffic seizes, and outdoor plans collapse. A shorter second rainy spell arrives in October and November.
