Ramadan, falling roughly in the first quarter through the late 2020s, is observed by a substantial Muslim minority in the north and among northern communities in the city, but Abidjan itself stays largely unaffected commercially. The Abissa festival at the old colonial capital along the coast runs for a week each autumn and is a public airing of grievances as much as a carnival, which makes it one of the more interesting things on the regional calendar.
abidjan.prosCons: The appeal is genuine energy: Abidjan is the economic engine of francophone West Africa, with a real restaurant and nightlife scene, excellent grilled fish and attieke, ocean and lagoon geography, direct flights across the region and to Europe, and a growing startup and fintech community that gives a visiting remote worker something to plug into. French is universally useful and the city feels cosmopolitan rather than provincial. Costs are high for what is delivered, the traffic is brutal and eats hours, and the nomad scene is effectively nonexistent, meaning almost no one is doing what a remote worker is doing and no community infrastructure exists to meet people through at all. Petty crime and phone snatching are a real concern after dark, especially in Adjame, Abobo and Treichville. Power cuts interrupt work, humidity is oppressive year round, air quality suffers during harmattan, and almost nothing outside expat zones runs in English.
abidjan.whoFor: Everybody who comes here has an actual reason to be in West Africa: someone working on African market entry, development or logistics, a francophone speaker who wants a large, functioning city rather than a beach town, or a traveller building a longer regional loop through Ghana, Senegal and Benin who wants a comfortable base with reliable flights. Anyone who values a lively restaurant and music scene over cheap living will find it rewarding. A first-time nomad, or anyone arriving without functional French, will find this hard going, and there is no ready-made community to fall back on: turning up with no contacts reliably produces a lonely first month. Skip it if the budget is tight, since $900 buys far more in Southeast Asia or Latin America, if reliable uninterrupted power is non-negotiable, or if walkability and calm are what the work day requires.

mombasa.costOfLiving: Around $800 a month is a realistic figure for a single nomad in Mombasa who rents monthly rather than nightly. A furnished one-bedroom in Nyali, Bamburi or on the Diani strip south of the ferry costs $300 to $550 a month on a longer lease, with beachfront apartments and serviced units running $600 to $900. Food is the strong point: $150 to $250 covers groceries plus regular eating out, with a plate of pilau or biryani at a local place under $3 and a beachfront dinner around $12 to $20. A Safaricom SIM with a large monthly data bundle costs $10 to $20, and Safaricom coverage is the single best utility in the country. Coworking desks run $70 to $130. Electricity and water land at $30 to $70, higher with constant air conditioning. Transport is $40 to $80. Overall value is strong, especially for the coastline and food on offer.
mombasa.whereToWork: Nyali is the practical base: a leafy suburb north of Mombasa Island with malls, supermarkets, apartment blocks and the majority of what passes for a coworking supply. Bamburi and Shanzu extend the same idea further north with more beach. Diani Beach, south across the Likoni ferry, is the more appealing lifestyle choice and has quietly become the coast's remote-work centre, with beachfront cafes, villa rentals and Kenya's small but visible coastal nomad crowd. Swahilipot Hub near the Old Town serves the local creative and tech community and is worth visiting. Old Town and Mombasa Island itself are atmospheric but hot, congested and not where anyone rents a desk. Fibre from Safaricom or Zuku in Nyali and Diani delivers 20 to 100 Mbps reliably, and Safaricom 4G is a strong backup almost everywhere. Power cuts happen regularly; check that any rental or cafe has an inverter or generator before committing. The port here is the sea gate for half a dozen landlocked countries inland, and the freight moving up the corridor towards Uganda and beyond is what the city actually does for a living. Tourism is the visible half and the smaller one, which is why the town keeps working when the beaches empty out.
mombasa.gettingAround: Bolt and Uber both operate in Mombasa and are the default for anyone working remotely, with typical rides costing $2 to $5 and a longer run from Nyali to the airport around $8 to $12. Little is a useful local alternative. Tuk-tuks are everywhere and cost $1 to $3 for short hops once a price is agreed, and boda-boda motorcycle taxis are cheapest but carry meaningful accident risk. Matatu minibuses serve fixed routes for well under $1. Moi International Airport sits on the western side of the island, roughly 30 to 45 minutes from Nyali in traffic. The SGR train to Nairobi leaves from Miritini and takes about six hours, a genuinely good alternative to flying. The Likoni ferry to the south coast and Diani is free for foot passengers, chaotic at rush hour, and the main friction of living south. Walkability is poor outside Old Town and beach strips; no car is needed.
mombasa.visas: Kenya abolished its traditional visa in January 2024 and now requires every visitor, including citizens of visa-exempt-sounding countries, to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival. The ETA is applied for online, costs roughly $30 to $35 plus processing, and is normally approved within a few days, so apply at least a week out. It grants a single entry with a stay of up to 90 days, and the immigration officer at the airport sets the actual period stamped, which can be shorter than requested. Extensions of a further 90 days are possible through the immigration eCitizen portal or the immigration office in Mombasa, giving a practical six-month ceiling. There is no Kenyan digital nomad visa despite persistent rumours and repeated announcements; do not plan around one. The East Africa Tourist Visa covering Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda still exists and remains useful for a regional loop. Yellow fever proof is required when arriving from an endemic country.
mombasa.bestTime: Mombasa is hot and humid all year, typically 26 to 33 Celsius, with the seasons defined by monsoon winds rather than temperature. The best stretch is December to March, when the northeast kaskazi wind brings clear skies, calm warm sea and the best diving and snorkelling visibility; this is also the peak tourist window with the highest prices, especially around Christmas and New Year. The long rains arrive in April and May and are the worst period by a wide margin: heavy downpours, high humidity, rough seas, and many coastal hotels and restaurants closing outright. June through September is cooler and breezier under the southeast kusi monsoon, drier than April, with more seaweed on the beaches but comfortable working weather and lower prices. Short rains fall in November. Ramadan matters on this coast, since Mombasa is heavily Muslim: daytime eating options thin out noticeably, and Eid brings several very lively days. The domestic holiday weeks fill the beach hotels with Kenyan families and set the rates more than any foreign season does, and they do not line up neatly with the best weather, so the busiest fortnight of the year is not always the most pleasant one to be here. Booking around them saves a good deal.
mombasa.prosCons: The strengths are obvious: Indian Ocean beaches, Swahili food that ranks among the best on the continent, Old Town's coral-stone architecture and centuries of trading history, Safaricom's excellent mobile network, M-Pesa making payments frictionless in a way most countries cannot match, and a low cost of living against a genuinely attractive lifestyle. Diani in particular has a small, real remote-work community. The drawbacks are equally clear: humidity is relentless and saps concentration, power cuts interrupt work weeks, and fixed-line internet quality varies sharply by building. Petty theft, phone snatching and scams targeting foreigners are common, walking alone on beaches after dark is inadvisable, and terrorism advisories still apply near the Somali border further north. The Likoni ferry is a daily bottleneck, traffic on the island is severe, malaria is present year round, and the professional nomad scene remains small enough that networking is largely accidental.
mombasa.whoFor: Mombasa and its coastline suit the nomad who wants ocean living on a modest budget and can work asynchronously without needing a dense professional community. It fits divers, surfers and kitesurfers, food-obsessed travellers, anyone combining remote work with safari and East African travel, and Europe-facing workers who benefit from the convenient UTC+3 timezone. Diani specifically works for those who want a small, sociable, low-key expat and nomad crowd rather than a city. Humidity here defeats people who do not do well in it, guaranteed power and fibre for live calls are not something the city can promise, and urban culture, nightlife variety and a peer network of any size are all thin on the ground. Nairobi is the better Kenyan choice for anyone whose priority is business connections, startup ecosystem access or a cooler climate. Solo travellers uneasy about petty crime and constant price negotiation should also think twice.

agadir.costOfLiving: Agadir runs comfortably at $900 a month for one person and can be done for less outside high season. A furnished one-bedroom apartment in the city centre, Talborjt or the Founty and Marina districts costs $350 to $600 monthly on a longer lease, with beachfront and marina units at the top of that range and long winter bookings negotiable. Groceries plus regular eating out cost $180 to $280: a tagine or grilled fish lunch at a local place is $4 to $7, souk produce is cheap, and a marina restaurant dinner is $15 to $25. A Maroc Telecom, Orange or Inwi SIM with a big data bundle costs $10 to $20. Coworking runs $80 to $150 a month. Utilities are $40 to $80, with winter heating rarely needed. Transport is $30 to $60. Value is good, and Agadir undercuts Essaouira, Marrakech and the Canary Islands for a beach base. An earthquake levelled the town in 1960 and killed a third of its people, and everything standing here was built after that, which is why the housing stock is modern, low and unromantic, and why rents run below the old imperial cities. The trade-off is that almost nothing here is older than living memory.
agadir.whereToWork: Agadir is not Morocco's coworking capital, so expectations should be calibrated: Marrakech, Casablanca and Taghazout have deeper supply. Within the city, base yourself in Founty near the beach for calm modern apartments, in the centre near Boulevard Hassan II for convenience, or at the Marina for cafes and restaurants. Talborjt is cheaper and more local. A handful of coworking spaces operate in the centre and near Founty, and Sun Desk in Taghazout, roughly 20 kilometres north, remains the anchor of the region's remote-work scene, pairing a proper coworking floor with the surf village lifestyle; many nomads simply base in Taghazout or Tamraght instead. Cafes along the beach promenade and in the marina are workable off-peak but noisy and often without power sockets. Fibre in newer buildings delivers 50 to 200 Mbps, and 4G and 5G coverage is strong. Power is stable; the real caveat is thin coworking supply and seasonal crowding. The fishing port lands more sardines than almost anywhere on earth and the processing plants behind it are the largest employer in the region, which is why the city keeps working through the months the beach empties. Agriculture on the plain inland is the other half, growing winter vegetables for European supermarkets, and the greenhouses stretch for kilometres along the road north.
agadir.gettingAround: Central Agadir is flat and walkable, with a long beach promenade linking the marina to Founty, so daily life often needs no vehicle at all. Petits taxis are orange, metered and cheap: most in-city rides cost $1 to $3, and drivers usually do run the meter, though confirming it before setting off avoids arguments. Careem operates in Morocco and Heetch has a presence in the larger cities, but coverage in Agadir is patchier than in Casablanca, so metered taxis remain the practical default. Local Alsa buses cover the city and the coast road cheaply, including a useful route north toward Taghazout for around $1. Grands taxis are shared, faster and better for intercity hops. Al Massira airport lies about 25 kilometres inland, roughly 30 minutes by taxi at $15 to $25, with a cheaper bus option. Long-distance CTM and Supratours coaches connect to Marrakech in three hours. A car helps for surf and mountain trips only.
agadir.visas: Morocco grants visa-free entry of up to 90 days to citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, with no application, no fee and no pre-registration required; a passport valid for the stay and an onward or return ticket are the practical requirements. The 90 days is per entry rather than a rolling allowance, which is why many long-stayers do a short exit to Spain, the Canary Islands or Portugal and re-enter for another 90 days, a routine that generally works but is at immigration's discretion and can attract questions if repeated often. Formal extensions inside Morocco are possible through the local police prefecture but are slow, poorly documented and frequently refused, so most people fly out instead. There is no Moroccan digital nomad visa. Anyone intending to stay beyond 90 days legitimately needs a residence permit, the carte de sejour, which requires local sponsorship, proof of income and considerable paperwork.
agadir.bestTime: Agadir claims roughly 300 sunny days a year and the climate is the main selling point: mild, dry and stable. Winter, from November to March, is the standout window, with daytime highs of 20 to 23 Celsius, cool nights around 10, and only occasional rain; this is when European long-stayers arrive and when apartment demand peaks. Spring, March to May, is close to ideal, with warm days and green hinterland. Summer runs June to September at 26 to 30 Celsius on the coast, tempered by Atlantic breeze and cool sea, making it far more bearable than Marrakech, which regularly exceeds 40; the exception is a chergui, a hot desert wind that briefly pushes temperatures into the high thirties. The Atlantic stays cold year round, around 17 to 21 Celsius. Ramadan, in the first months of the year through the late 2020s, quiets daytime cafes and shifts restaurant hours, though tourist areas adapt.
agadir.prosCons: Agadir offers a rare combination: reliable winter sun, a long sandy beach, a modern grid-planned city rebuilt after the 1960 earthquake, low prices, good fibre, two-to-four hour flights to most of Western Europe and a timezone aligned with London and only an hour off central Europe. Surf breaks at Taghazout and Tamraght sit half an hour away, the Anti-Atlas and Paradise Valley are close, and the city is calmer, cleaner and far less hassle-prone than Marrakech. The trade-offs start with character: Agadir is functional rather than beautiful, with little historic fabric and a package-tourism feel along the beachfront. The nomad community is small and concentrated in Taghazout rather than the city. Coworking options are limited, alcohol is restricted to hotels and licensed venues, the ocean is cold and often rough, French or Arabic is needed away from tourist zones, and administrative processes are opaque and slow.
agadir.whoFor: Agadir fits the European remote worker escaping winter who wants sun, cheap rent and a short flight home, and who values calm and routine over cultural intensity. It suits surfers using the city as a comfortable base for the Taghazout coast, budget-conscious workers who want beach living without Southeast Asian flight times, and anyone working European hours who benefits from being in the same timezone band. Families find it easy, safe and well supplied with supermarkets and apartments. It is the wrong choice for someone chasing Morocco's cultural depth, who should look at Fes, Marrakech or Essaouira, and for nomads who need a large peer network, coworking density and a busy events calendar. Anyone who wants warm swimming water, real nightlife or a walkable historic old town will find Agadir underwhelming and should treat it as a base rather than a destination.

algiers.costOfLiving: Algiers can be run near $800 a month, but the figure hinges entirely on the exchange rate used. Changing money on the parallel market, which nearly everyone does, yields substantially more dinars than the official bank rate and roughly halves the effective cost of living, so budget planning should assume cash euros or dollars exchanged locally. A furnished one-bedroom in Hydra, Sidi Yahia, Bab Ezzouar or near the centre costs $250 to $500 monthly at parallel rates, more if booked through international platforms in hard currency. Food is inexpensive: $150 to $250 covers groceries and eating out, with a plate of couscous or chorba at a local restaurant under $4. A Djezzy, Ooredoo or Mobilis SIM with data runs $8 to $15. Formal coworking is scarce; expect $60 to $120 where it exists. Utilities are $25 to $50, transport $30 to $60. Value is good, convenience is not. Import restrictions mean a good many ordinary goods are simply not on the shelves, and the ones that are carry a markup that has nothing to do with the exchange rate. Anyone attached to a particular brand of anything should bring it rather than expect to find it. Cash runs everything: cards are barely used and a foreign one will not work at all.
algiers.whereToWork: Coworking supply in Algiers is genuinely limited, with a handful of startup-oriented spaces and incubators clustered around Hydra, Sidi Yahia and the university and business zones near Bab Ezzouar; the Algiers startup ecosystem around Algeria Venture and similar public initiatives is where most desks and events sit. Beyond that, hotel lobbies, the newer cafes of Hydra and Sidi Yahia, and apartments are the working reality. Base yourself in Hydra or Sidi Yahia for the safest, best-serviced residential option, in El Biar or Ben Aknoun for quieter hillside living, or near the Bab El Oued and central Algiers waterfront for atmosphere and walkability at the cost of noise. Fixed internet has improved substantially, with Algerie Telecom fibre in central districts reaching 50 to 200 Mbps, though ADSL still lingers in older buildings and speeds are inconsistent. Nationwide internet shutdowns during school exam periods each June are a real and recurring disruption.
algiers.gettingAround: Algiers has the best public transport in the Maghreb: a clean modern metro line, several tram lines, extensive buses and cable cars climbing the steep hillsides, with fares under $0.50 a ride. The city is built on slopes above the bay, so central districts are walkable but tiring, and the metro plus a taxi covers most needs. Yassir is the dominant local ride-hailing app and works well, with typical rides costing $1.50 to $4; Heetch also operates in Algiers. Uber and Bolt do not. Street taxis exist and are negotiated rather than metered. Houari Boumediene airport sits about 20 kilometres east of the centre, roughly 30 to 50 minutes depending on traffic, with a Yassir ride around $8 to $15 and a metro plus bus combination far cheaper. Traffic congestion is heavy at peak hours. A car is unnecessary in the city and parking is difficult. The Sahara is reached by air rather than by road, because the distances south are enormous and the flights from here to the oasis towns are cheap and frequent, which is how anybody with a fortnight actually gets to see the desert. Overland it is days. Trains along the coast are slow but cheap and comfortable.
algiers.visas: Algeria has the hardest entry requirements in North Africa and this is the single biggest obstacle. Almost all Western nationals, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, must obtain a visa in advance from an Algerian embassy or consulate before travel; there is no e-visa for general tourism and no visa on arrival. The application requires a hotel booking covering the entire stay with a confirmation stamped and signed by the hotel, or a formal invitation letter from an Algerian host that has been certified by local authorities, plus bank statements, an itinerary, insurance and a return ticket. Processing takes weeks and refusals are routine without a clear reason given. Tourist visas are usually issued for 30 days, sometimes 90. A limited visa on arrival scheme exists for tourists booked on organised tours into the Saharan south via Djanet and Tamanrasset, but it does not cover independent travel to Algiers. There is no digital nomad visa. Extensions require police applications and are rarely granted.
algiers.bestTime: Algiers has a classic Mediterranean climate softened by the sea, so it never reaches the extremes of the interior. Spring, from March to May, is the best window: 18 to 25 Celsius, green hills, wildflowers and comfortable walking weather. Autumn, September through November, is nearly as good, with warm sea into October and the first rains arriving late. Summer, June to August, brings 28 to 34 Celsius with high humidity along the coast and heavy domestic tourism on the beaches; the interior and the Sahara become genuinely dangerous, exceeding 45 Celsius, so southern travel is off the table. Winter, December to February, is mild at 10 to 17 Celsius but is the wet season, with sustained rain and grey skies, and unheated apartments feel colder than the numbers suggest. Ramadan, falling in the first quarter through the late 2020s, transforms daily rhythm: daytime restaurants close, offices shorten hours, and nights become sociable.
algiers.prosCons: Algiers is one of the most striking and least visited capitals on the Mediterranean, with white terraced buildings stacked above a wide bay, spectacular French colonial and Ottoman architecture, the UNESCO-listed Casbah, excellent museums, a serious cafe culture and prices that, at parallel exchange rates, are extremely low. Roman sites at Tipaza and Djemila are day trips, the Kabylie mountains are close, and Algerians are notably hospitable to the few foreigners who arrive. The obstacles are substantial. The visa alone deters most people, and it must be secured before booking anything. There is essentially no nomad scene and very few foreign residents outside diplomatic and energy sectors. Foreign card payments are almost useless outside major hotels, so the economy runs on cash. Internet is inconsistent and subject to national exam-period shutdowns. French or Arabic is effectively mandatory, alcohol is hard to buy, bureaucracy is heavy, and travel outside the north is restricted.
algiers.whoFor: Experience and patience are the requirements, along with enough French or Arabic to function without English, and the reward is the architecture, the history and a country that almost nobody visits. It works for someone with a genuine tie to Algeria, family, business in energy or construction, or academic research, since the visa is far easier with a local host. Photographers, Roman-history enthusiasts and anyone who enjoys being the only foreigner in the room will find it unusually rewarding. It is the wrong destination for a first stint abroad, for anyone dependent on card payments, food delivery apps and coworking infrastructure, or for anyone who needs guaranteed uninterrupted internet for client calls. Nomads seeking community, nightlife, beach convenience or an easy administrative life should choose Morocco or Tunisia, both of which deliver a similar region with none of the entry friction.

isfahan.costOfLiving: Isfahan is extraordinarily cheap for a foreigner because the rial trades on a parallel market far weaker than any official rate, and $600 a month is comfortable rather than tight. Money must be brought in as physical euros or dollars and exchanged locally, since foreign cards do not function. A furnished one-bedroom apartment near Chahar Bagh, Julfa or the Si-o-se-pol area costs $150 to $350 a month, with older local apartments cheaper still. Food is the biggest bargain: $100 to $180 covers groceries and frequent restaurant meals, with a kebab plate or dizi under $4 and even a good traditional restaurant on Naqsh-e Jahan square rarely exceeding $10. An Irancell or Hamrahe Aval SIM with data costs $5 to $12. Formal coworking, where it exists, runs $40 to $90. Utilities are heavily subsidised at $15 to $40. Transport is under $30. Value is exceptional, access is the problem. Fuel is subsidised to a degree that has no equivalent anywhere, so a tank of petrol costs a couple of dollars and a domestic flight across the country costs less than a short taxi ride in Europe. Internal travel is effectively free once you are inside the borders. Bus and rail fares sit on the same scale, so distance stops being a budget consideration at all.
isfahan.whereToWork: The Julfa quarter, the historic Armenian district around Vank Cathedral, is the most pleasant base: walkable, full of specialty cafes with reliable wifi, and close to the Zayanderud bridges. The Chahar Bagh Abbasi axis and the streets north of Naqsh-e Jahan square are more central and better connected. Isfahan has a genuine startup and university scene tied to Isfahan University of Technology and the Isfahan Science and Technology Town, which hosts incubators and shared workspaces, but public coworking aimed at foreigners barely exists. Cafes are the default office and the local cafe culture is strong. The critical caveat is the internet. Iran filters aggressively: WhatsApp, Telegram, YouTube, Instagram, X, most Google services and many Western sites are blocked or throttled, so a working VPN installed and tested before arrival is mandatory. Speeds are modest, typically 5 to 30 Mbps, with international routing slow and periodic nationwide slowdowns or shutdowns during unrest. The river the city was built around now runs dry for most of the year, diverted upstream to steel mills and farmland, and the great bridges stand over sand. The water question is the single biggest constraint on the local economy and a live political grievance rather than a curiosity for visitors.
isfahan.gettingAround: Isfahan is one of Iran's most walkable large cities, with the historic core around Naqsh-e Jahan square, the bazaar, the Jameh Mosque and the river bridges all covered on foot. Snapp is the ride-hailing app everyone uses and it is startlingly cheap: most trips across the city cost $0.50 to $2, though registration requires an Iranian phone number, so buy a SIM on arrival. Tapsi is the main alternative. Street taxis operate as shared services along fixed corridors for pennies, and private hire is negotiated. A single metro line runs north to south through the centre and a bus rapid transit network fills gaps, with fares of a few cents. Isfahan Shahid Beheshti airport lies about 25 kilometres northeast, roughly 30 minutes by Snapp for a few dollars, though most visitors arrive by domestic flight or by the comfortable overnight train and bus links from Tehran and Shiraz. No car is needed.
isfahan.visas: Iran requires a visa in advance for nearly all Western nationals, obtained through an authorisation code process: an application is submitted, typically via an Iranian travel agency, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issues a reference or authorisation code, and the visa is then collected at an Iranian consulate or, for many nationalities, at the airport on arrival. Tourist visas are usually 30 days, extendable once or twice inside Iran at a provincial police immigration office, including in Isfahan, for a total of up to 90 days. Two hard rules dominate. Citizens of the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada cannot travel independently: they must book a guided tour or a licensed private guide accompanying them throughout, and the itinerary forms part of the visa application. Second, international sanctions mean Visa, Mastercard and foreign ATM cards do not work anywhere in Iran, so all money must be carried in cash or loaded onto a prepaid Iranian tourist debit card on arrival. No digital nomad visa exists.
isfahan.bestTime: Isfahan sits at roughly 1,570 metres on the arid central plateau, so the climate is dry with wide daily temperature swings and four distinct seasons. April and May are the best months, with highs of 22 to 30 Celsius, blossom in the gardens and the pleasantest conditions for walking the old city. October and early November are equally good, warm by day and cool at night. Summer, June through August, is hot and very dry at 35 to 40 Celsius, though low humidity and cool evenings make it more tolerable than Gulf heat; midday is still lost to the shade. Winter, December to February, is cold, with frost, occasional snow and highs near 8 to 12 Celsius, and poorly heated buildings. Nowruz, the Persian new year around 21 March, is the biggest holiday: everything is booked and crowded for two weeks. Ramadan closes daytime restaurants and requires visible discretion about eating in public.
isfahan.prosCons: Isfahan is one of the great historic cities of the world, with Naqsh-e Jahan square, the Sheikh Lotfollah and Shah mosques, the covered bazaar, the Safavid bridges and the Armenian quarter all within walking distance, and Iranian hospitality toward foreign visitors is genuinely exceptional. Costs are among the lowest anywhere for a comparable quality of urban life, food is superb, crime against foreigners is very rare, and the city is calm and orderly. The drawbacks are severe for a working nomad. The internet is filtered, slow internationally and occasionally cut entirely, which makes client-facing work precarious. No foreign bank card, payment app or international service functions, so income cannot be accessed locally and cash must be imported. There is no nomad community whatsoever. Dress codes and headscarf rules are enforced for women, alcohol is illegal, dual nationals face real detention risk, and geopolitical volatility can close airspace without warning.
isfahan.whoFor: Isfahan makes sense for the culturally motivated traveller rather than the conventional remote worker: someone spending weeks on Islamic architecture, Persian language study, carpets, miniature painting or regional history, who can front-load their income and work in low-bandwidth bursts. It rewards experienced independent travellers comfortable with cash economies, conservative social codes and unfamiliar bureaucracy, and it is a strong stop on an overland route through Tehran, Kashan, Yazd and Shiraz. Anyone whose work depends on stable video calls, cloud tools, foreign payment rails or predictable connectivity should not attempt to base here, and US, UK and Canadian passport holders face the additional cost and rigidity of a mandatory guide. Women unwilling to observe mandatory hijab, travellers who want nightlife or alcohol, dual Iranian nationals, and anyone who needs the reassurance of consular support should choose elsewhere entirely.

montegobay.costOfLiving: A single nomad running at roughly $1300 per month in Montego Bay is living carefully, because the resort corridor and the local town operate on two different price lists. A furnished monthly rental in a central or Ironshore apartment complex runs about $500 to $800, with Airbnb units on the Hip Strip or in Rose Hall asking $1000 and up for the same square footage. Groceries and mostly local eating come to $250 to $400; a patty and box lunch from a local cookshop is $3 to $6, while a Gloucester Avenue restaurant plate is $20 to $35. Digicel or Flow prepaid data sits at $15 to $30. Coworking, where available, is $80 to $150 monthly. Utilities with air conditioning are punishing at $80 to $180, since JPS electricity is among the costliest in the region. Local transport is $30 to $60. Verdict: liveable, but poor value against Latin America.
montegobay.whereToWork: Basing decisions matter more here than venue lists. Gloucester Avenue, the Hip Strip, puts cafes, beaches and nightlife within a walkable kilometre but charges tourist rates and attracts persistent vendors. Ironshore and Rose Hall to the east are quieter residential and resort zones with better apartment stock and reliable utilities, though a car or taxi becomes necessary. Freeport, on the peninsula, is calm, gated and popular with longer stays. Inland Montego Bay proper around Fairview and Bogue is where locals live and prices normalise. Dedicated coworking is thin: a handful of small operators and the Fairview shopping centre area cover the demand, so hotel lobbies, resort business centres and cafes carry most of the load. Flow and Digicel deliver fibre and LTE at roughly 20 to 100 Mbps in serviced buildings. Power cuts are routine, generators and a backup SIM are standard, and hurricane season outages can last days. The largest white-collar employer here is not tourism but the outsourcing industry: call centres in the free zone north of the airport employ thousands on shifts timed to the American day, which is why the roads are busy at hours that make no sense for a resort town.
montegobay.gettingAround: Route taxis are the backbone: shared white-plate cars running fixed corridors, flagged from the roadside, with fares around $1 to $2 per hop paid on exit. Etiquette is to state the destination before getting in, expect three passengers across the back seat and carry small notes. Buses cover longer local routes cheaply, and Knutsford Express coaches connect Montego Bay to Ocho Rios, Negril and Kingston in air conditioned comfort for roughly $12 to $30 one way, booked online. Uber operates thinly and unreliably; InDrive has better local traction, and charter taxis with red PP plates are the tourist default at $10 to $25 across town. Sangster International sits minutes from the Hip Strip, which is walkable end to end. A rental car helps for exploring the north coast, though driving is on the left, roads are potholed and night driving is best avoided. There is no fast route across the middle of the island, so the capital is reached the long way round the coast rather than straight over the mountains, which is why a three-hour journey on a map becomes four in practice. Parts of the north coast road are tolled.
montegobay.visas: Jamaica admits citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Australia and New Zealand visa free as visitors. Crucially, the length of stay is written by the immigration officer at the border rather than fixed by rule: grants commonly reach up to 90 days, but shorter stamps of 30 days or matched to a stated onward flight date are routine. Proof of onward or return travel and a confirmed accommodation address are asked for regularly and should be ready. Extensions are handled by the Passport, Immigration and Citizenship Agency, PICA, in person for a fee, and are discretionary rather than automatic. Jamaica has no digital nomad visa. Remote work for a foreign employer while on a visitor stamp is widely tolerated and not policed, but it is not formally authorised, so avoid discussing work at immigration. Working for a Jamaican employer requires a sponsored work permit.
montegobay.bestTime: December through April is the dry high season and the reason most visitors come: daytime highs around 29 to 31C, low humidity by Caribbean standards, cool evenings and reliably calm sea. It is also the priciest window, with accommodation and flights peaking from mid December to early April. May brings the first rainfall spike as the wet pattern establishes. June through November is the Atlantic hurricane season, with genuine risk concentrated from August to October when storms, flooding and multi day power outages are realistic. October is the second and heavier rain peak. July and August are hot, humid and sticky but busy, carrying Reggae Sumfest in July, the anchor event of the local music calendar. Carnival falls in the spring around April, and the Christmas and New Year stretch is festive, crowded and expensive. This coast faces north, which spares it the weed that fouls the eastern beaches in some years but leaves it open to winter swells rolling down from storms far out in the ocean. The sea can be flat for a fortnight and then unswimmable for three days.
montegobay.prosCons: The strengths are real: English is the working language with no adjustment period, direct flights from North America and Europe land at Sangster minutes from town, the beaches and north coast scenery are genuinely world class, and the music and food culture is lived rather than staged, with a warmth and humour that many nomads find hard to leave. The list on the other side is a difficult one. Jamaica has a persistently high national violent crime rate and area selection matters enormously, with some parishes and inner city zones effectively off limits. The resort strip runs a two tier pricing system and constant hustling of tourists wears thin. Dedicated coworking infrastructure is thin and unreliable, power cuts are routine, and hurricane season can shut down connectivity for days. Electricity and imported goods are costly, and the overall bill runs well above comparable Latin American bases.
montegobay.whoFor: Caribbean beach living with no language friction and short flights home is the offer, and it needs a budget with some room in it rather than one squeezed to the last dollar. Work that runs asynchronously and forgives the occasional outage is the practical condition. Repeat visitors who already know which streets and which complexes they trust have a far easier time of it than first arrivals, and the serious draw is Jamaican music and food rather than anything a resort brochure puts on its cover. It also fits short winter stays of one to three months, which sidesteps both hurricane season and the visa ambiguity. Skip it if cost per dollar is the deciding factor, since Colombia, Mexico and Brazil deliver more for less. Skip it too if a reliable coworking community, guaranteed uptime, casual late night walkability or a formal long stay visa pathway is non negotiable.

bansko.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $900 a month as a solo remote worker in Bansko, which makes it one of the cheapest bases in the European Union. A one-bedroom apartment near the gondola runs about $350 to $500 in summer and considerably more from December to March, when the ski season pushes short-term rates up and long leases signed in advance become the only sensible option. Groceries land around $200 if you shop at Lidl and the Saturday market rather than the tourist minimarkets. A mehana dinner with wine is $12 to $18, a coffee about $1.50, and a gondola day pass in winter roughly $50. Coworking membership at the established space in town is around $110 a month. The single biggest variable is whether you arrive before or after the season sets rents. A great many of the apartment blocks here went up in an off-plan building boom that collapsed around 2008, which is why the town holds more flats than it needs and why buying one costs so little. Maintenance charges on those blocks vary wildly and are levied by whoever ended up managing the building, so a cheap purchase in a badly run block is not the bargain it looks from the listing.
bansko.whereToWork: Bansko's reputation as a nomad town rests almost entirely on one institution: Coworking Bansko, which opened in 2016 and effectively created the scene here. It runs across two buildings, has fast fibre, standing desks, phone booths and a members' calendar that carries most of the town's social life through the winter. The annual Bansko Nomad Fest in June is its doing as well. Outside it, options thin quickly. A handful of cafes on Pirin Street have wifi and will tolerate a laptop for an hour, but Bulgarian cafe culture does not really run to all-day working, and in high season the seats go to skiers. Most residents work from their apartments and use the coworking space for company rather than for connectivity, which is generally good across town. The lift concession and the boundaries of the national park above the town have been fought over in the courts for years, environmental groups on one side and the operator on the other, and it is the one local subject on which nobody here is neutral. Everything else in the town is hotels, lifts and the trades that serve them, so the working population halves when the snow goes.
bansko.gettingAround: Bansko is small enough to cross on foot in twenty minutes, and most people never use anything else. The old town, the coworking space, the supermarkets and the gondola base station all sit within that radius. There is no local bus network worth the name. For the ski lifts a free shuttle loops the main hotels in season, otherwise it is a walk or a $3 taxi. Getting to Bansko is the harder part: it is about 160km from Sofia, roughly two and a half hours by road, with several daily buses from Sofia's central station for around $8. The train exists, is narrow gauge and scenic, and takes five hours. Many residents rent a car for the mountains, though winter tyres are a legal requirement from November. The gondola queue in high season is the town's running complaint and can swallow an hour on a Saturday morning, which is why residents ski midweek or walk up to the second station instead. Mountain roads south towards Greece stay open all year and put Thessaloniki within about four hours, which is a better airport connection than most people arriving here realise they have.
bansko.visas: Bulgaria is in the European Union and joined the Schengen area for air and sea borders in March 2024, with land borders following in 2025, so the standard Schengen rules now apply: EU and EEA citizens may live and work freely, and most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180. Bulgaria has no dedicated digital nomad visa, which is the main structural gap for anyone wanting to stay past three months. The usual routes are a freelance or self-employed residence permit, which requires a Bulgarian company or registered activity, or company formation, which is common enough here that local accountants advertise the service in English. Bulgaria's 10 percent flat corporate and personal income tax is the reason a number of long-term residents register a business rather than simply visiting.
bansko.bestTime: Bansko has two clearly separate seasons and a quiet gap between them. The ski season runs roughly mid-December to mid-April, brings the town to life, fills the coworking space and doubles rents. Summer, from June to September, is the season most remote workers prefer: daytime highs in the mid-twenties, cool nights at 900 metres, hiking straight into the Pirin national park, and accommodation at half the winter rate. June brings the Nomad Fest and the largest concentration of remote workers in the year. The shoulder months, late April to May and October to November, are cheap and very quiet, with many restaurants closed and the weather unreliable. If you want the community, come in winter or in June. If you want the mountains and the prices, come in September. Snow lingers on the high traverse into July most years, so an early summer walk above the tree line still wants proper boots and an ice axe, whatever the valley looks like from a terrace. Brown bears live in this range in real numbers, and the local advice about making noise on a quiet trail is meant seriously rather than offered as colour for visitors.
bansko.prosCons: Bansko's appeal is unusually easy to state. It is cheap by European Union standards, it has one genuinely excellent coworking space with a real community around it, the Pirin mountains start at the edge of town, and Bulgaria's flat tax makes it attractive to anyone with a registered business. Wifi is good and the town is safe. The catch is the size of the place. The nomad scene concentrates in one building, and if you do not click with it there is not a second one. Restaurant variety is limited and largely Bulgarian. English is common among the nomad crowd and much less so elsewhere. Winter rents can double, healthcare means a trip to Blagoevgrad or Sofia for anything serious, and the nearest international airport is two and a half hours away.
bansko.whoFor: European Union residency options and mountain access, on a budget that would not cover a room in Lisbon, is the whole proposition. Serious skiers and hikers are the core of it. Anybody running a registered business has Bulgaria's 10 percent rate to consider, and the town trades a large anonymous city for one strong community, which some people want badly and others find claustrophobic. It is a good first base for someone nervous about going far from Europe. Variety, nightlife, a large dating pool and a nearby major airport are all absent, and no season here changes that. Families will find the town safe and the schooling limited to Bulgarian state options. If your work depends on meeting clients in person, Sofia is the better address and Bansko the better weekend.

jerusalem.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $3,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Jerusalem, which makes it expensive by regional standards and comparable to a mid-sized Western European capital. A one-bedroom apartment in a central neighbourhood such as Nachlaot, Rehavia or the German Colony runs about $1,300 to $1,900, and rents are quoted in shekels but often discussed in dollars. Further out, in Kiryat Yovel or Pisgat Ze'ev, the same apartment is $900 to $1,200. Groceries run $400 to $550, noticeably less if you shop at Mahane Yehuda market rather than the supermarkets. A hummus lunch is $8, a restaurant dinner $25 to $40, and a monthly transit pass about $60. Utilities and municipal tax, the arnona, add $200 to $300 and catch newcomers out. Rent is often paid with a year of post-dated cheques handed over at signing, along with a guarantee from somebody local, which is a real obstacle for a newcomer with nobody to ask. Leases turn over in a single season keyed to the academic year, so arriving outside that window means taking what is left rather than choosing. A local bank account has to exist before any of it works.
jerusalem.whereToWork: Jerusalem has a real coworking market, mostly clustered downtown around Jaffa Road and in the Talpiot business area, and several spaces are aimed at the technology and non-profit sectors rather than at tourists. Desk rates run about $200 to $300 a month. Cafe working is normal and accepted: the streets around Emek Refaim and the lanes off Jaffa Road have plenty of places where a laptop and a long coffee raise no eyebrows. Wifi is fast and widely available, and mobile data is cheap and excellent, so tethering is a genuine fallback. The one thing to plan around is Shabbat: from Friday afternoon to Saturday evening most of the city closes, including many cafes and nearly all transport, and this is not a city where that rule bends. Offices here open on Sunday and shut on Thursday evening, which leaves the local weekend and the European one overlapping by a single day, so anybody with clients abroad ends up working six days to cover both. The last working day is a short morning at best. That mismatch is the biggest practical adjustment for somebody arriving from Europe or America, and it wants planning for before the first week rather than after it.
jerusalem.gettingAround: Jerusalem is walkable in its centre and hilly enough that walking is real exercise. The light rail runs a single main line through the middle of the city, from Pisgat Ze'ev through the Old City walls and down Jaffa Road, and is the fastest way along that corridor. Buses cover everything else and are frequent, with a rechargeable Rav-Kav card or a phone app for payment. A monthly pass is about $60. Everything stops for Shabbat, from Friday afternoon until Saturday night, when taxis and shared sherut minibuses are the only option and charge accordingly. Tel Aviv is an hour away by fast train from Yitzhak Navon station, which makes day trips easy. Driving in the city is slow and parking is genuinely difficult; most residents do not bother with a car.
jerusalem.visas: Israel grants most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, a 90-day visitor permit on arrival, issued as a paper slip rather than a stamp. Since January 2025 an ETA-IL electronic travel authorisation must be obtained online before flying. There is no digital nomad visa, and working remotely for a foreign employer on a tourist permit sits in the usual grey area. Extensions are possible through the Population and Immigration Authority but are discretionary and not reliable. Anyone Jewish or with Jewish ancestry has a separate and much simpler route through the Law of Return, which grants citizenship. Border questioning is thorough on both entry and exit, and travellers should expect detailed questions about where they are staying and who they know. Keep the paper entry slip somewhere safe, because it stands in place of a stamp in the passport and is what exempts a visitor from sales tax on hotel bills and some other services. Losing it means paying that tax and explaining yourself on the way out. Entry is often granted for less than ninety days at the officer's discretion, so read what was actually written on it rather than assuming the maximum.
jerusalem.bestTime: Spring and autumn are clearly the best times. March to May brings warm days, cool evenings and hillsides that are briefly green, and September to November does the same in reverse. Summer, June to August, is hot and dry, with highs in the low thirties, though Jerusalem's 750 metre elevation makes the nights far more bearable than on the coast. Winter, December to February, is cool and wet, occasionally cold enough to snow, and the stone city looks its best in it. Plan around the festival calendar rather than the weather: Passover in spring and the September or October cluster of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkot close much of the city and push accommodation prices sharply up. Ramadan changes the rhythm of the Old City entirely. The sharav blows in off the desert at the turn of the seasons, hot and dry, lifting the temperature ten degrees and filling the air with dust for a day or two at a stretch. On the Day of Atonement the country stops completely: no traffic at all, and children riding bicycles down empty motorways, which is worth seeing once. Nothing is open that day, the airport included.
jerusalem.prosCons: Few cities offer this much history in this small a space, and for anyone interested in archaeology, religion or the politics of the region, Jerusalem is unmatched. The food is excellent, the markets are among the best in the Mediterranean, connectivity is first-rate and Tel Aviv is an hour away. The city is compact and the light is extraordinary. It is expensive, the political situation is a live and sometimes dangerous reality rather than a background detail, and travellers should follow their government's current advice rather than any guide, including this one. Shabbat removes a day and a half of normal service every week. The nomad community is small, as most remote workers in Israel base themselves in Tel Aviv. Social tensions are visible and can be uncomfortable.
jerusalem.whoFor: Nobody arrives in this city without a specific reason to be here: research, faith, family, archaeology, or work connected to the region. It rewards curiosity and patience, and it punishes anyone hoping for a straightforward, cheap, easy base. A compact walkable city with serious food and several thousand years of history immediately outside the door is what is on offer, and the only real condition is a budget that can absorb what it costs. A large nomad community, cheap living, a beach and political calm are four things this city does not offer, and Tel Aviv, which is very close, answers most of them considerably better. Anyone considering it should check their own government's travel advice for the region before booking, and should understand that conditions here can change quickly.

ankara.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $880 a month as a solo remote worker in Ankara, which makes it appreciably cheaper than Istanbul for a similar standard of city living. A one-bedroom apartment in Cankaya, Kizilay or Bahcelievler runs about $300 to $450, and the newer districts out towards Cayyolu cost about the same for more space and a longer commute. Groceries land around $180 to $250, helped by neighbourhood pazar markets that undercut supermarkets on produce by a wide margin. A lunch of doner or pide is $3 to $5, a proper restaurant dinner with drinks $15 to $25, and a monthly transit pass about $25. Utilities run $60 to $110 and spike in winter, when Ankara's continental climate makes heating a real line item rather than an afterthought. Rent increases on a continuing tenancy were capped by law through the worst of the inflation and the cap has since lapsed, leaving a wide gap between what a sitting tenant pays and what a newcomer is quoted, which is why so many flats change hands quietly between people who already know each other. An agency takes its commission on a new let. A deposit of a month or two is standard and comes back slowly if at all, so expect to argue for it.
ankara.whereToWork: Ankara is a government and university city rather than a tourist one, and its working spaces reflect that. Coworking clusters around Kizilay, Cankaya and the technology parks attached to METU and Bilkent, where rates run about $90 to $150 a month and the other members are more likely to be Turkish founders and engineers than visiting nomads. Cafe culture is strong and laptop-friendly, particularly in the student areas around Bahcelievler and Tunali Hilmi, and third-wave coffee has arrived properly in the last few years. Fixed-line internet is fast and cheap, and mobile data is good, though foreign SIM cards get throttled after 120 days unless the handset is registered, which is a well-known and expensive piece of Turkish bureaucracy worth planning around. The defence and aerospace industry is concentrated in this city and nowhere else, and the engineering firms attached to it are the reason the technology parks exist at all. None of that work is open to a foreigner without clearance. What it does produce is a city full of engineers, a serious supply of technical meetups, and a professional culture that starts at half past eight in the morning and means it.
ankara.gettingAround: Ankara has a metro with four lines plus the older Ankaray light rail, and between them they cover the spine of the city from Kizilay outwards. Buses and shared dolmus minibuses fill everything else, and an Ankarakart smart card pays for all of it at roughly $0.40 a ride. The city is spread out and hilly, so walking works within a neighbourhood rather than between them. Taxis are metered, plentiful and cheap by European standards. The high-speed train to Istanbul takes about four and a half hours and to Konya under two, both from Ankara YHT station, and is much more pleasant than flying. Esenboga airport is 28km north with a frequent Havas bus. Traffic is heavy at rush hour and driving is not recommended for newcomers. The fast rail network keeps extending east from here, with a line to Sivas opened a couple of years ago, which makes the city the hinge of the whole system rather than one end of it. Journeys that used to mean a flight are now a morning on a train. Within the city the hills mean a metro station can sit a long way below the street, and the escalators at some of them take longer than the ride between stops.
ankara.visas: Turkey grants most Western passports a 90-day stay in any 180-day period, with EU, UK and Canadian citizens entering visa-free and some nationalities needing an e-Visa bought online in advance. Turkey has no digital nomad visa in the usual sense, but it does have a short-term residence permit, the kisa donem ikamet, which is the standard route for anyone staying longer. It is applied for online through the e-ikamet system, requires proof of address, health insurance and funds, and has become noticeably harder to obtain in Istanbul in recent years. Ankara is generally reported as more straightforward. Turkey also has a well-known citizenship-by-investment property route. Anyone planning to stay should start the residence process well before the 90 days expire. Every embassy in the country is in this city, which matters more than it sounds: applying for a visa to somewhere else, having a document legalised or replacing a lost passport all happen here rather than in the bigger city on the coast, and people travel up for a morning appointment. That is a real practical advantage of basing here. Appointment systems are online and the slots go quickly, so book before travelling rather than after arriving.
ankara.bestTime: Ankara sits on the Anatolian plateau at about 900 metres, which gives it a genuinely continental climate and four distinct seasons. Spring, April to early June, and autumn, September to October, are the best: warm days, cool nights, clear light and comfortable walking weather. Summer is hot and very dry, with highs in the low thirties, but the altitude keeps nights cool and the humidity is low, so it is far more bearable than the coast. Winter, December to February, is genuinely cold, regularly below freezing, with snow and grey skies, and air quality dips as heating ramps up. There is no tourist season to speak of, so accommodation prices are stable year-round, which is one quiet advantage of a city that does not live on visitors.
ankara.prosCons: Ankara is cheap, functional and largely undiscovered by remote workers, which is either its main appeal or its main problem depending on what you want. It has a real metro, excellent and inexpensive food, a serious university and technology sector, fast internet, and a central position that puts the whole of Anatolia within reach by good trains. It is far calmer and less crowded than Istanbul. It is not a beautiful city, the tourist sights amount to a strong museum and a hilltop citadel, and there is almost no international nomad community here at all. English is limited outside the universities and technology parks. Winters are cold and the air quality suffers. Anyone arriving expecting Istanbul's drama will find a working capital instead.
ankara.whoFor: The point of the place is living in Turkey properly rather than passing through it, which means learning some Turkish and valuing low costs and a functioning city over scenery and easy company. Anybody building ties to the Turkish technology sector has business here, and the rail network makes this the obvious base for working through Anatolia. A good many people arrive because Istanbul turned out to be either too much or too expensive. It is a reasonable choice for families, with safe neighbourhoods and good private schools. An English-speaking environment, an existing nomad crowd, a beach and nightlife on any scale are all missing here, and no amount of patience will produce them. Those wanting Turkey with all of that should look at Istanbul, Izmir or the coast.

olomouc.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Olomouc, which buys a standard of central European city living that would cost half as much again in Prague. A one-bedroom apartment in or near the historic centre runs about $450 to $600, and the panel-block districts a tram ride out drop that to $350 to $450. Groceries land around $220 to $280. A pub lunch with a beer is $7 to $9, a good restaurant dinner $18 to $25, and Czech beer remains cheaper than soft drinks at about $1.60 for half a litre. A monthly transit pass is roughly $18. Utilities add $90 to $150 and rise in winter. The city's student population keeps prices honest in a way that tourist-heavy Czech towns do not manage.
olomouc.whereToWork: Olomouc has a small but real coworking scene, mostly serving the university and a growing cluster of software companies, with desks at roughly $90 to $140 a month. The bigger asset is Palacky University, the second oldest in the country, whose 20,000 students support a dense network of cafes that are entirely comfortable with laptops and long stays. The lanes around Horni namesti and Univerzitni street have most of them. Czech fixed-line internet is fast and cheap, and mobile data is reliable if not especially generous. Because the city is compact, you can reasonably keep two or three regular working spots within a ten-minute walk of home, which is a practical advantage over larger cities where changing scene costs half an hour. The town's most famous product is a small pungent ripened cheese made nowhere else in the country under a protected name, and the factory that makes it sits up the road in a village that smells of it. The other steady employers are the hospital, the university and an army garrison, which between them keep the place working when the students are away. None of that hires from abroad, but it does mean the cafes stay open in August.
olomouc.gettingAround: Olomouc is a walking city first: the historic centre is about a kilometre across and closed to most traffic, and almost everything a resident needs sits inside or just beyond it. Beyond that, an efficient tram network with several lines covers the wider city, running from early morning to around eleven at night, with a monthly pass at about $18 and single tickets under a dollar. Cycling is popular and the terrain is flat. The main railway station is a fifteen-minute tram ride from the centre and puts Prague at two hours and twenty minutes, Brno at an hour, and Vienna, Krakow and Bratislava all within half a day. There is no airport; most people fly into Prague, Brno, Vienna or Katowice and take a train. The river through the city flooded catastrophically in 1997, and the defences built afterwards are why the newer embankments look the way they do. Day to day the flat ground makes a bicycle quicker than a tram for anything inside the ring, and the town has painted lanes along most of the main streets without much fuss about it. Trains east into the mountains leave hourly and are how people reach the walking.
olomouc.visas: The Czech Republic is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so EU and EEA citizens may live and work here without formality beyond registering after 30 days. Most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180-day Schengen period. Since 2023 the Czech Republic has operated a digital nomad visa, aimed at highly skilled non-EU remote workers from a defined list of countries, which grants a long-stay permit of up to one year and is one of the more usable schemes in central Europe. Outside that, the long-standing zivnostensky list, the Czech trade licence, remains the route many freelancers use, though it involves real bureaucracy and is best approached with a local accountant. Applications are made at Czech consulates abroad rather than in-country. A trade licence brings compulsory social and health insurance with it, charged at a monthly minimum whether or not anything was earned, which is the cost people discover in their second year rather than their first. An accountant files the annual returns and the fee is small against the penalties for getting them wrong. A registered address is needed for the licence, and a landlord has to consent to it in writing.
olomouc.bestTime: May to September is the clear window. Late spring brings long light evenings, the university in full session and the squares busy, while June to August is warm without the heat that makes southern Europe uncomfortable, with highs in the mid to high twenties. September is arguably the best month of all: warm days, thinner crowds, and the new academic year filling the cafes again. Autumn turns grey and wet through October and November. Winter, December to February, is cold, often below freezing, with short days and occasional snow that suits the baroque centre very well; the Christmas market on Horni namesti is one of the better ones in the country and far less crowded than Prague's. March and April are unreliable and best avoided. A large horticultural fair fills the exhibition gardens twice a year, once in spring and once in autumn, and it is the one occasion that pulls people here from the rest of the country. Cold still weather traps the air over this part of Moravia in the darkest weeks, and the smog that results is a regional problem rather than a local one. Snow here is reliable enough to plan around and rarely deep enough to be a nuisance.
olomouc.prosCons: Olomouc offers a UNESCO-listed baroque centre, a serious university, Czech prices well below Prague and a genuinely walkable scale, which together make it one of central Europe's better-value bases. Beer is cheap and excellent, trains connect it to half the region, the streets are safe, and the student population keeps the city young without making it loud. The drawback is simply that it is small. The international community is thin, the nomad scene barely exists, and English, while common among students, is not universal. There is no airport and winters are long, grey and cold. Anyone wanting mountains, sea or a large city's variety will find Olomouc limiting, and those needing frequent international flights will spend a lot of time on trains to Prague or Vienna.
olomouc.whoFor: Central European quality of life at a price that leaves room to save is the bargain, provided you are happy to supply your own social life or draw it from a university town. The Czech digital nomad visa or a trade licence is the usual route in. What the city adds is a position within a few hours of Prague, Vienna, Krakow and Brno without paying any capital-city rent for it, plus flat country for cycling and a country that drinks more beer per head than any other on earth. Couples manage well here, and so does work that needs long quiet stretches. An established nomad crowd, warm weather, an airport at hand and a large English-speaking professional network are all things somebody would have to go elsewhere to find. Brno is the obvious step up in size while keeping most of the price advantage.

pecs.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $850 a month as a solo remote worker in Pécs, which is among the cheaper options anywhere in the European Union. A one-bedroom apartment in the centre runs about $300 to $420, and the surrounding districts drop that to $230 to $320. Groceries land around $180 to $240, with the Saturday market on Vasarcsarnok cheaper than the supermarkets for produce. A menu lunch is $5 to $7, a restaurant dinner with wine $15 to $22, and Hungarian wine from the nearby Villany region is very good and very cheap. A monthly transit pass is about $16. Utilities add $80 to $150, more in winter. The university keeps a large stock of small flats in circulation, which holds rents down outside the September rush. Older flats in the centre are often still heated by a tiled stove in the corner, cheap to run on wood and an hour to get going, which is either charming or a chore depending on the morning. Blocks charge a monthly common cost covering the stairwell and the lift, and it arrives separately from the rent. Two months as deposit is the usual ask, and it comes back in cash rather than by transfer more often than not.
pecs.whereToWork: Pécs is a university city of roughly 20,000 students, and the working infrastructure follows from that rather than from any nomad economy. There are one or two small coworking spaces attached to the university's innovation ecosystem, with desks around $80 to $130 a month, but most people work from home or from cafes. The pedestrianised Kiraly utca and the streets around Szechenyi ter have a good density of places that will not hurry you along. Hungarian fixed-line internet is fast and cheap, among the better networks in the region, and mobile data is inexpensive. The main practical constraint is that very little of this is set up for foreigners: expect Hungarian menus, Hungarian signage and a certain amount of translation-app work in the first weeks. The porcelain works that made this city's name still runs, and the quarter built around it for a European culture year holds studios, galleries and a planetarium in what were factory buildings, which is the nearest thing here to a creative district. Uranium was mined in the hills until the nineteen nineties, and its closure took thousands of jobs out of the local economy inside a few years, which is why the city leaned so hard on the university afterwards.
pecs.gettingAround: Pécs is compact and hilly, built on the southern slope of the Mecsek, and the centre is comfortably walkable if you accept some climbing. A bus network covers the rest of the city, with a monthly pass at about $16 and single tickets under a dollar; there are no trams. Cycling works on the flat but is hard work towards the hills. The railway station is a fifteen-minute walk from the centre and connects to Budapest in about three hours, which is the main link most residents use. There is no useful airport: Budapest is the practical gateway, roughly three hours away by train or car. Within the region a car opens up the Villany wine country and the Danube, but nothing essential requires one. The motorway reached this city only in the last fifteen years, and the drive to the capital fell to roughly two hours and a half with it, which is why so much of what is written about how remote the place feels was written before that. The Croatian border is under an hour south, putting the coast within a long day. Up in the hills behind the city a television tower has a viewing platform, and the road to it is the standard Sunday outing.
pecs.visas: Hungary is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so EU and EEA citizens face no restrictions beyond registering a residence address. Most other Western passports receive 90 days in any 180-day Schengen period. Hungary operated a well-publicised White Card digital nomad residence permit, introduced in 2022 for non-EU remote workers earning above a set threshold from foreign sources, and it remains one of the few purpose-built schemes in the region; requirements and thresholds have been revised since launch, so check the current figures with a Hungarian consulate rather than relying on older summaries. Beyond that the usual routes are employment, study at the university, which has English-language medical and business programmes, or family reunification. Bureaucracy is real and generally conducted in Hungarian.
pecs.bestTime: Pécs enjoys a mild, almost Mediterranean pocket of climate by Hungarian standards, sheltered by the Mecsek hills, and it shows. May, June and September are the best months: warm, bright and comfortable, with the squares full and the surrounding wine country at its most pleasant. July and August get hot, into the low to mid thirties, though it is a dry heat and evenings on the terraces are the point of the season. Autumn is long and golden through October, and the Villany harvest festivals fall in this window. Winter, December to February, is cold, grey and damp rather than snowy, and the city is quiet with students away over Christmas. March and April are changeable. The academic year fills the city from late September. Almond trees flower on the hillsides here weeks before anything blooms elsewhere in the country, and a thousand-year-old one on the slope above the city is enough of a local emblem that the national tree competition began around it. That early blossom is the clearest sign of the sheltered pocket this city sits in. Fog fills the valley below on still cold mornings while the hill above stays in sun, which is worth the walk up to see.
pecs.prosCons: Pécs offers genuine European Union living at close to south-east Asian prices, with a two-thousand-year history that runs from Roman tombs through a surviving Ottoman mosque to a well-preserved Habsburg centre. It is warm by Hungarian standards, safe, walkable, and surrounded by good wine country. The university gives it energy and a supply of cheap flats. It pays for that in isolation: Budapest is three hours away and there is no airport at all. The international community is very small and the nomad scene effectively nonexistent. English is limited outside the university, and Hungarian is a difficult language with no useful cognates. Winter is long and grey. Anyone needing a professional network, frequent flights or an English-speaking environment will struggle here.
pecs.whoFor: Spend very little, live somewhere genuinely old and attractive, and provide your own company: that is the arrangement, and it suits a particular kind of person. The Hungarian White Card is the usual paperwork, and the university's English-language programmes account for most of everybody else. Writers and researchers come for the quiet, and anybody with a car and an interest in wine has the Villány region close by. Couples and solo workers who are comfortable in their own company will get the most from it. There is no existing foreign community to join, international travel means a long haul to Budapest first, and daily life cannot be conducted in English however willing the person opposite is. Budapest is the obvious alternative for those who want Hungary with all of that, at roughly double the rent.

rijeka.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Rijeka, which makes it markedly cheaper than Split or Dubrovnik for a city with better year-round infrastructure. A one-bedroom apartment near the centre runs about $500 to $700, and the hillside districts above the port drop that to $400 to $550. Because Rijeka is a working city rather than a resort, long leases are available on normal terms and do not vanish in summer, which is a real advantage over the Dalmatian coast. Groceries land around $250 to $320. A konoba lunch is $10 to $14, a restaurant dinner $22 to $32, and coffee about $2. A monthly transit pass is roughly $30. Utilities add $110 to $190, higher in the damp winter months. The changeover to the euro a couple of years ago rounded a great many prices upward and residents will tell you so at length, which is worth understanding when comparing figures written before it. Flats carry a monthly contribution to the building's reserve fund on top of the rent, small but separate. A tenancy registered with the tax office is what a residence application needs, and a landlord who would rather not register one is a landlord to walk away from.
rijeka.whereToWork: Rijeka has a modest coworking scene, with a few spaces in and around the centre charging roughly $110 to $180 a month, and the city's designation as European Capital of Culture in 2020 left behind some renovated cultural venues that double as working space. The Korzo, the main pedestrian street, and the streets running off it have plenty of cafes where a laptop is unremarkable, and Croatian coffee culture is famously unhurried, so nobody will move you along. Fixed-line internet is fast and mobile data is good and cheap within the EU roaming area. The practical advantage over the tourist coast is that all of this works in February as well as in August, when Split's cafes are full of visitors and its rents have tripled. The self-propelled torpedo was invented in this city in the eighteen sixties and the factory that built it still stands derelict by the water, which is the sort of industrial history the place has in quantity and has not yet decided what to do with. The shipyard up the coast has been in slow crisis for years. What that leaves is a city with cheap space and a great many unused buildings, which is why the cultural sector took root here rather than elsewhere.
rijeka.gettingAround: Rijeka is built on a narrow shelf between the Kvarner gulf and the hills, which makes it long, thin and steep. The centre is walkable end to end along the waterfront and the Korzo, but anything uphill is a serious climb and the city has stairs where other places have streets. An extensive bus network covers the rest, with a monthly pass at about $30. The main railway station connects to Zagreb in around four hours, which is slower than the bus at two and a half. Rijeka airport is on the island of Krk, 30km away, seasonal and small; Zagreb, Pula, Trieste and Ljubljana are all realistic alternatives within a few hours. Ferries run along the coast and to the Kvarner islands in season. A stone stairway of several hundred steps climbs from the river to the castle above the city, built as a pilgrims' route in the sixteenth century and still the most direct way up, which tells you something about how the place is arranged. The bridge out to the nearest island carries the airport traffic and is tolled. Buses to the villages along the coast run hourly through the summer and a good deal less often once the season ends.
rijeka.visas: Croatia is in the European Union, the Schengen area since January 2023, and the eurozone since the same date, so EU and EEA citizens may live and work here freely. Most other Western passports get 90 days in any 180-day Schengen period. Croatia was an early mover on remote work and its digital nomad residence permit, available since 2021, grants up to one year for non-EU nationals working for foreign employers, with an income threshold and proof of accommodation and health insurance required. It is not renewable directly, requiring a gap before reapplying. Notably, income earned under it is not subject to Croatian income tax, which is unusual among such schemes and one reason the permit has been popular. Years spent on the remote work permit leave no credit at all towards settlement, so it buys a year rather than a foothold, and the compulsory gap before reapplying means planning where to spend the months in between. A personal identification number is issued early in the process and is then asked for by every counter in the country. The criminal record certificate has to be apostilled where it was issued, which is the step people start too late.
rijeka.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months in Rijeka: warm, bright and free of the July and August crowds that fill the Kvarner coast. Summer is hot, into the low thirties, and the city empties towards the islands and beaches at Opatija and Lovran along the coast. Winter is mild by continental standards, around 10 degrees, but wet, and Rijeka is known for the bura, a fierce dry wind off the mountains that can blow for days and closes the coastal road. February brings the Rijeka Carnival, one of the largest in Europe and the single most distinctive thing in the local calendar. Because the city works year-round rather than seasonally, rents and services stay stable in a way the Dalmatian resorts do not manage.
rijeka.prosCons: Rijeka gives you the Croatian coast without the resort economy: real neighbourhoods, year-round rents, a working port, a university, and a cultural scene that outlasted its Capital of Culture year. It is cheaper than Split, better connected to central Europe, and has the Kvarner islands and the Ucka mountains within half an hour. The digital nomad permit is one of the better ones in the EU. It is not conventionally pretty: the centre is handsome Habsburg but the surroundings are industrial and socialist-era in equal measure. The bura wind is genuinely unpleasant.
