The coastal economy is tourism, cacao and what is left of the banana trade. Nothing here is hiring a foreigner, and the work permit rules are strict enough that the question rarely comes up.
puertoviejo.gettingAround: Puerto Viejo is a small town and the standard way to move is a bicycle: the coastal road running south through Playa Cocles, Chiquita and Punta Uva to Manzanillo is flat, shaded and lined with the beaches most people come for, and cycling it is a large part of the appeal. Scooters are common. Buses run along the coast and north to Limón and on to San José, a journey of about four and a half hours to the capital. There is no airport nearby; San José's Juan Santamaría is the international gateway, and the domestic strip at Limón has limited service. A car helps for supermarket runs to Limón but is not necessary for daily life. Panama is under an hour down the coast and the islands beyond that crossing are close enough that people go for a few days without much planning, which doubles as the standard way of resetting a stamp. The coastal road floods in the heavy months and the buses simply wait it out. Nothing along it is lit after dark, so a bicycle ridden home at night wants a lamp and a reflective strip rather than the optimism most people rely on.
puertoviejo.visas: Costa Rica grants most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, up to 180 days visa-free on arrival, which is one of the most generous allowances anywhere and covers a long stay without any paperwork. Costa Rica also introduced a digital nomad visa in 2022 for remote workers earning above a monthly threshold from foreign sources, granting one year with a one-year extension, exemption from income tax on that foreign income, and the ability to use a foreign driving licence for the duration. It is a well-designed scheme and one of the more attractive in the region. Longer-term residency routes include the pensionado, rentista and inversionista categories, all long established. Airlines check for onward travel before boarding and will refuse to carry somebody without it, which is a real problem for anyone intending an open-ended stay and the reason cheap throwaway bus tickets to the next country are sold specifically for the purpose. A departure tax is charged on the way out and is usually bundled into the fare, though not always. Anyone bringing a vehicle in on a tourist entry has to take it out again on the same timetable, and the two clocks are not linked.
puertoviejo.bestTime: The Caribbean coast runs on a different calendar from the rest of Costa Rica, which catches people out. The driest and most reliable months here are September and October, precisely when the Pacific side is at its wettest, and February and March are the other dry window. The heaviest rain falls in November, December, July and August. Temperatures barely move: it is around 30 degrees and humid all year. High season for visitors runs roughly December to April and again in July, when prices rise and the town is busy. Surf is best from December to March. Anyone planning around weather should ignore national dry-season advice and use the Caribbean pattern instead. Leatherback turtles come ashore to nest along this stretch of coast through the first half of the year, and the local project that patrols them takes volunteers on night walks, which is the best reason to be here outside the surf calendar. The reef break in front of town only works on a serious north swell and is heavy enough that most visitors watch rather than paddle out. Sandflies are worst on the sand at dawn and dusk, which nobody mentions until the first week is over.
puertoviejo.prosCons: Puerto Viejo is Afro-Caribbean Costa Rica: Creole cooking, calypso, English widely spoken alongside Spanish, and a stretch of coast where rainforest reaches the sand. The beaches south of town at Punta Uva and Manzanillo are among the best in the country, sloths and howler monkeys are ordinary daily sights, and Costa Rica's 180-day visa-free allowance and nomad visa make staying easy. It is expensive for the region, infrastructure is thin and the internet unreliable enough to matter, and the humidity never lets up at all. Petty theft is a known problem and requires ordinary care. The town has a party reputation that suits some and not others, and healthcare beyond a clinic means Limón or San José.
puertoviejo.whoFor: Jungle and Caribbean beach in one place, for anyone who can work around variable internet and whose budget absorbs Costa Rican prices. Surfers come first, and after them people who want wildlife within walking distance of where they sleep. The Costa Rican digital nomad visa and the long visa-free allowance both make the stay straightforward to arrange. The town is small, sociable and carries a long-stay foreign population that settled here years ago, not one that turns over every season. Guaranteed connectivity is not available, the heat is wet rather than dry, the costs are Costa Rican rather than cheap, and neither a coworking space nor a serious hospital is within easy reach. The Central Valley around San José and Atenas has the infrastructure; Tamarindo and Santa Teresa have the Pacific and more remote workers.

lafortuna.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,750 a month as a solo remote worker in La Fortuna, which is at the higher end for Central America and reflects both Costa Rican prices generally and this town's status as one of the country's busiest destinations. A one-bedroom place in town runs about $600 to $900 on a long lease, with properties out towards El Castillo or on the lake cheaper but requiring a car. Groceries land around $350 to $450. A casado at a soda is $6 to $9, a restaurant dinner aimed at visitors $20 to $35, and entry to the better hot springs $40 to $80, though the free river springs at Chollín cost nothing. Utilities add $70 to $130. Value added tax at thirteen percent sits on almost everything including services, and it is usually included in a quoted price but not always, so it is worth asking which. Imported goods carry duties on top of that, which is why a jar of something familiar costs several times what it would at home and why long-stayers learn to shop locally fast. Electricity is expensive by regional standards despite being generated close by, so a unit running all night shows up clearly on the bill.
lafortuna.whereToWork: La Fortuna has no coworking space and its economy is built almost entirely around tourism, so the working infrastructure is what your accommodation provides plus a handful of cafes in town that tolerate laptops. Connectivity is better than the setting suggests: fibre has reached the town centre and speeds are workable, though properties further out towards the lake or the volcano can be poor and should be tested before committing. Mobile 4G coverage is good in town and patchy in the surrounding forest. Power cuts happen in the wet season. Because the town runs on tourism, cafes are busy with day-trippers from mid-morning to late afternoon, which makes early starts the practical rhythm. The lake behind the town is a reservoir rather than a natural feature, dammed in the seventies for hydroelectricity, and between that and the wind turbines on its far shore the region generates a good share of the power the country runs on, which is a grid that is almost entirely renewable. Knowing that makes the occasional cut easier to understand, since the fault is usually a line down somewhere in the forest rather than a shortage. The tourism season sets the rhythm of everything else here.
lafortuna.gettingAround: La Fortuna is a small grid of streets around a central park with the volcano filling the sky to the west, and the town itself is walkable in fifteen minutes. Everything else requires transport: the hot springs, the waterfall, the hanging bridges and the national park entrance are all several kilometres out. Taxis are plentiful and cheap for short hops, and many residents keep a scooter or a car. Buses run to San José in about four and a half hours and to La Fortuna from Liberia and Monteverde. The famous jeep-boat-jeep transfer across Lake Arenal to Monteverde takes about three hours and is the standard route. San José's airport is the main international gateway. Private shuttles are how most visitors move between towns and they cost several times what the public bus does over the same ground, which is worth knowing when a hotel offers to book one. The road around the north side of the lake is slow, narrow and unsurfaced in places, so an hour on the map becomes most of a morning in practice. A four wheel drive is unnecessary in town and genuinely useful for anything up the side roads once the rains have set in.
lafortuna.visas: Costa Rica grants most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, up to 180 days visa-free on arrival, which is among the most generous allowances in the world and covers a very long stay with no paperwork at all. Costa Rica's digital nomad visa, introduced in 2022, offers one year with a one-year extension for remote workers earning above a monthly threshold from foreign sources, exempts that income from Costa Rican income tax, and lets holders use a foreign driving licence throughout. Longer-term residency runs through the well-established pensionado, rentista and inversionista categories. The country is politically stable and its immigration system is comparatively predictable, which is worth something in the region. Residency of any kind carries compulsory enrolment in the national health system, with a monthly contribution set against declared income, and it is a condition rather than a benefit to opt into. The generous entry allowance is granted at an officer's discretion rather than by right, and somebody who has been leaving and re-entering for years will eventually get a shorter stamp and a question about what they are doing. A driving licence from home stays valid only as long as the entry stamp does.
lafortuna.bestTime: La Fortuna sits in one of the wettest parts of Costa Rica, and rain is the defining variable. The driest stretch is roughly February to April, when the volcano is most reliably visible and the trails are firm. May to November is the green season, with rain most afternoons and heavier through September and October; mornings are often clear and this is when prices fall and the forest is at its most spectacular. Temperatures barely change: high twenties and humid all year. High season for visitors is December to April and again in July, when the town is busy and accommodation prices rise substantially. Arenal itself is frequently wrapped in cloud regardless of season, so patience is required.
lafortuna.prosCons: La Fortuna puts you under a near-perfect volcanic cone with rainforest, hot springs, waterfalls and Lake Arenal within a few kilometres, and Costa Rica's stability, healthcare and 180-day visa-free allowance behind it. Wildlife is abundant and ordinary here. The town is safe and well-serviced by regional standards. It is a tourist town first and a place to live second: prices are set for visitors, restaurants are aimed at them, and and the population turns over more or less constantly. It rains a great deal. There is no remote-work community, no coworking, and internet quality is address-dependent. Anything requiring a city, from specialist healthcare to a professional network, means San José four hours away.
lafortuna.whoFor: The idea is to live inside a landscape rather than in a town, which asks for Costa Rican money and work that tolerates a moderate connection. Hikers and birders are the core of it, along with anybody who wants rainforest and hot springs to be an ordinary feature of the day instead of an excursion. A few months on Costa Rica's long visa-free allowance is the natural shape of a stay. Couples and outdoor-minded solo workers do best. There is no nomad community, the weather is wet by design since that is what makes the rainforest, the costs are high for the region, and coworking and a beach are both absent. Costa Rica's Pacific coast towns and the Central Valley around Atenas answer those better, and Puerto Viejo offers the Caribbean alternative.

durban.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,050 a month as a solo remote worker in Durban, which makes it the cheapest of South Africa's three main cities by some distance. A one-bedroom apartment in Morningside, Glenwood or Umhlanga runs about $350 to $550, with secure complexes at the upper end and older buildings in the city centre far cheaper, though location matters here more than price. Groceries land around $250 to $320. A bunny chow, Durban's own dish, is $4 to $6, a good curry $8 to $12, and a restaurant dinner with wine $18 to $28. South African wine is excellent and cheap. Utilities add $90 to $170, and many residents budget for backup power given the country's load-shedding history. Electricity is usually prepaid on a meter topped up by app or at a shop, which makes the cost visible in a way a monthly bill never is and turns a cold snap into an immediate decision. A flat in a secure complex carries a monthly levy on top of the rent covering the guards, the grounds and often the water, and that levy is the figure to ask for rather than the headline. Municipal rates fall on the owner but are frequently passed through in the rent.
durban.whereToWork: Durban has a growing coworking scene, concentrated in Umhlanga Ridge to the north and in the Station Drive precinct and Glenwood closer to the centre, with desks at roughly $130 to $220 a month. Umhlanga in particular has become the business centre of the region and has the newer buildings and the more reliable infrastructure. Cafe working is normal in Glenwood, Morningside and Florida Road. Fixed-line fibre is widely available and fast in the better suburbs. Electricity was the critical local consideration for a decade and has stopped being one: South Africa's load-shedding ended in May 2025 and the grid carried the 2026 winter without a stage. The inverters the better buildings fitted are still worth asking about, because this coast loses power to summer storms on its own account. Local time is two hours ahead of London for half the year and one for the other half, so a European working day lands almost entirely inside the afternoon here, which is why the outsourcing industry set up in this country in the first place. That sector employs tens of thousands locally and is the most visible white-collar employer outside the port. Water interruptions are the other recurring risk alongside the electricity, and a building with a tank of its own is worth asking about.
durban.gettingAround: Durban is spread along the coast and a car is close to essential for most residents, which is the honest position for all of South Africa's cities. The Golden Mile beachfront promenade is excellent for walking and cycling and runs for several kilometres. Public transport exists in the form of the People Mover bus along the beachfront and minibus taxis covering everything else, though the latter are not generally recommended to newcomers. Ride-hailing apps are widely used, reliable and inexpensive, and many residents rely on them entirely rather than owning a car. King Shaka international airport is about 35 minutes north and connects to Johannesburg, Cape Town and a growing list of international destinations. The commuter rail network that once served this city was stripped and vandalised during the pandemic years and has only partially returned, which is why nobody plans a journey around it. The container port below the bluff is the busiest on the continent, and the trucks feeding it fill the inland highway for the first hour of any drive out. That highway climbs steeply towards the interior and carries most of the freight in this half of the country, which shows in the state of the surface.
durban.visas: South Africa grants most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, 90 days visa-free on arrival. In 2024 South Africa introduced a remote work visitor visa, its digital nomad visa, for foreign remote workers earning above a substantial annual threshold, which was a significant change after years of having no such route. Details and thresholds have been adjusted since introduction, so confirm the current requirements with a South African mission rather than relying on early coverage. Extensions of the visitor visa are possible but the process is slow. Longer-term routes include the critical skills work visa, which covers a defined list of occupations, and business or spousal visas. Long-term applications ask for a medical report and a chest radiograph alongside everything else, and both have to be recent enough that obtaining them too early simply wastes the fee. A points-based work route was introduced recently to sit beside the occupation list, which widened the field a little for people whose job title never appeared on it. Renewals go through a contracted centre rather than an office, and the appointment has to be booked before the current permit expires or the whole thing is treated as a fresh application.
durban.bestTime: Durban is subtropical and warm all year, which is its main draw within South Africa. April to September is the best window: dry, sunny, daytime highs in the low to mid twenties, and sea temperatures that stay swimmable through the winter, which is not true anywhere else in the country. This is also when Johannesburg residents come down for the school holidays, so July is busy. Summer, November to March, is hot and humid, into the low thirties with high humidity and afternoon thunderstorms, and the sea is very warm. The Sardine Run, when huge shoals move up the coast, usually falls between June and July. Cyclone risk is low but heavy rain events have caused serious flooding in recent years.
durban.prosCons: Durban gives you warm ocean twelve months a year, the best Indian food outside India, a long beachfront promenade, the Drakensberg mountains three hours inland and game reserves within reach, all at prices well below Cape Town. The city has a distinctive Zulu and Indian character that neither of the other big South African cities shares. Crime is a genuine and serious consideration that shapes daily decisions about where to live and walk, and this should be researched honestly rather than waved away or ignored. The city centre has declined and most middle-class life happens in the northern suburbs. Water interruptions occur, and load-shedding, which ended nationally in 2025, is no longer the drag on a working week that it was here for a decade. Public transport is inadequate and a car or ride-hailing budget is necessary.
durban.whoFor: Warm sea and low costs, on the condition that you take South African security seriously and organise your life accordingly. Surfers and divers are well served, the food alone justifies a longer stay, and the Drakensberg and the KwaZulu-Natal game reserves are both close enough to make this a base rather than a destination. It works for those on the new remote work visa or the critical skills route. It is a reasonable family option in the northern suburbs, which have good schools. Planning around crime is not optional here, living car-free is not realistic, and the international remote-work community that exists elsewhere in the country has not formed in this city. Cape Town has that community and the scenery, at roughly double the rent.

knysna.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Knysna, which sits in the middle of the South African range and reflects its status as a well-established Garden Route town. A one-bedroom place in Knysna proper or in Leisure Isle and Brenton runs about $400 to $650, with lagoon views commanding a premium and holiday-let demand tightening the market over Christmas and Easter. Groceries land around $260 to $330. Knysna oysters, the town's signature, are cheap at source. A pub lunch is $8 to $12, a restaurant dinner with wine $20 to $30. Utilities add $90 to $170, with backup power a common additional cost given South Africa's electricity record. Water is metered and restricted in dry years, and the municipal tariff steps up sharply once a household crosses a threshold, which makes a garden an expensive habit. Private medical cover is close to essential, since the public hospitals in the region are stretched, and it is a real monthly line rather than a precaution. Anything ordered online arrives slowly, because the courier networks treat this coast as a spur rather than a route, and the local shops price accordingly.
knysna.whereToWork: Knysna is a small town of around 70,000 and has a modest coworking presence serving a mix of local business and the semigration crowd who have moved down from Johannesburg and Cape Town, with desks at roughly $110 to $180 a month. Cafes around the waterfront and on Main Street are comfortable with laptops. Fibre has been rolled out well in the town and speeds are good, which is one reason Knysna has attracted remote workers. Electricity is no longer the persistent constraint it was: the national cuts ended in May 2025 and none has been scheduled since. Ask about backup power anyway, because the forest and the lagoon mean a lot of overhead line in a small area, and outages here have always owed as much to weather as to anything the national grid was doing. The clock here gives you the entire European working day without an early start, which is the best single reason to base a business in this country and why the relocation crowd keeps its European clients. Anyone working seriously keeps two connections, a fibre line and a mobile router on a different network, because the failure modes are independent of each other. The arrivals from the cities brought their own professional networks with them rather than joining a local one.
knysna.gettingAround: Knysna is strung along the N2 between the lagoon and the forested hills, and a car is effectively necessary: the beaches at Buffalo Bay and Brenton, the forest trails, and the neighbouring towns of Plettenberg Bay and Sedgefield are all a drive away. The town centre and the waterfront are walkable. There is minimal public transport beyond minibus taxis. The Garden Route is designed around driving and most residents and visitors do exactly that, with the N2 running from Cape Town in about six hours and Port Elizabeth in three. George airport is about an hour west and connects to Johannesburg and Cape Town, which makes Knysna far better linked than its size suggests. The tourist railway that once ran along this coast closed after storm damage in 2006 and was never restored, so the road is the only way through. Long-distance coaches stop here on the run between the two big coastal cities and are cheap and reliable, which is the alternative to driving for anyone travelling alone. Driving the rural stretches after dark is the thing residents avoid, rather than the towns themselves.
knysna.visas: South Africa grants most Western passports 90 days visa-free on arrival, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian citizens. The remote work visitor visa introduced in 2024 is South Africa's first purpose-built route for foreign remote workers and requires an annual income above a substantial threshold; the figures and conditions have been revised since launch, so check with a South African mission for the current position. Extensions to the standard visitor visa are possible but the process is slow and best started early. Other routes include the critical skills work visa for listed occupations, business visas, and retirement visas, the last of which has long been popular along the Garden Route. Any application longer than a visitor stamp wants a police certificate from every country lived in for more than a year, and assembling those takes longer than the rest of the file put together. Applications are lodged abroad through a contracted visa centre rather than at the mission itself. The visitor stamp is given on arrival without discussion, but the officer writes the date by hand, so it is worth reading what was actually written before leaving the desk.
knysna.bestTime: The Garden Route has a mild climate with rain spread across the year rather than concentrated in a season, which is unusual for South Africa. February to April is generally the best window: warm, settled, and after the December and January holiday crush has passed. Spring, September to November, is also good and brings wildflowers and whale watching along the coast, with southern right whales present from roughly June to November. Winter, June to August, is cool and damp, around 18 degrees in the day, and quiet. December and January are the South African summer holidays, when the population of the town multiplies, prices rise sharply and accommodation must be booked months ahead. The fires of 2017 came through the plantations and the edges of the town in a single afternoon, and fire season is now part of how residents read a hot dry wind rather than an abstraction. Whales pass close enough to be watched from the cliffs without a boat between winter and spring. The lagoon is at its best on a still morning before the wind gets up.
knysna.prosCons: Knysna sits on a lagoon between indigenous forest and the sea, and the setting is the whole point: it is one of the most attractive small towns in South Africa, with good fibre, a mild year-round climate, an established community of people who have relocated for exactly these reasons, and George airport an hour away. Costs are moderate and the food and wine are very good. The town is small and can feel closed, and a car is not optional here. The 2017 wildfires did significant damage and fire risk remains a live concern. Water restrictions appear in dry summers, and the national power cuts that shaped the last decade here ended in 2025, though the local lines still come down in a storm. Crime is lower than in the big cities but not absent, and the seasonal holiday influx transforms the town twice a year.
knysna.whoFor: Small-town South Africa with good infrastructure and dramatic surroundings, and a car. People who hike, sail, dive or mountain bike have the most to work with, and families relocating find decent schools in a quiet place. Anybody drawn to the Garden Route gets a base here with considerably more substance behind it than Plettenberg Bay has ever managed. Retirees and semigrants make up much of the incoming population. Living car-free is not possible on this stretch of coast, a professional network of any size does not exist here, and city amenities are six hours away in Cape Town. Cape Town is six hours away and answers all of those.

puertovaras.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Puerto Varas, which is mid-range for Chile and reflects the town's popularity with domestic tourists and relocating Santiaguinos. A one-bedroom apartment in town runs about $450 to $700, with lake views at the upper end and properties out towards Puerto Montt cheaper. Groceries land around $300 to $380; Chilean supermarkets are expensive relative to income and the local ferias are better value. A lunch menu is $8 to $12, a restaurant dinner with wine $22 to $32, and Chilean wine is excellent and inexpensive. Utilities add $110 to $200, with heating a substantial winter cost in a genuinely wet and cold climate. Rents and most contracts here are written in UF, an inflation-indexed unit rather than pesos, so the figure in the lease converts to a slightly different number every month and the peso amount is never quite what it was. A RUT, the tax identity number, is asked for at the supermarket till as well as by the bank, and obtaining one is the first administrative job of any stay. Landlords usually want a local guarantor or a large advance from a foreigner, which is the real barrier to a long let rather than the price itself.
puertovaras.whereToWork: Puerto Varas has a small coworking presence serving local business, tourism operators and a growing number of relocated professionals, with desks at roughly $130 to $200 a month. Cafes along the lakefront and in the centre are comfortable with laptops and the German-influenced kuchen culture makes the coffee stops pleasant. Chilean internet is among the best in Latin America: fibre is widely available, fast and reasonably priced, and mobile coverage is good. That reliability is a real advantage over most of the continent. Puerto Montt, 20 minutes south, is the regional commercial centre and has more of everything if a bigger city is needed occasionally. Salmon farming runs out of the port city south of here and dominates the regional economy, which is why the professional population skews towards engineers, veterinarians and logistics people rather than anything resembling a creative sector. The German-descended community keeps its own schools and clubs and has done since the nineteenth century settlement, and that network is a working part of local life rather than a heritage display. Working hours start early and the midday break is long enough to count as a real one.
puertovaras.gettingAround: Puerto Varas is compact and walkable, laid out along the shore of Lake Llanquihue with the Osorno volcano across the water. Local buses and colectivo shared taxis connect it to Puerto Montt, Frutillar and Puerto Octay cheaply and frequently. Most residents who plan to explore the Lakes District keep a car, which opens up Vicente Pérez Rosales national park, the Petrohué falls, the hot springs and the road towards Argentina over the Cardenal Samoré pass. Long-distance buses run north to Santiago, a long overnight journey, and El Tepual airport at Puerto Montt is 30 minutes away with frequent flights to Santiago and connections onward, including to Patagonia.
puertovaras.visas: Chile grants most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, 90 days visa-free on arrival. Chile does not operate a dedicated digital nomad visa, but it has a well-established temporary residence system, and the temporary residence visa for those with means or professional activity has historically been the route foreigners use. Chile's immigration law was substantially reformed in 2021 and applications for most categories must now be made from outside the country rather than converted in-country, which changed a long-standing practice and catches people out. Anyone planning more than 90 days should start the process from abroad and take current advice, as procedures have shifted since the reform. Leaving for a day and coming back resets nothing, since the reform closed the practice of stacking tourist entries and officers record the pattern. An application filed from abroad can take many months to resolve, and the applicant is expected to wait outside the country while it does. Anyone who does hold residence gets an identity number that unlocks contracts, banking and health cover, and almost everything in ordinary life runs through that number rather than through a passport.
puertovaras.bestTime: December to March is the southern summer and clearly the best season in Puerto Varas: long days, temperatures in the high teens to low twenties, the volcanoes visible, and the lake and the national parks at their best. This is also the domestic holiday season, so the town is busy and prices rise. Autumn, March and April, is quieter and often still fine. Winter, June to August, is cold, dark and very wet: this is one of the rainier parts of Chile, with rainfall spread through the year and concentrated in winter, and short days at 41 degrees south. Ski season at Osorno runs through it. Spring is unpredictable. Rain is possible in any month. Calbuco, the second volcano visible from the town, erupted without warning in April 2015 and put an ash column fifteen kilometres into the air, closing airports across the south and dusting the streets here. Both peaks are monitored continuously and the alert level is published, which is something residents check rather than worry about. The lake is large enough to make its own weather, so a clear morning across the water is not a forecast for the afternoon.
puertovaras.prosCons: Puerto Varas is one of the most attractive small towns in Chile: German-founded, wooden-shingled, set on a large lake with two snow-capped volcanoes across the water and Patagonia beginning just south. Chile has the best internet and the most stable institutions in South America, the food and wine are excellent, and the national parks are extraordinary. It rains a great deal here, and the winter is long, dark and properly cold. Costs are high for the continent. Chile's post-2021 immigration reform makes long stays harder to arrange than they once were. The nomad community is minimal, with most of Chile's remote workers in Santiago or Valparaíso, and Spanish is essential.
puertovaras.whoFor: The Chilean Lakes District as a daily backdrop, if you can handle rain and a long winter. Hikers, kayakers, climbers and skiers all have something to work with, and anybody heading to or from Patagonia gets a comfortable place to break the journey. Chile's infrastructure and its stability are the quiet argument underneath all of it. Couples and families are well served, in a town that is safe and where the local schooling holds up. Sun is rationed at this latitude, there is no nomad scene, the costs are Chilean rather than cheap, and no straightforward route exists for staying past ninety days. Santiago has the flights, the community and the jobs; Valparaíso has the coast and more life. Arriving for a southern summer and leaving before June is what most foreigners here actually do, and it is a defensible plan rather than a failure of nerve. Anyone intending to stay through a winter should rent somewhere with proper heating and ask what it costs to run before signing, because the answer separates a pleasant winter from a miserable one.

vinadelmar.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,450 a month as a solo remote worker in Viña del Mar, which is at the higher end for Chile outside Santiago and reflects its status as the country's main coastal resort. A one-bedroom apartment near the centre or in Reñaca runs about $500 to $750, with ocean views commanding a clear premium and the inland districts cheaper. Summer rents from January to February rise sharply as Santiago empties towards the coast. Groceries land around $300 to $380. A lunch menu is $8 to $12, a seafood dinner with wine $22 to $35, and coffee about $3. A monthly transit pass is roughly $30. Utilities add $90 to $170, with little heating needed in the mild coastal climate.
vinadelmar.whereToWork: Viña del Mar has a reasonable coworking presence, some of it shared with neighbouring Valparaíso, at roughly $130 to $210 a month, and the two cities function as a single labour market. Several Chilean universities have campuses here, which supports a good supply of laptop-friendly cafes, particularly around Plaza Vergara and along Avenida San Martín. Chilean internet is the best in Latin America: widespread fibre, fast, and reasonably priced, with strong mobile coverage. Valparaíso next door has more of the creative and startup community, and many people live in Viña for the flats and the beaches while working or socialising in Valparaíso, which is fifteen minutes by metro. A tax number is the key to ordinary life here, needed before a lease, a phone contract or a bank account, and it is issued to foreigners on an application that does not require residence, which makes it the first errand rather than the last. Invoicing runs through a state electronic system, so a freelancer billing locally files every invoice with the revenue service as it is issued. Earthquakes are a working consideration rather than a curiosity: the buildings are engineered for them, the power is not always, and anyone whose income depends on a connection keeps a charged battery.
vinadelmar.gettingAround: Viña del Mar is laid out on a grid behind its beaches and is walkable in the centre. The Metro Valparaíso commuter line runs along the coast, connecting Viña to Valparaíso in about fifteen minutes and inland to Limache, and it is clean, cheap and the backbone of local transport. Micros, the local buses, and colectivo shared taxis cover everything else. A car is not necessary. Santiago is about ninety minutes away by frequent intercity bus, which is comfortable and inexpensive, and the capital's international airport is the gateway for anything beyond South America. The coastal road north towards Concón and Maitencillo has the better beaches and is served by bus. The highway inland is tolled at two points and the booths back up badly on a Sunday evening when the weekend traffic goes home, which is the one time the bus is slower than the timetable claims. Within the city the grid ends where the hills begin, and the streets above it climb steeply enough that the buses take the long way round rather than the direct one. The dunes on the northern edge are a protected remnant of a much larger system and the coast road skirts them, which is why the drive north is prettier than a map suggests.
vinadelmar.visas: Chile grants most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, 90 days visa-free on arrival. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa. The temporary residence system is the route for longer stays, and Chile's 2021 immigration reform changed the practice substantially: most visa categories must now be applied for from outside Chile rather than converted from a tourist entry inside the country, which was the previous norm. This catches out people who arrive intending to sort it out later. Anyone planning to stay beyond 90 days should apply from abroad and take current advice, as the rules and processing times have continued to change since the reform took effect. Once a residence visa is granted there are two further steps that trip people up: registering with the investigations police within thirty days of entering, and then applying for the identity card at the civil registry, since that card is what every other counter will ask to see. Neither happens automatically and the clock on the first is short. Time spent on a tourist stamp counts for nothing towards permanent residence, so a year of coming and going leaves you exactly where you started when the permanent application is finally made.
vinadelmar.bestTime: December to March is the southern summer and the height of the season in Viña del Mar: warm, dry, and packed, as Santiago decamps to the coast in January and February. Prices rise and the beaches fill. The water, however, is cold year-round thanks to the Humboldt current, and swimming is a brisk business regardless of air temperature. Spring and autumn, October to November and March to April, are the pleasantest months for actually living here: mild, bright and far quieter. Winter, June to August, is cool and damp at around 14 degrees, with grey coastal cloud, though it rarely gets truly cold. The Viña del Mar International Song Festival in February is the town's largest event. Rain here falls almost entirely in the winter half of the year and there has been much less of it than there used to be, since central Chile has been in a long drought that has changed how the hills look and how the water is rationed. Morning cloud off the sea is the daily pattern for much of the year and usually burns off by midday. The new year fireworks over the bay pull hundreds of thousands of people onto this coast, and a bed for that night is booked months rather than weeks ahead.
vinadelmar.prosCons: Viña del Mar gives you a Chilean beach city with real infrastructure: a metro, universities, fibre internet, good healthcare and Valparaíso's culture fifteen minutes away, all ninety minutes from Santiago and its international airport. It is greener and more orderly than its neighbour, with parks, a casino and long beaches. Chile is the most stable and best-connected country in South America. It is expensive by continental standards, the sea is cold enough that swimming is rare, and the summer influx makes January and February both crowded and pricey at once. The nomad community is small and mostly in Santiago. Spanish is essential, and Chilean Spanish is famously fast and idiomatic.
vinadelmar.whoFor: A comfortable, well-serviced coastal base in South America, with excellent internet and a capital city an easy trip away. Valparaíso's arts and startup scene sits next door, which is most of the point of being here. Beaches and parks come without giving up urban infrastructure, and the rest of Chile opens out from this coast easily enough. Families are the group best served, with decent schools and a green, safe city to use them in. The Humboldt current keeps the water cold enough to discourage swimming, the costs are Chilean rather than low, very few other remote workers are around, and the long-stay visa position is awkward. Valparaíso is cheaper and more characterful; Santiago has the jobs, the flights and the people.

arugambay.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Arugam Bay, which makes it one of the cheapest coastal bases in Asia. A room or small apartment in or near the main strip runs about $200 to $350 on a long stay, with beachfront cabanas more and inland options in Pottuvil less. Prices swing hard with the season: from May to September rates rise with the surf crowd and from November to March many places close or negotiate heavily. Groceries land around $130 to $180. A rice and curry lunch is $2 to $4, a beachfront dinner $7 to $12, and a Lion beer about $2.50. A scooter rental is $60 to $90 a month. Boards, fins and anything technical carry heavy import duty, so replacing a snapped board here costs a multiple of what it would at home and everyone brings spares. A room rate agreed before the swell arrives holds for the season, while the same room asked about in the middle of it costs twice as much. Ask whether electricity is included, because a fan and a fridge running all day sit on a meter the owner reads, and a bill settled at the end of a month can be a shock.
arugambay.whereToWork: Arugam Bay has no coworking space and its infrastructure is that of a small surf village. Remote workers work from their guesthouse or from the cafes along the main road, several of which have grown up around long-staying surfers and are used to laptops. The genuine constraint is connectivity: fixed-line internet is limited and variable, and this is not a place to rely on a fixed connection. Most people work off mobile data, which is cheap in Sri Lanka and where 4G coverage in the bay is reasonable, and a local SIM with a generous data package is the standard first purchase. Power cuts occur. Anyone with heavy video-call requirements should test before committing. The surrounding area is largely Muslim and the surf strip is a thin layer over a town that runs on fishing and farming, which shows in what is open on a Friday and in how people dress away from the sand. Most of the businesses on the strip are staffed by people who come across the island for the season and leave when it ends, so whoever remembers you in July will not be here in December. Ramadan shifts the opening hours of everything not aimed at visitors.
arugambay.gettingAround: Arugam Bay is a single road running behind the beach for a couple of kilometres, and walking covers most of it. A scooter is the standard way to reach the surf points at Whiskey Point, Peanut Farm and Elephant Rock, and to get to Pottuvil town for the bank and the larger shops. Tuk-tuks are everywhere and cheap. Getting to Arugam Bay is the effort: it is on the far east coast, about eight to ten hours from Colombo by road or bus, though a domestic flight to Batticaloa or Ampara shortens that considerably. Kumana national park and the eastern route to Ella and the hill country both start from here. Wild elephants use the roads around here after dark and a collision with one is not survivable on two wheels, so the local advice about not riding at night is meant literally rather than offered as caution. A foreign driving licence has to be endorsed locally before it covers a motorbike, and riding without that endorsement voids most travel insurance as well as being an offence. Helmets are required and enforced on the main road, if not always on the sand tracks.
arugambay.visas: Sri Lanka requires most visitors to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorization before arrival, granting 30 days initially, which can be extended in-country to 90 days and in some cases up to six months through the Department of Immigration. The system and its fees have changed several times in recent years, including a period of free visas for selected nationalities, so check the current position before travelling rather than relying on older guidance. Sri Lanka has announced work on a digital nomad visa but as of writing the standard tourist visa and its extensions remain the practical route. Extension is done in Colombo or online and is generally straightforward. Buying land outright is not open to foreigners, who take a long lease instead, and a surf-town property advertised for sale to an outsider is usually a lease or a company structure rather than a title, which is worth having a lawyer explain before any money moves. A resident guest scheme exists for people bringing in a substantial sum and buys several years of residence. Overstaying is charged by the day and settled at the airport, and the officers there do check the arrival stamp against the calendar.
arugambay.bestTime: Arugam Bay runs on the opposite calendar to Sri Lanka's more famous west and south coasts, which is the single most important thing to know about it. The season here is roughly May to September, when the southwest monsoon brings dry, sunny weather to the east coast and the surf works: this is when the village is alive, the businesses are open and the crowd arrives. From November to March the northeast monsoon brings rain to this coast, most businesses close, and the bay is very quiet. April and October are transitional. If you want the community and the surf, come in the middle of the year; if you want solitude and low prices, come outside it and accept that little will be open.
arugambay.prosCons: Arugam Bay offers a world-class point break, a long sweep of sand, very low costs and a genuinely relaxed village atmosphere that has survived its growing fame better than most surf towns. Sri Lankan food is excellent, the people are welcoming, and the east coast is far less developed than the south. Kumana national park and the hill country are within reach. The infrastructure is basic, and that is the whole of it: the infrastructure is basic: internet is the weak point and should not be assumed, power is intermittent, and healthcare beyond a local clinic means a long drive. The village effectively closes for half the year. It is remote from Colombo, and Sri Lanka's economic difficulties since 2022 have made supply and prices less predictable.
arugambay.whoFor: Surfers who can work off mobile data and want to spend very little while living on a beach are the entire audience. The May to September east coast season is what the whole plan has to be built around, because outside it the place empties. Solo travellers find a social scene already assembled around the surf, and asynchronous work fits far better here than a calendar full of scheduled calls ever will. Connectivity cannot be relied on, the services close with the season, the nearest real hospital is hours away, and nothing here resembles a professional environment in any month. Colombo has the infrastructure, Galle and the south coast have the season that runs from November, and Ella has the hill country.

dianibeach.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $950 a month as a solo remote worker in Diani Beach, which is inexpensive for a coastline of this quality. A one-bedroom apartment or cottage a few minutes from the sand runs about $300 to $500 on a long lease, with beachfront and serviced options considerably more and inland Ukunda cheaper. Groceries land around $200 to $280, with local markets far cheaper than the supermarkets that stock imported goods for the expatriate market. A local meal is $3 to $5, a beach restaurant dinner $12 to $20, and a Tusker beer about $2. A tuk-tuk down the beach road is under a dollar. Utilities add $60 to $120, and many people budget for backup power. A night guard is an ordinary household line here rather than a sign of trouble, and one shared between a few houses on a lane costs very little each. Water on this coast often arrives by tanker in the dry months even where there is a mains connection, so a house with its own tank is worth more than the rent difference implies. Landlords commonly ask three or six months up front from a foreigner, which makes the first payment the real barrier rather than the monthly figure.
dianibeach.whereToWork: Diani has a genuine and slightly surprising remote-work scene: it has been promoted for several years as a base for the sector and has at least one established coworking space on the beach road, with desks at roughly $120 to $200 a month, plus several cafes and beach clubs entirely used to laptops. That makes it an outlier on the East African coast. Connectivity is the reason it works: fibre is available along the main road and Kenyan mobile data is cheap, fast and reliable, with M-Pesa handling payments for almost everything. Power cuts happen and a backup is normal. The community is small but real, and skews towards people staying months rather than weeks. Local time sits three hours ahead of London and one ahead of most of the continent to the north, which puts a European working day squarely inside the afternoon here and is a large part of why the place works for anyone billing to Europe. The season shapes the company: desks fill between about November and March and thin out afterwards, so a stay timed for the quiet months is cheaper and lonelier in equal measure. Nothing local hires foreigners outside the hotels and the dive schools.
dianibeach.gettingAround: Diani is a single road running parallel to about ten kilometres of beach, with side lanes down to the sand, and tuk-tuks are the universal transport: they cost a dollar or two for most trips and are everywhere. Matatu minibuses run the main road cheaply. Many residents rent a motorbike or a car for trips further afield. Ukunda airstrip is right in Diani and has daily flights to Nairobi, which is the practical route in and out and takes about an hour. Mombasa is roughly an hour and a half north including the Likoni ferry crossing, which can be very slow at peak times; the new Dongo Kundu bypass has improved this considerably. The standard gauge railway from the capital is the alternative to flying and takes about six hours to a terminus on the far side of the big city, from where a taxi finishes the job. It is comfortable and cheap and books out at holidays. Motorcycle taxis fill the gaps the three-wheelers leave and are how most people get down a sand lane to a house. The border with the next country south is under two hours away, which turns a visa run into a day trip rather than an expedition.
dianibeach.visas: Kenya moved in January 2024 from a visa system to an Electronic Travel Authorisation that all visitors must obtain online before arrival, which despite being described as visa-free is a mandatory paid application. It generally grants 90 days. In 2024 Kenya announced a Class N digital nomad work permit for remote workers earning above an annual threshold from foreign sources, aimed squarely at the coast and at Diani in particular, granting an initial period with renewal possible. Implementation details have evolved, so confirm the current requirements with a Kenyan mission. East African Tourist Visa arrangements covering Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda also exist for multi-country travel. The travel authorisation is granted for a single entry, so a weekend across a border means applying again and paying again, and that is what trips up anyone planning a loop through several countries. Extending a stay is done in person at an immigration office in one of the big cities rather than locally. Ordinary work permits are sponsored by a company and carry a serious annual fee, which is why the remote worker category was created at all and why the older routes were never realistic for a freelancer.
dianibeach.bestTime: December to March is the best season in Diani: hot, dry, and with the clearest water for diving and snorkelling on the reef. July to October is the second window, cooler and dry, and this is when the humpback whales pass. The long rains fall roughly from late March through May and are the wettest part of the year, when some businesses close and the sea is churned up; the short rains in November are lighter. Temperatures are consistently high, high twenties to low thirties, with humidity to match. The kaskazi and kusi monsoon winds shape the seasons and the kitesurfing calendar, with the best wind generally from December to March and again in June to August.
dianibeach.prosCons: Diani has one of the best beaches in the world by most measures, and unusually for East Africa it has the infrastructure to work from: fibre, a coworking space, an airstrip with daily Nairobi flights, and a small established remote-work community. Costs are low, the food is good, and Kenya's mobile money system makes daily life frictionless. Marine parks, Shimba Hills and a coral reef are all close. The Kenyan coast has a security history that requires attention to what the current government travel advice says, particularly regarding areas further north. Power cuts occur, healthcare beyond a good local clinic means Mombasa or Nairobi, and the beach road is developing fast and not always attractively.
dianibeach.whoFor: Diani suits remote workers who want a genuinely beautiful tropical coast with functioning infrastructure and low costs, and who are drawn to Africa rather than the well-worn Asian and Latin American circuits. Divers and kitesurfers are the obvious audience, and safari access is close enough to fold into the plan instead of standing as a separate trip. Solo workers and couples both settle in easily, and the community here is small enough that being isolated takes more effort than at most beach bases. Checking travel advisories before booking is not optional on this coast, first-rate healthcare means a flight to Nairobi, and the amenities of a large city are simply not part of the offer. Nairobi has the infrastructure and the professional scene; Zanzibar is the obvious regional alternative on the coast.

hurghada.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Hurghada, which makes it one of the cheapest places on any warm sea. A one-bedroom apartment in El Kawther, El Mamsha or Dahar runs about $200 to $350 on a long lease, and this is a market with enormous supply thanks to years of resort construction, so bargaining works and sea views are affordable. Groceries land around $130 to $190. A koshary or local lunch is $2 to $4, a restaurant dinner $8 to $15, and a coffee about $1.50. A dive with a local centre is $30 to $45. Utilities add $40 to $90, dominated by summer air conditioning. Egyptian currency movements make budgeting in dollars sensible.
hurghada.whereToWork: Hurghada has a small coworking presence catering to a mostly Russian, Ukrainian and German resident population, with desks around $70 to $130 a month, plus a good number of cafes along El Mamsha and in the newer districts that are entirely used to laptops. The remote-work population here is substantial but informal, and much of it is Russian-speaking, which shapes the social scene. Connectivity is decent: fibre has reached the main residential areas and Egyptian mobile data is cheap with good coverage. The recurring practical issues are power interruptions during summer peak load and Egypt's periodic restrictions on some voice-over-internet services, which is worth checking before relying on a specific calling platform. Diving is an industry here rather than a pastime, and the instructor and boat economy is what most foreign residents are actually employed in, which shapes everything from the rental market to when the bars are busy. Seasonality is sharper than the weather implies: the charter flights set the rhythm, and a town full in one month can be half empty in the next under the same sunshine. Anyone working to a European clock will find the offset small enough to ignore, and that is a quiet part of why this coast works at all.
hurghada.gettingAround: Hurghada is strung along about 40 kilometres of coast, from Dahar in the north through Sekalla and El Mamsha to the resort strips at Sahl Hasheesh and Makadi Bay in the south, so it is not a walking city between districts though each is walkable within itself. Microbuses run the main road for well under a dollar and are the local way to move. Taxis and ride-hailing apps are cheap and widely used. Many residents keep a scooter. Hurghada international airport is central and served by a large number of European charter and scheduled routes, which is one of the town's genuine advantages. Buses run to Cairo in about five hours and to Luxor in four. There is no railway anywhere on this coast, which is why every long journey begins on a bus, and the road inland to the valley crosses a range of bare mountains with checkpoints along it where a passport gets looked at. The coastal highway runs north for hours past resort after resort and is the way to reach the rest of the shoreline. Within town the microbuses have no route numbers and no stops, so the way to learn the network is to ask which direction a driver is going and get in.
hurghada.visas: Egypt grants most Western passports a 30-day visa on arrival, purchased at the airport, or through an e-Visa obtained online in advance, and this is renewable in-country at a passport office. Longer stays are usually handled by repeated renewals, which is a well-established if bureaucratic practice, and many long-term foreign residents in Hurghada operate this way. Egypt has discussed a digital nomad visa but as of writing has not implemented one, so there is no purpose-built route. Property ownership by foreigners is permitted and is a common basis for longer residence applications, which is one reason the Red Sea resorts have such a large permanent foreign population. Renewals are handled at the local passport office rather than in the capital, a real advantage of basing yourself on this coast, and the queue is shorter than the reputation of the system suggests. Bring the original entry card, since losing it turns a routine renewal into a week of letters. Overstaying is settled as a fine at the airport on the way out, and while people do it, the fine rises with the length and a long one can attract a ban on returning. Marriage and study are the two routes that produce a genuine multi-year status.
hurghada.bestTime: October to April is the comfortable season in Hurghada: daytime highs in the low to high twenties, sea temperatures still warm enough to dive comfortably with a thin wetsuit, and the whole town at its most pleasant. This is also high season for European visitors, particularly around Christmas and Easter. Summer, June to September, is extremely hot, regularly above 38 degrees and sometimes far more, and while the humidity is low and the sea is warm, it limits what can be done outdoors between mid-morning and late afternoon. The wind blows almost year-round, which is why Hurghada is a major kitesurfing centre, and it takes some of the edge off the heat. The khamaseen is the spring nuisance: a hot wind off the desert that lifts sand into the air for a couple of days together, cuts visibility underwater and coats everything left outdoors. It passes quickly, though it can still spoil a dive trip booked months earlier. Water temperature swings further than most people expect, warm enough in autumn for a shorty and cold enough late in winter that a five millimetre suit earns its place in the luggage. Mornings at the turn of the seasons want a fleece on an open boat.
hurghada.prosCons: Hurghada offers year-round sun, one of the world's best reef diving destinations on the doorstep, prices among the lowest for any coastal city, and an international airport in the middle of town with direct flights across Europe. There is a large, established foreign resident population, so the practicalities of settling are well trodden. It is a purpose-built resort city with little historic character and a great deal of unfinished construction around it. Summer heat is genuinely extreme. Egypt's currency instability and periodic internet service restrictions add friction. The foreign community is largely Russian and German rather than an English-speaking nomad crowd, and cultural norms outside the resorts require some adjustment.
hurghada.whoFor: Divers and kitesurfers who want warmth on very little money, and who would rather have a real international airport than charm, are the people who come. A European winter spent somewhere warm and inexpensive is the basic calculation, and it holds up. The Red Sea reefs become a regular part of the week rather than something saved up for once a year. It works for those comfortable in a Russian and German-speaking expatriate environment. Historic atmosphere is absent from a town built in the 1980s, the foreign community speaks Russian and German rather than English, the summers are brutal, and Egyptian politics offer no predictability to plan around. Dahab, four hours north in Sinai, is the smaller, more characterful alternative with a longer-established travelling crowd.

mindo.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $650 a month as a solo remote worker in Mindo, which is among the cheapest options anywhere with this quality of environment. A small house or apartment in the village runs about $200 to $350, with lodges and cabins in the surrounding forest available on longer terms. Ecuador uses the US dollar, which removes exchange risk entirely and makes budgeting unusually simple. Groceries land around $130 to $180, with the weekly market cheap and the small village shops limited in range. An almuerzo, the set lunch, is $3 to $4, a restaurant dinner $8 to $14, and a chocolate tour, one of the village's specialities, about $10. Utilities add $30 to $60. There is very little banking in a village this size and the one machine runs dry at weekends, so cash comes up from the city with you. Cooking gas arrives as a heavily subsidised cylinder and costs almost nothing, one of the few things here cheaper than anyone expects. Imported goods carry heavy duties, and a supermarket run into the city is what most long-stayers do monthly, since the village shops stock what the village eats and not a great deal else.
mindo.whereToWork: Mindo is a village of around 2,500 people and there is no coworking space. Remote workers here work from their accommodation, and the practical question is entirely the connection: fixed-line internet reaches the village and is adequate for most work but not fast, and it varies considerably between properties, with lodges further into the forest often much worse. Testing before committing is essential. Mobile 4G coverage is reasonable in the village centre and drops away quickly outside it. Power cuts happen, and Ecuador experienced significant scheduled electricity rationing during the 2024 drought, which is worth knowing about as a recurring risk. Several cafes on the main street have wifi and are laptop-friendly. The forest around the village is part of a biosphere reserve, and in a referendum a couple of years ago the people of the province voted to ban metal mining across it, a rare instance of a community deciding against an extractive industry and the reason the valley still looks as it does. The local economy is guiding, lodges, cacao and a little dairy. None of that is a client base. What it does mean is that the village itself has a direct interest in the forest staying as it is.
mindo.gettingAround: Mindo is a village of a few streets and everything in it is a five-minute walk. Getting to the surrounding attractions, the cloud forest reserves, the waterfall route, the tarabita cable car and the butterfly and hummingbird gardens, is done on foot, by bicycle, or by the pickup trucks that operate as shared taxis for a few dollars. There is no need for a car. Buses run to Quito in about two and a half hours over the pass, with the road descending steeply from the Andes into the cloud forest. Quito's Mariscal Sucre airport is roughly three hours away and is the international gateway. Cycling the main road is popular but the traffic requires care. Some buses do not enter the village at all and stop instead at the junction out on the main highway, from where a pickup runs the last few kilometres down the side road, so it is worth confirming which service you have bought. Landslides close that highway in the wettest months and the detour is a long one. The road itself drops steeply off the mountains and the temperature climbs as it goes, which is the most obvious way to understand where the village actually sits.
mindo.visas: Ecuador grants most Western passports, including EU, UK, US, Canadian and Australian, 90 days visa-free on arrival, extendable by a further 90 days in-country for a fee, giving up to 180 days in a year. Ecuador introduced a Rentista visa category widely described as a digital nomad visa, available to remote workers and others with a stable foreign income above a monthly threshold, granting two years with the possibility of renewal and a route towards permanent residence. Ecuador's use of the US dollar as its national currency removes exchange complications entirely. The country has faced serious security problems in its coastal cities since 2023, though the highland and cloud forest areas including Mindo have been far less affected.
mindo.bestTime: Mindo sits at about 1,250 metres in the western Andean cloud forest and is warm and wet year-round, roughly 18 to 24 degrees in the day. The drier months are broadly June to September and December to January, which are the best for hiking, birding and the waterfall routes; the wettest are February to May and October to November, when afternoon and evening rain is close to daily. It is a cloud forest, so mist and rain are the normal condition rather than an interruption, and anyone coming for dry weather has misunderstood the destination. Birding is excellent all year, with the greatest activity in the early morning regardless of season. Sitting almost on the equator, the day here is twelve hours long in every month, with light at six and dark at six, and the birding everyone comes for happens in the first two of those hours whatever the calendar says. The village has held the world record for the number of species counted in a single day during the annual bird census, which sounds like marketing until you stand on a road at dawn. Cloud usually builds through the middle of the day and breaks again by late afternoon.
mindo.prosCons: Mindo packs an extraordinary amount of nature into a very small place: it sits in one of the most biodiverse regions on earth, with several hundred bird species including dozens of hummingbirds, cloud forest reserves, waterfalls and cacao farms all within walking or cycling distance. It is cheap, it uses the US dollar, and it is two and a half hours from a capital city with an international airport. This is a village, and it shows: the internet is the limiting factor and should be verified, healthcare means Quito, and there is essentially no community of remote workers. It rains a lot. Ecuador's national security situation has deteriorated, though this has affected the coast far more than the highlands.
mindo.whoFor: Living inside a cloud forest, for work that tolerates a modest connection and a person who needs neither company nor amenities. It is an outstanding choice for birders, naturalists and photographers, and a good one for writers and anyone wanting quiet, cheap, focused time. The dollar economy and the Rentista visa make longer stays administratively simple. Couples have an easier time of it than people arriving alone. Fast reliable internet is beyond what a cloud forest village can deliver, nothing resembling a social life has formed among four hundred residents, healthcare is in Quito, and the weather is wet because the forest depends on it being so. Quito is two and a half hours away with all of it, and Cuenca is the more established Ecuadorian base for foreign residents.

sokcho.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $1,500 a month as a solo remote worker in Sokcho, which is well below Seoul while still being South Korea. A one-bedroom apartment or officetel near the centre or the beach runs about $450 to $700, and Korean leases traditionally involve a large deposit, the jeonse or wolse system, so short-term and foreigner-friendly options often come at a premium through agencies or serviced buildings. Groceries land around $350 to $450; Korean supermarket prices for fruit and imported goods are high. A bowl of noodles or a gimbap lunch is $6 to $9, a Korean barbecue dinner for two $30 to $45, and the fish market by the port is excellent and cheap. Utilities add $80 to $160.
sokcho.whereToWork: Sokcho is a city of about 80,000 and has no meaningful coworking scene; that sits in Seoul and Busan. Remote workers here work from their accommodation or from cafes, of which Korea has an extraordinary density even in small cities, and Korean cafe culture positively expects long laptop sessions. Connectivity is the reason Sokcho works at all as a base: South Korea has among the fastest and most reliable internet anywhere, fixed-line and mobile alike, and that holds outside the capital. Public wifi is ubiquitous. English is limited in daily life, and while translation apps handle most transactions, anything administrative is considerably easier with a Korean-speaking friend. Half the town was settled by refugees who came south from the far north during the war and expected to go back, and their descendants still run the market and the food stalls that carry those northern dishes, which is a piece of history you eat rather than read. The economy otherwise is fishing, the squid boats and whatever the national park brings in. None of it employs foreigners, so the work you do here is what you brought with you, and the compensation is a cost of living well under the capital.
sokcho.gettingAround: Sokcho is compact and spread between the beach, the port and the Cheongchoho lagoon, and much of it is walkable or cyclable on the flat. City buses cover the rest cheaply with a T-money card, and the same card works nationwide. Bus 7 and 7-1 run to Seoraksan national park, which is the main reason most people are here, in about twenty minutes. Express buses connect Sokcho to Seoul in around two and a half hours, and this is the standard route since the city has no railway station, though a KTX line to the east coast has been under development. Yangyang international airport is nearby with limited service; Incheon is the practical international gateway. The coast road north runs out after about an hour at a checkpoint, beyond which the civilian control zone begins and an observatory looks across the line into the other country, a reminder that this is a border province rather than simply a holiday one. Traffic on the mountain road west is heavy on autumn weekends, and a journey that takes an hour in spring can take three when the leaves turn. Bicycles can be hired by the lagoon and the flat loop around it is the pleasant local ride.
sokcho.visas: South Korea grants most Western passports 90 days visa-free, and requires many of them to obtain a K-ETA electronic travel authorisation before departure, though this requirement has been temporarily waived for a rotating list of countries, so check the current position. In 2024 Korea launched the F-1-D workation visa, a digital nomad visa for remote workers employed by foreign companies with more than a year of experience in their field and an income above roughly twice the Korean gross national income per capita. It grants one year with a possible one-year extension and allows accompanying family. It was a significant addition, as Korea previously had no route at all for remote workers. The remote work visa carries an insurance condition that is unusually specific: the policy has to cover medical costs up to a high fixed sum, and a standard travel policy will not satisfy it. Holders may not take work from a local employer at all, which is the line separating it from every other long-stay category. A criminal record certificate, apostilled and translated, is part of the file, and obtaining one from a home country usually takes longer than the rest of the application put together.
sokcho.bestTime: Autumn, late September through November, is the outstanding season in Sokcho: clear skies, cool air and the foliage on Seoraksan, which is one of the most celebrated autumn sights in Korea and fills the park and the town at weekends. Spring, April and May, is the second window, mild and with cherry blossom. Summer is hot and humid, into the low thirties, and July brings the monsoon rains, but this is also when the east coast beaches are the point and Sokcho fills with Korean holidaymakers. Winter is cold, often below freezing, and this stretch of coast gets heavy snow, which makes Seoraksan spectacular and the roads occasionally difficult. Book far ahead for autumn weekends. A dry wind comes off the mountains at the turn of the year and has driven serious wildfires through this region several times lately, and the emergency alerts that reach every phone in those weeks are not a formality. The squid season runs through the warmer months and the boats work at night under lamps bright enough to read by from the shore. Sea fog rolls in on summer mornings and clears before noon, which is why the early swimmers have the beach to themselves.
sokcho.prosCons: Sokcho gives you Korean infrastructure, which is to say some of the best internet, transport and healthcare in the world, in a small coastal city with a national park of granite peaks directly behind it and the East Sea in front. Costs are well below Seoul, the seafood is superb, and the country is exceptionally safe. English is genuinely limited and Korea is administratively demanding for foreigners: banking, phone contracts and rentals all involve their own hurdles. There is no foreign community in Sokcho and no nomad scene. The city is quiet outside the tourist seasons and busy within them. Winters are cold and snowy, and Seoul is a two and a half hour bus ride rather than a commute.
sokcho.whoFor: Korea without the cost and intensity of Seoul, for people who hike or climb and can operate in a mostly Korean-language environment. The new workation visa paired with somewhere genuinely quieter is a rare combination in Korea. Seoraksan is what draws most people in the first place, and the infrastructure and the safety are what keep them. Solo workers who came for focus get it, and couples manage too without much adjustment. Daily life runs in Korean and no app closes that gap, the nightlife is a handful of places by the harbour, and a professional network would have to be assembled from nothing by somebody who does not speak the language. Seoul and Busan have all of that, and Busan in particular offers a coastal city with far more happening.

trincomalee.costOfLiving: Budget roughly $650 a month as a solo remote worker in Trincomalee, which is among the cheapest coastal bases anywhere. A room or small apartment in town or out at Uppuveli and Nilaveli runs about $180 to $320 on a long stay, with beachfront guesthouses negotiable outside the season. Groceries land around $120 to $170, with the town market very cheap for produce and fish. A rice and curry lunch is $2 to $3, a beachside dinner $6 to $12, and a beer about $2.50. A scooter rental is $60 to $90 a month. Sri Lanka's economic difficulties since 2022 have made prices and supply less predictable than they once were, so budget with some margin. The economic crisis of recent years is still the backdrop to every price here, and the tax rise that followed it pushed anything imported well above what the exchange rate alone would suggest. Electricity tariffs went up sharply in the same period and did not come back down, which is why a guesthouse quoting a monthly rate usually caps air conditioning hours rather than absorbing them. Fish, fruit and rice from the town market are the part of the budget that stayed cheap, and a stay built around them costs a fraction of one built around imported food.
trincomalee.whereToWork: Trincomalee has no coworking space and its remote-work infrastructure is what a guesthouse provides. The connection is the central practical question: fixed-line internet in the town and along the Uppuveli and Nilaveli beach strip is variable, and this is not a place to depend on a fixed line. Mobile data is cheap in Sri Lanka and 4G coverage in Trincomalee town and the nearby beaches is generally reasonable, so most people work off a local SIM with a large data package. Power cuts have been a recurring feature of Sri Lankan life since the economic crisis and a battery backup for a router is a sensible precaution rather than a luxury. Tamil is the language of the town and Sinhala the language of the national administration, and the gap between the two is a live fact rather than a historical one, so a form filled in the wrong language goes to the back of the queue. The harbour is the reason the town exists, and the navy's eastern command sits on it beside an oil tank farm dating from the war years that governments are still negotiating over. None of that employs foreigners, which is why the working people you meet will be in tourism or in aid.
trincomalee.gettingAround: Trincomalee town is small and walkable around the harbour, the fort and the Koneswaram temple on Swami Rock. The beaches most people stay at, Uppuveli and Nilaveli, are six and sixteen kilometres north respectively, and a tuk-tuk or a scooter is how you cover that. Tuk-tuks are everywhere and cheap. Buses run along the coast and inland. The railway connects Trincomalee to Colombo in around eight hours, and buses do it in six to seven; the road across the island via Habarana and Dambulla passes the cultural triangle, which makes breaking the journey attractive. There is a small domestic airport at China Bay with limited seaplane and light aircraft service. Ride-hailing apps that work perfectly in the capital are thin to useless here, so a tuk-tuk fare is agreed before setting off and the going rate is better asked of a guesthouse than of a driver. Boats out to the island national park leave from the beach north of town in the morning and turn round in the early afternoon, and the park charges its own entry fee on top of the crossing. Long-distance buses are cheap and frequent, but the seats and the road together make an overnight journey a poor substitute for a night of sleep.
trincomalee.visas: Sri Lanka requires most visitors to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorization online before arrival, which normally grants 30 days and can be extended in-country to 90 days and in some cases longer through the Department of Immigration in Colombo.
