geelong.bestTime: December to March is the summer window, with daytime temperatures in the mid twenties and the bay warm enough to swim. Melbourne's reputation for four seasons in a day applies here too, and a February day can swing from thirty-five to eighteen when a cool change comes through. Autumn in March and April is the most settled weather of the year. Winter from June to August is cold and grey by Australian standards, with highs around fourteen, though it rarely freezes. Rain is spread across the year. Anyone planning around the Great Ocean Road should know it is busiest between December and February and considerably more pleasant in autumn. The ultraviolet index here is severe even on cool days, so sun protection is a year-round habit rather than a summer one. And the bushfire season runs through summer, which matters for anyone heading into the Otways or along the coast, where fire danger ratings are published daily and taken seriously. Southern right whales come into the coast between June and October, which gives the grey months a reason of their own.
geelong.prosCons: Geelong combines a rebuilt waterfront on Corio Bay, a university, an hour's train to Melbourne and the start of the Great Ocean Road, at rents meaningfully below the capital. Bells Beach and the Otways are close. Australian costs are high and do not bend, the visa position rules the city out for most non-Australians, the weather is unreliable, and the city is still working through the closure of the industries that built it, which shows in parts of it. The bay itself is shallow and calm rather than surf coast, so anyone expecting waves needs to drive to Torquay or Bells, half an hour south. The city has grown quickly as Melbourne's prices pushed people down the highway and the housing market has tightened accordingly, so the cost advantage over the capital is real but narrower than it was five years ago. And there is more cultural weight here than the industrial reputation suggests, with a serious regional gallery and a performing arts centre, though anyone wanting range rather than quality will still be catching the train.
geelong.whoFor: Australian work rights and a want of coastal living within reach of Melbourne without paying Melbourne rents, plus the surfers drawn to the Surf Coast. It works for anyone connected to Deakin. A foreign passport with no visa route attached gets nowhere here, a travelling budget will not survive Australian prices, and reliable warmth is not something this stretch of coast delivers even at the height of summer. It also suits families, since the city has the schools, hospitals and space that inner Melbourne makes expensive, and anyone whose work is in Melbourne but only two or three days a week. Among the Victorian regional cities the choice is between the coast and the goldfields: Ballarat and Bendigo are cheaper again, with grander nineteenth-century architecture and colder winters, while this one has the bay, the surf coast and the faster train. Torquay is the alternative for anyone whose priority is waves rather than a city. The clearest case here is the hybrid worker who needs Melbourne two days a week and would rather spend the other five near water.

newplymouth.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,650 a month as a solo remote worker in New Plymouth, which is among the cheaper options in New Zealand while keeping a full range of services. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $800 to $1,150. New Zealand grocery prices are high and imported goods carry a premium that surprises arrivals from Europe or Asia. The region's economy rests on dairy and on oil and gas, which keeps wages and some prices higher than a town this size would otherwise support. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. The local market is distorted from both ends. Fonterra's plant near Hawera is among the largest dairy factories in the world, and the payout to farmers swings the regional economy far harder than eighty thousand people ordinarily would, so a good season lifts rents and a bad one softens them. The energy sector pulls the other way, paying salaries the local labour market could not otherwise support and taking rents up with them. The effect for a remote worker is that costs here follow a milk price and a gas price, neither of which has anything to do with the town.
newplymouth.whereToWork: New Plymouth has limited formal coworking, with a small number of spaces serving the energy sector that dominates local professional employment. Fibre is widely available at reliable speeds and typical New Zealand pricing, and mobile coverage is comprehensive in town and patchy on the mountain and around the coast. The Len Lye Centre and the town's arts programme give the place a creative layer unusual for its size. As everywhere in New Zealand, confirm the connection at a specific property rather than assuming it is in place. Anyone whose work depends on being seen in person should understand that the nearest city of any size is four hours away by road. The first oil well in this country was drilled at Moturoa inside what is now the city, in 1865, which makes the region's energy history older than most of the industry anywhere. The Maui field offshore carried the national gas supply for decades and is now in decline, which is why the technical workforce here has been steadily retraining into wind, hydrogen and geothermal, and why a newcomer with engineering skills finds more technical conversation here than this far from a city has any right to offer.
newplymouth.gettingAround: New Plymouth is compact and the Coastal Walkway runs thirteen kilometres along the shore from the port to Bell Block, which functions as the town's main artery for walking and cycling rather than as a recreational path. A local bus network covers the suburbs. Egmont National Park and the trailheads onto Mount Taranaki are half an hour inland. The airport has domestic connections. Everything beyond the town, the Surf Highway, the Forgotten World Highway and the mountain, needs a car. The Surf Highway 45 runs around the coast from the town and is the route to almost every break in the region, which is what most people here use a car for. Egmont National Park is a near-perfect circle on the map, a boundary drawn in 1900 as a radius of about nine and a half kilometres from the summit, and the line between dark forest inside it and green farmland outside is sharp enough to be obvious from an aircraft. Every road onto the mountain stops at that edge, which is why the three main trailheads are the only realistic ways up and why they fill on a clear weekend.
newplymouth.visas: New Zealand's 2025 clarification that visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer changed the practical position considerably. Most Western nationals get an NZeTA and up to three months on arrival, extendable in some cases to a maximum of nine months within eighteen. Working Holiday visas cover a defined list of nationalities and ages with twelve months of work rights. Longer stays go through the accredited employer route or the skilled residence pathway. Immigration settings change frequently, so verify the current rules directly rather than relying on a guide. The region's oil and gas sector has historically sponsored skilled workers, which is one of the few employer-led routes into New Zealand outside the main centres. New Zealand charges an International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy on arrival, paid alongside the NZeTA rather than separately, and it was raised sharply in late 2024. It funds conservation and tourism infrastructure of exactly the kind the national park here depends on. Australians and a few other categories are exempt. It is small against the cost of a flight but it is a real line, and it falls again on a fresh visa rather than once per person.
newplymouth.bestTime: December to March is the warm half, with daytime temperatures around twenty-two and the sea swimmable. Taranaki is wet: the mountain catches weather off the Tasman and rain falls in every month, so a dry spell is luck rather than season. February is the most settled month. Winter from June to August is mild at sea level, with highs around thirteen, while the mountain holds snow and the ski field operates. The famous view of a symmetrical volcanic cone depends entirely on the cloud lifting. Locals will tell you the mountain is visible about one day in three, which is worth knowing before booking a trip around the view. The mountain makes its own weather and the numbers are stark: the summit takes several times the rainfall of the town below it, and conditions at the trailhead say very little about conditions two hours up. Search and rescue call-outs run high for a peak this accessible, because the walk starts easy and the last section is alpine. The Festival of Lights runs through Pukekura Park from December to February and is the reliable summer fixture whatever the cloud is doing.
newplymouth.prosCons: New Plymouth has one of the most striking settings of any town in this dataset: a near-perfect volcanic cone thirty minutes inland, a thirteen-kilometre coastal walkway through the middle, and consistent surf along the Surf Highway. The Len Lye Centre is a serious gallery for a town this size. It is remote even by the standards of New Zealand, the weather is genuinely wet, there is no international community, and the local economy's dependence on oil and gas makes its future a live local question. The town is also on the wrong side of the island for most itineraries, so it is rarely somewhere people pass through by accident. The mountain became a legal person in 2025, recognised as an entity holding its own rights and vested in a body that speaks for it, following Te Urewera and the Whanganui River, and its official name is now Taranaki Maunga. That settlement sits on top of a much harder history: Taranaki land was confiscated in the 1860s, and in 1881 the government sent troops into Parihaka, a settlement built on deliberate non-violent resistance, arresting its leaders and dispersing its people. The Crown apologised in 2017. Parihaka is forty minutes from the town and open to visitors.
newplymouth.whoFor: New Zealand work rights and a life organised around the mountain and the surf, in a town that has real services and an unexpectedly good arts scene. It works for climbers and trampers, since Mount Taranaki is a serious objective rather than a walk. No international community has formed here, the mountain makes dependable sunshine impossible to promise, and the professional network begins and ends with the energy sector. The cultural life here runs well ahead of the population. A serious kinetic art gallery and a WOMAD festival every March are not what a town this far from anywhere would normally sustain. It is not a place to arrive expecting company. It suits a surfer who does not need warm water, since the breaks along the coast road work on almost any swell and the crowd stays thin even in summer. It suits somebody with a professional reason to be here, because the energy transition arguments are live and the people having them are all in one town. Anyone coming for the cone on the postcard should build the trip around something else and treat a clear day as a bonus, which is the only way to arrive and not leave disappointed.

nadi.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Nadi, which is moderate for the Pacific and reflects an island economy where almost everything imported carries freight and duty. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $450 to $750. Local produce from the market is cheap and Indo-Fijian food costs very little, while anything Western-facing, particularly in the resort areas at Denarau, is priced for tourists. Alcohol and electronics are expensive. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a planning figure. The two-price pattern is the thing to learn quickly. The same meal, taxi or excursion carries a resort price and a local price, and the gap is wide enough that a month lived on the local side of it costs perhaps half what the same month costs on the other. Rentals are usually unfurnished and asked for with a bond plus a month in advance. Electricity is expensive and air conditioning is what drives the bill. Anyone staying a while should shop at the market rather than the supermarkets, where the difference is largest of all.
nadi.whereToWork: Connectivity is the weakest part of the case. Fiji has fibre in the main towns and Nadi has usable connections, but speeds are modest by international standards, reliability is inconsistent and data costs more than in Asia or Europe. Mobile coverage is reasonable along the western corridor and patchy elsewhere. There is minimal coworking. Power cuts occur, and cyclone season can take infrastructure down for days. Anyone with a demanding video schedule should test a specific connection carefully rather than assume the resort wifi is representative. Suva, four hours away, has the country's better infrastructure if a stretch of reliable work becomes necessary. The time zone is the other structural issue and it is rarely mentioned. Fiji sits twelve hours ahead of London and nineteen ahead of the American west coast, which puts it a day ahead of most clients and makes live overlap with Europe or North America genuinely awkward rather than merely inconvenient. Australia and New Zealand are the exception and are close. A local SIM with a data bundle is cheap enough to be the sensible backup, and coverage along the Queens Road corridor is the best in the country.
nadi.gettingAround: Nadi is small and the main town along Queens Road is walkable, though the airport, Denarau and the port are spread along a corridor that needs transport. Local buses are very cheap and taxis are inexpensive and metered in town. Denarau, where the marina and the boats to the Mamanuca and Yasawa islands leave from, is fifteen minutes west. The Coral Coast runs southeast and Suva is about four hours by road. The airport is the Pacific's main hub for onward connections. Driving is on the left and the Queens Road carries most of the island's traffic, with standards that require attention rather than confidence. The local buses are open-sided with no glass in the windows, which is the cheapest and much the most pleasant way to travel the coast in the heat. Boats to the islands run to a fixed daily schedule built around the flight arrivals rather than continuously, so a same-day connection needs its timings checked in advance. The Kings Road around the north of Viti Levu is the alternative route to Suva, longer and far more scenic, and it takes most of a day with stops.
nadi.visas: Fiji grants most Western nationals four months visa-free on arrival, which is unusually generous and extendable to six months in total. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa, though Fiji has actively courted remote workers and offers a longer-stay option through its investor and work permit routes. The four-month entry alone makes an extended stay straightforward without paperwork. Fiji is outside every regional visa bloc, so time here counts against nothing else. Check requirements close to travel, since Pacific entry rules change with little notice. Anyone island-hopping onward through the Pacific should note that Fiji is the regional aviation hub, so most routings pass back through Nadi. Proof of onward travel is checked at the gate rather than on arrival, and airlines enforce it more strictly than immigration does, so a one-way ticket is the most common reason people are stopped before they even leave. Extensions are applied for at the immigration office before the four months run out and are usually granted without difficulty. Working for a Fijian employer needs a permit and the visitor entry does not allow it, while remote work for a foreign employer occupies the same unlegislated space it does almost everywhere.
nadi.bestTime: May to October is the dry season and the reason to come: warm days around twenty-nine, lower humidity, reliable sun and calm seas for the island boats. That is also peak season, when accommodation prices rise. The wet season from November to April brings heavy afternoon rain, high humidity and the cyclone season, which runs to the end of April and is a genuine planning consideration rather than a formality, since Fiji is hit regularly and severely. Nadi itself sits on the drier western side of Viti Levu. Anyone planning around the island boats should also know the Yasawa transfers are weather-dependent and cancel in a strong swell. The shoulder weeks in early May and late October give dry-season weather at wet-season prices and are the best value of the year. Australian and New Zealand school holidays cause sharp local spikes that have nothing to do with the weather and are worth checking against any booking. Fiji's Indo-Fijian population also means Diwali is a public holiday and a genuinely lovely time to be here, falling in October or November depending on the year.
nadi.prosCons: Nadi is the arrival point for Fiji and the base for the Mamanuca and Yasawa islands, which are the reason most people come, with a four-month visa-free entry that makes a long stay easy. Fijian and Indo-Fijian cultures sit side by side and the hospitality is genuine. Connectivity is weak, and the town itself does a job rather than charm anyone, Pacific costs are higher than the tropics elsewhere, and the cyclone season is a real risk from November to April. The town is also a place most visitors pass through in a day on the way to the islands, which means the services are built for transit rather than for residents. Healthcare is limited, with the better private facilities in Suva and anything serious meaning evacuation to Australia or New Zealand, which is standard cover for anyone staying long. And Fiji's politics carry a history of coups, four of them since 1987, though the last was in 2006 and the country has since returned to elected government. That is context rather than a current warning, and it explains some of the caution older residents still carry.
nadi.whoFor: Divers, sailors and anyone whose plan is the islands rather than the town, plus travellers who value the generous visa entry. It works for people whose work can tolerate an unreliable connection. A demanding remote schedule and this island's bandwidth are not compatible, and Fiji has no nomad community for anybody to arrive into. Budget travellers should adjust their expectations before booking rather than after: Pacific island economics work nothing like Southeast Asian ones, and the difference shows up on the first grocery bill. Connections are the practical argument. Flights onward to Australia, New Zealand and the smaller island states run more reliably from here than from anywhere else in the Pacific, which makes this a hub rather than a terminus. Most people who stay months rather than weeks do not stay in the town itself. The Coral Coast an hour southeast, or Savusavu on Vanua Levu for anyone wanting somewhere genuinely quiet, is where the longer-term foreign residents actually are, and Nadi becomes the place you pass through for the airport. Families do well in Fiji, with international schooling available around both Suva and Nadi, and the culture is exceptionally welcoming to children.

portvila.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,500 a month as a solo remote worker in Port Vila, and understand that Vanuatu imports nearly everything, so supermarket prices are startling relative to local wages. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $500 to $850. The market produce is excellent and cheap, and eating at the market food stalls costs very little, but anything packaged or imported is expensive. There is no personal income tax in Vanuatu, which is a genuine part of the arithmetic. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Rent for anything aimed at expatriates is quoted in a different bracket from local housing, which is worth understanding before assuming a listed price is the going rate. Sales tax is fifteen per cent and there is no income tax at all, which is the arrangement the country is known for. Kava at a nakamal in the evening costs very little and is the ordinary social expense here rather than a bar tab, since drinking kava is what most of the town does after dark. Anything arriving in a container, which is nearly everything except the produce, carries freight and duty on top of the price it would have anywhere else.
portvila.whereToWork: Connectivity is the weakest thing about working here. Vanuatu is connected by a single submarine cable and outages have taken the whole country offline for days. Speeds in Port Vila are usable for email and light work, less so for anything demanding, and mobile data is expensive. There is essentially no coworking. Power is unreliable enough that a backup matters. The 2023 twin cyclones and the December 2024 earthquake both damaged infrastructure. Nobody should plan deadline-driven work here without a satellite fallback. Starlink has become the practical answer for anyone here who cannot afford to be offline, and is now common among businesses that depend on connectivity. The clock runs eleven hours in front of GMT, which puts the working day an hour ahead of Sydney for part of the year and makes Australian and New Zealand clients straightforward and European ones close to impossible. Offices open early and close in the middle of the afternoon, which is the tropical pattern and worth matching rather than fighting. Both French and English school systems operate here, a legacy of the joint colonial administration, and that shapes which professionals stay long enough to be worth knowing.
portvila.gettingAround: Port Vila is small and the seafront, the market and the centre are walkable. Minibuses circulate constantly and cost a dollar or two, flagged down anywhere and taking a roundabout route to wherever the other passengers are going, which is the normal way to move. Taxis are available. The airport is ten minutes out with connections to Australia, New Zealand and Fiji. Efate has a sealed ring road that circles the island in about three hours, and the other islands are reached by small aircraft or ferry. Driving is on the right, unusually for the region, and the ring road is sealed while most side roads are not. The minibuses carry a B on the plate and the taxis a T, which is the quickest way to tell them apart before one stops. There is no timetable and no route map because neither would mean anything: you say where you are going and the driver decides whether it fits the load already aboard. Walking back along the seafront after dark is ordinary enough, though the unlit stretches past the centre are where people take a bus instead.
portvila.visas: Vanuatu grants most Western nationals thirty days visa-free on arrival, extendable in country up to four months. There is no digital nomad visa, though Vanuatu is well known for a citizenship-by-investment programme that has attracted scrutiny and led several countries, including the European Union, to suspend visa-free access for Vanuatu passport holders. That is worth understanding as context rather than as a route. For a visitor the entry is simple. Vanuatu levies no income tax, which is the country's more legitimate financial draw. Anyone considering the investment programme should read the current international position on it carefully rather than the promotional material, since the restrictions on the passport have real consequences. The immigration office in town renews a stay a month at a time, which means a queue and a fee rather than a flight out, and that is how most people reach the four month limit. An onward ticket is asked for on arrival and checked at the departure airport more often than at this one. Paid work for a local business needs a permit tied to an employer, and the rules protecting ni-Vanuatu jobs are enforced rather than decorative.
portvila.bestTime: April to October is the dry season and the best window, with warm days around twenty-eight, lower humidity and calmer seas. The wet season from November to March brings heavy rain, high humidity and the cyclone season, which in Vanuatu is not a formality: the country is among the most exposed to natural disaster on earth by most risk indices, and Cyclone Pam in 2015 and the twin cyclones of 2023 both caused severe damage. Plan around that window rather than through it. The volcano on Tanna, one of the most accessible active craters anywhere, is reachable year-round but the flights are more reliable in the dry months. Land diving on Pentecost, where men jump from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles, runs between April and June and is the ceremony bungee jumping was copied from. It is a working ritual tied to the yam harvest rather than a performance, and reaching it takes a flight and an arrangement rather than a ticket. The dry months are also when the inter-island boats keep something like a schedule, which matters more than the weather to anyone planning to leave Efate.
portvila.prosCons: Port Vila offers a genuine Pacific capital with no income tax, some of the best wreck diving in the world at the SS President Coolidge on nearby Espiritu Santo, accessible active volcanoes, and a small but real expatriate community. Bislama makes communication easy for English speakers. Connectivity is poor and sometimes absent altogether, costs are high for what you actually get, the cyclone and earthquake exposure is genuinely serious, and the hospital cannot handle much, which makes evacuation insurance essential rather than advisable. Bislama, the national creole, is close enough to English that a visitor can follow a conversation within days, which makes the country unusually easy to be in. Million Dollar Point, where departing American forces bulldozed their own wartime equipment into the sea rather than ship it home, is now a dive site full of jeeps and bulldozers. The country also topped the Happy Planet Index when it was first published in 2006, a result that says as much about the index as about the place but that nobody here has stopped mentioning since.
portvila.whoFor: Divers, sailors and people connected to the development or maritime sectors of the region, and anyone whose income is flexible enough to survive a week offline. It works for those attracted by the tax position who understand what they are giving up in infrastructure. A demanding video schedule and Pacific bandwidth do not go together, serious healthcare means a flight to Australia or New Zealand, and the cyclone season is something to build a stay around rather than hope to miss. The outer islands are the real destination and this is how they are reached. Tanna's volcano and Espiritu Santo's wrecks and blue holes both begin with a flight from Efate rather than ending there. Domestic flights are the real budget line for anyone who came for the islands rather than the capital, since flying is the only practical way between them and the fares are not small. Two months here with three island trips inside it costs a good deal more than the monthly figure suggests. Anyone planning that should book the internal legs before fixing the dates, because schedules thin without much notice.

alula.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Al Ula, which is high for the region and reflects a place built around premium tourism rather than around residents. Accommodation is the problem: the valley's stock runs from a handful of mid-range guesthouses to Banyan Tree and Habitas at resort rates, and long-term rentals aimed at outsiders barely exist outside the staff housing attached to the Royal Commission's projects. Food is far cheaper than the room, with local restaurants at ordinary Saudi prices and imported goods marked up for the distance. There is no alcohol anywhere in the country, which removes a line most budgets carry. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Prices move with the season rather than sitting flat: a room in February can cost twice what the same room costs in June, and the cheap months are the ones nobody wants to be outside in. There is no rental market to speak of, so a month here is priced as thirty nights of accommodation rather than as rent, which is what makes the arithmetic so different from anywhere else on this site.
alula.whereToWork: Al Ula has no coworking scene in any meaningful sense. The hotels are where remote work actually happens, and the better ones have business-grade connections because the destination is built for international visitors. Saudi mobile data is fast and cheap by any standard, with 5G across the built-up parts of the valley and the main tourist sites, and a local SIM is the practical answer for anyone not staying somewhere with reliable fibre. Coverage thins quickly in the desert beyond the oasis, which matters if the plan involves working from the rock formations. The town is small enough that the same handful of cafes serve everybody, so expect familiarity rather than choice. Sunday to Thursday is the week here, so a Gulf client and a European one pull it in opposite directions, while the three-hour offset from GMT puts a European morning comfortably inside the afternoon. Many places still pause around the prayer calls, a twenty minute interruption several times a day rather than a serious obstacle, though it does shape where you sit and when.
alula.gettingAround: Al Ula is a strip of oasis along a valley, and the distances between the old town, the modern centre and the archaeological sites are too great to walk in the heat. A car is close to essential, though the destination runs a shuttle between the main sites and hotels that covers most visitor needs. Hegra itself can only be entered on a guided tour using the site's own transport, which is a rule rather than a suggestion. AlUla airport sits twenty minutes from the centre with connections to Riyadh and Jeddah and a seasonal handful of international routes. Taxis exist but thin out considerably outside the winter season. Hiring a car is straightforward with an international permit, and the roads are new, empty and well surfaced, which makes the drives between sites the easy part of the day. The old Hejaz Railway station in the valley is part of the archaeological area rather than a working one: the line that ran from Damascus to Medina was cut during the First World War and never rebuilt. Medina is about three hours south by road.
alula.visas: Saudi Arabia has no digital nomad visa. The eVisa covers around sixty nationalities, is valid a year for multiple entries and allows ninety days per stay up to a hundred and eighty in the year, which is the route almost every visitor uses. It is a tourist permission and does not authorise work for a Saudi employer; remote work for a foreign one sits in the same unaddressed space it does across the Gulf. Longer stays run through employer sponsorship or the Premium Residency programme, which carries a substantial fee. Rules here have changed quickly and repeatedly since the country opened to tourism, so check the current position directly rather than trusting a secondhand account. The eVisa price includes a compulsory insurance policy, bundled rather than optional. Foreign women have not been required to wear an abaya since 2019, though modest dress covering shoulders and knees is expected, enforced by social pressure rather than by police. Unmarried couples sharing a room, once a genuine obstacle, stopped being a practical problem under the same set of changes.
alula.bestTime: October to April is the only sensible window. Winter days sit in the low twenties with cold desert nights that drop close to freezing in January, which is exactly the weather the destination was built around. The Winter at Tantora season and the concert programme at the Maraya mirrored hall fall in these months and are when the valley is busiest and priciest. Summer from June to September pushes past forty degrees and the archaeological sites become genuinely unpleasant by mid-morning, which is why most of the tourism infrastructure quietens down. February and March are the best balance of open sites and thinner crowds. Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each year and changes the rhythm of everything while it runs: daytime eating in public is not done, restaurants open after sunset, and the working day shortens. The desert nights are properly dark and the valley has made something of that, with observatory programmes and night tours. Rain is rare enough to count as an event, but it arrives as flash flooding in the wadis when it does, which is why sites close rather than drain.
alula.prosCons: Al Ula holds Hegra, the Nabataean city that became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage site, with more than a hundred tombs carved into sandstone outcrops and almost none of the crowds that Petra carries three hundred kilometres north. The landscape around it is extraordinary and the air is clean. This is a managed destination rather than a city at all: there is no nomad community, no nightlife of any kind, no alcohol, and the cost of staying is set by hotels rather than by a rental market. Everything is a drive away. It is a place to spend a remarkable few weeks, not a base. Maraya, the concert hall out in the valley, is clad entirely in mirror and is recognised as the largest mirrored building anywhere, disappearing into the rock face from a distance, which is the point of it. The whole valley is being developed to a plan that runs to 2035, so anything written about the place has a short shelf life and the version you arrive to will not be the version in last year's account.
alula.whoFor: A stretch of desert quiet with genuinely world-class archaeology outside the door, and a budget that absorbs resort pricing. A short concentrated block of work slotted between site visits is the shape that fits, and the winter season, when the cultural programming runs, is when to do it. Company, nightlife, a rental market and a walkable city are four things this place has not been built to provide, and the accommodation arithmetic defeats a tight budget before anything else gets a chance to. Women travelling alone find it easier than the country's reputation suggests, though local norms still apply. Archaeologists and heritage professionals are the one group with a working reason to be here, and there are more of them around than the visitor numbers suggest, since the excavation and conservation programmes run all year. Anyone else is a visitor with a laptop. Two or three weeks is the natural length, long enough to see the sites properly and short enough that the absence of a rental market never becomes the problem it would be at three months.

abha.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Abha, which makes it one of the cheaper places to sit in Saudi Arabia and a fraction of what the Gulf coast cities cost. A furnished one-bedroom flat runs roughly $400 to $650, with the higher end for something new near the centre or with a view over the escarpment. Food is inexpensive if eaten locally, and the Asir region grows much of its own produce, which shows in the markets. Fuel costs almost nothing and there is no alcohol spend anywhere in the country. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. The rental market has an unusual shape: leases are typically annual and paid in one or two instalments up front rather than monthly, which is the norm across the kingdom and a large sum to produce on arrival. Short-term furnished apartments are the alternative, though their rates are set for the holiday trade and climb steeply in peak weeks. Air conditioning barely runs at this altitude, which removes the utility bill that dominates every other Saudi city, and winter heating is the smaller cost that replaces it.
abha.whereToWork: Abha has almost no coworking provision, and the cafes around the centre and the newer developments are where remote work happens in practice. Saudi mobile data is fast and inexpensive with strong 5G across the city, which is the reliable option; fixed connections in older buildings vary considerably by address. The city's summer role as the country's domestic hill station means hotels here are used to guests who stay for weeks, and the better ones have connections to match. Power is stable. English is limited outside the university and the tourism sector, so expect Arabic to be the working language of daily errands. The working week runs Sunday to Thursday, so a Friday deadline set by a European client lands on the local weekend and a Sunday one lands on a working Monday. And shops and many offices close briefly for each of the five daily prayers, which fragments the afternoon in a way that takes a fortnight to plan around rather than fight. A mobile hotspot is the sensible primary connection here, with the building's fixed line as the backup rather than the other way round.
abha.gettingAround: Abha sits at around 2,200 metres and is built across ridges and valleys, which makes it hilly rather than walkable in any continuous sense. A car is the normal way to move around, and fuel costs almost nothing by international standards. Ride-hailing works in the city and is the usual answer for anyone without a vehicle. The cable cars down the escarpment are tourist infrastructure rather than transport but are worth taking once. Abha airport has frequent domestic connections to Riyadh and Jeddah and a small number of regional routes. The mountain roads down to the Tihamah plain are spectacular and demand real attention. A foreign licence with an international permit covers a visitor for a limited period, after which a Saudi one is required, and women have been able to drive since 2018 so a rental is straightforward regardless. The escarpment roads carry a hazard of their own, and it is cloud rather than traffic: the mist that makes the summers pleasant sits directly on the road in places, and visibility can collapse inside a single bend. The descent to Rijal Almaa drops the scarp in a long series of switchbacks and is the best road in the region.
abha.visas: Saudi Arabia has no digital nomad visa. Most visitors arrive on the eVisa, which covers around sixty nationalities, runs for a year with multiple entries and allows ninety days per stay to a maximum of a hundred and eighty days in the year. It permits tourism, not employment by a Saudi entity, and remote work for a foreign employer is not addressed in the rules either way. Anyone wanting to stay longer needs employer sponsorship or the Premium Residency scheme and its fee. The country's visa policy has changed repeatedly since it opened to tourism in 2019, so confirm current conditions before planning a long stay. The eVisa bundles a mandatory health insurance policy into its fee, so that is one thing not to arrange separately. Women may travel and stay independently, a change from the pre-2019 rules that still surprises people. Non-Muslims may not enter Mecca, which matters for any overland route in the west of the country, and while dress rules have relaxed considerably, Asir is more conservative than Riyadh or Jeddah and modest dress is expected of everyone rather than requested.
abha.bestTime: Abha's altitude gives it the mildest climate in Saudi Arabia and the reason the rest of the country arrives here in July. Summer highs sit around the high twenties while Riyadh is above forty, and the monsoon fringe brings afternoon cloud and mist that rolls over the escarpment. That makes June to September the busiest and most expensive months, with domestic tourism filling the hotels. Spring and autumn are quieter and just as pleasant. Winter nights get genuinely cold for the region and can approach freezing at this elevation, and heating is not something every building here takes seriously. The greenest weeks follow the summer rains rather than accompanying them, so late August into September shows the terraces at their best. Timing around Eid matters more than timing around weather: both Eid holidays fill every hotel in the region with domestic visitors and prices follow, and because the Islamic calendar shifts each year those dates move backwards through the seasons. The Asir flower festivals in summer, where men of the region wear the herb and blossom crowns the area is known for, are the local events worth arranging a visit around.
abha.prosCons: Abha has weather no other Saudi city can offer, sitting high in the Asir mountains with green terraced slopes, cool summers and clean air, along with the stone tower houses at Rijal Almaa and the country's highest peaks nearby. Costs are low and the landscape is genuinely unusual. Not one remote worker is here to meet, English is scarce, there is no nightlife and no alcohol at all, and the region is conservative even by Saudi standards. Getting anywhere outside the kingdom means a domestic connection first. It is a place with real character and almost no international infrastructure to support a long stay. The region is also changing quickly, which cuts both ways. Large tourism developments are under construction on the escarpment above the city as part of the national diversification programme, and they will bring infrastructure that does not exist yet along with the crowds and the prices that follow. Set against the thin visitor provision, Asiri hospitality towards foreigners is genuine and often overwhelming, and a traveller with a little Arabic will be fed and directed far more than they expected.
abha.whoFor: Anyone already working in Saudi Arabia who wants a cooler base than the coast or the capital, or a traveller drawn to mountain landscapes and heritage architecture that almost no outsiders see. It rewards anyone with some Arabic and patience for a place that has not organised itself around foreign visitors. No international community has formed in these mountains, alcohol is illegal so a bar is not a category that exists, and work that depends on face-to-face meetings will find there is almost nobody here to meet with. Summer arrivals should book early against the domestic holiday season. Photographers and hikers get the most out of it, since the escarpment, the terraced villages and the road down to the coast are unlike anywhere else on the peninsula and almost none of it is photographed. For anyone weighing the Saudi hill stations against each other, Taif is easier to reach and busier, while Abha is higher, greener and further from everything. As a base it works best in weeks rather than months unless there is a job attached, because the practical support a long stay needs is simply not here yet.

fujairah.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Fujairah, which is well below Dubai and Abu Dhabi while still being the UAE. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $600 to $950 depending on how close it sits to the corniche, and the gap against Dubai rents is the main reason anyone chooses to live on this coast. Groceries are broadly Gulf standard, meaning imported goods carry a premium and local produce does not. Alcohol is available in hotels and licensed outlets and is expensive everywhere in the country. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Fibre runs about $80 to $150 a month, which is high for the speed and reflects a duopoly. Housing is normally paid in one to four cheques covering the year rather than monthly, which front-loads the cost substantially and is the arrangement most newcomers are unprepared for. A car is the other fixed cost, with hire from about $350 a month and fuel cheap by any standard. Rents on the corniche carry a premium of around a third over the inland streets, and the difference buys a sea view rather than better building.
fujairah.whereToWork: Fujairah has a small coworking presence relative to Dubai's, mostly attached to the free zone and serving the port and shipping businesses that drive the local economy. Internet across the UAE is fast and well built, with fibre widely available and comprehensive 5G, though prices are high and the country's blocking of most voice-over-internet services still catches people out; a VPN is standard practice among remote workers here. The port at Fujairah is one of the world's largest bunkering hubs, which gives the emirate a professional layer beyond its size. Dubai is ninety minutes away for anything the local network cannot supply. Fujairah's free zone offers company licensing at a fraction of mainland Dubai's cost and comes with a residence visa, which is the substantive reason some small consultancies register on this coast and work from anywhere in the country. The UAE moved to a Saturday and Sunday weekend in 2022, aligning with most of the world. Most professional and social life still happens in Dubai, and a good number of residents here drive over for a day or two each week rather than relocating.
fujairah.gettingAround: Fujairah is spread along the coast between the Hajar mountains and the Gulf of Oman, and like most of the UAE it assumes a car. The corniche and the area immediately around it are walkable, but everything else, including the dive sites north towards Dibba and the mountain roads inland, needs driving. There is no metro and the bus network is limited. Taxis and ride-hailing work in town. Dubai is about ninety minutes by road through the mountains, which is a genuinely good drive, and Fujairah has its own small international airport with a handful of regional routes. The road over the Hajar mountains from Dubai climbs through Masafi and is one of the better drives in the country. Snoopy Island off Sandy Beach is a shore dive reached by swimming out from the sand, which is unusual in the Gulf and is why the site is as busy as it is at weekends.
fujairah.visas: The UAE has one of the region's few real remote work visas: a one-year permit for people employed outside the country, requiring proof of around $3,500 a month in income, an employment contract of at least a year and health insurance valid in the country. It is renewable and can be applied for from abroad. Short visits run on visa on arrival for most Western nationalities, typically thirty or ninety days depending on passport. There is also the Golden Visa for longer horizons and defined categories. The remote work route is administratively straightforward by regional standards, which is a real point in the country's favour. The income threshold is checked against bank statements rather than a contract alone, so anyone with variable freelance income should look closely at how the last six months read. Emirates ID and a medical follow the visa and take a couple of weeks. Residence also unlocks a local bank account, which almost everything administrative in the country assumes you hold.
fujairah.bestTime: November to March is the comfortable half of the year, with daytime temperatures in the mid twenties, warm sea and the conditions that make the east coast diving worth the trip. This is also when the mountain wadis are at their best. Summer from June to September pushes past forty degrees with heavy humidity on the coast, and outdoor life effectively stops between mid-morning and evening. The east coast is marginally cooler and less humid than Dubai on the other side of the mountains, which is a difference locals notice, but it is still a Gulf summer and not somewhere to arrive unprepared. Ramadan reshapes the emirate's rhythm entirely, with daytime eating restricted in public, shortened working hours and social life moving to after sunset, and it moves earlier by about eleven days each year. The wadis inland fill and flow after the winter rains, which is brief and unpredictable and is the one time the mountains behind the coast look green.
fujairah.prosCons: Fujairah is the only emirate entirely on the Gulf of Oman, which gives it mountains directly behind the beach, the best diving in the country around Snoopy Island and Dibba, and the oldest mosque in the UAE at Al Bidyah. It costs meaningfully less than Dubai while keeping the same infrastructure, safety and visa options. You would be the only remote worker in town, the place is quiet enough to bore anyone used to a city, and the summer here is genuinely brutal. Most social and professional life still happens ninety minutes away on the other coast. Al Bidyah mosque dates to around 1446 and is built of stone and mud brick with four domes on a single central pillar, and it remains in use rather than being preserved as a monument.
fujairah.whoFor: The remote work visa, the safety and the connectivity of the Emirates without Dubai rents, and a beach with mountains behind it rather than a skyline. Divers in particular get more here than anywhere else in the country. It works as a winter block rather than a full year, given what the summer does to the coast. A community, a scene and a professional network are all things that mean driving to Dubai, and the drive is long enough that most people who need them regularly end up living there instead. Anyone without a car will find the emirate hard work from the first day. Shipping and bunkering are the exception to everything said above. This is the second-largest bunkering port in the world after Singapore, and the professional network around that trade runs genuinely deep for so small an emirate. Compared with Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah has the better diving and the worse road access, and both sit well under Dubai on price.

amasra.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Amasra, which is inexpensive even by Turkish standards and reflects a small Black Sea town rather than a city. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $200 to $350, with the peninsula and the two harbours at the top of that range and anything a short walk inland at the bottom. Fish is the local staple and cheap in season, and the region's produce keeps grocery costs low. Turkish inflation makes any figure here a moving target, so treat this as a working budget rather than a fixed one. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $10 to $20 a month where the building supports it, which is among the best value in Europe, and there is no coworking cost because there is no coworking. Summer rents on the peninsula can double when the domestic season starts in July, so a lease signed in May on annual terms is worth considerably more than a monthly booking made in August. Bartin twenty minutes inland has the supermarkets, the hospital and the bank branches, and most practical shopping happens there rather than in the town.
amasra.whereToWork: Amasra has no coworking spaces. This is a town of a few thousand people that fills with domestic tourists in summer and empties in winter, and remote work happens from apartments and a handful of cafes along the harbour. Turkish fibre reaches the town and mobile coverage is good, with data cheap by European standards, but connection quality varies by building and the older stock on the peninsula is the weakest of it. Anyone dependent on being online should test before signing anything longer than a month. Bartin, the provincial centre, is twenty minutes inland and has the services the town lacks. Turkey sits three hours ahead of GMT year-round since it dropped daylight saving in 2016, giving a full European overlap and an early-afternoon window with the American east coast. The town's population roughly triples in summer, and mobile data slows noticeably in July and August as a result. The town's summer influx is domestic rather than international, so English is no more useful in August than in February.
amasra.gettingAround: Amasra is built on a small peninsula between two bays and is completely walkable, which is much of its appeal; the castle, both harbours and the museum all sit within fifteen minutes of each other on foot. Buses run to Bartin and on to Safranbolu and Ankara, and the coastal road east towards Sinop is one of the better drives in the country. Istanbul is around six hours away by bus. There is no airport nearby, with the nearest useful connections at Zonguldak or a longer trip to Ankara. A car opens up the Black Sea coast but is not needed in the town itself. Safranbolu, an Ottoman merchant town that is a UNESCO World Heritage site, is about ninety minutes inland and is the standard excursion from here. The coastal road east through Kurucasile and Cide is slow, winding and among the least-travelled scenic drives in the country. Buses to Istanbul run overnight and are comfortable, which is how most people make that journey rather than driving it.
amasra.visas: Turkey allows most Western nationals ninety days within any hundred and eighty on arrival or through a straightforward e-visa, which covers a season comfortably. There is no digital nomad visa in the sense that other countries use the phrase, though Turkey introduced a Digital Nomad Identification Card in 2024 for citizens of a defined list of countries with a university degree and a minimum monthly income, which eases the residence permit process rather than replacing it. Short-term residence permits are the traditional longer route and have become notably harder to obtain in recent years, with many neighbourhoods closed to new foreign registrations. The residence permit quota is the practical obstacle rather than the visa: the interior ministry closes neighbourhoods to new foreign registration once foreigners exceed a set share, the list changes, and a small town like Amasra can be affected disproportionately by a handful of registrations.
amasra.bestTime: June to September is the season, with warm days, a swimmable Black Sea and a town that fills with Turkish holidaymakers who have known about it for generations. July and August are genuinely crowded and prices rise accordingly. May and September are the better months if the point is to work rather than to holiday. Winter on this coast is grey, wet and windy, with temperatures around eight degrees and much of the tourist infrastructure closed; the Black Sea gets far more rain than the Aegean or Mediterranean coasts and that is the defining fact of the off season. The number behind that is over a metre a year, roughly double Antalya's, and the storms are real weather rather than merely dreary, which is why the season here shuts down completely instead of slowing. The two harbours face different ways, so one is always sheltered whatever the wind is doing, which is why the town was settled where it is.
amasra.prosCons: Amasra is one of the prettiest small towns on the Turkish coast, a Roman and then Genoese harbour settlement on a peninsula with a castle around it, cheap fish and a beach on each side. Costs are very low and the setting is unusual. It is tiny, it has no international presence, English is barely spoken, and the winter is long, wet and thoroughly empty. The 2022 mine disaster in the wider Bartin coalfield is part of the region's recent history and its economy is not only tourism. Anyone imagining a Mediterranean summer should understand this is a different and much wetter sea. Amasra was the Roman colony of Amastris and the Genoese held it until 1460, and the castle walls still enclose part of the town, with houses built into and against them rather than the ruins being fenced off. The mine disaster in October 2022 killed forty-two workers and is recent enough that it remains a live subject locally.
amasra.whoFor: A genuinely cheap and genuinely quiet Turkish base with a working harbour and a walkable centre, for anyone happy to be the only foreigner in the room. It works best as a summer or shoulder-season stay of a few weeks rather than a year, given what winter does to the place. There is no nomad community in a town of six thousand, the internet is domestic rather than enterprise grade, and nothing here operates in English. Anyone considering a longer stay should look at Bartin or Safranbolu for the practicalities and keep Amasra for the weekends. Anybody working along the Black Sea coast properly should start at this end. The shoreline runs east from here through Sinop and on to Trabzon, and it takes a small fraction of the visitors that the southern coasts absorb every summer. Sinop is the nearest comparison, and Amasra is smaller, prettier and considerably closer to Istanbul.

sanliurfa.costOfLiving: Budget around $600 a month as a solo remote worker in Sanliurfa, which is among the cheapest figures anywhere on this site and reflects a large southeastern Turkish city with almost no international demand on its housing. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $150 to $300 depending on the district, and the newer developments away from the old centre are the better value. Food is remarkably cheap and remarkably good, built on the local kebab tradition and the isot pepper that defines it. Turkish inflation moves these numbers constantly, so treat the figure as a working budget. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $10 to $20 a month at good speeds, which is among the best value on this site. The lira's decline means rents quoted in it can be renegotiated upward mid-lease, a normal Turkish practice rather than a landlord acting badly, and anyone signing for a year should expect the conversation. Eating out is cheap enough that cooking for one rarely saves money here. Rents in Karakopru and the newer northern districts run below the old city and come with better wiring and cooling, which matters more here than character does.
sanliurfa.whereToWork: Sanliurfa has no coworking scene aimed at foreigners, though the city is large enough to have business centres and university facilities serving its own economy. Fibre reaches most of the modern districts and Turkish mobile data is fast and cheap, which is the practical answer for most people. English is very limited outside the archaeological tourism around Gobekli Tepe, and Arabic is widely spoken given the city's large Syrian population. Anyone working here should expect to do daily business in Turkish. Power and water are reliable, though summer demand on air conditioning is heavy across the whole region. Turkey sits three hours ahead of GMT year-round since it abandoned daylight saving in 2016, which gives a full European overlap and an early-afternoon window with the American east coast. The city's large Syrian population also means Arabic is genuinely useful here in a way it is not elsewhere in Turkey. The university is large and its archaeology department is closely tied to the excavations, which is the one professional network here that a foreigner might plausibly join.
sanliurfa.gettingAround: Sanliurfa is a spread-out city of two million and the old centre around Balikligol is the only genuinely walkable part, which is where most visitors spend their time anyway. City buses and dolmus minibuses cover the rest cheaply, and taxis are inexpensive by any standard. Gobekli Tepe is about twenty minutes out by road and needs a taxi or a tour; Karahan Tepe, the newer excavation, is further out and harder to reach. Sanliurfa airport has domestic flights to Istanbul and Ankara. Summer heat makes walking anywhere in the middle of the day genuinely unpleasant from June onwards. Gobekli Tepe is covered by a permanent shelter and boardwalk and takes about ninety minutes to see properly. Harran, with its distinctive beehive mud-brick houses and the ruins of one of the oldest universities in the Islamic world, is an hour south and usually combined with it. Nemrut Dagi, with its giant stone heads on a mountain summit, is three hours north and is usually done as an overnight rather than a day trip.
sanliurfa.visas: Turkey gives most Western nationals ninety days in any hundred and eighty, either visa-free or through a quick e-visa. The Digital Nomad Identification Card introduced in 2024 is open to citizens of a defined list of countries who hold a degree and meet a monthly income threshold, and it smooths the short-term residence permit process rather than being a visa in itself. Residence permits have become considerably harder to obtain, with many districts closed to new foreign registration once a quota is reached. Anyone planning to stay past the visa-free window should research the specific district rather than the country as a whole. Turkey issues a foreigner identity number alongside any residence permit, and it is what actually unlocks daily life, because banks, mobile operators, the health system and the tax office all key off that number rather than off a passport, so obtaining it is the milestone that matters rather than the permit card itself.
sanliurfa.bestTime: March to May and October to November are the only comfortable windows. Sanliurfa sits on the edge of the Mesopotamian plain and summer is severe, regularly above forty degrees through July and August with nights that stay warm, and it shapes everything about how the city runs in those months. Spring brings the plain briefly green and is the best time to see the archaeological sites without suffering for it. Winter is cool and can be wet, with daytime temperatures around ten degrees, and it is a perfectly workable season for anyone who does not mind grey. The isot pepper that defines the local cooking is sun-dried on rooftops through late summer, which is visible across the city in August and is the one thing worth being here in the heat for. Ramadan changes the rhythm of the whole city, with daytime eating restricted in public and the evenings coming alive after sunset, and it moves earlier each year.
sanliurfa.prosCons: Sanliurfa is next door to Gobekli Tepe, the eleven-thousand-year-old site that rewrote the timeline of monumental building, with Karahan Tepe and a dozen related excavations across the same plain. The old city around the Pool of Abraham is one of the most atmospheric places in Turkey, the food is exceptional and the cost of living is extraordinarily low. It is conservative, it is very hot, has essentially no international community, and English is rare. The Syrian border is around fifty kilometres away, which is worth understanding in context rather than as an alarm, and government travel advice for the region should be read directly. Gobekli Tepe predates pottery, metal and the wheel, and only a small fraction of the site has been excavated, which means the picture it gives of the Neolithic is still actively changing rather than settled. Balikligol, the pool of sacred carp beside the Halil-ur-Rahman mosque, is a genuine pilgrimage site rather than an attraction, and behaves like one.
sanliurfa.whoFor: A serious interest in archaeology or the ancient Near East, a wish to be near the sites rather than visiting them on a tour, and the ability to operate in a city that has not adapted itself for outsiders. The cost of living makes a long research stay unusually affordable. No foreign community exists here, alcohol is effectively unavailable in a conservative province, and the social environment is one to adapt to rather than one that will adapt. Anyone sensitive to heat should not consider the summer months here at all, whatever else the trip has going for it. Humanitarian work is the profession this city genuinely accommodates. It hosts one of the largest displaced populations in Turkey, and the concentration of organisations working on the Syrian response is here because of that. Put it beside Gaziantep and Sanliurfa is cheaper, hotter, more conservative and considerably closer to the sites.

oudtshoorn.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month as a solo remote worker in Oudtshoorn, which is inexpensive for South Africa outside the big cities and very cheap by the standards of anywhere with this much English spoken. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $300 to $500, and houses with land are within reach at figures that would be impossible on the coast. Groceries are cheap and local produce is excellent, with the Klein Karoo's wine and olive farms nearby. Budget separately for a vehicle and for power backup, both of which are practical necessities here. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $30 to $45 a month where it reaches. Load shedding was a national fact for a decade and left an inverter in most households as ordinary equipment rather than a precaution, though the cuts themselves ended in May 2025 and nothing has been scheduled since. A car is effectively mandatory here, since the Karoo distances are real and public transport between the towns is minimal, and fuel is the second-largest line after rent for most residents.
oudtshoorn.whereToWork: Oudtshoorn has no coworking provision to speak of, and remote work happens from homes and a few cafes on the main street. Fibre has reached much of the town and is reasonably priced, and mobile data on the main networks is workable though South African data costs remain high relative to local income. Electricity was the real planning issue for years, and it has quietly stopped being one: load shedding eased and then ended, with no stage imposed nationally since 16 May 2025 and the 2026 winter carried in full. Anyone whose work cannot pause should still want a property with an inverter and battery, because a Karoo town at the end of a long line loses power to weather without any schedule behind it. Most established rentals here now include some form of backup as standard. South Africa runs two hours ahead of GMT, which gives a full European overlap and is one of the reasons the country has drawn remote workers at all. The 2024 remote work visa applies here as anywhere in the country, requiring foreign employment above an income threshold, and is the first proper nomad route on the continent.
oudtshoorn.gettingAround: Oudtshoorn is a small grid town that can be crossed on foot, but everything that makes the region worth being in, the Cango Caves, the Swartberg Pass, the ostrich farms and Route 62, needs a car. Public transport between towns is limited to minibus taxis, which serve a different market. George is about an hour away over the Outeniqua Pass and has the nearest airport with domestic connections to Johannesburg and Cape Town. Cape Town itself is around five hours by road. Driving is on the left and the mountain passes demand attention rather than speed. Route 62 runs west from here through Calitzdorp and Barrydale and is marketed as the longest wine route in the world, which is a claim worth taking lightly and a drive worth taking seriously. The Swartberg Pass is gravel throughout and closes after heavy rain or snow, so the condition should be checked before setting out rather than discovered halfway up.
oudtshoorn.visas: South Africa introduced a remote work visa in 2024, open to people employed by a foreign company earning above roughly $36,000 a year, initially for up to three years, and the regulations around tax registration for longer stays have been clarified since. Before that, most visitors used the ninety-day visitor visa that many Western nationalities receive on arrival, which remains the simplest option for a short stay and is extendable once. The remote work route is a genuine improvement on what the country offered previously, though processing times through South African missions abroad vary considerably by country. The extension runs through VFS and has to be started well before the first ninety days expire, because it moves slowly enough to strand somebody who leaves it until the last fortnight. Overstaying triggers a ban that is enforced, so the dates matter more here than the paperwork does. The rules on when a holder of that visa has to register for local tax were settled only after the visa itself was announced, and they turn on how much of a three-year window is spent inside the country rather than on any single year. Anyone planning repeat stays should have that checked by somebody who has read the current regulations rather than the announcement.
oudtshoorn.bestTime: September to April covers the warm half, with hot dry summers that push into the mid thirties in January and February. The Klein Karoo is semi-arid and the heat is dry rather than oppressive, which makes it more bearable than the number suggests. Spring, from September to November, is the best combination of comfortable temperatures and green after the winter rain. The KKNK Afrikaans arts festival fills the town for a week each autumn. Winter nights get genuinely cold at this altitude and inland position, dropping close to freezing, and few older houses here are built for it. The town sits in the rain shadow of the Outeniqua mountains, which is why it is semi-arid while George on the other side of the pass is one of the wettest places in South Africa, and the drive between the two crosses that divide in about forty minutes. The night sky here is the thing nobody plans for and everybody remembers: almost no light pollution for hundreds of kilometres, and the Milky Way visible from a farm gate without any equipment at all. The same dryness that makes the days hot is what keeps the nights that clear.
oudtshoorn.prosCons: Oudtshoorn sits in the Klein Karoo with the Cango Caves and the Swartberg Pass on its doorstep, one of the most dramatic mountain roads in Africa, and it is the centre of the ostrich industry that gave the town its Victorian feather-boom architecture. Costs are low, English is universal and the air and space are exceptional. Nobody else is doing this here, a car is not optional, and South Africa's crime statistics call for the ordinary situational awareness the country demands everywhere. Load shedding belonged on this list until 2025 and no longer does, which removes the one constraint that used to make a working week here genuinely hard to plan. The town is quiet in a way some find restorative and others find limiting. Oudtshoorn's ostrich industry dates to the feather boom of the 1880s, when the trade briefly made the town wealthy enough to build the sandstone feather palaces that still stand, and the industry survives in a much reduced form as farming and tourism.
oudtshoorn.whoFor: Space, dry air and dramatic landscape at a low cost, with the whole Garden Route and Route 62 within a day of driving. A vehicle and a tolerance for small-town rhythms are the entry conditions. Anybody travelling with animals or with a family does unusually well out of it, because of how much house the money buys out here. The international community is a handful of people, public transport barely exists in a Karoo town of this size, and the nightlife finishes early. Anyone whose work cannot survive an outage should sort out power backup before the first week rather than after it. Garden Route travellers who want an inland base rather than a coastal one should look at this side of the pass. The Karoo is drier, cheaper and considerably quieter than the coast an hour south of it.

ifrane.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Ifrane, which is cheap by any international measure but not by Moroccan ones, since the university and the summer visitors keep local prices above what a town this size would otherwise charge. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $250 to $400, with the chalets near the centre at the top of that and Hay Riad and the outer streets below it. Food is inexpensive and the Middle Atlas produce is good. Heating is a real winter line item here in a way it is nowhere else in Morocco. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data. Heating is the line that separates Ifrane from the rest of Morocco: at 1,650 metres the winter is genuinely cold and a poorly insulated flat can cost $80 to $150 a month in gas between December and February, which nobody budgets for after reading about Marrakech. Fibre runs about $25 to $40 a month. The university calendar also moves the rental market noticeably, with the best options gone before term starts.
ifrane.whereToWork: Ifrane has no dedicated coworking, but Al Akhawayn University dominates the town and its presence changes what is available: the cafes around the campus are used to people working, English is spoken far more widely than in comparable Moroccan towns, and the general standard of infrastructure is higher. Moroccan fibre reaches the built-up area and mobile data on the main networks is fast and cheap. Power is stable. Anyone needing more than the town can offer has Fes about an hour and a quarter away, which has both coworking and the flight connections Ifrane lacks entirely. Al Akhawayn teaches in English on an American liberal arts model, which is why the town is anomalously anglophone for Morocco and why a foreigner working from a cafe here attracts no attention at all. Morocco runs on GMT+1 year-round, which puts it in the same working day as continental Europe and one hour ahead of the UK, among the best time zones on this site for European clients.
ifrane.gettingAround: Ifrane is small, laid out on a grid of wide streets and completely walkable, which is unusual enough in Morocco to be worth saying. Grand taxis run to Azrou fifteen minutes away and on to Fes and Meknes, and buses cover the same routes for less. The cedar forest with its Barbary macaques starts just outside town and the Michlifen ski area is twenty minutes up the road, both of which are easier with a car. Fes is the nearest airport at around ninety minutes. Winter snow occasionally closes the higher passes, which is a genuine consideration between December and February. Azrou, fifteen minutes away, is the market town and is where the weekly souk and the cheaper shopping are, so most residents make that trip regularly. The cedar forest between the two holds the Barbary macaques, the only macaque population in Africa and an endangered one, and feeding them is discouraged despite the roadside stalls that encourage it.
ifrane.visas: Morocco gives most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, which is generous and simple. There is no digital nomad visa despite periodic announcements, so anyone wanting longer works through the carte de sejour residence card, which requires a local sponsor, a lease or property, and proof of means, and is processed through the local prefecture rather than centrally. A common informal approach is a short exit to Spain or Ceuta and a fresh ninety days on return, though this is tolerance rather than entitlement and border officials have discretion. Anyone planning a year here should start the residence process early. The ninety-day reset by exiting to Ceuta or Melilla is well established but is a land border into Spanish territory and therefore into Schengen, so anyone using it needs to be counting Schengen days as well as Moroccan ones, which catches out people who assume the two are unrelated. Overstaying the ninety days is settled at the airport with a fine and a stamp that makes the next entry harder, and the officers do count. Anybody living here on repeated entries should keep the dates written down rather than in their head.
ifrane.bestTime: May to October is the comfortable window, with warm dry days that rarely feel hot at this altitude and cool evenings that require a layer. July and August are when Moroccans arrive from Fes, Casablanca and Rabat to escape the lowland heat, and the town is at its busiest and most expensive. Winter is the other reason to come: Ifrane sits above 1,600 metres, gets real snow, and holds the record for the coldest temperature ever recorded in Africa. Skiing at Michlifen is modest by Alpine standards but genuinely exists, which surprises most visitors. Ifrane recorded minus 23.9 degrees in February 1935, still the lowest temperature ever measured in Africa, which is the fact the town is best known for internationally. Michlifen and Mischliffen operate on natural snow only, so the season is short and unreliable and some winters barely produce one. When the university term ends the town empties to a degree that surprises anybody who arrived during it, with half the cafes shut and the streets quiet until the summer visitors come up from the plains. The academic calendar matters more here than the weather does.
ifrane.prosCons: Ifrane is unlike anywhere else in Morocco, an alpine town of pitched roofs and cedar forest built by the French in the 1930s, exceptionally clean, cool in summer and snowy in winter, with an English-language American-curriculum university at its centre. Air quality is among the best in the country. It is small and quiet, and there is no nomad community here, prices are high relative to the surrounding region, and much of the town's life follows the university calendar and empties in the holidays. Anyone coming to Morocco for medinas and coastline will find none of it here. The town holds the record for the coldest temperature ever measured in Africa, minus twenty three point nine degrees in February 1935, which is not what most people expect from Morocco and should shape how anyone plans to get through a winter here, since buildings in the country are generally put up without central heating whatever the temperature outside.
ifrane.whoFor: Clean mountain air, forest on the doorstep and a genuinely cool summer within reach of Fes, in a small, orderly town rather than a Moroccan city. The university connection makes it unusually workable for anyone in academia or education. There is no beach at fifteen hundred metres, no nightlife worth the name, and no nomad scene of any description. July fills the town with Moroccan families escaping the lowland heat, so that month books out and prices climb accordingly. It works best as a summer base or a winter curiosity rather than a year-round home. Summer visitors who cannot manage the lowland heat have exactly one good option in this part of Morocco. Fes and Meknes regularly pass forty degrees in July while this town an hour away sits in the high twenties with cool nights.

djerba.costOfLiving: Budget around $750 a month as a solo remote worker in Djerba, which is low even by Tunisian standards outside the capital and reflects an island whose economy runs on package tourism rather than on residents. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $200 to $400, with Houmt Souk and the beach strip at Sidi Mahrez costing more than anywhere inland. Food is very cheap if bought locally, and the island produces its own olives, dates and fish. The dinar is a closed currency, so bring the means to pay for things rather than assuming a card works. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The closed currency matters in practice: dinars cannot legally be taken out or exchanged abroad, so anything left over at the end of a stay is effectively spent or lost.
djerba.whereToWork: Djerba has almost no coworking provision, and remote work happens from apartments, hotel lobbies and the cafes of Houmt Souk. Tunisian fibre reaches the main towns and mobile data is inexpensive with reasonable coverage across the island, though speeds are modest by European standards and evening congestion is noticeable in the resort areas. Power cuts are occasional rather than routine. French is the practical second language for anything administrative, with English limited to the tourism trade, so anyone here for a stretch will get further with some French than without it. Speeds in the resort strip drop noticeably in the evenings when the hotels fill, so anyone with calls to make is better placed in Houmt Souk than on the beach.
