Pottery has been made at the village on the south coast for two thousand years, out of a local clay, and the workshops there still sell direct. It is one of the few trades on the island not tied to the hotels. The working population divides sharply between people employed by the resorts for six months and everybody else, and the two groups keep different hours and different calendars.
djerba.gettingAround: Djerba is flat, about five hundred square kilometres, and connected to the mainland by a Roman causeway that still carries the road, with a ferry at the other end of the island. Houmt Souk, the main town, is walkable, but the beaches, the synagogue at Erriadh and the villages are spread out and need transport. Scooters and rental cars are the usual answer and both are cheap. Louage shared taxis cover the longer routes. Djerba-Zarzis airport handles charter flights from across Europe in season, which is what makes the island unusually easy to reach for its size. The Roman causeway is the only fixed link and a single road, so an accident on it closes the island's main connection until it clears. A ferry at the western tip crosses to the mainland in a quarter of an hour and runs through the night, which is the alternative when the causeway is blocked and the shorter route south in any case. Riding a bicycle across it is realistic, though the villages sit further apart than a map on this scale prepares you for, and a long ride into a headwind in August is hard work rather than a pleasure.
djerba.visas: Tunisia allows most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, which is straightforward and rarely questioned. There is no digital nomad visa. Staying beyond ninety days means either leaving and returning, which is generally tolerated, or applying for a residence permit through the local authorities, a process that requires local sponsorship and patience. Anyone overstaying should know that a fine is levied at departure, calculated by the length of the overstay, which is an administrative matter rather than a serious one but is easily avoided. Rules are applied more consistently at the airport than at the land borders. Anyone leaving and returning to reset the ninety days should do so through the airport rather than a land border, where the practice is applied less consistently. Cash above a set threshold has to be declared on the way in, and the declaration slip is what allows the balance to be taken out again, so the form matters more than the amount does. Anyone working with a local partner should know that a foreign company cannot simply invoice from here without a registered presence, which is a tax question rather than an immigration one and catches people out later.
djerba.bestTime: April to June and September to November are the best months, with warm days, a swimmable sea and none of the summer crowds. July and August are hot, above thirty most days, and the island fills with European package tourists, which pushes prices to their annual peak. Winter is mild by any northern measure, with daytime temperatures around seventeen and very little rain, and it is a genuinely pleasant time to work here even though much of the resort infrastructure closes. The El Ghriba pilgrimage falls in spring and brings a security presence with it. Much of the resort infrastructure shuts between November and March, so a winter stay means the island to yourself and considerably fewer places open to eat. The sea here is shallow for a long way out and warms earlier in the year than the open Mediterranean does, which is why the swimming season starts weeks ahead of the northern coast. Desert wind reaches the island a few times each year and puts sand in the air for a day at a stretch. Dates come in through the autumn and the roadside stalls sell them still on the stem.
djerba.prosCons: Djerba is a flat island of whitewashed courtyard houses, palm groves and one of the oldest synagogues in the world at El Ghriba, with a settlement pattern UNESCO listed in 2023 and a street art project at Erriadh that brought artists from thirty countries to paint the village. It is cheap, warm and easy to reach from Europe. The island is dominated by all-inclusive resorts that keep their guests inside, there is no remote-working scene of any kind, little English is spoken, and anything beyond the tourist economy runs slowly. It is a place to be quiet in rather than to network. El Ghriba draws a pilgrimage each spring that is one of the oldest continuous Jewish observances anywhere, and the security around it is a visible reminder of why that is notable.
djerba.whoFor: Mediterranean warmth, very low costs and a short flight back to Europe, for anyone content with their own company. It works particularly well in the shoulder seasons, when the weather holds and the resorts have emptied. A professional community does not exist on the island, the internet is adequate rather than fast, and the nearest thing to a city is on the mainland. Anyone with French will find the island far easier to live in than anyone without. It rewards a month or two rather than a year, unless the appeal is precisely how little happens. Winter flights to Europe are shorter and more frequent from here than the island's size would suggest, because the charter network that serves the resorts keeps operating at reduced frequency through the cold months.

nanyuki.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Nanyuki, which buys considerably more here than the same figure does in Nairobi. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, and houses with gardens are within reach at figures that would be impossible in the capital, which is why the town has attracted a long-standing settler and expatriate farming community. Food is cheap and the produce from the Mount Kenya slopes is excellent. Budget separately for a vehicle and for a backup power arrangement. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Fibre where it reaches runs $40 to $70 a month and a Safaricom data bundle rather less, which is the arrangement most people actually use. A vehicle is the substantial line: a used four-wheel drive is a real purchase and hiring one is $60 to $100 a day, which is why residents buy rather than rent. Conservancy entry fees are $60 to $100 a day for non-residents, so anyone here for the wildlife should ask about resident rates.
nanyuki.whereToWork: Nanyuki has a small but real coworking presence, unusual for a Kenyan town this size, driven by the conservation organisations, the tourism operators and the resident expatriate community rather than by nomads. Fibre has reached parts of the town and Safaricom's mobile data is the reliable fallback almost everywhere, with 4G across the built-up area. Power cuts happen and anyone whose work cannot pause should assume an inverter or a generator. English is an official language and universally spoken, which removes the friction that a comparable town elsewhere in the region would carry. Nairobi is four hours by road. Kenya sits three hours ahead of GMT, which gives a full European working overlap and a late-afternoon window with the American east coast, and is one of the better time zones on this site for anyone working across both. M-Pesa handles nearly all everyday payment, and a Kenyan SIM and mobile money account are the first things to arrange on arrival rather than a card.
nanyuki.gettingAround: Nanyuki is a small town straddling the equator at around 1,950 metres, and the centre is walkable while everything that draws people here is not. Ol Pejeta and Lewa conservancies, the Mount Kenya trailheads and the surrounding farms all need a vehicle, and most residents have one. Matatu minibuses and boda boda motorcycle taxis cover local trips cheaply. The road to Nairobi takes around four hours and is in reasonable condition. Nanyuki has an airstrip with light aircraft connections to Nairobi and the northern conservancies, which is how most safari traffic arrives. The equator line runs through the town and is marked on the main road, which is a tourist stop rather than a landmark but does tell you exactly where you are. Mount Kenya's Sirimon and Chogoria routes both start within a couple of hours, and Point Lenana, the trekking summit at 4,985 metres, is a three to four day walk rather than a technical climb.
nanyuki.visas: Kenya replaced its visa system with an Electronic Travel Authorisation in January 2024, required of almost all arrivals and granting stays of up to ninety days. In late 2024 the government announced a digital nomad work permit for remote workers employed outside Kenya, with an income threshold reported at around $55,000 a year and an initial validity of one year. Implementation details have moved since the announcement, so confirm the current requirements with a Kenyan mission rather than relying on secondary reporting. The older route, a class of work permit tied to an employer or a business, remains available and remains slow. The ETA replaced visa-free entry even for nationalities that previously had it, including several African countries, which caused real confusion in its first year. It must be applied for before travel rather than on arrival, and approval usually comes within a few days. An ordinary work permit requires the employer to show that no citizen could fill the role, which is why almost every foreigner working here on a long contract is with a conservation organisation, a school or a mission rather than a company.
nanyuki.bestTime: Nanyuki sits high enough that the equator does not translate into heat, with daytime temperatures around the low twenties year-round and nights that get genuinely cold. The dry seasons, January to March and July to October, are the best for the mountain and the conservancies, and July to October is when Mount Kenya climbing is most reliable. The long rains from late March into May and the short rains in November bring afternoon storms rather than continuous wet, and the landscape is at its greenest immediately after. There is no bad season here, only a muddier one. The altitude is the thing to plan for rather than the latitude: nights drop to single figures year-round and houses here are built with fireplaces, which visitors expecting equatorial Africa find surprising. The long rains can make the conservancy tracks difficult in April and May. Sitting on the equator at nearly two thousand metres means the ultraviolet here is punishing even on a cool day, and anybody who judges the sun by the temperature gets caught out inside a week. A jumper is wanted after dark whatever the calendar says. Rain arrives as an afternoon event rather than a day-long one.
nanyuki.prosCons: Nanyuki sits on the equator at the foot of Mount Kenya, with Ol Pejeta and Lewa conservancies on the doorstep and some of the best air and light in East Africa. English is universal, costs are low, and there is a long-established resident community with the services that come with it. The town is small and professionally shallow, internet reliability depends on the particular arrangement rather than the address, power cuts are entirely routine, and a vehicle of your own is not optional here. The wider region's security situation varies by area, so travel advice north of the town should be read directly. Ol Pejeta holds the last two northern white rhinos on earth, both female and under permanent armed guard, which makes a visit there a genuinely singular experience rather than another game drive. Lewa's conservancy model is studied internationally and the community programmes around both are substantial.
nanyuki.whoFor: Mountains, wildlife and a temperate climate at low cost with English spoken everywhere, provided you are set up to work through the outages. It is unusually good for anyone in conservation, agriculture or field research, where the local network is genuinely deep. Families get space, and a set of schools that the expatriate community here has kept going for years. This is a market town rather than a city, the nightlife is a few bars, and no nomad scene has formed. Without a vehicle the landscape that justifies being here stays firmly on the other side of the window. Runners and cyclists get something here that money cannot buy elsewhere. Kenya's high-altitude training culture is centred not far away, and Iten, the town that has produced a generation of distance runners, is a manageable drive west.

lome.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Lome, which is low for a West African capital and reflects a city that has never had the oil or mining money that inflated some of its neighbours. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $200 to $400, with the beachfront and the diplomatic quarter well above that and the inland neighbourhoods well below. Street food is very cheap and the markets are excellent. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, which removes the currency volatility that complicates budgets elsewhere in the region. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre where it reaches runs $60 to $120 a month for speeds that would cost a fraction of that in Europe, which is the standard West African internet penalty. A zemidjan ride across town is well under a dollar. The CFA peg to the euro at a rate unchanged since 1999 means a European income holds its value here in a way it does not in Ghana or Nigeria next door.
lome.whereToWork: Lome has a small startup and coworking scene, concentrated in a handful of spaces serving the city's technology and logistics sectors, and it is more developed than the country's size would suggest thanks to the port. Fibre reaches parts of the city and mobile data on the main networks is workable, though West African internet pricing remains high relative to speed and evening congestion is real. Power cuts happen and most serious workplaces have a generator. French is the working language of everything administrative and English is limited, so operating here without French is genuinely difficult. Togo runs on GMT with no offset at all, which makes it the single easiest time zone on this site for anyone working with London and comfortable for continental Europe. Mobile money through Flooz and T-Money handles most everyday payment and a local SIM registered on arrival is the first practical step.
lome.gettingAround: Lome runs along the Gulf of Guinea coast with the Ghanaian border at its western edge, close enough that the frontier is effectively part of the city. Zemidjan motorcycle taxis are the dominant way to move and cost very little, though they demand a helmet and some nerve. Shared taxis cover the longer routes. The coastal road is the main axis and the Grand Marche sits at the centre of everything. Lome airport is a regional hub with connections across West Africa and to Europe, which makes the city considerably easier to reach than its profile suggests. The Ghanaian border at Kodjoviakope is walkable from the city centre, which makes a day in Aflao or a longer trip to Accra unusually easy. The coastal road east to Benin and Nigeria is the main regional artery and the buses along it are frequent, cheap and slow. The airline based at this airport was set up as a regional carrier with an East African partner, and it is why a city this size has direct flights to two dozen capitals across the continent. Connecting through here is often cheaper than routing through the bigger hubs.
lome.visas: Togo offers an eVisa and visa on arrival at Lome airport for most nationalities, typically for stays of seven to thirty days and extendable at the immigration office in the city, which is the normal route rather than an exception. There is no digital nomad visa. Anyone planning a longer stay applies for a residence permit locally, a process that requires documentation, patience and generally some French. Togo is part of ECOWAS, so overland travel to Ghana, Benin and beyond is straightforward for citizens of the bloc and requires separate consideration for everyone else. Yellow fever vaccination is required on entry. The visa on arrival is issued for seven days initially in many cases and must then be extended at the Service des Migrations in the city, which is a straightforward but in-person process that catches out anyone who assumed the airport stamp covered their whole stay. A regional visa exists covering this country and four of its neighbours on one document, which is worth asking about for anyone planning a circuit rather than a single stay, though not every consulate issues it readily and it is easier to obtain inside the region than outside it.
lome.bestTime: November to February is the dry season and the best time to be here, with less humidity than the rest of the year and daytime temperatures around thirty. The harmattan can bring dust down from the Sahara in December and January, which drops visibility and irritates anyone with a respiratory sensitivity. The long rains run from April to July and the short rains return in September and October, both bringing heavy downpours rather than continuous grey. Coastal humidity is a constant regardless of season and is the thing most arrivals underestimate about the climate here. There is a short dry break in August, the petite saison seche, which splits the rains and is a genuinely pleasant window that most guides miss. The harmattan months are also the coolest nights of the year, dropping to the low twenties, which is the closest Lome comes to relief. In the north of the country the July wrestling festival marks the initiation of young men over several days and draws the whole region, which is the most striking thing in the national calendar and a long drive from the coast. Nothing down here runs at that scale.
lome.prosCons: Lome is a genuinely underrated West African capital, with a long beach through the middle of the city, the vast Grand Marche, the Akodessewa fetish market that is unlike anything else on the continent, and an airport that connects across the region and to Europe. Costs are low and the port gives the city a commercial energy. There is no nomad community here whatsoever, French is close to mandatory in daily life, power and internet are both unreliable, and the city demands more situational awareness than most places on this site. It is a place for the experienced rather than the first trip. The Akodessewa market supplies the Vodun practice of the whole region and is a working religious supply market rather than an exhibit, which is worth understanding before visiting: it is photographed heavily and the fee for doing so is part of how it operates.
lome.whoFor: A low-cost coastal capital with excellent regional flight connections, for French speakers who already work in West Africa or want to. It works well as a base for anyone covering the region rather than as a destination in itself. Reliable infrastructure, an English-speaking environment and a nomad community of any kind are three things this city does not have in any usable form, and French is not optional. Anyone new to the region would be better served starting in Accra, two hours west, and coming to Lome from there. Logistics and shipping are why this city matters more than its size implies. The port here is the deepest on the West African coast and handles transhipment for much of the region, which is the commercial fact underneath everything else about the place.

tofo.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Tofo, which is low for the diving it buys but not as low as the surrounding country, since everything on this beach is priced for visitors. A room or a simple one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450 depending on how close it sits to the sand and whether it is high season. Food is cheap if bought at the market in Inhambane and considerably less so at the beach restaurants. Diving is the real budget line here. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data. Diving is the line that dominates any Tofo budget: a single dive runs $45 to $60, a ten-dive package considerably less per dive, and an Open Water certification $350 to $450. Anyone here for a month who dives most days should expect that to exceed their rent. Electricity is expensive and unreliable in equal measure, and a place with a working inverter is worth paying more for.
tofo.whereToWork: Tofo has no coworking and its internet is the honest weak point of the place. Mobile data on Vodacom or Tmcel is the primary connection for most people and speeds vary by hour and by weather. Fixed lines exist in a few of the better guesthouses and lodges. Power cuts are routine and most established places run on an inverter or a generator. Anyone whose work involves video calls should test thoroughly before committing to a month, and anyone who cannot tolerate an outage should look elsewhere on this coast. Mozambique runs two hours ahead of GMT, level with South Africa, which gives a full European overlap in the afternoon and makes European work genuinely practical when the connection holds. Starlink has appeared at some lodges since 2023 and is the single thing most likely to make a longer stay workable, so it is worth asking about by name. A permit to work is granted against a named employer, and the centres here sponsor only their permanent staff, so instructors passing through for a season are mostly doing it informally. None of that touches somebody billing a client abroad, which is the cleaner arrangement by a distance.
tofo.gettingAround: Tofo is a beach village and everything in it is within a fifteen-minute walk, which is a large part of why people stay longer than they planned. Inhambane, the provincial town with the market, the bank and the ferry, is about twenty-five minutes inland by chapa minibus or taxi. Inhambane airport has flights to Maputo and Johannesburg, which is the practical way in. The road from Maputo takes seven or eight hours by bus. Sand tracks lead to the quieter beaches at Barra and Tofinho, and a four-wheel drive or a walk are the only ways along them. Chapas run to Inhambane through the day and stop in the early evening, so an evening in town means arranging a taxi back. The dhow ferry across the bay from Inhambane to Maxixe is cheap, frequent and the pleasant way to make that crossing rather than driving around. Police checkpoints on the main highway are frequent and ask for a driving licence, a passport and the vehicle papers, so a hire car wants all three in the glovebox rather than one of them in a bag. Nothing about the stop is unusual once the documents are there.
tofo.visas: Mozambique removed visa requirements in 2023 for citizens of a long list of countries including most of Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia, allowing visits of up to thirty days, which transformed the practicality of getting here. Everyone else can obtain a visa on arrival at the main entry points or apply in advance. Extensions are handled at immigration offices in the provincial capitals, meaning Inhambane rather than the beach. There is no digital nomad visa. The policy shift was recent enough that some airlines and border posts have been slower than the rules, so carry the documentation anyway. The 2023 visa exemption covers tourism specifically and for thirty days, so anyone planning a longer stay is looking at an extension from Inhambane or a border run to Eswatini or South Africa. Carry proof of onward travel and accommodation, since the exemption is newer than some officials' habits.
tofo.bestTime: Tofo works year-round, which is unusual, because the whale sharks and manta rays that draw divers here are resident rather than seasonal. April to September is the dry half, cooler and clearer, with humpback whales passing through between roughly June and October and the best visibility for diving. October to March is hotter and wetter, with the warmest water and the highest chance of a cyclone, most likely between January and March. The Mozambique Channel has produced serious storms in recent years, and anyone booking in that window should follow the forecasts. Water temperature ranges from about twenty-two degrees in the cooler months to twenty-nine in the warm half, so a wetsuit matters between June and September. Manta cleaning stations at Manta Reef are most reliably productive in the cooler, clearer water, which is the opposite of what most visitors assume. South African school holidays in December and again in the middle of the year are what actually fill this beach, rather than any international season, and the prices and the noise both follow that calendar rather than the weather.
tofo.prosCons: Tofo is one of the few places on earth where whale sharks and giant manta rays are present all year, on a wide arc of beach with a diving community that has been here for decades and a research presence studying both species. It is warm, cheap by the standards of what it offers, and small enough to know within a week. The internet is genuinely poor and the power cuts are routine, medical facilities are very limited and the nearest real hospital is a long way off, and the village has almost nothing beyond diving and the beach. The Marine Megafauna Foundation was founded here and Tofo is one of the longest-running whale shark research sites in the world, so the diving community has a scientific spine that most beach destinations lack and volunteers and researchers pass through constantly.
tofo.whoFor: This is a place for a diver first and a remote worker second. Anyone whose work tolerates an unreliable connection and who wants to be in the water most days will find few better places at this price. A month or a season is the right length for this. A year is a different question entirely. A demanding call schedule will lose here more often than it wins, medical infrastructure means a long drive to Inhambane and a longer one to Maputo, and there is no professional community whatsoever. Bring a local SIM, a power bank and a tolerance for things happening slowly, and it repays all three. Marine research is a live activity here rather than a recreational veneer. The long-running study programmes take volunteers, and the scientists working on them make up a genuine part of the village's social life rather than passing through it.

boise.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Boise, which no longer makes it the bargain it was before 2020, when a wave of arrivals from the west coast reset the housing market permanently. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $1,100 to $1,500, with the North End and downtown at the top and the Bench and Garden City cheaper. Idaho has no local sales tax surprises beyond the state rate and utilities are reasonable. Health insurance is the line item that dominates any American budget and sits outside this figure. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Idaho's income tax is a flat rate in the high five per cent range and the state sales tax is six per cent, which is middling for the American west. Coworking runs $200 to $350 a month. The housing reset since 2020 is the number that matters most: Boise had one of the steepest percentage increases of any American metro in that period, so any figure from before then is badly out of date and locals will tell you so.
boise.whereToWork: Boise has a real coworking market for a city its size, built on a technology sector anchored by Micron and a startup scene that grew through the last decade. Desks run from roughly $200 a month. Fibre reaches most of the city at competitive American prices and mobile coverage is comprehensive. The professional network here is genuine rather than nominal, which distinguishes Boise from most of the smaller American cities on this site, and the state capital and university both add layers to it. Remote workers are common enough that no one finds the arrangement unusual. Boise sits in Mountain time, two hours behind New York and seven to eight behind most of Europe, so east-coast work starts early and European work is impractical. Micron's presence is the anchor of the technology sector and its expansion has continued, which is unusual for a city this size and is why the professional network holds up rather than being a handful of freelancers.
boise.gettingAround: Boise is flat where it matters and the downtown grid is walkable, though the city sprawls into the valley beyond it and most residents drive. The Boise River Greenbelt runs about forty kilometres along the water and is the spine of the city for cycling and walking, which is the single best thing about moving around here. Valley Regional Transit buses cover the main corridors and little else. The Ridge to Rivers trail network starts at the edge of the foothills within reach of downtown. Boise airport is fifteen minutes out with direct flights across the western United States. The Greenbelt is the single piece of infrastructure that defines daily life here, running from Lucky Peak through the middle of the city, and a good number of residents commute on it year-round. Bogus Basin is a non-profit community ski area rather than a resort, which keeps the season pass remarkably cheap by American standards and the crowds local. No passenger train has served this city in decades, so the airport ten minutes from downtown does everything, and the drive to the nearest larger city runs six hours in any direction you choose. That isolation is the thing residents either value or resent.
boise.visas: The United States has no digital nomad visa and no intention of creating one. Most Western nationals enter under the Visa Waiver Programme with an ESTA, which allows ninety days per visit for tourism or business meetings but explicitly not productive work, and remote work for a foreign employer sits in a grey area that the government has never resolved and border officers judge individually. The B1 and B2 visitor visas allow up to six months for those who need them. Anything longer requires a work visa tied to an employer, an investor category or family sponsorship, none of which is quick. As elsewhere in the United States, the practical reading is that this page describes a place for people who already hold work rights. Anyone entering on an ESTA should treat the ninety days as the ceiling it is and avoid the pattern of repeated back-to-back entries, which is precisely what secondary inspection exists to examine.
boise.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months, with warm dry days and cool nights that suit the trails and the river. Summer from July into August is hot and dry, regularly above thirty-five degrees, and wildfire smoke from the wider region has become a recurring feature of late summer that visibly affects air quality for days at a time. Winter is cold but not severe by northern American standards, with daytime temperatures around freezing and enough snow for Bogus Basin thirty minutes up the mountain, which is the reason many people here tolerate January. The Boise River is the summer social centre as much as the trails are: floating it from Barber Park to Ann Morrison is a city-wide ritual through July and August, and the shuttle and rental operation that supports it is run by the county. Smoke season increasingly overlaps the best of it. Floating the river on a rented tube from one park down to another is the town's summer institution, with a shuttle running people back upstream, and on a hot Saturday the water is busier than the path beside it.
boise.prosCons: Boise gives outdoor access that few American cities can match, with a forty-kilometre riverside greenbelt through the middle, foothill trails from the edge of downtown, a ski area half an hour away and whitewater within reach. It has a genuine technology employment base, a walkable centre and the largest Basque community in the United States with the food and festival culture to show for it. Costs here have risen sharply, the summer brings both heat and wildfire smoke, and the city is a long way from anywhere, with Salt Lake City and Portland both a serious drive. The Basque community is a genuine feature rather than a curiosity: the Basque Block downtown, the boarding house museum and the Jaialdi festival every five years make Boise the centre of Basque-American life, a legacy of the sheepherding migration of the late nineteenth century.
boise.whoFor: Trails, a river and a real professional network without a coastal price, for an American willing to drive for whatever the city does not stock itself. It is unusually good for anyone who skis, rides or paddles, since all three are within thirty minutes. Without American work rights there is essentially nothing to build on, since the visa system offers a remote worker almost no route, and the international community in Idaho is small enough to notice its absence. Late-summer arrivals should know what the smoke season does to the air here. Scale is the argument that keeps people here. This is a western American city with the trails and the airport of somewhere considerably larger, and it can still be crossed in twenty minutes, which is a combination that usually disappears as a place grows.

spokane.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Spokane, which is one of the cheaper mid-sized cities in the American west and roughly half what the same life costs in Seattle. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $900 to $1,300, with downtown and the South Hill at the top of that and the north side and Spokane Valley below it. Washington has no state income tax, which is a meaningful difference for anyone earning here rather than abroad. Health insurance sits outside this figure and dominates any American budget. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Sales tax runs close to nine per cent and is added at the register rather than shown on the shelf, which is the offsetting cost and the thing that catches anyone used to a displayed price being the price.
spokane.whereToWork: Spokane has a modest coworking market serving a healthcare, education and aerospace economy, with desks from roughly $150 a month and several spaces clustered downtown. Gonzaga University and the medical school give the city a professional layer beyond its size. Fibre is widely available at ordinary American prices and mobile coverage is comprehensive across the valley. Seattle is about an hour by air or four and a half hours by road, which is how most people here handle anything the local network cannot supply. Remote work is common enough in the city that it needs no explanation. The city sits in the Pacific time zone, which puts it three hours behind the American east coast and eight or nine behind most of Europe, so European work means very early mornings. An air force base west of the city is the single biggest employer for a long way around, and it is the reason the aerospace suppliers settled here at all, which the outdoor reputation gives no hint of. Healthcare is the other pillar, with two medical schools now training here, and together they support a professional population that depends on nothing seasonal. None of it competes for a remote worker's attention, which is rather the point.
spokane.gettingAround: Spokane is built around a river gorge with waterfalls running through the middle of downtown, which makes the centre unusually walkable for an American city of this size. Riverfront Park sits at the heart of it and the Centennial Trail runs sixty kilometres along the river towards Idaho, which is the best cycling here by a distance. The bus network covers the main corridors adequately and little else, so most residents drive. Spokane airport is fifteen minutes from downtown with direct flights across the west. Coeur d'Alene and its lake are forty minutes east over the state line. Snow closes the passes west over the Cascades several times each winter, which is worth knowing if the drive to Seattle is part of your plan rather than the flight. The long-distance train across the northern states calls here in the middle of the night, and this is where it splits, one half going on to the coast and the other to Portland, which is a piece of railway theatre performed at two in the morning to nobody at all. It is slow but genuinely pleasant if the schedule suits. Otherwise the interstate running east and west is the only road that matters.
spokane.visas: The United States offers no digital nomad visa. Most Western nationals enter under the Visa Waiver Programme with an ESTA, which permits ninety days for tourism or business meetings but not productive work, and remote work for a foreign employer occupies a grey area that has never been formally resolved and is judged individually at the border. B1 and B2 visitor visas allow up to six months for nationalities outside the waiver programme. Anything longer requires employer sponsorship, an investor category or family, and none of those routes is quick or cheap. Border officers judge the purpose of a visit rather than the location of an employer, so anyone entering under the waiver should be able to describe the trip as a visit and show onward travel. Tax residence is the trap rather than immigration: spending enough days here across three years triggers a presence test that can make somebody liable on worldwide income regardless of which visa they hold, and the counting formula is not intuitive. Anyone stringing visits together should run the numbers before the third year rather than after it. The travel authorisation is good for two years and any number of trips inside it.
spokane.bestTime: June, September and early October are the best months, with warm dry days, cool nights and the river at its most usable. July and August are hot and dry, often above thirty-two degrees, and wildfire smoke from the interior northwest has become a regular feature of late summer that can hold air quality down for a week at a time. Winter is cold and grey with real snow, daytime temperatures around freezing, and three ski areas within an hour and a half including Mount Spokane and Schweitzer over in Idaho. Spring comes late and wet. The smoke season is now predictable enough that residents track air quality daily through August and September, and an indoor filter is a normal household item rather than a precaution. The city calls itself after the lilac and holds a parade for it in May, which is when the gardens on the hill above downtown repay the climb. Cold air settles into the valley through the darkest weeks and can sit there for days, so a grey stretch down here is often bright a few hundred metres up on the ridge. The river runs hardest on snowmelt in April and the falls are loudest then.
spokane.prosCons: Spokane has a waterfall in the middle of downtown, sixty kilometres of riverside trail, three ski areas within ninety minutes and lakes across the Idaho border, all at costs that make Seattle look absurd. Hoopfest and Bloomsday give the city two of the largest events of their kind anywhere. There is no international circle here to join at all, the summer smoke season is a genuine health consideration, the winters run long and grey, and the city is isolated enough that most trips involve a flight. The professional network is real but shallow outside healthcare and education. Spokane is also the largest city between Seattle and Minneapolis, which gives it more medical and cultural infrastructure than its population would otherwise support.
spokane.whoFor: Outdoor access and a walkable downtown at a price the coast cannot match, for an American who does not mind a real winter. It is unusually good for anyone who skis, since three areas sit within easy reach and none of them carries resort pricing. American work rights are the gate, and without them the rest is academic. Beyond that, the international scene is thin and the professional network shallow outside health care and the university. Anyone with a respiratory condition should look closely at what late summer does to the air here. American east-coast hours are the reason to be here rather than somewhere warmer. The three-hour offset turns a nine-to-five into a six-to-two and hands back every afternoon for the trail.

burlington.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Burlington, which is expensive for a city of forty-five thousand people and reflects a tight housing market squeezed by the university and by very limited new construction. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $1,300 to $1,700, and finding one at all is harder than affording one, particularly around the start of the academic year. Vermont's grocery prices run above the national average. Health insurance sits outside this figure as it does everywhere in the country. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Vermont has no sales tax on clothing or groceries and a modest rate on everything else, which softens the housing figure slightly. Coworking runs $200 to $350 a month. Heating is the northern cost and a Vermont winter on oil or propane can add $150 to $250 a month between December and March, which is the line most people from warmer states get wrong.
burlington.whereToWork: Burlington has a coworking scene disproportionate to its size, built on a startup community, the University of Vermont and a long-standing culture of small independent business. Desks run from roughly $200 a month and several spaces sit within walking distance of Church Street. Burlington Electric has run the city on entirely renewable sources since 2014, which is a genuine distinction rather than a marketing line, and the grid is reliable. Fibre is available across most of the city. Montreal is under two hours by road for anything the local network cannot supply. Burlington sits in Eastern time, which makes it the rare American base with a workable European overlap: a London afternoon is a Burlington morning. Montreal being ninety minutes north also means a genuinely international city is closer than Boston, which is four hours, and that shapes weekends more than the map suggests. The state has more breweries per head than any other and this city is where most of them sell, which sounds like a novelty until you notice how much of the local small-business economy, from packaging through distribution to hospitality, is built on top of it.
burlington.gettingAround: Burlington is small enough to cross on foot, with the Church Street Marketplace as a genuine pedestrian centre rather than a token block, and the lakefront a few minutes downhill from it. The Island Line Trail runs north along Lake Champlain on an old causeway, with a seasonal bike ferry across the gap, and is one of the best rides in the northeast. Green Mountain Transit covers the county. Burlington airport is fifteen minutes out with connections through the eastern hubs. Stowe and Sugarbush are both under an hour, and Montreal is a straightforward drive north. The Amtrak Vermonter runs south to New York in about nine hours, which is slow but scenic and avoids the airport entirely. Lake Champlain ferries cross to New York State from three points along the shore, and the Burlington to Port Kent run is a seasonal shortcut into the Adirondacks that saves an hour over driving around the water.
burlington.visas: The United States has no digital nomad visa. Visa Waiver Programme nationals enter with an ESTA for up to ninety days, which permits tourism and business meetings but not productive work, and remote employment for a foreign company sits in the unresolved grey area that American immigration policy has never addressed. Longer visits run on B1 or B2 visitor visas of up to six months. Anything beyond that requires an employer-sponsored category, an investor route or family sponsorship. The Canadian border is forty-five minutes away, which is convenient but is not a reset mechanism for status. The proximity of the Canadian border is worth stating plainly rather than leaving implied: crossing to Montreal and returning does not reset an ESTA period, and a same-day turnaround is a well-known pattern that officers on both sides recognise immediately. State income tax is a separate question from the federal one: this state taxes people who spend more than half the year in it, and its rules do not depend on immigration status at all. Both sets of thresholds want looking at together before a stay is planned around either.
burlington.bestTime: September and early October are the reason people come, with clear cool days and foliage across the Green Mountains that draws visitors from across the country. Summer from June to August is warm, humid and the best time for the lake, and the city is at its most alive. Winter is long and genuinely cold, with January averages below freezing and heavy snow, which is excellent for the ski areas and hard on anyone unprepared for four months of it. Spring is the mud season locals warn about, wet and unattractive, and April is the month to skip. Foliage peaks in the Champlain valley around the first week of October and a week or two earlier in the mountains, and accommodation across the state books out months ahead for it. The lake moderates the city's climate noticeably, so Burlington is milder than the interior of Vermont in both directions. Whether the lake freezes over completely is recorded each year and has been for well over a century, and it now happens far less often than it once did, which is the local climate record everybody here cites. In the years it does, people walk out onto it.
burlington.prosCons: Burlington is a small city with the amenities of a much larger one: a real pedestrian centre, a lake with the Adirondacks on the far shore, a startup and food culture well beyond its size, and an electricity supply that has been fully renewable for over a decade. Skiing is under an hour and Montreal under two. It is expensive for what it actually is, housing is genuinely scarce, the winter is a long one, and a city of this size will be exhausted by anyone looking for scale. There is no meaningful international community. The renewable electricity claim is worth understanding precisely: Burlington Electric sources the equivalent of the city's annual use from renewables, largely a biomass plant, hydro and wind, rather than running islanded from the grid. It is still a genuine and unusual achievement for an American city.
burlington.whoFor: A walkable small city with mountains, a lake and a strong independent culture, for an American who actively likes winter rather than tolerating it. Food, the outdoor industry and climate work all have a local network here that runs a good deal deeper than the population would predict. Without United States work rights nothing else about this town matters, and anybody needing a large city is describing Boston rather than Vermont. Late August is the specific date to avoid: the student housing rush makes finding anywhere to live close to impossible for a fortnight. Portland, Maine is the usual comparison: Burlington trades the ocean for the mountains and gets closer to Montreal in the bargain. Vermont once paid remote workers to relocate here through a state grant scheme, which says something about its demographics: among the oldest and least populous states in the country, and actively trying to import working-age people.

nanaimo.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Nanaimo, which is meaningfully cheaper than Victoria and dramatically cheaper than Vancouver while sitting on the same coast. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $1,100 to $1,500, with the harbour and the north end at the top of that range. British Columbia's grocery and fuel prices are high by North American standards. The saving against the mainland is the entire reason the city has grown, and it has been narrowing steadily. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Ferries are the line most people underestimate, at roughly $70 each way for a car and driver to the mainland, which quietly reshapes how often you leave the island.
nanaimo.whereToWork: Nanaimo has a small coworking presence serving a local economy of healthcare, education, forestry and the growing population of people who left Vancouver. Vancouver Island University keeps a professional layer in the city. Fibre is widely available at Canadian prices, which are high, and mobile coverage is good in the built-up area and patchy once the island road heads inland. The float plane to downtown Vancouver takes about twenty minutes, which makes a meeting on the mainland a morning rather than a day and is the single most useful piece of infrastructure here. Coverage has real gaps on the highway north to Campbell River and west across to Tofino, which matters if your work involves calls taken on the move. The clock is the thing to think about before committing: eight hours behind London and three behind the eastern cities means a European call lands before breakfast and an eastern one eats the morning, which suits somebody billing westwards and punishes anybody billing east. Forestry is still a real employer here, though the mills have closed steadily for thirty years and the jobs that replaced them are in health, education and the public sector rather than in anything a newcomer walks into.
nanaimo.gettingAround: Nanaimo is strung along the coast and the downtown core near the harbour is walkable, but the city sprawls north and south along the highway and most residents drive. Two ferry routes cross to the mainland, at Departure Bay and Duke Point, taking around two hours to Horseshoe Bay and Tsawwassen respectively. Float planes and a passenger ferry serve downtown Vancouver directly. Victoria is ninety minutes south by road and Tofino around three hours west across the island. Saysutshun, the island in the harbour, is a ten-minute foot passenger ferry and a good afternoon. BC Transit covers the corridor between downtown and the university adequately during the day, then thins sharply in the evening, which is when the car becomes unavoidable. Sailings fill on summer weekends and a reservation costs extra on top of the fare, so turning up and waiting for the next boat is the alternative and it can mean hours in a car park. The island highway drops to two lanes for most of its length once you leave the corridor, and deer on it at dusk are a standing hazard rather than an occasional one. Winter tyres are required by law on the routes across the island between autumn and spring.
nanaimo.visas: Canada has no digital nomad visa, but its 2023 tech talent strategy confirmed what had been ambiguous: visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer during a standard visitor stay, normally up to six months. That is the practical route for most people and it requires only an eTA for visa-exempt nationalities. The International Experience Canada working holiday covers under-thirties or under-thirty-fives depending on country and gives full work rights for one or two years. Permanent routes run through Express Entry and the provincial nominee programmes, both of which are competitive and slow. The six months is at the border officer's discretion rather than an entitlement, so be ready to show ties abroad and onward travel. An extension is applied for online before the current stay expires and produces a visitor record, a document rather than a stamp, and applying in time preserves status while the decision is pending. Citizens of the country to the south need no authorisation at all and are simply waved through, a distinction that advice written for everybody else tends to bury. The province runs a stream of its own aimed at smaller communities, which is how a few people have turned a stay out here into something permanent.
nanaimo.bestTime: May to September is the dry half and the reason people put up with the rest, with warm days rarely above twenty-five, long light evenings and the water at its most usable. July and August are the busiest and the driest. October to April is the wet season, and the total rainfall is the defining fact of life on this coast: not cold, rarely below freezing, but grey and wet for weeks. The island's east coast, where Nanaimo sits, is considerably drier than the west, which is a difference worth understanding before choosing a town. The dry stretch has lengthened in recent years and summer water restrictions are now a routine part of an island summer rather than an exceptional measure. The herring spawn in late winter turns miles of water a pale milky green and brings sea lions, eagles and whales in behind it, which is the one genuinely spectacular natural event of the year here and is over inside a fortnight. At the other end, smoke from fires burning in the interior drifts across the strait some years and settles for days, turning a bright week hazy and orange. Neither is on any tourist calendar and both shape how residents plan.
nanaimo.prosCons: Nanaimo gives access to Vancouver Island at a price the island's better-known towns no longer offer, with a working harbour, a twenty-minute float plane to downtown Vancouver, forest and coast in every direction and Tofino across the island. English is universal and the city is safe and easy. The winter is relentlessly grey and wet, no remote-working scene has formed here at all, the city itself is workmanlike rather than beautiful outside the harbour, and Canadian internet and grocery costs are high. Everything beyond the island involves a ferry or a flight. Island healthcare capacity is stretched and finding a family doctor is a well-known local difficulty, which matters more for a stay of months than of weeks.
nanaimo.whoFor: The Pacific northwest coast without the Vancouver housing market, for anyone holding Canadian work rights or a working holiday and set up for a wet winter. Paddling, hiking and riding are all immediately accessible, which is most of why anybody chooses to live out here. Foreigners in numbers, a night out and a professional network with any depth all sit across the strait in Vancouver, and the ferry is long enough that they stay there. Victoria is worth visiting before deciding, since the price gap has narrowed and the character of the two is not the same. It also suits someone splitting time with the mainland, since the float plane makes a weekly day in Vancouver a practical routine rather than an expedition.

stjohns.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in St John's, which is the cheapest provincial capital in Canada and a real saving against anywhere on the mainland's populated coasts. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $900 to $1,300, and the colourful row houses downtown that appear in every photograph are within reach rather than aspirational. Groceries cost more than the Canadian average because everything arrives by ship or plane, which is the permanent condition of an island economy. Heating is a serious winter line item. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Heating through a Newfoundland winter is the line most newcomers get wrong, running $200 to $350 a month between November and April on electric or oil in an older downtown house, and the housing stock here is old. Fibre is around $80 to $110 a month at Canadian prices. Flights are the other structural cost: St John's is expensive to leave, and anyone planning regular trips to the mainland should price that before committing to a year.
stjohns.whereToWork: St John's has a small but real coworking and startup scene, built on an ocean technology sector, Memorial University and the offshore energy industry that shaped the city's last forty years. Fibre reaches most of the city at Canadian prices and mobile coverage is good in the built-up area. The time zone is the practical quirk: Newfoundland runs half an hour ahead of Atlantic time, which puts the city three and a half hours ahead of the American west coast and closer to European hours than anywhere else in North America, an advantage for anyone working with Europe. London sits only three and a half hours off by the clock, where the rest of the region is four or five, so a European afternoon call lands mid-morning here instead of over lunch. Memorial University charges the lowest tuition of any Canadian university by a wide margin, a deliberate provincial policy held for decades, which is why the student population is disproportionately large for a city this size.
stjohns.gettingAround: St John's is built on steep hills around a narrow harbour, and downtown is walkable if the gradients are acceptable; Signal Hill above the harbour entrance is a climb rather than a stroll. Metrobus covers the city adequately and most residents drive. The East Coast Trail runs for over three hundred kilometres along the coast south and north of the city, starting close enough to reach on a bus, and is the best thing about being here. St John's airport is fifteen minutes out with connections through the Canadian hubs and seasonal transatlantic service. Signal Hill and Cape Spear, the easternmost point of North America, are both within twenty minutes and both are where people go when the fog lifts. The East Coast Trail's southern sections around Petty Harbour and the Spout are reachable without a car, which is unusual for a Canadian trail network of that scale.
stjohns.visas: Canada has no digital nomad visa. The 2023 tech talent strategy clarified that visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer during a normal visitor stay of up to six months, which is the route most people use and requires only an eTA for visa-exempt nationalities. The International Experience Canada working holiday covers a defined list of countries and age ranges with full work rights. Newfoundland and Labrador runs its own provincial nominee stream and has actively recruited remote workers and skilled migrants, which makes it a more realistic permanent route than the competition elsewhere in the country. The Atlantic Immigration Program works from the opposite direction: employer-driven rather than points-based, covering all four Atlantic provinces, which suits someone who can line up a job offer more than someone optimising a ranking total. Finding a designated employer is the step that takes the time. This province is losing population faster than any other and recruits accordingly: its nominee stream and a separate priority-skills route are among the more accessible in the country, and the provincial government runs recruitment missions abroad rather than waiting for applications to arrive. Anybody weighing a permanent move to the country would do well to read what is offered here before assuming the big cities are the easier route.
stjohns.bestTime: June to September is the season and it is short, with daytime temperatures rarely above twenty, long evenings and the whales and puffins offshore. Icebergs drift down what locals call Iceberg Alley between roughly April and June, which is the single best reason to time a visit. Fog is a defining feature and St John's is among the foggiest cities in Canada. Winter runs long, wet and windy rather than deeply cold, with heavy snow and the occasional storm that closes everything for a day. Anyone considering a year should visit in February first. Iceberg Alley is best watched in late May and early June, and the icebergs are genuinely visible from shore at Cape Spear and along the northern coast rather than requiring a boat. Puffins arrive at Witless Bay from April and the colony there is among the largest in North America. There is a local name for the storm that blows through around the middle of March and is said to mark the end of winter, and people will tell you the season is not finished until it has come and gone.
stjohns.prosCons: St John's is the oldest European-founded city in North America, built in tiers of painted houses around a harbour with the open Atlantic beyond it, three hundred kilometres of coastal trail, icebergs in spring, and a music and pub culture that punches far above the city's size. It is the cheapest provincial capital in the country and its time zone suits European work. The weather is genuinely hard, and the fog and the wind are constant, the island is remote and flights are expensive, and there is no international nomad presence at all. George Street claims more bars per square foot than any street in North America, which is the kind of claim that is impossible to verify and entirely believable on a Friday. The traditional music scene behind it is genuine, with sessions running in several pubs most nights of the week.
stjohns.whoFor: A small, characterful, walkable city on the edge of the Atlantic, for anyone genuinely unbothered by weather, which is not a small requirement in this particular place. The time zone makes it unusually good for anyone working European hours from North America. Sunshine is rationed on this coast, the professional network is small outside ocean technology and the university, and flying anywhere from here costs more than the distance suggests it should. Anyone with Canadian ambitions should look at the provincial nominee stream, which has been more open to remote workers than most of its counterparts. The music is a reason on its own. What happens in the bars along George Street is a living tradition being played for the people in the room rather than a heritage performance arranged for visitors. Ocean technology is the sector that makes this city legible as a base. Memorial University's marine institute, the offshore energy industry and a working harbour have together produced a genuine cluster somewhere nobody would have predicted one.

manta.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Manta, and the useful thing about Ecuador is that the figure needs no conversion, since the country has used the United States dollar as its currency since 2000. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, with the Murcielago beachfront and Barbasquillo at the top of that and the inland neighbourhoods well below. Fish is exceptional and cheap in a city built on the tuna fleet. Imported goods carry a premium. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Using the US dollar removes exchange risk entirely, which is a genuine and underrated advantage for anyone earning in dollars, though it also means Ecuador cannot devalue and prices have crept up relative to its neighbours. A set almuerzo at lunch is $3 to $4 and includes soup, a main and a juice, which is what most of the city eats. Fibre runs $25 to $40 a month and a taxi across town $2 to $3.
manta.whereToWork: Manta has a small coworking presence, mostly serving the port, the fishing and canning industry and the local university rather than visitors. Fibre has reached the better neighbourhoods and mobile data is inexpensive with reasonable coverage, though speeds and reliability both sit below what a nomad would expect from the larger Latin American cities. Power is generally stable, but Ecuador has had scheduled outages during drought years when the hydroelectric system runs short, which is a real planning consideration. Spanish is essential; English is limited outside the university and a few businesses. Coworking desks, of which there are only a handful, run $80 to $150 a month. Ecuador sits five hours behind GMT with no daylight saving, level with New York in winter, which makes North American work straightforward and European work an early start. The drought-driven outages of recent years were scheduled rather than random and published in advance, so they are manageable if you know to look for the schedule.
manta.gettingAround: Manta runs along the coast and the Malecon and the Murcielago beach form the walkable spine of it, with the port and the fish market at one end. City buses are cheap and cover the rest, and taxis are inexpensive. Montecristi, where the hats the world calls Panamas are actually woven, is twenty minutes inland and worth the trip. Manta has its own airport with domestic connections to Quito and Guayaquil, the latter about three hours away by road. The coastal route north towards Canoa and Pedernales is the way to the quieter beaches. Long-distance buses from the terminal are cheap and frequent, with Quito around eight hours and Guayaquil three, and they are how most Ecuadorians travel. Montecristi's hat weaving is genuine rather than a tourist performance: the finest superfino pieces take months and sell for thousands, and the town's cooperative is the place to see it done rather than the roadside stalls.
manta.visas: Ecuador gives most nationalities ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable to a hundred and eighty within a twelve-month period, which is generous by regional standards. The country also has a remote work visa introduced in 2022 for people employed or contracted outside Ecuador, requiring proof of a monthly income of around three times the national basic salary and granting two years with a path to renewal. The application runs through a consulate abroad or through the foreign ministry locally. Documentation requirements are specific and apostilles are involved, so allow considerably more time than the process appears to need. Because that threshold is pegged and not fixed, it moves every year with the minimum wage, so the figure to plan against is the current one and never whatever an older guide happens to quote. Documents must be apostilled in the country that issued them, which is the step that adds weeks, so start it well before travelling.
manta.bestTime: December to May is the warm and wetter half, with hot humid days, the best sea temperatures and short heavy afternoon showers that pass quickly. June to November is drier and noticeably cooler, with grey overcast mornings that locals call garua and highs around twenty-five, and it is the more comfortable half for working even if it is the less attractive one for the beach. Humpback whales pass the coast between roughly June and September and are visible on day trips from the port, which is the strongest single reason to time a visit. The garua season produces genuinely grey mornings that burn off by midday, and visitors who arrive in July expecting equatorial sun are often surprised. Water temperature swings noticeably too, from around twenty-six degrees in the warm half to twenty-one or lower during the Humboldt-influenced months, which is wetsuit territory for anything longer than a swim. An El Nino year changes everything on this coast: the water warms, the rain arrives in quantities the drainage was never built for, and the fishing collapses for months. It is not an abstraction here but something households plan their budgets around. The overcast months are also when the town is at its cheapest.
manta.prosCons: Manta is a working port city with a long city beach, Ecuador's tuna fleet, whale watching in season and prices that make it one of the cheapest coastal places in the Americas, all denominated in dollars. Montecristi and the quieter beaches to the north are close. This is an industrial city and not a resort at all, the 2016 earthquake did serious damage to the region and its effects are still visible, Spanish is essential, and Ecuador's security situation has deteriorated in recent years, particularly in the coastal provinces. Read current government travel advice directly. Manta is also Ecuador's main tuna port and one of the largest in the Pacific, which is the city's economic engine and shapes everything from the smell near the harbour to the quality of the fish in the market. The 2016 earthquake killed hundreds in the province and reconstruction is visible in some districts and incomplete in others.
manta.whoFor: A genuinely inexpensive dollar-denominated coastal base with a real city behind the beach rather than a resort strip, and Spanish is the price of entry. The ocean is the point, and so is the fact that the city carries on with its own business whether or not anybody is visiting. Spanish is not optional here, the infrastructure is workable rather than strong, and the security picture on this coast has changed materially in the last decade. That last point deserves current research rather than an assumption carried over from an older guidebook or an older visit. The remote work visa deserves a proper look from anybody weighing a longer stay. Two years in a dollarised economy at Ecuadorian prices is a combination very few countries offer at all. Ecuador packs coast, Andes and Amazon inside a day's travel of one another, which is a geography no other country of its size offers. This makes a sensible coastal anchor for anybody planning to move between all three rather than settle in one.

belem.costOfLiving: Budget around $850 a month as a solo remote worker in Belem, which is low for a Brazilian state capital of two million people and reflects a city that sits a long way from the country's economic centre. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, with Nazare and Umarizal at the top of that and the outer bairros well below it. Food is the bargain here, with the market at Ver-o-Peso supplying produce from across the Amazon basin at prices that make eating well trivially cheap. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $20 to $35 a month for 200 to 500 Mbps and coworking $60 to $120, both cheap even against the rest of Brazil. Air conditioning is the utility line that matters in a city this humid, and running it overnight can add $40 to $70 a month. Acai here is not the frozen sweetened product sold abroad but a savoury staple eaten with fish or shrimp, sold fresh by the litre from stalls across the city for a couple of dollars, and it is a genuine daily food rather than a health fashion.
belem.whereToWork: Belem has a coworking scene appropriate to a capital of its size, concentrated in the newer commercial districts and around the federal university, and it grew considerably in the run-up to the thirtieth United Nations climate conference the city hosted in November 2025, which brought infrastructure investment the region had been waiting decades for. Fibre reaches the central neighbourhoods and Brazilian mobile data is cheap and fast. Power cuts happen in the heavy rain season. Portuguese is essential; English is rare outside the university and the hotel trade. Anyone working European hours will find the city sits three or four hours behind depending on the season, which is a workable overlap. That conference investment left the city with upgraded fibre backhaul, a rebuilt airport terminal and new hotel stock, which has changed the practical picture for anyone arriving now compared with five years ago. That said, much of the new capacity was built for a fortnight of international attention and how well it is maintained is an open question rather than a settled one.
belem.gettingAround: Belem sits where the Amazon meets the Atlantic and its historic core around Ver-o-Peso, the Estacao das Docas and the Theatro da Paz is walkable, shaded by the mango trees that give the city its nickname. Buses cover the rest and are cheap, and ride-hailing is widely used and the safer default at night. Boats leave the docks for Ilha do Marajo, the river island larger than Switzerland, and for the smaller communities upriver, which is the reason many people come. Belem airport has domestic connections and a small number of international routes. The boat to Soure on Ilha do Marajo takes about three hours and the island is famous for water buffalo, which arrived in the nineteenth century and are now ridden by the local police. Upriver services from the Hidroviario terminal run to Santarem and on to Manaus over several days in hammock class, which is the classic Amazon journey and costs a fraction of the flight. Ver-o-Peso has traded on the same waterfront since 1625 and its iron market hall was shipped in pieces from England, which is the kind of detail the rubber boom left all over the city.
belem.visas: Brazil launched a digital nomad visa in January 2022, open to remote workers employed or contracted outside the country who can show around $1,500 a month in income or $18,000 in savings, valid for a year and renewable for a second. It is one of the more accessible schemes in the region. Note that Brazil reinstated visitor visa requirements for citizens of the United States, Canada and Australia in April 2025 through an eVisa system, reversing the previous waiver, so travellers from those countries should not rely on older guidance about arriving visa-free. The eVisa for American, Canadian and Australian citizens is applied for online and typically returned within a few days, but it must be obtained before travel and airlines check it at boarding. European nationalities remain visa-free for ninety days, extendable once through the Policia Federal to a hundred and eighty in a twelve-month period. Time on the nomad visa counts toward residency in Brazil, which is unusual among such schemes and makes it a genuine first step rather than a dead end for anyone considering staying.
belem.bestTime: Belem is equatorial and hot all year, with daytime temperatures around thirty-two and humidity that never really drops. The practical division is between the wetter months from December to May and the drier ones from June to November, though drier here means the afternoon rain is less certain rather than absent. The famous local habit of setting appointments around the daily downpour is real. The Cirio de Nazare procession in October is one of the largest religious gatherings on earth and fills the city entirely, which is either the best or worst time to arrive. Cirio de Nazare draws around two million people and is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage, and accommodation across the city is booked out months in advance for the second Sunday of October. The rain in Belem is punctual enough that residents genuinely arrange meetings as before or after it, usually falling in the mid-afternoon. Belem receives around 2,900 millimetres of rain a year, roughly three times London's, which is the number behind the reputation rather than the anecdote about punctual downpours.
belem.prosCons: Belem is the gateway to the Amazon, with Ver-o-Peso, the largest open-air market in Latin America, a Belle Epoque centre built on the rubber boom, the best food in northern Brazil and a river system that starts at the docks. Hosting the thirtieth United Nations climate conference in 2025 brought the city visibility and infrastructure it had long lacked. The heat and the humidity are unrelenting, and little English is spoken, the safety picture requires real attention and is worse than the southern Brazilian cities, and there is no nomad community at all. The river itself is the compensation for all of it, since almost nowhere else puts the Amazon at the end of a city street. Belem also has a distinctive musical culture in carimbo and tecnobrega, the latter a local electronic style built around enormous sound systems called aparelhagens, which is unlike anything in southern Brazil and is best encountered in the outer neighbourhoods rather than the centre.
belem.whoFor: A serious interest in the Amazon, its food or its music, plus Portuguese, and what you get is a large Brazilian city that almost no foreign remote worker has considered. The cost of living and the quality of the eating make it exceptional value. Portuguese is not negotiable here, the equatorial heat and humidity never let up for a season, and no foreign community exists at the mouth of the Amazon to arrive into. Anyone coming should read current safety guidance for the city rather than generalising from Rio or Sao Paulo, since the conditions are not the same. Working on the Amazon professionally, in conservation, climate or journalism, changes the calculation entirely. This is the eastern gateway to the basin, and the institutional presence that built up around the climate conference has largely stayed rather than packing up afterwards.

bucaramanga.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Bucaramanga, which is cheaper than Medellin and considerably cheaper than Bogota for a city with much the same climate advantages. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $250 to $450, with Cabecera and the newer developments in Floridablanca at the top of that range and the areas north of the centre well below it. Food is inexpensive and Santander's cooking is among the more distinctive in the country. The metro area spreads across four municipalities, so the neighbourhood matters more than the city average. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $15 to $25 a month for 200 to 400 Mbps, which is among the best value on the continent, and coworking $80 to $150. The four-municipality spread matters financially as well as practically: Floridablanca and Piedecuesta are noticeably cheaper than Cabecera for the same standard, at the cost of a longer commute into the centre.
bucaramanga.whereToWork: Bucaramanga has a small coworking market serving a local economy of health services, engineering and the oil sector in the wider department, with desks from roughly $80 a month. The Universidad Industrial de Santander gives the city a technical base that shows in the workforce. Fibre is widely available in the newer neighbourhoods at low prices and Colombian mobile data is cheap with good 4G coverage. Power is reliable. Spanish is essential, with English limited to the university and a handful of businesses, which is the main practical difference from Medellin. Colombia sits five hours behind GMT with no daylight saving, level with New York in winter and an hour behind in summer, which makes North American work straightforward and gives a workable European morning. That time zone is a large part of why Colombia has drawn remote workers at all, and it applies here as much as in Medellin.
bucaramanga.gettingAround: Bucaramanga sits on a plateau at around a thousand metres with the metro area spilling down the slopes into Floridablanca, Giron and Piedecuesta, which makes it larger on the ground than it appears. The Metrolinea bus rapid transit runs the main corridors and city buses cover the rest cheaply. Ride-hailing is widely used. Giron, a preserved colonial town, is fifteen minutes away and worth choosing as a base. Palonegro airport sits on a plateau across the canyon about forty minutes out. San Gil and Barichara are two hours south on a spectacular road. Palonegro's position on a mesa across the canyon means the approach is dramatic and the road down and up again takes longer than the distance suggests. The Chicamocha cable car spans the canyon in about half an hour each way and is the standard way to see it without driving the switchbacks. The highway through here is the main road between the capital and the Caribbean coast, which is why the lorry traffic is what it is, and the pass north over the mountains climbs above three thousand metres and is genuinely cold at the top.
bucaramanga.visas: Colombia gives most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable once to a hundred and eighty days within a calendar year, which is straightforward and widely used. The country also introduced a dedicated digital nomad visa in late 2022, open to remote workers and freelancers employed outside Colombia who can show a monthly income of around three times the local minimum wage, valid for up to two years.
