nassau.gettingAround: New Providence is a small island and Nassau covers most of it. Downtown around Bay Street is walkable, though it is built for cruise passengers and empties when the ships leave. Jitney minibuses cover the island cheaply and are the way most residents move; they stop running in the early evening. Taxis are expensive and metered fares are frequently a negotiation. Driving is on the left in cars mostly imported with left-hand drive, which is as strange as it sounds. Lynden Pindling airport has more direct connections to the United States than any other Caribbean airport, and the Family Islands are short hops by light aircraft. The Exumas are a forty-minute flight or a longer ferry, and Eleuthera and Long Island are similar hops, which is how most permit holders actually use the country. Rock Sound and George Town both have airstrips with several services a day from Nassau. Jitneys run numbered routes from the depot near the British Colonial and stop when flagged, and the fare is a flat dollar and a quarter regardless of distance.
nassau.visas: The Bahamas Extended Access Travel Stay, known as BEATS, is a one-year renewable permit for remote workers and students employed or enrolled outside the country, with an application fee of around $1,000 plus a smaller processing charge. It is handled online and is one of the more straightforward schemes in the region. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to ninety days, and British citizens receive longer. There is no income tax on money earned under the permit, which is the substantive benefit alongside the length. Anyone applying should note that the permit covers the whole country, so it can be used from a Family Island rather than from New Providence. Applications are made online through the Bahamas Immigration portal and are usually decided within a few weeks, and the permit covers dependants at an additional fee per person. Renewal is straightforward for a second year.
nassau.bestTime: December to April is the dry, cooler season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-six, low humidity and the calmest seas, and it is when prices and crowds peak. May to November is hotter and considerably wetter, and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; the Bahamas sits directly in the track and Hurricane Dorian in 2019 was catastrophic for Abaco and Grand Bahama, though Nassau was largely spared. September and October carry the highest risk and the lowest prices. Junkanoo, the street parade with its costumes and goatskin drums, runs on Boxing Day and New Year's Day. Junkanoo starts in the small hours and runs until dawn on both days, and the competing groups spend the year building costumes for it, which makes it a genuine civic institution rather than a performance for visitors. Water temperature stays above twenty-four degrees all year, which makes the Bahamas one of the few places in the region where winter diving needs no wetsuit beyond a shorty. Sea temperature peaks near thirty degrees in August.
nassau.prosCons: Nassau has the best flight connections to the United States of any Caribbean capital, a one-year remote work permit, no income tax, and seven hundred islands behind it that almost no visitor reaches. The water in the Exumas is as good as anywhere on earth. Nassau itself is expensive to live in, dominated by cruise tourism along Bay Street, and carries a crime problem that residents and foreign governments both take seriously, with specific areas that visitors are consistently advised to avoid. The island is developed rather than beautiful, and the beauty is elsewhere in the chain. Andros, the largest island in the chain and one of the least visited, holds the third-longest barrier reef in the world and a blue hole system that is still being surveyed, and it is an hour from Nassau. Nassau's own beaches are decent rather than remarkable by Bahamian standards.
nassau.whoFor: American working hours and a Caribbean base a short flight from the east coast, with the paperwork solved for a year and no income tax on it. It works best for people who treat Nassau as the airport and the Family Islands as the point, since the Exumas, Eleuthera and Long Island are what the country actually offers. A budget will not survive Bahamian prices for long. Anybody moving here should also read the current safety guidance for New Providence properly, because a place that receives millions of tourists is not therefore uniformly safe, and the distinction matters by neighbourhood. Nobody has a better reason to be here than a sailor. The Exumas rank among the great cruising grounds of the Atlantic, and this is where boats get provisioned, cleared and repaired before heading down the chain. Next to Bermuda it is half the rent, twice the crime, considerably better islands behind it and a permit that costs a third as much.

roseau.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,500 a month as a solo remote worker in Roseau, which makes Dominica one of the cheaper Eastern Caribbean islands and considerably cheaper than its better-known neighbours. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $500 to $900, and houses outside the capital are within reach at figures that would be impossible on Barbados. Dominica grows a great deal of its own food, which is unusual in the region and keeps the market cheap; imported goods carry the usual island markup. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar, so budgeting is simple. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Fibre where it reaches runs $60 to $110 a month and a generator or an inverter is a normal household expense rather than a contingency, which is the line most budgets miss. A minibus fare anywhere on the island is a dollar or two, and hiring a four-wheel drive runs $50 to $70 a day, which is the realistic way to reach the trailheads. Sea Cat and dive operators charge $80 to $120 for a whale-watching trip and $100 or so for two tanks, and those are the two things most people come here to spend money on.
roseau.whereToWork: Connectivity is the honest weakness of the island. Fibre has reached parts of Roseau and Portsmouth and works well where it exists, but coverage is patchy outside the towns and speeds vary. Mobile data from Flow and Digicel is the practical fallback. Power cuts are not rare and the grid is still being rebuilt in places after Hurricane Maria in 2017, which destroyed much of the island's infrastructure. Anyone whose work cannot pause should ask about backup power before committing, and should treat a video-call-heavy schedule as a real constraint here. Starlink became available here after 2023 and has quietly transformed what is possible on the island, so it is worth asking a prospective landlord about by name rather than accepting a general assurance about wifi. Dominica sits four hours behind central European time and one ahead of New York in winter, which gives a European afternoon at the start of the day and a full American overlap after it. The 2017 rebuild buried a good deal of the distribution network, so outages are shorter and less frequent than they were, though they have not stopped.
roseau.gettingAround: Roseau is small and walkable, a grid of narrow streets between the river and the sea that can be crossed in fifteen minutes. Beyond it the island is mountainous and the roads are steep, winding and slow: Dominica is only 47 kilometres long but crossing it takes far longer than the distance suggests. Minibuses cover the main routes cheaply and stop early. A four-wheel drive helps for the trailheads. There is no international airport for large jets, so almost everyone arrives via a connection through Antigua, Barbados or Saint Martin into Douglas-Charles, an hour and a half from Roseau. The cruise berth in Roseau brings several thousand people ashore on ship days and empties the town again by late afternoon, which changes the character of the centre from one morning to the next. The Waitukubuli National Trail runs 184 kilometres in fourteen segments from the south to the north, and several segments start close enough to Roseau to be walked as day trips rather than as an expedition. Ferries run from Roseau to Martinique, Guadeloupe and Saint Lucia several times a week and are often cheaper and simpler than flying between the islands.
roseau.visas: Dominica's Work In Nature visa is an eighteen-month remote work permit, the longest single term offered anywhere in the Eastern Caribbean, open to people employed or self-employed outside the country who can show an annual income of around $50,000 and hold health insurance. The fee is roughly $800 for an individual. Applications are handled online. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities, typically for up to six months, granted at the border. Dominica also runs a citizenship by investment programme, which is a separate matter and should be researched independently rather than through the agents who market it. That length is the strongest practical argument for choosing Dominica, because it removes the mid-stay renewal that a shorter permit forces on anybody intending to settle in for a while. Applications are processed in a few weeks and the income bar of around $50,000 is lower than Barbados or Antigua ask, which makes it accessible to a wider range of people than most Caribbean schemes. Holders may bring dependants on the same permit, and time spent on it does not count towards permanent residence, which is a separate track entirely.
roseau.bestTime: February to May is the driest and most comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and the trails at their most passable. Dominica is one of the wettest places in the Caribbean by design of its geography: mountains over 1,400 metres wring rain out of the trade winds, which is why there are 365 rivers and why the island is green in a way its neighbours are not. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season, and Dominica is exposed; Hurricane Maria in 2017 damaged or destroyed the majority of buildings on the island. Plan around September and October. Sperm whales are resident year-round rather than migratory here, which is why Dominica is the only country in the world to have declared a marine protected area specifically for them, gazetted in 2023 and covering nearly eight hundred square kilometres of the western coast. Sightings are most reliable between November and March. The Boiling Lake walk is closed after heavy rain and guides are compulsory, so it needs a settled forecast as well as a free day.
roseau.prosCons: Dominica is the Nature Island and the name is earned: rainforest running to the waterline, the second-largest boiling lake in the world at the end of a hard six-hour walk, hot springs, whale watching that runs almost year-round because sperm whales live offshore, and the Waitukubuli Trail down the length of the island. It is cheap and the eighteen-month visa is the region's longest. The internet is genuinely unreliable, no remote-working scene exists here at all, getting here always requires a connection, and the island is exposed to hurricanes in a way that shapes everything. Dominica has committed to becoming the world's first climate-resilient nation after Maria, which shapes how the island rebuilds: buried power lines, reinforced roofs and a geothermal plant under development at Laudat that would make the island largely self-sufficient in electricity. The island has no chain hotels of any size and no cruise pier outside Roseau, which is deliberate policy rather than an accident of development. Dominica has instead built its tourism around hiking, diving and the whale population, which keeps visitor numbers low and means the trails are rarely crowded even in the dry season.
roseau.whoFor: Rainforest, rivers and hiking above all else, for a connection that will drop out and somebody who wants neither nightlife nor company. Divers and hikers get more from Dominica than from anywhere else in the Eastern Caribbean. A demanding call schedule will not hold up here. Anybody picturing white sand has the wrong island, since Dominica's beaches are volcanic and dark, and flying in or out at short notice is difficult enough that plans need building around the schedule rather than the other way round. Dominica against Saint Lucia is a plain trade: worse beaches and infrastructure, far better hiking, and a stay you can measure in months rather than weeks. The Kalinago Territory on the east coast is the only surviving pre-Columbian Carib community anywhere in the Caribbean. It has its own elected chief and governs its own land, and it is a place people live rather than a heritage exhibit arranged for visitors.

stgeorges.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in St George's, which is mid-range for the Eastern Caribbean. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $600 to $1,000, with anything near Grand Anse beach at the top of that range and the hillside neighbourhoods above the harbour cheaper. Grenada grows a serious amount of its own produce and the Saturday market is genuinely cheap; imported goods carry the standard island markup. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar. St George's University brings a large international student population that shapes the rental market. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $60 to $100 a month and coworking, where it exists, $120 to $200. The university's academic calendar drives the rental market hard: prices around Grand Anse and True Blue rise sharply when terms begin and soften between them, so the timing of a lease matters as much as its location. Minibus fares anywhere on the island are around a dollar. Utilities run high because Grenada generates almost all its electricity from imported diesel, and a flat with air conditioning will show it on the bill.
stgeorges.whereToWork: Grenada's connectivity is reasonable and improving, with fibre from Flow and Digicel reaching St George's, Grand Anse and the south of the island at workable speeds, and mobile data covering everywhere anyone lives. There is limited formal coworking, though the presence of St George's University, a large American medical school, means cafes and study spaces used to people working are easy to find. Power cuts happen but are not routine. The island runs four hours behind central European time and one ahead of New York in the northern winter, so a European afternoon lands at the start of the Grenadian working day and an American morning at the end of it. The medical school brings several thousand North American students to a country of 110,000, which is why the south of the island has the cafes, gyms and supermarkets it does. Term-time and vacation are visibly different seasons in a way that has nothing to do with the weather, and the quieter months are noticeably cheaper for a short let. Grenada's undersea cable connections improved with the East Caribbean fibre system, and speeds in the south now compare reasonably with Barbados rather than lagging it.
stgeorges.gettingAround: St George's is built around a horseshoe harbour with steep streets rising from it, which makes it beautiful and hard work on foot. The Carenage around the water is walkable; the rest is a climb. Minibuses run constantly along the main routes to Grand Anse and around the island for very little, and they are how most people move. Driving is on the left and the roads through the interior are narrow and mountainous. Maurice Bishop airport is fifteen minutes from town with direct flights to London, New York, Miami and Toronto, which is good connectivity for an island of 110,000. The Sendall Tunnel, cut through the ridge in 1895 and barely wide enough for one vehicle, still connects the Carenage to the western side of town and is the sort of infrastructure that explains why Grenadian drivers use their horns constantly. Grand Etang in the interior is a crater lake in cloud forest about forty minutes up from the coast. Buses stop by early evening and Sunday service is thin, so anyone living outside walking distance of the centre needs a plan for nights out.
stgeorges.visas: Grenada has no dedicated remote work visa, which is the main practical gap against its neighbours. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to three months, with extensions available through the immigration department in St George's, and Commonwealth citizens often receive longer. Anyone wanting to stay past that applies for an extension of stay locally or a residence permit, which requires more documentation and patience. Grenada also operates a citizenship by investment programme that includes an E-2 treaty route to the United States, which is a substantial and separate decision rather than a nomad option. The absence of a nomad visa is the gap, but the extension route is straightforward in practice: applications are made at the immigration office on the Carenage, cost little, and are routinely granted in monthly increments up to six months for people who present a clear case and proof of funds. Grenadian immigration expects a return ticket and evidence of accommodation on arrival, and applies both more consistently than most of its neighbours do.
stgeorges.bestTime: January to May is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine, lower humidity and the calmest sea. June to December is wetter, and the hurricane season runs June to November; Grenada sits at the southern edge of the belt and is hit far less often than the islands north of it, though Hurricane Ivan in 2004 devastated the island and Beryl in 2024 struck Carriacou hard. August brings Spicemas, the carnival, with the pre-dawn Jouvert that covers everyone in oil and paint. September and October are the quietest and cheapest. Grenada produces around twenty per cent of the world's nutmeg despite its size, and the crop runs year-round with a peak between January and June, so the processing stations at Gouyave and Grenville are working rather than staged whenever you visit. Carriacou and Petite Martinique, the two smaller islands to the north, run their own regatta each August and are reached by a ferry that is frequently rough.
stgeorges.prosCons: Grenada is the spice island and it smells like it: nutmeg, mace and cinnamon growing on the hillsides, and a working nutmeg processing station you can walk through. St George's harbour is among the most beautiful in the Caribbean, Grand Anse is a three-kilometre white beach ten minutes from town, and the underwater sculpture park off Molinere is the first of its kind in the world. No remote work visa exists, there is nobody else doing this here, and the connection is adequate rather than good, and the steep streets make the capital tiring to live in. The 1983 revolution and the American invasion that followed are within living memory for most Grenadians over fifty, and Fort George where Maurice Bishop was killed is open to visitors with almost no interpretation, which makes it a strange and sobering place to stand. The Bianca C sank in 1961 and lies at around fifty metres, which puts it beyond recreational limits for much of its length and makes it an advanced dive.
stgeorges.whoFor: A genuinely beautiful Caribbean town, hiking in the interior, and diving that takes in both the reefs and the Bianca C, the largest wreck in the Caribbean. The medical school gives the island an international layer most of its neighbours lack. Three months is the practical ceiling without paperwork, which rules out anybody who needs a long-stay visa. The other thing to know is the terrain: this town is built on hills and living here means climbing them several times a day. Time a visit around Spicemas in August if the carnival is the point, or avoid it entirely if it is not. It also suits sailors, since Grenada sits below the insurance line for the hurricane season and Prickly Bay and Mount Hartman fill each summer with cruisers waiting out the weather, which creates a transient but genuinely sociable community from June to November. It also suits chocolate specifically: Grenada's tree-to-bar producers process cocoa on the island rather than exporting beans, which is rare anywhere in the Caribbean.

castries.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Castries, which reflects an island where tourism sets prices along the west coast. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200, with Rodney Bay and Gros Islet in the north at the top of that and the areas around Castries itself cheaper. Saint Lucia grows bananas, cocoa and a good deal of its own produce, and the Castries market is where the price difference shows. Imported goods carry the usual markup. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. A minibus ride anywhere on the island is under $3 and a rental car about $45 a day, which is the single biggest variable in an island budget.
castries.whereToWork: Connectivity in Saint Lucia is workable rather than strong: fibre reaches Castries, Rodney Bay and the developed western coast at reasonable speeds, and mobile data from Flow and Digicel covers the populated areas. Coworking exists in a small way around Rodney Bay, which is where most of the island's remote workers and long-stay visitors end up rather than in Castries itself. Power cuts happen. The island runs four hours behind central European time, which makes a European afternoon a Saint Lucian morning and gives a reasonable overlap in both directions. Fibre packages run roughly $60 to $100 a month, high for the speeds delivered, so a mobile data bundle as a backup is standard rather than cautious. Bananas were the island's living until the preferential access it held into Europe was struck down in trade disputes, and the collapse of that trade in the nineteen nineties is why tourism now carries everything and why the interior holds so many abandoned plots. Understanding it explains a great deal about how the island talks about visitors. There is a small offshore financial sector, and beyond that almost every formal job is attached in some way to the hotels.
castries.gettingAround: Castries sits around a deep harbour that takes cruise ships, and the central grid is walkable though busy and hot. Minibuses cover the island cheaply and frequently, running north to Rodney Bay and south along the coast to Soufriere, and they are the practical way to move. Driving is on the left and the west coast road to Soufriere is spectacular and slow, with hairpins the whole way. Hewanorra, the international airport, is at the far southern end of the island, an hour and a half from Castries, which is a longer transfer than most visitors expect. Minibuses stop in the early evening and after that a taxi is the only option, charged against a published tariff rather than a meter, so agree the fare first. A second airport sits right beside the capital and takes regional turboprops, so a connection through a neighbouring island can land you fifteen minutes from town rather than ninety, and it is worth pricing that routing against the direct long-haul flight. Water taxis run along the west coast and are the pleasant way to reach the bays under the peaks. The road across the interior is shorter on a map and slower in practice than going round the coast.
castries.visas: Saint Lucia has no dedicated remote work visa, though it ran a Live It scheme during the pandemic that has not been maintained as a formal category. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to six weeks, with extensions available through the immigration department, and British and Commonwealth citizens often receive longer on arrival. Anyone planning a longer stay should ask for the maximum at the border and then extend locally, which is routine. Saint Lucia also operates a citizenship by investment programme, which is a separate decision and unrelated to remote work. Saint Lucia is part of the OECS, whose citizens move and work freely between member states, though that does not extend to visitors from outside the bloc. Arriving by sea means clearing in at a designated port rather than wherever is convenient, and a yacht that anchors first and reports afterwards can expect a fine. Skilled nationals of the wider regional community may work here on a certificate instead of a permit, a distinction that matters to anybody holding one of those passports. Everybody else needs an employer to sponsor a permit, and the fee is set high enough to discourage casual applications.
castries.bestTime: December to May is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine, lower humidity and calm seas, and it is when prices are highest. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season; Saint Lucia sits within the belt and has taken direct hits, most recently Tropical Storm Bret and its neighbours in recent years. Saint Lucia Jazz in May and Carnival in July are the two events worth planning around. September and October are the wettest, quietest and cheapest, and also the months when many hotels close for maintenance. Anyone booking into the June to November window should check whether their travel cover excludes named storms once one is forecast, which many policies do. Sargassum weed washes onto the Atlantic-facing side of the island through the warm months in some years and not others, and where it lands it smells and the beach clearing cannot keep up, which is why the sheltered western bays are where everybody swims. The trade winds strengthen around the turn of the year and sailors call them the Christmas winds, which is what makes the crossing season and the regattas fall when they do.
castries.prosCons: Saint Lucia has the Pitons, two volcanic plugs rising straight out of the sea at Soufriere that are a UNESCO World Heritage site and genuinely unlike anything else in the Caribbean, a drive-in volcano with sulphur springs, rainforest walks and a serious sailing culture around Rodney Bay. No remote work visa exists here either, and the airport sits a long way from the capital, Castries itself is a working port town rather than a place people choose to live, and the crime rate is higher than several of its neighbours, with the usual advice about specific areas. The centre empties and fills with the cruise schedule, so the character of Castries changes from one morning to the next depending on what is in the harbour.
castries.whoFor: Dramatic landscape within a short drive, on the understanding that you will base yourself in Rodney Bay or Soufriere rather than the capital. Sailors get a great deal from Saint Lucia, which sits on the main Windward Islands route and hosts the finish of the Atlantic Rally for Cruisers each December. There is no long-stay visa to apply for, which settles the question for anybody planning more than a season. Arrivals should also plan the transfer from Hewanorra in advance, because discovering that drive at the end of a long flight is nobody's preferred introduction. The Pitons are the reason to come and they are ninety minutes from the capital. It suits a stay of weeks rather than months, given that the visa-free default is six weeks and extending means dealing with the immigration department in person.

portofspain.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Port of Spain, which is cheap for the Caribbean and reflects an economy built on oil and gas rather than tourism. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $500 to $900, with Woodbrook, St Clair and Newtown at the top of that and the areas east of the city considerably cheaper. Food is inexpensive and Trinidad's is the best in the Caribbean by a distance, with doubles from a street cart costing almost nothing. Fuel is subsidised. The Trinidad and Tobago dollar floats within a managed band and foreign exchange can be hard to obtain locally. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $40 to $70 a month and a coworking desk $120 to $200. The foreign exchange constraint is the practical oddity here: the central bank rations hard currency, so buying dollars locally can mean a wait or a premium, and anyone paid from abroad should think about how money comes in before arriving. Fuel is subsidised heavily enough that running a car is cheap by Caribbean standards. Rents east of the city towards San Juan and Barataria run at half the Woodbrook rate, with the trade being the highway at peak.
portofspain.whereToWork: Trinidad's connectivity is good by regional standards, underwritten by an energy sector that needs it: fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches most of the developed western corridor at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive. There is a small coworking scene around Port of Spain, serving local startups rather than visitors. Power is reliable. The island runs four hours behind central European time. English is the only language required. The professional network here is real but concentrated in energy, finance and government, and it is not one a visiting remote worker plugs into easily. Trinidad sits four hours behind GMT with no daylight saving, level with New York in winter and an hour ahead in summer, which gives a workable European afternoon and a full American day. The energy sector's bandwidth requirements are why the connectivity here beats most of the Caribbean rather than matching it. Coworking here serves Trinidadian founders rather than visitors, so it is a place to meet locals rather than other foreigners.
portofspain.gettingAround: Port of Spain is compact around Independence Square and the Queen's Park Savannah, the largest roundabout in the world and the city's green centre, and that core is walkable by day. Maxi taxis, the colour-coded minibuses, and route taxis cover the city and the corridor east towards Arima cheaply. Traffic on the Churchill Roosevelt and Beetham highways is severe at peak. Most residents drive, on the left. Piarco airport is forty minutes east. The ferry to Tobago takes around three hours and is how most people reach the quieter island, which is where the beaches are. The Queen's Park Savannah is about three and a half kilometres around and is where the city walks and runs in the early morning and evening. Maracas Bay on the north coast, reached over the mountain road, is where Trinidadians go for bake and shark, and it is about forty minutes from the city. Route taxis run fixed routes and are hailed from the roadside, and the colour of the band on the number plate tells you where a maxi is going.
portofspain.visas: Trinidad and Tobago has no remote work visa. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days, and Commonwealth citizens generally receive the same, with extensions applied for at the immigration division in Port of Spain. The process is bureaucratic rather than difficult. Anyone planning to stay longer needs a work permit tied to an employer, or a residence permit through marriage or descent. The country is not organised around long-stay visitors and the immigration system reflects that; plan around ninety days rather than assuming an extension. Anyone coming for Carnival should apply well ahead if a visa is needed at all, since the weeks around it are the busiest the immigration system sees. The immigration division extends stays in person at Port of Spain and the process takes a morning rather than a week, but it is discretionary and a clear reason plus proof of funds and onward travel matter more than the paperwork. Tobago is the same jurisdiction, so no separate entry applies.
portofspain.bestTime: January to May is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around thirty-one and the lowest rainfall, and it contains the event that defines the calendar. Trinidad Carnival, on the Monday and Tuesday before Ash Wednesday, is the largest in the Caribbean and the reason a great many people come at all; the season of fetes and panyard rehearsals runs for weeks before it and the city is fully booked. June to December is the wet season, with heavy afternoon rain. Trinidad sits south of the hurricane belt and is rarely struck, which is a genuine advantage over the rest of the region. The panyards open for rehearsal in the weeks before Carnival and are free to walk into, which is the best way to hear steelpan properly and is something the Carnival itself does not really offer. Accommodation for Carnival is booked a year ahead and prices multiply rather than rise.
portofspain.prosCons: Trinidad invented the steelpan, calypso, soca and limbo, and its Carnival is the one every other Caribbean carnival is modelled on. The food is the best in the region, mixing African, Indian, Chinese, Creole and Syrian traditions on the same street. The Northern Range has rainforest and the Caroni swamp fills with scarlet ibis at dusk. It is cheap and outside the hurricane belt. The crime rate is the serious qualification here: Trinidad has one of the higher murder rates anywhere in the Americas, and both residents and foreign governments treat parts of Port of Spain as no-go areas. The Pitch Lake at La Brea in the south is the largest natural asphalt deposit in the world and has been mined continuously since the sixteenth century, and it is one of only a handful anywhere. Tobago sits outside the belt too.
portofspain.whoFor: Music, food and Carnival are the draw, and the price of admission is taking the security situation seriously and organising your movements around it rather than ignoring it. It is culturally the richest place in the Caribbean and almost no remote workers go there. Anybody after a beach city is on the wrong island, since Trinidad's coast is not what it is for and Tobago is a separate flight and a separate trip. There is also no long-stay visa route to build a year around. Read current government travel advice for Trinidad specifically, and take local advice on neighbourhoods seriously. Energy is the industry that makes this island a career rather than a stop. Trinidad is a major LNG and petrochemical producer, and the people working in it here are connected outward to Houston and Aberdeen rather than inward to the Caribbean. Put it beside Tobago and Trinidad has the culture and the food and Tobago has the beaches, and the ferry between them takes three hours.

georgetownguyana.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Georgetown, and note that this figure has been moving upward fast. Guyana began producing offshore oil in 2019 and has since been among the fastest-growing economies in the world, which has pushed rents in the capital up sharply as international companies arrive. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $500 to $1,000 depending on how close it sits to the areas the oil sector has taken. Food from the markets is cheap and the produce is excellent. Imported goods carry a heavy markup. This is our own estimate rather than measured data, and it dates faster here than elsewhere. The oil boom's effect on rents is the single most important thing to check before committing to anything, since figures more than a year old are likely to understate the market by a wide margin. Fibre runs $60 to $120 a month, which is expensive for the speed. A generator or an inverter is a normal household item rather than a precaution, and should be budgeted as one.
georgetownguyana.whereToWork: Georgetown's connectivity has improved with the oil money but remains the weak point: fibre reaches parts of the city at workable speeds, mobile data from GTT and Digicel is the fallback, and neither is dependable enough to plan a day around without a backup. Power cuts are frequent enough that generators are standard in any serious building. There is a small coworking presence serving the energy sector and local startups. English is the official language, which is unusual in South America and is Guyana's single biggest practical advantage for an English-speaking visitor. Guyana sits four hours behind GMT with no daylight saving, which gives a workable European afternoon and a full North American day, and is one of the better time zones on the continent for transatlantic work. Starlink became available in 2024 and has changed the practical picture for anyone who can install it. A local content law passed a few years ago requires the oil companies to hire and buy Guyanese first across a long list of services, which has created a scramble for qualified locals and made it harder rather than easier for a foreigner to pick up work here.
georgetownguyana.gettingAround: Georgetown is flat, laid out on a Dutch grid with drainage canals down the middle of several avenues, and much of it sits below sea level behind a seawall. The centre around Stabroek Market and the wooden St George's Cathedral is walkable by day. Minibuses cover the city and the coast road cheaply and drive alarmingly. Taxis are inexpensive and are the standard advice after dark. The interior is another matter entirely: Kaieteur Falls and the Rupununi savannah are reached by light aircraft, and there is no road network to most of the country. The seawall is where Georgetown walks in the evening and is the city's real public space. Kaieteur is a day trip by light aircraft costing a few hundred dollars, and the flights are weather-dependent and cancel often, so anyone determined to see it should allow more than one attempt in their plans. The bridge over the river west of the city floats on pontoons and is retracted on a published schedule to let ships through, stopping the traffic completely for an hour at a time, so a crossing has to be planned around that timetable rather than around the clock.
georgetownguyana.visas: Guyana gives most Western nationalities and all Commonwealth citizens visa-free entry for up to ninety days, granted on arrival, with extensions available from the immigration department. There is no remote work visa and no particular framework for long-stay visitors. Anyone wanting to stay beyond ninety days applies locally, and the process is manageable but slow. Yellow fever vaccination is required if arriving from an endemic country and is sensible regardless given the interior. Guyana is a member of CARICOM, so regional nationals move more freely. Anyone heading into the interior should also note that visits to Amerindian villages require a permit arranged through the tour operator rather than on arrival. Guyana's land borders are a separate matter from the airport: the crossing to Brazil at Lethem is remote and the Suriname ferry at Moleson Creek runs to a limited schedule, so an overland exit needs planning rather than improvisation.
georgetownguyana.bestTime: Guyana sits close to the equator and is hot and humid year-round, around thirty degrees every month. The calendar is set by rain rather than temperature, and there are two wet seasons: a long one from May to August and a shorter one from November to January. The drier windows, February to April and September to October, are the practical time to visit, and September is also when Kaieteur Falls is at its most dramatic against low water. Georgetown floods in heavy rain because the drainage system is old and the city is below sea level. Mashramani in February, marking the republic anniversary, is the country's largest festival and the best time to see Georgetown at its most alive. The seawall and the drainage kokers are worth understanding as infrastructure: the city depends on them entirely and a spring tide with heavy rain is a genuine flood risk. Cricket is the other thing that fills the calendar, with the regional Twenty20 tournament bringing a fortnight of full stands and a party atmosphere to the ground outside the city in late summer, and it is where the country is at its loudest and most itself.
georgetownguyana.prosCons: Guyana is South America's only English-speaking country, with a wooden colonial capital unlike anything else on the continent, Kaieteur Falls, the highest single-drop waterfall in the world at nearly five times the height of Niagara, and rainforest covering four-fifths of the country. Costs are low and the culture, mixing Indian, African, Amerindian, Chinese and Portuguese, is genuinely distinctive. Georgetown has a serious crime problem, and it is not one to take lightly, the infrastructure is weak, and the oil boom is changing prices and the city faster than any guide can keep up with. Guyana is also culturally part of the Caribbean rather than Latin America despite sitting on the South American mainland, belonging to CARICOM and playing Test cricket, which surprises visitors who arrive expecting a Spanish-speaking continent.
georgetownguyana.whoFor: An experienced traveller after somewhere genuinely off the remote work map, interested in the interior rather than the capital, who will organise the day around the security situation rather than hope. Anyone working in energy, conservation or development will find real professional depth here right now. This is the wrong place to begin a first trip to South America, reliable internet is not something the country can promise, and current travel advice needs reading properly rather than skimming before anybody commits to a stay. The interior is the reason to come; Georgetown is the way in. It also suits birders specifically, since the Rupununi and the Iwokrama rainforest hold species lists that draw serious ornithologists from around the world and the country has built its small tourism sector largely around them.

paramaribo.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Paramaribo, which is cheap by any measure and reflects a small economy that has been through serious currency instability. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $350 to $700. Food is the standout: Suriname's markets are cheap and its cooking, drawing on Javanese, Hindustani, Chinese, Creole and Dutch traditions, is among the most varied anywhere per head of population. The Surinamese dollar has devalued sharply in recent years, so any figure quoted in it dates quickly and locals often price in United States dollars. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre from Telesur runs about $40 to $80 a month for modest speeds, which is poor value by regional standards. Anybody signing a lease should establish which currency it is denominated in before anything else in the contract, because that single detail decides what the rent will actually cost a year from now. Groceries in the Chinese supermarkets, which dominate retail here, are noticeably cheaper than the Dutch-style shops. Imported goods carry a heavy markup because almost everything arrives through one port.
paramaribo.whereToWork: Paramaribo's connectivity is modest: fibre from Telesur reaches parts of the city at workable speeds, mobile data is the fallback, and neither is fast by international standards. Power cuts happen. There is essentially no coworking aimed at foreigners. Dutch is the official language and the language of all administration, with Sranan Tongo as the common tongue between communities; English is spoken by younger people and in business but is not something to rely on. Anyone with Dutch will find Suriname dramatically easier than anyone without, which is the main practical filter here. Suriname sits three hours behind GMT, which gives a comfortable European afternoon overlap and a full working day with the Americas, and is one of the better time zones on the continent for transatlantic work. Starlink became available in 2024 and is the practical answer for anyone who needs a connection the local network cannot supply. Telesur is state-owned and the effective monopoly on fixed lines, which is a fair part of why prices sit where they do and why service complaints have nowhere much to go. Digicel provides the main mobile alternative.
paramaribo.gettingAround: Paramaribo's historic centre is compact, flat and walkable, and the UNESCO-listed core of white wooden Dutch colonial buildings is genuinely the reason to be here. Minibuses and shared taxis cover the city cheaply. Most residents drive, on the left, in cars imported from Japan. Beyond the coastal strip the country is rainforest with almost no roads: the interior is reached by riverboat or light aircraft, and trips to the Upper Suriname River or Brownsberg are organised rather than improvised. Zanderij airport is an hour south with flights to Amsterdam, Miami and the region. Cars drive on the left, a Dutch colonial inheritance shared with almost nowhere else in South America, and the vehicles are almost all right-hand-drive imports from Japan. The ferry across the Suriname river to Meerzorg has been replaced by the Jules Wijdenbosch bridge, which is the landmark most visible from the waterfront. The Afobaka road south towards Brokopondo is the only sealed route of any length into the interior, and it stops well short of the rainforest proper, which is why almost everything beyond it goes by river.
paramaribo.visas: Suriname introduced an e-visa and a tourist card system that most Western nationalities can use, typically granting ninety days, and the process is done online before travel rather than at the border. There is no remote work visa. Dutch nationals have easier access given the historic relationship. Extensions are handled locally through the immigration service. Yellow fever vaccination is required for arrivals from endemic countries and strongly advised regardless. Check the current requirement directly, since Suriname has changed its entry rules more than once in recent years. Anyone crossing overland to French Guiana or Guyana should check both sides separately, since the river crossings have their own rules and hours. The tourist card is the cheaper and simpler of the two routes for most nationalities and is bought online for around $25, while the e-visa costs more and covers longer or multiple-entry stays. Both must be arranged before travel, and neither is issued at the airport. Anyone crossing to French Guiana should remember it is legally part of France and the European Union, so Schengen rules apply at that border despite the setting.
paramaribo.bestTime: Suriname has two dry seasons and two wet ones, which is unusual and worth planning around. The long dry season from August to November and the short one from February to April are the practical windows, with less rain and better river conditions for reaching the interior. Temperatures sit around thirty-one all year with humidity that never drops. The long rains from April to August make interior travel harder and the coast greyer. There are no hurricanes here: Suriname sits well south of the belt, which is a real advantage over the Caribbean islands. Leatherback turtles nest on the beaches at Galibi and Braamspunt between roughly February and July, which is the single best reason to time a visit, and the Galibi reserve is reached by boat from Albina on the French Guianese border. The short dry season in February and March coincides with the country's Holi Phagwa celebrations, which the Hindustani community observes on a scale that fills the streets of the capital and is one of the more striking things a visitor can time a trip around.
paramaribo.prosCons: Paramaribo has a UNESCO World Heritage centre of white wooden Dutch buildings that looks like nowhere else in South America, a cathedral that is among the largest wooden structures in the western hemisphere, and a street where a mosque and a synagogue stand side by side and share a car park. The food and the ethnic mix are extraordinary for a country of 600,000 people, and rainforest covers most of it. Dutch is close to necessary, the internet is slow going, the currency has been unstable for years, and there is no nomad presence whatsoever. Suriname is around ninety-three per cent forest, the highest proportion of any country on earth, and the Central Suriname Nature Reserve is a UNESCO site covering an area larger than several European countries with essentially no permanent population in it. Paramaribo's wooden architecture is built almost entirely without nails in the older buildings, using timber joinery that has survived two and a half centuries of equatorial humidity, and the restoration work along the Waterkant is ongoing rather than finished.
paramaribo.whoFor: Dutch, or the willingness to work in it, opens up a genuinely unusual South American base at very low cost, and the interior is the reason to bother. Anyone drawn to the mix of cultures will find more of it here per square kilometre than almost anywhere. Dutch does most of the work here and its absence is felt daily, a fast connection is not something the country can guarantee, and anybody expecting Brazilian infrastructure has misread which side of the border they are on. Getting to the rainforest requires organising a trip rather than a day out. Researchers working across the Guianas tend to end up here. Of the three capitals this is the most comfortable to live in and the easiest to reach from Europe, which settles the question for most fieldwork. The Maroon communities of the interior are a serious reason to come. They descend from people who escaped plantation slavery and built autonomous societies along the upper rivers, and several now run their own tourism on their own terms rather than through an operator in the capital. It also suits birdwatchers, since Suriname's forest holds species lists that rival anywhere in the Amazon basin with a fraction of the visitor pressure.

roatan.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker on Roatan, which makes it one of the cheapest Caribbean islands anywhere and by a distance the cheapest with diving of this quality. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700, with West End and West Bay at the top of that and the eastern half of the island considerably below. Food from the mainland keeps grocery costs reasonable, though imported goods carry a markup. Honduras uses the lempira, but Roatan runs substantially on United States dollars and most prices are quoted in them. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Electricity is the line that surprises people: Roatan's power is among the most expensive in Central America and running air conditioning through the night can add $150 to $250 a month on its own, which is why many long-stay rentals quote rent and utilities separately. Diving is the other structural cost and the reason most people are here, with a fun dive around $35 and a full Open Water certification $300 to $400, the cheapest anywhere. Water is trucked to much of the island and is billed accordingly.
roatan.whereToWork: Roatan's connectivity is the weak point and it is the reason people either love the island or leave it. Fibre has reached West End and parts of the developed western half at speeds that work, but coverage is uneven, and power cuts are frequent enough that most established places run on an inverter or a generator. Mobile data from Tigo and Claro is the fallback. There is a small coworking presence in West End that grew out of the diving community. Anyone with a call-heavy schedule should test a specific property for a week before committing to a month. Starlink has changed the picture materially in the last two years and a number of rentals and dive shops now advertise it, which is worth looking for specifically because it sidesteps the island's cable and its outages. The island runs on Central Standard Time with no daylight saving, which puts it level with Chicago in winter and an hour behind in summer, giving a good North American overlap and an impractical European one.
roatan.gettingAround: Roatan is a long thin island, about fifty kilometres end to end, with one main road running its length. West End is walkable and is where most visitors base themselves, a single street of dive shops and restaurants along the water. Collectivo taxis run the main road cheaply and are the standard way to move; private taxis cost several times more and the difference is worth understanding before getting in. Scooters and rented cars work for the eastern half. The airport is near Coxen Hole with direct flights to Houston, Miami and mainland Honduras, plus a ferry to La Ceiba. The collectivo and private taxi distinction is worth learning on day one: a collectivo along the main road costs a dollar or two and a private taxi ten times that for the same journey, and drivers will assume the latter unless you say otherwise. The road east past French Harbour deteriorates, and the far end of the island around Camp Bay is genuinely remote. Scooter hire runs about $25 a day.
roatan.visas: Honduras has no remote work visa. It belongs to the CA-4 agreement with Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua, which grants most Western nationalities ninety days across all four countries combined rather than ninety days in each, a detail that catches out anyone planning a regional loop. Extensions of up to ninety further days can be applied for in Roatan or on the mainland. Leaving to Belize or Costa Rica resets the clock; leaving to Guatemala does not. Anyone planning a long stay should understand the CA-4 rule properly before arriving. Extensions are handled at the immigration office in Coxen Hole and are routine rather than difficult, but they must be applied for before the ninety days expire rather than after. The CA-4 rule catches people repeatedly: a trip to Guatemala or Nicaragua does not reset anything, and the only nearby resets are Belize, Costa Rica or Mexico, all of which mean a flight or a long overland day.
roatan.bestTime: March to September is the drier half and the best for diving, with calm water, visibility often over thirty metres and daytime temperatures around thirty-one. October to February is the wet season, with heavier rain and occasional cold fronts from the north that stir up the sea. The Atlantic hurricane season runs June to November and Roatan is exposed; Hurricane Mitch in 1998 and the 2020 storms Eta and Iota all affected the island. Whale sharks pass Utila, the next island west, between roughly February and April, which is the trip most divers here add. Sargassum has become a seasonal factor on the eastern and southern shores between roughly May and August, though the West End and West Bay beaches on the sheltered side are far less affected. September and October are the quietest months on the island and the cheapest to rent in, with the trade-off that the weather is least reliable then.
roatan.prosCons: Roatan sits on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second-largest in the world, and is the cheapest place on earth to get a diving certification, which is why a diving community has grown here rather than a nomad one. Costs are very low, English is widely spoken because of the island's Bay Islands history, and the water is exceptional. The internet here is genuinely unreliable, Honduras itself has one of the higher homicide rates in the Americas even though Roatan itself is far calmer than the mainland, and the island's development has been fast and largely unplanned. Roatan is also a Bay Islands community with its own history: English-speaking, part Garifuna and part descended from British settlers, and culturally distinct from mainland Honduras in a way that is immediately obvious. Cruise ships dock at Coxen Hole and Mahogany Bay several times a week, which floods the western half for a few hours and then empties it again.
roatan.whoFor: A diver on a budget whose work survives a patchy connection, and anyone who would rather spend three months getting qualified than three days. The community around the dive shops in West End is real and easy to join, which is unusual in the Caribbean. Island bandwidth and a demanding call schedule pull against each other every day, there is no city here in any sense, and the CA-4 rule catches out anybody planning a long Central American loop who assumed four countries meant four separate allowances. The reef is the reason to be here and it is worth the compromises. Working up to a dive instructor qualification is one of the few things this island does better than almost anywhere. The concentration of shops means the whole ladder from Open Water to instructor can be climbed without leaving, at a cost that would be impossible in the Mediterranean or off Australia.

sanpedrobelize.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in San Pedro, which is expensive for Central America and reflects an island where everything arrives by boat or plane. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,300, with anything on the beach or north of the bridge at the top of that. Groceries cost considerably more than on the Belizean mainland, which is a short flight away and where many residents shop deliberately. The Belize dollar is pegged at two to the United States dollar and both circulate interchangeably. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Golf cart hire is the line nobody expects, running $60 to $90 a day or $500 to $700 a month, and it is how the island moves. Electricity is expensive at island rates and air conditioning through the hot months is the largest utility cost. Diving on the Barrier Reef runs $90 to $130 for a two-tank trip, and the Blue Hole day trip is $250 to $350, which is a once rather than a habit for most budgets.
sanpedrobelize.whereToWork: San Pedro's connectivity is adequate rather than good: fibre from Belize Telemedia reaches much of the town at workable speeds, and mobile data covers the island, but both are expensive relative to what they deliver and outages happen. Power cuts are not rare. There is a small coworking presence and a scattering of cafes used to remote workers, growing out of the Work Where You Vacation programme. English is the official language of Belize, the only country in Central America where that is true, which removes the friction that Spanish-speaking neighbours carry. Belize runs six hours behind GMT with no daylight saving, level with Chicago in winter, which makes North American work straightforward and European calls a late afternoon at best. Starlink has spread across the caye since 2023 and is worth asking about by name, since the older shared connections struggle when the island fills. The clock here stays on one offset all year, so the overlap with North American hours moves an hour in each direction across the year while nothing local changes at all. Anybody scheduling across that border learns it the hard way exactly once.
sanpedrobelize.gettingAround: There are almost no cars on Ambergris Caye. Golf carts are the transport, and renting one is the first thing most arrivals do; the town itself is small enough to walk. Three sand and concrete streets run parallel to the beach, and the island stretches north over a bridge into quieter, more expensive territory. Water taxis run to Caye Caulker and to Belize City, and light aircraft fly to the mainland in fifteen minutes. Everything on the reef, from Hol Chan to the Blue Hole, is reached by boat, and the Blue Hole is a long day trip rather than a morning. North of the bridge the road runs unpaved for kilometres and the carts get progressively more battered the further you go, which is roughly how the island grades its own neighbourhoods. The bridge itself carries a small toll each crossing, paid in cash, and the queue at either end at the start and end of the working day is the closest San Pedro gets to traffic.
sanpedrobelize.visas: Belize's Work Where You Vacation programme grants a six-month remote work stay to people employed outside the country who can show an annual income of around $75,000 and hold health insurance, with a fee of roughly $500 for an individual. It is not renewable in place. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for thirty days on arrival, extendable monthly at an immigration office for a fee, which many long-stay visitors use instead of the formal programme. Belize is not part of the CA-4 agreement, so time here does not count against a Guatemalan or Honduran allowance. The extension route is worth understanding as the default rather than the fallback: monthly renewals cost around $100 each and a good number of long-stay residents have run on them for years, which works out more expensive than the formal programme over a full year but requires no income proof at all. Land and property can be bought outright by foreigners here on the same terms as by citizens, with no restriction on nationality and no local partner required, which is unusual in this part of the world and is a large part of why the island has the resident population it does.
sanpedrobelize.bestTime: Late November to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine, low humidity, and the calmest water for diving and snorkelling. It is also the busy and expensive half. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season, and Belize is exposed; the island has been evacuated more than once. September and October are the wettest, quietest and cheapest. Sargassum seaweed has become a recurring problem on this coast between roughly April and August, and how much of it lands varies enormously year to year. The whale sharks that draw divers to Gladden Spit further south run from roughly March to June, which is a separate trip from the island. Lobster season opens in mid-June and closes at the end of February, and the opening is a genuine island festival rather than a marketing exercise. Conch runs on a separate calendar from October to June, so the menu shifts noticeably with the months rather than staying constant.
sanpedrobelize.prosCons: San Pedro puts you on the Belize Barrier Reef with Hol Chan Marine Reserve and Shark Ray Alley twenty minutes offshore and the Great Blue Hole reachable in a day, in the only English-speaking country in Central America, with a six-month remote work visa and golf carts instead of traffic. The Maya sites of the mainland are a short flight away. It is expensive for the region, the internet is no better than mediocre, the island is small and heavily touristed, and the sargassum seasons of recent years have been genuinely bad. Belize also uses a currency pegged at two to the United States dollar and unchanged for decades, so prices convert in your head instantly and there is no exchange risk at all, which is a small thing that makes a long stay noticeably simpler.
sanpedrobelize.whoFor: The reef and English in the same place, for a diver or snorkeller who can absorb prices closer to the Caribbean than to Central America. The stamp allows six months, and on an island this small that is a ceiling rather than a target. A Central American budget stretches a great deal further on the mainland, or even on Caye Caulker half an hour away, than it does on this island, and anything requiring a dependable connection has picked the wrong caye entirely. Compared with Caye Caulker, Caulker is cheaper, smaller and slower, which is the whole difference. Caribbean diving conducted in English on a North American clock is a rarer combination than it sounds, and it accounts for most of this island's practical appeal. Everywhere else in the region asks for Spanish, an awkward time zone, or both.

chisinau.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Chisinau, which makes it the cheapest capital in Europe by most measures. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $250 to $450, with the centre and Botanica at the upper end and the Soviet-era districts well below. Food is inexpensive and Moldova grows most of it: the markets are genuinely cheap and the wine is absurdly so, since this is a country with more vineyard per head than almost anywhere. Utilities in winter are the one line that rises sharply. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Gigabit fibre runs $8 to $12 a month, which is not a typo and is among the cheapest anywhere on earth for that speed. A coworking desk is $70 to $120 and a trolleybus fare a few cents. Heating through a continental winter is the one genuine seasonal expense, adding $50 to $100 a month between November and March in an older block. Restaurant meals run $5 to $10 and a good bottle of Moldovan wine at a shop is often under $5, which changes the shape of a social life here more than the rent does.
chisinau.whereToWork: Moldova's internet is its standout practical advantage: the country has consistently ranked among the fastest and cheapest in the world for fixed broadband, and gigabit fibre in Chisinau costs a fraction of what it does in western Europe. Mobile data is similarly cheap and fast. There is a real coworking scene, driven by an IT sector that the Moldova IT Park tax regime has deliberately grown, and desks are inexpensive. Power is reliable, though the country's energy dependence has been a live political issue since 2022. Russian and Romanian are both widely spoken; English is limited outside the technology sector. Moldova has repeatedly appeared in the top handful of countries worldwide for fixed broadband speed relative to price, which is a direct consequence of a small, dense, late-built network with no legacy copper to protect. The IT Park regime lets a registered company pay a single seven per cent levy on turnover covering income tax, social contributions and VAT, and it has drawn a genuine outsourcing sector to the city.
chisinau.gettingAround: Chisinau is flat, laid out on a Russian imperial grid, and the centre around Stefan cel Mare boulevard is easily walkable. Trolleybuses and minibuses cover the city for a few cents and run frequently. Taxis and ride-hailing are cheap. The city is compact enough that most people do not need a car. Chisinau airport has connections across Europe, though the choice narrowed after Ukrainian airspace closed and routes rerouted. Cricova and Milestii Mici, the underground wine cities, are half an hour out, and Transnistria, the unrecognised breakaway region, is an hour east and requires its own consideration. Transnistria requires a separate entry registration at the de facto border and is not recognised by any United Nations member, so anyone crossing should understand that consular assistance there is effectively unavailable. Trains are slow and limited; the overnight service to Bucharest exists but the bus is faster, and the rail link north into Ukraine has been reshaped by the war. Orheiul Vechi, a cave monastery cut into a limestone gorge an hour north, is the country's best-known sight and is reachable by marshrutka on a good day.
chisinau.visas: Moldova gives most Western nationalities ninety days visa-free within any hundred and eighty, which is the standard European arrangement. There is no digital nomad visa, though the Moldova IT Park regime offers a flat seven per cent tax on turnover to registered technology companies, which some remote workers use by incorporating locally. Longer stays run through a residence permit, applied for at the Bureau for Migration, which requires a local basis such as employment, study or property. Moldova is an EU candidate country and its rules are moving, so confirm the current position directly. The ninety-in-one-hundred-eighty rule runs on Moldova's own clock rather than Schengen's, so time here does not consume a Schengen allowance, which makes Chisinau useful as a reset for anyone cycling around the European Union. Moldova opened EU accession negotiations in 2024 and its visa and tax rules are likely to move over the coming years.
chisinau.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable half, with warm dry summers reaching the high twenties and long evenings. Late September and early October are the best of the year, when the wine harvest brings the National Wine Day festival to the main square and the countryside is at its most attractive. Winter runs from December to February and is properly cold, sitting around freezing with snow, and the shoulder months of March and November are grey and wet. Moldova has a genuine continental climate rather than a Mediterranean one, which surprises people who place it further south than it is. The festival falls on the first weekend of October and brings producers from every region into the centre, which makes it the one weekend genuinely worth planning a trip around. Milestii Mici holds the Guinness record for the largest wine collection in the world, at around two million bottles in two hundred kilometres of limestone tunnels.
chisinau.prosCons: Chisinau is the cheapest capital in Europe with some of the fastest and cheapest internet anywhere, a real IT sector, and a wine country on its doorstep that includes the largest underground cellar on earth at Milestii Mici. It is safe, walkable and almost entirely undiscovered by remote workers. English is limited, the city is architecturally plain outside a few streets, no remote-working scene has grown up here at all, and Moldova sits directly next to Ukraine, which is a live geopolitical consideration to think about before committing to a long stay rather than after one. Moldova is also among the least visited countries in Europe by a wide margin, which is part of the appeal and part of the reason nothing is set up for visitors: signage is thin, English-language information is scarce, and a good deal of the country runs on knowing somebody.
chisinau.whoFor: European time zones, gigabit fibre and very low costs, for anyone who needs neither a scene nor English to get by. Anyone with Russian or Romanian will find it dramatically easier. The visa-free allowance runs to ninety days, which is long enough to test the place properly without committing to it. There is no nomad community, and Chisinau was built for use rather than for looking at. The larger consideration is the war across the border in Ukraine, which makes current official guidance a thing to read properly rather than a formality to skip. The wine alone justifies a visit in September. Curiosity about a country nobody goes to is a legitimate reason on its own, and Moldova qualifies more completely than anywhere else on the continent: it receives fewer visitors than any other European state. Running a small software company cheaply and legally is what the IT Park regime was built for, and it is one of very few tax structures in Europe aimed squarely at businesses of one or two people rather than at corporations pretending to be small.

dushanbe.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Dushanbe, which is among the lowest figures on this site. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $200 to $400, with the centre near Rudaki Avenue at the top of that. Food from the bazaars is very cheap and the produce, particularly the fruit, is famously good; Tajikistan grows apricots, melons and pomegranates that the whole region buys. Imported goods and anything electronic are expensive and hard to find. The somoni is stable but not freely convertible outside the country. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fixed internet runs $30 to $60 a month for speeds that would cost a tenth of that elsewhere, which is the single worst value on this site. The somoni cannot be exchanged abroad, so bring dollars and change what you need locally, and expect cash to be the only option for most transactions. A marshrutka fare is a few cents and a taxi across the city a dollar or two. Rents in the Soviet-era blocks away from Rudaki run well below the centre and are what most residents pay.
dushanbe.whereToWork: Dushanbe's connectivity is the real constraint: Tajikistan has among the slowest and most expensive internet in the region, the state controls the backbone, and access has been restricted during politically sensitive periods. Fibre reaches parts of the capital at modest speeds and mobile data is the common fallback. Power supply in the capital is reliable, though the rest of the country still sees winter rationing. There is essentially no coworking. Russian is the working language of business and Tajik of daily life; English is rare. Anyone planning to work here should treat the connection as the thing to verify first. Tajikistan runs five hours ahead of GMT, which gives a European afternoon overlap and no useful American window at all. The state telecom holds the international gateway and pricing reflects that, which is the structural reason the internet is both slow and expensive rather than merely one or the other.
dushanbe.gettingAround: Dushanbe is a low-rise city laid out along Rudaki Avenue, a long tree-lined boulevard that most of the centre hangs off, and the walkable core is genuinely pleasant with fountains and parks along its length. Marshrutka minibuses and buses cover the city for very little, and taxis are cheap and usually unmetered, so agree the fare first. Dushanbe airport has connections to Istanbul, Dubai, Moscow and the region. The Pamir Highway, the second-highest road in the world, starts here and runs east towards the Wakhan Corridor and Kyrgyzstan, which is why most foreign visitors come at all. Rudaki Avenue carries what is claimed to be one of the tallest flagpoles in the world outside the palace, and the Navruz Palace and the national museum along it were built in the same wave of state construction. The road north to the Fann Mountains and Iskanderkul reaches genuinely alpine country within four hours. Shared taxis to Khujand through the Anzob tunnel take about five hours and are the standard way north, the tunnel itself having a poor reputation that has improved since its rebuild.
dushanbe.visas: Tajikistan operates an e-visa that most nationalities can obtain online in a few days, typically valid for forty-five to sixty days, and it is one of the more straightforward systems in Central Asia. There is no remote work visa. Anyone intending to travel the Pamir Highway needs an additional GBAO permit for the Gorno-Badakhshan autonomous region, which can be requested with the e-visa application and is checked at road posts. Registration with the authorities is required for stays beyond a set period, usually handled by the hotel. Rules here change, so confirm directly before booking. The GBAO permit is free when requested alongside the e-visa but is often refused or delayed during periods of tension in Gorno-Badakhshan, which has been closed to foreigners more than once in recent years. Anyone planning the Pamir Highway should check whether the region is currently open before booking anything.
dushanbe.bestTime: April to June and September to October are the comfortable windows, with warm dry days and the mountains accessible. Dushanbe sits low at around 800 metres and its summers are hot, regularly above thirty-five degrees in July and August, though the dry air makes that more bearable than the number suggests. Winter is cold and grey with snow, and the air quality in the capital drops sharply as coal heating comes on. The Pamir Highway season is short, roughly June to September, and the passes are closed by snow outside it. Navruz in late March is the largest holiday of the year and Dushanbe marks it on a scale that closes the city for several days. Winter air quality in the capital is genuinely poor, with coal and low-grade fuel burned for heating and the valley position trapping it. The mountains hold snow into June, so the high valleys open later than the capital's weather suggests, and the trekking season is correspondingly short.
dushanbe.prosCons: Dushanbe is the gateway to the Pamirs, which is one of the great mountain regions on earth and almost entirely unvisited, and the city itself is greener and more pleasant than its reputation, with a genuinely walkable central boulevard. Costs are among the lowest anywhere and the fruit is remarkable. The internet is slow and politically controlled, English is rare, not one remote worker is in evidence here, air quality in winter is genuinely poor, and Tajikistan is an authoritarian state where political topics are best left alone. The city was also rebuilt on a Soviet plan with the widest boulevards in Central Asia, which makes it feel larger and emptier than its population. Tajikistan is over ninety per cent mountain and the Pamirs contain peaks above seven thousand metres, including Ismoil Somoni, the highest in the former Soviet Union, which is the scale of what sits a day's drive from a very ordinary capital. Yagnob valley to the north still speaks a direct descendant of Sogdian, the language of the Silk Road merchants, and is one of the last places it survives.
dushanbe.whoFor: A traveller heading into the Pamirs needs somewhere to arrange permits, buy supplies and rest, and that is what this is rather than a place to sit and work for months. Anyone with Russian will find it far easier. Work that depends on a fast or uncensored connection cannot be done here, and that single fact disqualifies most remote workers before any of the other considerations get a hearing. Come for the mountains, plan the connection around what the country actually offers, and time it for the short Pamir season. Anyone attempting the Pamir Highway should also plan the GBAO permit and the vehicle before arriving, since neither is quick to arrange once here. It also suits cyclists specifically, since the Pamir Highway is one of the classic long-distance rides in the world and Dushanbe is where almost every attempt is provisioned and repaired. Central Asian water politics is a subject best studied from the country that controls the taps. Tajikistan holds the headwaters the whole region depends on, and the Rogun dam is the project the entire argument now turns on.

bandarseribegawan.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Bandar Seri Begawan, which is moderate for Southeast Asia and reflects an oil state with subsidised fuel and no income tax. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700. Food is inexpensive, particularly at the night markets and the Gadong food court, and Brunei's cooking sits between Malay and Bornean traditions. Petrol costs a fraction of the regional price. There is no alcohol spend because there is no legal alcohol sale, which removes a line most budgets carry. The Brunei dollar is pegged one to one with the Singapore dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $30 to $60 a month at good speeds. Petrol at around a third of the regional price is the reason everyone drives, and a car is effectively a required expense, with hire from about $300 a month. The absence of an alcohol line is genuinely material to a monthly budget in a way that surprises people comparing Brunei with Malaysia next door. Rents in Gadong and Kiulap sit above the older quarters near the river and put you closer to the malls and food courts where the city actually eats.
bandarseribegawan.whereToWork: Brunei's connectivity is good: fibre reaches most of the developed area at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, underwritten by a state that can afford the infrastructure. Power is entirely reliable. There is very little coworking, since the country has almost no visiting professional population, so remote work happens from apartments and the cafes around Gadong. English is widely spoken and is a language of instruction and business, which makes Brunei one of the easier places in the region to operate in. The country runs on the same time as Singapore and Kuala Lumpur. Brunei sits eight hours ahead of GMT, level with Singapore and Kuala Lumpur, which suits East Asian and Australian work and makes European clients an evening proposition.
