The country's oil wealth funds free healthcare and education for citizens, which is why the infrastructure is what it is despite a population under half a million. Coworking is limited to a couple of government-backed innovation spaces rather than a market.
bandarseribegawan.gettingAround: Bandar Seri Begawan is small and the centre around the Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque is walkable, but the country assumes a car and public transport is thin: buses exist and are infrequent, and there is no rail. Petrol is so cheap that everyone drives. Water taxis cross to Kampong Ayer, the water village of stilted houses that has stood on the river for centuries and still holds thousands of people, and they cost almost nothing. Brunei airport has connections across the region. Ulu Temburong National Park, primary rainforest reached by longboat, is the country's main draw and takes a full day. Kampong Ayer has been continuously inhabited for over a thousand years and Antonio Pigafetta, sailing with Magellan, described it in 1521 as the Venice of the East. Around ten thousand people still live there and the water taxis run all day for a dollar or so. The Temburong district is now reached by a thirty-kilometre bridge opened in 2020, which replaced a boat journey through Malaysian waters and cut the trip to under an hour.
bandarseribegawan.visas: Brunei gives visa-free entry to most Western nationalities, typically thirty days for British citizens and ninety for some others, granted on arrival, and the rules vary more by nationality than in most countries so check yours specifically. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require an employment pass tied to a local sponsor. Visitors should understand that Brunei applies Sharia law, that alcohol cannot be sold although non-Muslims may import a small personal allowance, and that public behaviour standards are stricter than elsewhere in Southeast Asia. Anyone travelling on to Sabah or Sarawak should note that Brunei splits Malaysian Borneo in two, so the overland route crosses several borders in a day. Alcohol may be imported by non-Muslims in a limited personal allowance, declared on arrival, and there are no bars or licensed premises anywhere in the country. Anyone relying on that allowance should read the current quantity before packing.
bandarseribegawan.bestTime: Brunei is equatorial and hot all year, around thirty-two degrees every month with high humidity, so the calendar turns on rain rather than temperature. January to May is the drier half and the better window, particularly for the rainforest at Ulu Temburong, where the canopy walkway and river journeys depend on water levels and weather. The wetter months from September to January bring heavy afternoon downpours. Ramadan changes daily life substantially, with restaurants closed during daylight and a quieter public rhythm, and it is worth knowing which weeks it falls in. Ulu Temburong is reached by longboat up the Temburong river and the canopy walkway there sits at around fifty metres, and the trip requires a permit arranged through an operator rather than turning up. Hari Raya at the end of Ramadan involves the Sultan opening the palace to the public for three days, which is one of the few occasions the country genuinely fills with visitors.
bandarseribegawan.prosCons: Brunei is one of the safest countries in the world, has some of the best-preserved primary rainforest in Borneo an hour from its capital, a water village that is a living settlement rather than an exhibit, and infrastructure paid for by oil. English works everywhere and there is no income tax. There is nothing that could be called nightlife, no alcohol, and no remote-working scene, very little at all to do after dark, and a legal and social framework considerably stricter than its neighbours. It is quiet in a way that suits few people for long. Brunei has kept around seventy per cent of its land under forest, one of the highest proportions in Asia, largely because oil revenue meant it never needed logging or palm oil, which is why the rainforest here is intact where Sabah and Sarawak's is not. The country has no rail and no domestic flights at all.
bandarseribegawan.whoFor: A very safe, very quiet, English-speaking base in Borneo with rainforest close by, for somebody who does not drink or does not mind that nobody else can. A few weeks built around Ulu Temburong and the water village is the right use of this country. A long stay is a much harder case to make. Nightlife, company and anything resembling a scene are all absent from a country where alcohol is banned outright. Anybody travelling with a partner should read the laws on personal conduct carefully before arriving, because they are stricter than most visitors assume and the penalties are not nominal. Business in Borneo is easier to run from here than from anywhere else on the island's northern coast, since Brunei combines the most comfortable infrastructure with the best connections outward. Tropical forest ecology is the field this country serves best. Brunei's primary lowland dipterocarp forest is among the best-preserved anywhere on earth, and the research station at Kuala Belalong hosts international work year-round. Kota Kinabalu is the comparison, and Brunei is safer, quieter, considerably drier socially and has the better-preserved forest.

dili.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Dili, which is moderate for Southeast Asia and higher than a country this poor suggests, because Dili's rental market was shaped by the international missions that followed independence. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700. Timor-Leste uses the United States dollar as its currency, so nothing needs converting, though the coins are local. Food from the markets is cheap and the coffee, which is the country's main export outside oil, is excellent and absurdly inexpensive. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The dollarised economy is a genuine convenience for anyone earning in dollars, though the local centavo coins circulate alongside American ones and small change is often given in either. Fibre where it exists runs $80 to $200 a month for speeds that would be unremarkable anywhere else, which is among the worst internet value on this site. Timorese coffee, mostly arabica grown in the highlands around Ermera, sells for a couple of dollars a kilo at the market and is exported to specialty roasters worldwide.
dili.whereToWork: Dili's connectivity is poor and it is the main practical obstacle: the country relies on a limited submarine connection, prices are high relative to speed, and outages are common. Mobile data from Telkomcel and Telemor is the usual fallback. Power cuts happen regularly and anyone whose work cannot pause needs a building with backup. There is essentially no coworking. Tetum and Portuguese are the official languages, Indonesian and English are widely understood, and English is more common than in most of the region because of the long international presence. Anyone working with Australia will find the time zone useful, since Dili sits within an hour of the eastern Australian working day. Dili runs nine hours ahead of GMT, level with Tokyo and Seoul and an hour ahead of Jakarta, which puts it inside the Australian working day and makes Sydney and Brisbane clients entirely practical. That is the strongest structural argument for basing here rather than elsewhere in the region. Starlink became available in 2024 and is the single change most likely to make a serious stay workable, so it is worth asking any prospective landlord about by name.
dili.gettingAround: Dili is a small coastal capital laid out along the waterfront, and the central strip from the Government Palace east towards the Cristo Rei statue is walkable. Microlet minibuses cover the city for a few cents and taxis are cheap. Most expatriates drive, and a four-wheel drive is needed for anywhere outside the capital, because Timor-Leste's roads are mountainous and in poor condition; the drive to Baucau or the south coast takes far longer than the distance suggests. The ferry to Atauro Island takes a couple of hours and is the trip most visitors come for. The Cristo Rei statue at the eastern end of the bay is reached by a long flight of steps and is where Dili exercises at dawn and dusk. Atauro's ferry runs on a limited schedule, a couple of times a week on the government boat with faster private options, so an island trip is planned around the timetable rather than dropped into a weekend.
dili.visas: Timor-Leste grants a thirty-day visa on arrival at Dili airport to most nationalities for a fee of around $30, and it is straightforward. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are available from the immigration service in Dili, and a longer stay can be arranged through a business or work visa with local sponsorship. Portuguese citizens and some others have separate arrangements. The land border with Indonesian West Timor has its own requirements and is not the same process as arriving by air, so check that route separately if planning it. The visa on arrival covers Dili airport specifically; arriving overland from Indonesian West Timor at Batugade requires a visa obtained in advance, which is the single most common planning mistake people make with this country. Extensions are handled at the Migration Service in Dili and are routine for a further thirty days. Accession to the regional bloc has been agreed and is being worked through, which over time should ease movement and trade across the wider region, though nothing about the position facing a visitor has actually changed yet. The airport handles a handful of flights a day and the visa desk closes along with them.
dili.bestTime: May to November is the dry season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around thirty-one, clear water for diving and the roads passable. December to April is the wet season, when heavy rain makes the mountain roads difficult and the sea murkier. Diving is the reason many people come and the visibility is best between roughly June and September. The waters around Atauro Island were found in a 2016 survey to have the highest average reef fish diversity recorded anywhere in the world, which is not a claim the country makes loudly enough. The figure behind it is 253 species per site, counted by Conservation International, and no other site surveyed anywhere has matched that number since. Whale and dolphin migration through the Ombai Strait peaks between October and December and is visible from the ferry.
dili.prosCons: Timor-Leste has the most biodiverse reef waters ever surveyed half an hour off its capital, mountains rising to nearly three thousand metres, coffee that is among the best in Asia, and almost no tourists at all. It is the youngest country in Asia and its independence history is recent and openly told, at the Chega and Resistance museums. The internet is genuinely bad and the roads are worse still, medical facilities are limited, prices are higher than the region for what you get, and there is no nomad infrastructure whatsoever. Timor-Leste joined ASEAN in principle in 2022 and has been working through accession since, which is expected to change trade, travel and investment considerably over the coming years and is the main reason the country's economics may look different in five years than they do now.
dili.whoFor: A diver, or someone working in development or conservation, who wants somewhere genuinely unvisited and whose work tolerates a poor connection. Atauro is the reason to come and it is extraordinary. A call-heavy schedule and the local bandwidth are in direct conflict, Southeast Asian prices do not apply in a dollarised economy that imports almost everything, and the infrastructure is thin in ways that shape every ordinary day. The country is easier for an English speaker than most of its neighbours, which is the one thing that consistently surprises people who go. Watching a country assemble itself from nothing is a genuine reason to be here. The institutions of Timor-Leste are younger than most of the people using them, which is a rare thing to observe at close range. Coffee at origin is a serious reason to come. The highland cooperatives around Ermera and Maubisse are reachable from here, and the harvest between May and September is when the country's main non-oil industry can actually be watched working rather than described.

thimphu.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,500 a month as a solo remote worker in Thimphu, and understand that the figure is dominated by one line rather than by rent. Bhutan charges most foreign visitors a Sustainable Development Fee of $100 per person per night, reduced from $200 in September 2023, which is roughly $3,000 over a thirty-day month before accommodation, food or anything else. Discount structures for longer stays have been introduced and changed more than once. Rent and food are cheap by comparison: a flat runs a few hundred dollars and eating locally costs very little. Indian, Bangladeshi and Maldivian nationals pay a far lower fee. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Nothing about how somebody chooses to live here changes that number. Taking a cheaper room or eating locally moves a monthly total by a few per cent, because the largest single line is charged by the day regardless of anything else. A month here costs more in fees than three months in most of the countries on this site cost in total, and any planning has to start from that number rather than from rent. Accommodation and food are genuinely cheap and almost irrelevant next to the nightly fee, which is the whole arithmetic of a Bhutanese stay.
thimphu.whereToWork: Thimphu's connectivity is adequate rather than good: fibre reaches parts of the city at modest speeds, mobile data from Bhutan Telecom and TashiCell covers the valley, and the whole country runs on a limited international link routed through India. Outages happen. There is no coworking. English is a language of instruction in Bhutanese schools and is widely spoken in the capital, which makes Bhutan far easier to operate in than its isolation suggests. The country runs six hours ahead of London and thirty minutes ahead of India, which is one of the world's few half-hour offsets. Bhutan's international bandwidth is routed through India, so an outage or a disruption on that link affects the whole country at once. The half-hour offset from Indian Standard Time is a deliberate marker of independence rather than a geographic necessity, and it catches out anyone scheduling across the border. Coworking does not exist and hotel wifi is the practical desk.
thimphu.gettingAround: Thimphu is the only national capital in the world with no traffic lights: an intersection in the centre is directed by a policeman in a decorated booth, and an attempt to install lights was abandoned because people disliked them. The city sits in a north-south valley and the central grid is walkable. City buses and shared taxis are cheap. Paro, with the country's only international airport, is an hour away on a mountain road, and the approach into it is among the most demanding commercial landings anywhere, flown only by a small number of certified pilots. Roads elsewhere are slow and winding. Paro's approach threads between mountains and requires a manual visual approach with no instrument landing, which is why only a few dozen pilots worldwide are certified for it and why flights are cancelled readily rather than attempted in poor visibility. Punakha, the old winter capital with its dzong at the confluence of two rivers, is three hours east over the Dochula pass.
thimphu.visas: Bhutan does not operate an ordinary tourist visa in the way other countries do. Almost every foreign visitor needs a visa applied for online through the Department of Immigration, costing around $40, and must pay the Sustainable Development Fee for every night of the stay. Independent travel has been permitted since 2022, so a guide is no longer mandatory outside protected areas, which was a substantial change. Indian nationals enter under a separate arrangement with a much lower fee. There is no remote work visa and no framework for long stays outside employment or study. The fee has moved twice since 2022, from $200 to $65 as a temporary measure and then to $100, and discounts for longer stays have been introduced and withdrawn, so the current published rate is the only one worth planning against. The fee is paid in advance with the visa application rather than on arrival.
thimphu.bestTime: March to May and September to November are the two good windows. Spring brings rhododendron across the hills and clear mountain views; autumn is drier still and holds the tsechu festival season, when masked dances are performed in the dzongs and the Thimphu tsechu fills the capital for three days. Thimphu sits at around 2,300 metres, so summers are mild rather than hot, reaching the mid twenties, and the monsoon from June to August brings cloud that hides the mountains. Winter is cold, dropping below freezing at night, with occasional snow and the clearest air of the year. Tsechu dates follow the Bhutanese lunar calendar and shift each year, so the Thimphu and Paro festivals move by weeks between one year and the next and need checking against the current calendar rather than a fixed month. Winter is the clearest season for mountain views and the cheapest for accommodation, though the fee does not move with the season.
thimphu.prosCons: Bhutan is the only country that measures itself on Gross National Happiness rather than output, the only one that is carbon negative, and the only one whose constitution requires that sixty per cent of its land stay forested. The dzongs, the Tiger's Nest monastery above Paro and the Buddha Dordenma above Thimphu are genuinely extraordinary, and the country is safe and orderly. The Sustainable Development Fee makes a long stay expensive in a way that no other country matches, the internet is middling at best, there is no nomad presence, and nightlife is essentially nonexistent. Bhutan absorbs more carbon than it emits, largely because of the forest cover requirement and hydropower exports, and it is one of very few countries anywhere that can make that claim on a measured rather than an offset basis. Television and the internet were legalised only in 1999, which is recent enough that many people here remember the change.
thimphu.whoFor: A deliberate, budgeted few weeks in a country that has decided not to compete on price, for Himalayan trekking and living Buddhist practice rather than a cheap base. Anyone interested in how a small state manages tourism deliberately will find Bhutan the case study. Anybody counting costs will find the daily sustainable development fee dwarfs rent, food and everything else combined. A long stay is not merely expensive but structurally discouraged, since the system was designed to limit visitor numbers rather than to welcome residents. Do the arithmetic on the fee before anything else. Anyone hoping to trek the Snowman Trek or the Trans Bhutan Trail should build the fee into the trip length from the start, since both take weeks. The Trans Bhutan Trail reopened in 2022 after sixty years closed, and it runs four hundred kilometres across the country. Most people walk it in sections rather than end to end, which makes it a reason to base here rather than to pass through. Measured against Nepal, Bhutan costs many times more per day and delivers a fraction of the crowds.

nosybe.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month as a solo remote worker on Nosy Be, which is cheap by international standards though noticeably more expensive than mainland Madagascar, because the island runs on tourism. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $500, with Ambatoloaka and the west coast beaches at the top of that and Hell-Ville, the main town, below it. Food from the market is very cheap and the seafood is excellent. Imported goods carry a heavy markup on an island this remote. The ariary has been weak for years, which helps a visitor and hurts everyone living here. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Mobile data bundles run $15 to $40 a month depending on how much you need, and that is the connection most people actually use rather than a fixed line. A scooter is around $12 a day or $200 a month. Boat trips to the surrounding islands are the discretionary line that adds up, at $30 to $70 a day depending on how far you go and whether the trip is shared. Rents in Hell-Ville run well below the beach strip and put you in the working town rather than the resort one.
nosybe.whereToWork: Nosy Be's connectivity is poor and it is the main constraint on working here. Mobile data from Telma, Orange and Airtel is the primary connection for most people and speeds vary by hour and location; fixed lines exist in a few hotels and better guesthouses. Power cuts are routine across Madagascar and the island is no exception, so an inverter or a generator is standard in anything aimed at visitors. There is no coworking. French is the language of business and administration, Malagasy of daily life, and English is limited to the tourism trade. Madagascar sits three hours ahead of GMT, which gives a full European working day and no useful American window at all. Starlink was licensed in Madagascar in 2023 and a few of the better lodges now have it, which is the single thing most likely to make a longer stay workable and is worth asking about by name rather than accepting a general assurance about wifi.
nosybe.gettingAround: Nosy Be is about twenty-five kilometres across and Hell-Ville, properly Andoany, is the administrative town at its southeast corner. Taxis, mostly ageing Renaults, and taxi-brousse minibuses cover the island cheaply, and scooters are the common rental. The roads are variable and get worse in the wet season. Fascene airport has seasonal direct flights from Milan and Paris and connections through Antananarivo, Nairobi and Reunion, which makes the island considerably easier to reach than most of Madagascar. Boats run constantly to Nosy Komba, Nosy Tanikely and the smaller islands, which is what most visitors come for. Nosy Komba, the lemur island, is twenty minutes by boat and Nosy Tanikely's marine reserve about forty. The mainland is reached by a car ferry to Ankify and then a long drive, which is why almost everyone flies in and out rather than combining the island with an overland trip. Roads on the island are unsealed in places and deteriorate through the wet season, so a scooter is fine in the dry months and a poor idea in February.
nosybe.visas: Madagascar grants a visa on arrival to most nationalities at the main airports, and since 2023 stays of up to fifteen days have been free of the visa fee, with thirty, sixty and ninety-day options available for a charge. The process is done at the airport and is straightforward, though queues can be long. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays run through a residence permit applied for locally, which takes time and local support. Check the current fee structure directly, since Madagascar has revised it more than once in recent years. The fee-free fifteen days is genuinely free rather than merely cheap, and for a short stay it removes the paperwork entirely. Anyone staying longer should have the exact fee in cash, since card payment at the airport counter is unreliable. Overstaying carries a fine payable at the airport on departure.
nosybe.bestTime: April to November is the dry season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around thirty and calm seas. The wet season from December to March brings heavy rain and the cyclone risk, and Madagascar is one of the most cyclone-exposed countries in the world; the northwest coast is hit less often than the east but is not immune. The wildlife calendar is the other consideration: humpback whales pass between roughly July and September and whale sharks arrive from September to December, which is the reason many divers time a trip for the end of the dry season. Ylang-ylang is distilled on the island between roughly October and December and the smell of it carries across the west coast during those weeks, which is where the island's old nickname of the perfume island comes from. Cyclone season formally runs November to April and flights are the first thing cancelled.
nosybe.prosCons: Nosy Be is the easiest way into Madagascar's wildlife, with lemurs in the Lokobe reserve on the island itself, whale sharks and humpbacks offshore in season, and Nosy Tanikely's marine reserve half an hour away by boat. The island grows ylang-ylang and smells of it. It is warm, cheap and reachable directly from Europe in season. The internet is bad and the power goes off often, French is close to necessary here, Madagascar's poverty is severe and visible, and petty crime around the tourist areas requires ordinary caution. The island is also considerably easier to reach than the rest of Madagascar, which is either its main convenience or the reason it feels less like the country. Madagascar split from Africa around 160 million years ago and roughly ninety per cent of its wildlife exists nowhere else, which is the reason the island is a destination at all and why the reserves are as strictly managed as they are. Lokobe is reached only by pirogue.
nosybe.whoFor: A diver or naturalist with some French, whose work tolerates a weak connection, and who wants the wildlife of Madagascar without the long overland journeys the mainland demands. A few weeks inside the dry season is the only version of this that really works. A call-heavy schedule will not survive here, French is doing all the work in daily life, and the direct European flights suggest an infrastructure the island does not actually have behind them. The rest of Madagascar is a different and much harder trip, which is worth understanding before treating this island as representative. Anyone planning to continue to Antananarivo or the southern reserves should treat that as a separate expedition rather than a side trip from here. Serious divers find rather more than the package brochures let on. The channel between Nosy Be and the mainland holds whale sharks, manta rays and reef systems that take a fraction of the traffic the Indian Ocean's better-known sites absorb. Next to Zanzibar, Nosy Be is quieter, harder work, and far ahead on wildlife.

blantyre.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Blantyre, which is low even by regional standards. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, with Nyambadwe and Sunnyside at the top of that and the areas towards Limbe cheaper. Food from the markets costs very little and Malawi grows most of what it eats. Imported goods are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable, since the country has repeatedly run short of foreign exchange. The kwacha was devalued by around forty-four per cent in late 2023, so any figure in it dates fast. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The foreign exchange shortage is not an abstraction and it shapes daily life: bank cards issued abroad often fail, ATMs run dry, and dollars change hands at a parallel rate well away from the official one. Bring cash, in good condition and in larger denominations, which attract a better rate. Landlords catering to foreigners frequently quote and want dollars, several months at a time. Fuel shortages have been recurrent, and queueing for it costs hours rather than money, which is its own kind of expense.
blantyre.whereToWork: Blantyre's connectivity is modest: fibre has reached parts of the city and works reasonably where it exists, and mobile data from TNM and Airtel is the common fallback, though Malawian data prices are high relative to income. Power cuts are frequent and scheduled load shedding is a fact of life, so anything serious runs on an inverter or a generator. There is a small coworking presence serving local business rather than visitors. English is an official language and the medium of education and business, which removes the language friction entirely and is Malawi's clearest practical advantage. Load shedding is published as a schedule rather than arriving at random, so the workable arrangement is to plan the day around it: the utility posts the rota by area and most residents structure meetings and heavy tasks accordingly. Malawi's power is largely hydroelectric from the Shire river, which means supply worsens when the water is low, so the dry season is also the difficult season for electricity. The time zone sits two hours ahead of London, giving a comfortable European overlap and an early start against North America.
blantyre.gettingAround: Blantyre spreads across hills, with the older commercial centre and the separate town of Limbe forming a twin core about eight kilometres apart. Minibuses cover both cheaply and are how most people move; they fill before they leave. Taxis and a growing number of ride-hailing options work in the centre. Most expatriates drive, on the left. Chileka airport is twenty minutes out with regional connections through Addis Ababa, Nairobi and Johannesburg. Mount Mulanje is an hour and a half east and Lake Malawi's southern shore about three hours north, which is what most weekends here are for. Driving between towns after dark is avoided by residents, since the roads are unlit, carry pedestrians and livestock, and the standard of other vehicles varies enormously. Fuel availability is the other planning constraint on any road trip, and filling up when you can rather than when you need to is the local habit. The Zomba plateau, about an hour north, is the third weekend destination alongside the lake and the mountain, and its escarpment road is one of the best drives in the country.
blantyre.visas: Malawi requires a visa of most nationalities, obtained through an e-visa system before travel or on arrival at the main entry points, typically costing around $50 for a thirty-day single entry with longer options available. The process is straightforward by regional standards. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at an immigration office in Blantyre or Lilongwe. Business and employment permits require local sponsorship and take considerably longer. Malawi has changed its visa fees more than once, so confirm the current schedule before travelling. Anyone travelling on to Zambia or Tanzania overland should check those requirements separately, since neither shares an arrangement with Malawi. A yellow fever certificate is required of anyone arriving from a country where the disease is present, which catches travellers routing through parts of East Africa rather than flying in from Europe. For work, the permit to know about is the temporary employment permit, which an employer applies for and which takes months rather than weeks, so nobody sensibly arrives and then sorts it out. Keep a copy of the entry stamp, since extensions are calculated from it and the original is the only record of it.
blantyre.bestTime: May to August is the cool dry season and the most comfortable window, with daytime temperatures in the low twenties at Blantyre's altitude and cold nights. September to November is hot and dry, building towards the rains, and can be genuinely uncomfortable in the lowlands. The wet season from December to April brings heavy rain that makes some roads difficult and the mountain hard going, though it is also when the country is greenest. Mount Mulanje, whose Sapitwa peak at just over 3,000 metres is the highest in central Africa, is best climbed between May and October. The chiperoni is the local word worth learning, a cold damp southeasterly that brings days of grey drizzle to the highlands in the cool season and surprises visitors expecting African sunshine. Malaria risk rises through and after the rains, so prophylaxis is not optional here. The rainy months are also the lean season agriculturally, before the harvest comes in, which shapes prices and the mood in rural areas far more than any tourist calendar does.
blantyre.prosCons: Malawi is called the warm heart of Africa and the reputation for friendliness is genuinely earned. Blantyre has Mount Mulanje on its doorstep, Lake Malawi within a morning's drive with freshwater snorkelling among hundreds of endemic cichlid species, and living costs among the lowest anywhere. English works everywhere. The power supply is thoroughly unreliable, the economy has been under severe strain with recurrent shortages of fuel and of foreign exchange, medical facilities are limited, and there is no remote-working presence and very little visitor infrastructure in the city itself. Blantyre is also the older of Malawi's two main cities and carries the colonial architecture that Lilongwe, built as a capital in the 1970s, does not. Bilharzia is present in Lake Malawi, which matters because the snorkelling is the reason people come. It is treatable and widely treated, and residents swim anyway while taking a course of praziquantel afterwards as a matter of routine, but anyone who swims should know that in advance rather than find out later. Serious medical problems mean evacuation to South Africa, and cover for it is standard for anyone posted here.
blantyre.whoFor: An English-speaking African base that costs almost nothing, with real mountains and a remarkable lake within reach, for work that survives load shedding. Anyone in development, conservation or health will find a substantial professional network here, since Malawi hosts a great deal of that work. Power here comes and goes on a schedule nobody publishes, and the foreign community is aid workers and missionaries rather than anything a remote worker joins. Anyone staying should sort out a power backup and a plan for the fuel shortages before they become urgent rather than after. Climbing Mulanje properly is worth organising a stay around. The massif rewards a week of hut-to-hut walking in a way that a day trip up and down cannot begin to approach. Within Malawi rather than this city specifically, Lilongwe has the diplomatic community, the better hospital and the international flights, while Blantyre has the commerce, the mountain and the older character. A third option suits a good many people better than either: basing on the lake itself, at Cape Maclear or Nkhata Bay, where the costs fall again and the connectivity, already imperfect here, becomes the accepted trade.

victoriafalls.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Victoria Falls, which is high for Zimbabwe and reflects a town whose entire economy is tourism. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700. Food and goods are priced for visitors in the centre and considerably less in the residential areas of Chinotimba. Zimbabwe's currency history is its own subject: the country uses United States dollars for most transactions alongside the ZiG, introduced in April 2024 after a series of failed currencies, and prices in dollars are the reliable ones. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Park entry to the falls is around $50 for non-residents each visit, so anyone staying a while should ask about the local rate rather than paying it repeatedly.
victoriafalls.whereToWork: Victoria Falls has better connectivity than most of Zimbabwe because tourism demands it: fibre reaches the town centre and the lodges at workable speeds, and mobile data from Econet and NetOne covers the area, though Zimbabwean data prices are high. Power cuts are a national problem driven partly by low water at Kariba, and load shedding is routine, so lodges and serious businesses run on generators or solar. There is no coworking. English is an official language and universally used, which makes Zimbabwe one of the easier African countries to work from. Data is sold in bundles rather than by the gigabyte and works out at several times European prices, which makes a lodge with its own fibre worth paying for. Zimbabwe has one of the highest literacy rates on the continent and an education system that was once the envy of the region, which is why the guides, drivers and lodge managers here are often far more qualified than the job requires and why so many of their contemporaries left. That history sits under every conversation about the economy. For an outsider it means a working relationship that is easy from the first day and unusually well informed.
victoriafalls.gettingAround: Victoria Falls is a small town and its centre is walkable, with the falls themselves a fifteen-minute walk from the main street, though warthogs and the occasional elephant on the roads are a genuine consideration rather than a joke. Taxis and shuttles cover the lodges. The Victoria Falls Bridge crosses to Zambia and Livingstone, and walking across it is straightforward with the right visa. Victoria Falls airport has direct flights from Johannesburg, Nairobi, Addis Ababa and Cape Town. Hwange National Park, one of Africa's great elephant reserves, is two hours south. Livingstone is fifteen minutes across the bridge and has its own airport, which is sometimes the cheaper way in or out of the region. An overnight train still runs south to the second city, leaving in the evening and arriving in the morning, and it is slow, unreliable and one of the great cheap journeys anywhere on the continent, with a sleeper berth costing a few dollars. The bridge across the gorge was finished in 1905 and carries a road, a railway and a bungee platform on the same deck, which is a strange combination to walk over with a passport in your pocket.
victoriafalls.visas: Zimbabwe issues visas on arrival to most nationalities at the airport and land borders, typically around $30 for a single entry and $45 for a double. The more useful option here is the KAZA UniVisa, roughly $50, which covers both Zimbabwe and Zambia for thirty days and allows unlimited crossings between them plus a day trip into Botswana at Kazungula, which matters a great deal in a town where the falls are split across a border. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require an extension applied for locally. The UniVisa is not always offered unprompted at the border and is worth asking for by name, since the alternative is paying twice to see both sides. The border posts keep fixed hours and close at night, so a day on the far side has a deadline attached and missing it means a hotel nobody planned for. The combined visa is not open to every nationality and the list is worth reading before counting on it. Employment by a local company requires a permit that the company itself has to sponsor, and it is a serious application, so a remote worker in practice lives on a visitor stamp renewed with care.
victoriafalls.bestTime: The falls are a different sight in every season and there is no single best time, only a choice. February to May is peak flow, when the Zambezi is at its highest and the spray is so heavy that the falls are often invisible from close range and the viewing paths are drenched. June to August is the balanced window, with strong water and clear views, and it is the busiest. September to December is low water, when the eastern cataracts can dry to bare rock but the Devil's Pool on the Zambian side opens and the rafting below the gorge is at its best. Rafting below the gorge closes during peak flow, roughly March to June, because the water is too high to run safely. When the river is full, the nights around a full moon throw a lunar rainbow across the gorge, and the park opens late for it on a few evenings each month, which is the one thing here that genuinely cannot be seen anywhere else on this scale. Game viewing works to the inverse of that calendar: once the bush dries out the animals concentrate at the waterholes, and that is when the park two hours away is at its best.
victoriafalls.prosCons: Victoria Falls is a kilometre and a half of river dropping a hundred metres into a gorge, twice the height of Niagara, and living beside it does not stop being remarkable. Hwange and Chobe are both within reach, the rafting below the falls is world class, and English is universal. The town is entirely a tourism economy and nothing else with the prices that implies, Zimbabwe's power and currency problems are constant background noise, there is no nomad community, and everything beyond the falls and the parks requires organising a trip. In high water the spray on the viewing path is heavy enough to soak a bag, which is worth knowing before walking down with a laptop in it.
victoriafalls.whoFor: Living beside one of the natural wonders of the world with a national park two hours away, for work that tolerates the power going off. Anything beyond a month or two starts to strain. This is a small town, and even a waterfall on this scale eventually stops stopping you in the street. Tourism pricing here applies to whoever is standing there, resident or not, which makes a tight budget difficult to hold. Reliable power is the other problem, and it is a national one rather than a local one. The UniVisa makes treating Livingstone as the same town entirely practical. It also works for anyone whose own work is seasonal, since the town follows the river and the low-water months are noticeably cheaper and quieter.

lusaka.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month as a solo remote worker in Lusaka, which is moderate for southern Africa. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $300 to $600, with Kabulonga, Rhodes Park and the areas around the embassies at the top of that and the townships far below. Food from the markets is inexpensive and Zambia grows its own maize, vegetables and beef. Imported goods carry a markup and fuel prices have been volatile. The kwacha has weakened substantially over the last decade, which is worth knowing when reading older figures. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs about $50 to $90 a month and a coworking desk $80 to $150. The line that dominates any budget here right now is backup power: a solar and battery system capable of carrying a working day costs $1,500 to $3,000 up front, and a property that already has one commands a premium worth paying rather than negotiating over. Diesel for a generator is the alternative and works out more expensive within months. Rents in Kabulonga and Sunningdale carry a premium for security and generator capacity rather than for the houses themselves.
lusaka.whereToWork: Lusaka's connectivity is reasonable: fibre reaches the better residential and commercial areas at workable speeds and mobile data from MTN, Airtel and Zamtel is widely used. The serious problem is electricity. Zambia depends on hydropower from Kariba, and the drought of 2024 pushed the country into load shedding measured in many hours a day, which is the single most important practical fact about working here right now. Anything serious runs on solar and batteries. There is a small coworking scene serving local startups. English is the official language and used throughout. Zambia sits two hours ahead of GMT, which gives a full European working day and a late-afternoon overlap with the American east coast. The Kariba shortfall is a structural problem rather than a bad year: the reservoir feeds both Zambia and Zimbabwe and its levels have been at or near record lows, so the rationing is expected to persist rather than resolve with one wet season.
lusaka.gettingAround: Lusaka spreads out along a few main arteries, with Cairo Road as the old commercial spine and the newer malls and offices scattered east and south. It is not a walkable city and the distances are real. Blue minibuses cover the routes cheaply and are how most people move, and ride-hailing works in the central areas. Most expatriates drive, on the left. Kenneth Kaunda airport is half an hour out with connections through Johannesburg, Nairobi, Addis Ababa and Dubai. South Luangwa, which invented the walking safari, is a long drive or a short flight east. South Luangwa is a nine-hour drive or a one-hour flight from Lusaka, and the Lower Zambezi is closer at around three hours by road. Both are seasonal, and the flights into the valley run to the camps' schedules rather than a public timetable. Traffic on the Great East Road at peak is severe enough that residents plan meetings around it rather than around distance.
lusaka.visas: Zambia removed visa requirements for citizens of a substantial list of countries in 2022, including the United Kingdom, most of the European Union and the United States, so many visitors now enter free for up to ninety days. Everyone else uses the e-visa system or obtains one on arrival. The KAZA UniVisa, covering Zambia and Zimbabwe for thirty days, is the practical option for anyone based around Livingstone. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a permit through employment or investment, applied for locally. Confirm the current list, since it has changed. The visa-free list is genuinely broad now and covers most of the countries this site's readers hold passports from, but it has been revised more than once since 2022 and airlines occasionally lag the policy, so carrying a printout of the current position is sensible. Anyone entering overland from Zimbabwe at Victoria Falls or Kazungula should ask for the UniVisa by name, since it is not always offered.
lusaka.bestTime: May to August is the cool dry season and the most comfortable, with daytime temperatures in the mid twenties at Lusaka's 1,280 metres and cold nights. September and October are hot and dry, reaching the mid thirties, and are also the best months for wildlife viewing as animals concentrate around the remaining water in South Luangwa. The wet season from November to April brings heavy afternoon storms and turns the country green, and many safari camps close entirely between January and March because the roads become impassable. Anyone planning a safari should note that the walking-safari season in South Luangwa runs roughly June to October and the camps simply close outside it. Kariba's water level is now part of the seasonal calculation as much as the rain is: a poor wet season means deeper load shedding through the following year, which is a planning factor for a stay rather than a background detail. Lusaka sits high enough that June and July nights drop to single figures, which surprises people who expect uniform African warmth.
lusaka.prosCons: Lusaka is a functional, safe-enough African capital with English throughout, a mild highland climate, and access to South Luangwa and the Lower Zambezi, two of the best and least crowded safari destinations on the continent. Costs are moderate and the country is politically stable by regional standards. The load shedding driven by the Kariba drought is severe and has been for over a year, the city itself is sprawling and hard to cross and short on character, there is no nomad community, and petty crime requires ordinary urban caution. The city is also the natural hub for the region, with better flight connections than Lilongwe, Harare or Gaborone and a more stable currency than Zimbabwe's. Zambia has been through several peaceful transfers of power at the ballot box, which is unusual enough in the region to be worth stating, and the 2021 election and the debt restructuring that followed are the context for the country's current economics.
lusaka.whoFor: Zambia as a base for the parks rather than for the capital, which needs English, a stable country, and an investment in solar and batteries before anything else. Anyone in conservation, mining or development will find real professional depth. Work that cannot survive a scheduled outage will struggle in a country where load shedding has run for hours at a stretch, and the city itself is spread out and functional rather than walkable or full of character. Treat Livingstone and the falls, six hours south, as the other half of what the country offers. Livingstone is smaller and prettier; Lusaka is where the work, the flights and the hospitals actually are. Mining and its supply chain are the professions this capital genuinely accommodates. Zambia is Africa's second-largest copper producer, and the Copperbelt's professional network is administered from here rather than from the mines themselves. Choosing between the two is really a choice between earning a living and looking at the country.

douala.costOfLiving: Budget around $950 a month as a solo remote worker in Douala, which is moderate for central Africa though the city is more expensive than its neighbours because it is the region's main port. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $300 to $600, with Bonapriso and Bonanjo at the top of that and the outer quarters well below. Food from the markets is cheap and Cameroonian cooking is among the best in the region. Imported goods carry a heavy markup. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, which removes currency volatility entirely. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The CFA peg is worth understanding properly: it is fixed to the euro at a rate that has not moved since 1999, which removes exchange risk against Europe entirely and means the currency does not absorb local shocks the way a floating one would. Fibre runs $50 to $100 a month for modest speeds, and a generator is a standard household cost rather than an unusual one.
douala.whereToWork: Douala's connectivity is workable rather than good: fibre reaches parts of the commercial districts, mobile data from MTN and Orange is the usual answer, and speeds are modest for the price. Power cuts are frequent and any serious office runs a generator. There is a small startup and coworking scene, more developed than the country's profile suggests, concentrated around Bonanjo and Akwa. French is the language of everything in Douala, which sits in the francophone Littoral region; English is Cameroon's other official language but you will not get far on it here. Cameroon sits one hour ahead of GMT, which puts it in the same working day as Europe and makes it one of the more convenient African bases for European clients. Mobile money through MTN and Orange handles most everyday payment, and a local SIM registered on arrival is the first practical step. Cocoa, timber and aluminium leave through this port, the smelter an hour south running on hydro power off the river, and the trading houses handling all of it are the commercial layer the city actually runs on.
douala.gettingAround: Douala is a large, hot, congested port city and it is not walkable in any meaningful sense. Yellow shared taxis are the standard way to move and cost very little, hailed by calling out your destination and a price. Motorcycle taxis, the bendskin, are faster and considerably more dangerous. Traffic is heavy and the rain floods the streets regularly. Douala airport has connections across Africa and to Paris and Brussels. Kribi, with beaches and the Lobe Falls that drop straight into the sea, is around three hours south and is the escape most residents take. The Wouri bridge is the single crossing between the port and the western districts and it is a bottleneck at both ends of the day. Douala's rain floods the low-lying quarters quickly and a heavy downpour can strand traffic for hours, which is a routine part of the wet season rather than an exceptional event.
douala.visas: Cameroon requires a visa of almost all visitors, and since 2023 an e-visa system has replaced most consular applications, issued for thirty or ninety days with an approval usually returned within days. A yellow fever certificate is required on entry. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a residence permit arranged through an employer or a local sponsor. Anyone planning travel beyond Douala should read current government advice carefully: the Far North faces a Boko Haram insurgency and the Northwest and Southwest regions have been in armed conflict since 2017. The e-visa is applied for online and collected on arrival, with the approval letter needed at check-in as well as at immigration, so it should be printed rather than left on a phone. Registration with the local authorities is expected for longer stays and is normally handled by an employer or a host. Photographing government buildings, bridges, the port or anybody in uniform is prohibited, and the rule is enforced rather than nominal, which is the single most common way a visitor here ends up in a long conversation with the police.
douala.bestTime: Douala sits just north of the equator on a wet coast and it is hot and humid all year, around thirty-one degrees with humidity that never drops. The calendar turns entirely on rain. December to February is the short dry season and by far the most comfortable window. The long rains from June to October are extraordinary: Douala is one of the wettest large cities in the world, and nearby Debundscha at the foot of Mount Cameroon is among the wettest places on earth. August is the peak and the city floods regularly. Debundscha, two hours west, records over ten metres of water in a year, and that number is what the long rains actually amount to along this stretch of coast. The short dry season in December and January is when anything outdoors is realistically planned. Humidity at this level attacks equipment rather than merely comfort: camera lenses grow fungus, leather goes green and a laptop shut in a cupboard for a fortnight comes out smelling of it. A dry box or a handful of silica packs earn their place in the luggage.
douala.prosCons: Douala is the economic engine of central Africa, with a port that serves several landlocked countries, a food culture that is among the continent's best, real business energy, and the euro-pegged CFA franc removing currency risk. Kribi's beaches and Mount Cameroon are within a few hours. The climate here is genuinely punishing, the city is congested and short on charm, French is essential to daily life, crime requires real caution, and the Anglophone conflict in the neighbouring Southwest region means the obvious excursions towards Buea and Limbe carry a security warning that should be read rather than assumed away. Mount Cameroon is an active volcano and West Africa's highest peak at just over 4,000 metres, with an annual race to the summit and back that is one of the hardest mountain races anywhere, though reaching it means the Southwest region and its current advisory.
douala.whoFor: A French speaker with business in central Africa needs the best flight connections in the region and its main port, and puts up with the heat and the congestion to get them. It is a working city rather than a destination. French is required and English will not substitute, the humidity is constant rather than seasonal, and this is a working port city rather than anywhere pleasant to sit for an afternoon with a laptop. Anyone planning to travel around Cameroon should read the current regional advisories properly before deciding where they can go. Anyone whose interest is Cameroon's landscape rather than its commerce should look at Yaounde or the west, since Douala is the port and behaves like one. Working across the CEMAC bloc effectively requires being here. The port and airport serve Chad, the Central African Republic and both Congos, which makes this the practical hub for a region that offers very few alternatives.

cotonou.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Cotonou, which is low even for West Africa. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $200 to $400, with Haie Vive and Cadjehoun, the districts around the embassies and the airport, at the top of that and the inland quarters well below. Food from the markets is very cheap and Beninese cooking is good, built on maize, cassava, peanut sauces and grilled fish from the lagoon. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, so there is no currency risk and no black market rate to navigate. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre where it reaches runs $60 to $120 a month for modest speeds, the standard West African internet penalty, and a generator or an inverter is a normal household cost rather than a contingency. A zemidjan ride across town is well under a dollar. The CFA peg has held at the same rate against the euro since 1999, which means a European income keeps its value here in a way it does not in Nigeria or Ghana next door. Rents in the inland quarters run at half what Haie Vive asks, and the gap buys proximity to the embassies rather than better building.
cotonou.whereToWork: Cotonou's connectivity is modest: fibre reaches parts of the city and mobile data from MTN and Moov is the usual answer, with prices high relative to speed as across West Africa. Power cuts are frequent and any serious business runs a generator. There is a small startup and coworking presence, helped by government efforts to position Benin as a digital services centre, though it serves locals rather than visitors. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, and English is genuinely rare, which is the main practical filter for working here. Benin runs on GMT+1 year-round, putting it in the same working day as continental Europe and an hour ahead of London, which is among the more convenient African time zones for European clients. Mobile money through MTN and Moov handles most everyday payment, and a local SIM registered on arrival is the first practical step. Sebou, the government digital services push, is why the coworking exists at all.
cotonou.gettingAround: Cotonou is flat, spread between the Atlantic and Lake Nokoue, and it is not a walkable city. Zemidjan motorcycle taxis, recognisable by their yellow shirts, are the dominant transport and cost very little, though they demand a helmet and some nerve. Shared taxis cover longer routes. Traffic on the main axes is heavy. Cotonou airport has connections across West Africa and to Paris and Brussels. Ganvie, the stilt village of some twenty thousand people built out on the lake, is half an hour away by boat, and Ouidah, the historic centre of the slave trade and of Vodun, is an hour west. The road east to Lagos is under two hours but the Seme border crossing can take considerably longer than the drive itself, and it has a reputation among overlanders that it has earned. The coastal highway west to Lome is faster and easier. Ganvie is reached by pirogue from Abomey-Calavi and the village has been on the lagoon since the seventeenth century, built there to escape slave raiders who could not follow onto water.
cotonou.visas: Benin has one of the most open visa policies in Africa: since 2019 it has been visa-free for all African nationals, and everyone else uses a straightforward e-visa applied for online, typically thirty or ninety days, approved within a few days. There is no remote work visa. A yellow fever certificate is required on entry. Longer stays run through a residence permit applied for locally. Benin is a member of ECOWAS, so travel to Togo, Nigeria and Ghana is straightforward for regional nationals and needs separate arrangements for everyone else. The e-visa is issued as an approval to be presented on arrival and airlines check it at boarding, so it should be printed rather than left on a phone. Benin's decision to drop visas for all African nationals was the first of its kind on the continent and remains among the most open positions anywhere.
cotonou.bestTime: November to February is the main dry season and by far the best window, with less humidity and daytime temperatures around thirty-one. The harmattan blows Saharan dust south in December and January, which drops visibility and irritates anyone with a respiratory sensitivity. The long rains run from April to July and a shorter wet spell returns in September and October. Coastal humidity is constant regardless of season. The Vodun festival on the tenth of January at Ouidah is the country's largest event and draws practitioners from across the diaspora. Pendjari National Park in the far north is only reliably reachable in the dry months, which is another reason the calendar matters here. Ouidah's beach holds the Door of No Return, a memorial arch on the sand at the end of the route enslaved people walked to the ships, and the annual festival brings visitors from Brazil, Haiti and the United States who trace their ancestry through it. The tenth of January is a public holiday.
cotonou.prosCons: Benin is where Vodun comes from, and it is a state religion here rather than a curiosity: the annual festival at Ouidah, the sacred forest at Kpasse and the Temple of Pythons are living practice. Ganvie on the lagoon is one of the most extraordinary settlements in Africa. Pendjari National Park in the north holds West Africa's best remaining wildlife. Costs are very low and the visa policy is open. French is essential, and the internet is weak, the power cuts are routine, and Cotonou itself is a hot, congested working city rather than an attractive one. The Royal Palaces of Abomey, ninety minutes north, were the seat of the Kingdom of Dahomey and are a UNESCO site, and the bas-reliefs there record the kingdom's history in a way almost nothing else in the region does.
cotonou.whoFor: An interest in West African history and religion, French, and work that survives unreliable power, in exchange for a very cheap base with an open visa policy. Anyone researching the slave trade, Vodun or the region's art will find Benin unusually rich. French is not optional, the infrastructure is unreliable in ways that shape a working week, and anybody picturing a beach city should know that the undertow along this coast makes swimming genuinely dangerous rather than merely discouraged. Ouidah and Ganvie are the reasons to be here rather than Cotonou itself. Anybody moving overland between Lagos and Accra passes through Benin, and this is the calmest place to stop along that road, which counts for a good deal after either of the cities at its ends. The restitution question is being settled here rather than debated in the abstract. France returned twenty-six royal treasures to Benin in 2021, and the museum built to hold them has made this city the live case that the whole argument now cites. Compared with Lome, Cotonou is larger, busier and has the more open visa policy, while Lome has the better beach and the calmer centre.

mahe.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month as a solo remote worker on Mahe, which makes Seychelles one of the more expensive places in this batch and reflects an island nation that imports almost everything. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,400, with Beau Vallon and the northwest coast at the top of that and the areas around Victoria and the south considerably cheaper. Self-catering is what keeps a budget here in one piece: restaurant prices are set for resort guests, while the market in Victoria and the local takeaways are a different economy entirely. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Electricity is a real line item on an island where almost everything runs on imported fuel, and air conditioning through the warmer months is what separates a comfortable budget from a tight one. Car hire is the largest discretionary cost most people meet here and can rival rent if it runs all month. Guesthouses will usually quote a monthly rate well below their nightly one if you ask directly, which is the single most effective thing a long-stay visitor can do about the cost of being here. Fish bought at the market is cheap; anything imported, from cheese to wine, is emphatically not.
mahe.whereToWork: Seychelles has better connectivity than its remoteness suggests: the country is served by submarine cable and fibre reaches most of Mahe at workable speeds, with mobile data from Cable and Wireless and Airtel covering the island. Prices are high. Power is reliable. There is very little coworking, so remote work happens from guesthouses and self-catering apartments. English is one of three official languages alongside French and Seychellois Creole, and it is used throughout government and business, which makes the country straightforward to operate in. Anyone working with Europe will find the offset convenient, since Seychelles sits two hours ahead of central European time for most of the year. A local SIM is worth buying on arrival rather than roaming, since data bundles are the cheapest part of the telecoms bill here and coverage follows the coast road closely. Anyone whose income depends on being reachable should keep a second SIM on the other network, because a single outage on a small island has nowhere to fail over to. Calls with North America are awkward from this longitude, landing either very early or very late, so the working day realistically points at Europe, the Gulf and East Africa instead.
mahe.gettingAround: Mahe is about twenty-seven kilometres long with a mountainous spine, and Victoria, the smallest capital in Africa, sits on its northeast coast. Buses cover the island cheaply and frequently, and the network genuinely works, which is unusual for a small island and means a car is optional rather than essential. The coastal roads are narrow and the cross-island routes steep. The airport is ten minutes from Victoria with direct flights to Dubai, Doha, Addis Ababa, Paris and Nairobi. Ferries run to Praslin and La Digue, the other main islands, in about an hour. Traffic drives on the left, a legacy of British administration, and the roads are well surfaced but genuinely tight in places, with buses taking their half of the width out of the middle. The bus network thins out after the early evening, so anyone planning a night in Victoria should agree a taxi in advance rather than assume one will appear. Most of the interior belongs to Morne Seychellois National Park and is reached on foot, and several of the best walks start from the cross-island road rather than the coast, which makes the bus a reasonable trailhead shuttle.
mahe.visas: Seychelles has the most open border policy in the world: it requires no visa of any nationality. Every visitor receives a visitor's permit on arrival, initially for up to three months, extendable up to a total of twelve months in any year on payment of a fee, provided you can show accommodation, means and a return ticket. There is no separate remote work visa because the ordinary permit already does the job. It is not a residence permit and does not allow working for a Seychellois employer, which is the one limit worth understanding. Seychelles requires an online Travel Authorisation, applied for and paid in advance, and airlines check it at boarding, so the absence of a visa is not the absence of paperwork. Extensions are handled at the immigration office in Victoria and are granted in blocks rather than all at once, with the fee rising at each renewal, so a twelve-month stay means several visits and a growing cost. Bring evidence of funds and onward travel to each one, since the same conditions are reassessed every time.
mahe.bestTime: Seychelles is warm all year, around twenty-nine degrees every month, and the calendar is set by two trade winds. The southeast trades from May to September bring cooler, windier, drier weather, better hiking and good conditions for sailing, though seaweed collects on some southeastern beaches. The northwest trades from November to March bring warmer, calmer, wetter weather with the best diving visibility and the flattest sea. April and October are the transition months and the most settled of all. The islands sit outside the cyclone belt, which is a real advantage in this ocean. Rain here usually arrives as a heavy shower that clears rather than a day lost, even in the wetter months, which is worth knowing before writing off December to February. Prices follow the European holidays rather than the weather: Christmas and the New Year, then July and August, are when flights and guesthouses cost the most and book out first. Whale sharks pass the west coast around September and October, and hawksbill turtles nest on the beaches from roughly October to February, so the quieter shoulder months carry most of the wildlife worth planning around.
mahe.prosCons: Seychelles has the granite boulder beaches that appear on every list of the world's best, an interior of mountain rainforest with the Vallee de Mai on Praslin holding the coco de mer palm found nowhere else, giant tortoises, and no visa requirement for anyone on earth. English works everywhere and the country is safe. Prices are high, the islands are small and quickly exhausted, and nobody else has come here to work, and the economy is so dominated by high-end tourism that the middle of the market barely exists. Prices also vary far more by island than visitors expect, with La Digue and Praslin costing noticeably more than the south of Mahe. Healthcare is adequate for ordinary problems, but anything serious means an evacuation flight, which is worth insuring for properly rather than assuming. And getting here is expensive from almost everywhere, with the cheaper fares concentrated on a handful of Gulf and East African carriers, so the cost of a stay is decided as much by the flight as by the nightly rate once you arrive.
mahe.whoFor: Extraordinary beaches and hiking with no visa paperwork at all, for somebody who will self-cater rather than eat out. The twelve-month extendable permit is quietly one of the most generous arrangements anywhere for a long stay. Seychelles prices defeat a tight budget within the first week, and the professional community here is tourism and fisheries or it is nothing at all. Anyone staying a while should use the bus network and rent in the south rather than the northwest, which is where the price difference on this island actually lies. Anybody who has been refused a visa somewhere else should know that Seychelles is the only country on earth that requires one of nobody at all, whatever passport they happen to hold. It rewards a particular kind of stay: solitary, focused work broken by water, which is why writers, divers and sailors tend to get more out of Mahe than most. The islands are safe and everything runs in English, which removes most of what makes a move hard with children. Anyone who needs a city, a scene, or somewhere new to go every weekend will run out of island faster than they expect, and the onward flights are too expensive to treat as a casual escape.

apia.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Apia, which is moderate for the Pacific and lower than most of the region's capitals. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700. Food from the market at Maketi Fou is cheap and Samoa grows taro, breadfruit and bananas in quantity; imported goods carry the heavy markup that every Pacific island pays for freight. The tala is stable. Fales, the open-sided beach huts let by families along the south coast, are a genuinely cheap way to stay outside the capital. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Imported goods carry the Pacific freight premium and most of what is not grown locally arrives from New Zealand, which sets the price of everything in the supermarkets. Fibre where available runs $60 to $120 a month. The Samoan custom of fa'alavelave, contributions to family and church obligations, shapes the local economy in ways a visitor does not pay into but will notice in how money moves here.
apia.whereToWork: Samoa's connectivity improved substantially with the Tui-Samoa submarine cable in 2018, and fibre now reaches Apia at speeds that work, though prices are high and coverage thins outside the capital. Mobile data from Digicel and Vodafone covers the populated coast. Power cuts happen. There is essentially no coworking. English is an official language alongside Samoan and is used throughout government and business. Samoa moved across the international date line in 2011 to align with Australia and New Zealand, so it now sits a day ahead of American Samoa two hours away. Working hours here align naturally with Auckland, which is where most of Samoa's business and diaspora connections run, and with Brisbane and Sydney an hour or two behind that. Anyone whose clients are in Europe or North America is looking at a genuinely inverted day rather than an awkward overlap, which is the single biggest practical filter on basing here. Most of the land in this country is held under customary title by extended families rather than owned outright, and it cannot be bought by anybody at all, which is why long leases are the only arrangement available and why the decision sits with a family council rather than with an individual.
apia.gettingAround: Apia runs along a harbour on the north coast of Upolu and its centre is walkable, with the market, the flag-tiled Immaculate Conception cathedral and the waterfront all within twenty minutes. Brightly painted wooden buses cover the island cheaply on no fixed timetable and are an experience in themselves. Most residents drive, and Samoa switched from driving on the right to the left in 2009, which makes it one of very few countries ever to have done so. Faleolo airport is forty minutes west with flights to Auckland, Fiji and Sydney. The ferry to Savaii takes ninety minutes. They have no fixed stops either. A passenger waves one down from the roadside and pays the driver on the way out, which is worth knowing before standing hopefully at what looks like a stop. To Sua Ocean Trench on the south coast and the Piula cave pool are the two trips most visitors make, both around an hour from Apia by road.
apia.visas: Samoa grants a free entry permit on arrival to citizens of most countries for up to ninety days, which is generous and requires only a passport, onward ticket and proof of accommodation. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for locally through the immigration office. Longer stays require a work or residence permit with local sponsorship. The simplicity of entry is one of Samoa's practical advantages over several of its Pacific neighbours, where the paperwork is heavier and the fees higher. Anyone island-hopping should note that American Samoa, two hours away by air, is United States territory and needs its own separate permission. Samoa grants a sixty-day entry permit free on arrival to most nationalities, which is longer than most Pacific states offer, and it is extendable in-country. Anyone arriving by yacht clears in at Apia, which is the only port of entry, and the Apia Marina is small enough that a berth should be arranged in advance.
apia.bestTime: May to October is the dry season and the comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine, lower humidity and the calmest seas. November to April is the wet season and also the cyclone season, and Samoa sits in the belt; the islands have taken serious hits, most memorably Cyclone Evan in 2012. The 2009 tsunami, caused by an offshore earthquake, killed nearly two hundred people on the south coast, and evacuation routes are marked there for good reason. Independence celebrations at the start of June are the biggest event of the year. Sunday observance is close to absolute in Samoa: villages hold a curfew for evening prayer, shops close, and travelling through a village during sa is a genuine breach rather than an inconvenience. Planning a week here means planning around it. Samoa jumped the date line at the end of 2011 and skipped the thirtieth of December entirely, moving from the last place on earth to see each day to the first, which put the country back on the same working calendar as Australia and New Zealand. The territory forty kilometres away did not follow.
apia.prosCons: Samoa is where fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, still orders daily life more visibly than tradition does almost anywhere: village councils, Sunday observance that closes the country, and a formality of manner that visitors notice within a day. The To Sua ocean trench, the Piula cave pool and the waterfalls of the south coast are remarkable, and Robert Louis Stevenson's house above Apia is a genuinely good museum. It is remote, it is expensive to reach, the internet is adequate rather than good, and Sunday closure catches out anyone who has not planned for it. The 2009 tsunami struck the south coast hard and the rebuilt villages and the memorials along that shore are part of what a visitor sees. Samoa also has one of the highest rates of land held under customary title anywhere, around eighty per cent, which means almost nothing here is bought and sold in the way a foreigner might expect.
apia.whoFor: A Pacific base with real cultural depth rather than a resort, for anyone comfortable with a slow pace and a country that stops entirely on Sundays. The ninety-day free entry makes a long stay unusually simple. Fast internet is not on offer this far into the Pacific, the nightlife amounts to a few venues, and any professional network has to arrive with you rather than be found on landing. Anyone coming should read a little about fa'a Samoa first, since the social rules here are more visible and more consequential than in most places visitors go. Savaii is the reason a lot of people end up staying. The larger and far quieter island has the lava fields and the blowholes, and hardly anybody crosses the strait to see them. A Polynesian base with a functioning capital behind it is a narrower proposition than it sounds. Apia has hospitals, flights and supermarkets that most of the region's smaller centres simply cannot offer, which is the difference between a posting and a stay.

nukualofa.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Nuku'alofa, which is moderate for the Pacific. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $350 to $650. Food from the Talamahu market is cheap and Tonga grows root crops, coconut and fruit in quantity, but almost everything else is imported and the freight cost shows on every shelf. The pa'anga is stable and remittances from Tongans abroad are a substantial part of the economy. Prices rose after the 2022 eruption and have not fully settled. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Imported staples carry the freight premium most visibly: a box of cereal or a block of cheese can cost several times what it would in Auckland, which is where most of it arrives from. Land here cannot be bought by anybody, foreigner or not: it belongs to the Crown and is held under a traditional allocation, so a long lease is the only arrangement on offer and the terms are settled with a noble estate rather than with an owner. Renting a house is straightforward enough, but any longer plan runs into that wall early. Kava circles in the evening are the standard social outing and cost next to nothing.
nukualofa.whereToWork: Connectivity is the honest weak point of a stay here. The country depends on a single submarine cable, and when the Hunga Tonga eruption severed it in January 2022 the entire nation was cut off from the internet for weeks. The cable has been repaired and a backup arrangement exists, but the vulnerability is structural. Fibre reaches parts of Nuku'alofa and mobile data from Digicel and TCC is the fallback. Power cuts happen. There is no coworking. English is an official language alongside Tongan and is widely used. Tonga sits thirteen hours ahead of GMT and is among the first places on earth to see each date, which puts a European afternoon in the Tongan small hours and makes European work close to impossible.
