A large share of the working-age population spends part of each year picking fruit in New Zealand or Australia under seasonal labour schemes, and the money that comes back is what builds the houses going up everywhere. That pattern shapes who is around and when. For an outsider it means an unusual amount of familiarity with life abroad, and very little curiosity about what a visitor does for a living.
nukualofa.gettingAround: Nuku'alofa sits on the north coast of Tongatapu, a flat coral island, and the centre around the market and the waterfront is walkable. Minibuses cover the island cheaply on loose schedules and taxis are inexpensive. Most residents drive, on the left. Fua'amotu airport is thirty minutes south with flights to Auckland, Sydney and Fiji. Ferries and small aircraft reach Vava'u and Ha'apai, the northern island groups, and Vava'u is where the sailing and most of the whale swimming happens, which is what brings most visitors to the country at all. Nothing runs on Sunday. The Sabbath is written into Tongan law, so ferries, buses, shops and most flights stop, and a week has to be planned around it rather than through it. A road runs right around the island and the circuit takes a couple of hours with stops, which is the standard way to see it: blowholes on the south coast that fire spray through the reef for a kilometre at a time, and trilithon stones inland older than anything else in this ocean. The surface away from the capital is rough, and a hire car takes longer over it than the distance implies.
nukualofa.visas: Tonga grants a visitor's visa on arrival to citizens of most countries for thirty-one days, free of charge, extendable in-country up to six months for a fee. It is simple and requires a passport, onward ticket and proof of accommodation. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a business or residence visa with local sponsorship. Anyone planning to swim with humpbacks should know that the activity is licensed and regulated, and that operating outside a licensed tour is not permitted. Anyone arriving by yacht should clear in at Nuku'alofa, Vava'u or Ha'apai, since those are the designated ports of entry for the kingdom. Extensions are granted a month at a time at the immigration office in Nuku'alofa, so a six-month stay means returning several times rather than applying once.
nukualofa.bestTime: May to October is the dry, cooler season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-six and lower humidity. It also contains the reason most people come: humpback whales migrate to Tongan waters to calve between roughly July and October, and Tonga is one of a very small number of places in the world where swimming with them is legal and regulated. November to April is the wet season and the cyclone season, and Tonga is exposed. The Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai eruption and tsunami of January 2022 was among the most violent volcanic events ever recorded. Whale season also sets the accommodation market: Vava'u fills from July and the good operators are booked months ahead, so a trip timed for the humpbacks needs arranging well in advance. The kingdom marks the monarch's birthday with a week of parades, dancing and a pageant in the middle of the year, and it is the largest thing in the national calendar by a distance. Preparing for cyclones is an ordinary seasonal chore rather than an emergency response, with shutters going up and water put by as a matter of course.
nukualofa.prosCons: Tonga is the only Pacific nation never colonised, still a kingdom, and the sense of a country running on its own terms is immediate. Swimming with humpback whales in Vava'u between July and October is something almost nowhere else permits. The Ha'apai group has genuinely empty islands. The internet is fragile in a way that has already cut the country off once, the infrastructure is limited across the board, there is very little to do in Nuku'alofa itself, Sunday closes everything by law, and the cyclone and volcanic exposure are real. Tonga is also low-lying and its exposure to sea level rise is not a distant concern here but a live subject of national policy, which shapes a good deal of the conversation on the islands.
nukualofa.whoFor: Nuku'alofa suits someone whose reason for coming is the whales, the sailing in Vava'u or the empty islands of Ha'apai, and who treats the capital as the way in rather than the destination. Work that tolerates an unreliable connection is close to a requirement. A call-heavy schedule and Tongan bandwidth are a poor match, nightlife is thin, and the country closes on Sundays by law rather than by custom, which is a real constraint on a working week and catches people out. Time the trip for the whale season or the case for coming weakens considerably. It also suits sailors, since Vava'u is one of the great cruising grounds of the Pacific and has a charter fleet to match. Anyone considering a longer stay should treat the single cable as the planning constraint it is, and keep work that can be done offline for the weeks when it cannot.

rarotonga.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker on Rarotonga, which is expensive for the Pacific and reflects an island that uses the New Zealand dollar and imports from New Zealand. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200. Groceries carry the freight cost that every remote island pays, and the difference between shopping at the Punanga Nui market on a Saturday and shopping at a supermarket is substantial. There is no local income tax on foreign earnings. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Fibre runs about $80 to $150 a month, which is the price of a small island buying its bandwidth wholesale, and it is the single line most people find steeper than expected. Scooter hire is around $150 a month and a car double that. Eating out is expensive outside the Muri night markets and the Saturday market, where a plate of ika mata, raw fish cured in lime and coconut cream, costs a few dollars and is what most residents eat. Rentals are found through noticeboards and word of mouth rather than listing sites, and a month's stay is usually cheaper arranged after arrival than before it.
rarotonga.whereToWork: The Cook Islands are served by the Manatua submarine cable, completed in 2020, which transformed connectivity from satellite-dependent to genuinely workable, and fibre now reaches most of Rarotonga at reasonable speeds. Prices are high. Mobile data from Vodafone Cook Islands covers the island. Power is reliable and increasingly solar. There is a small amount of coworking. English is an official language alongside Cook Islands Maori and is used everywhere. Rarotonga sits ten hours behind London and is a day behind New Zealand despite being two hours ahead of it in clock terms, which confuses everybody. The date-line confusion is worth stating plainly: Rarotonga is ten hours behind GMT and sits on the same side of the line as Hawaii, so when it is Monday morning in Auckland it is still Sunday afternoon here. Anyone coordinating with New Zealand is working a day apart on the calendar even though the clock difference is small. The Manatua cable links Rarotonga to Niue, Samoa, French Polynesia and on to the wider network, and it is the single change that moved the Cook Islands from impossible to workable for remote work within the last five years.
rarotonga.gettingAround: Rarotonga is thirty-two kilometres around and has exactly one ring road, which two buses circle all day: one clockwise, one anticlockwise, and that is the entire public transport system. It works. Scooters are the common rental and a local licence is issued at the police station, which used to involve a practical test and has become a formality. Cycling the ring road is easy and flat. The interior is mountainous and crossed by the Cross-Island Track past the Needle. The airport is on the ring road with flights to Auckland, Sydney and, seasonally, Los Angeles and Tahiti. The Cross-Island Track takes about four hours from Avatiu to Wigmore's Waterfall and is genuinely steep and slippery rather than a stroll. Aitutaki is fifty minutes by air and its lagoon is the one that appears in most photographs attributed to the Cook Islands.
rarotonga.visas: The Cook Islands grant thirty-one days on arrival to citizens of most countries with no visa and no fee, extendable in-country month by month up to six months for a modest charge. New Zealand citizens have open access. Cook Islanders hold New Zealand passports, since the country is in free association with New Zealand. There is no remote work visa, but the extendable thirty-one day permit does the same job with less paperwork than most schemes. Longer stays require a permit through employment or business. Anyone extending should do it before the permit lapses rather than after, since the immigration office treats an overstay far less lightly than the easy entry suggests. Extensions are handled at the immigration office in Avarua and cost a modest fee each month, which makes six months here considerably cheaper and simpler than most formal nomad visas elsewhere in the Pacific.
rarotonga.bestTime: April to November is the dry season and the comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-six, low humidity and the calmest lagoon. December to March is the wet season and the cyclone season, and while the Cook Islands are hit less often than Vanuatu or Fiji, the exposure is real. The shoulder months of April, May, October and November are the best combination of weather and price. The Te Maeva Nui festival at the start of August, marking self-government, is the largest cultural event of the year and worth timing around. Te Maeva Nui runs for about a week around the fourth of August and every island in the group sends a performing team, which makes it the one time the whole country is visibly in one place. Humpback whales pass Rarotonga between July and October and are often visible from the shore on the southern coast, which is an unusually easy way to see them without a boat.
rarotonga.prosCons: Rarotonga has one of the most beautiful lagoons in the Pacific at Muri, a mountainous green interior you can walk across in a morning, no building taller than a coconut palm by law, and a genuinely safe, easy, English-speaking society running on New Zealand dollars. The submarine cable made working here possible. It is expensive and very small, with no remote-working scene here at all, the choice of anything at all is limited by the size of the island, and getting here means Auckland for almost everyone. The law capping building height at a coconut palm is also the reason the island looks the way it does, and it is enforced. Land in the Cook Islands cannot be sold to foreigners and is held under customary title, leased rather than bought, which is why the island has no resort development of the scale seen in Fiji and why it looks as it does. Power runs on a mix of diesel and a large solar installation, and the island has been working toward full renewable generation for years, which for a country of seventeen thousand people is an unusually concrete commitment.
rarotonga.whoFor: An easy, safe, English-speaking Pacific island where the paperwork is trivial and the lagoon is the reason to be there. Anyone working New Zealand or Australian hours will find the time zone awkward but the flights simple. Most people find one or two months is the honest answer, even though the permit will stretch to six. Variety runs out on an island this size, there is no professional network beyond tourism, and importing everything across the Pacific keeps costs a long way above low. Aitutaki, an hour north by air, has the lagoon that Rarotonga is often mistaken for. Children do unusually well here. Rarotonga can be learned in a week, its crime rate is low enough to stop thinking about, and the lagoon around it stays shallow in a way very few Pacific destinations manage. New Zealand citizens have an advantage nobody else does: under the free association arrangement they can live and work here without asking anyone's permission at all. Fiji is the comparison, and the trade is far smaller, considerably safer, easier paperwork and no domestic flight network to speak of beyond Aitutaki.

papeete.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Papeete, which makes French Polynesia one of the most expensive places in this batch and among the most expensive in the Pacific. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,200 to $1,900. The cost of imported food is the standing local grievance and has driven protests more than once; a supermarket shop costs far more than in mainland France, which is where much of it comes from. The CFP franc is pegged to the euro. Eating from the roulottes, the food trucks that fill the waterfront at dusk, is the way locals manage it. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Local produce is the exception that makes a budget work. Fish, breadfruit, taro and tropical fruit bought at the market or from roadside stalls cost a fraction of the imported equivalent, and a diet built around them is a different financial proposition from one built around the supermarket. Electricity is expensive. Long leases work out cheaper per month than anything advertised to visitors, and rents fall noticeably away from the Papeete side of the island, which is part of why so many people commute.
papeete.whereToWork: French Polynesia is served by the Honotua and Natitua submarine cables, which give Tahiti connectivity well above the Pacific norm, and fibre reaches Papeete at good speeds. Prices are high. Mobile data from Vini and Vodafone covers the populated coast. Power is reliable. There is a small amount of coworking in Papeete. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, with Tahitian widely spoken; English is limited outside the tourism industry, which is the main practical filter here. Tahiti sits ten hours behind Paris, which is an awkward overlap with France. The offset that does work runs toward the Americas. Tahiti sits close to the United States west coast in time, which makes a Californian working day entirely manageable from here and is the single most useful scheduling fact about the territory. Business structures are French, so anyone already registered as a freelancer in France can operate here without reinventing anything. Connectivity drops away sharply outside Tahiti and Moorea, and while the Natitua cable has reached parts of the Tuamotus and Marquesas, an outer-island stay should be planned as a low-bandwidth one.
papeete.gettingAround: Papeete sits on the northwest coast of Tahiti and its centre, around the market and the waterfront, is walkable. Le Truck buses and their modern replacements cover the island's coastal road cheaply. Most residents drive and traffic into Papeete at peak is genuinely bad for a city this size. The ferry to Moorea takes thirty minutes and runs constantly, which is why many people who work in Papeete live there instead. Faa'a airport is on the edge of the city with flights to Paris, Los Angeles, Auckland, Tokyo and the outer archipelagos. Tahiti is really two islands joined at an isthmus, and the road rings the larger one in about four hours of easy driving, passing the surf at Teahupoo on the smaller. Inter-island flights are the main cost of exploring the territory and they add up quickly, which is why the Aranui, the mixed cargo and passenger ship serving the Marquesas, remains a genuinely popular way to reach the far archipelagos. Cycling the coast road is a pleasure outside the Papeete rush hour and thoroughly unpleasant inside it.
papeete.visas: French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France but is not in the Schengen area, so Schengen rules and Schengen day counts do not apply here. European Union citizens have freedom of movement and can live and work without a permit. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. There is no dedicated remote work visa. Longer stays for non-EU citizens run through a French long-stay visa applied for before travel, and the process is the French one, which is thorough. The separation from Schengen is the detail that catches people out in both directions. Both directions are worth spelling out, since that sentence hides the two mistakes people actually make. A Schengen visa does not admit you here, and a French visa has to be endorsed for French Polynesia specifically, which is checked at boarding rather than on arrival. Meanwhile time spent here does not consume a Schengen allowance, which makes the territory useful as a genuine pause for anyone managing that clock. For Europeans, freedom of movement covers residence, while some local employment is subject to territorial preference rules protecting the local labour market.
papeete.bestTime: May to October is the dry season and the comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, lower humidity and the calmest water. November to April is the wet season, hotter and more humid, with the cyclone risk concentrated in January and February, though French Polynesia is hit less often than the western Pacific. July is the Heiva festival, a month of dance and sport competitions that is the cultural event of the year and fills accommodation across the islands. Humpback whales pass between roughly August and October. Anyone planning the Tuamotus should also know that the diving there peaks with the grouper aggregation at Fakarava in June and July. The surf follows the opposite pattern to the tourism. The southern swells that make Teahupoo what it is arrive between roughly May and September, which happens to coincide with the dry season and the crowds. The wet months are the value window, with lower fares and emptier hotels, and the rain typically arriving as afternoon downpours rather than lost days. Anyone flexible on timing gets substantially more island for the money between November and March.
papeete.prosCons: Tahiti is the gateway to 118 islands across five archipelagos, with Moorea thirty minutes away by ferry, Bora Bora and the Tuamotu atolls beyond, and some of the best diving in the world at Fakarava and Rangiroa. The connectivity is unusually good for the Pacific and the French administration means the infrastructure works. The cost of living here is severe, French is close to necessary in practice, Papeete itself is a busy port city that most visitors pass through rather than stay in, and everything beyond Tahiti costs another flight. The cost of living has also been a live political issue for years, and the protests over food prices are a recurring feature rather than a one-off. France conducted nearly two hundred nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa between 1966 and 1996, and the health and compensation consequences are still a subject of active political argument here. On the practical side, healthcare in the capital is French-standard, which is a genuine and unusual advantage this far into the Pacific.
papeete.whoFor: The Pacific with functioning infrastructure, for a French speaker, ideally an EU citizen who can stay without a permit, and who can absorb the prices. Divers get more from the Tuamotus than from almost anywhere on earth. Nothing here is transacted in English, Polynesian prices will overwhelm a budget quickly, and anybody who pictured Bora Bora has confused the postcard with the capital: this is a working city of traffic, container ships and a very large port. Most people who stay a while end up living on Moorea and commuting by ferry. A European passport removes the visa problem that makes most Pacific bases awkward, and the combination of French Polynesia with EU documents is rarer and more useful than it first appears. Sailors are the other group who belong here, since Tahiti is the great crossroads of the Pacific crossing and the harbour fills each season with boats making the passage. Anyone comparing Pacific bases will find Hawaii better connected and cheaper to reach from North America, Fiji cheaper outright, and French Polynesia unmatched for the water itself. It rewards months rather than weeks, because the cost of getting here is only justified by staying a while.

basseterre.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in Basseterre, which is mid-range for the Eastern Caribbean. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $600 to $1,000, with Frigate Bay and the areas near the beaches at the top of that and the streets behind the capital well below. The islands import most of their food and the markup shows, though the Saturday market and the local fish are cheap. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar, so budgeting needs no conversion. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Ross University's veterinary school sits on the island and brings around a thousand American students through it at a time, which distorts the rental market more than anything else does: the apartments near Frigate Bay are built and priced for them, leases run on their semester calendar, and a foreigner arriving in January competes with an intake. Arriving between terms is cheaper and easier. It also means American groceries, American-style clinics and a supply chain aimed at people who expect them, which lifts both the floor on prices and the standard of what is available.
basseterre.whereToWork: Saint Kitts has reasonable connectivity for its size: fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches Basseterre, Frigate Bay and the developed south at workable speeds, and mobile data covers the island. There is very little formal coworking, so remote work happens from apartments and a handful of cafes. Power cuts are occasional rather than routine. English is the only language required. The federation sits four hours behind central European time and one ahead of New York in the northern winter, which gives a usable overlap in both directions. The cruise terminal at Port Zante brings several thousand people ashore on ship days, which changes how busy the centre feels from one morning to the next. Nevis has been drilling for geothermal power for years and sits on a genuine resource, with the ambition of running both islands on it and exporting the surplus. Progress has been slower than every announcement suggested. For a remote worker the relevance is the grid: power here is expensive and diesel-fired, which is why an outage costs a business real money and why the better rentals advertise a generator rather than mentioning it in passing.
basseterre.gettingAround: Basseterre is small and its centre around the Circus and Independence Square is walkable in twenty minutes. Minibuses cover the island cheaply and frequently along the coastal road, and they are the practical way to move. Driving is on the left and a local permit is required. The Saint Kitts Scenic Railway, built to carry sugar cane and now running a tourist circuit, is the last operating railway in the West Indies. A ferry crosses to Nevis in around forty-five minutes, several times a day. Nevis is a separate island with its own administration and its own rhythm, and the crossing is cheap enough to make a day there routine. The monkeys are not a novelty item. Vervets were brought by French settlers in the seventeenth century and now outnumber people on Saint Kitts, they raid crops and gardens across the island, and a rental car parked with a window down will be entered. The coastal road also passes Bloody Point, where English and French settlers together killed around two thousand Kalinago in 1626, an event the place name has carried for four hundred years without softening.
basseterre.visas: Saint Kitts and Nevis has no dedicated remote work visa. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days, with British and Commonwealth citizens often receiving longer, and extensions applied for locally at the immigration department. The federation runs the oldest citizenship by investment programme in the world, launched in 1984, which is a substantial and separate decision rather than a nomad route and should be researched independently of the agents who market it. Anyone planning a long stay should ask for the maximum on arrival. Anyone moving between the two islands should note that Nevis has its own immigration desk at the ferry terminal, though it is a formality for a visitor. Nevis is not simply the smaller island. It has its own assembly and premier, it holds powers Saint Kitts does not exercise over it, and it voted on leaving the federation in 1998, where sixty two per cent backed secession against a two thirds threshold. The arrangement has held since, but that separate desk at the ferry is a trace of something real rather than an administrative habit.
basseterre.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, lower humidity and the calmest sea, and it is when prices peak. May to November is hotter and wetter, and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Saint Kitts sits within the belt though it has been struck less often than several of its neighbours. Sugar Mas, the national carnival, runs from mid-December into early January rather than before Lent, which is unusual in the region and worth knowing. The rainforest interior is walkable year-round, and the crater at the top of Mount Liamuiga is a hard day out in any season. Hurricane exposure here is a matter of record rather than reassurance: Georges in 1998 and Hugo in 1989 both hit hard, and Irma and Maria in 2017 passed close enough to be felt without landing. Building codes tightened after Georges and it shows in what has gone up since. For a long stay the practical planning is insurance that covers named storms, an evacuation position agreed with a landlord, and an understanding that the airport closes before a storm rather than during it.
basseterre.prosCons: Saint Kitts has Brimstone Hill Fortress, a UNESCO World Heritage site and the most complete surviving fortification of its kind in the Americas, a working scenic railway, a rainforest interior below a dormant volcano, and Nevis forty-five minutes across the channel with its own peak and its own pace. It is quiet and safe by regional standards. There is no remote work visa, nobody else is working here remotely, and the island can be exhausted inside a month, and the economy leans heavily on cruise arrivals and citizenship sales. The closure of the sugar industry in 2005 also ended two centuries of the island's economy in a single year, which is visible in the abandoned estates. Saint Kitts was the first English colony in the Caribbean and the first French one at the same time, the two powers dividing a single small island between them in the 1620s, which is why it was called the mother colony of the West Indies and why the place names alternate between two languages along one road. Almost every other island in the region was settled from here.
basseterre.whoFor: A genuinely quiet Eastern Caribbean base with real history and easy English, for anyone content with ninety days rather than a year. The Nevis ferry makes a two-island stay practical, which is unusual. Neither a long-stay visa nor a professional network exists on the island, so a year here has to be assembled from ninety-day stays and colleagues who live somewhere else. Held up against Antigua or Barbados, Saint Kitts is smaller, calmer and less organised for visitors than either. Caribbean industrial history is unusually legible on this island. The railway, the abandoned estates and the fortress above them tell the sugar story end to end rather than in fragments. The vet school is the one substantial international institution on the island, and having a reason to be inside it is the difference between arriving with colleagues and arriving with only neighbours. It suits a reader of the American founding, since Alexander Hamilton was born on Nevis and the house is a museum, and Nelson married there in 1787. Anybody expecting a year should look at the ninety days twice, because there is no mechanism to extend that into a residence and the citizenship programme is a different order of decision entirely.

kingstown.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Kingstown, which makes Saint Vincent one of the cheaper Eastern Caribbean islands. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $450 to $800, and the Grenadines are a different economy entirely, with Mustique and Canouan priced for people who arrive by private aircraft. Saint Vincent grows a great deal of its own produce and the Kingstown market is genuinely cheap. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Electricity is expensive and diesel-generated, though the country has geothermal ambitions that have not yet arrived. Imported goods carry both freight and duty, so anything from a laptop to a jar of pasta sauce costs noticeably more than the rent would suggest, while local fish, breadfruit, mangoes and root vegetables are cheap enough to change a monthly figure if you cook from them. Budget for the ferries as well, since a habit of weekending down the chain adds up faster than most people expect. Rentals are usually unfurnished, with a deposit and a month up front.
kingstown.whereToWork: Connectivity in Saint Vincent is adequate rather than good: fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches Kingstown and the developed south at workable speeds, and mobile data covers the main island and the larger Grenadines. There is essentially no coworking. Power cuts happen and the 2021 volcanic eruption disrupted supply across the north of the island for months. English is the only language required. Anyone planning to work from Bequia or further down the chain should treat connectivity as considerably weaker than on the main island. Anyone working with Europe should note the four-hour offset behind central European time, which puts a European afternoon at the start of the Vincentian day. The professional world here is government, agriculture, the port and the yachting trade, and that is close to all of it, so a newcomer's network forms quickly and stays small. Work happens from home or from a hotel with a generator, since a cut during the working day is ordinary rather than notable. A call-heavy schedule needs a specific address proved over a full week rather than an afternoon, because the variation runs between buildings rather than between providers.
kingstown.gettingAround: Kingstown is compact, built along a harbour with the market and the cathedral within a few streets of each other, and it is walkable though hot and steep in places. Minibuses cover Saint Vincent cheaply and are how everyone moves. The Grenadines are reached by ferry from Kingstown, with Bequia an hour away and the smaller islands beyond, and the ferry timetable governs everything. Argyle International Airport opened in 2017 and finally gave the country direct flights from North America, which changed how easy it is to reach. Bequia is the practical Grenadine base for a longer stay, being large enough to have shops and a hospital while still an hour from the capital. Minibuses run when they fill rather than to a timetable, play music at a volume that is part of the experience, and stop wherever you ask. Driving is on the left and the coast roads are narrow, steep and blind in places, which makes the minibus the less alarming option for a newcomer. Several of the Grenadines have their own airstrips, so a light aircraft is the alternative to the ferry for Bequia, Canouan, Union Island and Mustique.
kingstown.visas: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines has no remote work visa. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to a month, extendable at the immigration department in Kingstown, and Commonwealth citizens often receive longer on arrival. The extension process is routine but must be started before the initial stay expires. Anyone planning several months should ask for the maximum at the border and then extend. The country also runs no citizenship by investment programme, which distinguishes it from most of its neighbours. Anyone arriving by yacht clears in at Kingstown, Bequia, Union Island or Chateaubelair, and the paperwork is separate from an arrival by air. CARICOM nationals move under a separate and far simpler regime, with skilled-national certificates allowing indefinite stay and work across member states, which is worth knowing for anyone holding a Caribbean passport. For everyone else, proof of onward travel and an address are asked for at the airport, and airlines enforce the ticket more strictly than immigration does. Extensions carry a monthly fee and are granted case by case rather than as of right, so arriving in good time and looking organised achieves more than any argument will.
kingstown.bestTime: January to May is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine and the calmest sailing conditions in the Grenadines, which is what most visitors come for. June to November is wetter and the hurricane season runs through it. The other consideration here is volcanic: La Soufriere at the northern end of Saint Vincent erupted explosively in April 2021, covering the island in ash and displacing tens of thousands, and it remains an active volcano that is monitored continuously. The Vincy Mas carnival falls in late June and early July, unusually late in the regional calendar, and is the island's largest event. The volcano is monitored by the university's seismic research centre and its alert levels are published, which is the thing to check rather than any general reassurance. Ash from 2021 still affects soil and water catchment in the northern parishes. The sailing season runs with the dry months, and charters book out around Christmas and Easter well ahead. Leatherback turtles nest on the windward beaches between March and July, which is the other argument for being here in the dry half.
kingstown.prosCons: Saint Vincent is the gateway to the Grenadines, a chain of thirty-two islands including Bequia, Mustique and the Tobago Cays, which together make one of the finest sailing grounds in the world. The main island has rainforest, waterfalls and the Botanical Gardens, founded in 1765 and the oldest in the western hemisphere. Costs are low. There is no remote work visa here, and the internet is mediocre, the volcano is genuinely active, and Kingstown itself is a working harbour town that people pass through rather than settle in. Saint Vincent is also one of very few Caribbean islands with black volcanic sand on much of its coast, which surprises people expecting the Grenadines. Medical care runs to a general hospital in the capital, with anything serious meaning Barbados or Trinidad, so evacuation cover is standard for residents rather than optional. Emigration has been heavy for decades and a large Vincentian diaspora lives in Canada, Britain and the United States, which shapes families here more than any statistic conveys. The new airport has begun to change the country's connection to the world, though its effect on prices and development is still being argued about locally.
kingstown.whoFor: A sailor above all: the Grenadines are the reason to be here and the whole geography of the country points at them. A cheap, green, English-speaking island with almost no other foreigners on it describes very few places, and Saint Vincent is one of them. No route exists for staying past the standard entry, and connectivity is unpredictable across the chain. Anybody drawn to the smaller islands should budget for the ferries and accept a plain rule of thumb: the further down the Grenadines you go, the worse the internet becomes, and it does not recover. Hikers get more from Saint Vincent than from most of its neighbours. The climb up La Soufriere and the Vermont nature trail rank among the best walking anywhere in the Eastern Caribbean. Anyone choosing an Eastern Caribbean base should weigh Grenada, which has a longer-stay visa and better infrastructure, and Saint Lucia, which has the flights and the tourism economy, against this country's real advantage, which is the sailing ground rather than the shore. A month tells you whether the pace suits, and most people who stay longer end up on Bequia rather than in the capital.

englishharbour.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker at English Harbour, which is expensive for the region and reflects a yachting economy. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,300, with anything on the water at the top of that and the villages inland considerably cheaper. Antigua imports nearly all of its food and the supermarket bill is the line most people underestimate. Eating at a local place in Falmouth or Liberta costs a fraction of the dockyard restaurants. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Rents move with the season more sharply here than anywhere else nearby: a place let by the month in September can cost twice that in February, when the boats are in and the crews need beds. Antigua has a chronic water problem and much of the supply is desalinated, so water charges are a real line rather than a rounding error. Sales tax runs at fifteen per cent and is usually inside the shelf price, though not always on a restaurant bill, which is worth checking before adding anything on top.
englishharbour.whereToWork: Antigua's connectivity is reasonable and better around English Harbour than the island average, because the yachting industry needs it: fibre reaches the dockyard area and Falmouth at workable speeds and mobile data covers the island. There is a small amount of coworking in St John's and around the harbour, some of it created for holders of the Nomad Digital Residence visa. Power cuts happen. English is the only language required, and the international sailing crowd means the working population here is unusually cosmopolitan for an island of ninety thousand. Anyone whose work involves the marine industry will find a genuine professional network here, in a way that is true of very few small islands. The working population turns over on a schedule: crews arrive with the boats in November and go again in May, so the people you meet in January are mostly not here in July. The marine trades are the one steady employer, from rigging and sailmaking to provisioning and yacht management, and they take on foreigners who turn up with a skill more readily than most industries on any small island. The quiet months are when the work actually gets done.
englishharbour.gettingAround: English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour sit next to each other at the southern end of Antigua and both are walkable, with Nelson's Dockyard, the restaurants and the marinas within twenty minutes of each other. Minibuses run to St John's, the capital, in about forty minutes for very little. Driving is on the left and a local permit is required. V. C. Bird International is the best-connected airport in the Eastern Caribbean, with direct flights to London, New York, Miami and Toronto, which is a genuine advantage of basing here. The walk up to Shirley Heights from the dockyard takes about forty minutes and is the standard way to reach the Sunday evening party. Buses do not run on Sundays and stop early on the days they do, which makes a car or a scooter close to necessary for living here rather than visiting. Taking a lift from a passing car is ordinary and safe on this island and accounts for a good deal of the local movement around the two harbours. The airport sits over on the other side of the island, which is the one journey that needs planning.
englishharbour.visas: Antigua and Barbuda's Nomad Digital Residence is a two-year remote work visa for people employed or self-employed outside the country who can show an annual income of around $50,000, with a fee of roughly $1,500 for an individual and more for a family. Two years is among the longest terms offered anywhere and the application is handled online. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to three months. The country also runs a citizenship by investment programme, which is a separate matter. Anyone applying should know that the two years run from approval rather than arrival, so it is worth timing the application to the intended stay. The residence carries no right to take local employment and does not lead to permanent status, which is the distinction people most often get wrong when they confuse it with the investment programme. Dependants can be added at extra cost. Opening a bank account here is the part that takes longest, and many holders never bother, running everything from accounts at home and drawing cash as they need it.
englishharbour.bestTime: December to April is the dry season and the sailing season, with steady trade winds, daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and the harbour full. Antigua Sailing Week at the end of April is the largest regatta in the Caribbean and fills every bed in the south of the island. May to November is hotter and wetter and the hurricane season runs through it; Antigua was spared in 2017 while Barbuda, its sister island, was rendered uninhabitable by Hurricane Irma and evacuated entirely. Barbuda is reachable by ferry or a short flight and is slowly being rebuilt, with its frigate bird colony among the largest in the world. The Classic Yacht Regatta runs in the week before it and brings in the older boats, which is the better event for anyone who would rather look at rigs than race them. Carnival falls at the end of July and the start of August and is held in St John's rather than down here, so the south of the island stays quiet through it. September is when much of the dockyard simply closes, which is worth knowing before a stay is booked inside it.
englishharbour.prosCons: Nelson's Dockyard is the only continuously working Georgian naval dockyard in the world, a UNESCO World Heritage site that is still a marina rather than a museum, and the Sunday sunset party at Shirley Heights above it has run for decades. Antigua has a two-year nomad visa, the region's best flight connections and a claimed beach for every day of the year. Costs are high, the few remote workers here are mostly sailors and heavily overlapping with the sailing one, and the island empties considerably outside the season. The dockyard's Georgian buildings are also still in commercial use as hotels, offices and marina facilities, which is why it feels like a place rather than an exhibit. Antigua's coastline is unusually indented for its size, which is what produced the natural harbours the navy wanted and what gives the island so many separate small beaches rather than a few long ones. The south is where the yachting money is and the north is where the resorts are, and the two economies barely touch, which is why the place can seem expensive from one end and ordinary from the other.
englishharbour.whoFor: A sailor, or someone who wants to be around sailing, with a two-year visa and the budget for a yachting town. The international crowd here is real and easy to join, which is rare on a small island. It works for a full year rather than a season. A tight budget does not survive a yachting harbour in season, and anybody wanting a city will find St John's forty minutes away and modest even then. Anyone arriving in Sailing Week should book months ahead. Families find Antigua easier than its size would predict, since the schools and the medical facilities here are better than most islands with this population manage to sustain. Two years is long enough to justify shipping possessions and registering a business, which turns a stay into a move, and that is why people choose here over an island offering twelve months. Anyone whose interest is the sailing rather than the island itself should know that the boats leave in May and that the harbour in August is a different and much quieter place.

roadtown.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Road Town, which is expensive and reflects an offshore financial centre and the world's busiest charter yacht base. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,200 to $1,800. Everything arrives by ship and the grocery bill is high even by Caribbean standards. The territory uses the United States dollar, which removes any conversion. Rents rose sharply after Hurricane Irma in 2017 destroyed much of the housing stock and have not fully settled. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Insurance is the line that changed after 2017 and has not changed back. Property and contents cover here is expensive and in some cases hard to obtain at all, which feeds directly into what landlords charge, and it is the reason rents rose faster than the rebuild alone would explain. Payroll deductions for social security and the national health insurance apply to anyone employed locally. Crew and seasonal staff mostly live in shared housing arranged through the charter companies, which is a parallel market a newcomer will not see advertised.
roadtown.whereToWork: The British Virgin Islands host tens of thousands of registered companies and the connectivity reflects that: fibre reaches Road Town and the developed parts of Tortola at solid speeds, and the professional services around the financial sector are substantial. Mobile coverage is good on Tortola and thinner on the outer islands. Power was rebuilt after Irma and is more reliable than before. There is a small amount of coworking. The territory runs on Atlantic time, an hour ahead of New York in the northern winter. Anyone working with London will find the four-hour offset workable, since a British afternoon lands at the start of the Virgin Islands day. The scale of the company registry is worth stating plainly, because it explains the town: several hundred thousand companies have been incorporated here, making this one of the largest offshore domiciles in the world, and the legal and accounting depth that supports it is genuinely international. That sector also lives under sustained external pressure over transparency, from the United Kingdom and from the European Union, and beneficial ownership rules have tightened repeatedly. Anyone joining it should expect a compliance-heavy working life rather than a sleepy one.
roadtown.gettingAround: Road Town is small and its waterfront is walkable, but Tortola is mountainous and everything else needs a vehicle; driving is on the left in cars mostly imported with the wheel on the left, which takes adjustment. Open-air safari taxis run the main routes. The real transport here is the ferry: boats leave Road Town and West End constantly for Virgin Gorda, Jost Van Dyke and the United States Virgin Islands, and the whole territory is organised around them. Terrance B. Lettsome airport handles regional connections only. The ferry to St Thomas takes about forty-five minutes and crosses an international border, so a passport and the American entry rules both apply. Ridge Road runs the spine of Tortola and the gradients on it are severe enough that hire companies specify low gear on the descents, which is advice worth taking rather than filing. A car barge crosses to Virgin Gorda for anyone who needs a vehicle at the other end, though most people simply hire again on arrival. Taxi fares are set by published tariff rather than negotiated, so asking the rate before setting off settles the question.
roadtown.visas: The British Virgin Islands have no dedicated remote work visa, though the territory ran a one-year Work in Nature programme after the pandemic that has not been maintained as a standing category. Most Western nationalities enter for up to thirty days on arrival, extendable at the immigration department, and British citizens receive longer. Anyone planning several months should ask for the maximum at the border and extend locally. Working for a British Virgin Islands employer requires a work permit, which is a separate and considerably harder process. Anyone arriving by yacht clears customs and immigration separately at Road Town, West End or Jost Van Dyke, and the fees differ by vessel and season. The thirty-day stamp is short enough that extending is the normal course rather than the exception, and the immigration department expects it, so arriving with evidence of funds and accommodation makes the first extension straightforward. The trap sits offshore: crossing to the American side enters United States territory, so anyone who would need a visa or ESTA to fly to Miami needs exactly the same to board that boat, and being turned away at the dock is a common and entirely avoidable surprise.
roadtown.bestTime: December to April is the dry season and the charter season, with steady trade winds, flat anchorages and daytime temperatures around twenty-eight. It is also when every mooring ball is taken and prices peak. May to November is hotter and wetter and the hurricane season runs through it; Hurricane Irma in September 2017 passed directly over the territory as a category five and destroyed most of the buildings on Tortola, which is still visible and still shapes what things cost. Anyone chartering should book the winter season many months ahead, since the fleet is finite and the good weeks go first. Christmas winds is the local name for the reinforced trades that blow through late December and January, and they make for spectacular sailing and uncomfortable anchorages on exposed sides. The Spring Regatta at the end of March is the territory's biggest event on the water. Emancipation Festival in early August is the biggest on land, running for days and an entirely different proposition from the charter season. Water temperature barely varies, which is why the diving holds up year-round.
roadtown.prosCons: The British Virgin Islands are the charter yacht capital of the world for a reason: sixty islands within sight of each other, consistent trade winds, short line-of-sight passages and anchorages like the Baths on Virgin Gorda and the beach bars of Jost Van Dyke. It is safe, English-speaking and uses the dollar. Prices are high, there is no remote work visa of any kind, Road Town itself is a functional port and financial district rather than an attractive town, and the hurricane exposure is not theoretical. Recovery from Irma also reshaped the territory's building code, and much of what has been rebuilt since is considerably more storm-resistant than what stood before. Governance here has been under scrutiny rather than quietly ticking over: a United Kingdom commission of inquiry reported in 2022, a premier was arrested that year in Miami, and constitutional reform has been under discussion since, which is live local politics rather than history. On a practical level, prices running above the neighbouring American islands send a steady traffic of residents across for a shopping day, which tells you most of what you need to know about the gap.
roadtown.whoFor: A sailor or somebody in offshore finance, and genuinely hard to justify for anyone who is neither. If the plan is to charter or crew, this is the best base in the Caribbean and the case makes itself. No long-stay visa exists, a budget will not hold in the British Virgin Islands, and anybody expecting a town should adjust that picture: this is a harbour with offices arranged around it. The ferries are the point; anyone who will not use them should look elsewhere. The offshore corporate sector is the one field in which this territory operates at genuine international depth rather than at the scale its population would suggest. Crewing is the route in that the guides omit. The charter fleet hires captains, mates, cooks and engineers every season, the qualifications are attainable, and it is how a good many people who now live here first arrived without capital or a company behind them. Anyone comparing the two Virgin Islands groups should know the American side is cheaper, better connected to the mainland and busier, while this one keeps the anchorages and the quiet.

charlotteamalie.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,700 a month as a solo remote worker in Charlotte Amalie, which is expensive even by American standards and reflects a territory that imports everything. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,300 to $1,900. Groceries cost substantially more than the American mainland and electricity is among the most expensive under the United States flag, which residents discuss constantly. There is no need to convert anything, since the territory uses the dollar and is part of the United States customs zone. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Electricity deserves its own line in a budget rather than a footnote, since the utility generates from imported fuel and a house with the air conditioning on can run to several hundred dollars a month by itself. Shipping a container of belongings from the mainland is how most people move here and costs accordingly. Property insurance is expensive and hurricane cover is not optional where there is a mortgage. What comes back the other way is the absence of any currency conversion, international banking or roaming charge, which removes costs that every other island on this site quietly imposes.
charlotteamalie.whereToWork: Connectivity is good: the territory is served by submarine cable, fibre reaches most of St Thomas at solid speeds, and American carriers operate here with domestic roaming, so a United States mobile plan works without international charges. That last point is a genuine practical advantage over every other Caribbean island. There is a small coworking presence. Power outages are more frequent than on the mainland and the grid was heavily damaged in 2017. The territory runs on Atlantic time year-round. Anyone with an American employer will also find payroll, banking and tax entirely domestic here, which removes a set of problems every other Caribbean base creates. A generator or a battery is normal household equipment here rather than a precaution, since outages remain more frequent than anything the mainland would put up with. The territory also runs an economic development programme offering qualifying businesses steep reductions in corporate and personal tax in exchange for relocating and hiring locally, which has drawn a steady trickle of small firms and is a serious proposition rather than a brochure. Anyone weighing it should take advice early, because the residency and hiring conditions are specific and they are audited.
charlotteamalie.gettingAround: Charlotte Amalie is built around a harbour on steep ground and the waterfront and Main Street are walkable, though the residential streets above involve the ninety-nine steps and several other staircases cut into the hillside. Safari taxis, open-sided trucks with bench seats, run the main routes cheaply. Driving is on the left, in cars almost all imported from the American mainland with the wheel on the left, which is genuinely disorienting. Ferries run to St John, St Croix and the British Virgin Islands. Cruise ships berth at Havensight and Crown Bay, and on a four-ship day the town centre is genuinely difficult to move through. A car earns its keep the moment you leave the waterfront, and the roads climb hard, turn tight and punish brakes rather than merely winding. A seaplane links St Thomas and St Croix in about twenty minutes, landing in both harbours, which is a considerably better experience than the ferry and not much dearer. The cruise schedule is published and worth consulting like a weather forecast, since it decides whether Main Street is passable on a given morning.
charlotteamalie.visas: This is United States territory, so for American citizens there is no visa question at all: no passport is required to travel from the mainland and there is no limit on how long you may stay or work. That makes the United States Virgin Islands the simplest Caribbean option available to Americans by a wide margin. Everyone else needs a United States visa or an ESTA under the Visa Waiver Programme, with the same ninety-day limit and the same prohibition on productive work that applies on the mainland. Anyone travelling on to the British Virgin Islands should note that is a separate country with its own entry rules, despite the forty-five minute ferry. A passport is still worth carrying despite not being required, because the return journey passes through United States customs and the process is markedly smoother with one. The territory has its own customs allowance, more generous than the mainland's, which is why the duty-free shops exist at all. Residents pay income tax to the territory rather than to Washington and cannot vote in presidential elections, a constitutional oddity worth understanding before a long stay.
charlotteamalie.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the highest prices, since this is when the cruise ships and the mainland arrive. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; St Thomas was hit by both Irma and Maria within two weeks in September 2017 and the recovery took years. Carnival on St Thomas runs through April and is the largest event of the year. St John's Virgin Islands National Park covers roughly two-thirds of that island and is reachable by a twenty-minute ferry in any season. Late April into June is the value window, after the ships thin out and before the heart of the storm season, and the water is warmest through the autumn rather than the winter. The island reverts to its residents through September and October, when a fair number of restaurants shut altogether, and those same weeks sit at the centre of the storm season, which is the trade being offered. Sargassum affects some windward beaches in some years between spring and late summer.
charlotteamalie.prosCons: For an American, the Virgin Islands are the Caribbean without any paperwork at all: no passport, no visa, no time limit, a domestic mobile plan and the dollar. Charlotte Amalie has a genuine Danish colonial core with Fort Christian dating from 1672, and St John, twenty minutes by ferry, is two-thirds national park. It is an expensive place, and the crime rate is high enough that both residents and the State Department name specific areas to avoid, and the town is heavily shaped by cruise retail. Electricity costs here are also among the highest anywhere under the American flag, which is a real and recurring line in any household budget. Medical care is the gap that surprises people who assumed a United States flag settles it. The hospital handles routine and emergency work, but anything specialist means a flight to Puerto Rico or Florida, and that is a normal part of living here rather than an exception. The Danish period also runs deeper than the fort: Denmark governed these islands for nearly two and a half centuries before selling them to the United States in 1917, and the street names, the architecture and the legal traces are all still Danish.
charlotteamalie.whoFor: An American remote worker who wants the Caribbean with no immigration friction whatsoever, and for that specific person nothing else on this site competes. It works indefinitely rather than for a season. Anybody without an American passport gets the full weight of United States visa rules here and none of the compensating benefits of being on the mainland, and a budget will not survive island import pricing either. Read current safety guidance for St Thomas rather than assuming a United States flag means low crime. Sailors are the exception. These islands sit at one end of the same chain the British Virgin Islands charter fleet works, which puts a world-class cruising ground within a day's sail. Among the American Caribbean options, Puerto Rico is worth a look too, which is larger, considerably cheaper, better connected by air and offers tax incentives of its own, while these islands are smaller, prettier and more expensive. Within the territory, St Croix is quieter and cheaper than St Thomas, and St John is the one people fall in love with. Families do reasonably well here, though the schooling question sends a good many to the mainland eventually.

providenciales.costOfLiving: Budget around $3,200 a month as a solo remote worker on Providenciales, which makes Turks and Caicos one of the most expensive places on this site. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,600 to $2,400, with anything near Grace Bay at the top of that. Groceries are the standing complaint: everything is imported, there is no local agriculture to speak of, and a supermarket shop costs well over double the American equivalent. There is no income tax and the territory uses the dollar. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Water is the cost that never appears in a comparison and should. There are no rivers and no aquifer worth the name, so supply is desalinated or caught from roofs into cisterns, and a villa with a pool consumes a startling amount of both. National Insurance and health surcharge contributions are deducted from local salaries and payable by the self-employed. Villa rentals are quoted weekly for the season and monthly out of it, and the difference between those two ways of pricing the same house is where a long stay finds its margin.
providenciales.whereToWork: Connectivity is good for a small territory: fibre reaches the developed parts of Providenciales at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive across the island. Prices are high. There is a small amount of coworking. Power is reasonably reliable and expensive. English is the only language required. The islands run on Eastern time with daylight saving, which keeps Providenciales aligned with New York year-round and makes it a straightforward base for anyone working American hours. There is no formal remote work programme to build a community around, so the foreign population here is resort staff and second-home owners rather than nomads. Anyone hoping to find other remote workers will have to look harder than the marketing suggests. The other economy here is offshore financial services, quiet, long-established and almost invisible beside the resorts, which is why the professional infrastructure, banking, company formation, legal advice, is better than a place this size would otherwise support. For day-to-day work the honest arrangement is a rental with a good line and a mobile bundle behind it, since the coffee-shop-as-office culture barely exists outside the Grace Bay strip.
providenciales.gettingAround: Providenciales is flat and spread out along a few main roads, and it is not walkable in any useful sense: the island assumes a car and most visitors rent one. Taxis exist and are expensive, with fares set by a published tariff rather than a meter. Driving is on the left. Grace Bay's hotel strip is the one stretch where walking works. Ferries run to North and Middle Caicos, and light aircraft reach South Caicos, Salt Cay and Grand Turk, the actual capital, which almost no visitor sees. Grand Turk, the actual seat of government, sits an hour away by air and receives a fraction of the visitors that Providenciales does. Hire cars are the single largest recurring expense after rent for most stays, so a monthly rate negotiated directly with a local firm beats the airport desks substantially. The main road, Leeward Highway, carries everything and its junctions are the island's real hazard, with a road safety record poor enough that residents drive defensively as a matter of course. Cycling is possible on the flat but the road has no shoulder and the traffic moves fast.
providenciales.visas: Turks and Caicos has no dedicated remote work visa. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days on arrival, and British citizens receive the same, with extensions available from the immigration department for a fee. The territory has discussed a formal digital nomad scheme more than once without introducing one. Anyone wanting to work for a local employer needs a work permit, which is expensive and tied to a sponsor. For a stay of up to three months the ordinary arrival stamp is all that is required. Anyone considering a longer stay should also know that property purchase does not confer residence here, despite how often the two are marketed together. Neither of the things that shape a long stay here is a visa. Belonger status is the local citizenship that governs land ownership, voting and unrestricted work, and it is difficult to acquire. The Permanent Residence Certificate can be bought through property investment above set thresholds, which grants the right to reside but not the right to work, and the two are commonly confused in marketing. Anyone intending to earn here still requires a work permit with a named sponsor, whatever property they hold.
providenciales.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the calmest water, and it is when the islands are busiest and most expensive. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Hurricanes Irma and Maria both affected the territory in 2017. September and October are the quietest and cheapest months and carry the highest risk. Water temperature stays swimmable all year, which is the argument for coming outside the season. Humpback whales pass through the Turks Island Passage between January and April, which is the one seasonal wildlife event worth timing a visit around. Sargassum reaches the south and east shores in some years through the warmer months, while Grace Bay, facing north behind its reef, is largely spared, which is one reason the whole island developed on that side. The steady winter trades that keep the humidity down also make Long Bay one of the better kitesurfing flats in the region between November and April. Late April into early June gives dry-season water and conditions without the peak-season rates.
providenciales.prosCons: Grace Bay is repeatedly named the best beach in the world and the claim is defensible: twelve kilometres of white sand over a reef-protected shelf with water that stays turquoise to the horizon. The barrier reef system here is the third largest on earth, the diving off West Caicos and French Cay is exceptional, and there is no income tax. Living costs here are severe, and there is no remote work visa either, the island is flat and undramatic once you leave the water, and almost everything is built for resort tourism. Land and who may own it is the live political argument here, since Belonger status governs it and the resort economy has bid property well beyond what local wages reach, which is a tension the brochures do not mention and residents discuss constantly. The reef, for all its scale, has suffered from bleaching events and from stony coral tissue loss disease, which has moved through the region since 2019 and which dive operators will discuss frankly if asked. Crime is low by regional standards without being absent, and residents are specific about which parts of the island to avoid late rather than vague about it.
providenciales.whoFor: A well-paid remote worker after a beach that is hard to better anywhere in the Caribbean, working American hours, and able to absorb prices closer to Bermuda than to the rest of the region. Divers get a great deal here. An ordinary budget does not reach these prices, and a stay beyond ninety days has no mechanism behind it, so the ceiling is fixed regardless of how much anybody likes the place. Set beside the Bahamas, the difference is that the Bahamas has a one-year permit and Turks and Caicos does not. There is one profile this island fits precisely: genuinely location-independent work paired with a salary large enough that accommodation stops being a line worth examining. Against the Cayman Islands, the other high-end offshore option, Turks and Caicos is smaller, quieter, has a far better beach and lacks the certificate that would let you stay a year, which is the whole difference. Sharing a villa is how people who are not on resort salaries actually make it work, and off-season monthly rates make that arithmetic plausible in a way the weekly headline never does.

philipsburg.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Philipsburg, which is expensive and reflects an island of forty thousand people that receives well over a million visitors a year. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $900 to $1,500. Groceries are imported and the markup is heavy, though the French side of the island has cheaper supermarkets and many residents shop there deliberately, which is a genuinely useful trick. The Netherlands Antillean guilder is pegged to the dollar and dollars circulate everywhere. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Power comes from imported diesel and the tariff shows it, ranking among the steepest anywhere in the region, so air conditioning decides a monthly bill more than the rent does. Rentals on the Dutch side are usually quoted in dollars and on the French side in euros, and the rate between them moves the real cost of a lease without anyone renegotiating anything. Prices in the town itself rise on heavy cruise days, which is precisely why residents do their shopping when the harbour is empty.
philipsburg.whereToWork: Sint Maarten's connectivity is reasonable: fibre reaches the developed parts of the Dutch side at workable speeds and mobile data covers the whole island, though a French SIM and a Dutch SIM behave differently on the two halves and roaming charges can appear without warning. There is a small amount of coworking. Power cuts happen. Dutch is official on the southern half and French on the northern, but English is the working language of almost everything commercial on both sides, which is what makes this island unusually easy to operate in. Storm season is the real infrastructure question rather than the daily service: a bad storm removes power and connectivity for weeks rather than days, as 2017 showed, and anyone whose income cannot pause needs a plan for that rather than an assumption. A generator is common in the better rentals and worth asking about by name. The working rhythm otherwise follows the American east coast, which suits anyone billing in dollars and leaves only the European afternoon as a usable overlap the other way.
philipsburg.gettingAround: Philipsburg is a narrow strip between Great Bay and the Great Salt Pond, and Front Street runs its length in twenty minutes on foot. Beyond that a car is needed, and the island is small enough to drive across in forty minutes. Minibuses cover the main routes cheaply. The border between the Dutch and French sides is marked by a monument and nothing else: there are no checks, no barrier and no formality, and most people cross several times a week without noticing. Princess Juliana airport sits at the western end of the island and its approach over Maho Beach, where aircraft pass a few metres above sunbathers, is the island's best-known image. Traffic on an island this small is worse than it has any right to be, since a single road ring carries everything and the causeway across Simpson Bay Lagoon is the only relief. Car hire is cheap and competitive, which is how most visitors get about. Ferries run from here to Anguilla, Saba, Statia and Saint Barthelemy, and the island works as the hub for all four, which is a large part of why the airport matters as much as it does.
philipsburg.visas: This is where the island gets complicated. Sint Maarten, the Dutch side, is a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands and grants most Western nationalities up to ninety days on arrival. Saint-Martin, the French side, is a French overseas collectivity outside the Schengen area, and European Union citizens have freedom of movement there. Because the border is unmarked, which side you are legally staying on is a question of where you sleep rather than where you walk, and the two sets of rules run in parallel. Anyone staying long term should establish clearly which side their lease is on, since that determines which set of immigration rules they are actually living under. Working on either side needs a permit, and both administrations protect local employment, so a visitor entry is for visiting. Dutch nationals have no automatic right to live and work on the Dutch side either, since Sint Maarten sets its own admission rules as a constituent country, which surprises people who assume a Netherlands passport settles the question. Extensions on the Dutch side are applied for locally and are not guaranteed, so a long stay is better built around leaving and returning.
philipsburg.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the highest prices, since this is when North America and the cruise ships arrive. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it. Sint Maarten's exposure is not theoretical: Hurricane Irma passed directly over the island in September 2017 as a category five, destroying most of the buildings and the airport terminal, and the recovery took years. Anyone visiting in the low season should check what is open before booking, since a substantial share of the restaurants close in September and October. The cruise calendar governs the town's mood as much as the weather does. On a four-ship morning Front Street is impassable and by mid-afternoon it is empty again, and the schedule is published if you want to plan around it. The Heineken Regatta in early March fills the island and is the largest sailing event in the Caribbean. May and early December give dry-season conditions without peak prices, and sargassum affects the windward east coast in some years while the western beaches stay largely clear.
philipsburg.prosCons: Sint Maarten is the smallest landmass in the world divided between two sovereign states, and the difference between the Dutch and French halves is real: different food, different prices, different administration, and no border to speak of between them. The airport is one of the best-connected in the Eastern Caribbean and the eating, particularly on the French side at Grand Case, is the best in the region. The place is expensive, heavily built for cruise tourism, and severely exposed to hurricanes when they come. The two sides also have different price levels on almost everything, so a household that shops deliberately across the border spends noticeably less than one that does not. Medical care is limited on both sides, with a new hospital built on the Dutch side after the storm and anything complex still meaning Guadeloupe, Puerto Rico or Miami. Petty crime is a genuine consideration around the busier tourist areas, and residents are matter-of-fact about which streets to avoid after dark. The rebuild since 2017 has been uneven, and there are still visible shells standing alongside finished hotels, which tells you something about how insurance and ownership worked out here.
philipsburg.whoFor: Two countries on one island, exceptional food, and the densest flight connections in the eastern Caribbean, for anyone who can absorb the prices. Anyone who cooks will find the French supermarkets genuinely change the budget. It works for ninety days rather than a year, since neither side offers a remote work visa. Quiet is not what a busy commercial island offers, and the cruise crowds are the specific problem: several thousand people come ashore on most winter mornings and the town is built around receiving them. Sailing is what this island is actually for. Simpson Bay Lagoon is among the largest enclosed anchorages in the Caribbean, and the bridge into it opens twice a day to a queue of masts. Against its neighbours this island is the practical one. Anguilla is quieter and far better set up for a year-long stay, Saint Barthelemy is more polished and considerably dearer, and both of them lean on the flights and the supermarkets here. Curacao, further west, is the Dutch Caribbean alternative, with a longer-stay visa and no hurricanes to speak of. Families manage well enough, though the schooling splits along the language line as everything else does.

kralendijk.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Kralendijk, which is expensive for a small island and reflects an economy built almost entirely on diving. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,300. Everything is imported and groceries carry a markup, though the Dutch supply chain keeps the choice wide. Bonaire uses the United States dollar rather than a guilder, which is unusual in the Dutch Caribbean and removes any conversion. Diving is the line that dominates any real budget here. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The switch to the dollar came on 1 January 2011, when the islands left the Netherlands Antillean guilder behind along with the country that issued it, and prices were rounded upward in the process in a way residents still mention. Health insurance works on the Dutch model and is far cheaper than a private Caribbean policy, which offsets some of the grocery markup for anyone entitled to it. The recurring costs specific to the island are tanks and fills, the annual nature fee that funds the marine park, and a truck to reach the entry points, none of it avoidable.
kralendijk.whereToWork: Bonaire's connectivity is good for its size: fibre reaches Kralendijk and the developed west coast at workable speeds and mobile data covers the island. Prices are high. Power is reliable and increasingly wind-generated, since the island runs a substantial wind farm. There is a small amount of coworking aimed at the long-stay diving population. Dutch is official and Papiamentu is the language of daily life, but English is widely spoken and Spanish is common given Venezuela is eighty kilometres away. Anyone working with Europe will find the offset behind central European time makes a European afternoon into a Bonairean morning, which is a workable overlap. Papiamentu here differs from the Curacao and Aruba versions in spelling as much as in sound, and Bonaire writes it phonetically where Aruba leans on Spanish convention. Dutch remains the language of schooling and government, so official business is conducted in it. Cruise ships berth directly in Kralendijk rather than at a separate terminal, so the town centre fills and empties on a schedule that matters if you work from a cafe there.
kralendijk.gettingAround: Kralendijk is small and walkable along its waterfront, but Bonaire's whole proposition requires a vehicle: the diving is from the shore, at some ninety marked entry points along the western coast identified by painted yellow stones at the roadside, and reaching them means a pickup truck with tanks in the back. That is what almost every visitor rents. The island is flat and cyclable in the south. Flamingo International airport is minutes from town with connections through Curacao, Amsterdam and Miami. The southern half of the island is salt pans and flamingo colonies, and the road around them makes a flat circuit that most residents cycle at least once. Rincon in the northern interior is the oldest settlement in the Dutch Caribbean, founded inland and out of sight of the sea so that raiders could not spot it from a ship.
