The road north continues into Washington Slagbaai, a national park occupying the whole top of the island, where the tracks are rough enough that rental agreements often exclude them. South of town the salt pans are still worked commercially, and the stone slave huts along that shore are barely large enough to sit up in.
kralendijk.visas: Bonaire is a special municipality of the Netherlands rather than a constituent country, which makes its status different from Curacao or Aruba, though it sits outside the European Union and outside Schengen. Dutch and European Union citizens can live and work here with minimal formality. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days on arrival. There is no dedicated remote work visa, but the ninety days plus the ease of a short exit to Curacao makes a longer stay practical for anyone willing to manage it. Anyone diving here must complete a short orientation and buy an annual marine park tag before entering the water, which is enforced rather than nominal. Residents of Bonaire vote in Dutch general elections and for the European Parliament despite the island sitting outside the European Union, an arrangement with few parallels anywhere. Since 2023 they also elect a college that votes for the Dutch Senate. For a non-Dutch visitor none of that helps, and the practical route to a long stay remains those ninety days plus a willingness to explain yourself on re-entry.
kralendijk.bestTime: Bonaire sits below the hurricane belt and is dry, warm and windy essentially all year, around thirty degrees every month with very little rain, so there is no season to avoid. That consistency is the island's quiet advantage over most of the Caribbean. The busiest and most expensive window is December to April. October to December brings what rain there is. Diving conditions barely change through the year, which is why the island's visitor numbers are far steadier than its neighbours'. Sea turtles nest on the beaches between May and December, and the marine park restricts access to some stretches of shore during the season. The Pekelmeer in the south is one of only four places in the world where Caribbean flamingos breed, and the colony there is closed to people entirely during nesting. The birds commute to Venezuela to feed, which is why the flights over the salt pans at dawn and dusk are so reliable. Carnival runs in the weeks before Lent and is the one time the island is loud. Regatta week in October fills every room on the island, so aim at that date or well clear of it.
kralendijk.prosCons: Bonaire made its entire surrounding sea a national park in 1979, one of the first marine reserves anywhere, and the result is shore diving of a quality that nowhere else offers from a roadside: ninety marked entry points, healthy reef within swimming distance of the shore, and no boat required for most of it. The island is safe, outside the hurricane belt and uses the dollar. It is expensive, very quiet, and small enough to exhaust quickly, and there is essentially nothing to do here that is not underwater. The island also runs a substantial share of its electricity from wind, which is unusual in the Caribbean and shows in a grid that is more reliable than most. Lac Bay on the east coast is the counterweight to all that diving: a shallow lagoon with steady trade winds that has produced a run of world-class windsurfers from a population of around twenty four thousand. The mangroves at its head are a nursery for the reef fish that make the west coast worth diving, which is the sort of connection a small island makes obvious.
kralendijk.whoFor: A diver, and the honest answer is that it is almost nobody else. For someone who wants to dive most days for months at a low marginal cost, Bonaire is arguably the best place on earth and the island is organised entirely around making that easy. Somebody who does not dive has removed the entire reason this island attracts anybody, and nightlife, a city and a workable budget are three further things it does not supply. Non-divers will find the island beautiful and be finished with it in a week. Beginners have an advantage here that experienced divers sometimes miss. Shore entries taken at your own pace build hours far faster than a boat schedule allows, and Bonaire is built entirely around them. It suits a windsurfer nearly as well as a diver, since Lac Bay is shallow enough to stand in and blows reliably almost every afternoon. Dutch administration paired with Caribbean weather is a narrow preference, but it is a real one and this is where it exists. Medical depth is the real limit: complex cases are flown to Curacao or the Netherlands, and the island is honest about that.

pointeapitre.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Pointe-a-Pitre, which is expensive for the Caribbean and reflects the cost structure of a French department where much of the food is shipped from Europe. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200. Groceries cost noticeably more than in mainland France, which has driven serious protests here more than once. The local markets and the lolos, the small Creole grills, are considerably cheaper. The euro is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Anyone comparing with the independent islands nearby should note that European healthcare and schooling are included in what the higher cost of living buys. Water is the cost that does not appear on any comparison and dominates local life. The distribution network leaks badly enough that large parts of the archipelago run on rota cuts, tours d'eau, with taps dry for a day or more at a time, and households buy bottled water and keep storage containers as a matter of routine. Ask about it before signing anything. A negotiated basket of capped-price staples exists in the overseas departments, the bouclier qualite-prix, and knowing which items are on it changes a weekly shop more than switching supermarket does.
pointeapitre.whereToWork: Guadeloupe has European infrastructure and it shows: fibre reaches the developed parts of the archipelago at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive, and French mobile plans work here without roaming charges, which is a substantial advantage for anyone based in Europe. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene around Pointe-a-Pitre and Le Gosier. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, with Guadeloupean Creole spoken among locals; English is limited outside tourism. Anyone working with mainland France should note the five-hour offset, which puts a French afternoon at the start of the Guadeloupean working day and makes mornings the overlap. The public sector and its salaries dominate the formal economy here, and the private sector outside tourism and construction is small, which shapes both the professional network and the price level. The Universite des Antilles has a campus at Fouillole with a real research population attached to it. For anyone working from home the practical constraint is not the connection but the water and power interruptions, so a laptop that holds charge and a filled kettle before a rota cut are the local adaptations rather than anything technical.
pointeapitre.gettingAround: Guadeloupe is shaped like a butterfly, with Grande-Terre's limestone plain on one wing and Basse-Terre's rainforest volcano on the other, joined by a bridge over a narrow channel. Pointe-a-Pitre sits at the join and is the commercial centre. Buses cover the main routes and most residents drive; the roads are European-standard and the traffic into Pointe-a-Pitre at peak is heavy. Ferries run to Marie-Galante, Les Saintes and La Desirade, and the airport has direct flights to Paris. Basse-Terre, confusingly, is both the name of the western wing and of the actual administrative capital, which sits at its southern end rather than in Pointe-a-Pitre. The Route de la Traversee runs across Basse-Terre through the rainforest and is the drive that explains the island, climbing from coast to coast past the Cascade aux Ecrevisses in under an hour. Road numbering follows the French system, so a departmental road here behaves exactly as it would in the Vosges. Cycling is a serious local sport rather than a leisure activity, and the Tour de la Guadeloupe each August closes roads across both wings for a week.
pointeapitre.visas: Guadeloupe is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union, though it lies outside the Schengen area, which is a distinction that catches people out in both directions. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here without any permit at all, which makes Guadeloupe one of the simplest Caribbean options available to any European. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Longer stays for non-EU citizens require a French long-stay visa applied for before travel. Anyone travelling on to Dominica or the independent islands nearby should note those are separate countries with their own entry rules, despite the short ferry. The archipelago was larger until recently, and knowing that clarifies the region's map: Saint-Martin and Saint-Barthelemy were both administered from here until 2007, when they were detached to become separate overseas collectivities with their own rules, which is why three French territories in these waters now operate three different arrangements. For non-Europeans, the residence permit issued here is a French one and carries the same conditions as the mainland's, applied for at the prefecture in Basse-Terre rather than anywhere closer.
pointeapitre.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, known locally as careme, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, lower humidity and the calmest sea. June to November is the wet season, called hivernage, and the hurricane season runs through it; Guadeloupe sits within the belt. Carnival here runs from January through to Ash Wednesday and is a serious, weeks-long affair rather than a single parade. The Route du Rhum, the transatlantic solo yacht race from Saint-Malo, finishes here every four years. La Soufriere, the volcano on Basse-Terre, is walkable year-round but is in cloud most days, so an early start is the only reliable way to see anything from the top. Sargassum is the seasonal problem that has grown rather than receded, arriving on the Atlantic-facing shores in variable quantity between spring and late summer and smelling as it decomposes, while the leeward coast where most visitors stay is largely spared. School holidays follow the French calendar, so the archipelago fills at Toussaint and in February when mainland families arrive. The sea stays swimmable in every month of the year, which makes the low season a genuine bargain for anyone who can tolerate the rain.
pointeapitre.prosCons: Guadeloupe gives you the Caribbean with European infrastructure, French healthcare, the euro and no visa question at all for Europeans, plus La Soufriere's rainforest volcano, the Cousteau reserve at Pigeon Island and the Carbet falls. The food is genuinely excellent, mixing French technique with Creole ingredients. French is all but required, and the cost of living is high and politically contentious with it, Pointe-a-Pitre itself is a working port rather than an attractive town, and unemployment on the islands is severe. The archipelago also includes Marie-Galante, Les Saintes and La Desirade, which are quieter and cheaper than the two main wings and reachable by ferry. The water crisis deserves stating as the structural problem it is, since it is the thing residents raise first and visitors discover late: decades of underinvestment in the network mean chronic shortages, rota cuts across whole communes and periodic protest about it, and no quick fix is in prospect. Unemployment runs high, particularly among the young, and the departure of a generation to mainland France is a demographic fact the islands discuss openly. The compensation is a landscape that ranges from limestone flats to active volcano within an hour's drive.
pointeapitre.whoFor: A French speaker, and especially a European Union citizen, who wants the Caribbean without any immigration process and with infrastructure that works. Divers get the Cousteau reserve and hikers get a volcano. Guadeloupe operates in French from the airport onward, which makes the language a requirement rather than an advantage, and European prices in the Caribbean make a budget stay difficult to construct. Guadeloupe and Martinique are similar in status and different in character, Guadeloupe being wilder and Martinique more polished. Families get something genuinely unusual here. The schools are French state schools and the healthcare is the French system itself rather than a Caribbean approximation of it, with everything that implies for a longer stay. The smaller islands are where a good many people who stay actually end up. Marie-Galante is flat, agricultural and slow, Les Saintes has the best harbour in the archipelago, and both are cheaper and calmer than either wing of the main island while remaining French in every administrative sense. Anyone coming for a season rather than a fortnight should look there before signing anything near the commercial centre, which is where the jobs are and very little else.

fortdefrance.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Fort-de-France, which sits at much the same level as Guadeloupe and reflects the same French department cost structure. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200, with Schoelcher and the Pointe du Bout side at the top of that. Imported food is expensive and the price of it has driven repeated protest movements across the French Caribbean. The market and the local snack bars are far cheaper. The euro is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The mechanism behind the prices has a name: the octroi de mer, a dock duty levied on goods arriving in the overseas departments, which funds local government and adds to the shelf price of nearly everything imported. It is why a supermarket basket here costs so much more than the same basket in mainland France, and it is the central grievance in the recurring cost-of-living campaigns. On the credit side of it, healthcare and schooling run on the French system, removing two costs that dominate budgets elsewhere in the region, and a car, while close to essential, is insured and serviced at French rather than island prices.
fortdefrance.whereToWork: Martinique's infrastructure is European: fibre reaches most of the developed west coast at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and French plans roam here without charge. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene in Fort-de-France and around Le Lamentin. French is the language of everything, with Martinican Creole spoken among locals, and English is limited outside the tourism industry. Anyone working with Europe will find the five-hour offset behind Paris workable in one direction and awkward in the other. Anyone in the rum trade will find genuine professional depth here, since Martinique produces the only appellation-controlled rum in the world. The offset that does work is westward. Martinique sits an hour ahead of New York, so a full North American business day is available without any early start, which makes the island a far better base for anyone working with the Americas than for anyone tied to Paris hours. Setting up as a freelancer uses the same French structures and online portals as the mainland, a genuine administrative advantage over every independent state in the region. Storm season is the one infrastructure caveat, since a serious hurricane takes power and networks down for days.
fortdefrance.gettingAround: Fort-de-France is built around a bay with the Savane park and the extraordinary Schoelcher Library at its centre, and the core is walkable. A ferry crosses the bay to Trois-Ilets and Pointe du Bout in twenty minutes, which is faster and pleasanter than driving around. Buses cover the island and most residents drive; the road north to Saint-Pierre and the Route de la Trace through the rainforest are both excellent drives. The airport has direct flights to Paris and across the region. The ferry across the bay is also the cheapest way to reach the beaches of the south, which are considerably better than anything in the city itself. The other boat worth knowing is the inter-island fast ferry, which runs to Dominica, Saint Lucia and Guadeloupe and turns a set of separate countries into day or weekend trips. On land, the morning traffic into the city from the suburbs is genuinely bad for an island this size and parking in the centre is difficult, which is a large part of why people who work in town so often live across the water and take the boat instead.
fortdefrance.visas: Martinique is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union while sitting outside the Schengen area. European Union citizens can live and work here with no permit and no time limit, which is the single most useful fact about the island for any European reading this site. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Non-EU citizens wanting longer need a French long-stay visa applied for before travel, and the process is the French one rather than a Caribbean one. Anyone travelling on to Saint Lucia or Dominica, both visible from the island on a clear day, should note those are separate countries with their own rules. The corollary of sitting outside Schengen is worth spelling out. Days spent in Martinique are not counted against a Schengen allowance, so a non-European can use the island as a real pause inside a longer European itinerary rather than as part of the same clock. A Schengen visa alone does not admit you, and a French visa has to name the overseas departments to be valid here, which is the detail that catches people at check-in rather than on arrival.
fortdefrance.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and lower humidity, and it is the busiest window. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season runs through it. Carnival, running for the five days before Ash Wednesday and ending with the burning of Vaval, is the island's largest event and quite unlike the Trinidadian version. The rainforest north of the island is wet in any season, which is why Mount Pelee is so often in cloud. The Tour des Yoles, a race of traditional sailing boats around the island each summer, is the sporting event Martinicans care about most. Sargassum seaweed affects the Atlantic-facing east coast in some years between roughly March and August, while the Caribbean side where most people stay is largely spared. And if the volcano is the reason for the trip, climb early: the summit is usually clear at dawn and wrapped in cloud by the middle of the morning, so an afternoon attempt almost always ends in white. May and November are the value months, either side of the crowds.
fortdefrance.prosCons: Martinique has Mount Pelee, whose 1902 eruption destroyed Saint-Pierre and killed thirty thousand people in minutes, leaving ruins you can walk through, along with rainforest, rum distilleries producing the only appellation-controlled rum in the world, and the Caribbean's most developed restaurant culture outside Trinidad. European infrastructure and no visa question for Europeans. French is essential, and costs are both high and contentious, and Fort-de-France has real urban problems of the kind the tourist brochures do not mention. The island also produced Aime Cesaire and Frantz Fanon, whose work shaped how the whole francophone world thinks about colonialism, and both are taken seriously here. Chlordecone, a pesticide used in the banana plantations for two decades after it had been banned elsewhere, has contaminated a large share of the soil and the coastal waters and will persist for centuries. It has brought fishing restrictions in some areas, elevated cancer rates, and a long-running political dispute with Paris over responsibility. It does not make the island unsafe to visit, and it is a live subject that anyone staying should expect to hear about.
fortdefrance.whoFor: French, ideally with a European Union passport behind it, and a wish for the Caribbean with functioning institutions and a serious food and rum culture. Anyone interested in volcanology will find Pelee and the ruins of Saint-Pierre remarkable. French is required rather than useful in a French department, and Martinique carries European prices with Caribbean shipping costs on top of them. Most long-stay visitors base themselves in Trois-Ilets or the south rather than in the capital, which is worth knowing before booking a flat in the city. Rum treated as a subject rather than a drink is well served on this island. The distilleries are working agricultural businesses that happen to admit visitors, rather than visitor attractions that happen to distil. Anyone choosing between the two French islands is choosing character rather than quality. Guadeloupe is wilder and more spread out across its two joined halves; Martinique is more urbane, better served by restaurants and easier to move around. Hikers do well here, since the trails on the volcano and through the northern rainforest are properly maintained in a way that is unusual in the region. Families benefit from the schooling and the healthcare, which is why so many French professionals take postings here.

cayenne.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker in Cayenne, which is expensive for South America and reflects a French department where almost everything is imported from Europe. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200. Groceries cost substantially more than in mainland France, and the cost of living has driven serious social movements here. The markets, particularly the Hmong market at Cacao and the Saturday market in Cayenne, are the exception and are genuinely good. The euro is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The same dock duty that inflates prices across the French overseas departments applies here, which is why a European product costs more in Cayenne than in Paris despite the shared currency and supply chain. Crossing to Suriname or to Brazil, where the same shopping costs a fraction, is an escape mainland France does not have, and many residents make the trip periodically. Housing is genuinely short in the city, and the gap between what is advertised and what is actually available is wider than the figures suggest. Healthcare and schooling come through the French system.
cayenne.whereToWork: French Guiana has European infrastructure in a South American setting: fibre reaches Cayenne and Kourou at workable speeds, mobile coverage is good along the coastal strip and effectively absent inland, and French plans roam here without charge. Power is reliable in the towns. There is a small amount of coworking, much of it connected to the space industry at Kourou. French is the language of everything, with Guianese Creole widely spoken; English is rare. The territory sits four hours behind Paris. Anyone working with mainland France should note the four-hour offset, which is the smallest of any French overseas territory and makes a full working overlap possible. The professional world is narrower than European infrastructure suggests and it has two poles: the space centre at Kourou, with the engineering and logistics economy around it, and the research institutions working on the forest, from the field stations in the interior to the agricultural and health institutes. Almost everything technical connects to one or the other. Anyone outside those will find the local network thin and is better off treating the territory as somewhere to work from rather than somewhere to work in.
cayenne.gettingAround: Cayenne is compact around the Place des Palmistes with its royal palms, and the centre is walkable. Buses are limited and most residents drive. The single coastal road runs west to Kourou and Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni and east towards the Brazilian border at Saint-Georges, and that road is essentially the whole road network: the interior is rainforest reached by river, and there is no road to Brazil's interior or to Suriname except a ferry across the Maroni. Kourou, with the European spaceport, is about an hour west along that road, and launches are visible from Cayenne on a clear night. A car is close to essential and the road itself is good, though the distances are longer than they look: Saint-Laurent is around three hours west and Saint-Georges about the same going east. Beyond the tarmac, travel is by pirogue, the motorised dugout that serves the Maroni and Oyapock rivers and every settlement along them, and a trip upriver is measured in days and arranged through the communities rather than booked. The Iles du Salut are reached by boat from Kourou.
cayenne.visas: French Guiana is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union, outside the Schengen area. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here without a permit. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Non-EU citizens wanting longer need a French long-stay visa obtained before travel. Yellow fever vaccination is mandatory for entry, which is unusual for European Union territory and is enforced. The land borders with Brazil and Suriname have their own procedures. Anyone crossing to Suriname takes a pirogue across the Maroni at Saint-Laurent, and anyone crossing to Brazil uses the bridge at Saint-Georges, each with its own hours. Both land crossings need the neighbour's paperwork sorted in advance rather than at the river. Suriname operates an online tourist card or visa, and Brazil reinstated visa requirements for several Western nationalities in 2025, so a day trip across is no longer the casual thing it once was. Inland, gendarmerie checkpoints on the coastal road are routine and identity documents are checked, which follows from the mining and border situation rather than being aimed at visitors.
cayenne.bestTime: French Guiana is equatorial and hot all year at around thirty-one degrees with high humidity. The calendar turns on rain: the long dry season from July to November is the practical window, with a short drier spell in March. The heavy rains from December to June make interior travel difficult. Leatherback turtles nest on the beaches near Cayenne and at Awala-Yalimapo between March and July, which is one of the great wildlife spectacles in the Americas and the reason to time a visit. Anyone hoping to watch a rocket launch should check the schedule well in advance, since dates move and the viewing sites are allocated rather than open. Carnival here is longer and stranger than most. It runs every weekend from Epiphany to Ash Wednesday, with the touloulous, masked women who invite men to dance and can be neither refused nor identified, at the centre of it, and it is the territory's biggest cultural event by a distance. Practically, mosquito-borne illness including dengue is a real and recurring risk on the coast, so repellent and covered evenings are ordinary precautions rather than fussiness.
cayenne.prosCons: French Guiana is the European Union on the edge of the Amazon: rainforest covering ninety-eight per cent of the territory, Europe's spaceport at Kourou launching Ariane rockets over the Atlantic, the penal colony ruins on the Iles du Salut where Papillon was set, and leatherback turtles nesting on the beaches. The infrastructure is French and the euro is the currency. It is expensive, French is essential here, the crime rate in Cayenne is high by any European standard, and the interior is genuinely hard to reach. Illegal gold mining in the interior is also a serious environmental and security problem that shapes what is possible outside the coastal strip. The population is among the most varied anywhere for its size, with Creole, Maroon, Amerindian, Hmong, Brazilian, Haitian and metropolitan French communities living alongside one another, and that shows in the food more vividly than in anything else. And the gold mining that damages the forest also releases mercury into the rivers, which has contaminated fish stocks that upriver communities depend on, making it a public health problem as much as an environmental one.
cayenne.whoFor: French, plus a serious interest in the rainforest or in space, and a wish for European institutions on a South American frontier. Anyone able to watch an Ariane launch from Kourou will remember it. French runs everything, South American prices do not apply in a European department, and overland travel is close to impossible: the road network ends at the coast and the interior is rainforest and river. Read current safety guidance for Cayenne rather than assuming European territory means European crime rates. Amazon research is easier to run from here than from almost anywhere else in the basin, because the forest is among the least disturbed on the continent and the institutional support behind it is French. The most rewarding version of a visit for most people is short and built around one thing: a launch, the turtles, or a river trip, each of which justifies the fare on its own and none of which needs a month. Anyone drawn to the Guianas more broadly should know that Suriname next door is far cheaper, that English is useful there, and that Paramaribo is one of the more interesting small capitals in the Americas, so a trip taking in both makes better sense than either alone.

thevalley.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month as a solo remote worker in The Valley, which is expensive and reflects an island of fifteen thousand people that imports everything and has positioned itself at the top of the Caribbean market. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,100 to $1,700. Groceries are heavily marked up and many residents shop in Sint Maarten, twenty minutes away by ferry, where prices are lower. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the dollar and both circulate. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Anguilla levies no income tax, no capital gains tax and no inheritance tax, which is a genuine part of the arithmetic for anyone spending a year here, though it does nothing about an obligation at home. Electricity is very expensive, generated from imported fuel, and air conditioning is what decides the size of the bill. The rental market is built around holiday villas, so a long lease is negotiated rather than listed and works out dramatically cheaper per night than the weekly rate. Restaurants run from beach shacks at modest prices to some of the most expensive tables in the Caribbean, with little in between.
thevalley.whereToWork: Anguilla's connectivity is good for its size: fibre reaches most of the island at workable speeds and mobile data is comprehensive, both of which the government invested in specifically to support its remote work programme. There is a small amount of coworking. Power is reasonably reliable and expensive. English is the only language required. The island runs four hours behind central European time and one ahead of New York in winter, giving a workable overlap in both directions for anyone splitting time between the two. Anyone needing anything the island does not have will find Sint Maarten twenty minutes away by ferry, with a far larger airport and considerably more choice. The infrastructure caveat is seasonal rather than daily: a serious storm takes power and connectivity down for longer than a mainland outage would last, because the repairs wait on parts arriving by boat. Anyone whose work cannot pause should have a plan for that rather than an assumption. Day to day the island is quiet enough that a working routine is easy to hold, which is the thing people who come for a year most often say they valued and had not expected.
thevalley.gettingAround: Anguilla is flat, sixteen kilometres long and has no traffic to speak of, which makes it one of the easiest islands anywhere to move around. A car is still needed since the settlements are spread out and there is no public transport worth the name; driving is on the left and a temporary local licence is required. The Valley is the administrative centre rather than a town in any real sense. Ferries and light aircraft run to Sint Maarten in twenty minutes, which is the practical connection to the wider world. The long-standing public ferry runs from Blowing Point to Marigot on the French side, while a private boat goes direct to the Sint Maarten airport, which costs more and is far less stressful with luggage and a flight to catch. Anguilla's own airport takes regional aircraft rather than long-haul. On the roads, roaming goats and unlit stretches at night are the two hazards worth naming, and cycling is pleasant on the flat but demands care in the heat and the near-total absence of shade.
thevalley.visas: Anguilla introduced a remote work programme in 2020 that grants stays of up to twelve months to people working for employers outside the island, with a fee of around $2,000 for an individual and more for a family, plus proof of health insurance and a clean record. It was one of the earliest such schemes anywhere and remains straightforward. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to three months. British citizens receive the same, since Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory. Anyone applying should note that the fee is not refundable if the application is declined, and that proof of income and insurance are both checked properly. The programme is applied for online and decisions come quickly by the standards of these schemes, which is part of why it worked. What it does not do is lead anywhere: there is no progression from the remote work permit to residence, so a year here is a year rather than a first step. Being a British Overseas Territory also does not make Anguilla part of the United Kingdom for immigration purposes, so a British passport brings easy entry but no automatic right to settle.
thevalley.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the calmest sea, and it is when the island is busiest and most expensive. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Anguilla is exposed and Hurricane Irma in 2017 caused severe damage across the island. Many restaurants and hotels close entirely between September and October, which is worth checking before booking a long stay in those months. Anguilla's boat racing season, with traditional wooden sloops raced by whole villages, runs through the summer and is the island's genuine national sport. The summer calendar peaks with Carnival at the start of August, when the boat racing, the music and the island's whole social year come together, and it is the one time a quiet place is emphatically not quiet. May and early December are the value windows, with dry-season weather at off-season prices. Sargassum seaweed has become a recurring problem on Caribbean windward shores in recent years, though the best-known beaches here face the calmer side and are less affected by it.
thevalley.prosCons: Anguilla has thirty-three beaches on a flat coral island with no rivers to muddy the water, which is why the sand at Shoal Bay and Rendezvous Bay is as white as it is. It has one of the earliest and most generous remote work visas anywhere, very low crime, and a restaurant scene disproportionate to its size, built on the same French Caribbean supply chain that feeds Saint-Martin. It is expensive and extremely quiet, and there is genuinely very little to do here beyond the beaches. The absence of rivers is also why Anguilla has no rainforest and almost no elevation, which is the trade-off that produces the water clarity. The dependence on Sint Maarten runs deeper than shopping. The hospital handles routine care and anything beyond it means a boat or a flight, and the international airport connecting the island to the world belongs to another country twenty minutes away. That works smoothly almost all of the time and not at all when a storm closes the crossing, which is the structural vulnerability of living on a small island beside a larger one.
thevalley.whoFor: Twelve months on an exceptionally beautiful, safe and quiet island, for an income that absorbs the cost and a temperament that takes the silence. The visa is one of the best available anywhere. Nightlife, a community and a city are three things Anguilla has never had, and work that draws its energy from what is happening outside the window will find very little happening. Anguilla is deliberately calm and it does not pretend otherwise, which is either exactly right or exactly wrong. Families looking for somewhere genuinely safe have a strong candidate here, since Anguilla records one of the lowest crime rates anywhere in the Caribbean and sixteen thousand residents keep it that way without much effort. A useful test before applying: this is a place where the week's plan is which beach, and people who find that restorative stay the full year while people who need a project outside their work tend to leave early. Couples and families do better than solo arrivals, simply because the island supplies scenery rather than company. Anyone comparing the remote work schemes should weigh Barbados for a larger island with more going on, against quiet and beaches that are hard to beat anywhere.

andorralavella.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Andorra la Vella, which is cheaper than the Alpine countries around it and expensive by Spanish standards. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $700 to $1,200, and the rental market is genuinely tight because the country is small and much of the housing stock is holiday property. The tax position is the real financial story: Andorra charges a maximum of ten per cent income tax and four and a half per cent value added tax, the lowest in Europe, which is why duty-free shopping fills the main street. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Social security contributions are the cost the headline tax rate hides. Residents pay into the Andorran system and it is not trivial, though it buys a health service that works well. Fuel, alcohol, tobacco and electronics are all noticeably cheaper than in France or Spain, which is what the coach parties on the main street have come for. Rents are usually asked with two months' deposit and a year's commitment, and finding anything at all outside the summer and ski seasons is the harder half of the problem.
andorralavella.whereToWork: Andorra has invested seriously in connectivity: the state telecoms company has rolled fibre to essentially every household in the country, which makes it one of the best-connected places in Europe per head, and speeds are high. Mobile coverage is complete in the valleys and patchy on the high passes. Power is entirely reliable. There is a small coworking scene, and the government has actively courted digital businesses with a residence category aimed at them. Catalan is the official language, with Spanish and French widely spoken; English is limited outside tourism and the newer arrivals. The telecoms company being a state monopoly cuts both ways: the network is excellent and there is no competition on price, so bills run higher than the infrastructure would suggest elsewhere. The clock matches Madrid and Paris, which puts the whole European market inside ordinary office hours. Anyone pursuing the digital residence route should understand that it requires an actual Andorran company with real substance rather than a nameplate, and the authorities have tightened what counts. The domestic market is eighty thousand people, so a business here sells outward or not at all.
andorralavella.gettingAround: Andorra la Vella and the neighbouring town of Escaldes-Engordany run together along a narrow valley floor and the whole strip is walkable, which is fortunate because the traffic through it is heavy. Buses cover the parishes and the ski areas cheaply. The country has no airport and no railway, so everyone arrives by road: Barcelona is around three hours by bus, Toulouse two and a half, and the nearest stations are at L'Hospitalet and Lleida. That isolation is the single most important practical fact about living here. The road tunnels under the high passes mean the country stays open through winter, which was not true within living memory. The frontier is a customs post rather than an immigration one, and the queue leaving on a Sunday evening, when the day-trippers go home with their shopping, is the one to plan around. Winter tyres or chains are required on the mountain roads in the cold months and the requirement is enforced. Airport buses from Barcelona and Toulouse fill in the ski season and should be booked ahead. Within the country a car is optional, since the bus network is genuinely good for a place this size.
andorralavella.visas: Andorra is not in the European Union and not in Schengen, though it has no border controls with France or Spain in practice and uses the euro. Visitors need whatever permission the Schengen states require to reach it, since there is no other way in. There is no remote work visa. Residence comes in two forms: active residence requires running a company here, and passive residence requires a substantial investment in Andorran assets plus an interest-free deposit with the state, currently in the region of several hundred thousand dollars. Anyone counting Schengen days should note that Andorra is not in the area, though reaching it requires crossing France or Spain, which are. Both residence routes carry a presence requirement rather than being a paper arrangement. Passive residents must spend a minimum period in the country each year and it is checked, while active residents are expected to actually run the business. Private health insurance is a condition of the passive route, and the number of those permits is capped annually, so timing matters. Anyone treating Andorran residence purely as a tax address should take advice, since the substance requirements have tightened considerably.
andorralavella.bestTime: December to April is the ski season and the busiest half, with Grandvalira and Ordino-Arcalis together forming the largest ski area in the Pyrenees and the reason most visitors come at all. June to September is the walking season, with the high valleys open, wildflowers and daytime temperatures in the low twenties at this altitude. May and November are the shoulder months when much of the country simply closes. Andorra la Vella sits above a thousand metres, so winters are properly cold and snow in the town itself is normal. The shopping trade runs to a different calendar from the mountains and fills the capital at weekends and public holidays throughout the year, so a quiet Tuesday and a busy Saturday are barely the same town. Caldea, the thermal spa complex at Escaldes, is the standard wet-weather answer and opens all year. Meritxell day on the eighth of September is the national holiday and effectively closes the country, with a pilgrimage to the sanctuary in the Valira d'Orient valley that draws a large share of the population out of the towns for the day.
andorralavella.prosCons: Andorra offers the lowest tax rates in Europe, fibre to nearly every home, the largest ski area in the Pyrenees, and a genuinely safe and orderly country of eighty thousand people in a mountain valley. It uses the euro without being in the European Union. There is no airport, and no train reaches the country, the residence routes require serious money rather than a job, the capital is a traffic-heavy shopping strip rather than an attractive town, and Catalan or Spanish is close to necessary for daily life. The country also has no army, no airport and no railway, and manages the highest life expectancy in the world, which is an odd combination of facts. The valley traps its own air in winter, and traffic through a narrow corridor with mountains on both sides produces days when the pollution is worse than the setting implies. Hospital care is good for a country this size, though anything highly specialised goes to Toulouse or Barcelona under arrangement. Housing pressure is the other structural problem, since a large share of the stock is second homes and the people who staff the ski season struggle to find anywhere at all.
andorralavella.whoFor: Serious skiing or walking, either on a Schengen allowance or through the residence rules and their cost, and a three-hour bus to the nearest airport. The tax position matters only if you actually establish residence. This is a town rather than a city, Spanish or Catalan is required for daily life, and the low tax rates that Andorra is known for apply to residents rather than to visitors, which is a distinction worth understanding before the accountant does. Cyclists have the clearest case of anybody. The climbs out of this valley are among the hardest in professional road racing, and the peloton comes here to train rather than only to compete. The school system here runs Andorran, French and Spanish streams in parallel, which turns choosing one into a genuine decision for an arriving family rather than a formality to be signed off. Anyone who wants the Pyrenees without the residence problem should look at the Spanish side around La Seu d'Urgell or the French side at Ax-les-Thermes, both within an hour, both far cheaper to live in, and both with the same mountains out of the window.

monaco.costOfLiving: Budget around $5,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Monaco, which makes it by a distance the most expensive place on this site. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $3,500 to $5,000 and that is the ordinary market rather than the top of it: Monaco has the highest property prices per square metre in the world. Groceries and restaurants are priced for the residents, though the market at La Condamine and a short trip into France are both considerably cheaper. There is no income tax for residents other than French nationals. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The obvious economy is geographic. Beausoleil begins at the top of the hill and is in France, with rents a fraction of Monegasque ones and a five-minute walk to the border, which is how a large share of the people who work in the principality actually live. Doing that forfeits the tax position entirely. Inside Monaco, a parking space is bought or rented separately and costs what a flat does in many European cities. Agency fees and several months of deposit are standard, and landlords select tenants rather than the other way round.
monaco.whereToWork: Monaco's infrastructure is as good as anywhere in Europe: fibre throughout, comprehensive 5G, and a state that has invested in being an early adopter of network technology. Power is entirely reliable. There is coworking, aimed largely at the financial and yachting sectors. French is the official language and the language of administration, with Italian and English both widely spoken given the international population; a majority of residents are not Monegasque. The principality sits in central European time and functions as part of the French Riviera economy. Anyone working with London should note the one-hour offset, which makes a British afternoon and a Monegasque one almost entirely overlapping. The professional world here is narrower than the infrastructure suggests, and it concentrates in a handful of sectors: private banking and wealth management, the yachting industry, motorsport and a growing sports-business cluster. Anyone outside those will find the local network of limited use and is better off treating Monaco as a place to work from rather than a place to work in. The rhythm follows the Riviera's, which means the principality empties of its business population in August and fills up with everyone else.
monaco.gettingAround: Monaco is two square kilometres and can be crossed on foot in half an hour, though it is built up a steep hillside and the walk involves a network of public lifts and escalators that residents use constantly and visitors rarely find. Buses cover the principality. There is a railway station, entirely underground, with frequent trains along the coast to Nice in twenty minutes and Ventimiglia in Italy. Nice airport is thirty minutes by road or seven minutes by the helicopter shuttle, which is a genuinely normal way to arrive here. The lifts are the thing to learn first, because they are public, free and open long hours, and they turn a punishing gradient into a flat city. A bike share is shared with the neighbouring French communes. Driving is the option to avoid: the streets are narrow, one-way and frequently closed for events, and public parking is expensive even by local standards. A coastal path runs west towards Cap d'Ail, which is the pleasantest way out of the principality on foot and takes about an hour to reach the first proper beach.
monaco.visas: Monaco is not in the European Union but is in the Schengen area in practice, with its border controls handled by France under a long-standing arrangement, so Schengen rules and Schengen day counts apply exactly as they would in France. There is no remote work visa. Residence requires proving accommodation in the principality, which given the property market is the real barrier, along with a substantial deposit with a Monaco bank, generally several hundred thousand dollars. The tax advantage applies to residents and to nobody else. Anyone considering residence should also budget for the annual renewal process, which requires demonstrating continued means and occupancy of the property. The residence card runs in stages, a first card of one year renewed annually, then longer terms and eventually a ten-year card for those who stay, and each renewal tests presence rather than paperwork alone: a holder who is rarely here can lose it. The exclusion of French nationals from the tax position is not an administrative quirk but a bilateral treaty dating from the 1960s, and it has no workaround. Applicants from outside the European Union need a French long-stay visa before they can apply at all.
monaco.bestTime: May to September is the warm half, with daytime temperatures in the high twenties and the Mediterranean swimmable from June. Two events dominate the calendar and both fill every room in the principality and along the coast: the Rolex Masters tennis in April and the Formula One Grand Prix over a weekend in late May, when the streets become the circuit and the whole place is closed to ordinary traffic. Winter is mild, around thirteen degrees, and the principality is noticeably quieter and cheaper. The Monaco Yacht Show in late September is the third of the events that fills the principality and is the largest of its kind anywhere. The Grand Prix needs a decision rather than a shrug. Grandstand seats are expensive and sell out far ahead, the free viewing spots on the Rock fill hours before the cars run, and accommodation along the whole coast prices up for the week, so anyone here for other reasons should either commit to it or leave. Winter has an advantage beyond the price: the ski resorts of the southern Alps are inside two hours, so a morning on snow and an afternoon by the sea is an ordinary thing to do.
monaco.prosCons: Monaco has the lowest crime rate in the world, no income tax for residents, a Mediterranean climate, the Oceanographic Museum that Jacques Cousteau ran for thirty years, and the Alps an hour inland. Nice airport is half an hour away with connections everywhere. The cost of accommodation is the entire story here: the residence requirement amounts to proving you have somewhere to live in the most expensive property market on earth, the principality is very small, and the social scene is narrow and heavily weighted towards wealth. The principality has also reclaimed a substantial part of its territory from the sea, and continues to, which is the only way it can grow at all. The principality is a permanent building site, since the only directions it can grow are upward and out into the sea, so construction noise and hoardings are a constant somewhere in view. And it is among the most closely watched places in the world, with dense camera coverage and a very high ratio of police to residents, which is precisely why the crime figures read as they do and which some people find reassuring and others find airless.
monaco.whoFor: Almost nobody reading this site should move here, and it is included because it is one of the few places whose figures are worth seeing plainly. As a base for ninety days on a Schengen allowance it is possible and expensive. As a residence it requires capital rather than income. Cost of living, a community to join and physical space are three things Monaco has arranged its entire existence around not providing to anybody arriving without means. Anyone drawn to the Riviera should look at Nice or Menton, both of which are ten minutes away and a different economy. Where it does make sense is narrow and specific: someone whose work is already in the yachting, motorsport or private banking worlds, or a family with the capital for whom the tax position and the safety together justify the property cost. For everyone else the useful version of this place is a day at a time from Nice or Menton, which costs a train ticket, shows you the whole principality in an afternoon and settles the question. Anyone treating the tax position as the reason should take advice on their own country's rules first, since residence here does not by itself end an obligation elsewhere.

vaduz.costOfLiving: Budget around $3,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Vaduz, which reflects Swiss prices without Swiss scale. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $1,600 to $2,400, and the rental market is very tight because the country has forty thousand people and strict planning rules. Groceries are Swiss-priced, which is to say among the highest in Europe, though many residents shop over the border in Austria where the same basket costs considerably less. The Swiss franc is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Health insurance is compulsory and privately purchased on the Swiss model, a substantial monthly cost that no rent figure includes, and it is the single biggest omission in any naive comparison with a European Union country. Personal tax rates are low by regional standards, which partly offsets it for anyone actually resident. Cross-border shopping has limits worth knowing, since there are allowances on what may be brought back duty free and Swiss customs rules apply here. The buses across the border are cheap and frequent enough to make the trip routine.
vaduz.whereToWork: Liechtenstein has the infrastructure of a wealthy Alpine state: fibre throughout, comprehensive mobile coverage, entirely reliable power, and a financial sector that requires all of it. There is very little coworking, because the country has almost no visiting professional population. German is the official language and Alemannic dialect is what people actually speak, which is difficult even for German speakers; English works in business and banking. The country sits in central European time and functions economically as part of the Swiss and Austrian Rhine valley. Anyone working with London should note the one-hour offset, which leaves a British and a Liechtenstein working day almost entirely aligned. The economy is more industrial than the banking reputation suggests, and that is the more interesting fact about it. Liechtenstein has one of the highest ratios of industrial output to population anywhere, anchored by a handful of engineering and dental-materials firms with global reach. More people commute in to work each day than live in the country, mostly from Switzerland and Austria, which is why the roads are busy at eight in the morning and the towns are quiet again by nine in the evening.
vaduz.gettingAround: Vaduz has around five thousand inhabitants and can be walked end to end in twenty minutes. Liechtenstein has no airport and no railway station of any consequence, though the Austrian line clips the northern corner. Buses run frequently within the country and across the border to Buchs and Sargans in Switzerland and Feldkirch in Austria, and they are how almost everyone travels. Zurich airport is around ninety minutes by train and bus. Malbun, the small ski area, is half an hour up the valley. The Rhine footbridge to Sevelen in Switzerland is a covered wooden crossing and one of the pleasanter ways to leave the country on foot. The bus network is the thing to understand, since it is effectively the national transport system: one operator runs it, a monthly pass is inexpensive by regional standards, and the timetable is dense enough that a car is genuinely optional here in a way it is not across most of the Alps. The Rhine cycle route runs the length of the country on a flat separated path, which makes the whole of Liechtenstein rideable in an afternoon and is much the best way to see it.
vaduz.visas: Liechtenstein is not in the European Union but is in the European Economic Area and in the Schengen area, so Schengen rules and day counts apply. It is also in a customs and currency union with Switzerland. There is no remote work visa. Residence is genuinely difficult: the country operates a strict annual quota on residence permits for European Economic Area nationals, allocated partly by lottery, and permits for everyone else are rarer still. This is the hardest country in Europe to move to legally. Anyone counting Schengen days should note that Liechtenstein is inside the area, so time here counts exactly as time in Switzerland or Austria would. The quota is small enough to be worth stating plainly: a few dozen permits a year against a resident population of forty thousand, which is why that population grows so slowly. The route most people take instead is to live over the border and commute in, which requires none of this and takes twenty minutes. Family reunification is the other realistic path, and between the two of them they account for most new arrivals who do settle.
vaduz.bestTime: June to September is the walking season, with the high paths above Malbun and Steg open, alpine flowers and daytime temperatures in the low twenties. December to March brings snow and a small but genuine ski area at Malbun, which is uncrowded because almost nobody outside the region knows it exists. The Rhine valley floor where Vaduz sits gets fog and inversions through the winter, so the mountain villages are often above the cloud when the capital is under it. National Day on the fifteenth of August is the one big public event. National Day is unusual enough to plan around: the prince invites the entire country up to the castle grounds for a drink, which is among the few occasions anywhere that a head of state does anything like it. For walkers, the Fuerstensteig is the classic route, a cliff path with fixed cables that opens once the snow has gone, usually from June. May and October are quiet, cheap and often clear, with the valley fog not yet settled and the lower paths already open.
vaduz.prosCons: Liechtenstein is safe, orderly, wealthy and spectacularly located, with the Alps rising directly behind the Rhine valley and walking paths from the capital into the mountains. The infrastructure is Swiss-standard and the country is small enough to know completely. It is very expensive, and there is essentially nothing at all to do after dark, the residence quota makes moving here close to impossible, and Vaduz is a town of five thousand people rather than a city, with all that implies for company and choice. The prince's castle above the town is also a private residence rather than a museum, so it can be walked to and not entered. The Kunstmuseum holds a serious modern collection, and the princely art collection is among the most important in private hands anywhere. And the constitutional arrangement is a genuine curiosity: after a referendum in 2003 the prince holds veto powers unusual for a European monarch, which makes this the most politically powerful royal house on the continent, and a subject locals discuss with far more nuance than a visitor expects.
vaduz.whoFor: Private banking or the trust sector with a reason to be here, or a walker spending a Schengen allowance in a beautiful and largely unvisited corner of the Alps. It works for weeks rather than years, because the residence system is built to keep the population where it is. Settling here is close to impossible by design, since residence permits are allocated by lottery in tiny numbers, the costs are Swiss, and a social life would have to be conducted across the border. Sargans and Feldkirch, both twenty minutes away, are where most people actually go out. Walkers on the Rhine or the Alpine passes have a practical reason to stop, because Liechtenstein's marked paths run straight into the Swiss and Austrian networks without a break at either border. For most visitors the right shape is a base in Feldkirch or Sargans, both cheaper and better connected, with the country walked and ridden from there, which costs a fraction and loses nothing at all. It is small enough that staying inside it confers no real advantage beyond the address. Anyone who wants the novelty can still buy a passport stamp at the tourist office for a couple of francs, which is the only place in Europe that sells one.

torshavn.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Torshavn, which is expensive and reflects a North Atlantic archipelago that imports nearly everything except fish and lamb. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $900 to $1,400 and the rental market is tight, since the islands have fifty-four thousand people and a housing shortage. Groceries are Nordic-priced and eating out is expensive. Heating is a substantial year-round line rather than a winter one. The Danish krone is the currency, issued locally as Faroese notes. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The sub-sea tunnels are tolled and the charges are billed automatically to the vehicle, so a car used between islands accumulates a monthly bill worth budgeting for. Alcohol is sold only through the state monopoly and is expensive even by Nordic standards. And ordering from Denmark, which is how a good deal of shopping gets done, attracts handling on arrival that removes part of the saving. Set against all that, the local lamb and fish are outstanding and cheap, and much of the heating comes from local hydro.
torshavn.whereToWork: The Faroes are among the best-connected small territories anywhere: submarine cables to Denmark and Iceland, fibre to essentially every household, and mobile coverage through a network of sub-sea tunnels that link the main islands. Speeds are high and reliable. Power is reliable and increasingly wind and hydro. There is a small coworking presence in Torshavn. Faroese is the language of daily life and Danish is taught throughout; English is widely and comfortably spoken, particularly by anyone under fifty. Anyone working with the United Kingdom will find the islands on the same clock through the year, which is a smaller adjustment than the geography suggests. The tunnels also carry mobile signal, so a drive between islands does not drop a call. The economy behind all that infrastructure is narrow. Fishing and salmon farming account for the overwhelming majority of exports and the public sector employs much of the rest, so the professional network here is small and centred on those. What it means for a visiting worker is that the connection is excellent and the local market is not, which is the right way round for anyone bringing their own income with them.
torshavn.gettingAround: Torshavn is small and its centre, including the turf-roofed peninsula of Tinganes where the government has sat since the Viking age, is walkable in half an hour. The islands are connected by a remarkable network of sub-sea tunnels, one of which contains the world's first undersea roundabout, along with ferries and helicopters run as public transport at subsidised fares. Buses within Torshavn are free. Vagar airport is around forty-five minutes away by road and tunnel, with flights to Copenhagen, Reykjavik and a handful of European cities. The helicopter service to the outlying islands is subsidised as public transport and is one of the cheapest scheduled helicopter flights anywhere. The helicopter has rules that catch visitors. Seats are limited, residents have priority, and the routes exist to serve the islands rather than to sightsee, so a same-day return on the same route is generally not permitted and a trip out usually means a ferry back. Weather cancels all of it regularly. On foot, many of the best walks cross private land and a fee is now charged at several of the well-known sites, which is a change from a few years ago and is clearly signposted.
torshavn.visas: The Faroe Islands are an autonomous territory of Denmark but are not in the European Union and not in the Schengen area, which is the detail that catches almost everyone out: a Schengen visa does not admit you here, and time spent here does not count against a Schengen allowance. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a Faroese residence permit, which is administered separately from the Danish system. Anyone flying via Copenhagen should note that the Faroe leg is treated as an external border crossing despite both being Danish territory. A practical consequence of that border: carry a passport rather than a national identity card even when travelling from Denmark, since this is an external crossing and the checks are real. Routing matters too, because the islands are also reachable from Edinburgh and Reykjavik depending on the season, and arriving from somewhere other than Denmark avoids a Schengen entry and exit entirely, which is worth planning for anyone watching that allowance closely.
torshavn.bestTime: May to September is the practical window, with long days, temperatures in the low teens and the puffin colonies at Mykines occupied between roughly May and August. The Faroes have some of the most changeable weather anywhere: locals say you can experience all four seasons in an afternoon and they are not exaggerating, with fog, sun and horizontal rain in the same hour. Winter is dark, wet and windy rather than cold, rarely below freezing, with storms that close the tunnels and cancel flights. The Olavsoka festival at the end of July, marking the opening of parliament, is the largest gathering of the year and fills Torshavn entirely. Daylight swings hard, from about nineteen hours in June to five in December, and the summer light is what makes a trip here feel longer than it is. Mykines has a season of its own, since the ferry runs only in the summer months and the island closes to visitors outside them. For anyone flexible, late August and early September hold most of the light with fewer people and lower fares, and the G! Festival in July puts a very good music weekend on a beach in the north.
torshavn.prosCons: The Faroe Islands are eighteen basalt islands rising vertically out of the North Atlantic, with sea cliffs, grass-roofed houses, a waterfall that falls off a cliff into the ocean at Gasadalur and some of the emptiest landscape in Europe. The connectivity is excellent, the country is exceptionally safe, and English works everywhere. The weather is genuinely difficult and the prices are high with it, there are almost no trees and very little daylight in winter, and the grindadrap whale hunt is a real thing that visitors should read about rather than discover. On the whale hunt, the facts rather than the argument. The grindadrap is a non-commercial drive hunt of pilot whales, the meat is distributed within the community, it is regulated under Faroese law, and it is not a tourist event or something a visitor will stumble into, though it can happen at short notice and is confronting to see. Opinion within the islands is not monolithic either. Separately, healthcare is good and Danish-standard, with anything specialist meaning a flight to Denmark.
torshavn.whoFor: A photographer, a walker, or anyone who genuinely likes weather rather than merely tolerating it, and whose work benefits from excellent connectivity in an extremely quiet place. The islands are outside Schengen, which makes them useful for anyone managing a European day count. Sun is scarce at this latitude, the population of the whole country would fill a small town, and no scene of any description has ever formed in the islands. Anyone considering a winter stay should understand that the darkness and the wind are the defining experience rather than a footnote. Fishing and sailing are what these islands are organised around. The waters rank among the most productive in the North Atlantic, and the harbours are working ones rather than marinas dressed up for visitors. Iceland is not really the same choice at all. Iceland has the volume of tourism, the range of landscape and the flights, while the Faroes are smaller, greener, emptier and considerably less prepared for visitors, which is the whole appeal for some people and the objection for others. A stay of a few weeks suits most, since the islands can be covered thoroughly in that time and what follows is repetition rather than discovery.

nuuk.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Nuuk, which is expensive and reflects a town of nineteen thousand people that everything must be shipped or flown to. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $1,100 to $1,700 and housing is genuinely scarce, with waiting lists that are a standing feature of Greenlandic life. Groceries are Nordic-priced with an Arctic freight premium on top, and fresh produce is limited and expensive. Heating runs all year. The Danish krone is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Eating out is expensive enough that most people do it rarely, and the handful of restaurants in town are priced accordingly. The supermarkets carry a narrower range than a European shopper expects, and the price of anything fresh reflects how far it has flown. Local fish and, in season, game from the fjord are the exception and are genuinely good value bought at the market. Alcohol is heavily taxed. The largest hidden cost of a Greenland stay is usually the flying: one trip north to see anything beyond the capital can cost more than a week of accommodation.
nuuk.whereToWork: Greenland's connectivity has improved substantially with submarine cable to Iceland and Canada, and fibre reaches Nuuk at workable speeds, though prices are high and capacity outside the main towns is limited. Mobile coverage exists in the settlements and nowhere between them. Power is reliable and largely hydroelectric. There is a small amount of coworking. Greenlandic is the official language and Danish is universally taught; English is widely spoken among younger people and in business, which makes Nuuk considerably easier than its remoteness suggests. Anyone working with Europe should note that Greenland sits several hours behind, which makes a European afternoon into a Greenlandic morning. Data plans still carry caps that a video-heavy working day can reach, so it is worth checking the limit rather than assuming the fibre speed tells the whole story. Katuaq, the cultural centre, and the university are the two places in town with dependable public seating and power for a working afternoon. The compensation for the time zone is a very long uninterrupted morning: European colleagues do not come online until the middle of the Greenlandic day, which makes the first half of it the most productive stretch most people find anywhere.
nuuk.gettingAround: Nuuk is compact enough to walk across in forty minutes and has a small bus network. The important fact about Greenland is that there are no roads between towns, anywhere in the country: every journey beyond the immediate area is by aircraft, helicopter or boat, and weather cancels all three regularly. Nuuk's new international airport opened in late 2024, giving the capital direct flights from Copenhagen for the first time and ending decades of routing everyone through Kangerlussuaq. Ilulissat, with its UNESCO-listed icefjord, is a further flight north and is the trip most visitors add to a Nuuk stay. Build buffer days around any internal flight, because a cancellation for weather is normal rather than exceptional and the next seat may be days away. The coastal ferry is the slower alternative along the west coast in the ice-free months and is a journey in its own right. In town, taxis are plentiful and cheap by local standards. Ice underfoot is the real winter hazard, and studded overshoes are what residents wear from roughly November; the mountain behind the town, Store Malene, is walkable straight from the last streets in summer.
nuuk.visas: Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark but is not in the European Union, having left in 1985, and is not in the Schengen area. A Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance, which is the detail that matters most for planning. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a Greenlandic residence permit, administered separately from Denmark's. Anyone flying via Copenhagen should note that the Greenland leg is an external border crossing, with passport control in both directions. The consequence people actually use is the reset: a stay in Greenland does not consume Schengen days, so it can sit inside a longer European itinerary as genuine time off the clock. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a visitor stay sits in the same unlegislated grey area as most places, and is not the same thing as taking Greenlandic work, which needs a permit. Health cover is worth checking closely, since a European health card does not extend here and evacuation from Greenland is expensive in a way few policies anticipate.
nuuk.bestTime: June to August is the summer, with temperatures around ten degrees, very long days and the fjords ice-free and navigable, and it is when almost all visitors come. September to April brings the northern lights, which are visible from Nuuk on clear nights through the whole dark half of the year. Winter is cold but moderated by the sea, sitting around minus eight in Nuuk rather than the extremes further north. Ice conditions rather than temperature govern what is possible in any given month. Nuuk sits just below the Arctic Circle, so there is no true midnight sun here, though June nights never get properly dark. March and April make up the season most residents would recommend and most visitors miss: the light has come back fully, the snow is still good, and the aurora is still visible on a clear night, which is a combination the summer cannot offer. Whales are in the fjord from roughly June to September. Autumn storms are severe and can shut the airport for days at a time. Mosquitoes are a real nuisance inland in July, though far less so on the coast at Nuuk itself.
nuuk.prosCons: Nuuk sits at the mouth of one of the largest fjord systems on earth, with icebergs drifting past the town, whales in the fjord in summer and the northern lights overhead for half the year. It is the world's northernmost capital and, since 2024, directly reachable from Europe. Greenlandic culture is living rather than preserved. It is expensive, and housing is genuinely hard to find, the winter darkness is severe indeed, and no road connects the town to anywhere else, which shapes every plan you might make. Greenland is also the largest island in the world with one of the smallest populations, at around fifty-six thousand people across two million square kilometres. Nuuk is also a small town in all the ways that follow from the number: a handful of restaurants, limited shopping, and a social world in which anonymity is not really available. Greenland carries real social difficulties that a visitor should not pretend away, and they are discussed more openly here than outsiders expect. What the town gives back is a scale at which a newcomer can actually become known within a single season, which is rare anywhere.
nuuk.whoFor: A real reason to be in the Arctic, whether research, photography or a long-held pull towards it, work that tolerates weather-dependent travel, and accommodation arranged before arrival rather than after. The new airport has made a short stay far more practical than it was. Greenlandic prices defeat a budget immediately, the winter takes the daylight away almost entirely, and there is no road to the next town from here or from anywhere else in the country: every journey between settlements is a boat or a plane. Self-government is being worked out here in real time rather than settled. Greenland has been steadily taking powers back from Denmark since 1979, and the argument about how far that goes is a live one in every election. A first visit is better kept short and timed for the light, because whether the Arctic suits you is not a decision that can be made in advance. It rewards people content with a small number of very good days and long stretches of weather in between, and it suits anyone whose outdoor life is hiking, sea kayaking or skiing rather than anything that needs a crowd. Anyone needing constant variety, warm evenings outdoors or cheap escapes will not last a winter.

gibraltar.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Gibraltar, which is expensive and reflects six and a half square kilometres with thirty-four thousand people on it. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $1,400 to $2,000 and the housing market is one of the tightest in Europe, because there is no land. Groceries are cheaper than the United Kingdom on some things and dearer on others, and a great many residents shop in Spain, where the same basket costs substantially less. The Gibraltar pound trades at par with sterling. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. There is no value added tax, replaced by a lower import duty, which makes fuel, alcohol, tobacco and electronics noticeably cheaper than in Britain or Spain and explains why the frontier queue runs in both directions. Income tax rates sit below the United Kingdom's, with neither capital gains nor inheritance tax levied at all. A parking space is a genuine expense in return, on a peninsula with no room, and the arbitrage most residents actually use is to earn in Gibraltar and live in Spain, where the same rent buys several times the space.
gibraltar.whereToWork: Gibraltar's economy runs on online gaming, financial services and shipping, all of which require serious connectivity, and it has it: fibre throughout, comprehensive mobile coverage and reliable power. There is a small coworking market. English is the official language and universally used, with Spanish widely spoken and llanito, the local mix of Andalusian Spanish and English, heard constantly. The territory sits in central European time, an hour ahead of the United Kingdom, which is a small but real consideration for anyone working British hours.
