Anyone considering the gaming sector should know it is the territory's largest private employer and the reason much of the infrastructure exists at all. Office space is scarce enough that the government has reclaimed land to build more, and rents reflect it, which is why so many smaller operations run from home or a shared desk. The workforce crosses the frontier daily in large numbers, mostly Spanish nationals from the surrounding towns, and that flow is the thing every business here plans around. Regulation is itself a draw for the gaming and insurance sectors, since Gibraltar licenses quickly and supervises seriously, and that reputation is the asset the territory guards most carefully.
gibraltar.gettingAround: Gibraltar is walkable end to end, though the Rock rises 426 metres above the town and getting up it means the cable car, a taxi tour or a serious walk. There is a small bus network. The airport runway crosses Winston Churchill Avenue, the main road to Spain, so the road closes whenever an aircraft moves, which is exactly as strange as it sounds. The land border with Spain at La Linea is a few minutes' walk from the centre, and the queue to cross it can be anything from nothing to two hours. A road tunnel now runs beneath the runway, which has taken much of the sting out of the closures, though the queue at the frontier itself is unaffected and remains the real variable. Crossing on foot or by scooter is far quicker than by car at almost any hour, which is what most commuters do. Algeciras, twenty minutes around the bay in Spain, has the ferries to Tangier and Ceuta, so Africa is genuinely a day trip from here rather than a notional one.
gibraltar.visas: Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory outside both the European Union and the Schengen area, and its status since Brexit has been under negotiation for years without a concluded treaty, which means the arrangements at the Spanish border can change. British citizens have the right of abode. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for short visits. There is no remote work visa. Anyone planning to live here and cross into Spain regularly should follow the current position, since a Schengen day count may or may not apply depending on how the border is being run. Working here is a separate question from entering. Non-British nationals need a Gibraltar work permit, obtained by the employer rather than the worker, and European Union nationals lost their automatic right after Brexit along with everyone else. Residence for the wealthy runs through Category 2 status, which caps the tax payable in exchange for approved accommodation and substantial assets, and it is a deliberate policy rather than a loophole. Anyone whose plan depends on the frontier staying open exactly as it is today should treat that as an assumption under active negotiation rather than a settled fact.
gibraltar.bestTime: April to June and September to October are the best months, with warm dry weather in the mid twenties and the migration seasons, when Gibraltar sits directly under one of the busiest bird flyways in the world and raptors cross the strait in thousands. July and August are hot and crowded with day visitors from the Costa del Sol. Winter is mild at around sixteen degrees and wetter, with the levanter, an easterly wind that pins a cloud over the top of the Rock for days at a time. The Barbary macaques on the upper Rock are present year-round and will take anything carried in a bag, which is a warning rather than a charm. The levanter does more than sit on the summit. It also closes the airport with some regularity, so a tight connection out of Gibraltar in an easterly is a gamble and Malaga, ninety minutes up the coast, is the fallback. National Day on the tenth of September fills the streets in red and white and is the one date locals plan around. The raptor migration runs north in spring and south in late summer, and the September crossing is the heavier of the two.
gibraltar.prosCons: Gibraltar is British, English-speaking and sits at the mouth of the Mediterranean with Africa visible across the strait, dolphins in the bay and the only wild monkeys in Europe on the upper Rock. The tax regime is favourable and the professional sector in gaming and finance is real. It is very small, and its housing market is brutal, the border queue into Spain is a daily frustration that recurs, and the unresolved post-Brexit status is a genuine uncertainty rather than a technicality. The Rock is also honeycombed with more than fifty kilometres of military tunnels, considerably more tunnel than road, most of it dug during the Second World War. Health care runs through the territory's own authority and is good for routine work, with anything complex referred to Spain or the United Kingdom under arrangement. Socially the place is small enough that everyone is known, which people either value or find airless. And the territory keeps growing outward rather than only upward: a substantial share of the flat land here did not exist a few decades ago and was reclaimed from the bay, because it is the only direction left.
gibraltar.whoFor: Online gaming, shipping or financial services, or a British passport and a wish for Mediterranean weather with British institutions and English throughout. Birdwatchers get one of the great migration crossings in the world. Six and a half square kilometres is genuinely small and the walls close in on some people within a fortnight. The land border is the other daily fact, since a bad morning at the frontier can cost two hours and there is no alternative route. Most people who work here live in Spain and cross daily, which is worth understanding before committing. Divers do better here than the setting suggests. The bay holds a substantial number of wrecks, and the water on this side of the strait runs noticeably warmer than the Atlantic on the other. Anyone comparing English-speaking Mediterranean bases will find Malta larger, cheaper and inside the European Union, with a similar gaming and finance economy and none of the border question, which makes it the obvious alternative to weigh. British-curriculum schooling and a level of safety that surprises visitors are what a family gets, and the commute is short enough to be a real quality-of-life argument to anybody who has endured a long one.

douglasiom.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Douglas, which is broadly comparable to a prosperous British provincial town with a tighter housing market. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $900 to $1,400. Groceries are close to United Kingdom prices, since the supply chain is the same, though everything crosses the Irish Sea and the freight shows in some categories. The island has its own income tax with a cap on total liability, which is why a number of high earners live here. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Housing is the pressure point rather than the price level. Supply is genuinely tight, the government has been trying to grow the population for years, and a rental search takes longer than most arrivals plan for. Rates are charged instead of council tax and are modest. The recurring cost that catches newcomers is travel: a household visiting Britain regularly will spend a great deal on ferries and flights across a year, and fares rise steeply for the TT fortnight. Healthcare runs on the island's own system, with a reciprocal arrangement covering United Kingdom residents.
douglasiom.whereToWork: The Isle of Man has invested heavily in connectivity because its economy depends on it: the island hosts substantial e-gaming, financial services and insurance sectors, fibre reaches most of Douglas and the main towns at solid speeds, and mobile coverage is comprehensive. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking market. English is the only language required, though Manx Gaelic is taught in schools and appears on signage. The island keeps the same time as the United Kingdom, which removes any offset for anyone working British hours. The island also runs its own top-level internet domain and its own postal service, which is the kind of independence that surprises people who assume it is part of Britain. The professional world is small and interconnected in a way that is an advantage and a constraint at once: a newcomer can meet the relevant people in a sector within weeks, and a reputation, in either direction, travels the island quickly. Most employment sits in Douglas itself, so commutes are short and the working population is concentrated. Anyone arriving without a job should know that employers handle the work permit, which makes the job the gateway rather than the paperwork.
douglasiom.gettingAround: Douglas is built along a two-mile sweep of bay with a promenade the length of it, and the centre is walkable. The island has a genuinely unusual transport heritage still in daily use: a horse-drawn tram along the Douglas promenade, the Manx Electric Railway north to Ramsey, the Snaefell Mountain Railway to the island's only peak, and a steam railway south to Port Erin, all of them Victorian and all still running. Buses cover the rest. The ferry to Liverpool and Heysham takes a few hours and the airport has connections across Britain and Ireland. Parts of the island outside the towns carry no general speed limit, a fact that draws a certain kind of visitor and that residents treat with far more caution than outsiders expect. The heritage railways run to a seasonal timetable rather than all year, so they are transport in summer and closed attractions in winter. A car is optional in Douglas itself and close to necessary anywhere else on the island, and the sea crossing is exposed enough that a winter sailing can be cancelled at short notice, which is worth remembering before booking a tight onward connection on the other side.
douglasiom.visas: The Isle of Man is a Crown Dependency, not part of the United Kingdom and never part of the European Union, though it sits within the Common Travel Area with Britain and Ireland. British and Irish citizens can live and work here freely. Everyone else needs the island's own immigration permission, which is administered separately from the United Kingdom's and includes a work permit system. There is no remote work visa. Arrivals from Britain and Ireland face no routine border control, which is the practical consequence of the Common Travel Area. The point most people get wrong is that a United Kingdom visa confers no right to be here. The island runs its own immigration rules, and someone with indefinite leave to remain in Britain still needs Manx permission to work. The routes that exist are employer-led, with the permit tied to a specific job, and there is a separate business migration route for those establishing a company. Tax residence is determined by presence on the island rather than by the permit, and national insurance is administered separately from Britain's while broadly mirroring it.
douglasiom.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable half, with daytime temperatures in the high teens, long days and the coastal paths at their best. The calendar is dominated by one event: the Isle of Man TT, a motorcycle road race held on closed public roads over a fortnight in late May and early June, which fills every bed on the island and is the reason many people have heard of the place at all. Winter is mild but wet and windy, sitting around seven degrees, with ferry cancellations in a serious blow. Tynwald Day on the fifth of July is the national day, when the parliament meets outdoors at St John's in a ceremony that has run for a thousand years and at which anyone may present a petition. The Festival of Motorcycling in late August is the TT's quieter sibling and fills the island again on a smaller scale. Outside those weeks, late summer into September is the value window: the weather is at its most settled, beds are available, and the coastal path is at its best before the autumn gales arrive.
douglasiom.prosCons: The Isle of Man has the oldest continuous parliament in the world, Tynwald, which has met since around 979, a coastal path running the whole way round the island, Victorian railways still in service, and a genuine financial and e-gaming sector for an island of eighty-four thousand people. It is safe, English-speaking and an hour from Britain. The weather is grey and wet, and the island is small, immigration for non-British arrivals is far from straightforward, and the TT fortnight makes normal life on the island impossible. The island is also a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in its entirety, the only whole nation to hold that designation, which shapes how the countryside is managed. Specialist medical treatment usually means travelling to Liverpool, so a serious diagnosis comes with a travel arrangement attached to it. And the island is small enough socially that privacy is limited and a newcomer stays visible for a long time, which suits people who want to belong somewhere and grates on anyone who came to be left alone.
douglasiom.whoFor: E-gaming, insurance or fund administration, or a British or Irish passport and a wish for a quiet, safe island with real institutions and no immigration friction. The tax cap matters only to genuinely high earners. Sunshine is not an Irish Sea speciality, anybody outside the Common Travel Area needs a work permit before anything else is possible, and arriving during the TT without a booking made a year ahead means finding nowhere at all to sleep. Walkers can circle the entire island on the Raad ny Foillan coastal path in about a week, which is an unusually complete thing to be able to say. Motorcyclists need no explanation at all. The Calf of Man at the southern tip is a bird observatory reachable by boat in summer. Anyone comparing the Crown Dependencies is choosing between similar tax positions and very different characters: Jersey and Guernsey are warmer, smaller and closer to France, while this island is wilder, cheaper and better connected to northern England. Families settle well here. Anyone considering a move should come outside the TT and outside high summer, when the place is simply itself and the weather is doing what it does for most of the year.

sanmarino.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in San Marino, which is broadly similar to the surrounding Italian region and slightly cheaper on some things because the republic sets its own indirect taxes. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $600 to $1,000, and much of the affordable housing is in the lower towns of Borgo Maggiore and Dogana rather than on the mountain itself. Groceries are Italian-priced, which is to say reasonable. The euro is the currency although San Marino is not in the European Union. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The republic levies a single-stage import tax called the monofase instead of value added tax, which is why fuel, tobacco and some electronics come out below Italian shelf prices while most other things do not. Property purchase by non-residents is restricted, so buying is not the shortcut into the country that it is in some small states. Renting is done through local agencies and word of mouth, and the stock is small enough that anything decent moves before it is advertised widely.
sanmarino.whereToWork: San Marino's connectivity is good: fibre reaches the populated areas at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with the surrounding Italian networks also reaching most of the republic. Power is reliable. There is very little coworking, since the republic has almost no visiting professional population. Italian is the only language of daily life and administration; English is limited outside the tourism economy on the mountain. The republic sits in central European time and functions economically as part of Emilia-Romagna. Anyone working with the rest of Europe will find no offset at all, since the republic keeps central European time like the country entirely surrounding it. The economy is more industrial than the tourist shops on the ridge suggest, with ceramics, furniture, packaging and precision engineering employing a large share of residents, and thousands of Italians crossing in each morning to work in it. The banking sector went through a serious crisis and restructuring in the 2010s and is much diminished. The republic passed blockchain and tokenisation legislation to attract digital business, which has produced more announcements than companies so far.
sanmarino.gettingAround: San Marino is built on and around Monte Titano, and the historic city on top is entirely pedestrian, reached by road, by a cable car from Borgo Maggiore below, or on foot up a serious climb. The republic has no airport and no railway; the old electric line from Rimini closed in 1944 and its tunnels are still visible. Buses run to Rimini in about fifty minutes, which is where the nearest station and the coast are. Bologna airport is around two hours away. Rimini's beaches are close enough that a great many Sammarinese treat the Adriatic coast as their summer, and the bus runs frequently in season. Getting up the mountain is the daily logistics question, and the answer most residents use is the chain of public lifts and escalators built into the rock beside the multi-storey car parks, which turns a hard climb into a two-minute ride. Parking on the ridge itself is limited and priced accordingly. The bus to Rimini is cheap and frequent, and it is the connection that makes the republic function, since the coast holds the station, the hospital specialists and the airport link.
sanmarino.visas: San Marino is not in the European Union and not formally in Schengen, but it has open borders with Italy on every side and no border controls at all, so in practice reaching it means entering Schengen through Italy and the day count applies there. There is no remote work visa. Residence in San Marino is tightly controlled and generally requires either substantial investment or a genuine employment relationship with a Sammarinese company, and the process is slow. Anyone counting Schengen days should treat time in San Marino as time in Italy, since there is no border and no separate record of entry. The republic negotiated an association agreement with the European Union alongside Andorra and Monaco, which has been years in the making and would change movement and market access if it is ratified, so anyone planning around the current arrangement should watch it. Citizenship comes through descent or, for a spouse, after a long qualifying period measured in decades rather than years. Ordinary residence permits are granted sparingly and are attached to employment or family rather than to means.
sanmarino.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months, with warm dry weather, clear views across to the Adriatic and fewer of the day-trippers who come up from the Rimini beaches in summer. July and August are hot and the mountain is busy. Winter is cold and often in cloud at this altitude, with the city on the ridge frequently sitting above or inside a bank of fog while the plain below is clear, which is either atmospheric or oppressive depending on the day. The Medieval Days festival at the end of July fills the old city with re-enactment and crossbow competitions, which is the republic's largest event. The third of September is the Feast of Saint Marinus and the republic's national day, marking a founding in the year 301 and observed with a formality that a state of thirty thousand people carries off surprisingly well. The Rimini beach season pulls the working population downhill at weekends through July and August, which is precisely when the mountain fills with visitors going the other way, so the two flows pass each other on the same road.
sanmarino.prosCons: San Marino claims to be the oldest surviving sovereign state and the oldest constitutional republic in the world, founded by a stonemason in the fourth century, and its three towers on the ridge of Monte Titano are visible for fifty kilometres. It is safe, cheap by Western European standards, and the views across to the Adriatic are exceptional. It is tiny, Italian is essential here, the historic centre is largely given over to duty-free shops and tourist retail now, and there is no airport or railway. The republic also issues its own stamps and coins, minted in euro but with Sammarinese designs, which are collected far beyond the country itself. Healthcare is the republic's own service, small but well regarded, with an agreement covering treatment in Italy for anything it cannot handle, which in practice means Rimini or Bologna. San Marino keeps no standing army beyond a ceremonial militia and has never been at war in any modern sense, having stayed neutral through both world wars and sheltered a refugee population many times its own size in 1944, which is the fact that most repays looking into.
sanmarino.whoFor: An Italian speaker after a very quiet hilltop base within an hour of the Adriatic coast and two of Bologna, spending a Schengen allowance rather than trying to settle. The republic is more pleasant out of season than its reputation suggests, once the day-trippers have gone. Italian is required, there is no community of foreigners to join in a republic of thirty thousand, and the sovereignty does not translate into an easier residence route than Italy's. If anything the route is narrower, because the numbers admitted are smaller. Cyclists working Emilia-Romagna should build this into the week. The climb up Monte Titano is a serious piece of work, and the descent runs thirty kilometres to the sea without much pedalling. The honest comparison is not with other microstates but with the coast below: Rimini is cheaper, larger, better connected and thirty minutes away, and most of what makes this region worth a stay is down there rather than up here. The mountain earns a stay for the silence and the view, which are real, and for anyone whose work benefits from being somewhere with almost nothing to do in the evening.

libreville.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Libreville, which is expensive for Africa and reflects an oil economy with a small population and heavy import dependence. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200, with Quartier Louis and the areas near the embassies at the top of that. Groceries are expensive and much of what is on the shelves is French. Gabon has consistently ranked among the costlier African capitals for expatriates. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, which removes currency risk entirely. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Gabon has repeatedly appeared near the top of expatriate cost-of-living surveys for Africa, and the reason is structural rather than temporary: a small domestic market, almost no manufacturing and a food supply that arrives by ship. Fibre where available runs $80 to $150 a month for modest speeds, among the worst value on this site. A vehicle is close to essential and fuel, while subsidised, is one of the few genuinely cheap things here.
libreville.whereToWork: Libreville's connectivity is modest: fibre reaches parts of the city and mobile data from Airtel and Moov is the usual answer, with prices high relative to speed. Power cuts happen and any serious office runs a generator. There is very little coworking. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, and English is genuinely rare, which is the main practical filter for working here. The country sits in central European time in the northern winter, which makes it one of the easiest African bases for anyone working European hours. The time zone is the practical advantage worth naming: Gabon runs one hour ahead of GMT year-round, so a London morning is a Libreville morning and the whole European working day is available without either side compromising. Coworking barely exists, so a flat with a generator and a reliable connection is the arrangement to look for rather than a desk. Oil output has been falling for years and the state has pushed hard into timber and manganese instead, banning the export of unprocessed logs to force the milling to happen here. That policy is the reason the industrial zone outside the city exists, and it is where most of the new work is.
libreville.gettingAround: Libreville stretches along the Atlantic coast with the Boulevard du Bord de Mer running its length, and that seafront is the most pleasant part of the city to be in. Shared taxis, hailed by calling out a destination and a price, are the standard way to move and cost very little. Traffic is heavy on the main axes. Leon Mba airport is close to the centre with flights to Paris, Istanbul and across West and Central Africa. The national parks, which are Gabon's real case, are reached by internal flight or a long drive. Reaching the parks is the expense that defines a stay here: Loango is an internal flight to Port-Gentil then a boat and a drive, or a very long road journey, and the lodges are priced accordingly. Ivindo and Lope are reached by the Trans-Gabon railway, which is slow, scenic and the cheapest way into the interior by a wide margin.
libreville.visas: Gabon operates an e-visa system that most nationalities can apply for online before travel, with approval usually returned within a few days and the visa issued on arrival, typically for stays of up to ninety days. A yellow fever certificate is required for entry. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a residence permit arranged through an employer or local sponsor, which is slow. Gabon has changed its entry procedures more than once in recent years, so confirm the current position directly rather than relying on older guidance. Gabon suspended and then restored various entry procedures around the 2023 transition, and airlines have not always tracked the changes, so carrying printed approval matters more here than in most places. The yellow fever certificate is checked properly on arrival rather than waved through. This country belongs to the central African bloc rather than the western one, and the regional passport that lets member-state citizens move freely is of no use to anybody holding another one, so a trip to a neighbouring capital means a second visa arranged in advance rather than a stamp at the border.
libreville.bestTime: Gabon sits on the equator and is hot and humid all year at around thirty degrees. The calendar turns entirely on rain, and there are two dry seasons: a long one from June to September and a short one in December and January, which are the practical windows. The long rains from February to May and the shorter ones in October and November are heavy. The long dry season is also when the beaches at Loango are best for seeing forest elephants and buffalo come out onto the sand, which is Gabon's signature image. The long dry season from June to September is also when the surf picks up on the Atlantic beaches and when the humpbacks pass Gabon's coast, which is a lesser-known migration than the East African one and largely unvisited. Humidity stays high even in the dry months, so the seasons differ in rainfall rather than in comfort.
libreville.prosCons: Gabon protects around eleven per cent of its territory in national parks, created in a single decision in 2002, and the country is nearly ninety per cent forest with a population of two and a half million. Loango National Park has elephants and hippos on Atlantic beaches, which exists nowhere else. Libreville is expensive, French is unavoidable, and the connection is weak, the country has had its share of political instability including a coup in 2023, and reaching the parks requires organisation and money rather than a bus ticket. The country is also one of the few in Africa where forest cover has increased rather than fallen, largely because the oil economy never required logging revenue. The 2023 coup ended fifty-five years of rule by one family and the transition is ongoing, so the political situation is genuinely unsettled rather than merely noted, and anyone planning more than a short stay should be following it rather than assuming stability.
libreville.whoFor: Central African wildlife and the budget to reach it, or work in oil, timber or conservation, which is where the contacts actually are, and French throughout. French is essential, oil-economy prices make Libreville expensive on any budget, and the national parks that justify Gabon on paper are not reachable from the capital in a way that a weekend allows. Read current guidance on Gabon's political situation before planning a long stay rather than after arriving. Anybody researching gorillas or forest elephants comes here by necessity rather than preference, because Gabon holds the largest remaining populations of both anywhere in Central Africa. Carbon markets and forest policy are a live professional reason to be here. Gabon has deliberately made itself the test case for paying a country to leave its forest standing, and a good deal of the international activity around that idea passes through this capital.

freetown.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Freetown, which is genuinely cheap and reflects one of the lower-income countries anywhere. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $500, with Aberdeen and the peninsula near the beaches at the top of that and the central and eastern districts well below. Market food costs very little and Sierra Leonean cooking is good. Imported goods are expensive. The leone was redenominated in 2022, dropping three zeros, so older prices quoted anywhere need checking. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre where it reaches runs $60 to $120 a month for modest speeds and a generator is a normal household cost rather than a precaution. A poda-poda ride across town is well under a dollar and an okada a little more. Rents on the peninsula at Lakka or Tokeh are comparable to Aberdeen and put the beaches at the door rather than an hour away. Aberdeen and Lumley carry a premium for proximity to the international community and the restaurants that serve it.
freetown.whereToWork: Freetown's connectivity is weak: fibre has reached parts of the city and works where it exists, mobile data from Orange and Africell is the common fallback, and neither is fast. Power cuts are frequent and generators are standard in anything serious. There is a small startup and coworking presence, more developed than the country's profile suggests. English is the official language and the medium of education and government, with Krio, an English-based creole, as the lingua franca across the country. That combination makes Sierra Leone far easier for an English speaker than its neighbours. Sierra Leone runs on GMT with no offset at all, which makes it one of the easiest time zones on this site for anyone working with London and comfortable for continental Europe. Orange Money handles most everyday payment and a local SIM registered on arrival is the first practical step. Starlink was licensed in Sierra Leone in 2023 and is now the practical answer for anyone who needs a connection the local network cannot supply, particularly out on the peninsula.
freetown.gettingAround: Freetown sits on a mountainous peninsula and the city climbs steeply from the harbour, which makes it hard going on foot and heavily congested by vehicle. Poda-poda minibuses and okada motorcycle taxis are how most people move and both cost very little. The airport is at Lungi, across the estuary from the city, and reaching it means a ferry, a water taxi or a long drive around, which is the single most awkward piece of logistics in the country and should be planned rather than improvised. The peninsula road south from the city to Tokeh and River Number Two passes a string of beaches and is the best drive in the country. The Lungi water taxi takes about thirty minutes and runs to the flight schedule, while the road around the estuary takes four hours or more, so the crossing is the option rather than the alternative. Missing the last boat means an overnight on the wrong side. Traffic on the single road into the city centre is severe enough that residents plan around it, and a journey of five kilometres can take an hour at peak.
freetown.visas: Sierra Leone requires a visa of most nationalities, available through an e-visa system before travel or on arrival at Lungi airport, typically for thirty days with longer options. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at the immigration department in Freetown. The country is a member of ECOWAS, so regional nationals move freely. Entry procedures have changed several times in recent years, so confirm the current requirement rather than relying on an older account. Anyone travelling on to Guinea or Liberia overland should check those requirements separately, since neither shares an arrangement with Sierra Leone. The e-visa is applied for online and issued as an approval to present on arrival, and airlines check it at boarding. Sierra Leone dropped visa requirements for several African nationalities in recent years as part of a wider continental push.
freetown.bestTime: November to April is the dry season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around thirty and the beaches at their best. The harmattan blows Saharan dust down in December and January. The rains from May to October are among the heaviest in West Africa: Freetown receives well over three metres a year, the mountain slopes above the city are prone to landslides, and the 2017 Regent landslide killed more than a thousand people. Plan around August, which is the wettest month by a distance. Turtles nest on the peninsula beaches between September and March, and Tiwai Island's primate reserve is most accessible in the dry months. Freetown receives around 3,500 millimetres of rain a year, among the highest of any capital city in the world, and the peninsula's mountains are what wring it out of the Atlantic air. Bunce Island in the estuary was a British slave-trading fort and is reached by boat from Freetown, and it remains largely unrestored.
freetown.prosCons: Freetown was founded in 1792 by freed slaves from Nova Scotia and the history is present in the architecture, the Krio language and the Cotton Tree that stood at the centre of the city until it fell in 2023. The peninsula beaches south of the city are as good as anything in West Africa and almost nobody visits them. English works everywhere and costs are very low. The internet is poor here, the airport transfer is genuinely awkward, the infrastructure is limited, and the country is still recovering from a civil war and an Ebola epidemic. Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary sits in the forest above the city and is a genuine rehabilitation centre rather than a zoo, and Sierra Leone made the chimpanzee its national animal in 2019 largely through its advocacy. The Cotton Tree fell in a storm in May 2023 after standing for centuries, and its loss was treated as a national event.
freetown.whoFor: An experienced traveller after an English-speaking West African base at very low cost, with work that can live with a connection that drops, treating the peninsula beaches as the reason to be there. Anyone in development or public health will find a substantial professional network. A first trip to West Africa should not begin here, reliable power is not something the grid provides, and the Lungi airport crossing needs planning before departure rather than on arrival, because it involves water and it does not wait for anybody's flight time. The music is a reason in itself. Sierra Leonean palm-wine guitar and everything that grew out of it remain a living tradition here rather than a recovered one. Climate adaptation is studied here because the city had no choice about learning it. Landslide and flood exposure made Freetown a case study, and the urban tree-planting programme run in response is among the more ambitious anywhere in Africa. Measured against Accra, Freetown is cheaper, considerably harder work and has beaches that Ghana cannot match.

serrekunda.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Serrekunda, which is among the cheapest figures on this site. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $200 to $400, with the coastal strip at Kololi and Bijilo at the top of that and the inland streets well below. Market food is very cheap and the Gambia grows a good deal of its own produce, with the fish from Tanji among the best value anywhere. Imported goods carry a markup. The dalasi has weakened steadily, which helps a visitor. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Landlords usually want six months or a year in advance and in cash, which is the largest single obstacle a new arrival meets and is more negotiable than it first appears. Electricity runs on a prepaid meter and costs more per unit than the low rents would lead you to expect, so a place with air conditioning shifts the monthly figure substantially. Prices along the tourist strip climb from November when the charter flights start and drop again in May, while the inland streets barely move at all.
serrekunda.whereToWork: Connectivity is modest: fibre has reached parts of the coastal strip and mobile data from Africell, QCell and Gamcel is the usual answer, with prices high relative to speed and evening congestion common. Power cuts are frequent and any serious business runs a generator. There is a small coworking presence around the tourist coast. English is the official language and the medium of education and government, with Mandinka, Wolof and Fula the languages of daily life, which makes the Gambia unusually straightforward for an English speaker in a francophone region. The clock is a quiet advantage. The Gambia keeps GMT all year and never shifts, so it lines up exactly with London through the winter and falls an hour behind in the British summer, which is about as frictionless as African time zones get for European work. Buy two SIMs on different networks, because coverage and congestion vary street by street and the evening slowdown is real. An inverter with a decent battery will carry a laptop and a router through most cuts, and that combination is what local businesses use rather than running a generator all day.
serrekunda.gettingAround: Serrekunda is the country's largest town and runs into Bakau, Kololi and the coastal resort strip without much of a break, and the whole area is flat and walkable in parts. Shared taxis and gelly-gelly minibuses cover it cheaply. The Gambia is essentially a strip of land either side of one river, three hundred kilometres long and rarely fifty wide, so most travel is either along the coast or up the river by boat or road. Banjul International airport is twenty minutes away with charter flights from northern Europe. The river trip upcountry to Janjanbureh and the Wassu stone circles takes several days and is the part of the country almost no visitor sees. Taxis come in two kinds and the difference matters: green ones are licensed for tourists and charge several times what the yellow shared taxis ask for the same journey. The ferry across the river mouth from Banjul to Barra is the link to the north bank and to Senegal beyond it, and it runs on a schedule bearing only a loose relationship to its timetable. Roads deteriorate quickly away from the coastal strip, and the rains make some of them impassable.
serrekunda.visas: The Gambia grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries and a number of European states for up to ninety days, with everyone else obtaining a visa on arrival or in advance. The rules vary more by nationality than in most countries, so check yours specifically. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at the immigration department. The country is a member of ECOWAS, so regional nationals move freely, and a yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries. Anyone travelling on to Senegal, which surrounds the Gambia entirely, should note the border crossings have their own hours and their own paperwork. Because Senegal wraps around the country on three sides, almost any overland journey involves leaving and re-entering, and a single-entry Gambian visa will not survive that, so the multiple-entry version is the one to ask for. Extensions are granted at the immigration department in Banjul for a fee and are usually straightforward when applied for before expiry. Longer residence is tied to work or investment and moves slowly, which is why most foreigners here run on repeated visitor entries instead.
serrekunda.bestTime: November to May is the dry season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around thirty-two, low humidity and the charter flights running from Europe. This is also the birdwatching season, and the Gambia's bird list is enormous for a country this size, which is why a substantial share of its visitors carry binoculars. June to October is the wet season, hot and humid with heavy rain, and much of the tourist infrastructure closes entirely. The harmattan brings dust in December and January. Kartong and the southern beaches are quieter than the main strip in any season, and the fish landing at Tanji is worth an early morning. Malaria transmission rises sharply with the rains and stays high into November, so prophylaxis is a conversation with a doctor before departure rather than a decision made on arrival. The Gambia is overwhelmingly Muslim and Ramadan reshapes the working day for a month each year, moving earlier through the calendar as it goes. Marine turtles nest on the southern beaches through the wet months, which is one of the few arguments for coming in the season everyone else avoids.
serrekunda.prosCons: The Gambia is the smallest country in mainland Africa, a strip along one river, and it is genuinely easy: English throughout, a short flight from Europe, very low costs, long Atlantic beaches and some of the best birdwatching on the continent. The internet is weak here, the tourist strip has a well-documented problem with hustling and worse and with sex tourism that visitors should be aware of, the economy is fragile, and there is very little to the country beyond the coast and the river. The Gambia also has one of the highest densities of bird species per square kilometre anywhere, which is why the country's guides are among the best in Africa. Medical facilities are limited, and anything serious means Dakar or a flight to Europe, so evacuation cover is not an optional extra here. The political picture has been considerably calmer since the long dictatorship ended in 2017, and elections since have passed without the upheaval many expected. Set against the hustling on the strip, Gambians away from it have a reputation for hospitality that travellers who get off the coast confirm without being asked.
serrekunda.whoFor: A birdwatcher, or anyone after a very cheap English-speaking West African base within six hours of Europe, with work that copes when the signal comes and goes. The river trips upcountry are the part most visitors miss and the part worth doing. Reliable internet and a professional community are both missing. Anybody staying on the tourist strip should also prepare for persistent approaches from people selling and guiding, which is the single most common complaint visitors make about the country and the one most likely to shape how a month feels. Anybody tracing West African history should know what sits upriver. Juffureh and Kunta Kinteh Island are central to that story and both are reachable and back inside a single day. The single change that most improves a long stay is where you sleep. Taking a place in Fajara, Bakau or one of the inland streets rather than on the resort strip removes most of the friction visitors complain about, and costs less. Dakar is the alternative worth weighing for anyone choosing a West African base, being larger, better connected and home to a real professional scene, though it is francophone and considerably more expensive. Women travelling alone report the coast as manageable but persistent.

djibouti.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Djibouti, which is expensive for the region and reflects a small country that imports almost everything and hosts several foreign military bases whose personnel set the rental market. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $600 to $1,000, with the European Quarter and Heron at the top of that and the Balbala districts far below. Imported food is costly and local produce is limited by the climate. The franc is pegged to the United States dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Fibre runs $100 to $200 a month for modest speeds, among the worst value anywhere on this site, and the state monopoly is the reason. Air conditioning is not optional for most of the year and can add $150 to $300 monthly. The military presence is the structural distortion behind the rental market: French, American, Japanese, Italian and Chinese bases all house personnel here and the rents they support are what an ordinary tenant competes with. Groceries in the French supermarkets are priced for the expatriate and military market and cost several times what the same goods do in Addis Ababa, six hundred kilometres inland by rail.
djibouti.whereToWork: Djibouti sits at the landing point of several of the submarine cables that carry traffic between Europe and Asia, which is a genuinely unusual asset, though the domestic market is a state monopoly and retail prices are high relative to speed. Fibre reaches the city at workable speeds and mobile data covers the populated areas. Power is reliable and expensive. There is very little coworking. French and Arabic are the official languages, Somali and Afar are the languages of daily life, and English is limited outside the military and shipping sectors. Djibouti sits three hours ahead of GMT, which gives a full European overlap and a workable late-afternoon window with the American east coast. The irony of the cable landings is worth naming: some of the world's most important internet infrastructure comes ashore here and almost none of the benefit reaches the domestic retail market. Coworking barely exists and the practical arrangement is an apartment in the European Quarter with its own connection, which is what the international staff here do.
djibouti.gettingAround: Djibouti City is compact and the European Quarter around Place Menelik is walkable, though the heat makes that a morning and evening activity for much of the year. Shared taxis and minibuses cover the city cheaply. The country is small enough to cross in a day: Lac Assal, the lowest point in Africa at 155 metres below sea level, is two hours west, and Lac Abbe's limestone chimneys are a longer drive. The railway to Addis Ababa, rebuilt in 2017, takes around twelve hours. The ferry across the Gulf of Tadjoura to Obock and Tadjoura itself is the pleasanter way to reach the northern coast and the diving. Lac Assal sits in the Afar depression and its salt crust is thick enough to walk on, with the water around ten times saltier than the sea. Lac Abbe's chimneys are on the Ethiopian border and the drive is rough enough to need a guide and a four-wheel drive rather than a hire car. The Djibouti-Addis railway is Chinese-built, electrified and the first cross-border electric line in Africa, and it carries passengers as well as the freight it was built for.
djibouti.visas: Djibouti operates an e-visa system that most nationalities can apply for online before travel, typically for stays of up to ninety days, with approval returned in a few days. Visas on arrival have been available at times and the policy has shifted, so the e-visa is the reliable route. A yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a residence permit through an employer, and the military and shipping sectors account for most of them. Anyone travelling on to Ethiopia by the railway should arrange that visa separately and well ahead, since it is not issued at the border. The e-visa is issued as an approval letter to be presented on arrival, and airlines check it at boarding, so it should be printed rather than left on a phone. Djibouti has periodically suspended visa on arrival without notice, which is why the online route is the one to use.
djibouti.bestTime: November to February is the only comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and manageable humidity. The rest of the year is severe: Djibouti is one of the hottest inhabited places on earth, and from June to August temperatures regularly exceed forty-five degrees with the khamsin wind off the desert making it worse. The whale shark season in the Gulf of Tadjoura runs from roughly October to February, which is both the coolest period and the reason most independent visitors come. Anyone hoping to see the whale sharks should book ahead for December and January, since the licensed operator capacity is genuinely limited. Lake Assal, the lowest point in Africa at a hundred and fifty five metres below sea level, is only sensibly visited in the cool months, and even then at first light, because the salt pan throws back everything the sun delivers.
djibouti.prosCons: Djibouti has Lac Assal, the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest bodies of water in the world, the otherworldly limestone chimneys of Lac Abbe, and whale sharks gathering in the Gulf of Tadjoura every winter in numbers that are internationally significant. It sits at one of the world's great strategic chokepoints, which is why so many countries have bases here. It is very expensive for what it actually is, brutally hot for the greater part of the year, French is close to necessary, and there is little to do in the city. The Bab el-Mandeb strait a short distance east carries a substantial share of world trade and has been the focus of shipping disruption since 2023, which is the reason the foreign bases are here and a live factor in the country's economy.
djibouti.whoFor: A French speaker with a specific reason to be there, whether shipping, the military, development work or the whale sharks, rather than anyone looking for a general base. The landscape is genuinely extraordinary and almost entirely unvisited. Daily life is conducted in French, the heat ranks among the most extreme anywhere people live, and the budget question has an unusual cause: several foreign militaries are based here, and their presence holds prices far above what the local economy would otherwise sustain. Geologists have a reason to be here that nowhere else can offer. The Afar triple junction is among the very few places on earth where a continent can be watched pulling itself apart at the surface. It also suits divers specifically, since the whale shark aggregation in the Gulf of Tadjoura is one of the more reliable in the world and the reef diving off the Sept Freres islands is essentially unvisited. Be honest about the scale before committing: a fortnight covers the place, and what it offers is intensity rather than variety.

saotome.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Sao Tome, which is moderate for the region and higher than a country this small might suggest, because almost everything is imported and the islands sit a long way off the West African coast. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $350 to $650. Market food is cheap and the fish is exceptional. The dobra was redenominated in 2018 and is pegged to the euro through an arrangement with Portugal, which removes currency volatility. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. The roças are where the country's accommodation economy quietly sits. These estates, built for cocoa and long since idle, survive in every condition from restored guesthouse to roofless shell with families living in the old workers' quarters, and a room in one is often cheaper and always stranger than a hotel in town. Electricity is expensive and rationed in practice by the cuts. Everything imported arrives through a single small port, so a delayed ship empties the shelves of particular items for weeks at a time and nobody can tell you when they will return.
saotome.whereToWork: Sao Tome's connectivity is weak and it is the main practical constraint. The islands are served by a single submarine cable and domestic prices are high relative to speed, with mobile data from CST and Unitel the usual fallback. Power cuts are frequent and generators are standard in anything serious. There is no coworking. Portuguese is the official language and the language of everything; Forro and the other creoles are spoken at home, and English is genuinely rare. Portuguese is close to necessary here. Anyone working with Europe will find the offset trivial, since the islands keep the same time as London through most of the year. The economy is thinner than the scenery suggests and worth understanding before arriving. Oil was found in the maritime zone shared with Nigeria and a generation of national planning assumed it would arrive, which it has not, leaving cocoa, fishing and aid as the actual pillars. There is no professional network for an outsider to join. What works in practice is a routine built around the power: heavy tasks in the morning when supply is steadier, and everything important saved locally rather than in a browser tab.
saotome.gettingAround: The city of Sao Tome is small and its centre around the cathedral, the fort and the market is walkable in half an hour. Shared taxis and motorcycle taxis cover the island cheaply. The main island is only fifty kilometres long and a road runs most of the way round it, though the southern section is rough. Principe, the smaller island, is reached by a short flight or a long boat crossing, and it is quieter and considerably more expensive to stay on. Obo National Park covers roughly a third of the country and its trails start close to the road, which makes the forest unusually accessible. Getting to Principe is the trip that needs planning rather than improvising. The domestic flight takes half an hour on a small aircraft with a strict baggage allowance and sells out around holidays, while the boat is slow, infrequent and genuinely uncomfortable in a swell. Once there, the island has almost no vehicles for hire and lodges arrange transport themselves. On the main island, the road down the east coast is the good one and the western route past the plantations deteriorates the further south it runs.
saotome.visas: Sao Tome and Principe abolished visa requirements for citizens of the European Union, the United States and several other countries in 2017, granting stays of up to fifteen days visa-free, with a straightforward e-visa available for longer. That makes entry unusually easy for a country this obscure. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays run through a residence permit applied for locally. A yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries. Confirm the current position directly, since the policy has been adjusted more than once. Anyone flying in should note that connections run mainly through Lisbon, Accra and Libreville, and that the schedules are thin enough to shape a trip. Almost every route in passes through Lisbon, and the transit is where the paperwork actually bites: these islands ask for very little, while Portugal is Schengen and admits nobody without whatever their passport requires of them. That reshapes more itineraries than the entry rules here ever do. For a longer stay the residence application is handled locally and slowly, and the country has no scheme aimed at remote workers, so the honest position is that this is a place to visit properly rather than to base yourself.
saotome.bestTime: June to September is the gravana, the main dry season and the practical window, with less rain and daytime temperatures around twenty-eight. A shorter dry spell runs through January and February. The islands sit on the equator and are hot and humid throughout, with the southern half of Sao Tome among the wettest places in Africa. Sea turtles nest on the beaches between October and March and whales pass between July and October, both of which are reasons to time a visit. The southern beaches around Praia Jale and Praia Piscina are the ones worth the drive, and the road to them is rough in any season. Rainfall here varies more by place than by month: the southern half of the main island receives several metres a year while the northeast is comparatively dry, so a wet forecast for the country means very little without knowing which side of it you will be on. The cocoa harvest runs through the second half of the year and the estates are at their most active then. Ilheu das Rolas, off the southern tip, sits on the equator itself with a marker on the line, and a boat out to it is the standard day trip.
saotome.prosCons: Sao Tome and Principe are two volcanic islands on the equator, once the largest cocoa producer in the world, whose abandoned plantation houses stand in the forest with trees growing through them. Principe is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve with a fraction of a thousand visitors a year. It is safe, the fish and cocoa are exceptional, and almost nobody goes. The internet is poor, Portuguese is essential here, flights are both limited and expensive, and there is very little infrastructure of any kind aimed at visitors. The country also produces some of the finest cocoa in the world from the old plantation estates, several of which now run their own small chocolate operations. Malaria is the health fact that has actually improved here, and dramatically: sustained spraying and bed-net programmes cut cases by a very large margin from the early 2000s, though transmission continues and prophylaxis remains a conversation with a doctor. Anything beyond routine care exceeds what the country's one hospital can offer. Set against the thin infrastructure, the islands have no history of political violence to speak of, elections have changed governments peacefully, and the safety of walking around is not something anyone here worries about.
saotome.whoFor: A Portuguese speaker after somewhere genuinely unvisited and beautiful, with work that does not depend on bandwidth, and an interest in the plantation history or the birdlife, which includes a remarkable number of endemic species for so small a country. Portuguese is doing the work here, the internet is not reliable enough to plan a week around, and anybody on a schedule should reckon with a flight list that is short and a cancellation rate that is not unusual. It also suits birdwatchers, since the islands hold around thirty endemic species in an area smaller than most national parks, which is a density found almost nowhere else. Divers get uncrowded reef with no operators competing for it. Chocolate is the reason a specific sort of traveller comes, since the estates producing single-origin cocoa run tours and several make their own bars, and the quality is taken seriously by people who take that seriously. The realistic stay is two or three weeks, split between the main island and Principe, with slack for the flights. Anyone who wants the Gulf of Guinea with functioning infrastructure should look at Libreville or Douala instead and accept a far less interesting place.

maseru.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Maseru, which is low and reflects a small economy closely tied to South Africa's. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450. Food is cheap and much of it comes across the border from South Africa, which is where a great many residents shop deliberately, since Bloemfontein is around two hours away. The loti is pegged one to one with the South African rand and rand circulate freely alongside it. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Lesotho sits inside the Southern African Customs Union, which is why prices track South Africa's so closely and why so little is made locally; it is also the source of a large share of government revenue. Practically it means South African banking, retail and mobile networks all work here with minimal friction, and a card issued in Johannesburg behaves normally. Rents are usually monthly with a deposit and negotiated directly with the owner. Electricity and water are cheap by regional standards, since both are produced domestically.
maseru.whereToWork: Maseru's connectivity is modest: fibre has reached parts of the city and mobile data from Vodacom Lesotho and Econet is the common fallback, with prices high relative to income. Power comes largely from the Muela hydropower station and is more reliable than in several neighbouring countries, though cuts happen. There is very little coworking. English is an official language alongside Sesotho and is the medium of education, government and business, which removes the language barrier entirely and is Lesotho's clearest practical advantage. Anyone working with Europe will find the offset small, at one or two hours ahead of London depending on the season, which is a workable overlap. The professional economy is narrow and worth knowing before arriving: garment manufacturing for export, the water project that sells the country's rivers to South Africa, government, and a substantial development sector. Almost every foreign professional here is attached to one of those. In practice people work from home or from hotel lobbies, and a South African SIM roaming across the border is a common backup, since the networks are the same operators and coverage across the lowlands is continuous.
maseru.gettingAround: Maseru sits on the border, with the Maseru Bridge crossing into South Africa at the edge of the city centre, and the town itself is compact enough to walk in parts. Minibus taxis cover the city and the country cheaply. Beyond the lowland strip Lesotho is mountainous and the roads are serious: the Sani Pass, one of the highest road passes in Africa, requires a four-wheel drive and is one of the great drives on the continent. Moshoeshoe I airport has limited connections, and most people fly into Johannesburg. The Lesotho Highlands Water Project dams in the interior are worth the drive in their own right, and the road to Katse is tarred the whole way. The border posts have opening hours rather than running continuously, and the main bridge closes overnight, which is the detail that strands people arriving late from Bloemfontein. Maputsoe further north is the alternative and keeps longer hours. Up in the highlands the honest answer is often that there is no road at all: villages are reached on horseback or on foot, and the Basotho pony remains working transport rather than a tourist attraction.
maseru.visas: Lesotho grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries, the European Union and the United States for up to fourteen or ninety days depending on nationality, with an e-visa available for everyone else. The rules vary by passport more than in most countries, so check yours. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for locally. Because Lesotho is entirely surrounded by South Africa, anyone arriving overland needs South African entry first, and the two sets of rules both apply to any land journey. Anyone crossing at Maseru Bridge should allow time at month end and on holidays, when the queues of people working in South Africa are longest. A trip into Lesotho and back consumes a South African entry each way, so anyone on a ninety-day South African allowance should check whether their visa is single or multiple entry before crossing. Travellers arriving by air avoid the issue entirely, which is occasionally the cheaper answer despite the fare. Keep the Lesotho entry slip, since an extension is calculated from it.
maseru.bestTime: March to May and September to November are the best months, with mild dry weather and the mountain passes open. Lesotho is the only country in the world entirely above a thousand metres and the altitude governs everything: summers from December to February are warm in the lowlands and stormy in the mountains, and winters from June to August bring real snow to the highlands, with skiing at Afriski, one of only a handful of ski resorts in Africa. Maseru itself sits at 1,600 metres and gets frost. Afriski above Butha-Buthe runs from roughly June to August and is one of only two ski areas in southern Africa, which surprises most visitors. Lesotho has among the highest lightning strike densities in the world, and the afternoon storms in the highlands are genuinely dangerous for anyone exposed on a ridge, so walks are started early and finished early. Flash flooding closes mountain roads without warning in the same season. The Morija Arts and Cultural Festival, usually falling in the spring window, is the country's main cultural gathering and worth timing a visit around.
maseru.prosCons: Lesotho is the Mountain Kingdom and the name is literal: the entire country sits above a thousand metres, the Maloti range runs through it, Sehlabathebe National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Maletsunyane Falls drops two hundred metres in a single sheet. English works everywhere and costs are very low. Maseru itself is a functional border town and not in any sense an attractive city, the connection is poor, the country has one of the highest HIV rates in the world, and everything beyond the lowlands requires a serious vehicle. The health statistic deserves context rather than a bare number. Lesotho's HIV prevalence is among the world's highest, and it is also one of the countries where treatment coverage has expanded most, with antiretroviral access now reaching the large majority of those diagnosed. It is a fact about the country's history and its health system rather than a risk to a visitor taking ordinary precautions. Altitude is the more practical concern on arrival, since even the lowlands sit around 1,500 metres and the passes climb far higher.
maseru.whoFor: An English-speaking base for the Maloti mountains at very low cost, particularly for a walker, a rider or anyone drawn to Basotho pony trekking, which is the traditional way to travel here. It works as a gateway rather than a destination. This is a border town rather than a city, connectivity is unreliable, and without a vehicle equal to the mountain roads the whole of Lesotho stays out of reach, which is the only reason to come. Dinosaur trackways are an unexpected draw. Lesotho's sandstone holds some of the best-preserved footprints found anywhere, and several of the sites are open to anybody who makes the drive. Anyone drawn by the Maloti and the Drakensberg should know they are the same range seen from two sides, and the South African approach through Underberg is better organised for visitors while the Lesotho side is emptier and cheaper. It suits a skier, improbably: Afriski in the Maloti runs a short winter season on the only lift-served snow in southern Africa, and Lesotho is the only country on earth lying entirely above a thousand metres, which is the same fact that explains the cold, the ponies and the emptiness.

mbabane.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month as a solo remote worker in Mbabane, which is low and reflects a small economy inside South Africa's customs union. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $300 to $550. Food is cheap and largely South African, and many residents shop across the border or in Manzini, the larger commercial city half an hour away. The lilangeni is pegged one to one with the South African rand and rand circulate freely. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Anyone comparing with South Africa should note that the customs union keeps most goods at similar prices, so the saving is in rent rather than in shopping. Fibre runs about $40 to $80 a month and a coworking desk, where one exists, $60 to $120. Because the lilangeni is pegged to the rand, a South African card works everywhere and there is no exchange cost at all crossing the border, which makes the two economies effectively one for a visitor's purposes. Rents in the Ezulwini valley between the two cities sit above Mbabane itself and are where most of the country's expatriate staff live, since the hotels, the reserves and the craft markets are all along that road.
mbabane.whereToWork: Eswatini's connectivity is modest: fibre has reached parts of Mbabane and Manzini and mobile data from Eswatini Mobile and MTN is the common fallback. Power comes largely from South Africa and is affected when that grid is under strain. There is very little coworking. English is an official language alongside siSwati and is the medium of education, government and business, which removes the language barrier. The country sits two hours ahead of London in the northern winter, which is a workable offset for European hours. Anyone needing anything the capital lacks will find Manzini half an hour east, which is larger and holds most of the country's commerce. Eswatini imports most of its electricity from Eskom, so South African load shedding used to reach here directly. Those cuts ended in May 2025, which removed the scheduled outages without removing the dependency that transmits them, and a property with an inverter is still worth the premium for the same reasons it is across the border. Johannesburg is the practical hub for anything the country cannot supply professionally. Coworking is effectively limited to hotel business centres and a couple of small spaces in Manzini, so a flat with a reliable line is the arrangement to look for rather than a desk.
mbabane.gettingAround: Mbabane is a small highland capital and its centre is walkable, though the town is built across steep ground. Minibus taxis and kombis cover the country cheaply. Eswatini is small enough to cross in a few hours: Manzini is thirty minutes east, Hlane and Mkhaya game reserves an hour or so beyond that, and Mlilwane Wildlife Sanctuary sits in the Ezulwini valley between Mbabane and Manzini, close enough to visit on an afternoon. King Mswati III airport has limited connections and most people fly into Johannesburg, four hours away by road. Kombis run to fixed destinations from the ranks in Mbabane and Manzini and leave when full, and the fare anywhere in the country is a couple of dollars. Driving is on the left and the roads between the main towns are good. Malolotja in the northwest holds Africa's longest zipline canopy tour and some of the oldest mining evidence anywhere, with iron ore workings dated to over forty thousand years ago at Ngwenya.
mbabane.visas: Eswatini grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries, the European Union and the United States for up to thirty or ninety days depending on nationality, with an e-visa available for everyone else. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at the immigration department. The country belongs to the Southern African Customs Union with South Africa, Botswana, Lesotho and Namibia, which governs trade rather than movement, so each border still has its own immigration process. Anyone entering overland from South Africa or Mozambique should check the border post hours, since several of the smaller crossings close in the early evening. The country was still called Swaziland until 2018, so older insurance policies, airline systems and reference material sometimes still carry the previous name, which occasionally needs explaining at a desk and is worth checking on any document bought in advance.
mbabane.bestTime: April to September is the dry season and the comfortable window, with warm days in the low twenties at Mbabane's altitude and cold nights. October to March is the wet season, hotter and with heavy afternoon storms, and it is when the lowveld game reserves are greenest. The Umhlanga reed dance in late August and the Incwala kingship ceremony around December and January are the two great national events, both of them living ceremonies rather than performances for visitors. The Ezulwini valley between Mbabane and Manzini holds most of the country's craft markets and the Mantenga cultural village, and is pleasant year-round. Umhlanga runs over several days in late August and involves tens of thousands of unmarried women, and Incwala is closed to photography entirely, which is worth knowing before arriving with a camera. Mbabane sits at around 1,150 metres and is noticeably cooler than the lowveld reserves an hour east, where summer temperatures climb well into the thirties.
mbabane.prosCons: Eswatini packs a great deal into a small area: Mlilwane and Hlane hold rhino, elephant and big cats within an hour of the capital, Malolotja is serious mountain walking country, and the Ezulwini valley is genuinely beautiful. English works everywhere, it is cheap, and the country is calmer and safer than most of its neighbours. It is one of the last absolute monarchies left in the world and the pro-democracy protests of 2021 were met with force, the HIV prevalence is the highest anywhere, and Mbabane itself is very quiet. Eswatini changed its name from Swaziland in 2018 by royal decree, and both names remain in circulation internationally, which matters when searching for anything official or recent. The country's HIV prevalence among adults has been the highest in the world for two decades, though treatment coverage is now among the best in Africa and life expectancy has recovered substantially since the worst years.
mbabane.whoFor: An English-speaking southern African base with game reserves and mountains within an hour, at a fraction of South African prices, for anyone content with a very small capital. It works well as part of a longer regional trip rather than alone. Mbabane is a small administrative town rather than a city, and whatever professional network Eswatini has is in Manzini or across the border in South Africa. Anyone staying should read about the country's political situation rather than treating it as a purely scenic destination. Swazi craft is a working industry rather than a visitor attraction. The candle, glass and weaving workshops in the Malkerns valley are businesses that export, and they let people watch because it costs them nothing. Anybody crossing between South Africa and Mozambique passes through this country whether or not they meant to, and the Lomahasha border puts Maputo about two hours away from here. Next to Maseru in Lesotho, Eswatini is warmer, greener, has the better game reserves and considerably less mountain.

saintdenis.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Saint-Denis, which is expensive for the Indian Ocean and reflects a French department where much of the food arrives from Europe. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $700 to $1,100. Groceries cost noticeably more than mainland France and the price of living here has driven serious protest movements, including the gilets jaunes actions that were more sustained on Reunion than almost anywhere. The euro is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Anyone comparing with Mauritius nearby should note that Reunion costs considerably more and offers European healthcare and schooling in exchange. The same dock duty applied across the French overseas departments is the mechanism, and it is why an identical product costs more here than in Marseille despite the shared currency. The escape is local. The markets at Saint-Paul and in the capital sell fruit, vegetables and fish grown and caught on the island at a fraction of supermarket prices, and Reunion produces a great deal of its own. A car is close to essential, and both the purchase and the fuel cost more than they would in mainland France.
saintdenis.whereToWork: Reunion has European infrastructure: fibre reaches most of the coastal ring at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and French plans roam here without charge, which matters for anyone based in Europe. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene in Saint-Denis and Saint-Pierre. French is the language of everything, with Reunion Creole spoken among locals, and English is limited. The island sits three hours ahead of Paris in the northern winter, which makes a French morning into a Reunionese afternoon. Anyone working with mainland France should note that the offset flips with European daylight saving, which changes the overlap by an hour twice a year. Everything administrative runs on the same French systems as the mainland, so a freelancer already registered in France can operate here without building any new structure, which is a real advantage over the independent islands nearby. The university and the volcano observatory give the island a research population, and the public sector is the largest employer by a distance. Unemployment on Reunion is high, which shapes the local job market and is worth understanding before assuming work can be found here.
saintdenis.gettingAround: Saint-Denis sits on the north coast and its centre, with the Creole townhouses along the Rue de Paris and the Barachois seafront, is walkable. A coastal road rings the island and the new coastal highway west of the capital is one of the most expensive roads ever built in France, running partly on a viaduct over the sea because of rockfalls. Buses cover the ring. The interior, with its three cirques and the volcano, is reached by mountain roads and on foot. Roland Garros airport has direct flights to Paris. Traffic on the ring road is the daily reality: the population is concentrated on the coast, there is one route, and the peak is slow enough that residents plan around it. The roads into the cirques are the compensation. Cilaos is reached by a famous climb of some four hundred bends, and the Salazie road runs through tunnels cut into the gorge. Mafate has no road at all and is supplied by helicopter, which is why walking in is the only way. A hire car is close to mandatory for anything beyond the capital.
saintdenis.visas: Reunion is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union while sitting outside the Schengen area, which is the detail that matters: a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here with no permit. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Longer stays for non-EU citizens require a French long-stay visa applied for before travel. Anyone travelling on to Mauritius, forty minutes away by air, should note that is a separate country with its own entry requirements. As elsewhere in the French overseas departments, a visa issued for France has to name Reunion to be valid here, and it is checked at boarding rather than on arrival. Regional travel is one of the island's quieter advantages, with Madagascar, Mauritius, the Seychelles and South Africa all a short flight away and each with its own rules, so a stay here can be built as a circuit rather than a single destination. Yellow fever certificates are asked for from travellers arriving from affected countries.
saintdenis.bestTime: May to November is the dry, cooler season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-five on the coast and the hiking trails in the cirques at their best.
