longyearbyen.whereToWork: Connectivity is excellent and surprises people. Longyearbyen sits at the end of a dedicated fibre link to the mainland, laid to serve the satellite ground station on the plateau above town, which downloads data from polar-orbiting satellites on every pass. That gives a settlement of about two and a half thousand people better internet than most European towns. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking presence and several cafes people work from. The time zone is central European, the same as Oslo, so working with Europe is straightforward and the darkness is the only complication. The professional community is smaller and more concentrated than the population suggests: the university centre, the research stations and the tourism operators are effectively the whole economy, and a newcomer meets most of it within a month. The polar night is the real working variable. With no sunrise to anchor the day, routines drift badly, and the residents who cope best are ruthless about fixed hours, daylight lamps and getting outside even when outside is dark. It is an occupational hazard rather than a mood.
longyearbyen.gettingAround: Longyearbyen is walkable end to end in twenty minutes and that is essentially the whole road network: about fifty kilometres of road exist in all of Svalbard and none of it leaves the settlements. Beyond the town you travel by snowmobile in winter, by boat in summer, or on foot with a rifle, because polar bears are present across the archipelago and carrying protection outside the settlement is a legal requirement. Svalbard Airport is three kilometres out and connects to Oslo and Tromso daily in season, which is a genuinely good link for somewhere this far north. Rifles are rented in town and the shops that hire them expect you to know how to use one, so most visitors sensibly join a guided trip instead, which is also how the insurance tends to work. A small custom worth knowing before your first evening out: shoes come off at the door almost everywhere, including some restaurants and the hotel lobbies, a habit inherited from the coal-dust years. Taxis run to the airport and around the settlement, and the road east towards Mine 7 is about as far as driving goes.
longyearbyen.visas: Svalbard is unlike anywhere else. The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 gives citizens of every signatory country the right to live and work here without a visa, a residence permit or a work permit, regardless of nationality, and that has never been repealed. Svalbard is not part of the Schengen area, so time here does not count against a Schengen allowance, but you will pass through Schengen to reach it. The catch is practical: there is no welfare system, and anyone unable to support themselves can be required to leave. Anyone planning to stay should arrange work and housing before arriving, because the treaty gives the right to be here and no right at all to be supported here. The practical catch is the journey rather than the destination. Almost every route runs through mainland Norway, so a nationality that needs a Schengen visa needs one to transit even though Svalbard itself asks for nothing, and that is the detail that trips people up most often. Anyone staying beyond a short visit registers with the Governor's office, and private health insurance is strongly advised, since the local hospital stabilises and evacuates rather than treats.
longyearbyen.bestTime: March to May is the best combination, with snow still on the ground for snowmobiling and dog sledding, returning daylight and temperatures around minus ten. June to August is the midnight sun, with continuous daylight, boat access to the fjords and temperatures a few degrees above freezing. Late October to mid-February is the polar night, when the sun does not rise at all and the town runs on street lighting and northern lights, which is either the reason to come or the reason not to. There is no month here that is warm. Late February and early March bring the blue light, a few weeks when the sun sits just below the horizon and the whole landscape turns an even cobalt for hours, and the town marks the sun's actual return with a week of events in early March. Wildlife follows the season closely: the bird cliffs are occupied from May to August, and the boat trips that reach the walrus haul-outs only run once the ice has gone.
longyearbyen.prosCons: Nowhere else combines genuine Arctic wilderness, excellent internet, Norwegian standards of safety and services, and the right to simply turn up and stay for as long as you like. Glaciers, polar bears and the Global Seed Vault are all within sight of the town. Four months of darkness affects people more than they expect it to, costs sit above the mainland's and the mainland is not cheap, finding somewhere to live is the obstacle most arrivals underestimate, and leaving the settlement at all means equipment, a rifle and, for most visitors, a guide who knows the ground. Svalbard also has no burial ground in use, because bodies do not decompose in permafrost, and seriously ill residents are flown to the mainland rather than treated locally. The community is unusually transient, with a large share of residents on two or three year postings, so friendships form fast and end on a schedule. And the place is changing visibly: Svalbard is warming faster than almost anywhere on earth, the permafrost is degrading under buildings, and after a fatal avalanche in the town a decade ago parts of it were rebuilt or abandoned outright. None of that is an abstraction here.
longyearbyen.whoFor: Researchers, guides, photographers and anyone whose work is genuinely location-independent and who wants somewhere extreme with functioning infrastructure. It suits people who like winter rather than tolerate it. The visa freedom makes it unusually accessible to nationalities that struggle everywhere else. The sun does not rise at all for four months, hiking outside the settlement legally requires carrying a rifle against polar bears, and arriving without accommodation arranged is not a plan that works in a town where housing is allocated rather than rented casually. Anybody whose passport makes ordinary travel difficult should know what the Svalbard Treaty does. The right to live and work here applies regardless of nationality, and there is nowhere else on earth where that is true. Come first in the dark half rather than the light one, because anyone can manage Svalbard in June and the polar night is what actually decides it. Families do live here and there is a school, though most arrive because one partner was posted rather than by choosing the place from a distance. The people who struggle are the ones who came for the idea of it: the scenery is astonishing and the daily reality is a small town with one supermarket, limited privacy and weather that cancels plans.

mariehamn.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month, which is Nordic pricing without a Nordic city's choice. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, cheaper than Helsinki or Stockholm and not by as much as the size difference suggests. Groceries are Finnish prices, which are high, and the archipelago's ferry logistics do not help. Eating out is expensive and the choice is limited outside the summer season. The compensations are real: heating is included in most rentals, public services are excellent and the tax-free status of the islands within the European Union means alcohol and some goods are cheaper on the ferries. The euro is the currency. Rental supply is the real constraint rather than the price. Summer demand pulls a good part of the stock into short lets, so a long lease is far easier to sign in September than in May, and the market is small enough that listings circulate by word of mouth as often as they appear online. Budget separately for leaving: every trip off the islands is a ferry or a flight, and a household that hops to Stockholm or Turku monthly will watch that line grow quickly. Healthcare and schooling come through the Finnish system and cost almost nothing at the point of use.
mariehamn.whereToWork: Connectivity is excellent. Aland has Finnish infrastructure, which means fibre through the town, comprehensive mobile coverage and entirely reliable power. There is a small coworking scene and the islands have actively marketed themselves to remote workers, with the local government running programmes to attract residents to a place with a shrinking population. Everything administrative is digital and works. The time zone is eastern European, two hours ahead of GMT in winter, which gives a workable overlap with the rest of Europe and an early finish against anything in the Americas. The one real friction is language rather than infrastructure: business, government and daily life run in Swedish, and while English is widely understood, the meetings, the noticeboards and the paperwork are not in it. The islands run a relocation service staffed by people whose job is to answer exactly the questions an arriving remote worker has, which is not something most places offer. Practically, winter is the productive half of the year here. Summer is short, everyone is outdoors and on the water, and trying to hold a normal working rhythm through July is a fight most residents stop picking.
mariehamn.gettingAround: Mariehamn is small and flat and the bicycle is the default: Aland has an extensive network of cycle paths and the islands are laid out for them. Buses connect the main island's villages. Beyond that, the archipelago runs on ferries, most of them free or nearly so between the inhabited islands, and working out the timetables is part of living here. Mariehamn Airport has limited connections to Helsinki and Stockholm, but the practical route is the ferry: large ships run to both Stockholm and Turku daily and take five to six hours. A car still earns its place for anyone living outside the town, mostly because the bus timetable is built around school hours rather than working ones. Plenty of people cycle straight through the winter on studded tyres, since the terrain is flat and the roads are cleared promptly. If you are taking a vehicle onto an archipelago ferry, reserve it: the boats are small, the sailings are few, and being turned away means waiting for the next one, which on the outer routes can be the following day.
mariehamn.visas: Aland is part of Finland and part of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens can live and work here with no permit and everyone else needs the same Schengen visa or residence permit they would need for mainland Finland. The islands do sit outside the European Union value added tax area, which is why the ferries sell duty free, but that is a tax arrangement rather than a border. One genuine local rule: acquiring land and full residency rights requires hembygdsratt, a regional citizenship with a five year qualifying period. What that regional citizenship actually gates is worth stating precisely, because it sounds more restrictive than it is day to day: it governs owning land, voting in the islands' own elections and holding certain trades, and it leaves renting, working and living here entirely unaffected. Acquiring it takes five years of residence and a working command of Swedish. One further consequence of the demilitarised status is that holders of Aland regional citizenship are exempt from Finnish conscription, which is a real legal distinction rather than a historical footnote.
mariehamn.bestTime: June to August is the season, with long days, temperatures around twenty degrees, the archipelago open by boat and the islands at their busiest. May and September are quieter and still pleasant. Winter from December to March is cold, dark and very quiet, with the sea sometimes freezing enough to close the smaller ferry routes, though the main Stockholm and Turku ships run all year. The islands empty out of visitors entirely between October and April, which is either a drawback or the reason to come. Anyone planning around the ferries should note that the Stockholm and Turku routes are also the islands' duty free lifeline and are busiest on Friday and Sunday evenings. Midsummer is the fixed point of the local calendar and effectively closes the islands for several days, which makes it either the best week to be here or the worst to need anything done. The June light is the real draw: it barely gets dark at all, and the archipelago in flat evening water is what brings people back. In a cold winter the frozen sea becomes usable for skating and walking, which is a genuine pleasure the summer visitors never see.
mariehamn.prosCons: Aland is a demilitarised, Swedish-speaking, self-governing archipelago inside the European Union, with Nordic infrastructure, almost no crime, an enormous amount of water and space, and a government that actively wants more residents. Winter here is long and dark, the population is small enough to limit both the social and the professional scene, and the language is settled by law rather than preference, since Swedish is what the islands run on and arriving with Finnish will not help you at all. Prices are high and the choice of everything is narrow. Aland also fought a quiet diplomatic battle in the 1920s to join Sweden and lost it at the League of Nations, which is why the autonomy and the demilitarisation exist at all. Anything medical beyond the ordinary means a trip to Turku or Helsinki, so a specialist appointment is a day of travel rather than an afternoon. And the population is small enough that a professional falling-out is difficult to walk away from, which people who have lived in small places will recognise immediately and those who have not tend to underestimate.
mariehamn.whoFor: Aland suits Swedish speakers, sailors, cyclists and anyone who wants Nordic quality of life in a place with genuine space around it. It suits European Union citizens especially, since the paperwork disappears entirely. It suits families, given the schools and the safety. A town of eleven thousand is not a city, the winters are dark in the way Baltic winters are, and Swedish is genuinely required here rather than merely useful. Aland is monolingually Swedish by constitutional arrangement, so the Finnish-English fallback that works in Helsinki does not exist. Maritime history has a particular anchor here. The Pommern, a four-masted barque moored in the harbour, is the last of the grain-trade windjammers preserved unaltered rather than restored into something tidier. The islands reward a trial run in February rather than July, because anyone can enjoy Aland in summer and the winter is the half that decides it. It suits people who arrive with their income already secured, since the local job market is small and largely Swedish-speaking: a poor place to look for work and a good one to bring it. Aland against Gotland or the Stockholm archipelago really means choosing between self-government and better connections.

sthelier.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month, and Jersey is genuinely expensive. A one-bedroom runs roughly $1,400 to $2,000, and housing is tightly controlled: the island operates a residential qualification system that restricts what most newcomers may rent or buy, which pushes new arrivals into a smaller and pricier part of the market. Groceries cost more than mainland Britain because everything ships in, though the island's own dairy, potatoes and seafood are excellent. Eating out is expensive. Income tax is a flat twenty per cent with no capital gains or inheritance tax, which is the reason a great deal of money is here. The tax picture has two footnotes the headline rate omits: a goods and services tax applies at a low rate on most purchases, and social security contributions are levied separately and are not trivial for the self-employed. On housing, the part of the market open to newcomers is largely lodging and shared accommodation rather than whole flats, which is a different product at a similar price. Travel is the recurring cost that catches people, since every trip off the island is a flight or a ferry and fares rise sharply through the summer.
sthelier.whereToWork: Connectivity is outstanding. Jersey rolled out fibre to every property on the island years ahead of most of Europe, and gigabit connections are standard rather than premium. Mobile coverage is complete and power is entirely reliable. There is a real coworking scene serving the finance and digital sectors, and Digital Jersey runs a hub in St Helier. The time zone is the same as London, including daylight saving, so working with the United Kingdom is seamless and Europe is an hour away. This is one of the best-connected small islands anywhere. The constraint here is regulatory rather than technical, and it is the mirror image of the infrastructure. Starting a business or taking on staff generally requires a licence under the island's control of housing and work law, granted according to what the government judges the island needs, so the question is not whether you can get online but whether you are permitted to trade. Jersey maintains its own data protection regime aligned with European standards, which is one reason the digital and finance sectors here serve European clients without friction.
sthelier.gettingAround: St Helier is walkable and the island is only about fifteen kilometres across, so a bicycle covers most of it, helped by the green lanes where vehicles are limited to twenty five kilometres an hour and give way to walkers and cyclists. LibertyBus runs a decent network. Driving is easy but parking in St Helier is a permanent irritation and uses a paycard system. Jersey Airport connects to London, Southampton, Manchester and several European cities, and ferries run to Saint-Malo, Guernsey and Poole. Anyone driving should know that the island's speed limits are low even by British standards, topping out at about sixty four kilometres an hour, and are enforced. Filter in turn, marked at junctions with a yellow box and a sign, requires each vehicle to take strict alternate turns, and getting it wrong is the fastest way to identify yourself as a visitor. The Saint-Malo ferry makes France a day trip rather than a holiday, which is a genuine feature of living here. There are no motorways on the island and no need for any.
sthelier.visas: Jersey is a Crown Dependency, not part of the United Kingdom and not part of the European Union, with its own immigration rules that broadly mirror British ones. Most visitors who can enter the United Kingdom can enter Jersey, and the Common Travel Area means no routine passport check arriving from Britain. Working is a different matter: Jersey controls employment tightly through a registration card system tied to residential status, and taking a job without the right permission is not possible. There is no remote work visa. Anyone planning to stay longer than a visit should resolve the housing qualification first, since it determines what may be rented and is not something an employer can waive. The system has names worth knowing, because everything else follows from which one applies. Registered is where a newcomer starts, Licensed is granted to an employee the island has decided it needs, Entitled to Work usually arrives through marriage or long residence, and Entitled, the full status, generally takes ten years of continuous residence. Each tier unlocks more of the housing market. None of it is quick, and all of it is administered by the island rather than by any British authority.
sthelier.bestTime: May to September is the season, with temperatures around twenty degrees, long evenings and the beaches at their best. Jersey has the mildest climate in the British Isles and the second largest tidal range in the world, around twelve metres, which means the island grows by roughly a third at low tide and the seabed at Seymour Tower is walkable with a guide. Winter is mild but wet and windy, and the tourist infrastructure thins considerably. Late spring is when the island looks best, before the summer crowds arrive. Anyone visiting in summer should book the Ecrehous or Minquiers boat trips early, since the offshore reefs are only reachable on certain tides and the operators are few. Liberation Day on the ninth of May marks the end of the German occupation and is the island's national day, observed seriously rather than as a pretext for a long weekend. The Battle of Flowers in August is the largest event of the summer and fills whatever accommodation is not already taken. Between the two, late May and June give the best combination of weather, daylight and space, before the school holidays arrive.
sthelier.prosCons: Jersey puts exceptional infrastructure on a small, safe, mild island, with gigabit internet everywhere, low tax, excellent seafood, beaches and cliff paths, and an hour to London. Cost is the first objection and control the quieter one. Housing is expensive and rationed by a qualification system that treats most newcomers as temporary, the island is small enough to feel closed after a while, and the finance industry dominates the economy and much of the conversation. The German occupation of 1940 to 1945 is still a live part of the island's memory. Jersey is not in the National Health Service, so seeing a doctor costs money at the point of use, and insurance or a budget for it is a requirement rather than an optional extra. Hospital care is largely funded and general practice is not. The island's finance industry also draws sustained external scrutiny over tax transparency, which is part of the background of living here and shapes how the place is discussed elsewhere, whatever view you take of the substance.
sthelier.whoFor: Jersey suits people working in finance, law or digital services who want a low-tax base with British systems, and anyone with a family who values safety and schools. It suits sea swimmers, cyclists and walkers. Arriving without a job or a housing route is close to futile, because the residential qualification system decides what a newcomer is allowed to rent and it decides against most of them. Anybody looking for a cheap island is also in the wrong part of the Channel. Occupation history is unusually complete on this island. The Jersey War Tunnels and the coastal fortifications together form some of the most intact Atlantic Wall remains surviving anywhere in Europe. The sequence matters more here than almost anywhere: the job comes first, the licence follows the job, and the housing follows the licence, so anyone planning it in reverse stalls at the first step. A purely remote worker with no local employer has no route in beyond a visit, which is the honest answer to the question this site usually asks. Anyone comparing the Channel Islands will find Guernsey quieter and cheaper under a similar system, and the Isle of Man wilder and further from France.

stpeterport.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,500 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $1,300 to $1,900, and like Jersey the island restricts its housing market, dividing it into Local and Open markets with the Open market considerably more expensive and the route most newcomers take. Groceries cost more than mainland Britain. Eating out is expensive but the seafood is exceptional and the island's own dairy is famous. Income tax is a flat twenty per cent with a cap on very high incomes, and there is no capital gains, inheritance or value added tax, which is the reason the finance sector is here. Social insurance is charged separately from income tax and falls on the self-employed at a higher rate than on employees, which catches people who arrive assuming the headline rate is the whole story. Everything comes by boat, and the freight buried inside a shelf price is why a supermarket basket runs above what the same basket costs on the mainland. A property charge based on rateable value is billed annually and is modest by most standards, but it is another line the headline description of the tax system leaves out.
stpeterport.whereToWork: Connectivity is very good. Guernsey has invested heavily in fibre and most of the island now has it, with reliable power and complete mobile coverage. There is a small but real coworking and digital sector alongside the finance industry, and Digital Greenhouse in St Peter Port is the hub. The time zone matches London, including daylight saving, so United Kingdom work is seamless. Guernsey is slightly less far along on fibre than Jersey and slightly cheaper, which is a fair summary of the difference between the two islands generally. Anyone comparing the two islands should also weigh the sector: Guernsey's finance industry leans towards insurance and funds where Jersey's leans towards banking and trusts. The finance sector sets the working day and it is a conventional one, so the town empties at half past five and the restaurants fill immediately afterwards. The island's cables run to two countries, and a fault on one has taken services down for a day more than once, which is why redundancy matters to anyone whose work cannot stop. The professional community is small enough that reputation travels faster than a reference does.
stpeterport.gettingAround: St Peter Port is compact and steep, built up the hill from the harbour in narrow lanes and steps, and walkable if you accept the gradient. The island is about ten kilometres across with a decent bus network at a flat low fare. Cycling works well. Guernsey Airport connects to London, Southampton and Jersey, and ferries run to Jersey, Saint-Malo and Poole. The smaller islands of Herm and Sark are reachable by boat in twenty and fifty minutes, and Sark famously has no cars at all. Anyone driving should be ready for the filter in turn system at unmarked junctions, which is a local convention rather than a rule and works better than it sounds. The island speed limit tops out at thirty five miles an hour, and a network of lanes designated as quiet roads caps it at fifteen, with walkers, riders and cyclists given priority over cars by law rather than by courtesy. Nothing is more than a twenty minute drive from anything else, which changes what a car is even for. Parking in town is controlled by a clock disc on the windscreen rather than by payment, and the limits are enforced.
stpeterport.visas: Guernsey is a Crown Dependency with its own immigration rules that broadly mirror British ones, and the Common Travel Area means no routine passport check arriving from Britain. Most people who can enter the United Kingdom can enter Guernsey as a visitor. Working and living here is controlled through the population management regime, which ties employment and housing together and issues permits by category. There is no remote work visa, though the island has an Open market housing route that gives more flexibility than Jersey's system does. Anyone planning to stay should resolve the housing category first, since Local and Open market properties carry different rights and the distinction governs everything else.
stpeterport.bestTime: May to September is the season, mild at around twenty degrees, with the cliff paths on the south coast at their best and the sea warm enough to swim. Guernsey shares Jersey's enormous tidal range and mild maritime climate. Winter is mild but wet and windy, and the island is very quiet. Victor Hugo wrote through fifteen winters here in exile and found them productive, which is one way to read the season. Late spring, when the cliff paths are in flower, is when the island looks best. Anyone visiting should try to reach Sark on a clear day, since it has no cars, no street lighting and was designated the world's first Dark Sky Island in 2011. The tidal range means a beach that exists in the morning can be under water by mid-afternoon, which is why the tide tables are printed in the local paper rather than looked up. Autumn gales ground the planes more readily than winter cold does. The coastal footpaths on the south side are at their best in late May, when the flowers are out and the summer visitors have not yet arrived.
stpeterport.prosCons: Guernsey is a smaller, quieter and slightly cheaper version of Jersey, with the same tax treatment, better preserved lanes and a genuinely lovely capital of narrow streets rising above a working harbour. Hauteville House, where Hugo wrote Les Miserables, is open and extraordinary. Everything that weighs against Jersey weighs here too, including an expensive and rationed housing market, a finance-dominated economy, and an island small enough that the social scene is quickly exhausted. Flights are fewer than Jersey's and the weather closes the airport more often than people expect. The occupation of 1940 to 1945 also runs deeper here than on Jersey, since Alderney held the only Nazi concentration camps on British soil and the sites are still visible.
stpeterport.whoFor: Guernsey suits finance and legal professionals wanting a low-tax base, and anyone who prefers a quieter island to Jersey's slightly busier one. It suits walkers, sea swimmers and anyone drawn to the smaller islands nearby. Without either an Open Market housing route or an employment permit there is no way in at all. Flights are the other constraint, since fog grounds them often enough that anybody who needs to be somewhere on a particular day should build a spare one into the plan. A genuinely walkable harbour town is rarer than it should be, and this is one. The stepped lanes and Regency terraces here are among the best preserved anywhere in the Channel Islands. Half a year will tell you whether the size of the place suits, and the housing category decides whether half a year is even on offer. Anyone coming for the finance sector should have the role agreed before moving, because the permit and the flat are both issued against it.

vaticancity.costOfLiving: Nobody rents in Vatican City, so the figure here is really Rome around it: budget about $2,500 a month to live within walking distance of St Peter's. A one-bedroom in Prati or Borgo runs roughly $1,200 to $1,800, and those two districts carry a premium for the address and the calm. Groceries at the Trionfale market a few streets north are among the best value in Rome. Eating out ranges from tourist prices on the Via della Conciliazione to genuinely cheap in Prati's back streets, and the difference is a two minute walk. The euro is the currency and Italian banking applies. Prati is one of the few central Roman districts built on a grid with wide streets, which is why it commands its premium: the flats are larger and lighter than the centro storico's. A coworking desk runs $180 to $300 a month. Rome's tourist tax applies to short stays and is charged per night on top of the rate, and anyone renting for months should expect to pay several months up front plus an agency fee, which is standard practice rather than a negotiation.
vaticancity.whereToWork: Practically speaking you work in Rome. Fibre reaches most of Prati and Borgo at good speeds, mobile coverage is complete and Italian plans work throughout. Power is reliable. There is a reasonable coworking market in Prati and across the river in the centre, and the cafes around the Vatican walls are quieter than anywhere near the Pantheon. Vatican City itself has its own telephone country code, its own postal service, its own radio station and its own internet domain, none of which a visitor uses. The time zone is central European, so European work is straightforward. Italian bureaucracy is the practical obstacle rather than the infrastructure: a residence permit, a tax code and a bank account each take longer than they should, and a fibre installation can take weeks. The codice fiscale is the key that unlocks the rest and is obtainable relatively quickly, so it is worth doing first. Coworking in Prati runs $180 to $300 a month and is quieter than anything across the river.
vaticancity.gettingAround: Everything here is walking. Vatican City is under half a square kilometre and you cross it on foot in minutes, with the museums entrance on the north wall and St Peter's Square on the east. Rome's metro line A stops at Ottaviano and Cipro, both a few minutes from the walls, and buses and trams run along the river. Roma San Pietro station is a short walk south. Fiumicino airport is about forty minutes by taxi or a train from Termini, and Ciampino is further out and mostly serves budget carriers. The Vatican Museums and St Peter's have separate entrances on opposite sides of the walls and there is no public route between them without leaving and walking around, which is a fifteen-minute detour that catches most first-time visitors. Rome's buses are frequent and unreliable in equal measure; the metro is limited but punctual, and line A is the one that matters here.
vaticancity.visas: Vatican City has no border control and no visa of its own: you enter from Italy and the entry rules that matter are Italy's, which means the Schengen ninety day rule for most non-European visitors and free movement for European Union citizens. Time spent here counts against a Schengen allowance in practice because you are in Italy to get here. Residence in the Vatican itself is granted only to those working for the Holy See, and its citizenship is functional and temporary rather than something anyone acquires by living here. Italy operates its own digital nomad visa, introduced in 2024, for highly qualified remote workers meeting an income threshold, which is the realistic route for a non-European wanting more than ninety days near the Vatican. It requires an Italian tax code, health insurance and proof of accommodation, and is applied for at a consulate before travel rather than after arrival. The state issues its own passports and has a few hundred citizens, almost all of whom hold that status because of the post they occupy rather than where they were born, and it lapses when the job ends. There is no route into it and no particular reason to look for one.
vaticancity.bestTime: April to June and September to October are the best months, warm at around twenty three degrees and without the July and August heat that regularly pushes past thirty five. Winter is mild at around twelve degrees and much quieter, which makes it the best time to see the museums without queuing for an hour. Easter and Christmas bring enormous crowds to St Peter's Square. The Sistine Chapel and the museums are open most weekdays and closed on Sundays except the last Sunday of the month, when entry is free and the queues are correspondingly long. A papal audience fills the square on Wednesday mornings and the Angelus does the same on Sundays at noon, so anyone living here quickly learns which two half-days to avoid crossing it. August empties Rome of Romans and fills it with visitors, and a good number of the neighbourhood restaurants simply close for two or three weeks.
vaticancity.prosCons: The draw is simple and hard to argue with: the Sistine Chapel, the Raphael Rooms, the Laocoon and St Peter's Basilica sit within a few hundred metres of each other, and living beside them means seeing them on a Tuesday morning rather than in a two hour queue. Prati is a genuinely pleasant Roman neighbourhood. What you pay for it is living in the most tourist-saturated square kilometre in Europe, where prices reflect exactly that, and the Vatican itself closes at night, so the area empties in a way central Rome does not. The Vatican Gardens can be visited by booked tour only and are the one part of the state most residents of the surrounding streets never see. The museums also run occasional evening openings in the warmer months, which is by some distance the best way to experience them.
vaticancity.whoFor: This suits art historians, students of the Renaissance, and anyone whose interest in Rome is specifically the Vatican collections, which reward repeated visits far more than a single one. The appeal is a quieter, more residential Rome than the centro storico offers, without giving up the ability to walk to everything worth walking to. No nomad community exists in the smallest state on earth, the surrounding Roman prices are what they are, and the flow of pilgrims and tour groups is continuous rather than seasonal, which wears on some people within days. Attending a papal audience is more straightforward than most people assume. The general audience on Wednesday mornings costs nothing, and tickets come from the Prefecture of the Papal Household if requested in advance. Business at one of the pontifical universities or the institutes around the Borgo changes the picture entirely, since the academic community here is considerably larger than the size of the state would ever suggest.

minsk.costOfLiving: Budget around $750 a month, which makes Minsk one of the cheapest capitals in Europe. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, with the centre and the areas near the metro at the top and the Soviet-era microdistricts considerably cheaper. Groceries are inexpensive and Belarusian dairy and produce are good. Eating out is genuinely cheap: a full meal in an ordinary cafe costs a few dollars and even the better restaurants are modest by European standards. Utilities are low and heating is centralised. The Belarusian ruble was redenominated in 2016, so older prices need a factor of ten thousand applied. The practical difficulty is not the price level but paying anything at all. Foreign cards frequently fail, so most visitors run on cash exchanged locally, and how much you bring in becomes a planning decision rather than an afterthought. Rentals are usually arranged through an agency for a fee, and a landlord will need your registration details, since foreigners must be registered at their address. Imported goods have narrowed in range and risen in price under sanctions, so the cheapness applies most to what Belarus makes itself, which is a good deal of the food.
minsk.whereToWork: Connectivity is good and this is not an accident. Belarus built a serious software industry through its High Technology Park, which produced World of Tanks and Viber among others, so fibre is widespread, speeds are decent and prices are low. Mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. Coworking exists in the centre and the standard is reasonable. The complication is not technical: international payment cards issued abroad often do not work, several Western services are unavailable, and sanctions make banking and receiving money genuinely awkward. Plan the money side before arriving. A large part of that software industry relocated, to Poland, Lithuania, Georgia and elsewhere, so the sector that built the infrastructure is considerably thinner on the ground than the infrastructure itself suggests. And a number of Western sites and services are blocked or unreliable, which makes a VPN standard equipment for most foreign workers here, though the legal position on that is ambiguous rather than settled and is worth checking rather than assuming. Russian is the working language of almost everything.
minsk.gettingAround: Minsk has a clean, cheap and fast metro with three lines, and the fare is a few cents. Buses, trolleybuses and trams cover the rest, and the city was rebuilt after 1944 on a scale that makes it easy to navigate and long to walk: Independence Avenue runs fifteen kilometres in a straight line. Taxis and Yandex Go are cheap. Minsk National Airport connects to Moscow, Istanbul, Dubai and a shrinking set of other destinations, since European Union carriers no longer fly here and European airspace is closed to Belarusian ones. Getting in is now the harder part of any trip here. Most travellers arrive by air through Istanbul or Dubai, or overland from Russia, while the land borders with Poland, Lithuania and Latvia have been variously restricted, closed or reduced to a handful of crossings with long queues. Rail links to Moscow are frequent and comfortable, and the once-easy train to Vilnius no longer runs. From the airport a bus and a train both reach the centre in about an hour, and taxis are cheap enough that most visitors simply take one.
minsk.visas: Belarus operates a visa-free scheme that has expanded considerably: citizens of most European countries, including the whole European Union, may enter for up to thirty days without a visa. The conditions matter. The visa-free entry generally applies when arriving at Minsk National Airport or by certain land crossings, requires medical insurance, and specifically excludes arrival from or departure to Russia, because that border is not an international one and has no controls. There is no remote work visa. Check the current rules directly, since this policy has changed repeatedly. Anyone entering overland should also note that Belarus requires compulsory medical insurance bought locally at the border, and that the paperwork is checked rather than assumed. Foreigners staying beyond a short period must register their place of residence, which a hotel does automatically and a private landlord generally does not, and it is checked on the way out. The Russia exclusion works in both directions and catches people planning to leave overland towards Moscow, which is not a legal exit for a visa-free visitor. Anyone holding Belarusian citizenship alongside another should take specific advice, since Belarus does not recognise the second one.
minsk.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable window, with temperatures around twenty two degrees in July and long evenings. Winter from December to February is properly cold, often around minus five to minus ten, with snow on the ground for months, though the city clears it efficiently and the metro makes it manageable. April and October are grey and wet. Minsk is greener than its reputation suggests, with large parks along the Svislach river, and summer is when that shows. Independence Day on the third of July is the biggest event in the calendar. Winter days are short as well as cold, with the light gone by four in December, and that does more to shape a stay than the temperature does. Summer empties the city at weekends, when a large share of residents leave for dachas outside it, so August here is quiet in a rather pleasant way. Kupalle at midsummer is marked with bonfires and water outside the city, and the autumn mushroom season is a national preoccupation rather than a pastime.
minsk.prosCons: Minsk trades on cost, order and a coherent architectural idea: the city was almost entirely destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt in Stalinist neoclassicism on a monumental scale, which produces something genuinely unlike anywhere else. It is clean, very safe from street crime, the metro works and living costs are a fraction of the rest of Europe. The objection is political rather than practical. Belarus is an authoritarian state, the 2020 protests were suppressed severely, sanctions complicate money and travel, and the war next door shapes everything. The city's Great Patriotic War museum and the memorial at Khatyn also make plain how completely Belarus was destroyed between 1941 and 1944, which explains a great deal about the country. Photographing government buildings, police or infrastructure attracts attention, and political conversation can put a local at risk even where the visitor faces nothing worse than inconvenience. Check as well whether your travel insurance is valid here at all, since a number of policies now exclude the country outright and people tend to discover that at the point of claiming.
minsk.whoFor: A specific reason is what brings people: family connections, business ties, Russian-language study, or an interest in Soviet urbanism, which the city offers in an unusually complete form. It suits developers, given the local industry. Western banking does not function smoothly here and sanctions make that unlikely to change soon. Political expression carries real consequences in Belarus, which anybody considering a stay should weigh honestly rather than assume around, and the flight options out have narrowed to the point where an easy visa run is no longer available. Belovezhskaya Pushcha on the Polish border justifies the trip by itself. It is the last surviving stretch of the primeval woodland that once covered the whole European plain, and wild bison still live in it. Anyone looking for a cheap, Russian-speaking base without the complications should look at Georgia or Armenia first, which is where most of the people who would once have considered this city have gone. Journalists, researchers and anyone with a public record of political writing should take specific advice before travelling rather than rely on general guidance. For everyone else it works better as a visit of weeks than as a base of months.

bujumbura.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $500, with the Rohero and Kiriri areas near the embassies at the top. Market produce is very cheap and Burundi grows good coffee, bananas and vegetables. Imported goods carry a heavy markup and the supermarkets serving the expatriate community are expensive. Fish from Lake Tanganyika, particularly mukeke and the small ndagala, is cheap and excellent. Utilities are modest but power cuts are frequent. Burundi is one of the poorest countries in the world by income per head, which is visible everywhere and shapes what the low prices mean. The currency is the complication. Burundi has run a wide gap between the official exchange rate and the parallel one, which means the cost of a stay can differ substantially depending on how money is changed, and the rules around it shift. Rent at the expatriate end is often quoted in dollars and asked for several months at a time. A generator or an inverter is a normal household expense rather than a luxury, and fuel shortages have been recurrent, which turns a cheap utility into an unpredictable one.
bujumbura.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. Burundi is landlocked and its bandwidth arrives overland through Tanzania and Kenya, which makes it expensive and slow, and fibre reaches only parts of Bujumbura. Mobile data from Lumitel and Econet is the usual fallback. Power cuts are frequent enough that any serious office runs a generator. There is almost no coworking. Anyone with call-heavy work should treat this as a real constraint rather than a nuisance. The time zone is two hours ahead of GMT, which gives a workable European overlap and an early start against the Americas. In practice the reliable workspaces belong to organisations rather than to the public. The international hotels and the larger offices have generators and better lines, and a stay of any length usually means arranging desk access through whoever you are here with. French is the language of business and administration alongside Kirundi, and English is limited outside the international sector. Anyone who cannot arrange that kind of access should test a specific address over several days before committing to it, because the variation between buildings is larger than the variation between providers.
bujumbura.gettingAround: Shared minibuses and motorbike taxis cover Bujumbura cheaply and are how most people move. Taxis are available and inexpensive by the hour. The city is spread along the northeastern shore of Lake Tanganyika and is flat near the water, rising steeply into the hills behind, which is where the better housing sits. Bujumbura International Airport is about eleven kilometres north and connections are limited: Nairobi, Addis Ababa, Kigali and Dar es Salaam, mostly on regional carriers. The road to Kigali takes about six hours and is the common overland route. Travel outside the city after dark is generally avoided, by residents as much as visitors, and most organisations operate a rule against it. Hiring a driver for the day costs little and solves the roads and the language at once, which is why almost everyone working here does that rather than drive themselves. The lake is a route as well as a view: boats run down the shore and Kigoma in Tanzania is reachable across the water, though the schedules are irregular enough that it takes planning rather than turning up.
bujumbura.visas: Burundi requires a visa of most nationalities. An e-visa system operates and is the usual route, with visas issued for thirty days and extendable in Bujumbura, and visa on arrival has been available at times but is not something to rely on. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. The rules have changed more than once in recent years and the fees are payable in United States dollars, so confirm the current position directly with the immigration department before travelling. Anyone crossing overland to Rwanda should note that the border has closed and reopened several times in recent years and the current status is worth confirming the week before travelling. Carry a copy of the passport and the visa at all times, since identity checks are routine and being without documents is an avoidable problem rather than a serious one. Extensions are handled in the capital and are best begun well before the thirty days run out, because the process is not quick. Fees are paid in cash dollars in good condition, and worn or older notes are refused, which is a small detail that has stranded travellers at more than one border in the region.
bujumbura.bestTime: June to August is the long dry season and the practical window, warm at around twenty eight degrees on the lake shore with clear skies. There is a shorter dry spell in December and January. The rains from February to May and again from September to November are heavy, and Bujumbura floods, with the roads out of the city sometimes cut. Temperatures on the lake shore are consistently warm while the hills behind are noticeably cooler, and the difference of a few hundred metres is worth several degrees. Anyone visiting Kibira National Park in the north should note that its trails are close to impassable in the rains and that the chimpanzee tracking is a dry season activity. Malaria is present all year and rises after the rains, so prophylaxis is a matter for a doctor rather than a decision to make on arrival, and it is one of the few genuinely non-negotiable preparations for this destination. The lake is calmest and clearest through the dry months, which is when the beaches are worth the trip. The coffee harvest runs from around April into July and is the busiest stretch of the rural year.
bujumbura.prosCons: Bujumbura sits on Lake Tanganyika, the second deepest and second oldest lake in the world, with sand beaches at Saga and Karera that would be famous anywhere else, alongside genuinely low costs and a compact centre that is easy to walk. Burundian drumming is UNESCO-listed and unlike anything else. Burundi carries severe poverty, a fragile political situation left by the 2015 crisis, real street crime, weak medical care and limited infrastructure, and none of that is an exaggeration of the risk. This needs current government advice, not assumptions. The country's political capital also moved to Gitega in 2019, so Bujumbura remains the economic centre while the government has largely relocated inland. Lake Tanganyika looks like a beach and is not one. It holds hippos and crocodiles, and safe swimming is confined to specific stretches that residents know, so it is a question to ask rather than judge by eye. Medical evacuation cover is standard for anyone posted here and sensible for anyone else, given that serious treatment means Nairobi. Set against all of that, Burundians are widely described as among the most welcoming people in the region, and visitors say so consistently.
bujumbura.whoFor: Development, health and humanitarian workers, and there are a good many of them here, along with researchers working on the Great Lakes. It suits anyone with a regional connection through Rwanda or Tanzania. This is not a destination and treating it as one leads to a bad month. Connectivity and power are both unreliable, and without an existing support network the practical difficulty of ordinary days runs a great deal higher than the price level would ever suggest. Lake Tanganyika is why researchers keep a presence on this shore. It holds hundreds of cichlid species found nowhere else, which has made it one of the most closely examined bodies of fresh water on the planet. Anyone drawn to the region rather than to this country specifically will find Kigali a few hours away doing almost everything more easily, with better connectivity, simpler entry and a functioning services sector, and that is where most independent remote workers in the Great Lakes actually base themselves. Bujumbura makes sense with a posting, a project or a personal connection attached to it. It also rewards anyone seriously interested in music, since the drumming here is a living tradition rather than a performance staged for visitors.

gustavia.costOfLiving: Budget around $3,600 a month, which makes Saint Barthelemy among the most expensive places on this site. A one-bedroom runs roughly $2,000 to $3,000 and villa rates in high season run into thousands per night, which is the market this island serves. Groceries are imported through Saint Martin and priced accordingly, with a French supermarket selling French products at a substantial markup. Restaurants are excellent and expensive throughout. There is no meaningful budget tier: the island decided decades ago what it was going to be. The euro is the currency and French banking applies. Off-season rentals from May through November fall a long way below the winter rates, and someone able to be here in the quiet months experiences a substantially different island economically. Water is desalinated and expensive, which shows in the bills for anything with a pool. Saint Barthelemy also has its own tax status within France, with residents of five years or more falling outside French income tax, which is part of why the permanent population is what it is.
gustavia.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Saint Barthelemy has fibre in Gustavia and the main settlements, French mobile networks with roaming that costs European visitors nothing, and reliable power. The infrastructure was rebuilt substantially after Hurricane Irma in 2017. There is no coworking in any formal sense, but the villas and hotels are equipped for people who work. The time zone is four hours behind GMT, which gives a comfortable overlap with both the eastern United States and, in the morning, with Europe, and that combination is one of the genuine practical arguments for the eastern Caribbean. The working population is seasonal in a way that shapes everything: the island fills with crew, hospitality staff and villa managers for the winter and empties through the autumn, so the people around you in March are not the people around you in September. The resident professional world is yachting, hospitality and property and almost nothing else. For anyone bringing their own work that is fine and rather the point; for anyone hoping to find work here, the season decides it and staff housing is the binding constraint.
gustavia.gettingAround: You need a small car, and small is the operative word: the roads are steep, narrow and full of hairpins, and the island's rental fleet is mostly Mini Mokes and compact hatchbacks for that reason. Gustavia itself is walkable. Saint Barthelemy is only about twenty five square kilometres, so nothing is more than fifteen minutes away. Gustaf III Airport has one of the shortest and most demanding commercial runways in the world, approached over a hill and landing towards a beach, served by small aircraft from Saint Martin and San Juan. The ferry from Saint Martin is the alternative to that landing and takes about forty five minutes, which is the sensible choice for anyone with luggage, since the small aircraft enforce tight weight limits and bags occasionally follow on a later flight. Scooters are common and suit the roads, though the gradients and the loose gravel on the steeper corners argue for some experience first. Parking in Gustavia is limited and the harbour front fills early, which is the one place on the island where arriving late actually costs you something.
gustavia.visas: Saint Barthelemy is a French overseas collectivity, part of the French Republic but outside the European Union customs and Schengen areas, so a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. French and European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and may live and work here without a permit. Most other Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days. There is no remote work visa. Arriving through Sint Maarten means clearing that territory's entry rules first. Anyone arriving by the small aircraft from Saint Martin should also note that the two territories keep separate records, and that the flight is treated as an international one. The customs status is the other half of that arrangement and it is why the island is a duty-free port, which shows up in the price of alcohol, tobacco and perfume rather than in anything else. Saint Martin is the French side and Sint Maarten the Dutch, which is a trap worth avoiding when booking: they are the same island under two administrations, and the international airport and most connections are on the Dutch side of it.
gustavia.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, the high season and the reason the island exists economically, with temperatures around twenty seven degrees, low humidity and the harbour full. Prices in that window are extraordinary and everything books months ahead. May, June and November are the shoulder months and the best value. Hurricane season runs June to November and Irma in 2017 caused severe damage across the island. August and September are the quietest months, when many restaurants close entirely and the island belongs to residents. The Saint Barth Bucket Regatta in March and Les Voiles de Saint-Barth in April are the two events that fill the harbour, and accommodation around them is booked a year ahead. New Year is the island's extreme. The harbour fills with the largest yachts afloat, restaurant tables are allocated rather than booked, and prices for those two weeks are unlike anything else in the Caribbean, so anyone who wants the island rather than the scene should avoid it entirely. Winter also brings northerly swells that close some of the north-facing beaches for a few days at a time, which is worth knowing if a particular beach is the whole plan.
gustavia.prosCons: Saint Barthelemy is genuinely beautiful and genuinely safe, with fourteen beaches to a population of about ten thousand, French food and wine at the standard you would expect, and infrastructure that simply works. Gustavia's Swedish street grid and warehouse buildings, left from the century when Sweden owned the island, give it a character no other Caribbean harbour has. Price filters everything here, and so does scale, since this is a small island with one town and a single season that pays for the whole year. Gustavia is also the only Caribbean harbour named after a Swedish king, and the street names, the belfry and the three forts are what remains of that period. Medical care runs to a small hospital, and anything serious means Saint Martin, Guadeloupe or Miami, so evacuation cover matters here as much as anywhere less polished. And the island's own housing shortage is severe, because almost every building that could be a home is worth more as a rental, which is a live local issue and the reason so much of the workforce commutes in from Saint Martin.
gustavia.whoFor: Saint Barthelemy suits people with the budget to be here and a reason to want the eastern Caribbean specifically: the time zone works for American and European clients on the same day, the island is safe, and the food is excellent. It suits sailors. An ordinary budget has no business on St Barts, no community of remote workers has formed there, and variety is limited by an island this small where the season dictates what is open, what is full and what any of it costs. Pilots treat the approach into Gustaf III as a qualification in its own right. Flying it requires a specific certification, and it appears on every list of the most demanding commercial landings in the world. There is a cheaper way in that the island does not advertise: come in the quiet months, take a long let rather than a nightly rate, and the arithmetic changes considerably while the beaches do not. Anyone comparing the northeastern Caribbean will find Anguilla quieter and better set up for a long remote-work stay, Saint Martin far cheaper and busier, and this island the most polished and the least forgiving of a modest budget.

marigot.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month on the French side, which is expensive by Caribbean standards and considerably cheaper than Saint Barthelemy next door. A one-bedroom runs roughly $900 to $1,400, with Terres Basses and the Baie Nettle strip at the top. Groceries in the French supermarkets are imported and pricey, though crossing to the Dutch side for some shopping is normal and legal, since there is no border post. Restaurants in Grand Case, which markets itself as the gourmet capital of the Caribbean, are excellent and expensive. The euro is the currency on this side and dollars are widely accepted. The octroi de mer levied across Guadeloupe and Martinique is simply not charged on this side, and that single exemption is why several categories of imported goods cost less here than on the departments to the south. Rent is where the money goes instead, since the housing stock never fully recovered from 2017 and demand from the yachting and hospitality trades keeps the pressure on year-round rather than seasonally.
marigot.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable. Fibre reaches parts of Marigot and the main settlements, French mobile networks operate with free roaming for European visitors, and power is generally reliable, though the recovery from Hurricane Irma in 2017 took years and some infrastructure still shows it. There is limited coworking. The time zone is four hours behind GMT, which gives a good working overlap with the eastern United States all afternoon and with Europe in the morning, one of the more genuinely useful positions on this site for anyone with clients on both sides. Administration is the friction rather than the infrastructure. This is a collectivity with its own competences, so tax and some regulation are local while social security and the courts remain French, and working out which office handles a given question is a genuine time cost for anyone setting up. A great many residents on this side work on the Dutch side, where the jobs in the airport, the marinas and retail concentrate, so the daily flow across an unmarked border is the island's real economy. Marigot itself is administrative and quiet by comparison.
marigot.gettingAround: A car is the practical answer. The island is about eighty seven square kilometres shared between France and the Netherlands, with a single ring road and no border checks between the two halves, though the road narrows and the traffic backs up badly around Marigot and Simpson Bay. Shared minibuses run the main routes cheaply. Marigot itself is walkable. Princess Juliana International Airport on the Dutch side is the island's air link and one of the busiest in the eastern Caribbean, with direct flights to Europe and North America. Anyone crossing to the Dutch side regularly should also know that the two halves use different currencies and different plug standards, which catches people out more often than the border does. The Anguilla ferry leaves from here rather than from the Dutch side, running from Marigot to Blowing Point several times a day, which makes this the practical jumping-off point for that island and a reason to stay on this half. Taxi fares are set by a published tariff and are high enough that most residents drive. Parking in Marigot is manageable except on market mornings, when Wednesday and Saturday fill the waterfront and the streets behind it.
marigot.visas: Saint Martin is a French overseas collectivity, part of France and the European Union but outside the Schengen area, so a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. European Union citizens may live and work here without a permit. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for ninety days. The Dutch side, Sint Maarten, is a separate country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands with its own rules, and although nobody checks the internal border, the two sides do keep separate records. Anyone planning a long stay should also weigh which side to base on, since the French side offers European Union rights and the Dutch side offers a lower cost of living. The 2007 reorganisation is the thing to understand: this side was detached from Guadeloupe to become a collectivity in its own right, which is why its rules differ from the departments to the south despite everything looking equally French. Social security and health cover run through the French system, so a European card works here as it does in Paris. For non-Europeans the long-stay route is the French one, applied for before travel, and there is no local scheme that shortcuts it.
marigot.bestTime: December to April is the dry season and the high season, warm at around twenty seven degrees with low humidity and the whole island busy. May, June and November are quieter and better value. Hurricane season runs June to November, and this island took the full force of Irma in 2017, which was the strongest Atlantic hurricane on record at landfall and destroyed a large part of the built environment. Recovery has been substantial but uneven. September is the quietest month and much of the tourist economy shuts. Carnival on the French side runs in February and March before Lent, while the Dutch side holds its own in April, so the island effectively gets two. The eleventh of November is the island's own day, marking the saint the place was named for and celebrated jointly across both halves at the obelisk on the border, and no other divided island marks its shared identity in quite that way, so it repays timing a visit around. February and March bring the French side's carnival. Sea grape and flamboyant flower through the early summer, and the light in the weeks after the rains breaks is when photographers say the island looks best.
marigot.prosCons: The French side sells itself on food, which at Grand Case is genuinely a cut above anything else in the region, along with the beaches, the ability to live in France while working American hours, and freedom of movement for European Union citizens. Two legal systems on one small island produce useful arbitrage in several directions. Saint Martin also has real crime problems by regional standards, the recovery from Irma is incomplete, the traffic is bad, and the island leans heavily on a cruise and charter economy that it does not control. Healthcare on this side runs through a French public hospital with the standards that implies, which is a genuine advantage over most of the eastern Caribbean and the reason people cross from neighbouring islands for treatment. Schooling is the French state system, free and in French. The collectivity also carries serious social problems, with unemployment among the young high and the post-Irma reconstruction of public housing still unfinished, and those are visible rather than tucked away out of sight of the beaches.
marigot.whoFor: Saint Martin suits European Union citizens who want a Caribbean base with no immigration friction and a time zone that works for both sides of the Atlantic. It suits sailors, since the lagoon is one of the largest in the Caribbean and a major charter hub. It suits anyone who takes food seriously. Quiet is not on offer, the security situation is something to research honestly rather than assume, and anybody hoping for a cheap Caribbean island has picked one of the more expensive ones. The arrangement itself is the curiosity. The 1648 Treaty of Concordia that split this island between France and the Netherlands is among the oldest border agreements anywhere in the world still in force. For a European Union citizen this is one of very few places in the Caribbean offering full residence rights, a French hospital, French schools and a working American time zone at once, a set of things almost nowhere else offers together, and the strongest argument this island has. Families do well on this side for exactly those reasons. Anyone whose priority is cost rather than paperwork should look at the Dutch half or further down the chain, since neither the rent nor the restaurants here are forgiving.

brades.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $600 to $1,000, and the housing stock is limited because the population fell from about twelve thousand to under five thousand after the volcanic crisis and much of what was built is in the exclusion zone. Groceries are imported and expensive, with the supply chain running through Antigua. Local produce and fish are cheaper. Utilities are moderate. Eating out is limited to a handful of places at modest prices. Montserrat uses the East Caribbean dollar, which is pegged to the United States dollar at a fixed rate. Land in the safe zone is scarce and dear for the same reason housing is: everything the island had in the south sits inside the zone and can neither be built on nor insured. Import duty applies to almost everything arriving by boat or small aircraft, and the freight cost per box is what lifts the shopping bill rather than any markup at the till. There is no chain supermarket, so stock arrives on a boat schedule and the shelves empty in a pattern residents learn to read. Cash still matters more than a card in the smaller shops.
brades.whereToWork: Connectivity is adequate. Montserrat has a submarine cable connection and fibre reaches the inhabited north, with speeds workable for normal remote work, and mobile coverage across the safe zone. Power is reasonably reliable. There is no coworking. The island has actively marketed a remote work visa and has infrastructure adequate to support one, which is unusual for somewhere this small. The time zone is four hours behind GMT, giving a good overlap with the eastern United States and a workable morning with Europe. Anyone considering the remote work stamp should confirm the current income threshold and insurance requirement directly, since the scheme has been adjusted since it was introduced. The public sector is the economy here: government is by some distance the largest employer, and the British budget support that keeps it running is a standing fact of life rather than an emergency measure. The observatory, the airport, the ferry and the hospital account for much of the rest. That means the professional network available to an outsider is small and mostly public, and the private businesses are family firms of long standing. Anyone hoping to plug into a local industry should understand that there is essentially one, and it is administration.
brades.gettingAround: You need a car. The habitable northern third of the island is about ten kilometres across, with steep, winding roads and no public transport beyond a few minibuses. Brades, Salem and Little Bay are the main settlements and none of them is walkable to the others. John A Osborne Airport in the north is served by small aircraft from Antigua several times a day, a fifteen minute flight, and a ferry also runs from Antigua. The exclusion zone in the south is entered only with permission and a guide. Anyone taking the ferry from Antigua should allow for it being weather-dependent, and for the schedule changing seasonally in a way the airline connection does not.
brades.visas: Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory and grants visa-free entry to citizens of the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States, Canada and most Commonwealth countries for up to six months. It also operates a Remote Work Stamp, a formal one year visa for remote workers with proof of employment outside Montserrat, minimum income and health insurance, which is one of the more straightforward such schemes in the Caribbean. Arriving requires transiting Antigua, so that country's entry rules apply first. Anyone applying for the remote work stamp should budget for the application fee and for proof of income, both of which are checked rather than taken on trust. Because every arrival transits another country, the practical itinerary involves two sets of formalities on the same day, and a delayed connection can mean a night on the other island rather than an hour in a lounge. The stamp asks for a police certificate and a bank statement alongside the employment letter, and the file is read by a small office rather than processed by a system, which cuts both ways: slower, but it is possible to ask a question and get an answer from a person. Renewal is a fresh application rather than a stamp in a passport.
brades.bestTime: December to April is the dry season and the practical window, with temperatures around twenty seven degrees and low humidity. The rains from June to November are heavier and this is also the hurricane season. The volcano is the other calendar: Soufriere Hills has been intermittently active since 1995 and its state determines what is accessible, with the Montserrat Volcano Observatory publishing the current hazard level. Ash falls happen. The observatory itself is open to visitors and is the best introduction to what happened here. The Saint Patrick's Day festival in March is the island's biggest event and marks a 1768 slave rebellion, which is why Montserrat's Irish heritage is commemorated the way it is. The carnival here runs from the middle of December into the new year rather than before Lent, a pattern several of the smaller islands follow, and it makes the Christmas fortnight the busiest stretch of the year. A calabash festival takes the July slot. Ash advisories, when they come, are issued as routine and specify which districts should keep their windows shut rather than telling anybody to leave, and residents treat them roughly the way other places treat a wind warning.
brades.prosCons: Montserrat comes with a formal remote work visa, an English-speaking British administration, genuine safety, and a landscape unlike anywhere else in the Caribbean, since the buried town of Plymouth is visible from the viewing points and is the only abandoned capital city anywhere in the Americas. The island is green, quiet and largely undeveloped. The island is tiny and quiet in return, with a population under five thousand, minimal shopping, a single flight route in, and a volcano that has never once stopped being active. Montserrat is also where George Martin built AIR Studios in 1979, and the Rolling Stones, Dire Straits and Paul McCartney all recorded here before Hurricane Hugo destroyed it in 1989.
brades.whoFor: Montserrat suits remote workers who want a formal visa, a quiet English-speaking base and low prices, and who genuinely mean it about quiet. It suits geologists and anyone drawn to the volcano, which is among the most studied in the world. It suits birdwatchers, since the Montserrat oriole exists nowhere else. Choice, nightlife and company are all in short supply among five thousand people. The volcano is the real question: it is active, the exclusion zone is enforced, and anybody who would find that unsettling should take the feeling seriously rather than override it. It also suits divers, since the reefs off the north coast are almost entirely unvisited and the volcanic activity has created new underwater terrain since the 1990s. Three months is long enough to see whether the quiet is restful or oppressive, and that is the question the island turns on rather than any of the practical ones.

stpierre.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, and the housing stock is small, wooden and brightly painted, which is the town's defining look. Groceries arrive by ship from Halifax and by air, and prices reflect that: this is French retail with North Atlantic freight on top. The local fish is excellent and cheap. Heating is a serious budget line, since the winters are long and the buildings are old. Eating out is limited to a handful of restaurants but the bread, cheese and wine are genuinely French, shipped from France. The euro is the currency. Value added tax simply does not exist here, since the archipelago sits outside the European customs area, and what stands in its place is a local duty charged on goods as they land, which is why the shelf price of an imported item bears no simple relation to what the same thing costs on the mainland. Fuel oil arrives by ship and is bought by the tankful, and what an old timber house gets through between October and May is the number that decides whether a year here is affordable. Social security runs through a local fund rather than the national one, with its own rates and its own card.
stpierre.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Saint Pierre and Miquelon has a fibre connection through Canada and French telecoms infrastructure on the islands, so speeds in the town are workable and reliable, with mobile coverage across the inhabited areas. Power is reliable. There is no coworking. The time zone is unusual and worth noting: the archipelago runs three hours behind GMT, which is thirty minutes ahead of Newfoundland next door and an hour ahead of the Canadian mainland, and it observes European daylight saving dates rather than North American ones. The archipelago uses the euro while everything within reach of it runs on Canadian dollars, so a shopping trip to Newfoundland means a currency change as well as a border, and card acceptance here is patchier than in France.
stpierre.gettingAround: Saint-Pierre is walkable end to end in twenty minutes and the island is only about twenty six square kilometres, with a road network you exhaust in an afternoon. Cars exist and are barely needed. Miquelon, the larger island, is reached by a ferry that takes about an hour and has its own small settlement and a long sand isthmus with wild horses on it. Saint-Pierre Airport connects to Montreal, Halifax and St John's, and a ferry runs to Fortune in Newfoundland in about ninety minutes. Anyone crossing to Newfoundland should book the ferry ahead in summer and expect it to be cancelled in rough weather, which happens often enough to build slack into any plan. A small boat runs in summer to the abandoned village on the island across the harbour, which was still inhabited within living memory and is kept now as an open-air museum with a church, a school and a wreck on the shore. It is the best half day here. Driving is on the right with plates and rules from the mainland, and the fuel comes in at a price nobody from either neighbouring country would recognise. Bicycles work in summer and are pointless for half the year.
stpierre.visas: Saint Pierre and Miquelon is a French overseas collectivity, part of France but outside the European Union and outside Schengen, so a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. French and European Union citizens have freedom of movement and may live and work here. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days.
