Arriving overland means transiting Canada, so Canadian entry rules apply first, and that catches out people who assumed a French territory would be simple. Anyone flying in from Canada should also carry proof of onward travel, since the airline checks it and the archipelago's schedules leave little room to improvise a departure. A pet travelling with you has to satisfy two sets of rules rather than one, because almost every route in crosses another country first and that country applies its own conditions to an animal in transit. The same logic catches anybody carrying prescription medicines or professional equipment. Carry the rules in writing, because a check-in desk will not know them. Freedom of movement here comes attached to a labour market of a few thousand jobs, most of them public, so the right to work and the chance of work are quite different propositions.
stpierre.bestTime: July to September is the season, and it is a short one: temperatures reach around eighteen degrees, the fog lifts more often and the ferry and flight schedules are at their fullest. Winter from December to March is cold, windy and snowy, with the sea often too rough for the ferry. Fog is the defining weather here and can sit over the islands for days in any season, which is why the approach to the airport is so often diverted. Spring is late and cold. The Basque and Breton festivals in August are the liveliest weeks of the year, and they are when the archipelago's fishing heritage is most visible in the town. The capelin roll in early summer brings small silver fish onto the beaches in their millions to spawn, and everyone goes down to watch and to gather them, which is the clearest sign the season has finally turned. Snow clearing is a municipal operation that runs through the night, and the streets are usually passable by morning however much fell. Midwinter is the social season in a town this size, with the halls booked solid between the feasts and nobody going anywhere else in any case.
stpierre.prosCons: This is genuinely France, with French administration, French food, French schools and the euro, sitting twenty kilometres off the coast of Newfoundland, and no other place on earth offers quite that combination. The town is small, safe and remarkably pretty in its painted timber. The weather is the price: cold, wet and foggy for most of the year, on top of the isolation, a population of about six thousand, and a stock of things to do that runs out inside a single week for most people. The islands also hold the only guillotine ever used in North America, which was shipped from Martinique in 1889, used once, and is now in the museum.
stpierre.whoFor: This suits French speakers who want North America without leaving France, anyone drawn to the North Atlantic, and people with a working reason to be here in fisheries or administration. The Prohibition era ran through these islands on an enormous scale. Liquor moved from here into the United States all through the 1920s, and the warehouses that held it are still standing. Sunshine, choice and company are three things six thousand people on a fogbound North Atlantic archipelago cannot supply, and French is required, because English is thin on the ground here despite Canada being twenty kilometres away. It suits anyone with time rather than a schedule, since arriving means either the ferry from Fortune in Newfoundland or a small aircraft, and both defer to the fog that can close the islands for days together.

stanley.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100 and the rental market is very small, with most housing tied to employment or government. Groceries arrive by ship from Britain roughly monthly and by air, so the shelves depend on when the last delivery came and prices are high. Local lamb and fish are cheap and excellent. Heating is a substantial cost given the wind and the cold. Eating out is limited to a few pubs and restaurants. The Falkland Islands pound is pegged to sterling at par and British notes circulate alongside it. Housing is allocated more than it is rented. Most of the decent stock belongs to the government or to employers and comes with a post, so arriving without a job attached means competing for a very small private market where listings circulate by noticeboard and word of mouth rather than online. Wool and fisheries are what the private economy actually runs on, and the squid season sets the rhythm of the year. Anything ordered from Britain arrives with freight attached and on the ship's timetable, so households buy in quantity when something is available.
stanley.whereToWork: Connectivity is the weakest thing about the islands. There is no submarine cable, so all bandwidth arrives by satellite, which makes it slow, expensive and metered in a way that shapes daily life. Data allowances are a normal topic of conversation here. Mobile coverage exists in Stanley and thins to nothing in Camp, the term for everywhere outside the town. Power is reliable and increasingly wind-generated. Anyone with bandwidth-dependent work should treat the Falklands as genuinely difficult rather than merely slow. Anyone planning an extended stay should price the data allowance carefully, since exceeding it is expensive and video calls consume it far faster than most people expect. Satellite bandwidth is shared rather than dedicated, which means the speed you get depends partly on what everyone else in Stanley is doing at that moment, and evenings are noticeably worse than mornings. Plan anything heavy for early. The professional world is government, fisheries administration, farming and the military support economy, and it is small enough that a newcomer meets most of it within a fortnight. There is no scenario in which this works as a base for someone whose income depends on being reliably reachable by video.
stanley.gettingAround: Stanley is small and walkable along its waterfront. Beyond the town, Camp is reached by unsealed roads and four-wheel drive, or by the Falkland Islands Government Air Service, which flies small aircraft to the settlements and outer islands on a schedule published the evening before. Mount Pleasant airport, about fifty kilometres west, handles the military airbridge from Britain and the weekly LATAM flight from Santiago via Punta Arenas, which is the only commercial connection to South America. Anyone flying to the outer islands should expect the schedule to be confirmed by radio the night before, and to be reshuffled by weather without much notice. Distances in Camp are deceptive because the tracks, not the map, decide the time: a settlement forty kilometres away can take three hours across peat and stone, and getting stuck is common enough that nobody travels without telling someone the route. Vehicles here are almost universally four-wheel drive for that reason. Within Stanley everything is close enough to walk, and the harbour front takes fifteen minutes end to end.
stanley.visas: The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own immigration rules. Citizens of the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States and most Commonwealth countries receive up to twenty four months as visitors, subject to proof of onward travel, accommodation and sufficient funds, all of which are genuinely checked on arrival. Working requires a work permit arranged by an employer in advance. There is no remote work visa. Anyone arriving on the South America route needs to satisfy Chilean transit requirements as well. Anyone arriving on the military airbridge from Brize Norton should note that seats are limited, that priority goes to service personnel, and that civilian bookings are made well in advance. The sovereignty dispute has practical consequences for travel rather than merely political ones. Argentina does not recognise the islands' administration, the air links across South America have been restricted and renegotiated repeatedly, and the single weekly commercial flight is therefore a genuine chokepoint rather than one option among several. Anyone building an itinerary should treat that flight as the fixed point and everything else as flexible, and should hold insurance that covers a long unplanned wait.
stanley.bestTime: October to March is the southern summer and the only realistic window, with temperatures around thirteen degrees, long daylight and the wildlife at its most active. Penguin colonies are busiest from October to February, black-browed albatross nest through the summer, and elephant seals haul out in spring. Winter from May to August is cold, dark and windy with limited flights. The wind is the constant here rather than the temperature: it blows hard in every season and is what makes thirteen degrees feel considerably colder. Anyone hoping to see king penguins at Volunteer Point should allow a full day, since the drive across Camp takes several hours each way in a four-wheel drive. Weather here is a scheduling problem more than a comfort one. Flights to the outer islands, boat crossings and even the road to Volunteer Point are all cancelled by wind rather than by rain, and a fortnight in the islands should assume at least one day lost to it. Daylight in December runs to seventeen hours, which is what makes the summer trip worth the effort, while June gives barely seven and the town turns inward for the winter.
stanley.prosCons: Wildlife here comes on a scale that is hard to convey, with five penguin species, enormous albatross colonies, elephant seals and sea lions, all of it approachable and almost entirely unvisited outside the short cruise season. The islands are safe, English-speaking and orderly. The internet arrives by satellite, the costs are high, the wind is constant, the isolation is real, and the 1982 war and the continuing sovereignty dispute with Argentina shape the place in ways a visitor notices within days. Landmines were only fully cleared in 2020. The islands also run one of the most valuable fisheries in the South Atlantic, and the squid licences it sells fund most of the government's budget. Medical care is the constraint that shapes a long stay: one hospital serves the whole territory, and anything it cannot handle means an evacuation flight to Chile or Britain, which is expensive and weather-dependent in equal measure. Around three and a half thousand people live here, a number at which anonymity simply does not exist, and residents are candid that the arrangement suits some temperaments and defeats others entirely.
stanley.whoFor: The Falklands suit wildlife photographers, biologists and anyone whose priority is birds and marine mammals rather than comfort. They suit people with a working reason to be here in fisheries, government or the military. They do not suit anyone with bandwidth-dependent work, because satellite internet cannot support it, and they do not suit anyone who wants warmth, shelter from the wind, or the option of leaving on short notice. The 1982 conflict has not been tidied away into a museum. Goose Green, Tumbledown and Mount Longdon are all reachable, marked and explained on the ground where the fighting actually happened. The comparison worth making is with South Georgia and the Antarctic gateway ports, since anyone drawn here for the wildlife is usually weighing those too: Ushuaia and Punta Arenas are cheaper, better connected and have the ships, while these islands have the colonies you can walk to without booking a voyage. A month is a realistic stay for a photographer or a researcher, and anything longer generally means a job.

malabo.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month, which is expensive for central Africa and reflects an oil economy with a small population importing almost everything. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,200, with the areas near the embassies and the newer developments at the top. Groceries in the supermarkets serving the oil sector are very expensive; the local markets are far cheaper and the produce is good, since Bioko island is volcanic and fertile. Eating out ranges from cheap local canteens to expensive hotel restaurants with little in between. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro. The peg to the euro means no currency risk, which is unusual in the region, but it also means the country cannot devalue its way out of an oil price fall, so prices follow the oil cycle rather than local supply. Cash is the default and card acceptance is confined to a handful of hotels. The two-tier market is the thing to grasp about any price quoted: there is an expatriate rate and a local rate for the same goods and the same taxi, and which one you are offered depends on where you are standing and who introduced you.
malabo.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. Equatorial Guinea has a submarine cable connection and fibre reaches parts of Malabo, but the market is effectively a state monopoly, prices are high and reliability is poor. Mobile data is the usual fallback. Power cuts happen and generators are standard in anything serious. There is no coworking. Access to information is also restricted in ways that matter: internet shutdowns have occurred around elections. The time zone is one hour ahead of GMT, which makes European working hours straightforward. Anyone planning a stay should also arrange a local contact in advance, since almost everything here works through introduction rather than through published information. Spanish carries all official business, but French and Portuguese were both added as official languages later, French in 1998 for the regional trade bloc and Portuguese in 2010 as the price of joining the Lusophone community, and neither is spoken by many people. Bubi is the first language on Bioko and Fang on the mainland, and the distinction between those two is politically loaded rather than merely linguistic.
malabo.gettingAround: Shared taxis are the normal way to move around Malabo and are cheap, flagged down on the street and shared with whoever is going the same way. The city is small and the colonial centre is walkable. A car helps for reaching Pico Basile or the south of Bioko island, and the road up the volcano is spectacular. Malabo International Airport is about seven kilometres from the centre with connections to Madrid, Addis Ababa, Casablanca and regional West African cities, plus the domestic hop to Bata on the mainland. Anyone travelling to the mainland region of Rio Muni should note that Bata is a separate flight and that the new planned capital, Ciudad de la Paz, is being built inland from it. The city sits on the rim of a drowned volcanic crater, which is what gives the old harbour its shape and why the ground rises immediately behind the colonial centre. The airport road and the seafront were rebuilt during the oil years and are in better condition than almost anything else in the region, which can mislead a visitor about the state of the roads once the tarmac ends.
malabo.visas: Equatorial Guinea has one of the most difficult visa regimes in Africa. Most nationalities need a visa applied for in advance at an embassy, with an invitation letter, proof of accommodation and often a yellow fever certificate, and the process is slow and inconsistent. United States citizens are a notable exception and may enter without a visa. There is no remote work visa. Photography is restricted around government and military installations and this is enforced seriously. Register your plans and confirm requirements well ahead. Anyone photographing anything at all should ask first, since cameras attract official attention here in a way that visitors from most countries find surprising and occasionally expensive. The American exemption dates from the oil investment of the 1990s and is the only significant one: no European nationality shares it, which reverses the usual pattern and surprises people who assume an EU passport travels further. Where a visa is needed the invitation letter is the binding document rather than the form itself, and obtaining one generally means having a contact in the country before you start.
malabo.bestTime: December to February is the driest window on Bioko and the most comfortable, warm at around thirty degrees. The rest of the year is wet, and the south of the island is extraordinarily so: Ureca receives among the highest rainfall in Africa. Temperatures barely move all year. Turtle nesting on the southern beaches runs roughly November to February and is the island's great natural event, though reaching those beaches requires a serious expedition in any season. Anyone climbing Pico Basile should arrange a permit and a guide in advance, since the road passes military installations and the summit is a restricted area. The rain gradient across Bioko is what protected it: the southern slope facing the ocean is too wet and too steep to have been cleared, so the forest there is primary and the seven primate species are still in it, while the north where the city sits was planted with cocoa a century ago. Forty kilometres separates the two, and almost no road crosses between them.
malabo.prosCons: Bioko has an active volcano rising three thousand metres straight out of the Gulf of Guinea, primary rainforest holding several endemic primates, nesting turtles, and Spanish colonial architecture in Malabo that survives better than most of the region's. Spanish is the working language, which is unusual in Africa. What stands against that is the state itself: Equatorial Guinea is among the most closed and most authoritarian countries in the world, the visa process is genuinely obstructive, and the oil wealth has not reached most of the population. The country is also the only Spanish-speaking state in Africa, a legacy of Spanish rule that ended in 1968 and is still visible in the architecture and the schooling. Cocoa was the entire economy before oil, worked on Bioko by contract labour brought from Nigeria and elsewhere, and the abandoned plantation houses along the northern road are the visible remains of it. The oil that replaced it gave the country one of the highest income figures per head on the continent alongside some of the region's worst health and schooling outcomes, and holding those two numbers together is the honest way to look at the place.
malabo.whoFor: A working reason in oil, gas, diplomacy or conservation, and Spanish specifically, since Spanish opens everything here and English opens very little. It suits biologists working on Bioko's primates or turtles, which is real and ongoing research. It does not suit independent travellers, given the visa regime, and it does not suit anyone uncomfortable in a country where photography and movement are restricted and questions are unwelcome. Bioko's drill monkeys are among the most endangered primates in Africa, and the long-running conservation programme built around them is one of the few things on the island a visitor can genuinely take part in. It suits somebody who already has the introduction and almost nobody who does not. That is the plain summary of a country where the invitation letter, the contact and the stated reason for being present determine whether a stay works, and where turning up to see what happens is not a viable plan. Anyone considering it for the wildlife should approach through one of the established research programmes rather than independently, because the access, the permits and the logistics all run through them.

luanda.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month. Luanda was repeatedly ranked the most expensive city in the world for expatriates through the 2010s, and while the kwanza's fall has changed that, costs for anyone living an imported lifestyle remain high. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,300, with the Ilha and the Marginal at the top. Imported groceries are very expensive; the local markets are cheap and the fish is excellent. Eating out splits sharply between local canteens at a few dollars and expatriate restaurants at European prices. The kwanza has devalued substantially and cash still matters. Housing splits into two markets that barely touch. Expatriate compounds and serviced apartments are priced in dollars against oil-company budgets, while the ordinary rental market runs in kwanza at a fraction of that, and which one you enter depends almost entirely on whether an employer is paying. At the upper end, paying for security is simply part of what a household spends. The state built enormous satellite developments to house the middle the city lacked, of which Kilamba south of town is the best known, and they filled slowly and expensively.
luanda.whereToWork: Connectivity is moderate. Angola has submarine cable capacity and Luanda has fibre in the better districts, with speeds workable for normal remote work, though prices are high relative to income. Mobile data from Unitel and Africell is widespread and Africell's entry improved both price and coverage. Power cuts happen and generators are standard. There is a small but growing coworking scene aimed at the local startup community. The time zone is one hour ahead of GMT, which makes European hours straightforward. Anyone planning to work here should also budget for a generator or a building that has one, since the outages are frequent enough to interrupt a working day regularly. Oil is the whole economy and everything else follows from it: the sector funds the state, sets the exchange rate and determines whether the country is in an expansion or a contraction, and the diversification programmes have not yet changed that. Chinese firms built much of the visible infrastructure over the past two decades under oil-backed arrangements, which is why the construction is recent and the debt is long. For an outsider the practical effect is that professional life runs through personal introduction rather than open advertisement.
luanda.gettingAround: Luanda's traffic is the defining daily experience: the city has grown far faster than its roads and journeys that look short take an hour. The blue and white candongueiro minibuses cover the city cheaply and chaotically. Taxis and Yango are available and reasonable. A new light rail and the expanded Marginal have helped a little. Dr Antonio Agostinho Neto International Airport opened in 2023 about forty kilometres south, replacing the old Quatro de Fevereiro, with connections to Lisbon, Sao Paulo, Dubai and across Africa. Anyone travelling to the new airport should allow considerably more time than the distance suggests, since the road south leaves the city through some of its worst traffic. Sea traffic is the underused alternative. Boats cross the bay to the Ilha and run down the coast, which avoids the roads entirely for some journeys, and residents who have worked out the routes use them. Nobody walks between districts, both because of the distances and because the pavements are not built for it. Ride-hailing has changed the city considerably for anyone without a driver, though surge pricing in the evening rush makes a short trip cost what a long one does at noon.
luanda.visas: Angola transformed its visa regime in 2018 and again since, and it is now far more open than its reputation. Citizens of a long list of countries, including much of Europe, the United States and Brazil, receive up to thirty days visa-free on arrival, and an e-visa covers most of the rest. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a work or residence visa applied for in advance, and the process remains slow. Anyone extending a stay should start the process early, since Angolan administrative procedures are slow and overstaying carries fines that are enforced at the airport. Angola signed a mutual visa waiver with Portugal and several other lusophone states, part of a wider Community of Portuguese Language Countries arrangement, which covers most of the traffic that actually moves in and out of the country. Work permits are employer-sponsored and slow, and the local partner requirements for foreign companies are substantial, so anyone planning to operate rather than visit should get legal advice from someone who has done it in Angola specifically rather than in the region generally.
luanda.bestTime: May to September is the cacimbo, the cool dry season, and the practical window: temperatures around twenty four degrees with overcast skies and almost no rain. October to April is the hot rainy season, humid and up to thirty degrees, with heavy downpours that flood parts of the city. The Benguela current keeps the coast cooler than its latitude suggests, which is why Luanda is drier and milder than Kinshasa on the same parallel. The beaches south at Cabo Ledo are best in the dry season. Anyone heading south should note that Kissama National Park is about seventy kilometres away and that the Benguela railway inland reaches the highlands in a day. The cacimbo brings a low grey overcast rather than rain, and visitors expecting African sunshine in July are consistently surprised by weeks of flat cloud that never quite breaks. It is still the right season to come, since the alternative is heat and flooding. Carnival in February and March is a serious national event with parades along the Marginal, and it falls squarely in the wet half, which is the trade for seeing it.
luanda.prosCons: The setting is genuinely dramatic, a city curved around its bay, with a Portuguese colonial core, one of the most energetic music scenes in Africa in kuduro and semba, and an economy opening up after decades of closure. Angolan cooking is excellent. The cost is high, the traffic is worse, and a serious gap runs between the wealth on the Marginal and the musseque settlements immediately behind it. Street crime is a real concern, infrastructure is uneven, and the civil war that ended in 2002 still shapes the country. Luanda's Ilha, the sand spit closing the bay, also holds most of the city's beach bars and restaurants and is where the city goes at weekends. The gap between the Marginal and the musseques is the defining social fact rather than a footnote, and Angola's inequality is among the most extreme measured anywhere, which a visitor sees within an hour of arriving. Healthcare for anything serious means Portugal or South Africa, and the companies that post people here carry that cover as standard. Set against all of it, the country has been at peace since 2002 and a generation has now grown up with no memory of the fighting, which has done more to the city than any building programme.
luanda.whoFor: Work in oil, gas, construction, diplomacy or development, and Portuguese especially, since business runs in it and English will get you nowhere. Angolan music is exported across the whole continent, and both semba and kuduro came out of this city rather than being adopted by it. It does not suit budget travellers, anyone who needs to move around a city quickly, or anyone without a local network, because Luanda is difficult to navigate without one and expensive to navigate badly. The Atlantic slave trade ran through this city more heavily than through any other. Luanda was its largest single port, and the Museu Nacional da Escravatura stands on the site of the chapel where captives were baptised before embarking. The honest framing is that almost nobody comes to Angola independently, and the ones who do arrive with a contract, a posting or a family connection. Costs assume an employer. Anyone drawn to Portuguese-speaking Africa with a free hand should look at Cape Verde or Mozambique first, both of which are far easier to enter and to move around. What Luanda offers that neither does is a real capital city, with the scale, the music and the friction that implies.

moroni.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,000 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $500. Market produce is cheap and the islands grow their own cassava, banana and coconut, along with the vanilla, ylang-ylang and cloves that are the country's main exports. Imported goods carry a heavy markup because the shipping is infrequent. Fish is cheap and good. Utilities are unreliable rather than expensive, with power cuts a daily fact. Eating out is limited and inexpensive. The Comorian franc is pegged to the euro through an arrangement with France, which removes currency risk. Remittances are the economy's quiet foundation. A very large Comorian community in France sends money home continuously, much of the better housing in Moroni was built with it, and the flow shapes prices in ways a visitor notices without being able to explain. The grand mariage, the traditional wedding that confers social standing, is the other force: families save for years or decades for one, and it is a serious financial institution rather than a colourful custom.
moroni.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. The Comoros are served by a submarine cable and fibre reaches parts of Moroni, but capacity is limited, prices are high and outages are common. Mobile data from Comores Telecom and Telma covers the populated areas. Power cuts are frequent and prolonged, and generators are essential for any serious work. There is no coworking. The time zone is three hours ahead of GMT, which gives a workable European overlap in the afternoon and an early start with Asia. Anyone planning to work here should assume the power will fail at some point in every working day, and should treat a charged laptop battery as the actual infrastructure. French is the language of business and administration alongside Comorian, with Arabic used in religious and some official contexts, and English is genuinely rare. The week runs to Friday prayers rather than a Western weekend, which reshapes when anything official can be done. For a European client base the afternoons here line up neatly, and most people who work remotely from the islands structure the day around that and around whatever hours the electricity happens to cooperate.
moroni.gettingAround: Shared taxis run the roads on Grande Comore for a low fixed fare and are the normal way to move. Moroni's medina is walkable and genuinely medieval in layout, with narrow lanes and carved doors. A car is useful for the road around the island and the climb towards Mount Karthala. Prince Said Ibrahim International Airport is about twenty kilometres north with connections to Dar es Salaam, Nairobi, Addis Ababa, Paris and Mayotte, and inter-island flights and boats reach Anjouan and Moheli. Anyone travelling between the islands should allow generous margins, since the inter-island flights and boats are both unreliable and the sea crossing can be rough. The road that rings Grande Comore is surfaced in stretches and broken in others, and the drive around the island takes far longer than the distance implies. Getting between the three islands is the real constraint: the small aircraft and the boats both run to schedules that bend, and a missed connection can cost days rather than hours. Mayotte is visible from Anjouan on a clear day, which makes the political division of the archipelago feel closer than any map conveys.
moroni.visas: The Comoros are straightforward. Almost every nationality receives a visa on arrival at Moroni airport, valid for forty five days and issued for a modest fee payable in euros, with extensions available in-country. There is no remote work visa. A yellow fever certificate is required from travellers arriving from endemic countries. Anyone travelling on to Mayotte should understand that it is French territory with entirely different requirements, and the Comoros dispute its status, which makes that route politically loaded. Anyone arriving should carry euros in cash for the visa fee, since card payment is not available at the airport and the amount is fixed rather than negotiable. The country's recent history bears on any dealing with its institutions. The Comoros ran an economic citizenship programme in the late 2000s, selling passports in bulk to Gulf states as documentation for stateless residents, and the resulting scandal reached the presidency and still colours how Comorian travel documents are received elsewhere. Extensions of the arrival permit are handled in Moroni and are routine, though the process is unhurried and best begun well before the forty five days run out.
moroni.bestTime: May to October is the cool dry season and the practical window, warm at around twenty six degrees with lower humidity and calmer seas. November to April is the hot wet season and the cyclone season, and Cyclone Kenneth caused severe damage in 2019. Whale season runs roughly July to October, when humpbacks pass through the Mozambique Channel, and turtle nesting on Moheli runs through much of the year. Climbing Mount Karthala, one of the largest active craters in the world, is a dry season undertaking. Anyone climbing Karthala should also budget two days and a guide, since the ascent starts near sea level and the crater rim is above two thousand metres. Ramadan is observed strictly across the islands and the daytime economy contracts to match, with restaurants outside the hotels closed and official business slowed to a crawl; the dates shift earlier against the Western calendar every year. Wedding season concentrates in the dry months, and a grand mariage in the neighbourhood means several days of drumming, feasting and closed streets, which is better understood as an invitation than an obstruction. Cyclone risk runs from January to March, and the channel between the islands is at its roughest then.
moroni.prosCons: The Comoros get fewer visitors than almost any country on earth, and they have better reasons to be seen than that record suggests: Mount Karthala's crater, the Swahili stone town of Moroni with its old Friday mosque on the water, whale watching, and Moheli's marine park. Costs are low. The infrastructure barely functions, the power cuts are frequent, connectivity is weak, medical care is limited, and the political history runs to roughly twenty coups and attempted coups since independence in 1975. The Comoros also produce most of the world's ylang-ylang, the flower distilled for perfume, and the small distilleries on Grande Comore can be visited. Separatism is the political thread that runs through everything here. Anjouan and Moheli have both attempted secession, foreign troops have intervened more than once, and the rotating presidency between the three islands exists precisely to hold the union together. Medical provision is thin enough that residents with means travel to Réunion or Tanzania for anything serious, and that is the assumption to plan around rather than the exception.
moroni.whoFor: The Comoros suit divers, anyone drawn to Swahili coast culture, and travellers who genuinely want somewhere unvisited. They suit French speakers, since French is the working language alongside Comorian and Arabic. They do not suit anyone needing reliable power or internet, anyone on a schedule, or anyone expecting tourist infrastructure, because outside a handful of hotels there is essentially none. The coelacanth is this archipelago's strangest claim. A fish believed extinct for sixty million years was landed off these islands in the twentieth century, and preserved specimens are held in the capital to prove it. The country is also among the least visited on earth, which for some travellers is the entire argument. The trip that works best is a fortnight built around one thing, the volcano, the diving off Moheli, or the stone towns, with generous slack for the inter-island transport to misbehave. Anyone drawn to the wider region should know that Zanzibar offers the Swahili coast with infrastructure attached and Madagascar offers the wildlife, while this archipelago offers the version of both that almost nobody has seen, at the cost of everything working. Researchers and conservation staff are the foreigners who mostly end up staying.

mamoudzou.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month, and Mayotte is expensive in a way that causes genuine political tension: it is the poorest department of France while carrying French import costs, and the gap between the two is the source of recurring protest. A one-bedroom runs roughly $600 to $1,000. Supermarket groceries are French products at a heavy freight markup. The local markets are far cheaper. Utilities are moderate but water shortages are a serious recurring problem. Eating out is limited and mostly Comorian and Malagasy at modest prices. The euro is the currency. Public servants posted from France receive an indexed salary supplement, so a large part of the formal economy is paid well above the local wage and the upper end of the rental market is priced for them rather than for anyone else. And the annual flight to France is a substantial planned expense that many households build a year around. During rationing the cost of bottled water becomes a real household line rather than an afterthought, and vehicles, imported and taxed, cost far more than they would on the mainland.
mamoudzou.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable by regional standards. Mayotte has French telecoms infrastructure and submarine cable capacity, so fibre reaches Mamoudzou and mobile coverage is good, with French plans roaming without charge. Power is mostly reliable. There is very little coworking. The bigger practical constraint is water: Mayotte has suffered severe droughts with rationing that cut supply to households for days at a time, which affects everything about daily life. The time zone is three hours ahead of GMT, giving a workable European afternoon overlap. Anyone planning a long stay should also check the current water situation directly, since the rationing schedules change and they determine a great deal about daily life. Everything professional runs in French and to French administrative norms, since the department's institutions are the same ones as the mainland's, which makes the paperwork familiar to anyone who has worked in France and opaque to anyone who has not. In practice people work from home or from the few hotels with dependable air conditioning, because a public workspace culture has not developed here. A power bank and a plan for a rationing day are both worth having, since interruptions are scheduled rather than random.
mamoudzou.gettingAround: Mamoudzou is on Grande-Terre and the airport is on Petite-Terre, so the barge across the lagoon is part of daily life and runs frequently and cheaply. Shared taxis cover Grande-Terre. Traffic into Mamoudzou in the morning is heavy for a place this size. A car is useful but the roads are limited and congested. Dzaoudzi-Pamandzi International Airport connects to Paris, Reunion, Madagascar and the Comoros, with the Paris route long and expensive but direct. Anyone landing at night should note that the barge runs on a reduced schedule after dark, and that the crossing is the only practical link between the two islands. The road network is essentially one coastal route around Grande-Terre with spurs inland, so a single accident or landslide can sever the practical link between north and south for hours, and the rainy season makes that more likely. Shared taxis fill and leave rather than run to a timetable, which works well once you understand it and is bewildering before. Walking after dark in Mamoudzou is not generally advised, and most residents drive or take a taxi even for short distances at night.
mamoudzou.visas: Mayotte is a French overseas department and part of the European Union, but it is outside the Schengen area and operates its own entry rules, which are stricter than mainland France's. A Schengen visa does not admit you and a Mayotte visa does not admit you to Schengen. European Union citizens have freedom of movement and may live and work here. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for ninety days. Immigration enforcement here is intense, given the scale of irregular arrivals from the Comoros. Anyone travelling on to the Comoros should understand the sovereignty dispute, since the Comoros claim Mayotte and the route is treated as sensitive on both sides. A French visa is not automatically valid here: it has to carry a specific endorsement for Mayotte, and travellers regularly discover this at check-in rather than before. Identity checks are frequent and routine on the roads and at the barge, so carry documents rather than leave them at home. Mayotte voted to become a full French department in 2009 and the change took effect in 2011, which is why the legal framework here is metropolitan while the entry rules stubbornly are not.
mamoudzou.bestTime: May to October is the dry, cooler season and the practical window, at around twenty six degrees with better visibility in the lagoon. November to April is hot, humid and wet, and Mayotte lies in the cyclone belt: Cyclone Chido caused catastrophic damage in December 2024 and recovery is ongoing. Whale season runs roughly July to October when humpbacks calve in the lagoon, which is one of the largest and best enclosed in the world, and that is the island's outstanding natural asset. Anyone diving the lagoon should aim for the passe en S on the western barrier, which is the best known site and is a dry season dive for visibility. Mayotte is overwhelmingly Muslim, so Ramadan shapes the working day and opening hours for a month each year, and the date moves earlier annually. Turtles nest on the beaches through much of the year rather than in a narrow window, which is unusual, and it makes Saziley and the southern beaches worth an evening in almost any month. February is the most uncomfortable stretch, hot and wet at once, and the cyclone risk concentrates from January to March.
mamoudzou.prosCons: The lagoon is the draw here, enormous and double-barriered, holding dugongs, turtles and calving humpbacks, all of it inside French territory with European healthcare and schooling behind it. What weighs against it is substantial and worth stating plainly: Mayotte has the highest poverty rate in France, serious problems with crime and gang violence, chronic water shortages, and severe social tension around immigration from the Comoros. Cyclone Chido destroyed a large share of the informal housing in 2024. The island also voted overwhelmingly to become a French department in 2009, which is why its status differs so sharply from the rest of the archipelago. The maternity unit in Mamoudzou is the busiest in all of France, on an island with a fraction of the resources of any mainland department, and the health system runs permanently above capacity as a result. The gap between what the island is entitled to as part of France and what it actually receives is the subject of most local politics, and a visitor should expect that to be a live and openly argued subject rather than background.
mamoudzou.whoFor: Mayotte suits French public servants, teachers and medical staff on posting, of whom there are many, and divers and marine biologists drawn to the lagoon. It suits French speakers, since French is essential. It does not suit independent travellers looking for an easy island, anyone uncomfortable with the security situation, or anyone who would find the water rationing and the visible poverty hard to live alongside. Mayotte's dugongs are among the last of their kind in this ocean. The population in the lagoon is small and threatened, and very few others survive across the whole western Indian Ocean. For most independent remote workers the honest answer is that Reunion does nearly everything Mayotte does with far fewer difficulties, and anyone drawn to the region for the diving and the French administration should look there first. Mayotte makes sense when there is a reason specific to it: the lagoon as a research subject, family on the island, or a posting. Anyone who does come should arrive with the language, a vehicle arranged and a realistic picture of the water situation, because none of the three can be improvised once you are there.

nouakchott.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,000 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $500, with Tevragh Zeina, the diplomatic and business quarter, at the top and the older districts considerably cheaper. Market produce is inexpensive and the fish landed at the Port de Peche is among the best value anywhere on the Atlantic coast, sold straight off the boats in the afternoon. Imported goods carry a heavy markup. Utilities are modest and power is generally available. Eating out is limited and cheap, mostly Mauritanian and Senegalese. The ouguiya was redenominated in 2018, so older prices need a factor of ten applied. Rent is commonly asked for three months or six at a time rather than monthly, and a foreigner without a local guarantor will usually be quoted the longer term. Banking is limited and card acceptance close to nonexistent outside a handful of hotels, so the practical arrangement is cash drawn in bulk and kept carefully. Mobile money has spread faster than the banks have, and topping up a phone is how a great many small payments get settled. Fuel is subsidised and the shared taxis price accordingly, which is why moving around costs so little.
nouakchott.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak but improving. Mauritania has submarine cable capacity landing at Nouakchott and fibre reaches parts of the city, with speeds workable for ordinary remote work in the better districts. Mobile data from Mauritel, Mattel and Chinguitel covers the populated areas and is the usual fallback. Power is reasonably reliable in the centre. There is almost no coworking. Sand is a genuine equipment hazard here and gets into everything. The time zone is GMT with no daylight saving, which makes European and West African work straightforward. Anyone staying through the harmattan should also plan for dust, since it works into laptop fans and connectors and is a genuine cause of hardware failure here. Business runs in French and administration in Arabic, and the two are not interchangeable depending on which office you happen to be standing in. English turns up in the mining and fisheries sectors and almost nowhere else. The professional day starts early and stops through the middle of the afternoon in the hot months, which is worth matching rather than resisting, since very little gets answered between two and five in any case.
nouakchott.gettingAround: Shared taxis and minibuses cover Nouakchott cheaply and are the normal way to move, though the city is spread out and largely low-rise across a flat sandy plain, which makes walking unrewarding. A car helps considerably. Nouakchott-Oumtounsy International Airport opened in 2016 about twenty five kilometres north with connections to Paris, Casablanca, Istanbul, Dakar and Nouadhibou. The other route out is the iron ore train from Nouadhibou, which is among the longest trains in the world and carries passengers free on top of the ore. Anyone taking the ore train should know it runs about seven hundred kilometres, takes the better part of a day, and offers no shelter at all on the open wagons. Addresses are approximate and directions are given by landmark rather than by street, which matters more than it sounds as soon as something has to be delivered or a driver has to find you. Sand drifts across the tarmac after a windy night and the crews clear the main routes first, so the outer districts can be slow going in the morning. Fuel stations are frequent, and the coast road north is the one stretch in consistently good condition.
nouakchott.visas: Mauritania issues visas on arrival at Nouakchott airport and at the main land borders for most nationalities, valid for thirty days and payable in euros in cash, which is the part people are unprepared for. Applying in advance at an embassy is also possible. A yellow fever certificate is required from travellers arriving from endemic countries. There is no remote work visa. Travel to the north and east of the country carries security advisories and the border regions with Mali should be checked carefully before any overland plan. Anyone arriving overland from Morocco should also allow several hours at the Guerguerat crossing, which involves a stretch of unmarked no man's land between the two posts.
nouakchott.bestTime: November to March is the only comfortable window, warm at around twenty eight degrees with cooler nights and the Atlantic breeze taking the edge off. April to October is very hot, regularly above forty degrees inland, and the harmattan carries Saharan dust across the city for weeks at a time. Rain is negligible in any month. The Banc d'Arguin National Park north of the city, a UNESCO site where the Sahara meets the Atlantic, is best in winter when the migratory birds are present in enormous numbers. Anyone visiting Chinguetti should aim for the cooler months as well, since the town sits deep in the Adrar and the manuscript libraries are family-run and open on request. The fishing fleet comes ashore in the late afternoon and the beach south of the port becomes a market for an hour, which is the one daily fixture everybody here plans around. Cooler nights arrive from November, and the difference between a December day and a June one is the difference between a place you can walk in and one you cannot.
nouakchott.prosCons: Mauritania holds a landscape and a set of experiences that nowhere else can match: the iron ore train, the Adrar's desert oases at Chinguetti and Ouadane with their medieval libraries, and the Banc d'Arguin where millions of migratory birds meet the edge of the desert. Costs are low and the Atlantic fish is exceptional. Nouakchott itself is a functional rather than an attractive city, connectivity is limited, the heat is severe for most of the year, and security advisories still cover much of the country outside the capital itself. Mauritania also only abolished slavery in law in 1981 and criminalised it in 2007, and the practice persists in forms that human rights organisations continue to document.
nouakchott.whoFor: A working reason in mining, fisheries, development or diplomacy, or a traveller using the city as the base for the Adrar and the ore train. It suits French and Arabic speakers, since English is genuinely rare. Comfort was not part of how this city grew, connectivity is weak, and summer is not a season to negotiate with: the heat on the edge of the Sahara is the kind that decides what is possible each day rather than the kind that is merely endured. It also suits birdwatchers, since the Banc d'Arguin is one of the most important wintering sites on the East Atlantic flyway and holds millions of shorebirds each season. The foreign population is almost entirely institutional, meaning embassies, mining companies, fishing agreements and aid organisations, and a newcomer with none of those attachments finds the social world closes quickly at the edge of it. Anyone planning to move beyond the coast should take the current advice seriously rather than as boilerplate, since the advisories here distinguish sharply between regions and those distinctions have held. A fortnight in the desert with a base in the capital is a more honest plan than treating the country as somewhere to settle.

bissau.costOfLiving: Budget around $850 a month, which makes Bissau one of the cheapest capitals in West Africa. A one-bedroom runs roughly $200 to $400. Market produce is very cheap and the country grows good cashew, rice and fruit, with cashew nuts making up most of its exports. Fish and seafood from the estuary and the Bijagos are inexpensive and excellent. Imported goods carry a markup and the supermarkets are limited. Eating out is cheap, with Portuguese-influenced Guinean cooking and grilled fish the mainstays. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, which removes currency risk. The CFA franc is worth understanding rather than merely noting. Guinea-Bissau is the only Portuguese-speaking member of the West African monetary union, so it shares a currency, a central bank and a euro peg with seven francophone neighbours, which makes prices stable and regional travel financially frictionless in a way that is rare on this continent. The cashew harvest sets the economic mood: a good price in April and May means money circulates all year, and a poor one is felt in everything from rents to what the market carries.
bissau.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. Guinea-Bissau has limited submarine cable capacity and fibre reaches only parts of Bissau, with mobile data from MTN and Orange the usual answer at prices that are high relative to income. Power cuts are frequent and prolonged, and generators are standard in anything serious. There is no coworking. Anyone with call-heavy work should treat this as a genuine constraint. The time zone is GMT with no daylight saving, which makes European work straightforward and is one of the few unambiguous practical advantages here. Anyone working here should budget for a generator or an inverter, since the public supply is intermittent enough that a working day cannot be planned around it. Portuguese is the language of government and paperwork while Crioulo is what the country actually speaks, and the two are close enough that a Portuguese speaker picks up the second within weeks. That combination makes Bissau far easier for a lusophone visitor than the surrounding francophone region. The Lisbon flights matter more than they look, since they put the country a single hop from Europe and are the reason the diaspora connection runs through Portugal rather than France.
bissau.gettingAround: Shared taxis, painted blue and white and shared with whoever is going the same way, cover Bissau for a low fixed fare and are the normal way to move. The old colonial centre around the Praca dos Herois Nacionais is walkable. Roads outside the capital vary sharply and several are impassable in the rains. Osvaldo Vieira International Airport is about eight kilometres from the centre with connections to Lisbon, Dakar and Casablanca. Boats to the Bijagos archipelago leave from the port and the schedules are approximate. Anyone heading to the Bijagos should allow days rather than hours, since the pirogues and the ferry both depend on tides and on having enough passengers to sail. Tides run the transport here more than timetables do. The Bijagos boats sail when the water allows, the channels between the islands dry to sandbanks, and a crossing planned for the morning may leave at dusk or the following day. In the capital, walking the colonial grid is pleasant by daylight and the potholes are the main hazard rather than anything else. A motorbike is what most residents outside the taxi routes actually use.
bissau.visas: Guinea-Bissau requires a visa of most nationalities. An e-visa system operates and is the usual route, with visas issued for thirty to ninety days, and visa on arrival has been available at the airport for those who apply online first. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for in Bissau. The country has had repeated coups and attempted coups since independence, so the current political situation is worth checking before any plan. Anyone applying for the e-visa should print the approval and carry it, since the airport process still runs on paper and the online record is not always accessible there. Regional movement is the part worth planning around. Guinea-Bissau belongs to ECOWAS, so citizens of member states enter freely and overland travel to Senegal and Guinea is straightforward for them, while everyone else needs each country's own paperwork arranged separately before setting out. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries has also agreed mobility arrangements among its members, which is a slow-moving framework rather than an open door but is worth checking if you hold a lusophone passport.
bissau.bestTime: November to May is the dry season and the practical window, warm at around thirty degrees with lower humidity, and it is also the best time for the Bijagos. June to October is the wet season and Guinea-Bissau is genuinely wet, with roads outside the capital deteriorating badly and some becoming impassable. Carnival in February is the biggest event in the calendar and is a serious one, with masks and drumming from across the country converging on Bissau for several days. Anyone visiting the Bijagos should aim for the dry months, since the islands' accommodation is limited and several of the lodges close entirely during the rains. The cashew harvest between roughly February and June is when the country is busiest and most of its money moves, and the roads fill with the trade. Ramadan matters here as well, since about half the population is Muslim, and it reshapes daytime hours for a month that shifts earlier each year. The Bijagos have their own calendar of initiation ceremonies that outsiders are not generally present for, and asking before photographing anything on the islands is the minimum courtesy.
bissau.prosCons: The Bijagos are what bring the few visitors who come: an archipelago of eighty eight islands that is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, matrilineal in its social organisation, home to saltwater hippos and nesting turtles, and seen by almost nobody. Bissau itself has a decayed Portuguese colonial core that is genuinely atmospheric. Costs are very low. Weigh that against instability, weak infrastructure, unreliable power, limited medical care, and the country's long-standing role as a transit point in the cocaine trade, which shapes its politics. The country also has one of the highest cashew dependencies in the world, so the annual price of a single crop moves the whole economy and the mood with it. Guinea-Bissau has never had a president complete a full term without interruption since independence, which is the plainest way to state the instability, and it is history a visitor should know rather than a daily experience of walking around the capital. Serious medical treatment means Dakar, which is a road journey or a short flight away. For all of that, the welcome is genuine, the visitor numbers are close to nil, and the Bijagos are why anybody makes the effort at all.
bissau.whoFor: Guinea-Bissau suits travellers heading for the Bijagos, conservation and development workers, and Portuguese speakers, since Portuguese and Crioulo are the working languages and English is very rare. It suits birdwatchers and anyone drawn to matrilineal societies, which the Bijagos genuinely are. Reliable infrastructure does not exist here, a fixed schedule will meet something that breaks it, and Guinea-Bissau's politics have a history of changing abruptly, so the position needs checking against current reporting rather than against an older impression of the place. Poilao in the Bijagos hosts one of the largest green turtle rookeries in the Atlantic. It is also a sacred island, which means access runs through the Bijagos communities and their own rules about who may land and when. Across lusophone Africa, Cape Verde is far easier and has a remote work visa, Sao Tome is prettier and calmer, and this is the one with the archipelago nobody has seen and the infrastructure to match. The realistic trip is short and built around the islands, arranged through a lodge that handles the boats, rather than an independent attempt at the same thing. Portuguese is close to essential and Crioulo is what will actually be spoken back.

mindelo.costOfLiving: Budget around $950 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, with the streets near the Praca Nova and the seafront at the top. Market produce is reasonable and the fish is excellent and cheap, though Sao Vicente is dry and grows little of its own food, so much arrives from Santo Antao across the channel or from the mainland. Imported goods carry a markup. Utilities are moderate and water is desalinated. Eating out is inexpensive and good, with grogue, the local cane spirit, cheap everywhere. The escudo is pegged to the euro. The escudo peg to the euro removes exchange risk for European earners and makes budgeting genuinely predictable, which is rarer than it sounds at this price level. Long stays are negotiated directly and monthly, and asking in Portuguese or Creole changes the number offered more than any other single factor. Remittances form a large share of the local economy, so the town is used to money arriving from outside and to the price distortions that follow, which shows in what a foreigner is quoted first.
mindelo.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable. Cape Verde has submarine cable capacity and fibre reaches Mindelo at workable speeds, with mobile data from CVMovel and Unitel covering the island. Power is generally reliable. There is a small coworking presence and the country has actively courted remote workers with a formal visa, which has brought a modest but real community, mostly to Sal and Santa Maria rather than here. The time zone is one hour behind GMT, which gives an excellent European overlap and a workable American afternoon. Anyone comparing the islands should note that Sal and Boa Vista have the larger remote worker presence and the direct European charter flights, while Sao Vicente has the culture. The cafes around the Praca Nova are unhurried about a laptop on a table, and most people alternate between one of those and their own flat. The structural caution is inter-island logistics: anything that must arrive physically, a replacement machine, a bank card, routes through Praia or Sal first and takes longer than the distances suggest. Worth knowing too is that the creative economy here is not decorative, with studios, festivals and a recording tradition giving the town a professional layer unusual at this size.
mindelo.gettingAround: Mindelo is compact and walkable, laid out around Porto Grande bay with the main streets running back from the water. Shared minibuses, called hiaces, cover the rest of Sao Vicente cheaply. Taxis are inexpensive. The ferry to Santo Antao takes about an hour and is the reason most visitors come, since that island holds the best hiking in the archipelago. Cesaria Evora Airport is about seven kilometres out with connections to Lisbon, Praia and the other islands. Anyone hiking Santo Antao should take the morning ferry and stay over, since the Ribeira Grande valleys and the Cova crater need a full day and the last boat back is early. The inter-island ferries are the weak link and their reliability has been a national complaint for years, with cancellations and schedule changes common, so an itinerary that depends on a specific sailing needs a fallback. Flying between islands is quick and not expensive, and for anything time-critical it is the sensible choice. Within Sao Vicente the roads are good, and a hired car for a single day covers everything outside the town without difficulty.
mindelo.visas: Cape Verde abolished visa requirements for citizens of the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States and several other countries, who now register online through the EASE system before travel and pay an airport security fee on arrival, for stays up to thirty days. Everyone else applies for a visa. The country also operates a formal Remote Working Programme, a six month renewable visa for remote workers with proof of income and insurance, which is among the more straightforward such schemes anywhere. Anyone using the remote working visa should apply before travelling, since it is issued in advance rather than converted from a tourist entry after arrival. The remote working visa carries a tax position worth understanding: income earned from outside the country is not taxed locally under the scheme, which is what makes six months here financially straightforward rather than merely legal. Renewal is possible for a further six months. Mindelo sits on Sao Vicente, so anyone flying in through Sal or Praia clears immigration there and continues domestically, which matters because the international entry point and the island you actually want are rarely the same one.
mindelo.bestTime: November to June is the best window, warm at around twenty five degrees with steady trade winds and low humidity. The winds are strongest from December to March, which is why Sao Vicente and neighbouring Sal are serious kitesurfing and windsurfing destinations. August to October is warmer and marginally wetter, though Cape Verde is dry in every month and drought is a recurring national problem. The Baia das Gatas music festival in August and Mindelo's carnival in February are the two events that fill the town. Anyone coming for the wind should note that the strongest and steadiest months are December to March, which is also when the international kitesurfing events are held. Dust is the seasonal factor nobody mentions. The harmattan carries Saharan haze across the archipelago mainly between December and February, cutting visibility and settling on everything, and it coincides with the windiest and otherwise best months. Drought is a chronic national condition rather than an event, and water restrictions surface periodically. The August festival on the beach at Baia das Gatas draws the diaspora home, which makes flights and rooms scarce for a fortnight either side of it.
mindelo.prosCons: Mindelo is the cultural capital of Cape Verde and feels like it from the first evening: Cesaria Evora sang the morna here, live music runs most nights, the carnival is the biggest in the country, and the setting on Porto Grande bay under Monte Cara is genuinely striking from any angle. Add a formal remote work visa, a European time zone and low costs. Sao Vicente is also dry and largely barren, water is scarce, and the island runs out of new ground fairly quickly without the ferry across to Santo Antao next door. More Cape Verdeans live abroad than in the country, in Portugal, the Netherlands, France and New England, and that shapes the place profoundly: money, music and returning families all arrive from outside, and almost every household here has someone away. Serious illness means Praia or a flight to Lisbon, a longer chain than it looks on a map. The island's dryness is no passing inconvenience either, and desalination is what keeps Sao Vicente inhabited at all.
mindelo.whoFor: Musicians and anyone drawn to Cape Verdean music, which is the genuine claim of the island, along with kitesurfers and hikers using it as the gateway to Santo Antao. It suits remote workers who want the formal visa and a European time zone at low cost. Anybody picturing lush landscape has the wrong island in the archipelago, because Sao Vicente is dry and bare and that is its whole character. Seventy thousand people also do not add up to a city, whatever the music scene suggests. Mindelo's claim rests largely on the morna. UNESCO added it to the intangible heritage list in 2019, and it is still played live here most nights of the week, in bars that are not putting on a show for anybody. Musicians, and anyone who arrived because of a record, are who this town rewards most, and the live scene is the reason to choose it over the islands where the charter flights land. Portuguese matters more here than it does there. It repays months rather than a fortnight, since the place reveals itself slowly and the ferry timetable discourages hurry in any case. Anyone whose priority is a beach holiday should go elsewhere in the archipelago and come here for the carnival.

ashgabat.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,000 a month, though costs here are difficult to state plainly because Turkmenistan operates parallel exchange rates and the gap between the official and unofficial manat has been very wide. A one-bedroom runs roughly $300 to $600 at official rates. Subsidised utilities were a national policy for decades and have been progressively withdrawn. Local bazaar produce is cheap; imported goods are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable. Eating out is inexpensive by international standards. Bring cash: international cards frequently do not work and withdrawing money can be genuinely difficult. Shortages are a more useful thing to plan around than prices. Queues for subsidised staples have been a recurring feature, imported goods appear and vanish from the shelves, and what a given month costs depends heavily on what is available rather than on any published figure. Bring dollars in good condition and in reasonable quantity, since changing them is the routine mechanism and worn notes are refused. Accommodation for foreigners is generally arranged through the tour operator or an employer rather than found independently.
ashgabat.whereToWork: Connectivity is the worst on this site. Turkmenistan has among the most restricted and slowest internet in the world, with a state monopoly, extensive filtering that blocks most social media and messaging services, and speeds that make video calls impractical. VPNs are blocked and their use is discouraged in ways that carry risk. There is no coworking. Anyone whose work requires open internet access should treat Turkmenistan as unworkable rather than difficult. The time zone is five hours ahead of GMT. Anyone with work that depends on cloud services, messaging or video should assume none of it will function reliably, and should not plan to be productive here. What organisations posted here actually do is worth stating, since it explains the gap between the country existing and being workable: embassies and international companies run their own satellite links, and everyone else accepts that the connection is not a tool they can rely on. There is no consumer route to that. A stay here is therefore either short, or supported by an institution, or unproductive, and the third of those is the one people discover after arriving rather than before.
ashgabat.gettingAround: Ashgabat is laid out on a monumental scale with wide boulevards and enormous distances between buildings, so walking is possible but slow and the summer heat makes it unpleasant. Taxis are cheap and plentiful, including informal ones, and buses cover the city. The city holds a Guinness record for the highest density of white marble buildings, and the effect is striking and strange. Ashgabat International Airport connects to Istanbul, Dubai, Moscow and a small number of other cities, with Turkmenistan Airlines operating most of them. Anyone photographing the city should also be careful, since government buildings, the presidential palace and many public monuments cannot be photographed and this is enforced. Internal travel is not free movement either. Several border regions and areas near the Caspian require separate permits arranged in advance, and the assigned guide accompanies journeys outside the capital as a matter of course rather than as an option. Distances are long and the desert roads are hard on vehicles. Within the city, the scale that looks impressive in photographs means a walk between two landmarks can take forty minutes across open marble with no shade at all.
ashgabat.visas: Turkmenistan has one of the most restrictive visa regimes in the world. Independent tourism is effectively not permitted: almost every visitor needs a letter of invitation obtained through a licensed local tour operator, an approved itinerary and a state-assigned guide, and the application is frequently refused without explanation. A five day transit visa exists for those crossing between two neighbouring countries and is also frequently refused. There is no remote work visa and no realistic route to a long independent stay. Anyone applying should also allow months rather than weeks, since the letter of invitation is processed by the state migration service and the timeline is entirely unpredictable. Registration follows arrival for anyone staying beyond a few days, handled through the operator, and it is checked on departure. The transit visa deserves its own warning: it fixes both the entry and the exit point and the number of days, all of which are decided by the state rather than requested, and overstaying or deviating from the route is a serious matter rather than an administrative one. There is no mechanism anywhere in the system for extending a stay because you liked it.
ashgabat.bestTime: April to May and September to October are the only comfortable windows, warm at around twenty five degrees. Summer from June to August is severe, regularly above forty degrees in a city surrounded by the Karakum desert, and winter can drop below freezing. Rainfall is negligible year round. The Darvaza gas crater, the burning pit in the desert north of the city, is best visited in the cooler months and requires an overnight camp, which is one of the few things the tour operators reliably arrange. Anyone visiting Merv or Kunya-Urgench should note that both are a long way east and north of the capital and that internal travel is arranged through the same operator. The national calendar is worth checking against a trip, since public holidays here are elaborate state occasions that close offices and restrict movement in the capital. Melon Day in August celebrates the Turkmen melon with genuine national ceremony and is not a joke at the country's expense. Novruz in March marks the spring equinox and is the more widely observed. The desert swing between day and night is severe in the shoulder months, so a Darvaza camp needs warm clothing regardless of the afternoon temperature.
ashgabat.prosCons: There is nothing else like Ashgabat anywhere: a capital rebuilt almost entirely in white marble and gold since the 1990s, with monumental architecture, empty boulevards and a personality cult expressed in stone on every corner. Nearby Nisa is a UNESCO-listed Parthian city and Merv, further east, was once among the largest cities in the world. Everything else about it argues the other way: the visa regime, the surveillance, the internet restrictions, the heat, and a state that controls what visitors see and where they go. The Darvaza crater has also been burning since a Soviet drilling accident, and the government has repeatedly announced plans to extinguish it without doing so. The human rights position belongs in any honest account rather than in a footnote: Turkmenistan sits at or near the bottom of international press freedom and civil liberties rankings, independent journalism does not operate, and the surveillance a visitor notices is the visible part of something more thorough. That is not a reason nobody should go, and it is a reason to go informed, to be careful about what you photograph and who you put at risk by asking questions.
ashgabat.whoFor: Turkmenistan suits determined travellers collecting difficult countries, archaeologists working on Parthian and Silk Road sites, and people posted here by an employer. Remote work is not possible here in any sense: the internet cannot carry it, and the visa regime does not allow the stay in the first place. Anyone going should understand that they will be accompanied, that photography is restricted, and that the country is among the most closed in the world. The Akhal-Teke horse is the national symbol and one of the oldest surviving breeds anywhere, and the state maintains it with a degree of ceremony that says a good deal about how this country sees itself. Uzbekistan next door is the comparison that clarifies this one: it holds Silk Road cities of the same rank at Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, it has opened up substantially, and it can be travelled independently and worked from. Almost anyone whose interest is the region's history rather than its strangeness should go there instead. This country rewards the traveller who specifically wants the strangeness, has time for the paperwork, and is content to see it from inside an arranged itinerary.

erbil.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $500, with the areas near Empire World and the newer compounds considerably higher and aimed at the international sector. Market produce is cheap and Kurdish cooking makes good use of it. Imported goods are available and reasonably priced given the trade with Turkey. Eating out is inexpensive and the kebab and the breakfast culture are both excellent. Utilities cost more than the headline suggests because private generator subscriptions are normal alongside the grid. The Iraqi dinar is used and United States dollars circulate widely. Fibre runs about $50 to $100 a month. The generator subscription is the line nobody budgets for and it is not optional: households pay a neighbourhood operator by the ampere, typically $30 to $80 a month depending on how much you want to run during the daily grid outage, and air conditioning through an Erbil summer pushes that to the top of the range. International cards work in very little here, so the practical arrangement is dollars carried in and changed at a money exchange, which is normal, quick and gives a better rate than any bank counter.
erbil.whereToWork: Connectivity is moderate. Erbil has fibre in the newer districts and the international compounds, with speeds workable for normal remote work, and mobile data covers the city. Power is the constraint rather than bandwidth: the grid does not supply full-time electricity and almost every building is also connected to a neighbourhood generator, which is billed separately and is simply how the city works. There is a small coworking scene. The time zone is three hours ahead of GMT, which gives a good European overlap. Anyone renting here should ask specifically about the generator subscription and its amperage, since that number determines what you can run during the daily grid outages. The Kurdistan Region has its own government, budget and security forces, and its relationship with Baghdad over oil revenue has repeatedly affected public salaries and services here, which is background worth understanding rather than an abstraction. Coworking is limited and clusters around the newer developments west of the citadel. English is more widely spoken here than anywhere else in Iraq, a consequence of two decades of international presence, and Kurdish rather than Arabic is the working language.
erbil.gettingAround: Erbil is built in concentric rings around the citadel mound, which makes the layout unusually easy to understand and the traffic unusually circular. Taxis are cheap and plentiful and are the normal way to move, with ride-hailing apps available. The bazaar and Shar Park at the foot of the citadel are walkable. Erbil International Airport is about five kilometres west with connections to Istanbul, Dubai, Doha, Frankfurt and much of the region, and it has been the Kurdistan Region's link to the world for two decades. Anyone driving to Sulaymaniyah or Duhok should expect checkpoints along the way, which are routine, orderly and require a passport rather than causing any difficulty. The citadel itself has been almost entirely emptied for restoration, with a single family maintained in residence so the claim of continuous habitation is not broken, which is a decision that tells you a good deal about how seriously the site is taken.
erbil.visas: The Kurdistan Region issues its own entry permits separately from the federal Iraqi government, and they are considerably easier to obtain. Citizens of the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States and a number of other countries receive a visa on arrival at Erbil or Sulaymaniyah, valid for thirty days and extendable. A Kurdistan Region permit does not automatically allow travel to federal Iraq, which requires a separate federal visa. There is no remote work visa. Confirm the current position, since both regimes have changed repeatedly.
