Anyone intending to continue to Baghdad or the south should arrange the federal visa separately and in advance, since the regional permit does not cover that travel. Extensions are handled at the residency office in Erbil and are routine for a further thirty days. The regional permit is issued on arrival for eligible nationalities and does not require anything in advance, which is the single biggest practical difference from federal Iraq.
erbil.bestTime: March to May and October to November are the best windows, warm at around twenty five degrees, with the spring bringing green hills across the region that surprise people who expect only desert. Summer from June to September is severe, regularly above forty five degrees, and the city largely moves indoors or to the mountains at Shaqlawa and Rawanduz. Winter is cool and wet at around ten degrees with snow in the mountains. Newroz, the Kurdish new year on the twenty first of March, is the biggest event of the year. Shaqlawa and Rawanduz in the mountains north are ten to fifteen degrees cooler than the city in summer, and a good part of Erbil relocates there for weekends through July and August rather than enduring the heat. Newroz is marked with fires on the hillsides and a public holiday that closes the region for several days, and Akre north of the city holds the largest celebration in Kurdistan.
erbil.prosCons: The citadel mound has been continuously occupied for perhaps six thousand years, which makes it one of the oldest inhabited sites on earth and UNESCO-listed on that basis, and it sits above a working bazaar in a city that is genuinely calm and, by regional standards, inexpensive. The mountains north are beautiful. This is still Iraq, and while the Kurdistan Region has been far more stable than the rest of the country, the security situation is regional, changeable, and worth checking against current advice rather than a headline from last year. Erbil's bazaar at the foot of the citadel is a working market rather than a restored one, and the tea houses around it are where the city's social life actually happens, which is the thing most visitors remember. The region also runs its own visa regime, budget and peshmerga forces, which is why its stability has diverged so sharply from the rest of the country over twenty years.
erbil.whoFor: Energy, reconstruction, diplomacy or humanitarian work, of which there is a considerable amount, and archaeology, since the region holds an extraordinary density of sites. It suits travellers drawn to Kurdish culture and hospitality, which is genuine and much remarked on. The security picture in this region changes and needs watching rather than assuming, uninterrupted mains power does not exist here, and high summer in the Kurdish plain is a season to leave rather than to work through. Mesopotamian archaeology is reopening here after a long closure. Nineveh, Nimrud and a dozen other sites sit within a few hours of the city and are slowly becoming accessible to researchers again. Oil and gas is the one sector with genuine depth. The region's fields and the international companies working them have made this city the industry's base for the whole of northern Iraq, and the professional network on the ground reflects that exactly. Set beside Sulaymaniyah, Erbil has the international flights and the business, while Sulaymaniyah has the reputation for culture and a more liberal feel.

asmara.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month, though as in Turkmenistan the figure needs a caveat: Eritrea has a closed economy, a fixed official exchange rate and strict currency controls, and what things cost depends heavily on which rate applies. A one-bedroom runs roughly $200 to $400 at official rates. Local produce and bread are cheap. Imported goods are expensive and often simply unavailable, which is the more relevant constraint. Eating out is inexpensive and the Italian legacy means genuinely good coffee and pasta alongside Eritrean food. Cash is essential and declaring foreign currency on arrival is compulsory. The currency itself has a history that shapes daily life: in 2015 the government replaced every nakfa banknote and capped withdrawals, a move aimed at the black market that also wiped out savings held in notes. The limits have stayed tight since. No foreign card works at any machine in the country, so everything you will spend has to be brought in and accounted for again on the way out, which means budgeting in advance rather than adjusting as you go.
asmara.whereToWork: Connectivity is the worst in Africa and among the worst anywhere. Eritrea has the lowest internet penetration in the world, no meaningful mobile data for most of its history, and dial-up-era speeds in the internet cafes that serve as most people's access. Fibre exists in a very limited form. Power cuts are frequent. There is no coworking and no realistic way to run a remote job from here. The time zone is three hours ahead of GMT, which is academic given the connection. Anyone needing to reach clients should plan on doing so before arriving and after leaving, because the connection here cannot be relied on for anything time-sensitive. Eritrea has no independent domestic media at all, and has sat at or near the bottom of the world press freedom index since it closed the private press in 2001, with journalists held without charge since then. That context matters for a working visitor in a practical way: what you research, download or ask about is not a neutral activity here, and the constraint is on more than bandwidth.
asmara.gettingAround: Asmara is walkable and genuinely pleasant to walk, which is unusual for an African capital: the centre is compact, the streets are ordered on the Italian plan, and the altitude keeps it cool. Buses and shared taxis are very cheap. The Eritrean Railway to Massawa, built by the Italians and rebuilt by hand with original locomotives, runs occasional excursions down the escarpment. Asmara International Airport has limited connections, mainly to Cairo, Dubai and Addis Ababa since the 2018 rapprochement with Ethiopia. Anyone travelling beyond the capital should apply for the internal permit several days ahead, since it names specific destinations and is checked at posts on every road. The Italians also built a cableway from the coast up to the highlands, seventy five kilometres of it, the longest in the world when it opened in 1937 and dismantled by the British for scrap a decade later. Its concrete pylons still stand along the escarpment and are visible from the road, which is how most people first register how much engineering went into a colony of this size.
asmara.visas: Eritrea requires a visa of every nationality, applied for in advance at an embassy, with an invitation or a booking and a process that is slow and frequently refused. There is no visa on arrival and no e-visa. Travel outside Asmara requires a separate internal travel permit, applied for in the capital and issued for specific destinations, and this is enforced at checkpoints. There is no remote work visa. Photography is restricted and military and government buildings must not be photographed at all. Anyone applying should also expect to be asked for a detailed itinerary, and should understand that refusal without reason is common and carries no route of appeal. The rapprochement with Ethiopia briefly opened the land border in 2018 and then closed it again, and the crossing has not been dependably open since, so no plan should rest on it. Djibouti and Sudan are the other land neighbours and neither is straightforward at present. Overstaying is treated seriously, and the exit formalities at the airport are as thorough as the entry ones.
asmara.bestTime: September to March is the best window, dry and mild at around twenty two degrees thanks to the altitude of about 2,300 metres, which makes Asmara far more comfortable than its latitude suggests. The main rains fall from June to August and are heavy but short. Nights are cool year round and a jacket is needed. The coast at Massawa is a different climate entirely and is brutally hot for most of the year, so the descent from the highlands is best made in the cooler months. Anyone visiting the Dahlak archipelago off Massawa should aim for the cooler months, since the Red Sea coast is among the hottest inhabited places on earth in summer. Rain here comes as a hard afternoon storm rather than a day of drizzle, so the wet months stay workable if the plan allows for a soaked hour around four. Independence day on the twenty fourth of May brings the whole capital onto the main avenue, and the week around it is the hardest stretch of the year in which to find a room.
asmara.prosCons: Asmara is an intact Italian modernist and Art Deco capital, built in the 1930s and barely altered in the ninety years since, and it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017 for exactly that reason. The Fiat Tagliero service station, shaped like an aeroplane, and the Cinema Impero are among the finest buildings of their period anywhere. The state is the reason so few people come: Eritrea runs indefinite national service, imposes extensive restrictions on movement and expression, and has effectively no internet for ordinary users. The city's evening passeggiata along Harnet Avenue is also a genuine daily ritual, and it is the clearest surviving trace of the Italian period in ordinary life. Against the architecture sits the emigration: Eritreans have for years been among the largest groups arriving in Europe by sea relative to the population at home, and open-ended conscription is the reason most of them give. A visitor sees a calm and orderly city, and the calm and the exodus are the same fact seen from two directions.
asmara.whoFor: Architects and anyone drawn to twentieth century modernism, for whom the city is close to unmatched, along with travellers who want somewhere genuinely unvisited and are prepared for the constraints. It suits people with family connections. Remote work will not run on this connection, and that is only the first obstacle. Internal travel permits, checkpoints and restrictions on photography are all ordinary conditions of being here, and anybody who would find those hard to accept should not come at all, because none of it is negotiable. It also suits cyclists, since Eritrea is the most cycling-obsessed country in Africa, the Tour of Eritrea is a national event, and the sport is another Italian inheritance. Daniel Teklehaimanot rode for the polka dot jersey at the Tour de France in 2015, the first African to hold it, and he learned on these roads: the climb from the coast to the highlands gains more than two thousand metres in one ascent. It suits a photographer with patience and permission, and nobody holding only one of the two, because pointing a camera at the wrong building is a serious matter rather than an awkward one.

pakse.costOfLiving: Budget around $620 a month, which puts Pakse among the cheapest places on this site. A one-bedroom runs roughly $150 to $350, with the riverfront and the newer blocks near the centre at the top. Market food costs very little and the Bolaven plateau above the town grows the country's best coffee, so a good cup is cheap here in a way it is not elsewhere in Laos. Imported goods carry a markup, and Thailand across the river is where people go for anything the town does not stock. Utilities are inexpensive. The kip has lost a great deal of value in recent years, which helps a visitor and hurts residents considerably. Cash is the system here: card acceptance barely exists outside a couple of hotels, machines dispense kip in small amounts with a fee each time, and dollars or Thai baht are useful to carry. The slide in the local currency has also made prices quoted in it unreliable between one visit and the next, so guesthouses and tour operators increasingly quote in dollars or baht instead, which changes how a negotiation starts.
pakse.whereToWork: Connectivity is workable rather than good. Fibre reaches the centre of Pakse at speeds adequate for video calls on a good day, and mobile data from Unitel and Lao Telecom covers the town and the main roads. Power is reasonably reliable, though cuts happen in the wet season. There is no coworking, so most people work from guesthouses or the riverfront cafes, several of which have understood what a laptop customer wants. The time zone is seven hours ahead of GMT, which gives a comfortable European afternoon overlap and works well with the rest of Southeast Asia. Anyone with call-heavy work should test the connection before committing to a month. Redundancy here means a second SIM rather than a second router, since the fixed line and the mobile network fail for different reasons and rarely at the same moment. A hardware failure is the harder problem: nothing in town stocks a replacement laptop charger, so it means ordering from Bangkok and waiting, or crossing to Thailand to buy one, which is a day either way.
pakse.gettingAround: Pakse is small enough to walk across in half an hour and flat, so bicycles work well. Tuk-tuks and jumbos cover the rest cheaply, and rented motorbikes are the usual way people reach the Bolaven plateau, which is the point of being here: the loop takes two or three days past waterfalls and coffee farms. Pakse International Airport is a few kilometres northwest with flights to Vientiane, Bangkok, Siem Reap and Ho Chi Minh City. Buses run south to Si Phan Don, the four thousand islands where the Mekong splits, and east into Vietnam. The Thai border at Chong Mek is about forty kilometres west and is a straightforward crossing. Khone Phapheng at the bottom of Si Phan Don is the largest waterfall in Southeast Asia by volume and the reason the Mekong never became a trade route into China: the French could not get past it, so they built a seven kilometre railway across two islands to portage boats around it. The locomotive and part of the track are still there, and that line was the only railway the country had for the next century.
pakse.visas: Laos issues visas on arrival at Pakse airport and at the main land borders for most nationalities, valid for thirty days for a fee in United States dollars in cash, and an e-visa is also available in advance. Extensions of a further thirty days are applied for at the immigration office in town. There is no remote work visa and working on a tourist visa is not permitted. Overstaying carries a daily fine that is enforced on departure. Anyone crossing to Thailand and back should note that the Lao visa is not multiple entry by default, so a return means paying for a new one at the border. The e-visa is accepted only at a defined list of entry points, which does not include every land border, so anyone arriving overland from Cambodia or Vietnam should confirm that the specific crossing takes it rather than assuming. Visa on arrival wants cash dollars and a passport photograph, and what it costs depends on which passport you hold rather than being one flat figure, with a surcharge outside office hours at some posts.
pakse.bestTime: November to February is the cool dry season and the best window, with temperatures around thirty degrees, low humidity and clear skies. March to May is very hot, regularly above thirty five and uncomfortable on the plateau road. The rains from June to October are heavy and the waterfalls on the Bolaven are at their most spectacular then, which is the argument for coming in the wet season despite the mud. The Mekong is high and fast from August to October and low enough to expose sandbars by March. Boun Bang Fai, the rocket festival, falls in May and is worth arranging a trip around. The Vat Phou festival falls at the full moon of the third lunar month, usually February, and turns the temple an hour south into a three day pilgrimage with boat races, music and processions, drawing people from across southern Laos and northeast Thailand. Lao New Year lands in mid-April at the hottest point of the year, and three days of water throwing in forty degree heat is either the best or the worst time to be here depending on temperament.
pakse.prosCons: Pakse is a genuinely relaxed river town at very low cost, with the Bolaven plateau's waterfalls and coffee farms immediately above it, the Khmer temple of Wat Phou an hour south, and the Mekong islands of Si Phan Don a few hours further downstream. It is far less visited than Luang Prabang and considerably cheaper. Pakse itself is a modest town rather than a destination, the connection is fine for calls and not much more, medical care is limited enough that Ubon Ratchathani in Thailand is the serious option, and there is nothing here that could be called a remote working community. Air quality in the March burning season is poor. Laos is the most heavily bombed country per head in history, and the provinces immediately east of here took much of it because the Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through them. Unexploded ordnance is still being cleared in Salavan, Sekong and Attapeu, which is why walking off marked paths in those provinces is not a decision to make casually. The town itself and the main plateau routes are not the problem; the ground beyond them can be.
pakse.whoFor: Motorcyclists and anyone drawn to the Bolaven loop, coffee people, and travellers moving slowly through southern Laos who want a base rather than a stop. It suits anyone whose budget is the binding constraint, since very few places offer this quality of life at this price. Client calls need a connection this town cannot guarantee, there is nothing to do after dark and nobody to be professional with, and somebody unwilling to get on a motorbike has cut themselves off from the plateau, the waterfalls and the coffee farms, which is everything worth coming for. Families will find the medical situation the main concern rather than anything else. It suits a coffee person more precisely than most places do, since the plateau farms sell direct and several will take somebody for a week who wants to understand processing rather than only drink the result. It suits anyone writing or reading seriously, because the town gives you nothing to do in the evening, and that is either the flaw or the point. It fits badly for work with a hard deadline in a fixed week, since a wet-season outage or a cancelled flight is not unusual and there is no fallback.

mawlamyine.costOfLiving: Budget around $550 a month, which is very low even by Myanmar's standards. A one-bedroom runs roughly $120 to $300. Market produce is cheap and Mon State grows a great deal of its own food, so fruit, fish and vegetables cost very little. Restaurant meals are inexpensive and Mon cooking is one of the best regional cuisines in the country. Imported goods are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable. Utilities are cheap but the supply is the problem rather than the price. The kyat has been extremely volatile since 2021 and the gap between official and market rates is wide, so any figure here needs checking against current conditions rather than trusted. The banking position matters more than the prices do. International cards are largely unusable, transfers into the country are difficult under sanctions and restrictions, and most foreigners operate entirely on cash brought in and changed locally, which is a security question as much as a logistical one. Notes are inspected closely and anything marked or folded can be refused outright. Generator fuel is the household cost that has risen most, since the cheap electricity in the tariff is not the electricity that is actually available.
mawlamyine.whereToWork: Connectivity is poor and the reason is political rather than technical. Myanmar's military authorities have imposed sustained internet restrictions since 2021, including shutdowns, VPN blocking and throttling, and Mon State has been affected along with the rest of the country. Fibre exists in Mawlamyine and mobile data works, but neither can be relied on and the interruptions are deliberate rather than accidental. Power cuts are frequent and prolonged, with generators standard in any business. There is no coworking. The time zone is six and a half hours ahead of GMT. Anyone considering remote work here should treat the connection as unavailable rather than unreliable and plan accordingly. There is a further dimension that no bandwidth figure captures. A cybersecurity law passed in 2025 criminalises unauthorised use of a VPN, which shifts the question from whether a connection works to whether the means of restoring it carries legal risk, and that risk falls hardest on residents rather than on visitors. For anyone weighing this town as a place to work from, the honest position is that the constraint is not infrastructure that might improve but policy that may not.
mawlamyine.gettingAround: Mawlamyine is walkable along the riverfront and up to the pagoda ridge, and trishaws and motorbike taxis cover the rest very cheaply. The town sits on the east bank of the Thanlwin at one of the widest river mouths in Myanmar, with Bilu Kyun, the large island opposite, reached by ferry and worth a day for its craft villages. Buses run north to Yangon in six or seven hours and south towards Dawei and the Thai border at Myawaddy. The railway line north crosses the Thanlwin bridge, one of the longest in the country. The airport has limited domestic service and schedules change without much notice. Overland travel is what has changed most since 2021. Roads in the southeast pass through areas affected by the conflict, checkpoints are common, and routes that were routine for years now close and reopen without notice, so any journey needs local confirmation on the day rather than a timetable. The trains are very slow even by regional standards and the ride is rough, which is part of their charm in ordinary times and a poor bet when nothing about a schedule can be relied on.
mawlamyine.visas: Myanmar requires a visa of almost every nationality, obtained through the e-visa system in advance, with twenty eight days the standard tourist grant and extensions difficult. There is no remote work visa. The more important point is not procedural: most Western governments advise against all or all but essential travel to Myanmar following the 2021 coup and the conflict since, and insurance is likely to be void against that advice. Conscription was introduced in 2024. Entry and internal travel restrictions change frequently and some regions are closed entirely. Read current government advice before making any plan involving this country. Most consulates have sharply reduced their presence, so the assistance a traveller would normally expect in an emergency may not exist in practice. And a policy voided by government advice does not merely decline to cover a cancelled flight; it declines to cover medical evacuation, which in this part of the country would be the expensive part. Dual nationals of Myanmar carry additional exposure, including under the conscription law, and should take specific advice.
mawlamyine.bestTime: November to February is the cool dry season and the only comfortable window, at around thirty degrees with low humidity. March to May is very hot and reaches the high thirties. The southwest monsoon from June to October is exceptional here: Mon State is among the wettest parts of Myanmar and Mawlamyine receives close to five metres of rain in a normal year, which makes half the year genuinely difficult to move around in. The Thanlwin runs high and brown through the monsoon. Thadingyut, the festival of lights in October, is the year's biggest celebration and marks the end of Buddhist Lent. The monsoon compounds everything else here rather than simply being wet. Power failures increase, roads flood, and the river crossings that make ordinary movement possible become unreliable, so the season that is merely inconvenient elsewhere is the one that most restricts what is possible. April is the hottest month and holds Thingyan, the water festival marking the new year, though its scale has been much reduced since 2021 in a country where public celebration has itself become a political question.
mawlamyine.prosCons: Mawlamyine is a beautiful and almost unvisited colonial river town, with the Kyaikthanlan Pagoda on the ridge that Kipling wrote about, Mon culture that is distinct from the Burmese majority, the enormous reclining Buddha at Win Sein Taw Ya nearby, and prices that are among the lowest anywhere in Asia. The obstacle is the country, not the town: the 2021 coup, the conflict since, the deliberate internet restrictions, the currency instability and the travel advice against going at all. Medical care is limited. This is a place to understand and to watch rather than one to plan a stay in at present. The remaining problem is ethical rather than practical. Tourist spending in Myanmar is difficult to direct: hotels, transport and permits often route money to entities connected with the military, and organisations working on the country have argued both that visitors sustain ordinary livelihoods and that the revenue helps sustain the administration. There is no clean answer to that, and anyone who does travel should at least know which side of the argument they are choosing rather than discover it afterwards.
mawlamyine.whoFor: A working reason to be in Myanmar, in humanitarian work, journalism or academic research on Mon State, or a long history in the country and informed decisions about risk. The colonial-era town is far more intact here than in Yangon, which has spent thirty years rebuilding over its own version of the same thing. Remote work cannot be planned around a connection the state interrupts at will. Beyond that, most governments advise against travel here, and anybody going anyway should understand exactly what that does to their insurance and to what a consulate would be able to do for them if it came to that. The recommendation this guide would actually make is to keep the place in mind rather than book it. Mawlamyine has been one of the most rewarding towns in Southeast Asia for the traveller who reached it, and it will be again, and nothing about that argues for going now. Anyone whose interest is Mon culture can find a great deal of it in the diaspora communities across the border in Thailand, which are reachable, safe and welcoming, and which is where a good many people from this region now live.

madurai.costOfLiving: Budget around $470 a month, which makes Madurai one of the least expensive cities on this site. A one-bedroom runs roughly $100 to $250, with the areas near the temple and the newer suburbs at either end of that. Market produce is very cheap and Tamil Nadu grows a great deal of its own food. Eating out costs almost nothing: a full meal on a banana leaf at one of the mess halls runs a couple of dollars and is among the best food in India. Utilities are cheap. Imported goods and Western groceries carry a markup and the choice is limited compared with Chennai or Bengaluru. Fibre runs about $8 to $12 a month for 100 to 300 Mbps, which is among the best value anywhere on this site. A full South Indian meals plate on a banana leaf costs well under a dollar and is what most of the city eats at lunch. Autorickshaws are a dollar or two across the centre, and the main variable in a monthly budget is whether the flat has air conditioning for the hot months, which it should.
madurai.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable. Fibre from Jio, Airtel and BSNL reaches most of the city at good speeds and low prices, and mobile data in India remains among the cheapest anywhere. Power cuts happen but are shorter and less frequent than they were. There is a small coworking scene serving the local IT and startup sector, which is real but modest next to Chennai's. The time zone is five and a half hours ahead of GMT, which gives a full European working overlap in the afternoon and an early morning with East Asia. Summer heat makes air conditioning a working requirement rather than a comfort from April onwards. Coworking desks run about $50 to $90 a month, which is modest even by Indian standards. The city's economy is textiles, temple tourism and increasingly software services, and the professional population that supports what coworking exists comes from the local engineering colleges rather than from anywhere else.
madurai.gettingAround: Madurai is dense and best covered by autorickshaw, which is cheap and everywhere, with ride-hailing apps working reliably. The area around the Meenakshi temple is walkable and closed to vehicles in parts, which makes it the most pleasant part of the city on foot. City buses are very cheap and crowded. Madurai Junction is a major railway station with overnight services to Chennai, Bengaluru and Kerala, and the trains are the sensible way to move around south India. Madurai Airport has domestic flights and a small number of regional international ones to Colombo, Dubai and Singapore. Rameswaram and the Pamban rail bridge are about three hours southeast, and the new vertical-lift bridge that replaced the century-old cantilever opened in 2024. Kodaikanal in the Western Ghats is a similar distance west and around 2,100 metres up, which is the standard escape from the April heat. Overnight buses leave for the hill country to the west every evening, climbing out of the plain and over a state line while everybody sleeps, which is how most people here take a weekend away from the heat. The mountain section is done in the dark, restful or alarming depending on the passenger.
madurai.visas: India requires a visa of almost every nationality. The e-Visa is the practical route: a tourist e-Visa is issued for thirty days, one year or five years depending on the option chosen, applied for online several days before travel, and it is valid for arrival at Madurai among other airports. Business and employment visas are separate categories with their own requirements. There is no remote work visa, and working on a tourist visa is not permitted. Overstaying is taken seriously. Registration is required for some longer visa types within a fortnight of arrival, which catches people out. On the longer versions each individual stay is capped at ninety days or a hundred and eighty depending on nationality, which trips up anybody assuming a five-year document means five continuous years in the country. There is no nomad visa and FRRO registration applies beyond a hundred and eighty days, so a long stay is built around exits and fresh entries.
madurai.bestTime: November to February is the only comfortable window, warm at around thirty degrees with lower humidity and cooler evenings. March to June is severe, regularly above forty and among the hottest periods anywhere in India, with the city visibly slowing down in the afternoons. The northeast monsoon brings rain in October and November, heavy but not usually disruptive. The Chithirai festival in April and May is the year's great event, when a million people come for the celestial wedding of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar, and accommodation is impossible without booking months ahead. The Jallikattu bull-taming events around Pongal in January take place in villages near the city and draw very large crowds, and the practice was the subject of a Supreme Court ban and a subsequent state law that restored it, which makes it politically charged as well as popular. The jasmine grown around this city carries a protected name of its own, and the flower market opens well before dawn with the whole day's crop weighed, sold and gone by seven in the morning. The scent of it through the older streets in the hot months is the strongest argument anybody has for being up that early.
madurai.prosCons: The Meenakshi Amman temple is not a monument but a working temple that fifteen thousand people pass through every day, with fourteen gopurams covered in thousands of painted figures and a hall of a thousand carved pillars at its centre. The city has been continuously inhabited for well over two thousand years and appears in Greek and Roman records. Food is exceptional and costs nothing. The heat is punishing, the air quality is poor, the traffic and the noise are both constant, and the city makes very few concessions to visitors. There is almost no remote worker presence. The temple's Pottramarai Kulam, the golden lotus tank, and the surrounding concentric streets follow a plan laid out on Vastu principles, so the city's whole street grid radiates from the sanctuary in a way that is visible on any map and unusual even in south India.
madurai.whoFor: Anyone interested in living Hindu practice rather than monuments, since the temple is the centre of daily life at a scale that is difficult to find anywhere else. It suits people who take food seriously, because Tamil vegetarian cooking is at its best in these streets. It suits anyone on a tight budget. Quiet, clean air and Western comfort are three things a dense Tamil temple city does not set out to provide. March to June is the specific window to avoid, because the heat then is genuinely dangerous rather than merely unpleasant and it kills people every year. Madurai was the seat of the Sangam academies, and it claims a continuous urban record longer than almost any other city in India, which makes Tamil literature and history a serious reason to be here and not a footnote to the temple.

shillong.costOfLiving: Budget around $560 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $150 to $350, with Laitumkhrah and the areas near the golf course at the top and the outer neighbourhoods considerably cheaper. Market produce at Iewduh, one of the largest markets in northeast India, is cheap and the region grows excellent oranges, pineapple and the fiery bhut jolokia chilli. Eating out is inexpensive and Khasi cooking, which uses a great deal of pork and rice, is quite different from mainland Indian food. Imported goods carry a markup because everything comes up the road from Guwahati. Utilities are modest and heating is unnecessary at this altitude. Fibre runs about $10 to $15 a month where it reaches, and an inverter is a normal household purchase rather than a contingency. The road dependency on Guwahati is the structural cost driver: everything from cement to imported groceries comes up the same three-hour highway, and a landslide closing it in the monsoon moves prices within days.
shillong.whereToWork: Connectivity is adequate. Fibre reaches parts of Shillong at reasonable speeds and mobile data from Jio and Airtel covers the city and the main roads, though the northeast is served by fewer routes than the rest of India and outages happen. Power cuts are common enough that an inverter is standard. There is a small coworking presence aimed at the local student and startup population. The time zone is five and a half hours ahead of GMT, and Shillong sits far enough east that the sun rises before five in summer, which is a genuine oddity of a country with a single time zone. India runs a single time zone despite spanning nearly thirty degrees of longitude, which means Shillong's sun rises around half past four in June and sets by six, and the working day feels permanently misaligned with the light. There has been a long-running campaign in the northeast for a separate time zone precisely because of this.
shillong.gettingAround: Shillong is hilly and spread across ridges, so walking works within neighbourhoods and not between them. Shared taxis are the local institution: they run fixed routes for a few rupees and you share with whoever is going the same way, which is how almost everyone moves. Private taxis and ride-hailing exist. The city has no railway and no working airport for most purposes, so the road down to Guwahati, about three hours through the hills, is the practical connection to the rest of India. Cherrapunji and Mawlynnong are day trips, and the living root bridges at Nongriat are a serious hike. Shared taxis are the thing to learn on day one: you flag one going your direction, say where you are headed and pay a fixed few rupees, and the driver fills the car. The Nongriat double-decker root bridge is a 3,000-step descent and climb from Tyrna and is a serious half-day rather than a viewpoint. The road down to the plains carries all the freight for the state as well as its people, and a landslide or a convoy of trucks can turn three hours into six with no warning, so an early start is the local habit rather than an eccentricity.
shillong.visas: India's e-Visa applies here as elsewhere, issued for thirty days, one year or five years depending on the option chosen and applied for online before travel. Meghalaya no longer requires an Inner Line Permit, unlike several neighbouring states, so a standard Indian visa is enough. Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Mizoram do have additional permit requirements, which matters if you plan to travel on. There is no remote work visa and working on a tourist visa is not permitted. Foreigners are required to register with the local authorities on some visa types. Meghalaya dropped its Inner Line Permit requirement, but the state does require foreigners to register with the district authorities within twenty-four hours of arrival in some circumstances, which hotels usually handle. Anyone continuing to Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland or Mizoram needs a separate permit arranged in advance. The Bangladesh border is under two hours south and the crossing there is open to foreigners, though an Indian visa specifying a land exit is needed and a standard electronic one may not permit it, so the port of exit has to be confirmed before relying on that route.
shillong.bestTime: October to April is the dry season and the best window, cool at around twenty degrees by day and genuinely cold at night in December and January, which is why Shillong was built as a hill station. May to September is the monsoon, and this is the wettest region on earth: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, both within an hour, hold the world records for annual rainfall, and Shillong itself gets more than two metres. The waterfalls are extraordinary in the monsoon and the roads are difficult. Autumn, after the rains stop, is when the hills are greenest and clearest. Mawsynram averages around 11,800 millimetres of rain a year and Cherrapunji holds the records for the wettest month and the wettest year ever measured anywhere, both within an hour of the city. Visiting in the monsoon means seeing the waterfalls at full force and accepting that the roads and the views will both be unreliable. The Nongkrem dance at the Khasi royal seat outside town each autumn is the state's principal traditional festival, several days of ritual and dancing that is a religious occasion rather than a performance, and visitors are welcome on exactly those terms.
shillong.prosCons: A cool hill climate in the tropics is the start of it, along with a Khasi culture that is matrilineal and quite unlike the rest of India, the best live music scene in the northeast by a wide margin, and access to landscapes with no equivalent anywhere: living root bridges grown from rubber fig over generations, the wettest places on the planet, and clear rivers in limestone gorges. Everything comes through Guwahati, which is the isolation in one sentence, the monsoon is less a season than a condition here, and the infrastructure lags the rest of the country. Khasi society is matrilineal, with property and family name passing through the youngest daughter, which is genuinely unusual in India and shapes everything from inheritance to how households are organised, and it is worth reading about before arriving rather than discovering as a curiosity.
shillong.whoFor: Anyone drawn to northeast India, which is culturally and visually a different country from the plains, along with hikers, cavers and musicians, since the local rock scene is a genuine phenomenon and English-language music has been part of Khasi life for generations. It suits English speakers particularly, because Meghalaya is one of the more anglophone states in India. Getting anywhere quickly is impossible when the road to Guwahati is the only way out, and five months of rain in a town that competes annually for the world's highest rainfall is a genuine test of temperament rather than a statistic. It also suits cavers specifically: Meghalaya's limestone holds the longest cave systems in the subcontinent, including Krem Liat Prah at over thirty kilometres, and expeditions run here most years with a genuine international caving community behind them.

gilgit.costOfLiving: Budget around $480 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $120 to $280 and the rental market is small and mostly informal, arranged through contacts rather than listings. Market produce is cheap and the region's apricots, cherries and apples are exceptional in season and dried for the winter. Eating out is inexpensive and the food is more Central Asian than Pakistani, with more meat and bread and less spice. Imported goods are expensive and the choice is limited by the road. Utilities are cheap but supply is intermittent, and winter heating is a real cost and a real logistical problem. Fibre where it exists runs $20 to $40 a month for speeds that will frustrate anyone used to a city connection. Winter heating means wood or gas cylinders rather than a utility bill, and both have to be stockpiled before the roads deteriorate, which is a genuine seasonal task rather than an expense. A shared jeep to Hunza costs a few dollars and a private vehicle for the day $60 to $100. Cash is essential outside the main bazaar, since card acceptance is minimal and ATMs in the smaller valleys are unreliable or absent.
gilgit.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak and this is the single biggest constraint. Gilgit Baltistan is served by limited bandwidth up the Karakoram Highway, speeds are modest and outages are frequent, and mobile data thins to nothing as soon as you leave the main valleys. Power cuts are routine, particularly in winter when the hydropower runs low. There is no coworking. The time zone is five hours ahead of GMT, which gives a workable European afternoon. Anyone whose work requires reliable video calls should treat Gilgit as difficult, and anyone heading further into the valleys should assume no connection at all. Gilgit Baltistan's bandwidth arrives up the same road as everything else and a landslide that closes the Karakoram Highway can degrade the connection as well as the supply chain. Starlink is not licensed in Pakistan, so the usual workaround for remote places is unavailable here, which is worth knowing before planning around it.
gilgit.gettingAround: Gilgit town is small and walkable, and shared jeeps and minibuses handle everything beyond it. The Karakoram Highway is the spine of the region, running north to Hunza and the Khunjerab pass into China and south towards Islamabad, and it is one of the great roads in the world and also a landslide-prone one. Journeys take considerably longer than the distance suggests. Gilgit Airport has flights to Islamabad that are spectacular and are cancelled often, since the approach requires visual conditions through the mountains. The road to Islamabad takes fifteen to twenty hours. The Karakoram Highway was built jointly with China over twenty years and around a thousand workers died constructing it, which is the context for a road that still requires constant repair. The Khunjerab pass at 4,693 metres is the highest paved international border crossing in the world. Shared jeeps leave when full rather than to a timetable, so an early start matters more than a booking does for anything beyond Hunza.
gilgit.visas: Pakistan operates an online visa system that has become considerably easier: most nationalities can apply for a tourist e-visa in advance, often with approval in days, and a visa on arrival scheme exists for some countries through approved tour operators. There is no remote work visa. Gilgit Baltistan itself no longer requires a separate permit for most areas, though the Khunjerab pass, some border zones and certain peaks do need permits arranged in advance. Registration with police is required in some districts. Check current requirements directly, since Pakistan's visa policy has changed repeatedly in recent years. The e-visa is applied for through the NADRA portal and most nationalities no longer need a sponsor for tourism, which is a substantial change from a decade ago. The Khunjerab pass into China is the highest paved border crossing in the world and shuts for the winter, usually from around December until spring, so the overland route to Kashgar exists for only part of the year.
gilgit.bestTime: May to October is the season, with temperatures around twenty five degrees in summer, the passes open and the valleys accessible. The Khunjerab pass into China opens roughly in May and closes at the end of the year. Autumn from late September to October is when the poplars and apricot orchards turn and the light is at its best, and it is the photographers' month. Winter from November to March is cold, the higher roads close, and Gilgit itself sits at fifteen hundred metres and gets genuinely cold. Spring blossom in the Hunza valley in April is the other reason people time a trip. Cherry and apricot blossom moves up the valleys through April, starting lower near Gilgit and reaching Hunza and Nagar a week or two later, and the timing shifts year to year enough that it is worth watching before booking. The Shandur polo festival in July, played at 3,700 metres on the pass between Gilgit and Chitral, is the region's largest event and a genuine spectacle.
gilgit.prosCons: Position is everything here: this is where the Karakoram, the Hindu Kush and the Himalaya meet, five of the world's fourteen peaks above eight thousand metres stand within the region, and the Hunza valley two hours north is one of the most spectacular inhabited landscapes anywhere on earth. Costs are very low and the hospitality is genuine and much remarked on. Connectivity, the road, the winters and limited medical care all pull against it, and the security picture needs current government advice rather than guesswork, since parts of the wider region carry serious warnings of their own. Nanga Parbat, the ninth-highest mountain in the world and one of the most dangerous, sits at the southern end of the region, and the Fairy Meadows viewpoint below it is reached by a jeep track with a reputation of its own. Rakaposhi rises seven thousand metres almost directly from the valley floor, one of the steepest rises on earth.
gilgit.whoFor: Mountaineers, trekkers and photographers above all, for whom this ranks among the great destinations on earth and is reason enough to accept everything else. It suits anyone travelling the Karakoram Highway in either direction. It suits people with a working connection to the region through development or research. The connection will not carry remote work, and a fixed schedule is the other thing to leave at home: landslides, weather and cancelled flights make every timing in this valley approximate rather than firm, and no amount of planning in advance changes any part of that. The Wakhi and Burusho communities of the upper valleys speak languages unrelated to almost anything around them. Burushaski in particular has no established relatives anywhere on earth, which has kept it among the standing puzzles of Asian linguistics. Hunza's Ismaili population is studied for good reason. Literacy rates and social organisation there differ strikingly from the rest of Pakistan, and the Aga Khan network that built much of it is visible in every village school and clinic in the valley. Be clear before booking that this is a staging post rather than a destination, and that Karimabad in Hunza is where most visitors actually settle for a while.

jaffna.costOfLiving: Budget around $620 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $150 to $350, and the market is small, with much of the housing stock either rebuilt since the war or still showing it. Market produce is cheap and the peninsula grows its own vegetables, mangoes and palmyra. Eating out is inexpensive and Jaffna cooking, which uses more coconut, chilli and crab than the south, is regarded by many as the best food in Sri Lanka. Imported goods carry a markup and Colombo is where people go for choice. The rupee's collapse in 2022 and the recovery since mean prices have moved a great deal. Fibre runs about $15 to $25 a month and mobile data less, which is among the better value in South Asia and one of the practical reasons a longer stay works here. A rice and curry lunch at a local place is well under two dollars, and the crab curry that Jaffna is known for costs a few dollars even at the restaurants people travel for. Autorickshaw rides across town are a dollar or two. The one line to budget properly is a fan or air conditioning through the hot months, which is not optional on this peninsula.
jaffna.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable. Fibre reaches central Jaffna at workable speeds and mobile data from Dialog and SLT covers the peninsula, with prices low by regional standards. Power is more reliable than it was during the 2022 crisis, when scheduled cuts ran for hours daily, but the underlying situation is fragile. There is a small coworking presence and the university brings a young population. The time zone is five and a half hours ahead of GMT, which gives a good European afternoon overlap. Anyone planning a longer stay should have a mobile data fallback, since it has been the more reliable option during power problems. The University of Jaffna is the largest institution in the north and its presence explains most of what coworking and cafe culture exists, so the town is livelier in term time than out of it. Anyone staying through a power problem should know that the mobile networks held up considerably better than the grid during 2022, and that a data-heavy plan and a power bank were what kept people working. Dialog's coverage on the outer islands is patchier than on the peninsula itself.
jaffna.gettingAround: Jaffna town is flat and compact, which makes it the most bicycle-friendly city in Sri Lanka and cycling the way most residents move. Autorickshaws are cheap and everywhere. The peninsula's islands are reached by causeways and a ferry, and Delft with its wild ponies and baobab trees is a genuine day out. The Yal Devi train from Colombo takes about seven hours on a line that was destroyed in the war and rebuilt in 2014, which is itself part of the story. Jaffna Airport reopened in 2019 with flights to Colombo and Chennai. Bicycles can be hired for a couple of dollars a day and are genuinely the best way to see the peninsula, which is flat, quiet and full of small roads between palmyra palms. The causeway to Kayts and the ferry onward to Delft take most of a day each way, so the outer islands are a planned trip rather than an afternoon. Buses run to Point Pedro and the northern coast frequently and cost almost nothing.
jaffna.visas: Sri Lanka has moved between visa systems repeatedly and the current position needs checking. Most nationalities need an Electronic Travel Authorisation applied for online before arrival, issued for thirty days and extendable to six months in-country, and the country has at various points offered free or waived tourist visas to selected nationalities as a tourism measure. There is no remote work visa, though a digital nomad visa has been discussed. Extensions are handled in Colombo. Overstaying carries fines. Confirm the requirement and the fee directly rather than relying on older guidance. Sri Lanka has changed its visa arrangements repeatedly since 2023, including a period of free entry for selected nationalities and a contested switch of the processing contract, so the fee and the process should both be confirmed on the official portal rather than through a third-party site, several of which charge a substantial markup for the same thing.
jaffna.bestTime: January to March is the best window, dry and warm at around thirty degrees, and it is also when the peninsula's festivals fall. The dry season runs roughly from February to September, which is the opposite of Sri Lanka's southwest and is worth knowing, since Jaffna is a good destination exactly when the southern beaches are wet. The northeast monsoon from October to December brings the region's rain. The Nallur festival in August is the great event of the year, twenty five days of processions culminating in enormous crowds around the temple, and accommodation is impossible without booking. The dry season here running February to September is genuinely the inverse of the southwest coast, which means Jaffna is at its best exactly when Galle and the south are wettest, and a Sri Lankan itinerary that uses both can stay dry year-round. Nallur's twenty-five days in July and August fill every room on the peninsula, so a stay in that window needs booking months out.
jaffna.prosCons: Jaffna holds a Tamil culture that is quite distinct from the rest of Sri Lanka, a Dutch fort on the lagoon that is among the largest colonial fortifications in Asia, the Nallur Kandaswamy temple, exceptional food, and a peninsula of islands, palmyra and lagoons that almost nobody troubles to visit. It is also a place actively rebuilding after a thirty year war that ended in 2009, which is visible everywhere. The heat and the limited infrastructure are the everyday objections, and the war's aftermath, including unresolved questions of accountability and land, remains politically live and is not something anybody should be casual about. The peninsula's landscape is also unlike anywhere else in the country: flat limestone, palmyra palms, salt lagoons and islands reached by causeway, with none of the hills or rainforest that define the south. Delft's wild ponies descend from Dutch colonial stock and the island's baobabs were planted by Arab traders, which gives some sense of how many layers are here.
jaffna.whoFor: Anyone interested in Tamil culture, in post-conflict recovery, or in the parts of Sri Lanka that the beach and hill country circuit misses entirely. It suits cyclists, since the flat peninsula is genuinely made for it. It suits people who take food seriously. The north of Sri Lanka is not set up for beaches and comfort and does not pretend to be. The larger thing is the war, which ended within living memory and is present here in the buildings, the demographics and the conversations, so anybody who would rather not encounter that should choose the south. The Tamil diaspora runs back to this town. Communities in Toronto, London and Sydney trace their origin to Jaffna, and a great deal of the reconstruction visible in the streets was funded from them, which makes the last two decades of the town's history readable on the ground rather than only in an account of it.

luangnamtha.costOfLiving: Budget around $540 a month, which is very low. A one-bedroom or a long-stay guesthouse room runs roughly $120 to $280, and the market here is informal enough that a monthly rate is a conversation rather than a listing. Market produce is cheap and the valley grows its own rice, vegetables and river fish. Eating out costs a few dollars and the night market is where most people do it. Imported goods carry a markup because everything comes up the road. Utilities are inexpensive. The kip has weakened substantially in recent years, which makes a foreign income go a long way here and makes local life harder. Fibre where the guesthouses have it runs $20 to $35 a month and a Unitel data bundle a few dollars, which is the arrangement almost everyone actually uses. A motorbike is $6 to $10 a day or around $90 a month, and a bicycle a dollar or two, which covers most of the valley. A guided two-day trek into Nam Ha costs $60 to $110 depending on group size, and that fee is the main discretionary line in a month here. Nothing else in the town is expensive enough to plan around.
luangnamtha.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. Fibre exists in the town at modest speeds and mobile data from Unitel covers the valley and thins quickly in the hills, which is where you would actually want to be. Power cuts happen, particularly in the wet season. There is no coworking and the guesthouses are the working environment by default. The time zone is seven hours ahead of GMT, giving a comfortable European afternoon. Anyone whose income depends on video calls should treat Luang Namtha as a place to visit between contracts rather than a base, because the connection will not carry a normal working week reliably. Starlink has begun appearing at a few of the better guesthouses since 2024 and is the one thing that would change the calculation, so it is worth asking about specifically rather than accepting a general assurance. The Laos-China railway has also improved the backhaul into northern Laos, and speeds in the town are better than they were three years ago, though the hills beyond it remain a different matter entirely.
luangnamtha.gettingAround: The town is a single main street and is walkable end to end in twenty minutes. Bicycles and rented motorbikes cover the valley, and the villages, waterfalls and the Nam Ha protected area beyond it. Songthaews handle longer local routes. Buses run south to Luang Prabang in about eight hours on a road that has improved considerably, north to Boten and the Chinese border, and west to Huay Xai for the slow boat down the Mekong. The airport has occasional flights to Vientiane. The Laos-China railway does not serve Luang Namtha directly, but Boten and Oudomxay are within reach of stations on it. The Boten crossing into China is the busiest land border in Laos and the traffic through it has grown sharply since the railway opened, which is visible on the road north. Muang Sing, an old opium-trade town near the Chinese border with a Sunday market drawing Akha and Hmong villagers down from the hills, is two hours northwest and is the trip most people make from here.
luangnamtha.visas: Laos issues visas on arrival at the main international entry points and via an e-visa applied for in advance, valid for thirty days for a fee payable in United States dollars in cash, with a thirty day extension available in-country. Luang Namtha's own airport and the Boten land crossing both handle visa on arrival, though the land border's hours are worth confirming. There is no remote work visa. Trekking in the Nam Ha protected area is done through licensed operators, which is a conservation arrangement rather than a permit requirement, and the fees go partly to the villages. The e-visa clears in a few working days and what it costs varies by nationality. At the Boten crossing from China there is no card payment at all, so the money has to be in hand before arriving. Extensions are handled in Vientiane or through an agent, so a sixty-day stay means planning that trip rather than assuming it can be done locally.
luangnamtha.bestTime: November to February is the cool dry season and the best window, with days around twenty five degrees and cold nights that surprise people who expect Laos to be uniformly hot. March and April are hot and, more importantly, are the burning season, when agricultural fires across the northern uplands fill the valleys with smoke for weeks and the air quality becomes genuinely poor. The rains from May to October make the trekking routes muddy and the leeches active, but the hills are at their greenest. October, just after the rains, is the clearest month of the year. Readings through those two months regularly reach levels that would trigger a public health warning anywhere with proper monitoring, and there is not enough wind at this altitude to move any of it along. Anyone with asthma should simply not come in those two months. The rice comes in through November and the whole valley turns gold and then stubble inside a fortnight, which is the best few weeks of the year to be looking at any of it.
luangnamtha.prosCons: The Nam Ha National Protected Area is why anyone comes: one of the better-run community-based ecotourism projects in Southeast Asia, where trekking fees are shared with the villages and guide numbers are capped by agreement. The valley is beautiful, the town is quiet and friendly, and the cost is negligible. Connectivity is poor, the town is a long way from anywhere, the burning season is grim, and there is very little going on beyond the trekking. Medical care is basic and the serious option is a long way south. There is no remote worker community at all. The Nam Ha project was set up with UNESCO support in the late 1990s and is one of the earliest community ecotourism schemes in the region, which is why the guiding standard and the village arrangements are noticeably better organised than the equivalent elsewhere in Laos.
luangnamtha.whoFor: Trekkers and cyclists, and anyone pulled towards the hill communities of northern Laos, which are Akha, Khmu, Hmong and Tai Dam rather than lowland Lao and are a genuinely different world. It suits people crossing overland between China, Laos and Thailand. It suits anyone whose work can go offline for a fortnight. A normal working schedule does not fit here. March and April demand a tolerance for smoke that most people do not have, and choice, whether in food or in company, is not something this town can offer much of at all. Anybody working the northern Laos loop slowly should build a week into it here. The town sits between Huay Xai on the Thai border and Oudomxay and Nong Khiaw to the east, which makes it the natural place to stop properly when everybody else stops for a single night.

miri.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month, which is moderate for Malaysia and low by any international measure. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, with the newer condominiums near the marina at the top. Hawker food is exceptional value and Miri's mix of Malay, Chinese, Iban and Indian cooking means the range at a few dollars a meal is genuinely wide. Groceries are reasonable and the supermarkets carry a good deal of imported stock because of the oil industry. Utilities are cheap and subsidised fuel makes driving inexpensive. The ringgit's weakness in recent years has made Malaysia noticeably cheaper for foreign earners. Condominium rents usually include a pool and a gym, which is standard rather than premium in Malaysia and changes what the figure buys compared with Europe. Expect two months' deposit plus a utilities deposit and a stamped tenancy agreement. Private healthcare is inexpensive and good, and the hospitals here serve a catchment reaching into Brunei, where costs are higher. A car is the main discretionary purchase, and second-hand prices in Malaysia are high because of the duty structure, so many longer-stay foreigners rent rather than buy one.
miri.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre from TM Unifi and Maxis reaches most of Miri at decent speeds and prices, and mobile coverage is comprehensive across the city, which is a real difference from most of Sarawak. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking presence and a number of cafes set up for it. The time zone is eight hours ahead of GMT, which is Malaysia's single national zone and gives a workable overlap with Australia and an early morning with Europe. Miri's oil and gas sector means the city has better business infrastructure than its size would otherwise support. The oil economy also explains the English. The city grew around Shell's first Malaysian well and the sector has run in English ever since, which makes professional dealings noticeably easier than the size of the place suggests. Regional haze from agricultural burning can affect air quality for stretches of the drier months, and an air purifier is a reasonable precaution. And the working day starts early while the heat peaks in the afternoon, so most people front-load anything demanding.
miri.gettingAround: A car or a motorbike is the practical answer: Miri is spread out along the coast and the public bus service is limited, though Grab works and is cheap. The city centre and the waterfront are walkable. Miri Airport is the busiest in northern Sarawak, with flights to Kuala Lumpur, Kota Kinabalu, Kuching and, crucially, the small aircraft to Mulu, which is how almost everyone reaches the caves. Buses run north to Brunei in about four hours and south down the coast. The road to Bario in the Kelabit Highlands exists and is a serious undertaking. The Mulu flight deserves planning rather than assumption. The aircraft is small, the baggage allowance is strict and enforced, and seats sell out well ahead in the dry months, so it is the first thing to book rather than the last. Going north, the road to Brunei involves two border crossings in quick succession because of the way the sultanate is divided, which surprises people expecting one. An international driving permit covers a visitor for a rental car.
miri.visas: Malaysia grants ninety days visa-free on arrival to most Western nationalities, and Sarawak operates its own immigration control, which means a separate entry stamp when you fly in from peninsular Malaysia and a limit that Sarawak sets rather than the federal government. Malaysia also runs the DE Rantau Nomad Pass, a twelve month renewable visa for remote workers earning above a stated threshold, which is one of the better schemes in the region. Extensions in Sarawak are handled by the state immigration department. Overland entry from Brunei is straightforward. The Brunei border is close enough that a short crossing and return is a common way to reset the clock, though anybody doing it repeatedly should expect questions at the counter rather than a formality. Sarawak commonly grants thirty days to visitors rather than the ninety the federal rules imply, and the length is at the officer's discretion, so look at the stamp before leaving the desk rather than discovering the difference a month later. The DE Rantau pass is applied for online before travel and covers dependants, which is the feature that makes the paperwork worthwhile for anyone considering a year.
miri.bestTime: March to September is the drier half and the practical window, with temperatures around thirty two degrees and high humidity throughout the year. The northeast monsoon from November to February brings heavier rain and rough seas, which affects diving on the Miri-Sibuti reefs and can close the small aircraft to Mulu. Mulu itself is wet in every month, since it sits in rainforest, and the caves are visitable year round. The bat exodus from Deer Cave happens most evenings when it is not raining, which is the qualification everyone forgets to mention. Gawai Dayak at the start of June is Sarawak's harvest festival and effectively closes the state for several days, with longhouse celebrations that a visitor invited to one should accept. Borneo Jazz, held in the city since the mid-2000s, is its own event and its main claim on the wider region. For anyone planning around the caves, the drier months are also when haze is most likely, which is the trade the calendar offers.
miri.prosCons: Miri is a comfortable, well-serviced small city with genuinely good food, low costs and reliable internet, sitting an hour's flight from Gunung Mulu National Park, a UNESCO site with the largest cave chamber in the world and a nightly exodus of millions of bats at dusk. The Niah Caves with their forty thousand year old human remains are two hours south. Miri itself is a functional oil town rather than an attractive one, its beaches are genuinely unremarkable, and there is very little left to do in the city once the food has been worked through, which takes about a week of steady eating. The city is very safe and unusually relaxed, including at night, which is not universally true of oil towns. And the position is genuinely useful, with Brunei an hour and a half north and Kota Kinabalu a short flight away, so it works as a hinge rather than a dead end. The countervailing fact is the logging and palm oil that have reshaped much of Sarawak's interior, which is plainly visible from the air on the way to Mulu.
miri.whoFor: Cavers, divers and anyone using the town as the base for Mulu, Niah and the Kelabit Highlands, which is the honest reason to be here. It suits remote workers who want Malaysian costs and infrastructure away from the crowds of Penang and Kuala Lumpur, particularly with the DE Rantau pass available. It suits English speakers, since Sarawak is comfortably anglophone. Beauty, a beach and a nightlife scene are three things an oil town on the Sarawak coast has never had any reason to develop, and none of them has arrived since. Bario in the Kelabit Highlands can be reached only by small aircraft or by a very long logging road, which leaves it among the last truly remote inhabited places anywhere in Borneo, and this city is where that trip begins. Anyone choosing a Sarawak base rather than a jumping-off point should look at Kuching first, a genuinely handsome city with more to do and better food again, and treat this one as the place to fly into for the caves and the highlands. A month or two attached to a specific plan is what this town is for, and families posted here through the oil sector generally report liking it a good deal more than they expected to.

aktau.costOfLiving: Budget around $750 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, with the seafront microdistricts at the top. Market produce is cheap and Kazakhstan's meat and dairy are good, though the Mangystau region is desert and most fresh vegetables arrive from elsewhere at a markup. Eating out is inexpensive, with Kazakh, Uzbek, Russian and Turkish food all easily found. Utilities are cheap. Aktau's oil and gas industry pushes some prices above the Kazakh average, particularly rents. The tenge has weakened considerably against the dollar over the past decade, which makes a foreign income go further than it once did. Fibre runs about $10 to $15 a month and a taxi across the city a couple of dollars, so the fixed costs of working here are among the lowest anywhere with this level of reliability. Every drop of fresh water in this city is desalinated from a sea that is itself salty, and for decades the plant doing it ran on a nuclear reactor on the shore, shut down at the end of the nineteen nineties. Water is therefore metered, priced and thought about here in a way it simply is not elsewhere in the country.
aktau.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable. Fibre reaches most of the city at moderate speeds and prices, and mobile data from Kcell and Beeline covers Aktau and the main roads out. Power is reliable, supported by the region's own generation. There is limited coworking, mostly aimed at the oil sector. The time zone is five hours ahead of GMT, giving a full European working overlap in the afternoon. Kazakhstan has imposed internet restrictions during periods of unrest, most notably in January 2022 when a national shutdown lasted several days, which is worth knowing rather than expecting. Coworking desks aimed at the energy sector run roughly $80 to $150 a month, which is high against local rents and reflects who they are built for. Much of the energy workforce lives on rotation, a few weeks on and a few weeks off, flying in from elsewhere in the country and going home again, which means a sizeable part of the population is always in transit. That shapes the bars, the flight schedules and the rental market in equal measure, and it is why short lets are easier to find here than in most cities of this size.
aktau.gettingAround: Aktau has an unusual navigation problem: the Soviet planners gave it no street names, only numbered microdistricts and building numbers, so addresses read as a sequence of digits and taxi drivers work from landmarks. The city is compact and the seafront promenade is walkable. Buses and cheap taxis, including informal ones flagged from the roadside, cover the rest. Aktau International Airport has flights to Almaty, Astana, Istanbul, Baku and Dubai. The Caspian ferry to Baku runs on no fixed schedule and is a well-known adventure rather than a transport option. Bozjyra and the Ustyurt plateau are three to four hours out on unsealed tracks and effectively require a hired four-wheel drive with a driver, which is the standard arrangement rather than an indulgence. Fuel costs almost nothing by any outside standard, which is what makes hiring a vehicle for the desert affordable in the first place and why distances that look punishing on a map get treated casually by residents. North along the coast the road runs out to an old fort and a line of cliffs dropping straight into the water, which makes a good half day and needs nothing special to reach.
aktau.visas: Kazakhstan is among the more open countries in the region. Citizens of most European countries, the United Kingdom, the United States and a long list of others receive thirty days visa-free on arrival, with registration handled automatically at the airport for most arrivals. There is no remote work visa, though Kazakhstan has introduced a Digital Nomad Visa for IT specialists with its own criteria. Longer stays require a work or residence permit. Anyone entering overland should confirm the registration position, since the automatic system does not always apply at land borders. The Digital Nomad Visa is aimed at IT specialists specifically rather than remote workers generally, so most people reading this page will be on the thirty-day visa-free entry instead. Arriving by sea rather than by air puts the registration question squarely in play, because the automatic system covering airport arrivals does not always reach a ferry berth, and the remedy afterwards is a visit to the migration police rather than a formality. Anyone crossing the water should photograph the entry stamp on the day it is given, before anything else happens to the passport.
aktau.bestTime: May and September to October are the best windows, warm at around twenty five degrees with the Caspian swimmable in late summer. June to August is hot, regularly above thirty five in a desert with almost no shade, and the wind off the steppe carries dust. Winter from December to February is cold and windy, hovering around freezing with the Caspian occasionally icing at the northern end. Rainfall is minimal in any month. Spring, when the desert briefly flowers, is the best time to go out to Bozjyra and the Ustyurt plateau. The Caspian is at its warmest in August and September and the city genuinely swims in it, which is not something most people expect of a desert oil town.
aktau.prosCons: Everything worth seeing is in the Mangystau region around the city: Bozjyra's chalk formations, the underground mosques at Beket-Ata and Shakpak-Ata carved into cliffs, and the Ustyurt plateau, which together make one of the strangest and least visited landscapes in Central Asia. The city has a swimmable sea, low costs and reliable services. Aktau itself is an unlovely Soviet oil city with almost no old town and little atmosphere, the desert summers are severe, the region cannot be seen without hiring something with high clearance, and English is rare once you leave the hotels. The Caspian ferry to Baku deserves its reputation: it sails when the cargo is ready rather than to a timetable, and a wait of several days at the port is normal.
aktau.whoFor: Oil, gas or shipping work, of which there is a good deal, and travellers using the city as the base for Mangystau, which is the real reason to come and increasingly known among photographers and overlanders. It suits anyone crossing the Caspian between Central Asia and the Caucasus. This is a Soviet planned city on a desert coast rather than an attractive one, Russian does most of the work and its absence has to be actively worked around, and the numbered address system with no street names strikes some people as a curiosity and others as a daily irritation. The Caspian is the largest inland body of water on earth, and it is not in good health. Its sturgeon fishery and its retreating shoreline are both subjects of serious study, and Aktau is one of the few places that work gets done from. The port is the western end of the overland Central Asia route and the only practical Kazakh crossing point, which is why overlanders and cyclists turn up here in numbers the city otherwise would not see.

matsuyama.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month, which makes Matsuyama noticeably cheaper than Tokyo or Osaka for a comparable standard of living. A one-bedroom runs roughly $400 to $700, with the areas near the castle and Dogo at the top. Groceries are reasonable and Ehime's citrus, particularly the mikan oranges, is a local point of pride. Eating out is inexpensive by Japanese standards and the local speciality, taimeshi, sea bream on rice, is worth the trip. Utilities are moderate. The yen's weakness against most currencies over recent years has made Japan considerably cheaper for foreign earners than it was. Fibre runs about $35 to $50 a month and is among the fastest anywhere. Dogo Onsen's public baths cost a few dollars for the basic entry, which makes a daily onsen a realistic habit rather than an indulgence. The larger financial consideration is administrative: Japanese rentals often demand key money, a deposit and a guarantor, which can mean several months up front, and short-term furnished apartments carry a premium precisely because they sidestep all of that.
matsuyama.whereToWork: Connectivity is excellent, as it is everywhere in Japan: fibre is ubiquitous and fast, mobile coverage is complete, and power is entirely reliable. There is a small coworking market and the city has actively courted remote workers as part of a national effort to move people out of Tokyo. The time zone is nine hours ahead of GMT, which is difficult for European clients and impossible for American ones, and that is the main practical constraint. Anyone whose income comes from Europe should expect to work evenings. Japanese banking and paperwork remain the other friction. The national relocation push is concrete rather than rhetorical: Ehime and several other prefectures have offered relocation grants and subsidised trial stays to people moving from the Tokyo area, and while those target Japanese residents, the infrastructure they funded is what a visitor benefits from. A pocket wifi router or a data SIM remains the practical answer for a stay under a year, since fixed contracts assume residency and a Japanese bank account.
matsuyama.gettingAround: Matsuyama has a tram network, including the Botchan Ressha, a working replica of the nineteenth century steam train that Natsume Soseki's novel made famous, and it runs on ordinary tram lines through the city. Bicycles work well and the city is flat. The castle is reached by ropeway or on foot up the hill. Matsuyama Airport has flights to Tokyo, Osaka and Seoul. Ferries cross the Seto Inland Sea to Hiroshima in about three hours, and the Shimanami Kaido, the cycling route across six islands to Honshu, starts about an hour north at Imabari. The Shimanami Kaido is the reason a good number of people come to this part of Japan at all: seventy kilometres across six islands on dedicated cycle paths with rental bikes returnable at either end, and it is widely rated among the best cycle routes in the world. Ferries across the Inland Sea to Hiroshima are faster than the land route around through Okayama.
