There is a real coworking scene and a substantial business services sector: Bydgoszcz has become a location for shared service centres and software work, which means the professional infrastructure is better than the city's profile suggests. The time zone is central European. Administrative processes have improved but still involve queues and paper more often than the Baltic states, which is worth knowing before comparing the two. Polish technology works differently from most of Europe and it is worth understanding before negotiating anything: the large majority of developers here contract through their own registered business rather than take employment, which shifts tax, holiday and notice onto the individual and produces headline rates that look higher than they are. A preferential rate on income from intellectual property exists for qualifying software work and is a substantial saving for anyone eligible. Rates for this city sit below Warsaw and Krakow, which is precisely why the service centres came.
bydgoszcz.gettingAround: Bydgoszcz is flat and has an extensive tram network, which makes getting around cheap and simple, with buses filling the gaps. The centre is walkable and the Brda river and the canal system run through it, with a genuine island in the middle of the city. Bicycles work well. Bydgoszcz Ignacy Jan Paderewski Airport has limited service, so Gdansk two hours north or Warsaw three hours southeast are the practical air connections. The railway station is well connected, and Torun, a UNESCO-listed medieval town, is forty five minutes away. Anyone using the airport should check the schedule carefully, since the routes served have changed repeatedly and Gdansk is often the more practical option despite the distance. The water tram runs along the Brda through the middle of the city in the warmer months and is public transport rather than a tourist boat, which is a pleasant oddity. Trains to Warsaw take under three hours on a line that has been steadily upgraded. Cycling is genuinely easy on flat ground with a decent network, and the towpaths along the canal run for miles out of the city towards the Vistula.
bydgoszcz.visas: Poland is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here without a permit, registering for residence after three months. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a temporary residence and work permit for longer ones, and Poland's system is notoriously slow, with waits of many months in some voivodeships. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa. Poland does offer a Business Harbour programme for IT specialists from certain countries, which has been the practical route for many. The residence card process is the part that tests patience, and the mechanism that saves people is the stamp: submitting a complete application before your current permission expires legalises your stay while it is considered, however long that takes, though it does not let you leave and return. Plan travel around that. A PESEL number is the other thing to obtain early, since it is the identifier that health care, banking and the tax office all run on and almost nothing proceeds without it.
bydgoszcz.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable window, with July around twenty four degrees and the riverside and the island at their best. Spring and autumn are pleasant and short. Winter from December to February is cold, often around freezing or below, with grey skies for weeks and the air quality problem that affects much of Poland: coal heating in the surrounding region pushes winter particulates well above guidance. The Bydgoszcz Music Festival and the Camerimage cinematography festival, which is internationally significant, both fall outside the summer. Anyone here in November should look at the Camerimage schedule, since the festival brings cinematographers and directors from across the world and fills the city's hotels. Late summer into October is when Poland is at its best and the forests around the city fill with people collecting mushrooms, which is a national preoccupation with its own etiquette and its own poisonings each autumn. The June light is long, with dusk after nine. Winter is the season to plan indoors around, and the city's opera and philharmonic both run full programmes through it, which is more culture than a place this size has any business supporting.
bydgoszcz.prosCons: Bydgoszcz is a genuinely handsome and much underrated Polish city at low cost: a granary-lined river, an island park in the centre, extensive Art Nouveau and eclectic architecture from its Prussian period, and the Man Crossing the River sculpture suspended above the water, which has become the city's emblem. Camerimage brings serious international attention each November. Winter air here is bad enough to matter, the flight connections are limited, the immigration system is slow for non-Europeans, and few people outside Poland have ever heard of the place at all. The city was also part of Prussia until 1920, which is why its centre looks more German than most of Poland and why the granaries and the canal exist at all. Poland's public health service charges nothing to those insured through work and is chronically overstretched, so most people with means carry a private subscription costing very little by Western standards and use it for anything routine. The city is safe by any European measure. Its quieter problem is demographic: Bydgoszcz has been losing population for two decades as people move to Warsaw or abroad, which is visible in the schools and in which parts of the centre are thriving.
bydgoszcz.whoFor: Software or business services, since there is a real employer base here, and anyone after a Polish city without the tourism of Krakow or the prices of Warsaw. It suits cinematographers and film people during Camerimage, which is among the most respected festivals in its field. It suits European Union citizens, for whom the paperwork is light. Winter smog in Polish cities is bad enough to change what somebody with asthma can do outdoors, the airport serves a handful of destinations and nothing beyond them, and a non-EU passport turns the residence paperwork into a project measured in months. Torun is forty five minutes away and worth the trip repeatedly. The medieval town came through the war intact, holds a UNESCO listing for it, and is where Copernicus was born. Among Polish cities of similar size, Wroclaw is prettier and far busier, Poznan is wealthier and better connected to Berlin, Gdansk has the coast, and this one is cheaper than all three with a decent employer base. Polish is difficult, and while younger people and the service centres speak English, a post office counter will not. It suits somebody who wants a functional, inexpensive European base and does not need the city to be a destination in itself.

aberdeen.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,600 a month, which makes Aberdeen noticeably cheaper than Edinburgh and considerably cheaper than London. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, and the market has softened as the oil industry contracted, so there is more choice than there was. Groceries are ordinary British prices. Eating out is moderate and the seafood is genuinely good. Utilities are a real cost, since the winters are long, though Scotland's housing is generally better insulated than England's. Council tax is a separate annual charge that catches people out when they compare with mainland Europe. Scottish tenancies work differently from English ones and in the tenant's favour: the private residential tenancy is open-ended with no fixed term, notice from the tenant is short, and the deposit goes into a government-approved scheme. That makes a trial stay far less risky here than in most of Europe. The market has a student rhythm, tightening through August and September around the two universities and loosening afterwards. Heating is the line that moves most, and a granite tenement with single glazing costs a great deal more to keep warm than a modern build.
aberdeen.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Aberdeen at reasonable speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. There is a real coworking scene and a substantial professional base, since the city has been the centre of the North Sea oil and gas industry for fifty years and is now trying to convert that expertise into offshore wind and hydrogen. The universities add a research layer. The time zone is GMT with British summer time, which is the most convenient position on this site for anyone splitting work between Europe and North America. The professional culture here is unusually contractor-shaped, a legacy of an industry that has always hired in project cycles, which means freelance and day-rate working is normal and understood rather than unusual. Robert Gordon University and the University of Aberdeen anchor the research side, the latter founded in 1495. The offshore wind build-out in the North Sea is where the money and the hiring have moved, and anyone with subsea, marine or project engineering experience will find this one of the few cities in Britain actively short of them.
aberdeen.gettingAround: Aberdeen is walkable in the centre along Union Street and compact enough to cover on foot or by bicycle, though the wind and the rain temper the enthusiasm. Buses cover the city and First Aberdeen runs a decent network. Aberdeen Airport has flights across the United Kingdom, to several European cities and, unusually, a great many helicopter movements to the offshore platforms. Trains run to Edinburgh in about two and a half hours and to London in seven. The ferry to Orkney and Shetland leaves from the harbour. Anyone driving north should know that the coast road towards Peterhead and Fraserburgh passes some of the best cliff scenery in Scotland and takes about an hour. The bypass, opened in 2019, changed driving in and around the city considerably and is the reason the coast and Deeside are as quick to reach as they now are. There is no tram or metro and none is planned, so buses and the park-and-ride sites do the work. Cycling infrastructure is improving but patchy, and the wind is a more serious deterrent than any of the hills.
aberdeen.visas: The United Kingdom requires most non-visa nationals to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival, which has been phased in and now covers most visitors, and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. Visitors may not work for a United Kingdom employer, though remote work for an overseas employer during a visit is permitted within limits. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays require a sponsored work visa, the Global Talent route, or one of the other categories, and the salary thresholds have risen substantially since 2024. Anyone working remotely for an overseas employer while visiting should read the current visitor rules carefully, since the permitted activities are defined narrowly and have changed recently. Nothing here is specific to Scotland: immigration is reserved to the United Kingdom government, so a Scottish job or a Scottish university confers no separate route, whatever the political argument about that. The graduate route lets students stay and work for a period after finishing, which is how a good many people first arrive in this city, and the immigration health surcharge is payable up front for the whole length of the visa, which is a substantial sum to find at the application stage.
aberdeen.bestTime: May to September is the best window, with July around eighteen degrees and long days: Aberdeen sits far enough north that midsummer light lasts past ten at night. April and October are cool and changeable. Winter from November to March is dark, wet and windy, with sunrise after eight and sunset before four in December, and the North Sea weather makes it feel rawer than the temperature suggests. Snow falls but rarely settles long in the city. The beach is beautiful and cold in every month. Anyone visiting in summer should also consider the dolphins at Torry Battery, where the Moray Firth population is regularly visible from the headland above the harbour mouth. The haar, a cold sea fog, can sit on the city for days in late spring and early summer while the countryside a few miles inland is in sunshine, which is a particular Aberdeen disappointment. And the northern latitude occasionally works in winter's favour: the aurora is visible from this coast on strong nights, and the dark months that make the city feel long are exactly when it appears. Spectra, the winter light festival in February, exists for that reason.
aberdeen.prosCons: Aberdeen is built almost entirely from local granite, which gives it an architectural coherence found nowhere else in Britain and which genuinely sparkles in sunlight, and it comes with a long beach, Royal Deeside and the Cairngorms an hour west, and a professional job market that few cities this size can match. Costs are well below the rest of urban Britain. The weather is grey and windy for much of the year, and the economy is still working out what comes after oil, a question the city has been asking for a decade. Union Street, the granite mile that is the city's signature, has struggled badly with retail vacancy as the oil contraction and online shopping arrived together, and the regeneration is under way but visibly unfinished. In its favour, the city is safe, the beach is a genuine two-mile stretch of sand a short walk from the centre, and the food has improved sharply of late as money that came for oil stayed for other reasons. Aberdeen also feels further from London than it is, which cuts both ways.
aberdeen.whoFor: Energy professionals, engineers and researchers, since the transition from oil to offshore wind is happening here and the expertise is concentrated. It suits hillwalkers and skiers, given the Cairngorms. It suits anyone working across Europe and North America, since the time zone serves both. Sunshine and mild winters are not what the north-east of Scotland offers, the international community is oil-sector rather than general, and anybody arriving from outside the United Kingdom without a sponsored job will find the visa routes narrow and the fees substantial. Aberdeenshire holds more castles per square mile than anywhere else in Britain, and several of them stay open right through the year, not only for the handful of summer months. Anyone choosing a Scottish city should know the trade plainly: Edinburgh is prettier and far more expensive, Glasgow is larger and has the culture, Dundee is cheaper again, and Aberdeen has the salaries, the mountains and the worst weather of the four. The schools are good and nobody commutes far, which matters a great deal more with children than without. Liking a northern winter is a genuine preference and not a pose, and it turns out to be the single best predictor of who ends up staying rather than leaving after one year.

inverness.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,550 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, and the market is tight because the Highlands have a genuine housing shortage made worse by short-term lets. Groceries cost a little more than the Scottish average, since everything comes up the A9. Eating out is moderate, with good local seafood, beef and game. Utilities are a serious cost given the winters, and rural Highland properties are often on oil or electric heating rather than gas, which is more expensive again. Council tax applies on top of rent. Delivery surcharges are a constant small irritation, since a great many retailers treat the Highlands as a separate shipping zone and either charge extra or decline to send at all, which is worth checking before ordering anything bulky. Rural fuel poverty is a policy problem here rather than a phrase, because off-gas properties heated by oil or electricity cost far more to warm than the mainland average. Short-term let licensing, brought in by the council, has begun returning some property to the long-term market after years of movement the other way.
inverness.whereToWork: Connectivity is better than the Highlands' reputation suggests. Fibre reaches most of Inverness at good speeds and the Scottish Government's rural broadband programmes have extended coverage, though it thins quickly once you leave the city. Mobile coverage in Inverness is comprehensive and becomes patchy in the glens. Power is reliable, with occasional weather-related outages. There is a small coworking scene and a growing remote worker presence, since the Highlands have actively marketed themselves to people leaving cities. The time zone is GMT with British summer time. Anyone planning to work from a rural cottage should test the connection before committing, since coverage in the glens varies enormously and satellite is sometimes the only answer. The economy is narrower than a regional capital's usually is: healthcare, public administration, tourism, and the energy work around the Cromarty Firth, where the yards service offshore wind and the freeport designation is meant to build on it. The University of the Highlands and Islands is spread across campuses rather than concentrated here, a different shape from a normal university town. For a remote worker that thinness is no obstacle, though it does mean the professional network is small and almost entirely local.
inverness.gettingAround: Inverness is small and walkable, laid out along the River Ness with the castle above it, and covering the town on foot takes twenty minutes. Buses cover the city and the region, with Stagecoach running the Highland network. A car is close to essential for anything beyond the town, since the glens and the coast are where the interest is. Inverness Airport has flights to London, Amsterdam and several United Kingdom cities. The railway runs south to Edinburgh in three and a half hours and the Kyle line west to Skye is among the great scenic routes. The sleeper train from London arrives in the morning and is the civilised way in, running six nights a week. Driving north or west means single-track roads with passing places, and the etiquette around them, pulling in, waiting, acknowledging, is expected rather than optional. The A9 south has a long-running dualling programme still unfinished and average-speed cameras along its length. Winter tyres are not required by law, but the passes close in snow and the ferries to the isles cancel in wind, so a Highland itinerary needs slack in it.
inverness.visas: The United Kingdom requires most non-visa nationals to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival, and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. Visitors may not work for a United Kingdom employer, though remote work for an overseas employer during a visit is permitted within limits. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays run through sponsored work visas, the Global Talent route or family categories. Scotland has argued for a distinct migration route to address rural depopulation, and it does not currently exist. Anyone working remotely for an overseas employer while visiting should read the current visitor rules carefully, since what is permitted is defined narrowly and has changed recently. The route that most often fits someone wanting a Highland year is the Youth Mobility Scheme, open to citizens of certain countries aged under thirty or thirty-five according to the agreement, allocated in part by ballot, and carrying an unrestricted right to work for two years. The seasonal worker route covers agriculture and, more recently, some hospitality, which is what staffs a good deal of the Highland summer. Irish citizens sit inside the Common Travel Area and need none of this at all.
inverness.bestTime: May to September is the season, with July around seventeen degrees, long days and the Highlands at their most accessible. Late May and early June are ideal: the days are long, the hills are green and the midges have not yet reached full strength, which they do from late June through August and which is a genuine consideration rather than a joke. September and October give autumn colour and clear air. Winter from November to March is dark and wet, with the northern lights occasionally visible on clear nights. Anyone walking between June and August should carry midge repellent and consider a head net, which locals use without embarrassment and which visitors usually buy on day two. Daylight swings hard at this latitude, from close to eighteen hours in June to under seven in December, and that does more to shape a winter here than the temperature does. Highland games run through the summer in towns across the region and are genuine community events rather than displays laid on for coaches. Aurora sightings are likeliest between September and March on clear nights away from the town's lights, and this is among the better parts of Britain for them.
inverness.prosCons: Inverness is the only real town in the Highlands and the way in to some of the best landscape in Europe: Loch Ness at the door, the Cairngorms an hour south, Skye and the west coast two hours away, and the North Coast 500 route starting from the town itself. It is safe, English-speaking and small enough to know quickly. The housing shortage, the weather and the midges all count against it, and the town is genuinely quiet, with a limited job market outside tourism, healthcare and public services of one kind or another. What the landscape hides is distance. Raigmore is the region's only major hospital, so an emergency from a remote glen can mean a long ambulance journey or a helicopter, and rural GP provision has thinned in places. The housing shortage carries a social edge as well, since holiday lets and second homes price out the people who staff the schools and the care homes, and that argument is live in every Highland community rather than confined to the council chamber. Gaelic is visible on the road signs and audible in the western isles, far less so in the town itself.
inverness.whoFor: Hillwalkers, climbers, cyclists and anyone whose priority is being close to the Highlands rather than being in a city. It suits people who already work remotely and want a British base with landscape at the door, and the Highlands actively want incomers. It suits whisky people, since Speyside is an hour east. City amenities are not what a Highland town of sixty thousand provides, local work is scarce enough that arriving without a job already arranged is a poor plan, and the winter here is wet and dark for long enough to affect people who did not expect it to. Culloden is four miles east of the city. The 1746 battle fought there ended the Jacobite rising for good, and the visitor centre built beside the field is among the better ones anywhere in Britain. Anyone choosing a Highland base should weigh Aviemore for skiing with the Cairngorms at the door, Fort William for the west coast and the climbing, and this town for being the one place with a hospital, an airport and a supermarket that stays open. The schools are good and a family settles in quickly. A move is worth trialling in the dark half of the year rather than the light one, because the summer recruits people the winter then has to keep.

dundee.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,400 a month, which makes Dundee one of the cheaper cities in the United Kingdom. A one-bedroom runs roughly $600 to $950, kept moderate by a very large student population across two universities. Groceries are ordinary British prices. Eating out is inexpensive by British standards and the city has more good independent places than it once did. Utilities run through a cold winter. Council tax applies separately. Dundee has among the lowest average incomes of any Scottish city, which is reflected in the cost of living and in other things too. Council tax should be priced before signing anything, because Scottish bands are set by council and this city's rates sit at the higher end while its property values sit at the lower, so the bill takes a larger share of the monthly cost than the rent alone suggests. Water and sewerage are collected with it rather than billed separately as in England. Students are exempt entirely, which is part of why so much of the private rental stock is aimed at them and why September is the wrong month to be looking for a flat.
dundee.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of the city at reasonable speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with reliable power. There is a genuine coworking and creative scene, driven by the universities and by a video games industry that has been here since the 1980s: Grand Theft Auto and Lemmings both came out of Dundee, and the sector still employs a substantial number of people. The time zone is GMT with British summer time, which serves both Europe and North America better than almost anywhere else on this site. Anyone in the games industry should know that Abertay University runs the oldest computer games degree in the world, which is why the sector settled here in the first place. The other pillar is life sciences. The University of Dundee's school is among the most cited in the world for its size and its drug discovery unit works with the pharmaceutical industry directly, which means the professional layer here runs to games and biology rather than the finance and energy that dominate other Scottish cities. Neither sector recruits casually, but both hold conferences and talks a newcomer can walk into.
dundee.gettingAround: Dundee is compact and walkable, with the waterfront redevelopment putting the V&A, the station and the Discovery within a few minutes of each other. Buses cover the city cheaply and cycling works, though the Law and the hills behind the centre are steep. Dundee railway station is on the east coast line, with Edinburgh about seventy minutes away and London around six hours. Dundee Airport has a limited service to London. The Tay road and rail bridges cross to Fife, and St Andrews is half an hour away. Anyone heading for the hills should note that Glen Clova and the Angus glens are within an hour, and that they are far quieter than the Cairngorms proper. The stumps of the first Tay rail bridge still stand in the water beside the current one. It collapsed in a gale on the twenty eighth of December 1879 with a train crossing it, killing everyone aboard, and the piers were left in place when the replacement went up alongside. Crossing by train means passing them, which is a quietly unnerving thing to notice from a window.
dundee.visas: The United Kingdom requires most non-visa nationals to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival, and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. Visitors may not work for a United Kingdom employer, though remote work for an overseas employer during a visit is permitted within limits. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays run through sponsored work visas or the Graduate route, which is relevant here given the universities and lets international graduates stay and work for two years after finishing. Anyone working remotely for an overseas employer while visiting should read the current visitor rules carefully, since the permitted activities are narrow and were tightened recently. Scotland runs its own student funding and its own graduate policy, but immigration is reserved to Westminster, so nothing about being in Scotland changes a visa position. What does change is the local sponsorship landscape: the two universities and the games studios are the employers here holding sponsor licences, and outside them a job offer in this city that can carry a visa is rare. That narrows the realistic routes to the Graduate route after study, or arriving with an income that needs no British employer at all.
dundee.bestTime: May to September is the best window, with July around eighteen degrees and Dundee benefiting from being on the drier east coast, which gets noticeably more sunshine than Glasgow. April and October are cool and changeable. Winter from November to March is dark and cold rather than snowy, with short days and a good deal of grey. The city's position on the Tay estuary means haar, the cold sea fog, rolls in on some summer days and drops the temperature abruptly, which is a local speciality. Anyone visiting in July should look at the Dundee Flower and Food Festival, and anyone here in September at Discovery Film Festival, both of which fill the waterfront. Latitude shapes a working year here more than temperature does: midsummer daylight runs past eleven at night, and a midwinter afternoon is finished before four. The two football grounds stand two hundred metres apart on the same street, closer than any other pair in the country, so a Saturday with both at home changes the whole city rather than one end of it.
dundee.prosCons: Dundee has genuinely reinvented itself over the last decade: the V&A Dundee, designed by Kengo Kuma and opened in 2018, anchored a waterfront rebuild, and the UNESCO City of Design designation reflects a design and games sector that actually exists rather than a marketing exercise. Costs are low, the universities keep it young, and the east coast light is good. The city still has severe deprivation in parts, a drug death rate that has been among the worst in Europe, and a job market outside the universities and games that is thin enough to be the reason many people leave. The old summary of this place was jute, jam and journalism, and one of the three is still here. DC Thomson has published from Dundee since the nineteenth century and still does, which is why The Beano and Oor Wullie are local products and why a bronze Desperate Dan stands on the High Street. The jute went back to Bengal and took the mills with it, leaving the largest of them as a museum, and the jam rests on a founding story about Seville oranges off a wrecked ship that is probably too neat to be true. Three industries, one survivor, and a waterfront built on the bet that design would be the fourth.
dundee.whoFor: Designers, game developers and academics, since those are the three sectors with real depth here. It suits students and graduates, given the universities and the Graduate route. A low-cost British base with good rail connections and the whole east coast close by is what this amounts to. The regeneration here is genuine and it is also unfinished, reaching the waterfront and a few streets behind it rather than the whole city. General professional work is also scarce: without a remote income or a fit with games, design or life sciences there is not much to walk into. Polar history has a physical anchor here. Captain Scott's ship the Discovery was built in Dundee and now sits at the waterfront beside the V&A, which is a stranger pairing than it sounds. It suits a designer who wants to be near the making rather than the market, since the V&A, the games studios and Duncan of Jordanstone put a great deal of practice inside a small radius. It suits somebody willing to live in a city that is honest about its problems rather than one that hides them, because Dundee discusses its drug deaths and its deprivation openly and a newcomer will hear about both within a week.

derry.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,350 a month, which makes Derry among the cheapest cities in the United Kingdom and Ireland. A one-bedroom runs roughly $550 to $850, well below Belfast and a fraction of Dublin two hours south. Groceries are ordinary British prices, and the border means many people shop on whichever side the exchange rate favours that month. Eating out is inexpensive. Utilities run through a wet rather than a cold winter. Rates, Northern Ireland's version of council tax, apply separately. The cost gap with the Republic across the border is a genuine and much-discussed local feature. Home heating oil rather than gas is what most houses here run on, which is unusual for this part of the world and means buying a tankful at a time at whatever the price happens to be that week rather than paying a smooth monthly bill. A tank lasts a few months through winter and the price moves with the oil market. Landlords sometimes include the rates in the rent and sometimes do not, and the difference runs to several hundred over a year, so the question belongs in the first conversation rather than the last.
derry.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Derry at reasonable speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with reliable power. There is a small coworking scene and a growing technology and business services presence, helped by Ulster University's Magee campus and by the city's push to attract investment. The time zone is GMT with British summer time, which serves Europe and North America equally well. One practical oddity: mobile phones near the border regularly roam onto Irish networks and back, which can produce unexpected charges if the plan does not cover it. The expansion of the university campus here has been argued over for decades and is the issue most likely to come up in any conversation about the city's economy, because the shortfall in student places is understood locally as the reason graduates leave. Financial services and contact centre operations are the largest private employers, drawn by costs well below the regional capital. Anyone working for a firm on the far side of the border should take advice on which tax system applies, since living on one side and working on the other has consequences that are not obvious.
derry.gettingAround: Derry is compact and the walled city is best covered on foot, with the mile-long circuit of the seventeenth century walls itself the obvious walk. Buses cover the city and Translink runs the regional network. The Peace Bridge and the Craigavon Bridge cross the Foyle. The railway to Belfast takes about two hours and is among the most scenic lines in Ireland, running along the coast at Castlerock and Downhill. City of Derry Airport has limited service. Donegal, in the Republic, begins about ten minutes away by road. Anyone crossing into Donegal should note that the Republic uses the euro and kilometres while the North uses sterling and miles, and the change happens without any sign to mark it. A ferry crosses the mouth of the lough in the summer months and turns a long drive around into a fifteen minute crossing, which is how most people reach the beaches on the far peninsula. Coaches run direct to Dublin airport several times a day and are how most people leave the island. The walls have seven gates, and directions here are given by them rather than by street name.
derry.visas: Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom, so United Kingdom rules apply: most non-visa nationals need an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. There is no digital nomad visa. The Common Travel Area means no routine passport control on the land border with the Republic of Ireland, but the immigration rules of each jurisdiction still apply, and crossing does not extend or reset either. Anyone planning to move between the two regularly should understand that distinction properly. Anyone driving across the border regularly should also check that their vehicle insurance covers both jurisdictions, since it does not always and the crossing is unmarked.
derry.bestTime: May to September is the best window, with July around eighteen degrees and long evenings. Derry is on the wet side of Ireland and rain is a constant possibility in every month, so the difference between the seasons is daylight rather than dryness. Winter from November to February is dark and damp rather than freezing. The Halloween festival at the end of October is the city's great event, among the largest in Europe, and fills every bed in the city and a good part of Donegal. Anyone coming for Halloween should book accommodation many months ahead, since the festival draws tens of thousands and the city has nowhere near enough beds for them. The other fixture is the maritime festival on the quays, held when the round-the-world race fleet calls in, which takes over the waterfront for a week. Daylight in June runs past ten in the evening at this latitude, which is the compensation for a December afternoon finished by four. Snow is rare enough that the few occasions it arrives are remembered by the year.
derry.prosCons: Derry is the last completely walled city built in Europe, with the seventeenth century circuit intact and walkable, and its recent history is presented with unusual honesty: the Bogside murals, the Museum of Free Derry and the Bloody Sunday memorial all stand within a few minutes' walk of the walls. Costs are low and Donegal's coast is on the doorstep. The city still carries real division, visible in flags, murals and the interfaces between neighbourhoods, along with high unemployment and flight connections that amount to very little at all. The name itself is contested, with Derry and Londonderry both in official use, and which one a person says is often read as a statement about something else entirely.
derry.whoFor: Anyone interested in the Troubles and their aftermath, which this city addresses more directly than anywhere else in Northern Ireland. It suits walkers and surfers, given Donegal and the Causeway coast. A very low-cost British base that still has a genuine sense of place is a narrow category, and this town belongs squarely in it. Political identity is visible on the streets here in murals, flags and kerbstones, and somebody who would rather not live alongside that should say so to themselves early. Getting out by air means Belfast or Dublin, and both are a drive of substance rather than a quick hop to a terminal. Irish traditional music is played properly here. The pubs around Waterloo Street host sessions most nights of the week, and the standard is high without any of it being staged for an audience. A year is long enough to see the city through both its winter and its festival, and both matter to the decision. Anyone coming for the university or the services sector should line the work up first, because the private job market here is narrower than the population would suggest.

kilkenny.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,650 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $800 to $1,200, and Ireland's housing shortage is the defining economic fact here as everywhere in the country, with supply tight and rents having risen sharply over the past decade. Groceries are expensive by European standards. Eating out is expensive, though Kilkenny has an unusually good restaurant scene for a town of its size. Utilities are moderate and heating runs through a mild damp winter. Local property charges apply to owners rather than renters, unlike the British system. Anyone comparing with Dublin should note that rents here run well under half the capital's, which is the main reason people have moved out along the railway line. Deposits are capped at one month and tenancies must be registered with the state board, which gives a tenant somewhere to go when a deposit is not returned. Many houses outside the town run on heating oil or solid fuel rather than gas, so heating means buying a delivery rather than paying a bill. Electricity here is among the dearer in Europe, and an old house with poor insulation turns that into a serious winter number.
kilkenny.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Kilkenny at reasonable speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with reliable power. Ireland's National Broadband Plan has extended fibre well into rural areas around the town. There is coworking, and the government has funded a network of remote working hubs across the country as a deliberate policy of moving jobs out of Dublin, several of which are within reach. The time zone is GMT with Irish standard time, which serves Europe in the afternoon and North America comfortably in the evening. Anyone considering one of the state-funded remote working hubs should look at the Connected Hubs network, which lists them nationally and is genuinely well organised. Employees working from home can claim relief on a share of heat, electricity and broadband, set out in the tax code rather than left to an employer's goodwill. The hubs the state funded came with a national booking system, so a desk in one town works exactly like a desk in another. The practical limit here is that the professional community is small enough that everyone in it already knows everyone else.
kilkenny.gettingAround: Kilkenny is small and entirely walkable, with the castle at one end of the Medieval Mile and St Canice's Cathedral at the other, and the whole route takes twenty minutes. Buses cover the town and the region. The railway runs to Dublin in about ninety minutes and to Waterford in forty. Dublin Airport is roughly two hours by road or by direct bus. A car helps for reaching the countryside, and the Nore valley, Jerpoint Abbey and the Wicklow mountains are all within reach. Anyone walking the Medieval Mile should pick up the trail map, since the route links the castle, the cathedral and a dozen buildings that are easy to walk past unnoticed.
kilkenny.visas: Ireland is a member of the European Union but not of the Schengen area, so it operates its own visa system: European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, and most Western nationalities enter visa-free for ninety days. Ireland is not in Schengen, so time here does not count against a Schengen allowance, which is a genuinely useful feature for anyone managing that limit. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays require an employment permit or one of the other immigration categories. Anyone using Ireland to pause a Schengen clock should keep the entry and exit evidence, since proving where you were is your responsibility rather than the border's. The travel area shared with Britain means an Irish stamp and a British one are separate things that happen to permit the same crossing, and the rules of each apply independently once you are inside. A PPS number is the identifier for tax, banking and health services, issued on proof of an address and a reason to need one. Anyone arriving to look for work rather than with it already arranged should check which stamp category permits that, since several do not.
kilkenny.bestTime: May to September is the season, with July around nineteen degrees and long evenings. Ireland's weather is unreliable in every month, so the difference is daylight and probability rather than certainty. The Cat Laughs comedy festival in June and the Kilkenny Arts Festival in August are the two events that fill the town and are both genuinely good. Winter from November to February is mild, wet and dark, rarely freezing but persistently grey. Spring comes early and the countryside is green in every month, which is the compensation. Anyone visiting during the arts festival in August should book early, since the town's accommodation fills and prices in that week bear no relation to the rest of the year. Hurling fills the summer here in a way that is difficult to convey to anyone who has not seen a championship crowd: the county colours go up in June and stay up until the team is beaten. The rivers run high after winter rain and the Nore path floods in places most years. Frost is rare enough that gardens keep something green through every month.
kilkenny.prosCons: Kilkenny is a medieval city that survived: black limestone buildings, a castle held by the Butler family for six centuries, a thirteenth century cathedral with a round tower you can still climb, and slipways and lanes that follow the lines they were first laid out on. It has a genuine arts and craft scene and better food and pubs than a town of twenty seven thousand should support. Irish costs apply in full, the housing market is under real strain, and the range of almost anything here is what a small town can carry. Alice Kyteler was tried here for witchcraft in 1324, the first such case recorded in the country, and escaped while her servant was burned in her place, which is the sort of local history the town tells without embarrassment. The black limestone that gives the buildings their colour was quarried a few miles away and polishes to something close to marble, which is why it was shipped as far as it was.
kilkenny.whoFor: An Irish base outside Dublin with real character and good rail links, particularly for people working remotely for European or American employers. It suits craftspeople, since the Kilkenny design tradition is genuine and the workshops are working ones. It suits anyone who takes pubs seriously. Irish prices and a tight budget are simply incompatible, this is a medieval town rather than a city, and turning up with nowhere booked is the specific error to avoid here: the Irish rental market is difficult in a way that genuinely surprises people arriving from elsewhere in Europe. It also suits hurling supporters, since Kilkenny is the most successful county in the sport's history and Nowlan Park on a championship day is a genuine spectacle.

ostend.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,550 a month, which is moderate for Belgium and cheaper than Brussels or Ghent. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, with the seafront apartments at the top and the streets behind the station considerably cheaper. Groceries are ordinary Belgian prices. Eating out is where Ostend spends: the seafood, particularly the grey shrimp and the sole, is genuinely good and priced accordingly. Utilities are moderate. Belgium's tax and social contributions are among the highest in Europe, which matters for anyone employed here rather than remotely. Anyone comparing with the rest of the coast should note that Knokke to the northeast is considerably more expensive and De Panne to the southwest a little cheaper. Rent is indexed once a year to an official price measure rather than negotiated, so the increase is a calculation instead of a conversation, and for a badly insulated home that indexation is capped or blocked outright by the energy label on the building. The deposit goes into a blocked account that the tenant owns, and it is released only on both signatures or a judgment. The lease itself has to be registered by the landlord with the tax office, and an unregistered one leaves the tenant with more rights rather than fewer.
ostend.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Belgium has extensive fibre and cable, with comprehensive mobile coverage and reliable power, and Ostend is well served. There is a small coworking presence. The time zone is central European. The genuine practical advantage here is position: Ostend is an hour from Bruges and Ghent, ninety minutes from Brussels, and within reach of Lille, and the train network makes all of it straightforward without a car. Anyone working across Europe will find the connections better than the town's size suggests. Anyone registering with the commune should allow several weeks and bring more documents than the list requires, since Belgian administration is thorough rather than quick. Administration here runs in Dutch and only in Dutch, which surprises people who assume the country works in French as well, since the region sets the language of its own services and this one does not translate. The port has become the maintenance base for the offshore wind farms out in the North Sea, and the crew transfer vessels leaving at dawn are the visible end of a technical sector that barely existed fifteen years ago. That is where the engineering jobs are, and it is seasonal only in the sense that winter weather stops the boats.
ostend.gettingAround: The Kusttram, the coastal tram, runs the entire sixty seven kilometres of the Belgian coast from De Panne to Knokke and passes through Ostend, which makes it the longest tram line in the world and the practical way to move along the coast. The town itself is flat, compact and made for bicycles. Trains to Brussels take about ninety minutes and to Bruges fifteen. Ostend-Bruges Airport has limited service. The port handles ferries and freight, and the beach runs the length of the seafront. The passenger ferry to England stopped running in 2013, so a Channel crossing now means driving to Dunkirk or Calais, or taking the Eurostar out of Brussels, neither of which is the short hop the harbour still looks like it should offer.
ostend.visas: Belgium is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here without a permit, registering with the commune within days of arriving, which is a genuine requirement rather than a formality. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones. There is no digital nomad visa. Belgian administration is famously layered, with federal, regional and communal responsibilities, and the commune is where most practical business is done. Anyone staying beyond three months should start the commune registration immediately on arrival, since the residence process runs from that date rather than from any later application. A neighbourhood officer calls at the address to confirm somebody actually lives there before the registration completes, and until that visit happens nothing else can move, so being out when they call sets the whole process back. The identity card issued afterwards carries a chip that signs tax returns and official forms, and it is genuinely used rather than ceremonial. Anybody moving between municipalities has to deregister and register again, because the record lives locally rather than nationally.
ostend.bestTime: June to September is the season, with July around twenty degrees and the beach and the tram both busy. Belgian coastal summers are unreliable and the sea is cold in every month, which locals accept and visitors find surprising. April, May and October are quiet and often pleasant. Winter from November to March is grey, wet and windy, with the seafront blasted by North Sea weather, though the town does not empty entirely the way smaller resorts do. The light in winter is what drew the painters here. The Theater Aan Zee festival at the end of July fills the town with performance for ten days and is the cultural high point of the year here. The coast runs on weekends as much as on seasons: the trains out of the interior fill on a Saturday morning in any month with sun, and the same town can be crowded on the Sunday and empty on the Tuesday. Beach huts go up in the spring and come down in the autumn, and those dates are a better guide to the local calendar than the weather is. Storms in the cold months shift enough sand that the town rebuilds its dunes with fences every year.
ostend.prosCons: Ostend is a seaside town with a real year-round population, excellent rail connections to the rest of Belgium and beyond, genuinely good food, and an artistic legacy more substantial than the beach suggests: James Ensor lived and worked here and his house is open, and the Mu.ZEE collection is worth an afternoon. The coastal tram is a genuine pleasure. The weather and the wind work against it, so does a certain postwar architectural bleakness along the front, and the prices are Belgian rather than cheap in any sense. Ostend was also Leopold II's favourite resort and much of the grand seafront architecture dates from that period, which the town's museums address rather than avoid.
ostend.whoFor: A beach, fast trains and no need for a car, inside the European Union, which suits people working across several European time zones. It suits cyclists, since the coast and the Flemish interior are both flat and comprehensively provided for. It suits anyone who takes seafood or Belgian beer seriously. The North Sea does not do Mediterranean weather in any month. Anybody wanting a picturesque old town should note that Bruges is fifteen minutes away and this is emphatically not Bruges, and Belgian prices leave little room for a tight budget. James Ensor's house on the seafront is preserved as he left it, and his masks and skeletons are still among the strangest things anybody in Belgium has ever put on a canvas.

vigo.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,150 a month, which makes Vigo cheaper than Madrid or Barcelona and comparable with the rest of Galicia. A one-bedroom runs roughly $500 to $800, with the areas near the marina and Samil beach at the top. Market produce is very good and cheap, and the Mercado da Pedra sells the seafood that Vigo lands in enormous quantities. Eating out is inexpensive and the standard is high: this is one of the best places in Spain to eat, and the prices do not reflect that. Utilities are moderate and heating runs through a wet mild winter. The menu del dia is the mechanism that makes eating out this cheap: a set lunch of several courses with a drink, served in most places on weekdays, and it is still the best value meal in Spain. Damp rather than cold is what costs money in a Galician winter, since a flat that is not heated regularly will show it on the walls, so budget for running heating even on mild days. Contracts usually run for a year with one or two months' deposit, and because Vigo is a working city rather than a tourist one, prices hold steady through the summer instead of spiking.
vigo.whereToWork: Connectivity is very good. Spain has extensive fibre at high speeds and low prices, mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. There is a real coworking scene in Vigo, helped by the university and by an automotive and technology sector that is substantial: the Stellantis plant here is one of the largest car factories in Europe. The time zone is central European, which is an hour ahead of solar time in Galicia and shapes the very late Spanish day. Spain's digital nomad visa applies here as elsewhere. Anyone working from Galicia should also expect the local rhythm, since lunch runs from two until four and the working day finishes correspondingly late. The other half of the local economy is the sea, and not only fishing: Vigo builds and repairs ships, freezes and processes catch for export, and the university's marine science work follows from that. It gives the city a technical professional base with nothing to do with tourism. Galician is used comfortably alongside Spanish in offices and meetings, and while nobody expects it of an outsider, understanding a little of it goes further here than a lot of English does.
vigo.gettingAround: Vigo is built up a steep hillside above its ria, so walking is hard work in one direction and easy in the other, and the city has installed a series of public escalators and lifts to deal with it. Buses cover the city cheaply. The Ave high speed line reaches Madrid in about four hours and Porto is two hours south by road. Vigo Airport has domestic and limited European flights. The ferries to the Cies Islands, which are the reason many people come, leave from the port in summer. The most useful connection is southward. Porto's airport is a straightforward drive or bus ride away and offers far more international routes than Vigo's own, so a great many residents fly from Portugal by default, and a cross-border train runs down as well. Locally, passenger ferries cross the ria to Cangas and Moana in about twenty minutes, which turns the far shore into a commutable place to live and a very easy afternoon out. Cycling is for the determined given the gradient, though the seafront out to Samil is flat and pleasant.
vigo.visas: Spain is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, registering for an NIE number and on the padron once resident. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones. Spain operates a digital nomad visa under its 2023 startups law, valid for up to a year initially and renewable to five, with an income threshold and a favourable tax regime for qualifying applicants, and it has become one of the most used schemes in Europe. The practical bottleneck is not eligibility but appointments. Booking a slot at a Spanish consulate, or at the relevant office for the in-country route, can take longer than the application itself is meant to, and this is the stage where most timelines slip. Family members can be included on the same application, which is one of the scheme's more useful features and is often missed. The favourable tax treatment has to be requested rather than granted automatically, and it is worth proper advice given how much turns on it.
vigo.bestTime: June to September is the season, with July around twenty four degrees and the Cies Islands accessible, though the ferry requires a permit that is capped daily and books out. Galicia is the wet corner of Spain and rain is a genuine feature: Vigo gets more than most Spanish cities and the winter is grey and damp rather than cold. May and October are pleasant and quiet. The Festa da Reconquista in March, when the city dresses in period costume to commemorate expelling Napoleon's troops, is the local event. Anyone hoping to reach the Cies should apply for the permit online well in advance, since the daily visitor number is capped and the summer allocation goes quickly. Galicians distinguish between rain and orvallo, the fine drizzle that hangs in the air for days without ever quite falling, and it is the orvallo rather than the downpours that defines a winter here. There is a compensation the summer visitors miss entirely: shellfish is at its best in the cold months, and the Christmas season in particular is when the percebes and the scallops are worth the trip on their own.
vigo.prosCons: Seafood and setting carry this place: Vigo is Europe's largest fishing port by value of catch, the ria is beautiful, and the Cies Islands half an hour offshore hold a beach that British newspapers once ranked the best anywhere, now protected as a national park with capped daily visitor numbers in summer. Costs are well below the Spanish cities people have heard of. The rain is persistent, the city is industrial and steep rather than pretty, and Galician is spoken as widely as Spanish in the streets around the port and the old market. Vigo is genuinely safe, including at night and including the parts that look industrial, which is not universally true of Spanish port cities. And the old town around A Pedra, small as it is, is where the oyster sellers work the street and is far better than its size suggests. The airport's route map is thin enough that most international travel starts with a journey to Porto or Santiago, which adds a couple of hours to every trip out of the city.
vigo.whoFor: Anyone who takes seafood seriously, which is the honest headline, along with sailors, walkers on the coastal Camino, and people on the Spanish nomad visa who want the Atlantic rather than the Mediterranean. It suits anyone working European hours. Coming to Spain for sunshine and arriving in Galicia is a category error, since this is the green corner and it is green for a reason. The historic centre is also small, and the city wrapped around it is a working port rather than anything charming. The coastal route of the Portuguese Camino to Santiago runs straight through Vigo, which makes the city a natural stage on the walk and not a detour off it. Anyone choosing within Galicia should know the trade. Santiago is prettier and smaller, A Coruna is more elegant, Pontevedra is the most pleasant to walk, and Vigo has the jobs, the transport and the lower rents. This is a working city and not a set piece. That is the whole of the appeal for some people, and families do well in it. It is also a sensible base for anyone who wants Portugal within easy reach without paying Lisbon or Porto prices.

evora.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,050 a month, which is moderate for Portugal and considerably cheaper than Lisbon. A one-bedroom runs roughly $450 to $750, though the university and the tourist market together keep the centre tighter than the town's size suggests. Market produce is cheap and the Alentejo produces excellent bread, cheese, olive oil and wine, most of it locally. Eating out is inexpensive and the regional cooking, heavy on pork, bread and coriander, is distinctive. Utilities are moderate, with summer cooling the main cost rather than winter heating. Anyone comparing with Lisbon should note that rents here run well under half the capital's, which is why a good number of people have moved inland since the Lisbon market tightened. Coworking desks, where the town has them, run about $90 to $140 a month, and a menu do dia at lunch is $10 to $14, which is what most people here actually eat.
evora.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Portugal has extensive fibre at reasonable speeds and prices, comprehensive mobile coverage and reliable power. There is a small coworking presence, helped by the University of Evora, which was founded in 1559 and is among the oldest in Portugal. The time zone is GMT with Western European summer time, which gives a good overlap with the rest of Europe and a workable afternoon with the eastern United States. Portugal's digital nomad visa and the broader D7 route both apply here and have brought a substantial number of people to the country. The university term shapes the town more than the tourist season does, so cafes and the rental market both loosen noticeably between June and September. The reservoir built on the river east of here is the largest artificial lake in western Europe, and it turned a dry province into irrigated farmland, which is why olive and almond plantations now run in rows to the horizon where there used to be cork oak and pasture. That is the biggest thing to have happened to this region in a century, and opinions on it locally are not settled.
evora.gettingAround: Evora inside the walls is small and entirely walkable, which is the point: the historic centre is a compact grid of whitewashed houses that has changed little since the sixteenth century. Buses cover the modern town outside the walls. The train to Lisbon takes about ninety minutes and buses are frequent. A car is needed to see the Alentejo properly, since the megalithic sites, the cork oak plantations and the hill towns are spread across an emptier landscape than most of Europe still has. Lisbon Airport is the practical air connection. Trains to Lisbon are infrequent rather than slow, running a handful of times a day, so the timetable matters more than the ninety minutes does when planning a trip. Motorway tolls here are collected electronically with no booths, so a hire car needs a transponder fitted or the charges arrive later with penalties attached, and this catches out more visitors than any other piece of Portuguese administration. Away from the motorway the plain carries so little traffic that a drive becomes a pleasure rather than a chore, which is an unusual thing to be able to say anywhere in Europe now.
evora.visas: Portugal is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, registering with the local council. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones. Portugal operates a digital nomad visa introduced in 2022, with a temporary stay version for up to a year and a residence version renewable towards permanent residence, both requiring proof of remote income above a threshold. The D7 passive income route is the other common one. Portugal ended its golden visa route for residential property in 2023, so anyone researching older guidance should be aware the investment options have narrowed considerably since. The tax regime that drew so many people to this country was closed to new entrants and replaced by a narrower one aimed at research and qualified professions, so anybody working from advice written before that is planning around something which no longer exists. A local bank account and a registered lease are both needed before an application will even be accepted, which is a circular problem most people solve with a short let first.
evora.bestTime: March to May and September to October are the best windows, warm at around twenty two degrees with the Alentejo green in spring and golden in autumn. Summer from June to August is severe: the Alentejo is among the hottest parts of Portugal and forty degrees is normal in July, with the town emptying into the shade in the afternoons. Winter is mild at around twelve degrees and wet, and the plains can be foggy. The wildflowers across the Alentejo in April are one of the better sights in southern Europe. Cork is stripped across the Alentejo between June and August, which is why the oaks stand bare-trunked and painted with a number through the summer, each tree cut once every nine years. The plains east of here hold one of the first certified dark sky reserves anywhere, with almost no light pollution across an area the size of a small country, and the clear dry nights of late summer are when it is at its best. Stargazing is a local industry here rather than a novelty, with observatories that take bookings and villages that have rewired their street lighting for it.
evora.prosCons: Evora is a walled town that UNESCO listed in 1986 and that genuinely earns it: a Roman temple standing in the middle of it, a cathedral, a Chapel of Bones lined with the remains of five thousand people, and an aqueduct that houses have been built into over the centuries. The Alentejo around it holds more megaliths than anywhere in the Iberian peninsula. Costs are low and the food and wine are excellent. The summer heat is serious, the winter is very quiet, and most people exhaust a town of this size inside a single season of living here. Evora is also small enough to be walked end to end inside the walls in twenty minutes, which is either the appeal or the limit depending on how long you intend to stay.
evora.whoFor: Anyone drawn to Roman and medieval Portugal, to megalithic archaeology, or to wine, since the Alentejo produces a great deal of the best in the country and the estates are visitable. It suits people using Portugal's residence routes who want somewhere quieter and cheaper than Lisbon or the Algarve. It suits walkers and cyclists in spring and autumn. The Alentejo summer is genuinely hot rather than pleasantly warm, and anybody who cannot tolerate forty degrees should come in another season or not at all. Fifty thousand people also make a town rather than a city, and it behaves like one in every way that matters. A Portuguese residence route still requires somewhere to live, and the rental market here is effectively a different country from Lisbon's, where the gap has now widened to more than double for the same kind of flat.

banjaluka.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month, which is very low for Europe. A one-bedroom runs roughly $200 to $400, with the streets near the centre and the Vrbas at the top. Market produce is cheap and the region grows a great deal of its own food, with the produce markets genuinely good. Eating out is inexpensive: a full meal with drinks runs under fifteen dollars almost anywhere, and the grilled meat is the regional speciality. Utilities are moderate and heating runs through a proper continental winter. The convertible mark is pegged to the euro, which removes currency risk. Fibre runs about $15 to $25 a month for fast speeds and a coworking desk $70 to $130, both among the better value in Europe. District heating in the older blocks is billed by building rather than by use, so an inefficient block costs the same as a careful tenant, and it is worth asking which system a flat is on before signing. Rents in Borik and the outer neighbourhoods run a third below the centre for the same space. Health insurance for a non-resident is cheap here and private clinics are used routinely rather than exceptionally, which is worth budgeting as a small monthly line.
banjaluka.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Bosnia has extensive fibre at low prices in the cities, with comprehensive mobile coverage and generally reliable power, and Banja Luka is well served. There is a small coworking scene and a growing software outsourcing sector, which is one of the country's few genuine growth industries. The time zone is central European, so European work is straightforward. The practical friction is banking and administration rather than technology: Bosnia's divided governmental structure means procedures vary by entity and can be slow and opaque. Anyone opening a bank account should allow time and paperwork, since Bosnia's two entities and the district each run their own administration and the rules differ between them. Bosnia sits one hour ahead of GMT, giving a full European working day and a late-afternoon overlap with the American east coast. The outsourcing sector here works largely for German and Austrian clients, which is why the time zone and the language skills matter more locally than the cost does.
banjaluka.gettingAround: Banja Luka is flat along the Vrbas and easy to walk, with the centre, the fortress and the riverside all within twenty minutes of each other. Buses cover the rest cheaply and taxis are inexpensive. Bicycles work well. Banja Luka International Airport has very limited service, so Zagreb, about three hours by road, is the practical air connection, with Belgrade about five. Buses run to Sarajevo in around five hours on a slow mountain road. The Vrbas canyon upstream is where the rafting happens and is half an hour away. The Vrbas canyon road upstream towards Jajce is one of the better drives in the country, following the river through limestone gorges, and Jajce itself has a waterfall in the middle of the town. Rafting operators run from Karanovac, twenty minutes out. Zagreb Airport is the practical gateway and the bus takes about four hours including the border, which is the journey most arrivals actually make rather than flying into Banja Luka.
banjaluka.visas: Bosnia and Herzegovina grants visa-free entry of ninety days in any one hundred and eighty to citizens of the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia and a long list of others, which is generous and straightforward. Bosnia is not in the European Union or Schengen, so time here does not count against a Schengen allowance, which makes it a genuinely useful base for people managing that limit. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays require a temporary residence permit, applied for locally, and the process is slow. Bosnia is an EU candidate country and its visa arrangements are likely to change over the coming years, but for now the ninety days runs on its own clock, which is the single most useful thing about it for anyone managing a Schengen allowance across a year.
banjaluka.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable window, with July around twenty seven degrees and the Vrbas at its best for rafting and swimming. Spring and autumn are pleasant and short. Winter from December to February is cold, often around freezing with snow, and brings the region's serious air quality problem: coal and wood heating across the valley pushes particulate readings among the worst in Europe during still winter weeks, which is the single biggest health consideration here. Summer air is clean by comparison. The thing to watch is the particulate reading rather than the forecast, and the worst of it arrives in the windless spells rather than the coldest ones, which is not what most people expect. The Vrbas is meltwater-fed and runs highest in April and May, which is when the rafting is at its most serious and when the canyon is at its most impressive rather than merely pleasant. Kozara National Park an hour north is the nearest proper hiking and is thickly forested rather than alpine, which suits walking better than climbing.
banjaluka.prosCons: Banja Luka is a green, walkable riverside city on the Vrbas at very low cost, with the canyon and its rafting half an hour upstream, thermal springs nearby, and a ninety day visa-free allowance that does not touch a Schengen clock. The Kastel fortress and the rebuilt Ferhadija mosque are both central. Winter air quality here is genuinely bad, the flight connections are very limited, and the politics matter: Banja Luka is the seat of Republika Srpska, and the entity's relationship with the Bosnian state has been a source of recurring instability for thirty years now. The Ferhadija mosque was destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt from its original stones, many recovered from a rubbish tip and the river, and reopened in 2016, which is a piece of the city's recent history that is legible in the building itself. Thermal spas at Slatina and Laktasi are twenty minutes out and are used year-round.
banjaluka.whoFor: European costs at a fraction of European prices without spending Schengen days, particularly for people working European hours who need somewhere to sit out the ninety day limit. It suits rafters, kayakers and anyone drawn to the Vrbas. It suits software people, given the local sector. The winter air in this valley turns poor enough to be worth a second thought for asthmatics, flights are few, and Bosnia's unresolved politics are present in daily conversation rather than confined to the news, which some people find interesting and others find wearing. The Vrbas canyon is what fills the hotels in spring. Rafting runs from the meltwater right through the summer, and in April the river is genuinely serious water rather than a scenic float down a gorge. The Dayton settlement is argued over more openly in Banja Luka than in any other Bosnian city, which makes the constitutional arrangement something a visitor runs into rather than reads about, because the politics are impossible to miss. Put it beside Sarajevo and Banja Luka is flatter, cheaper, considerably less atmospheric and has the better air in summer and the worse in winter.

namur.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,650 a month, which makes Namur cheaper than Brussels and considerably cheaper than Luxembourg an hour and a half east. A one-bedroom runs roughly $750 to $1,100, with the streets near the confluence and the old town at the top. Groceries are ordinary Belgian prices, which are moderate by western European standards. Eating out is reasonable and Wallonia's beer, cheese and charcuterie are all good and local. Utilities run through a damp rather than a cold winter. Belgium's tax and social contributions are among the highest in Europe, which matters if you are employed here rather than remotely. Belgian leases come with an etat des lieux, a formal inventory of the property's condition drawn up and signed at entry and checked against on departure, and skipping it leaves a tenant liable for whatever was already broken. Rents are indexed annually to inflation by a published formula, so the figure in the contract is not the figure in year three. Registration of the lease itself is the landlord's legal duty and protects the tenant, so it is worth confirming it happened.
namur.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Belgium has extensive fibre and cable coverage, with comprehensive mobile service and reliable power, and Namur is well provided as a regional capital. There is a small coworking presence, helped by the university and by the parliament of Wallonia being based here. The time zone is central European, so European work is straightforward and the American afternoon is reachable. The practical friction in Belgium is administrative rather than technical: registering with the commune is a genuine requirement within days of arrival and the process is thorough rather than quick. Anyone going self-employed here meets the statut d'independant and the social insurance fund that comes with it, where quarterly contributions are provisional and reconciled against real income two years later, which produces a bill people are genuinely unprepared for in their third year. Budget for it from the start. Hosting Wallonia's government also makes the professional economy administrative rather than commercial, so consultancies and public bodies dominate and there is little startup culture to plug into.
namur.gettingAround: Namur is compact and walkable, laid out where the Sambre meets the Meuse with the citadel on the ridge above and a cable car up to it. Buses cover the rest and cycling along both rivers is good, with the RAVeL network of former railway and towpath routes running for hundreds of kilometres from here. Trains reach Brussels in about an hour, Luxembourg in ninety minutes and Liege in forty five, which makes this an unusually well connected small city. Brussels Airport is around ninety minutes by direct train. Anyone cycling the RAVeL should know that the network runs on disused railway lines and canal towpaths, which means it is almost entirely flat and separated from traffic. Belgian rail runs on a dense network and season tickets are the normal way to use it, which changes the arithmetic of living here and working in Brussels or Luxembourg. The citadel's cable car reopened in 2021 after decades without one. Parking in the centre is metered and the old streets are narrow enough that most residents who own a car keep it outside the ring and walk in.
namur.visas: Belgium is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here without a permit, though registration with the commune within eight days of arrival is a legal requirement rather than a formality. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones, with the single permit combining work and residence for most employment routes. There is no digital nomad visa. Belgian administration is layered across federal, regional and communal levels, and the commune is where most practical business happens. The commune, not the country, is where residence actually happens. Registration triggers a visit from the local police to confirm you live where you say you do, which is standard practice and surprises almost everyone, and only afterwards does the identity card follow. Belgium recognises the single permit for most employment, but the application is lodged by the employer with the region, in this case Wallonia, rather than federally, so the process differs from Flanders and Brussels in ways that matter.
namur.bestTime: May to September is the season, with July around twenty three degrees and the rivers and the citadel at their best. Belgian summers are unreliable and rain is possible in every month, which locals accept. April and October are quiet and often pleasant. Winter from November to March is grey, damp and dark rather than cold, rarely freezing hard. The Fetes de Wallonie in September fill the city for several days and are the biggest event in the region, and Namur's Christmas market runs through December. The citadel's underground tunnels stay cool through the summer and are among the few genuinely comfortable places in the city during a heatwave. The rivers are a seasonal risk as well as the city's setting: the Meuse basin flooded catastrophically in July 2021, with the worst damage further east around Liege and Verviers, and flood defences and insurance have been live topics in Wallonia since. Summer heatwaves are becoming more frequent in a housing stock built for damp cold rather than heat. The walking and cycling season along both valleys runs comfortably from April into October.
