Coimbatore International Airport has domestic connections plus flights to Singapore, Sharjah and Colombo. The Nilgiri hills start an hour north, and the road up to Ooty through the Western Ghats is one of the good drives in South India. Avinashi Road is the artery and also the bottleneck, so a flat on the wrong side of it can add forty minutes to a trip that looks short on a map. The airport sits close enough to the eastern suburbs that a taxi in takes fifteen minutes rather than an hour. Mettupalayam, about thirty five kilometres north, is where the narrow gauge mountain railway begins its climb behind a steam locomotive, a line listed by UNESCO and much the slowest and best way up into the tea country above.
coimbatore.visas: India's e-visa covers most nationalities and comes in 30-day, one-year and five-year versions, applied for online in advance. The one-year and five-year e-tourist visas allow multiple entries but cap each stay, usually at 90 or 180 days depending on nationality, so read the conditions for your passport rather than assuming. There is no digital nomad visa. Working remotely for a foreign employer on a tourist visa is a grey area India has not clarified, and the employment visa is genuinely aimed at employment with an Indian entity. Registration with the FRRO is required for stays over 180 days. Extensions are difficult; most long stayers leave and return instead. An e-visa is valid only at a designated airport or seaport, and that list does not cover every airport with international flights, so check it against the one you intend to land at rather than assuming. A tourist visa cannot be converted into another category from inside the country, so a change of plan means a flight out. Overstay penalties are charged in bands by length and settled before departure. Anyone on a category that requires registration has fourteen days from arrival to complete it, and the clock does not wait for a flat to be found.
coimbatore.bestTime: Coimbatore sits at a break in the Western Ghats, and the Palakkad gap funnels wind through the city, which is why it is noticeably cooler and breezier than the Tamil plains around it. December to February is the pick: highs around 30C, nights near 20C, dry and clear. March to May is hot, reaching 36C or more, though the evening breeze through the gap takes the edge off. The southwest monsoon from June to August is comparatively light here because the Ghats catch most of it on the Kerala side, and the wind is strongest then. The heavier rain comes with the northeast monsoon in October and November, which is also when the hills are greenest.
coimbatore.prosCons: Coimbatore is an industrial and university city with real infrastructure behind it: decent coworking, fast cheap fibre, good hospitals and a workable airport, and all of it at $520 a month. The Palghat gap keeps it cooler than most of Tamil Nadu, the Western Ghats and Ooty are an hour away, and the food is excellent and very cheap. English is widely spoken in the professional city. There is essentially no foreign nomad scene at all, the city is spread out and traffic is heavy, air quality is mediocre and worse near the arterial roads, and nightlife is close to non-existent because Tamil Nadu's alcohol retail is state-run and bars close early.
coimbatore.whoFor: India for the cost and the food rather than for a community of other foreigners, and infrastructure valued over atmosphere. Work that needs a reliable connection and a proper desk is what this city is actually good for, and it doubles as a base for the Nilgiris, for Kerala and for the Western Ghats. Engineers and anyone with business in Indian manufacturing will find it more useful than Goa. It does not suit someone looking for the nomad-hub experience, for nightlife, or for a walkable historic centre. It is also not the easiest first city in India; Bangalore or Kochi are gentler introductions with more people doing the same thing.

bhubaneswar.costOfLiving: Bhubaneswar runs about $480 a month for one person, which is low even against other Indian state capitals. A furnished one-bedroom in Saheed Nagar or Jaydev Vihar is $110 to $200; a room in a shared flat near KIIT is half that. A thali at a local place is under a dollar, and dinner for two at a good restaurant is $10 to $14. Coworking exists around Infocity and Chandrasekharpur at $50 to $100 a month for a hot desk. Autos are $1 to $3 across town and the city runs an app-based e-rickshaw network. Fibre at 100 Mbps is $8 to $12 monthly, and utilities add $25 to $40 depending on air conditioning use. Leases here are written for eleven months rather than a year, a convention that exists to stay outside the registration requirement, and they roll over by agreement rather than automatically. A broker takes a month for finding the flat and the owner takes two or three months as advance, so the first payment is far larger than the monthly figure suggests. Cooking gas arrives as a cylinder booked by phone and swapped at the door, which is a cost nobody budgets for until the first one runs out mid-week.
bhubaneswar.whereToWork: The IT corridor at Infocity and Chandrasekharpur is where the coworking is, serving the software companies and the KIIT and NISER campuses rather than visitors. A hot desk is $50 to $100 a month and private cabins run higher; the spaces are practical and quiet and the connections are business grade. Home fibre from BSNL, Airtel or a local operator delivers 100 to 300 Mbps for $8 to $15, which is the cheapest good internet you will find anywhere on this site. Cafes in Saheed Nagar and around the Esplanade mall are workable for a couple of hours. Power is more reliable here than the region's reputation suggests, though a UPS is standard in most flats. The state runs on mining and steel, and although the pits and the plants are hundreds of kilometres inland, the head offices, the regulators and the consultants that go with them all sit in the capital, which is the quiet engine behind the demand for desks. Administration works in the local script as well as in English, and a form that arrives in one may need to go back in the other. The professional day starts late by regional standards and runs well into the evening, so an early European call is easier to arrange than a late one.
bhubaneswar.gettingAround: Bhubaneswar is unusual in India for having been planned, first by the Kalinga kings and again in 1948 by the German architect Otto Konigsberger, so the newer parts are laid out on a grid with wide roads. Autorickshaws are cheap and Ola and Uber both work. The Mo Bus city network is clean, air conditioned on some routes and costs pennies. Distances are real, so a scooter at $60 to $80 a month is worth it if you are staying. The airport is 4km from the centre with domestic flights and connections to Bangkok, Singapore and Dubai. Puri and the sun temple at Konark are 60 and 65km away, both easy day trips by train or car.
bhubaneswar.visas: India's e-visa system covers most nationalities in 30-day, one-year and five-year forms, all applied for online before travel. The longer versions allow multiple entries but limit each individual stay, commonly to 90 or 180 days depending on your passport, so check the specific conditions rather than assuming a year means a year. There is no digital nomad visa, and remote work for a foreign employer sits in a grey area India has never clarified. Stays beyond 180 days require FRRO registration. In-country extensions are hard to obtain for tourists, so long stayers generally plan an exit and a fresh entry rather than counting on an extension. Every hotel is required to file a form with the immigration bureau for each foreign guest, which is why a passport is copied at check-in everywhere, and why staying informally with a friend puts that obligation on the host instead. A local mobile number is issued against the passport and the visa page together, takes a day to activate, and is the thing most other services quietly depend on. Journalism and research are separate visa categories rather than activities a visitor may undertake, and the distinction is taken seriously enough that academics arrive on the right document.
bhubaneswar.bestTime: November to February is the season, with highs in the high 20s, cool mornings and dry air, and it is also when Odisha's festival calendar is busiest. March to May is severe: Bhubaneswar regularly passes 40C in April and May and the humidity from the Bay of Bengal makes it worse. The southwest monsoon arrives in June and runs to September, dropping well over a metre of rain and turning the temple stone dark and green. October is the transition month and often pleasant. Cyclone season is a genuine consideration on this coast, with the higher risk in October and November and again in May; the state's evacuation planning is among the best in India. The chariot festival in the temple town down the coast falls in the first weeks of the rains and pulls a crowd counted in the hundreds of thousands, which closes the road south for days and is either the reason to be here or the week to be elsewhere. A dance festival is staged against the sun temple in December, outdoors and after dark, and it is the one cultural event worth planning a trip around. Winter mornings inland are cool enough for a jacket, which surprises anybody who came expecting heat.
bhubaneswar.prosCons: What Bhubaneswar has is historical depth at a very low price. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited temple cities in India, with several hundred Kalinga-style shrines still standing, the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves on its edge, and Puri and Konark an hour away. It is also a planned city with a functioning IT corridor, cheap fast fibre, good hospitals and a real airport. April and May are punishing, the monsoon is heavy going, the cyclone risk is real, air quality is mediocre, and there is essentially no foreign community. English is common in the professional city but less so elsewhere, and nightlife is limited.
bhubaneswar.whoFor: An interest in India rather than in a nomad scene, and a want of somewhere cheap with functioning infrastructure and a great deal to look at. If temple architecture, archaeology or Indian history is the reason you are travelling, few cities on this site offer more per dollar. Two or three months over the winter is what most people should plan for, with Puri, Konark and the Chilika lagoon taken as trips out of the city. Other foreigners are scarce here, the city sprawls rather than gathering into a walkable centre, the nightlife is minimal, and a summer stay in coastal Odisha is not something to attempt on purpose. Anyone new to India would have an easier time starting in Bangalore, Kochi or Jaipur.

indore.costOfLiving: Indore runs about $500 a month for one person. A furnished one-bedroom in Vijay Nagar or New Palasia is $120 to $220; older areas near the Rajwada are cheaper at $80 to $150. Street food is the city's defining pleasure and costs almost nothing: a plate of poha with jalebi for breakfast is well under a dollar, and an evening working through Sarafa Bazaar rarely passes $5. A restaurant dinner for two is $10 to $15. Coworking around Vijay Nagar and the AB Road corridor is $55 to $110 a month. Autos are $1 to $3. Fibre at 100 Mbps costs $8 to $12 and utilities add $25 to $40. The cleanliness has an engine behind it rather than a campaign: the city separates waste at the door into six streams, sends none of the wet fraction to landfill, and runs a plant at Devguradia that turns food waste into compressed gas which fuels the municipal buses. Residents pay a small monthly collection charge for it, one of the few municipal fees a tenant here actually notices, and enforcement against dumping is real rather than nominal.
indore.whereToWork: The coworking cluster is along AB Road and around Vijay Nagar, driven by Indore's IT services firms and the presence of both an IIT and an IIM in the city. A hot desk is $55 to $110 a month, private cabins two to three times that, and the spaces are aimed at local startups rather than visitors. Home fibre from Jio, Airtel or a local operator gives 100 to 300 Mbps for $8 to $15, which is the practical answer if you take a flat. Cafes around 56 Dukan and New Palasia are fine for a few hours but get loud in the evening. Power is reliable by regional standards and cuts are short. The local IT sector is largely services rather than product, working for clients in the United States and Europe, which means the professional rhythm already accommodates odd hours and a foreigner's timezone is unremarkable. The IIM's executive programmes bring a steady flow of mid-career people through the city, and its public events are among the few places a visitor can meet the local business layer without an introduction.
indore.gettingAround: Indore is spread out and an auto or a scooter is the default. Autorickshaws are cheap and Ola and Uber both operate; a cross-city trip is $2 to $4. The city bus network, iBus, runs on dedicated lanes along AB Road and is genuinely useful. A metro line has been under construction for years and partial services have begun on the eastern corridor. Scooter rental is $60 to $80 a month. The airport is 8km out with good domestic connections and some Gulf flights. Ujjain is 55km, Mandu about 90km and Maheshwar 90km on the Narmada, all comfortable day trips and all worth the drive. Ujjain, an hour north, was the prime meridian of Indian astronomy: classical Sanskrit texts measured longitude from a line through the city, and the eighteenth century observatory there is still used to compute the Hindu calendar. It is also one of the four Kumbh sites, which means that once every twelve years the road you are driving carries tens of millions of people rather than a few thousand. Mandu, in the other direction, is a ruined Afghan capital spread across a plateau and takes a whole day rather than an afternoon.
indore.visas: India's e-visa covers most nationalities in 30-day, one-year and five-year forms, applied for online before you travel. The longer versions are multiple entry but cap each individual stay, usually at 90 or 180 days depending on your passport, so check the conditions attached to your nationality rather than assuming a one-year visa means a year in the country. There is no digital nomad visa. Remote work for a foreign employer on a tourist visa is a grey area India has not addressed. Stays over 180 days require FRRO registration, and in-country extensions are hard for tourists, so most long stayers plan an exit and a fresh entry. Madhya Pradesh carries no protected area restrictions of the kind that complicate the northeast or the Andamans, so a standard e-visa covers everything reachable from here without a supplementary permit. The document worth carrying is a printed copy of the visa and the passport page, because hotels must file a form for every foreign guest and a phone screen at a reception desk at midnight is slower than a photocopy. Registration is done by the property rather than by you, but the property cannot do it without the paperwork.
indore.bestTime: October to March is the good stretch. Indore sits on the Malwa plateau at about 550m, which makes its winters noticeably cooler than the plains: December and January nights can drop under 10C with daytime highs in the mid 20s. April to June is hot, regularly past 40C, and dry. The southwest monsoon arrives in late June and runs to September, and Malwa gets a proper soaking that turns the surrounding countryside and the Vindhya escarpment green. September and October are the pleasant tail of it. If you are here for the food, the winter months are when the night markets are busiest and most comfortable to walk. The plateau's winter is why people from Delhi and Mumbai keep second homes here, and it is also when the air is worst: cool still nights trap crop-residue smoke and traffic exhaust across the Malwa, so December and January deliver the best temperatures and the poorest air of the year together. That trade-off decides the month for anyone sensitive to it. The monsoon brings the cleanest air and the most difficult roads, which is the opposite bargain.
indore.prosCons: Indore is famous for one thing above all others: it has topped India's national cleanliness survey every year since 2017, and the difference shows on the street. The street food is arguably the best in the country, the plateau keeps winters mild, there are two national institutes bringing a young professional population, coworking is real, fibre is cheap and fast, and Mandu, Ujjain and Maheshwar are all within a couple of hours. April to June is genuinely hot here, the air is mediocre and worse again in winter, there is no foreign nomad community at all, alcohol is available but nightlife is thin, and the city is sprawling rather than walkable. Mhow, twenty five kilometres southwest, is where Ambedkar was born, which puts the man who chaired the drafting committee of the Indian constitution on this city's doorstep, and the memorial there is a pilgrimage for Dalit visitors from every state. Indore also runs on a Maratha inheritance rather than a Mughal one: the Holkars ruled from here, and Ahilyabai Holkar, who governed from Maheshwar down the road, is remembered nationally for rebuilding temples in cities she never controlled.
indore.whoFor: A comfortable, well-run Indian city to work from cheaply, for anyone who will take good infrastructure and outstanding food over an international scene. It is one of the easier large Indian cities to live in day to day, which is a real consideration if this is a three-month stay rather than a week. It is a strong base for central India: the Malwa forts, the Narmada temple towns and the Ujjain Kumbh cycle are all reachable. Other remote workers are effectively absent, the historic core is small against a very spread-out city, and neither a beach nor a nightlife is available anywhere in Madhya Pradesh. Nor is it a summer destination under any circumstances. It suits somebody with a tolerance for heat and a serious interest in food, because Sarafa after dark is not a night market in the tourist sense but a jewellery bazaar that converts, and eating through it properly takes several evenings and a local to explain what is in front of you. It suits a student of Indian politics, given Mhow. Anybody whose plan involves other foreigners should understand there are essentially none here, which is either the point or the problem depending on why you came.

nagpur.costOfLiving: Nagpur runs about $490 a month for one person. A furnished one-bedroom in Dharampeth or Ramdaspeth is $110 to $200; Civil Lines is dearer and the newer eastern suburbs cheaper. Food is inexpensive even by Indian standards: a thali is around a dollar, Saoji mutton at one of the local places is $3 to $4, and dinner for two at a good restaurant is $10 to $14. Coworking around Civil Lines and the IT park at Parsodi is $50 to $95 a month. Autos cost $1 to $3 and the metro is cheaper still. Fibre at 100 Mbps is $8 to $12, and utilities run $25 to $50 because summer air conditioning is not optional. Almost every payment now moves through UPI, the instant transfer system, and a foreigner without an Indian bank account is locked out of it, which means carrying cash in a city where locals have stopped doing so. Leases run eleven months by convention rather than a year, because a longer term triggers registration requirements, and the deposit is usually two or three months held without interest. Brokerage on a flat is customarily one month of rent. The city is known for its oranges, and the winter crop is sold off handcarts everywhere, cheap enough to be a daily habit rather than a treat.
nagpur.whereToWork: Coworking in Nagpur is modest but real, concentrated in Civil Lines, Dharampeth and near the IT park at Parsodi, and priced at $50 to $95 a month for a hot desk. The demand comes from local software and logistics firms rather than visitors, so expect functional offices with reliable business connections and little in the way of community programming. Home fibre from Jio, Airtel or a local ISP delivers 100 to 300 Mbps for $8 to $15. Cafes around Dharampeth work for a couple of hours. Power supply is dependable and cuts are brief, though building generators and inverters are common because summer load is heavy. Indian Standard Time sits at a half-hour offset from everywhere else, and that half hour is the part that causes trouble, since every invitation from abroad lands on a fractional boundary and half the scheduling tools handle it badly. The overlap with Europe is comfortable in the afternoon, while the American east coast needs an early start or a late night. Offices in many sectors work Monday to Saturday with alternate Saturdays off, so a local counterpart may well be at a desk when a Western client assumes the weekend has begun.
nagpur.gettingAround: Nagpur has India's most usable mid-sized metro, with two lines crossing at Sitabuldi in the centre, and it is clean, air conditioned and very cheap. Beyond it, autorickshaws and app cabs cover everything for $1 to $4. The city calls itself the centre of India and the Zero Mile Stone marks the old survey reference point downtown. The railway station is one of the busiest junctions in the country, with trains in every direction. The airport is 8km out with domestic flights and a growing cargo operation. Pench is 90km north and Tadoba-Andhari about 150km south, which is the real reason many people come.
nagpur.visas: India's e-visa is available to most nationalities as a 30-day, one-year or five-year tourist visa, applied for online before travel. The longer options allow multiple entries but restrict how long each stay may last, typically 90 or 180 days by nationality, so read the conditions for your own passport. There is no digital nomad visa and no formal permission to work remotely on a tourist visa, which is an unresolved grey area rather than a settled allowance. FRRO registration applies to stays past 180 days. Extensions are difficult to secure, so long stays are usually built around leaving the country and returning on a fresh entry. The application asks for a reference in the country and an address for the stay, and a hotel booking satisfies both, but the form is unforgiving about any inconsistency between what is typed and what is printed in the passport. Entry is permitted only at listed airports and seaports, which rules out arriving overland from Nepal or Bangladesh on this class of visa. The fee varies by nationality rather than following one published price. Nothing about the process moves quickly once a question has been raised.
nagpur.bestTime: November to February is the only comfortable working season, with highs in the high 20s and cool nights. Nagpur sits in the middle of the subcontinent with no coast to moderate it, and its summers are famously brutal: May routinely reaches 45C and has passed 47C. April through June should simply be avoided. The monsoon breaks in mid June and runs to September, bringing relief and heavy rain, and it is when the surrounding forest is greenest, though the tiger reserves are closed for much of it. October is warm and pleasant. Tiger safari season at Tadoba and Pench runs October to June, with the best sightings in the hot months. The loo, the dry wind that crosses central India in May, is what makes the heat dangerous rather than merely uncomfortable, and the local advice is to stay indoors between eleven and four rather than to drink more water and carry on. Diwali falls in October or November and effectively closes business for a week, which is worth knowing before promising a deadline inside that window. The orange harvest runs through the cool months and is the one season the city markets itself on, which tells you how little else competes for the title.
nagpur.prosCons: Position and price are the two things Nagpur has. It sits at the geographic centre of India with rail links in every direction, has a genuinely good metro, cheap fast fibre, functional coworking and one of the lowest costs of living of any Indian city this size. Two major tiger reserves are within a three-hour drive. Deekshabhoomi, where Ambedkar and hundreds of thousands of others converted to Buddhism in 1956, is a site of real historical weight. The summer heat is among the very worst in India and rules out four months of the year, air quality is poor through the winter, there is no foreign community, and the city is short on the kind of sights that fill a weekend.
nagpur.whoFor: India as a base rather than a destination: somebody who travels a lot by train, wants cheap rent and reliable internet in a city with a working metro, and does not need other foreigners nearby. Wildlife photographers and anyone drawn to Tadoba and Pench will find it the obvious place to sit between trips. Anyone interested in Ambedkar and the Dalit Buddhist movement has a reason to be here that no other city offers. This makes a poor first visit to India and a worse summer one. Nightlife, walkability and any kind of scene are all absent, and none of the three is coming. Pune and Bangalore do the comfortable-Indian-city job better if cost is less tight.

multan.costOfLiving: Multan runs about $420 a month for one person, which makes it one of the cheapest cities anywhere on this site. A furnished one-bedroom in Gulgasht or Model Town is $90 to $170, and older parts of the city are cheaper again. Food costs very little: a plate of nihari or a seer of Multani sohan halwa is a couple of dollars, and a full restaurant meal for two rarely passes $10. There is essentially no coworking market, so budget for home internet instead. Fibre or cable broadband is $10 to $18 a month. Rickshaws are under a dollar across the centre. Utilities are the variable, since summer cooling can add $40 to $70. Electricity bills carry so much in taxes, fuel adjustments and surcharges that the units consumed are often the smaller half of the total, which is why residents talk about the bill rather than about the tariff. Piped gas reaches the older districts and is cheap, though the pressure drops in the coldest weeks when demand peaks. Rent is often asked half a year in advance and paid in cash, since a foreigner without residence will find opening a local account slow going. Almost nothing outside the newer supermarkets takes a card.
multan.whereToWork: Multan has no meaningful coworking sector, so working here means a flat with a good connection. Fibre has reached Model Town, Gulgasht and Cantt through PTCL, Nayatel and local operators, delivering 20 to 100 Mbps for $10 to $18 a month, and it is the single most important thing to check before signing for a place. Mobile data from Jazz or Zong is a workable backup and cheap. Cafes exist around Bosan Road and the newer commercial strips but are social spaces rather than places to sit with a laptop. The real constraint is load shedding: scheduled power cuts are still common in summer, so a UPS or an inverter is essential rather than optional.
multan.gettingAround: Multan is flat and the old city around the shrines is walkable, though the traffic on the arterial roads is not. Autorickshaws and the Qingqi share-rickshaws cover the city for well under a dollar, and Careem and inDrive both operate. The Multan Metrobus runs a dedicated corridor across the city and costs a few cents. A motorcycle is what most residents use. The railway station puts you on the main line between Karachi and Lahore, with Lahore about four to five hours by fast train. Multan International Airport handles domestic flights plus Gulf routes to Dubai, Sharjah, Doha and Jeddah, which makes arriving from outside Pakistan reasonably simple. The motorway network reached the city in the last decade and a half, with a southbound stretch opened in 2019 that cut the run to the port cities to a single long day of driving, and the coaches that use it are air conditioned and punctual in a way the trains are not. Within the city the ring road is the way to avoid the centre entirely, and it is worth the extra distance at almost any hour. Motorcycle rickshaws take the narrow lanes of the walled city where a car simply cannot go, which is most of the historic quarter.
multan.visas: Pakistan overhauled its visa system and most nationalities can now apply online through the NADRA visa portal, with tourist visas commonly issued for three months and business visas for longer. Processing is usually quick and a sponsor is no longer required for tourism from most countries. There is no digital nomad visa. Extensions are handled online but are not guaranteed. The practical constraint is not the visa but the travel advice: several governments advise against travel to parts of Pakistan, and southern Punjab is treated more cautiously than Lahore or Islamabad. Foreigners in some districts are subject to police registration and occasionally to a mandatory escort, which affects how freely you can move. Anyone with a parent or grandparent born in the country can apply for an origin card instead of a visa, which removes the entry question altogether and is the route most of the diaspora uses. A no objection certificate is needed before travelling to several districts and is applied for through the interior ministry rather than arranged locally, so a plan involving the western provinces has to be made weeks ahead. Insurance is the practical block rather than the paperwork: a policy that excludes countries under a government advisory will not pay out here at all.
multan.bestTime: November to March is the only sensible window. Winter days are mild at 20C to 25C with cold nights, and December and January bring fog that regularly disrupts flights and road travel across Punjab. April to June is extreme: Multan is one of the hottest cities in Pakistan and 45C is a normal May afternoon, with dust storms on top. The monsoon reaches here weakly in July and August, adding humidity to the heat without much relief, though it can also flood. September and October are hot but improving. Urs festivals at the shrines of Bahauddin Zakariya and Shah Rukn-e-Alam are the events worth timing around, both in the cooler half of the year. Ramadan moves through the calendar by eleven days a year, and when it lands in the hot months the whole city inverts: nothing is open in daylight, everything is open at night, and a visitor who has not planned for it will find the working day unrecognisable. The mango orchards around the city ripen in sequence through the worst of the heat, variety after variety, and the crop is the one thing that makes the hot season worth being here for. Dry heat gives way to a sticky kind once the rains arrive further east.
multan.prosCons: History and price are the reasons to come to Multan. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in South Asia, its Sufi shrines are extraordinary and the blue-tiled Multani kashi work on them is unlike anything else in the region, and the whole month costs less than a week in Western Europe. The mangoes are the best in the country. Food is superb and cheap. What is stacked against it runs long, and it runs like this: no coworking, no foreign community, summer heat that makes four months unworkable, load shedding, poor air quality, limited English outside educated circles, and travel advisories that will complicate your insurance. Alcohol is effectively unavailable and nightlife does not exist.
multan.whoFor: An experienced traveller with a specific reason to be in southern Punjab: Sufi architecture, Pakistani history, family connections, or work in the region. It is not a place you drift into. If you have been to Pakistan before, know how the registration rules work in your district and have a flat with fibre and an inverter, the cost of living is remarkable and the city rewards attention. South Asia should be learned somewhere else first. Nobody else is working remotely here to fall in with, insurance that excludes advisory areas will not cover a stay, and April to June is a stretch nobody should choose deliberately. Lahore is the sane entry point to Pakistan for a newcomer.

mandalay.costOfLiving: Mandalay runs about $600 a month for one person, though prices have been unstable since the kyat's collapse and figures in local currency move faster than any guide can track. A furnished apartment in the central grid is $180 to $350, less in the outer townships. Street food is very cheap: a bowl of mohinga is under a dollar and a full meal at a local restaurant is $2 to $4. There is little in the way of coworking, so the desk line is coffee and home internet. A motorbike rents for $60 to $90 a month. Budget generously for electricity, since long outages mean generator fuel or a solar and battery setup. Cash dollars are the working currency for anything large, since foreign cards do not reliably work at the machines, and clean unfolded notes get a better rate than worn ones, which is a convention rather than a swindle. The gap between the official rate and the street rate has been wide enough at times to change the cost of a month by a third, so the figure above is an approximation over a moving target rather than a price.
mandalay.whereToWork: Mandalay's coworking sector was small before 2021 and has largely not survived, so working here means your own room and your own power. Internet runs through Ooredoo, ATOM, MPT and fixed-line providers; speeds are adequate for email and documents but video calls are unreliable, and the government has periodically restricted mobile data and blocked VPNs, which is a working constraint rather than a rumour. Power is the harder problem: the national grid supplies only part of each day in much of the city and a battery, inverter or generator is standard. Cafes around 78th Street have wifi when the power is on. Plan for interruption rather than around it. Load shedding follows a published rotation in some townships and no pattern at all in others, so people work around the hours their own street gets rather than around a city-wide schedule. Satellite internet is not licensed and using it is a legal risk rather than a clever workaround. The setup most residents settle on is a phone tether as the primary connection, a fixed line as the fallback, and a battery big enough to keep a laptop and a router alive through a four-hour cut.
mandalay.gettingAround: The centre of Mandalay is laid out on a numbered grid, which makes navigation unusually easy: streets run one way and avenues the other, and an address is a pair of numbers. Most people ride a motorbike or take one of the shared pickups and taxis; Grab does not operate but local ride apps come and go. A trishaw or taxi across the centre is $1 to $3. Amarapura, with U Bein Bridge, is 11km south; Sagaing and Inwa are within 20km, and the ferry to Mingun runs upriver in an hour. Roads and river routes beyond the immediate area cross checkpoints and can close without notice. The palace and its moat occupy a square kilometre at the middle of the grid, which is why the centre feels arranged around an absence: the compound is a military site and the building inside it is a reconstruction. Mandalay Hill is climbed barefoot up covered stairways from the south and takes about forty minutes. The international airport is an unusually long way out, around forty kilometres south, and that drive is the longest part of any arrival.
mandalay.visas: Myanmar's e-visa is available to most nationalities and normally grants 28 days for tourism, with a business e-visa allowing 70 days and multiple entry. Applications are made online in advance and are generally processed within days. There is no digital nomad visa. Overstay is fined per day at the airport. The visa is not the real question here. Several governments advise against all travel to Myanmar, insurance is difficult or void in much of the country, land borders are variably closed, and internal travel permits and checkpoints apply on many routes. Anyone considering this needs to read their own government's current advice rather than a page like this one. Foreigners must stay in accommodation licensed to take them, which rules out an ordinary rented flat unless the landlord registers you with the immigration office, and that registration is not a formality anyone treats lightly at present. Hotels report their guests nightly. Anyone flying in and out should expect their route and their reason for being in the country to be asked about directly, which is a change from the years before 2021.
mandalay.bestTime: November to February is the only comfortable season, with highs around 29C to 32C, low humidity and clear skies, and it is when the Irrawaddy light is at its best. March to May is severe: Mandalay sits in the central dry zone and April routinely passes 40C with very little shade or breeze. The southwest monsoon runs June to October but is comparatively weak here because the Rakhine mountains take most of it, so the rains are lighter than in Yangon and the heat persists. The 7.7 earthquake of March 2025 caused heavy damage across Mandalay and Sagaing, and reconstruction of both housing and heritage sites is still under way. Thingyan, the water festival that marks the Burmese new year, falls in the middle of April and stops the country for days at a time, landing in the hottest part of the year. River levels drop through the dry months, so the boats upstream to Bhamo run only in the period after the rains while the stretch down to Bagan stays easier. The cool season is also when the dust is worst, since nothing settles it until the rains return.
mandalay.prosCons: Mandalay is the cultural centre of Myanmar: the last royal capital, the gold-leaf workshops, the Mahamuni Buddha, U Bein Bridge across Taungthaman Lake, and Sagaing, Inwa and Amarapura all within twenty kilometres of the city. Costs are very low and the food is good. The other side of it is much heavier, and it should be read first. The country has been in armed conflict since the 2021 coup, electricity is intermittent, the internet is censored and unreliable, most governments advise against travel, travel insurance is unlikely to cover you, and the March 2025 earthquake damaged the city badly. Banking and card payments barely function for foreigners. Kuthodaw Pagoda holds what is often called the world's largest book: the Pali canon carved onto seven hundred and twenty nine marble slabs, each standing in its own small white stupa, in rows you walk between. The city is the centre of Burmese Buddhist learning, and the monasteries on the far bank of the river hold a monastic population in the thousands, which is why so much of the region's craft and scholarship sits here rather than in Yangon.
mandalay.whoFor: This page exists because Mandalay is a real place people ask about, not because it is a sensible base right now. It suits, at most, someone with an existing connection to Myanmar: journalists, aid and development staff, researchers, and people with family there, all of whom will have their own security guidance that supersedes anything written here. For an ordinary remote worker choosing where to spend a month, the answer is no: the power supply alone makes the work impractical, and the risk profile is not comparable to anywhere else in Southeast Asia. If Burmese culture is the draw, Chiang Mai and the Thai border towns are where much of that community now is. Anyone whose interest is the country rather than the city should know that the practical work on Myanmar is now done largely from outside it, from the Thai border towns and from Bangkok, and that arriving in person can create risk for the people you meet rather than only for yourself. That is the consideration that ought to decide it, and it is not one an itinerary can solve.

whangarei.costOfLiving: Whangarei runs about $1,650 a month for one person, which makes it one of the cheaper places to live in New Zealand but still expensive against most of this site. A one-bedroom flat near the Town Basin or in Kensington is $700 to $950; a room in a shared house is $400 to $550. Groceries are the surprise for newcomers, at $350 to $450 a month for one, because so much is imported. A flat white is $4 and a pub meal $18 to $25. Coworking is limited but exists at around $200 a month. Fibre is $50 to $70 for gigabit, power $70 to $110, and a car is close to unavoidable. Fifteen per cent goods and services tax sits inside every advertised price, so the shelf figure is the final one. A tenancy bond runs to four weeks of rent and is lodged with a government service rather than held by the landlord, which makes getting it back at the end far simpler than in most countries. Contents insurance is cheap and close to universal.
whangarei.whereToWork: Whangarei is small, so the coworking options are few but the internet is excellent: New Zealand's fibre rollout reached the city early and gigabit connections are standard in town at $50 to $70 a month. There is a coworking space near the Town Basin and desks in the Old Municipal Building precinct, generally around $200 monthly, and the Hundertwasser Art Centre area has cafes that tolerate a laptop through the morning. Most remote workers here work from home, which is easy given the housing stock is houses rather than apartments. Mobile coverage from One NZ, Spark and 2degrees is solid in town and patchy on the Tutukaka coast and out towards the harbour heads. An IRD number is needed before any local income can be paid properly and takes a few days to obtain online, which is worth starting early even for somebody who will never invoice locally, since the banks ask for it too. Cuts are rare, but the region sits at the end of a long transmission line and a storm can take the area out for a day. The library by the river is the quiet fallback when the house stops working.
whangarei.gettingAround: You need a car. Whangarei's bus network, CityLink, covers the main suburbs on weekdays with a limited weekend service, and the town centre and Town Basin are walkable, but everything that makes Northland worth being in is a drive: Whangarei Heads and Ocean Beach are 35km, the Tutukaka coast and the Poor Knights boats 30km, Whangarei Falls a short trip north of the centre. Petrol runs about $2.20 a litre. Auckland is 160km south on State Highway 1, roughly two and a half hours, and the Bay of Islands about an hour north. There is a small airport with flights to Auckland but no international service. The road south crosses the Brynderwyn hills, which slipped badly in the 2023 storms and closed for months, and that single stretch is what the region's freight and travel both depend on. The railway up here carries freight rather than passengers, so there is no train option at all. A second-hand car is cheap to buy, and the annual roadworthiness check is strict enough to be worth attending to before any purchase.
whangarei.visas: New Zealand's visitor visa allows most Western nationalities up to 90 days visa free, or 180 days for British citizens, entering under the NZeTA which is requested online for a small fee before travel. Since 2023 New Zealand has explicitly permitted visitors to work remotely for an overseas employer while on a visitor visa, one of the clearest positions of any country, though the tax residency rules still apply once you pass 183 days. Working holiday visas for 12 months are available to under-30s or under-35s from many countries and are the usual route for a longer stay. There is no separate digital nomad visa and none is needed. The travel authority itself lasts two years and covers multiple visits, so the ninety days are counted per entry rather than per authority. Anyone intending to stay long enough to trigger tax residence should take advice before the clock runs rather than after, since the country taxes worldwide income once you are resident. The working holiday route closes on a birthday, which is the detail people leave too late.
whangarei.bestTime: Whangarei is the warmest city in New Zealand and Northland is genuinely subtropical, so the seasons are gentler than the rest of the country. December to March is summer: highs of 24C to 26C, long evenings, warm sea, and the Poor Knights diving at its best with visibility often over 30 metres. It is also when the whole country takes holidays, so book accommodation early for January. Winter from June to August is mild at 15C to 16C but genuinely wet, and Northland gets more rain than most of the country. April, May and October are the quiet, pleasant months and the best value. Humidity is high year round. Ex-tropical cyclones reach this coast in February and March in some years, arriving as heavy rain and wind rather than as the thing that formed them, and the 2023 storms were the worst in decades. Pohutukawa along the coast flower red through December, which is what the country uses instead of a Christmas tree. Water temperature trails well behind the air here, so the diving is warmest in late summer rather than at midsummer.
whangarei.prosCons: Whangarei has the mildest climate in New Zealand at the cheapest big-town prices in the country, with gigabit fibre, a rebuilt waterfront around the Town Basin marina, the Hundertwasser Art Centre, and some of the best temperate diving anywhere in the world, half an hour offshore at the Poor Knights Islands marine reserve. Auckland is a two-and-a-half-hour drive and the Bay of Islands an hour. It is safe, clean, and English speaking. It is still expensive by global standards, a car is mandatory here, the remote-working population here is essentially nil, nightlife is a handful of pubs, winter is properly wet, and Northland has a real socioeconomic divide that is visible in parts of the city. The refinery at Marsden Point closed in 2022 and became an import terminal, which took a large block of skilled work out of the district and is part of why the economy feels thinner than the population would suggest. Abbey Caves on the edge of town are undeveloped limestone caves with glowworms, entered with a torch and no ticket office, which is the sort of thing the region has instead of attractions.
whangarei.whoFor: New Zealand without Auckland rents, for anyone whose leisure is outdoors: diving, sailing, sea kayaking, tramping, or surfing the east coast beaches. It works well on a working holiday visa for a year, or as a three-month summer base for someone with a business that runs on European or American hours, since the time zone puts you a day ahead of almost everyone. New Zealand prices will finish off a tight budget, a driving licence is not optional out here, and neither a nomad scene nor a nightlife exists to be found. If you want New Zealand with more people doing the same thing, Wellington and Queenstown are where they are. Anyone comparing the warm end of the country should know that Tauranga is larger, busier and costs a great deal more, and that this is the cheaper version of the same climate. The hospital here is the regional base for all of the north, which matters more than it sounds for anybody living an hour further up. Families do well and single arrivals under thirty tend not to stay.

nelspruit.costOfLiving: Nelspruit runs about $900 a month for one person, cheap for a South African provincial capital. A furnished one-bedroom in Sonheuwel or West Acres is $330 to $500, and a room in a shared house $180 to $280. Groceries are $200 to $280 a month, and a restaurant main is $8 to $14. Coworking exists in a small way at $90 to $150 a month. Fibre at 50 to 100 Mbps is $30 to $45. A car is close to essential and fuel runs about $1.20 a litre. The line most people forget is backup power: an inverter and batteries became normal household kit here through the load shedding years, and most properties kept them after the national cuts ended in May 2025. The Lowveld grows what the rest of the country buys: macadamias, avocados, mangoes, bananas and citrus, and South Africa is now among the world's largest macadamia exporters with much of that crop coming from within an hour of here. The practical effect is a farm stall economy where fruit is bought at the gate for a quarter of the shelf price and the seasons announce themselves rather than needing looking up. Meat is the other line, and a braai pack from a butcher undercuts a restaurant so far that most people simply stop eating out.
nelspruit.whereToWork: Fibre has reached most of Nelspruit's suburbs through Vumatel, Openserve and others, and 50 to 100 Mbps costs $30 to $45 a month, which is the foundation of working here. Coworking is limited to a few small spaces around Riverside and the town centre at $90 to $150 monthly, plus hotel business lounges. Most remote workers set up at home. The problem used to be electricity rather than bandwidth, because an outage takes the fibre ONT down with the lights unless you have an inverter and a battery. Eskom's load shedding eased through 2024 and then stopped altogether on 16 May 2025, with the 2026 winter carried without a single stage, so that battery now covers local faults rather than a published timetable. Budget for that before you budget for a desk. The city has been officially called Mbombela since 2009, meaning a crowded place in siSwati, and both names remain in daily use: the stadium and the municipality carry one, while most people and many road signs still use the other. It matters when searching for an address or a service provider, because a listing under one name may not surface under the other. siSwati and Xitsonga are the first languages here rather than Afrikaans, though English handles all business.
nelspruit.gettingAround: You need a car in Nelspruit. Minibus taxis run the main routes and are cheap but are aimed at commuters rather than visitors, and there is no useful municipal bus network. Uber and Bolt operate in town and cover most trips for $3 to $7. The town itself is compact around Louis Trichardt Street, but the reason to be here is what surrounds it: the Numbi and Malelane gates into Kruger are 50 to 65km, the Lowveld National Botanical Garden is on the edge of town where the Crocodile and Nels rivers meet, Sudwala Caves 35km, and the Blyde River Canyon and God's Window about 100km north on the escarpment. Barberton, forty five minutes southwest, sits under the Makhonjwa Mountains, listed by UNESCO in 2018 for holding some of the oldest exposed rock on the planet at around three and a half billion years. Geologists come here to study the earliest traces of life, and NASA has used the same rocks as a stand-in for Mars. The Geotrail is a marked drive over the pass into Eswatini with panels at each stop, and it is one of the stranger things available on a Saturday.
nelspruit.visas: South Africa gives most Western nationalities 90 days visa free on arrival, extendable once by another 90 days through VFS, though the extension process is slow and needs to be started well before expiry. In 2024 South Africa introduced a remote work visa for people earning above a set annual threshold from a foreign employer, valid up to three years, which is the first proper nomad route on the continent; the requirements and the threshold have been revised more than once, so check the current regulations rather than a summary. There is also a general work visa and a retired person visa. Overstaying triggers a ban, and enforcement is real. The border position is the practical visa fact here. Eswatini is about an hour away through Jeppe's Reef and Mozambique about ninety minutes through Komatipoort, so a reset here means a day on the road rather than a flight, which very few South African bases can say. Both are separate immigration regimes with their own requirements, and Mozambique in particular has revised what it grants at the post several times, so the trip needs checking afresh rather than repeating whatever worked last quarter.
nelspruit.bestTime: Nelspruit sits in the Lowveld at about 660m and is warm year round. April to September is the season: dry, sunny, highs of 24C to 27C, cool nights, and it is also the best time for Kruger because the bush thins out and animals concentrate at water. October to March is the wet summer, with highs near 30C, high humidity and heavy afternoon thunderstorms, and the malaria risk in the Lowveld and Kruger is at its highest then, which is worth a conversation with a travel clinic. The escarpment above the town is often in cloud in summer. June and July nights can drop to 8C, so bring something warm. The Lowveld's seasons are read off the bush rather than the calendar. By August the grass is down and the trees are bare, which is why the game viewing peaks then, and the first rains in October green everything within a fortnight and the animals disperse. The Panorama Route works the other way round: the waterfalls on the escarpment are worth the drive in the wet months and disappointing in the dry, so the two halves of what this town offers peak in opposite seasons.
nelspruit.prosCons: Nelspruit is the most practical base there is for Kruger and the Panorama Route, with an international airport 27km away, good fibre, a proper hospital, big supermarkets, and costs that sit well under those of Cape Town or Johannesburg. The Lowveld climate means shorts in July. The botanical garden and the river gorges are in the town itself. There is a car requirement, crime rates that need ordinary South African precautions rather than paranoia but do need them, seasonal malaria risk in the surrounding Lowveld, a nomad community of essentially nobody, and a town centre that is functional rather than charming. Load shedding led that list for years and came off it in 2025. Kruger's rhino are the hard fact behind the safari brochure. The park held the largest white rhino population on earth and lost most of it to poaching across roughly a decade, the count falling by thousands, and the response has run to dehorning, armed anti-poaching units and relocations to private reserves. A visitor will see fences, patrols and helicopters and may see no rhino at all. The stadium at the edge of town is the lighter counterpoint, built for the 2010 World Cup with floodlight pylons shaped like giraffes and seating striped like zebra, which is either charming or absurd depending on the day.
nelspruit.whoFor: The bush is the reason to be in South Africa here: wildlife photographers, guides, researchers, or anyone planning to be in and out of Kruger for weeks rather than days. It is also a reasonable landing point for the new remote work visa if you want space, sun and a low cost base rather than a city. It works far better with a car and a backup power setup than without. Walkable urban life is not what a Lowveld town built around a highway offers, the nightlife is thin, no coworking community exists, and the nearest beach is in Mozambique. Cape Town remains the obvious South African choice for a first stay, at roughly double the cost. It suits a geologist as squarely as a wildlife photographer, which is not a sentence many towns earn: the Makhonjwa rocks are a working research site and the Barberton greenstone belt turns up in undergraduate textbooks worldwide. It suits somebody with a Mozambique or Eswatini interest, since both are within a morning. Anybody wanting to live without a car should look elsewhere entirely, because the distances here are the whole proposition and none of them are walkable.

oran.costOfLiving: Oran runs about $700 a month for one person, though what you actually pay depends heavily on how you change money, since Algeria's parallel exchange rate differs substantially from the bank rate and most visitors use the former. A furnished apartment near the Front de Mer or in Hai Es Salem is $200 to $400. Food is cheap: a plate of couscous or a sandwich karantika is a dollar or two, a sit-down restaurant meal $6 to $12, and coffee well under a dollar. There is no real coworking market. Home ADSL or fibre from Algerie Telecom is $15 to $30 a month. Local transport costs pennies and taxis a few dollars. Cards issued abroad do not work here in any practical sense, so the money for a whole stay arrives as notes and gets changed in stages rather than drawn down as needed. Prices lift through July and August when the diaspora comes back from France, and a flat let by the week in that period earns what it would otherwise earn in a month. Cigarettes, coffee and bread anchor the bottom of the cost of living and have barely moved in years, which is why the monthly figure looks the way it does beside the price of anything imported.
oran.whereToWork: Oran has very little coworking, a handful of small startup spaces linked to the university and incubator scene, so the practical answer is a flat with a fixed connection. Algerie Telecom's fibre rollout has reached parts of the city and delivers usable speeds for $15 to $30 a month, while older ADSL lines are slow and worth avoiding if you can choose. Mobile data from Djezzy, Mobilis or Ooredoo is inexpensive and 4G coverage in the city is good, which makes tethering a reasonable backup. International bandwidth is the weak point: local browsing is fine but video calls to Europe or North America can be unstable at peak hours. Test before committing. A national startup label introduced in 2020 gives registered young companies tax relief and access to a state fund, and the incubator space attached to it is most of what passes for a shared-desk sector in the country. Power is dependable and the outages that trouble neighbouring countries are not a feature. Printing, scanning and stamped copies remain a daily part of doing business, so the photocopy shops beside any administrative building are busier than the cafes.
oran.gettingAround: Oran has a modern tram line running from Es Senia to Sidi Maarouf across the city, which is clean, cheap and the easiest way to cover distance. Buses fill in the rest and cost pennies, while yellow taxis and shared taxis are a dollar or two for most trips; agree the fare first. The centre around Place du 1er Novembre and the Front de Mer is walkable, and the climb up to Santa Cruz above the bay is a walk or a short taxi. Es Senia airport is 10km south with flights to Paris, Marseille, Barcelona, Istanbul and the Gulf. Trains run east to Algiers in about four hours. Ferries cross to Spain and to the south of France and carry a great many people who would rather not fly, particularly families travelling with a car and a season of luggage. Booking a sailing in July takes months of notice. Driving in the city is assertive rather than hostile and the lane markings are advisory, which is worth understanding before renting anything. The coastal rail service is slow and cheap, with carriages comfortable enough to work in.
oran.visas: Algeria is among the harder countries to enter independently. Most nationalities need a visa arranged in advance at an embassy, with a hotel booking or an invitation letter, proof of funds and a specific itinerary; processing is slow and refusals are not explained. A visa on arrival exists but only for organised tourism in the far south around Djanet and Tamanrasset, and it does not apply to Oran. There is no digital nomad visa and no remote work provision. Extensions are handled by the local wilaya police and are not straightforward. Anyone planning this should start the application months ahead and expect the paperwork to be the hardest part of the trip.
oran.bestTime: Oran has a proper Mediterranean climate and is comfortable for most of the year. April to June and September to early November are the best windows, with highs of 22C to 28C, warm sea and clear light. July and August are hot at 30C to 33C, humid on the coast, and the city fills with Algerians on holiday and with the diaspora returning from France, which pushes up prices and fills the beaches west towards Ain El Turk. Winter from December to February is mild at 16C to 18C but this is when the rain falls, mostly in short heavy bursts. A sirocco off the Sahara can spike temperatures sharply in any warm month. Rai came out of the cabarets here in the 1970s and the city still treats the music as its own property, with concerts through the summer advertised locally and almost nowhere else. The sea stays swimmable into November, which is longer than most of the northern shore manages. Spring brings a short green season across the hills behind the city that has gone entirely by June and surprises anyone who expected desert.
oran.prosCons: Oran is a large, lively Mediterranean port, with a century of layered Spanish, Ottoman and French building, a real beach coast running west of the city, and the birthplace of rai music, all of it at a cost most Mediterranean cities cannot come anywhere near. The Santa Cruz fort above the bay is one of the great views in North Africa. Food is excellent and cheap and the city has genuine energy. The visa is a serious obstacle in itself, international internet is unreliable, there is no coworking and no foreign community, alcohol is restricted and expensive, English is little spoken so French or Arabic is close to necessary, and cash and card infrastructure barely works for foreigners.
oran.whoFor: A French or Arabic speaker with a reason to be in Algeria and the patience to get the visa: family ties, research, journalism, or a wish to see the least touristed large city on the Mediterranean and a willingness to work for it. If you can handle bureaucracy and carry enough cash, it is one of the more rewarding places on this list. Stable video calls are not something Algeria's connection delivers, French is required throughout, no nomad community exists, and the visa process makes booking a flight for next month an unrealistic plan rather than a spontaneous one. Tunis and Casablanca deliver a similar coast with a fraction of the friction. Six weeks is a more realistic plan than six months, given how much of the effort goes into the paperwork and how little of it can be repeated easily. Anyone with family here has a completely different experience of the city from anyone without, and the gap is wider than in most places.

constantine.costOfLiving: Constantine runs about $650 a month for one person, a little under Oran, and as elsewhere in Algeria the figure depends on whether you change money at the bank rate or the parallel rate that most visitors use. A furnished apartment in the newer districts is $180 to $350, and older flats in the centre less. Eating is very cheap: street food is a dollar or two and a full restaurant meal $6 to $11. There is no coworking sector to budget for. Fixed internet from Algerie Telecom costs $15 to $30 a month. The cable car and buses cost pennies, and taxis a couple of dollars. Heating is a real winter cost at this altitude. Two exchange rates have coexisted for years, the bank one and the street one, and the spread between them effectively sets two price levels inside the same city, which is why almost every foreign visitor changes money outside a bank. Bread, semolina, milk and fuel are all subsidised and cost a fraction of the same basket across the Mediterranean, which is what holds the monthly figure down even as imported goods stay dear. Rent is often paid a year in advance rather than monthly, and that arrangement surprises new arrivals more than the price does.
constantine.whereToWork: Constantine has no coworking market to speak of, though the university, one of the largest in Algeria, has generated a small incubator scene. Practically, you work from a flat, so the fixed connection matters more than anything else: Algerie Telecom fibre reaches parts of the city at usable speeds for $15 to $30 a month, while the old copper lines are slow. Mobile 4G from Djezzy, Mobilis and Ooredoo is cheap and works well in the city, and tethering is a sensible backup. The recurring problem is international routing rather than local bandwidth, so calls to Europe can stutter at peak times even on a good line. Test before you commit to a month. The weekend falls on Friday and Saturday, so a Sunday here is an ordinary working day and a European Friday afternoon reaches nobody at all. Arabic is official, while business, engineering and most of the older professional class run in French, and English is gaining ground in the universities and almost nowhere else yet. The university is among the largest in the country by enrolment, which gives the city a young population and a bookshop trade that outlasts most of the retail around it.
constantine.gettingAround: Constantine is built on a plateau split by the Rhummel gorge, so the topography does most of the work of deciding how you move. Seven bridges cross the chasm, including the Sidi M'Cid suspension bridge of 1912 and the modern Salah Bey viaduct, and walking between them is the best way to understand the city. A cable car runs from the centre across to the hospital side and is cheap and quick. A tram line serves the newer districts, buses cover the rest, and taxis cost a couple of dollars. Mohamed Boudiaf airport is 9km south with flights to Paris, Marseille, Istanbul and the Gulf. Algiers is about four hours by road.
constantine.visas: Algeria requires most nationalities to obtain a visa before travel from an embassy or consulate, supported by a hotel booking or an invitation, proof of funds and an itinerary. Processing takes weeks and refusals come without explanation. The visa on arrival introduced for tourism applies only to the Saharan south around Djanet and Tamanrasset and is of no use for Constantine. There is no digital nomad visa and no provision for remote work. Extensions go through the wilaya police and are slow. Practically, this is a destination you plan several months ahead, and the paperwork is a larger obstacle than anything you will meet once you arrive. Foreign currency above a threshold has to be declared on the arrival form, and that declaration matters on the way out, since leaving with more than you brought and no paperwork is easier to avoid than to explain. Hotel bookings are checked against the application rather than assumed, and a mismatch between the two is a common reason for refusal. Anyone invited by a company or a relative needs the invitation legalised locally before it is of any use at a consulate.
constantine.bestTime: Constantine sits at about 640m on the edge of the Tell Atlas, which gives it a genuinely continental climate rather than a Mediterranean one. April to June and September to October are the good months, with highs of 22C to 28C and clear air over the gorge. July and August are hot and dry at 33C to 35C, hotter than the coast because there is no sea breeze. Winter is the surprise: December to February brings highs of only 11C to 13C, cold nights, heavy rain and occasional snow, and older buildings are poorly heated. The gorge is at its most dramatic after winter rain, when the Rhummel actually runs. Ramadan changes the working day completely, with offices on short hours and restaurants shut until sunset, and the date moves eleven days earlier each year, so it is worth checking against the calendar before booking anything. The malouf festival brings the city's Andalusian music tradition into public for a few days a year. Snow settles on the plateau in some winters and the city handles it badly, since neither the roads nor the buildings were built with it in mind.
constantine.prosCons: Nothing about Constantine resembles anywhere else, and the setting is the whole of it. A city of half a million built on a rock, cut off from the plateau by a gorge two hundred metres deep, crossed by seven bridges, continuously inhabited since it was Cirta and the Numidian capital. The Emir Abdelkader mosque, the Ahmed Bey palace and the malouf music tradition are all here, and it costs $650 a month. The visa is a major obstacle of its own, winters are cold and wet in badly heated buildings, the international links are unreliable, neither coworking nor a foreign circle exists, English is barely spoken, and card payments are largely unusable.
constantine.whoFor: French or Arabic, a specific interest in North African history, architecture or music, and the patience for Algerian bureaucracy. It is a spectacular place to spend a month if your work is self-contained and you do not depend on video calls. Photographers in particular will find few cities that reward walking as much. Reliable international connectivity is not available, French carries daily life and English does not, there are no other remote workers to find, and Algerian visas make short-notice travel close to impossible to arrange. If North Africa is the goal and the visa is the obstacle, Tunisia and Morocco offer most of the same appeal on arrival. A month is the right unit here, long enough to stop being a visitor in a city that takes some reading and short enough that the visa does not become the dominant fact of the stay. Anyone who arrives in winter should budget for heating that the building will not provide.

sfax.costOfLiving: Sfax runs about $650 a month for one person, a little cheaper than Tunis and considerably cheaper than the coastal resort towns. A furnished one-bedroom apartment near the centre or in Sfax El Jadida is $200 to $350, and further out $130 to $220. Food is inexpensive: a plate of couscous or a bowl of lablabi is $2 to $4, a full restaurant meal $8 to $14, and the fish landed at the port is both excellent and cheap. There is a small coworking scene at $60 to $120 a month. Fixed internet is $15 to $30 for a usable connection. Louages and buses cost pennies and taxis a couple of dollars. Bread, fuel and a handful of staples are subsidised, which is why the gap between a local shopping basket and an imported one is so wide, and why the price of a baguette has almost nothing to do with the cost of making it. The power company invoices on a two month cycle and the tariff steps up in bands, so a summer with air conditioning lands in a higher band and costs more than twice a mild one. A municipal charge on the dwelling is billed annually and usually falls to the tenant.
sfax.whereToWork: Sfax has a modest but genuine coworking sector, driven by the University of Sfax and a local software industry that is larger than the city's reputation suggests, with desks at $60 to $120 a month. Fixed internet from Tunisie Telecom, Ooredoo or Orange runs $15 to $30 monthly, with fibre available in parts of the city and ADSL elsewhere; ask which one an apartment actually has. Mobile 4G is cheap, widely available and a reasonable primary connection if you are staying a few weeks. International routing to Europe is decent, better than most of North Africa, and video calls generally hold. Cafes are plentiful but are social spaces first. Business runs in French and in Arabic, and a meeting will switch between them mid sentence without anyone noticing, which is harder to follow than either language on its own. The city has a reputation across the country for commerce and for keeping its money, and the family firms that earned it are not advertising for foreign staff. There is an export company regime that lets a business incorporated locally sell abroad under a lighter tax and customs arrangement, and it is the structure most outsourcing operations here use.
sfax.gettingAround: The medina at the centre of Sfax is compact, still enclosed by its walls, and walking is the only way to see it. Beyond that the city is spread out and you will use louages, the shared inter-city taxis, or the yellow city taxis which are metered and cheap at $1 to $3. A local rail line, the Metro du Sahel equivalent here being the Sfax suburban service, plus buses cover the suburbs. The ferry to the Kerkennah Islands leaves from the port and takes about an hour, and is the standard weekend escape. Sfax-Thyna airport is 6km out with limited flights; Tunis is three hours by train or road for wider connections. A car is the thing most residents aspire to and the thing a visitor least needs, since the shared taxis leave when they fill and go everywhere, which in practice is more frequent than any timetable. Cycling is rare and the drivers are not expecting it. The medina is safe to walk at night and is one of the few in the region where doing so involves no tourist economy at all, just people going home. Through traffic from the port keeps the southern approach heavy with lorries at every hour.
sfax.visas: Tunisia is one of the easier North African countries to enter. Most European, North American, Japanese and several other nationalities get 90 days visa free on arrival, with no advance paperwork. Extensions beyond 90 days require an application to the local police and are not routinely granted, and overstaying carries a fine payable on departure. There is no digital nomad visa, though Tunisia has discussed one for several years. A long-stay residence permit, the carte de sejour, exists but is aimed at people with local employment, study or family ties. Most remote workers here simply use the 90 days and leave, which is straightforward given the flight connections to Europe. The currency is the constraint nobody mentions: the dinar cannot legally leave the country and cannot be changed anywhere outside it, so converting back at the airport requires the receipts from converting in, and without them the money stays. Keep every exchange slip. Cards work in the cities and cash is still what most of the country runs on. A departure stamp is given without fuss and there is no exit formality beyond it, which makes the ninety day pattern as simple in practice as it looks on paper.
sfax.bestTime: Sfax has a hot semi-arid climate, drier than Tunis and drier than most of the Tunisian coast. April, May, October and November are the best months, with highs of 22C to 28C and comfortable evenings. July and August are hot at 33C to 36C and humid near the water, and the city empties somewhat as people head to Kerkennah or the beaches. Winter from December to February is mild at 16C to 18C, with the year's modest rainfall arriving then in short bursts. The olive harvest runs from November into January and is the region's economic heartbeat, since Sfax sits at the centre of one of the largest olive-growing areas in the world.
sfax.prosCons: Sfax is a working Tunisian city rather than a resort town, with a medina that is intact, walled and almost entirely free of tourists, a genuine software and university sector of its own, excellent seafood, and a monthly cost of living that comes to around $650. The visa is free on arrival for most people, flights to Europe are short, and the Kerkennah Islands are an hour away by ferry. It is an industrial port and it looks like one in several places, air quality near the phosphate plants is genuinely poor, the summers are hot, the foreign presence is small, English is limited so French helps enormously, and there is very little nightlife.
sfax.whoFor: North Africa without the tourist infrastructure, some French, and a preference for a real city over a pretty one. The combination of visa-free entry, low cost, short flights to Europe and a functioning local tech scene makes it a more practical base than its profile suggests. A month or two in spring or in autumn is the sensible window, and that is time enough to learn whether a city which makes no effort for visitors suits you. This is a working industrial port rather than a beach town, the nightlife is negligible, French and Arabic do the work rather than English, and no community of other remote workers has formed here. If Tunisia is the goal and company matters more than authenticity, Tunis and Hammamet are where the foreigners are.

portsaid.costOfLiving: Port Said runs about $600 a month for one person, which is cheap even by Egyptian standards for a coastal city. A furnished apartment near the corniche or in the centre is $150 to $300, and away from the water considerably less. Food costs very little: koshari is under a dollar, a plate of grilled fish from one of the port restaurants $4 to $8, and a full meal for two $10 to $16. There is no coworking market to budget for. Internet from Telecom Egypt or one of the mobile operators is $12 to $25 a month. Microbuses and the canal ferry cost pennies, and taxis a dollar or two. The Egyptian pound is what makes any figure here provisional. It has been devalued repeatedly since 2016 and floated again in March 2024, roughly halving against the dollar within days, which is excellent for somebody earning abroad and brutal for anybody paid locally. Landlords increasingly ask for dollars or index the rent, and a long lease signed in pounds at a fixed rate is a bet the landlord is unlikely to take.
portsaid.whereToWork: Port Said has no coworking sector, so this means an apartment with a working connection. Telecom Egypt's fixed lines cover the city and fibre has reached parts of it, giving 30 to 100 Mbps for $12 to $25 a month; older copper connections in the historic district are much slower and worth checking before you sign anything. Mobile data from Vodafone, Orange or Etisalat is cheap and 4G coverage is good, making tethering a sound backup. Egypt periodically throttles or blocks VoIP services, so test whichever calling platform your work depends on before committing to a stay. Cafes along the corniche have wifi but are places to sit rather than to work. The city's other economy is the free zone. Port Said has held duty-free status since the 1970s and Egyptians still travel here to buy imported goods, which is why shops in the centre carry electronics and appliances at prices the rest of the country does not see. For a remote worker the practical upshot is that a replacement laptop or router can be bought here rather than requiring a trip to Cairo, which is not true of most Egyptian cities this size.
portsaid.gettingAround: Port Said is long and narrow, squeezed between the Mediterranean and the canal, so the centre is walkable and the corniche runs its full length. Microbuses cover the length of the city for pennies and are how most residents move. Taxis cost a dollar or two and app services operate patchily. The free ferry across the canal to Port Fouad runs constantly and takes a few minutes, and is worth doing simply to watch the shipping. Cairo is about three hours by road or bus, Ismailia an hour and a half south along the canal, and Damietta an hour west. There is no useful passenger airport; fly into Cairo. The ferry to Port Fouad crosses between continents. This bank is in Africa and the far one is in Asia, so a free five minute crossing that residents make to visit relatives is also an intercontinental journey, which is the sort of thing this city does without remarking on it. The canal itself has no locks and runs at sea level for its whole length, which is why the hulls slide past the end of a street at what looks like walking pace, apparently travelling overland.
portsaid.visas: Egypt issues a 30-day tourist visa on arrival to most Western nationalities for $25 in cash at the airport, or through an e-visa applied for online in advance, which is the smoother option. Extensions are handled at the Mogamma or a local passport office and are usually granted, though the process takes a morning and some patience. There is no digital nomad visa. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a tourist visa is not addressed in Egyptian law and is not enforced against, but it is not authorised either. Longer stays are normally built on repeat entries or on a residence permit tied to study, work or property.
