zermatt.visas: Switzerland is not a member of the European Union, but it is part of the Schengen Area, so the familiar Schengen rules apply for most visitors: you can generally stay up to 90 days within any rolling 180-day period without a visa if you hold a passport from an eligible country, and days spent elsewhere in Schengen count against the same allowance. That window suits a scenic slow-travel stint or a ski season chunk, but it is not a route to living here long term. Anything beyond 90 days, or any intention to work locally, moves you into Swiss residence and permit territory, which is its own strict, quota-driven system tied to employment, study or means. Rules change and individual situations vary, so treat this as editorial orientation rather than legal advice, and confirm current requirements with official Swiss sources or a qualified advisor before you commit.
zermatt.bestTime: Zermatt is a genuine two-season destination. Winter, roughly December to April, is prime time for world-class skiing across an enormous linked area that spills over to Cervinia in Italy, with reliable snow, buzzing apres-ski and the village at its liveliest. Summer, around July to September, is the sweet spot for hikers: hundreds of kilometers of trails open up, the Matterhorn stands crisp against clear skies on good days, and you can even ski on the glacier in the mornings. The shoulder seasons, late spring and late autumn, are the quiet, cheaper flip side: fewer crowds and calmer streets, but also reduced lift service and some hotels, restaurants and cable cars closed for maintenance. For working and slow travel, summer or the early-winter lull offer the best balance of open infrastructure, good weather and slightly softer prices.
zermatt.prosCons: Zermatt trades on a simple, powerful promise: some of the most breathtaking alpine scenery on earth, wrapped in Swiss efficiency. The car-free streets are clean and quiet, the air is crisp, safety is excellent, and the internet is genuinely fast and reliable, which is more than many prettier places manage. Getting into the mountains is effortless thanks to the rail and cable-car network. The honest downside is cost, which is punishing, and character: this is a tourism-driven resort with a tiny permanent community, so it can feel transient and, outside the apres-ski scene, the nightlife is quiet. It is also strongly seasonal, with a different rhythm and different closures depending on when you arrive. None of that is a flaw so much as a fit question. Come for scenery, air and activity, not for a bustling social scene or a bargain.
zermatt.whoFor: Zermatt suits a specific kind of nomad: the scenic, active, well-funded slow traveler who values mountains and quiet over cost and crowds. If you can work a focused morning and then be on a glacier or a high trail by lunch, and if your budget comfortably absorbs Swiss resort prices, few places reward you more. It is ideal for skiers and hikers, for couples or solo travelers who want calm and nature, and for anyone who treats a stay here as a memorable splurge rather than an economical base. It is a poor fit for budget nomads, for people who need a large ready-made social or coworking community, and for night-owls seeking a big-city scene. Come with the right expectations, a healthy budget and a love of the outdoors, and Zermatt is unforgettable. Come chasing cheap rent or nightlife, and you will be disappointed.

zhangjiajie.costOfLiving: Zhangjiajie is genuinely affordable, even by Chinese standards, because it sits in Hunan province away from the pricey coastal megacities. A single nomad can live comfortably on roughly $600 to $1,200 a month, with the higher end covering a nicer apartment near Wulingyuan, frequent restaurant meals, and park passes. Rent is the biggest variable: a simple studio in the city center runs cheaper than a tourist-facing serviced room near the forest park gates. Food is a highlight and a bargain, since spicy Hunan and Tujia dishes at local canteens cost only a few dollars. Your main splurges will be national park admission, cable cars, and the occasional intercity trip. Bring a payment plan, because most transactions expect mobile pay.
zhangjiajie.whereToWork: Be honest with yourself before committing: this is a scenic tourist city, not a nomad hub, so there is no real coworking scene. You will work from hotel rooms, apartments, and a handful of laptop-friendly cafes. Local fixed-line internet is generally decent and fast in the city and in Wulingyuan town, and most hotels and guesthouses offer reliable wifi. The catch is China's Great Firewall: Google, Gmail, WhatsApp, Instagram, Western news, and many work tools are blocked, so you will almost certainly need a reputable VPN installed and tested before you arrive. Download and configure it in advance, because VPN provider sites are themselves often blocked once you are inside China. Mobile data on a local SIM is fast and cheap and works well as a backup for calls and hotspotting.
zhangjiajie.gettingAround: The name Zhangjiajie covers two things worth separating: the prefecture city center (Yongding district) and the famous scenery about 32 kilometers away around Wulingyuan. Most visitors base themselves in Wulingyuan town, the main gateway to Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, since it puts you minutes from the entrances. Inside the park, free eco-shuttle buses ferry you between valleys, and cable cars, the Bailong glass elevator, and mountaintop monorails handle the vertical distances. Between the city and the park, regular intercity buses and taxis are cheap and frequent. Tianmen Mountain, with its glass skywalk and 99-bend road, sits right beside the city center and is reached by a long cable car from downtown. The city has its own airport (DYG) and a high-speed rail station connecting to Changsha and beyond.
zhangjiajie.visas: China is one of the more demanding destinations for entry, and Zhangjiajie has no special status that changes that. Most nomads arrive on a tourist (L) visa, typically arranged in advance through an embassy, consulate, or authorized visa center, often with proof of itinerary, accommodation, and funds. Rules shift, and some nationalities benefit from limited visa-free transit windows or specific bilateral exemptions, so always verify the current policy for your passport before booking. China does not offer a dedicated digital-nomad visa, and working locally on a tourist visa is not permitted, so treat this as a place to visit and do remote work quietly rather than a long-term base. This is general editorial guidance, not legal advice; confirm everything with an official source close to your travel date.
zhangjiajie.bestTime: Spring (April to June) and autumn (September to November) are the clear winners, with mild temperatures, greener forests, and the best odds of the atmospheric mist that drapes the sandstone pillars and makes the scenery so unforgettable. That signature fog is common year-round and is part of the appeal, though it can occasionally hide the peaks entirely. Summers are hot, humid, and coincide with peak domestic tourism, so expect long queues at cable cars and the Bailong elevator and busy shuttle buses. Winters are cold and quieter, and the higher peaks like Tianzi Mountain sometimes get a dusting of snow that looks spectacular but can close attractions. If you want the classic misty pillars with manageable crowds, aim for weekdays in shoulder season and start early each day.
zhangjiajie.prosCons: Zhangjiajie's appeal is simple and enormous: it is one of the most jaw-dropping natural landscapes on earth, the quartz-sandstone pillars that inspired the floating mountains of Avatar, all for a very low cost of living and with excellent everyday safety. The trade-offs are equally clear. This is a tourism-focused city, not a community of remote workers, so you will not find the cafes-full-of-laptops scene of Chiang Mai or Lisbon. The Great Firewall means constant reliance on a VPN, English is limited outside tourist channels, and China's visa regime is comparatively strict. Crowds at peak times are intense. Come for the scenery, the food, and the affordability; do not come expecting a plug-and-play nomad ecosystem or frictionless access to your usual Western apps.
zhangjiajie.whoFor: Zhangjiajie suits the nomad who ranks nature and novelty above networking, and who can work independently without needing a coworking crowd. If you are an experienced China traveler, or at least comfortable with a VPN, mobile payments, and translation apps, you will get enormous value from a base this cheap next to scenery this dramatic. It is ideal for hikers, photographers, and anyone who wants their off-hours filled with cable cars, glass skywalks, and misty ridgelines rather than co-working happy hours. It is a poor fit for first-time nomads who want easy English, an instant community, or hassle-free connectivity to Western tools. Treat it as a spectacular medium-length stop within a wider China or Asia itinerary rather than a year-round home base.

abudhabi.costOfLiving: Abu Dhabi sits at the expensive end of the Gulf spectrum. Expect to spend significantly more than in Southeast Asia or Eastern Europe, though you get serious infrastructure and zero income tax in return. Rent: A one-bedroom in central areas like Al Maryah Island, Corniche, or Al Khalidiya runs $1,770-2,450/month. Moving further out to Al Nahyan, Mushrif, or Khalifa City drops that to $1,090-1,500/month. Groceries: Shopping at Lulu or Carrefour costs roughly $270-325/month if you buy local and regional brands. Imported Western products push costs noticeably higher. Eating out: A meal at a mid-range restaurant costs $14-27. Budget shawarma or cafeteria meals run $4-8. Business lunches are generally reasonable at $16-25. Coworking hot-desk: $135-270/month for a dedicated hot desk membership. Local transport: Public buses cost $0.50-1.50 per ride ($0.55-1.37). Taxis and ride-hailing apps run $4-11 per trip depending on distance. Most nomads rely on taxis or a car. Total monthly range: $2,450-4,900/month covers a comfortable nomad setup with mid-range housing. Budget-conscious choices bring this closer to $2,040; a more comfortable lifestyle climbs to $5,450+ ($5,450).
abudhabi.whereToWork: Abu Dhabi has a solid and growing coworking scene, though it is smaller than Dubai's. The main options are concentrated around Al Maryah Island, Al Khalidiya, Reem Island, and Yas Island. Haibu Space at Abu Dhabi Mall is one of the largest, with a 30,000 sq ft facility, daily passes from $26, and monthly memberships from $260. Cloud Spaces at Yas Mall offers a quieter environment starting at $33/day. Altspace in Al Khalidiya's Shining Towers is a premium 24/7 option with gym access. WeWork operates at Hub71 on Al Maryah Island, suited to those wanting a more corporate feel. GlassQube on Reem Island and at the ADGM is popular with finance and tech workers. Cafe work culture exists but is more limited than in Bali or Bangkok. Staff at most cafes tolerate laptops, but you will rarely find a packed "laptop cafe" scene. Good options include Joud Coffee (Al Muntazah), Coffee Architecture (Saadiyat), and The Third Place Cafe (Corniche Road). WiFi in coworking spaces is reliably fast; Abu Dhabi averages around 220 Mbps download on fixed broadband. Hotel lobbies and malls also have decent connectivity. Note that VoIP calls (WhatsApp, FaceTime) over public networks are technically restricted in the UAE, so a VPN is standard practice for video calls.
abudhabi.gettingAround: Abu Dhabi is not a walking city. Distances between key areas are long, summer heat makes outdoor walking impractical for most of the year, and pavements are patchy outside the Corniche and central grid. Plan your life around transport. Buses run on an extensive network using the Hafilat smart card, with most rides costing $0.50-1.50. They are air-conditioned and reliable but slow due to infrequent stops and traffic. Taxis are plentiful and regulated, identifiable by silver bodies and yellow roofs. Careem and InDriver also operate ride-hailing in the city. Taxis are the practical default for most nomads. Car rental or ownership is common among long-term residents. Roads are good and parking is generally free or cheap outside malls. There is no metro in Abu Dhabi yet. A metro system is planned but not operational as of 2026. Airport: Abu Dhabi International Airport (AUH) is around 30-40 minutes from the city center by taxi ($16-25). No direct metro connection exists currently. The new Terminal A opened in late 2023 and significantly improved the airport experience.
abudhabi.visas: Citizens of most Western countries (US, UK, EU, Australia, Canada) enter the UAE visa-free for 30-90 days depending on nationality. Most get 30 days on arrival, extendable once for another 30 days from within the UAE. The UAE offers a dedicated Remote Work Visa (sometimes called the digital nomad visa), administered by Abu Dhabi. It grants one-year residency without a UAE employer or local sponsor. Requirements include proof of employment by a company outside the UAE, a minimum average monthly income of $3,500, and valid health insurance covering your stay. The processing fee is around $287 and takes 15-20 days. It is renewable for a second year. The UAE also offers a Golden Visa for investors, highly skilled professionals, and exceptional talent, granting 10-year residency. Requirements and costs vary. Always confirm current requirements and entry rules with the official UAE government portal or your nearest UAE consulate before traveling, as rules change.
abudhabi.bestTime: Abu Dhabi has one of the harshest summer climates of any major city. From late May through September, temperatures routinely hit 40-45°C (104-113°F) with high humidity. These months are survivable only because the city is entirely air-conditioned, but outdoor life essentially stops. Expect sky-high electricity bills if renting, and limited motivation to leave your apartment. The sweet spot for remote workers is November through March. Daytime temperatures sit at a pleasant 22-28°C (72-82°F), evenings are cool, and the Corniche and outdoor areas are actually enjoyable. This is peak tourist season so hotel rates rise, but for longer-term stays you get full access to what the city has to offer. April-May and September-October are shoulder months: warm but manageable, with fewer crowds and slightly lower rents. July and August are the most brutal months and best avoided unless you have a compelling reason to be there.
abudhabi.whoFor:
Abu Dhabi works well for remote workers who value safety, stability, and strong infrastructure above all else. If you earn in USD or EUR and want a tax-free base with excellent flight connections, fast internet, and a genuinely cosmopolitan lifestyle, the city delivers. It suits people who prefer a calmer, less chaotic pace than Dubai while still having access to world-class restaurants, cultural venues like the Louvre Abu Dhabi, and beach access on Saadiyat Island.

It is also a good fit for remote professionals who travel frequently for work, given Etihad's strong hub connections, and for anyone who wants to use the UAE Remote Work Visa to establish legal residency in a low-tax jurisdiction.

Skip Abu Dhabi if you are on a tight budget, hate car dependency, want a vibrant street-level nomad scene with packed cafes and spontaneous community events, or if the summer heat will genuinely trap you indoors for months. Dubai offers more social infrastructure for nomads; Southeast Asia offers a fraction of the cost. Abu Dhabi sits in a specific niche and rewards those who fit it.

alexandria.costOfLiving: Alexandria is significantly cheaper than Cairo for equivalent accommodation, and dramatically cheaper than most European or North American cities. The Egyptian pound trades at roughly 49-50 EGP per USD as of mid-2026, so small amounts in local currency go a long way. Expect to pay $125-175 per month for a furnished one-bedroom in a central area like Sporting, Roushdy, or Sidi Gaber. Head further out toward Smouha or Saba Pasha and you can find similar apartments for $59-88. Groceries from local markets run around $23-39 per month if you cook Egyptian staples. A meal at a local foul and falafel spot costs under $2; a full seafood dinner for two at a mid-range restaurant runs $12-20. A hot-desk at one of the city's coworking spaces costs roughly $88-115 per month. The tram and local buses are very cheap, with a monthly transit pass around $13; taxis and ride-hail apps add perhaps $16-29 per month depending on your habits. Home broadband averages around $12 per month. A comfortable but modest nomad budget lands in the range of $650-1,100 per month all-in, or $1,100-1,600 if you want a nicer apartment, regular restaurant meals, and coworking membership.
alexandria.whereToWork: Alexandria has a small but functional coworking scene. Workstation in Smouha is one of the most established options, offering 50-plus seats, 200 Mbps internet, four private rooms, a printer, lockers, and a full kitchen. Hive Space in Roushdy provides a quieter atmosphere with complimentary drinks, a lounge, yoga studio, and a rooftop terrace, and draws consistent praise for its internet reliability. Flux Coworking Space on El-Horya Street in the Loran district is the largest single space in the city, with capacity for over 100 people, though some users report WiFi inconsistency during peak hours. Cafe culture has grown considerably, and chains like Zanilli's Coffee (branches in Sporting, Montazah, and near City Center Mall) are popular among remote workers for their hours and seating. That said, many traditional coffeehouses do not have reliable WiFi and are better suited for reading than video calls. The honest WiFi picture: home and coworking broadband in Alexandria delivers 15-40 Mbps download in better spaces, which is enough for Zoom and cloud work. Mobile data via Vodafone, Orange, or Etisalat SIM cards fills the gaps reliably. Public cafe WiFi is hit-or-miss, so carry a local SIM as a hotspot backup, especially if you are on calls.
alexandria.gettingAround: Alexandria runs along a long coastal strip, which means much of the city is linear and navigable. The tram network (Raml Tram and Al-Madina line) is cheap, slow, and often crowded, but covers the central coast. City buses and minibuses serve most districts at very low fares but can be confusing to navigate without some Arabic. Ride-hail apps (Uber and Careem both operate here) are the most practical option for tourists and nomads; fares are low by Western standards. The Corniche is pleasant to walk in good weather, and central neighborhoods like Raml Station, Roushdy, and Smouha are walkable within themselves. However, the city is not built for pedestrians across long distances, and the heat from June through September makes walking unpleasant for most of the day. Getting to and from Borg El Arab Airport (Alexandria's main international airport, about 45 km west of center): a taxi takes roughly 50 minutes and costs around $5-8. Bus route 555 runs from the airport to Al-Raml Bus Terminal for around $1. There is no train link to the airport. If you are arriving via Cairo, the train between Cairo Ramses and Alexandria Sidi Gaber takes 2-2.5 hours and is comfortable, with frequent departures.
alexandria.visas: Most Western passport holders (US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia) can obtain a 30-day tourist visa on arrival at Borg El Arab Airport for $25-30 in cash, or apply in advance via the Egyptian e-visa portal. The e-visa is single-entry and also valid for 30 days. A multiple-entry e-visa (valid 6 months) is available but less straightforward to obtain. Egypt does not have a formal digital nomad visa as of mid-2026. You can extend a tourist visa at the Mogamma building in Cairo or at the Passport and Immigration Office in Alexandria for a further 30 days; extensions beyond that require leaving and re-entering the country or applying for a resident permit, which requires more documentation and is mainly used by long-term expats. The 2025 five-year multiple-entry visa program allows up to 180 days per visit, but this is primarily marketed at frequent high-spend travelers rather than standard tourist arrivals. Always verify current entry requirements with the official Egyptian e-visa portal or your embassy before travel.
alexandria.bestTime: Alexandria has a Mediterranean climate moderated by sea breezes, which makes it meaningfully cooler in summer than Cairo, though still warm. The best windows for remote work comfort are October to November and March to May, when daytime highs run 20-28 degrees C (68-82F), evenings are pleasant, and the Corniche is enjoyable. The city is also at its least crowded outside of July and August. July and August see Egyptian families flooding the city from the interior, accommodation prices rise, and daytime temperatures regularly hit 32-35 degrees C with humidity. If you arrive in summer, expect a noisier, more crowded city and plan to work during the cooler morning hours. Winter (December to February) is mild, around 15-20 degrees C by day, and quiet, making it a decent budget season, though some days are grey and windy off the sea.
alexandria.whoFor: Alexandria suits nomads who prioritize low costs and cultural depth over infrastructure and convenience. If you are comfortable navigating a large Egyptian city with limited English, want Mediterranean weather without Mediterranean prices, and enjoy seafood and a slower coastal pace, Alexandria delivers well. History enthusiasts, budget-conscious solo travelers, and anyone already spending time in Egypt will find it worth a month or two. Skip Alexandria if you need rock-solid internet for heavy video production or engineering builds, want a buzzing expat social scene, or rely on nightlife and bars to decompress. Cairo is the better bet for those needing more digital infrastructure, a larger international community, or easier access to the full range of coworking options in Egypt.

annecy.costOfLiving: Annecy is one of the most expensive mid-sized cities in France. Its alpine setting, proximity to Geneva, and strong demand from Swiss cross-border workers push prices well above the French national average. Rent: A one-bedroom apartment in or near the Old Town (Vieille Ville) runs roughly $1,040-1,610/month. Moving to quieter outer neighborhoods like Cran-Gevrier or Meythet brings that down to $805-1,090/month. Short-term furnished lets add a 20-40% premium. Groceries: Expect to spend $345-520/month shopping at standard supermarkets like Carrefour or Casino. Local market produce is excellent but pricier. Eating out: A weekday lunch menu (plat du jour) costs $14-18. Dinner at a mid-range restaurant runs $29-52 per person without wine. A coffee at a cafe is $3-4. Coworking hot desk: Dedicated coworking membership typically costs $175-405/month depending on the space and access hours. Day passes run $17-35. Local transport: A monthly SIBRA bus pass costs around $58-69. The city is compact enough that many residents rely on bikes rather than buses. Total monthly range: Budget $2,070-2,760/month for a frugal lifestyle sharing a flat and cooking most meals. A comfortable solo setup with coworking and regular dining out lands around $2,880-4,030/month.
annecy.whereToWork: Annecy has a small but functional coworking scene. La Jardinerie Coworking is one of the most distinctive, offering individual wooden cabin workspaces 50 meters from the train station, with fast WiFi and drinks included. La Cordee Annecy on Rue Saint-Francois de Sales is a well-known national coworking chain with a terrace, meeting rooms, and flexible day access from $40/month. Carav'Annecy on Chemin de la Prairie has a relaxed, community feel and all-inclusive pricing around $245/month. DRIP, a specialty coffee shop on Chemin des Fins Sud, doubles as a laptop-friendly space with declared fast WiFi, making it a good option for shorter sessions. Cafe-work culture exists but is more limited than in Paris or Lyon. Many traditional cafes expect you to order regularly and do not advertise WiFi. Third-wave coffee shops are your best bet for longer working sessions. The real WiFi situation is worth noting honestly: average speeds in Annecy run around 25-35 Mbps on typical connections, which is adequate for video calls and standard work but not fast by European standards. Fiber is available in most apartments, so your home setup will likely outperform public spaces.
annecy.gettingAround:
Annecy is compact and walkable at its core. The Old Town, lake promenade, and most coworking spaces are within a 20-minute walk of the train station. Cycling is very popular: the SIBRA-operated Velonecy bike-share system offers over 200 pedal and electric bikes, and dedicated cycle paths ring the lake.

The SIBRA bus network covers the wider agglomeration reliably, with routes connecting outer neighborhoods like Cran-Gevrier and Seynod to the center. A single ticket costs around $2, and monthly passes are $58-69.

Getting to and from the airport: Annecy has a small regional airport (NCY) with limited connections. For serious travel, Geneva Airport (GVA) is your main hub. You can reach it by shuttle bus in 60-90 minutes or by car in 40-45 minutes via the A41 autoroute. There is also a train connection via Leman Express Line 2, though it requires a connection and takes closer to 100 minutes. Budget for the Geneva option when planning longer trips.

Owning a car is not necessary for daily life in the city center but is helpful for exploring the surrounding Alps and lake villages.
annecy.visas:
France is part of the Schengen Area. Citizens of the EU, EEA, and Switzerland can stay and work indefinitely. Most other common passport holders (US, UK, Canada, Australia) can enter visa-free for up to 90 days within any 180-day period.

France does not currently offer a dedicated digital nomad visa. To stay longer than 90 days, non-EU citizens need a long-stay visa (visa de long sejour). The most relevant option for remote workers is the "visiteur" visa, which allows residence without working for a French employer. You must demonstrate sufficient income, typically at least the French minimum wage of around $1,670/month net, and hold comprehensive health insurance. The application is submitted at your home country's French consulate before arrival, and the fee is around $115. Processing typically takes 1-3 months.

Always verify current requirements directly at france-visas.gouv.fr before making plans.
annecy.bestTime:
Late spring and early autumn are the best windows for remote work combined with quality of life. May, June, and September offer mild temperatures (16-22 degrees C), fewer crowds than peak summer, and good outdoor conditions for hiking and cycling around the lake.

July and August are busy: tourist numbers spike significantly, accommodation prices rise, the Old Town is packed, and temperatures can hit 30+ degrees C with high humidity. Working becomes harder if you do not have air conditioning, which is rare in local buildings.

Winter (November-March) is cold, often grey, and wet at lake level. Ski season brings a different crowd if you are into winter sports, but expect some venues and cafes to run on reduced hours. For pure remote work output, winter can actually be productive if you are comfortable with the cold and fewer social distractions.

Spring and autumn hit the sweet spot: reasonable prices, manageable crowds, comfortable temperatures, and the landscape at its most photogenic.
annecy.whoFor:
Annecy suits remote workers who prioritize quality of life and natural beauty over cost efficiency. If you want to ski, hike, or cycle in the Alps while maintaining a productive work schedule, few places in Europe match this combination. It works especially well for people who already have stable, well-paying remote income and do not need to stretch a budget.

It is also a solid pick for those who want a quieter, slower pace than Paris or Lyon, or who plan to use Geneva Airport frequently for client travel. Couples or small families will appreciate the safety and livability.

Skip Annecy if you are on a tight budget, rely heavily on networking or a large expat nomad community, need consistently fast public WiFi, or are looking for active nightlife. Those coming primarily for cost-effective European basing will find better value in cities like Lyon, Bordeaux, or Lisbon.

bari.costOfLiving: Bari is one of the most affordable cities in Italy for remote workers. Your biggest expense is housing: a one-bedroom apartment in the central Murattiano district or the historic Bari Vecchia runs around $520-750/month, while quieter residential neighborhoods like Libertà or Japigia drop to $405-520. Utilities add roughly $69-105. Groceries at local markets cost around $35-52 per week, especially if you lean into the abundant fresh produce, fish, and cheese. Eating out is genuinely cheap: a sit-down trattoria lunch runs $10-15, and street food (focaccia, panzerotti) costs $2.50-6 a pop. Coworking hot-desks run about $9 per day or $140-205 per month. A monthly public transit pass is just $29, and the city is walkable enough that many nomads skip it entirely. A realistic total monthly budget: $1,380-1,840 for a comfortable lifestyle including housing, food, coworking, and some entertainment. Budget-focused nomads can get by on under $1,270.
bari.whereToWork: The dedicated coworking scene is small but functional. Impact Hub Bari, near the Fiera del Levante seafront district, is the longest-established coworking community in the city and part of the international Impact Hub network, which is what gets a visiting member a desk without a negotiation. It offers networking events and a genuinely collaborative atmosphere, though the location is a 20-minute bus ride from the old town. MeetingRoomBari on Corso Italia, steps from Bari Centrale train station, is a more professional meeting-room-style space rated 5.0 on Google and praised for fast internet and reliable amenities. Regus on Corso Alcide de Gasperi covers the Murattiano district for those who want a predictable multinational setup. Cafe work culture exists but is not as developed as in northern European cities. Traditional bars expect you to drink your espresso at the counter and leave. However, a handful of specialty coffee shops actively welcome laptop workers. Cosmico on Via Melo da Bari and Il Caffettaio on Via Calefati are the best bets, with decent seating and solid WiFi. Expect fiber-optic connections of 100-300 Mbps in modern buildings and coworking spaces. Older accommodation and some cafes can be patchier, so a local SIM with 50-100 GB of 4G data costs $17-35 per month and is a sensible backup.
bari.gettingAround:
Bari's city center is compact and mostly walkable. The old town, the Murattiano grid, and the lungomare are all within 15-20 minutes on foot of each other. The public transit network covers buses, trams, and a metro line, with a monthly pass at $29. Cycling is practical on the flat terrain, and secondhand bikes run $58-115.

Getting to and from the airport is straightforward. Bari Karol Wojtyla Airport (BRI) is about 8 km northwest of the city center. The Tempesta shuttle bus runs regularly and costs around $4.50-6. A taxi is roughly $23-29. Ryanair, Wizz Air, and easyJet connect Bari to major European cities for $46-115. Train connections to nearby cities are solid: Lecce is about one hour by regional train ($12-17).
bari.visas: EU/EEA citizens can live and work in Italy indefinitely with no visa required. Most other nationalities, including US, UK, Canadian, and Australian passport holders, can enter Italy visa-free under the Schengen agreement for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. This covers short-to-medium stays but is not a long-term solution. Italy launched a dedicated Digital Nomad Visa (National Type D) for non-EU remote workers. Key requirements: a minimum annual income of $32,230, health insurance covering at least $34,530 valid in Schengen countries, proof of remote work for a company based outside Italy, and either a university degree or 6 months of verifiable remote work experience. The visa is valid for 12 months and renewable. It allows travel throughout the Schengen Area. Applications are made through an Italian consulate in your home country before arrival. Always verify current requirements at the official Italian consulate website or consnewyork.esteri.it before making any plans.
bari.bestTime:
Spring (April to mid-June) is the sweet spot for remote work in Bari. Temperatures sit between 18-25 C, the city is not yet overrun with tourists, and outdoor cafe work is pleasant. Autumn (September to November) is equally good, with warm evenings and fewer crowds than summer.

July and August are challenging. Temperatures regularly exceed 32 C, humidity is high, and many local businesses close for ferragosto in August. Older apartments often lack air conditioning. Some nomads adjust by working early mornings and late evenings, but productivity takes a hit. Winter (December to February) is mild by northern European standards, around 8-14 C, and very affordable, but the city feels quieter and the beach lifestyle disappears.
bari.whoFor:
Bari suits nomads who prioritize cost efficiency and genuine cultural immersion over a polished expat infrastructure. If you enjoy food-led travel, Mediterranean pace, and can get by with limited English support, Bari will feel like a discovery. It works well for solo workers who are self-sufficient with their setup (good laptop, reliable SIM, coworking membership), and for anyone who wants a southern Italian base to explore Puglia, the Adriatic coast, and beyond.

It is less suited for nomads who rely on a dense community of English-speaking peers, need a wide choice of coworking spaces, or plan to work through the peak of summer without climate-controlled accommodation. Those accustomed to the coworking density of Lisbon, Berlin, or even Milan may find Bari's options thin. Couples and those planning a 3-6 month stay on the Digital Nomad Visa will get more value out of the city than pure fly-in, fly-out short-timers.

barranquilla.costOfLiving: Barranquilla is one of Colombia's most affordable major cities, partly because it sits off the typical tourist trail. Prices have not inflated to the degree seen in Medellin or Cartagena, making it genuinely budget-friendly for remote workers. A furnished one-bedroom apartment in northern neighborhoods like El Prado or Alto Prado runs roughly $435-685 per month. In more central or southern areas you can find studios from $220-345, though you sacrifice location and sometimes safety. Monthly groceries from a supermarket come to around $155-220. Eating out at a local restaurant costs $3.50-6 per meal; a sit-down dinner at a mid-range spot runs $16-28 per person. A hot-desk at a coworking space costs $28-47 per day or $180-220 per month. Local transport by TransMetro or bus is $1 per trip (under $1); a Uber or Didi ride across town is typically $2.50-5.50. Estimated monthly total: USD 900-1,400 for a comfortable single nomad lifestyle, or as low as USD 700 if you live simply and cook at home.
barranquilla.whereToWork:
Barranquilla has a growing but still developing coworking scene. The city is not a nomad hub, so the ecosystem is smaller than Medellin's, but it is functional. Dedicated spaces like Monokuko Innova Space, MacondoLab (affiliated with Simon Bolivar University), WeWork on Carrera 53, and Regus Green Towers all offer reliable fiber internet, air conditioning, meeting rooms, and flexible day or monthly passes. Prices are competitive by Latin American standards.

Cafe culture for working is less developed here than in Bogota or Medellin. Some Juan Valdez locations and Starbucks branches are acceptable for a few hours with WiFi, and The Fit Bar Cafe in the north is a local favourite for laptop workers. However, you should not rely on cafe work as your daily routine the way you might in other Colombian cities.

Home internet in the northern residential zones is generally strong, with fibre connections from Claro, ETB, and Tigo widely available. You should confirm speeds before signing a rental. Overall, WiFi reliability in dedicated coworking spaces is good; in cafes, it is inconsistent. A local SIM with data is cheap and useful as a backup.
barranquilla.gettingAround:
Barranquilla is not a walkable city. Distances between neighborhoods are large, the heat is intense, and the sidewalk infrastructure is patchy outside the northern zones. You will rely on transport for most daily movement.

The TransMetro BRT system covers several major corridors with a rechargeable card; it is cheap and reasonably efficient during off-peak hours but crowded at rush hour. Traditional buses and minibuses (busetas) fill the gaps. For convenience, Uber, Didi, and Cabify all operate in the city and are the recommended option for most trips, especially after dark. Fares are low by international standards.

Ernesto Cortissoz International Airport (BAQ) is located roughly 10 km south of the city centre in Soledad. A taxi from the official airport queue or a ride-share app gets you to the northern residential areas in 20-35 minutes depending on traffic, for around $9.50-16. There is no metro or direct rail link to the airport.
barranquilla.visas: Citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, all EU/Schengen countries, Australia, New Zealand, and roughly 100 other countries enter Colombia visa-free. You are normally granted 90 days on arrival. Before your initial 90 days expire, you can apply to Migracion Colombia for a one-time 90-day extension, giving you up to 180 days total in a calendar year. Colombia offers a dedicated Digital Nomad Visa (Type V) for remote workers. It requires proof of monthly income of at least three times the Colombian minimum wage, roughly USD 1,100-1,200 as of 2025, sourced from clients or employers outside Colombia. You also need private health insurance valid in Colombia. The visa is granted for up to two years and is renewable. Processing takes two to four weeks. You must complete the Check-Mig immigration form online before each entry into Colombia. Always verify current requirements with Migracion Colombia (migracioncolombia.gov.co) or the Colombian consulate before you travel, as rules and income thresholds change.
barranquilla.bestTime:
Barranquilla sits on the Caribbean coast and is hot year-round, averaging 28-29 degrees Celsius (82-84 degrees Fahrenheit) every month. There is no temperate season. The dry season runs from December to April, when trade winds from the northeast offer some relief and humidity drops slightly. This is the most comfortable window for outdoor activity and the most practical for remote work with fewer power interruptions from storms.

The famous Carnaval de Barranquilla takes place every year in February or March, just before Ash Wednesday. It is the second-largest carnival in the world and brings extraordinary energy to the city, but also crowds, higher accommodation prices, and noise if you need quiet to work.

The rainy season runs from May to November, peaking in September and October. Rain comes in heavy short bursts rather than all-day drizzle, so productive work days are still very possible. Flooding in lower-lying and poorer neighborhoods can be a practical problem. For pure remote work productivity, December through April is the best window.
barranquilla.whoFor:
Barranquilla suits you well if you want to live cheaply in a real Colombian city without tourist inflation, you are comfortable navigating daily life in Spanish, and you value cultural immersion over a curated expat bubble. It works particularly well for solo nomads or couples on a tight budget who want to stay for one to three months and genuinely experience Caribbean Colombian life. People interested in salsa, Caribbean music, and Carnaval culture will find Barranquilla uniquely rewarding.

It is a good base if you have corporate or BPO contacts in Colombia, since the city has a significant professional business community. The airport connections also make it practical as a hub for exploring the Caribbean coast.

Skip Barranquilla if you rely on a large English-speaking nomad network, need a wide selection of laptop-friendly cafes, find sustained heat draining, or prefer the polished infrastructure and established nomad scenes of Medellin or Bogota. It also demands more patience and street smarts than either of those cities, and you should stick to the northern neighborhoods as your operational base.

basel.costOfLiving: Basel is one of the most expensive cities in Switzerland, which means it sits near the top globally. You are not going to find budget nomad territory here, but the infrastructure and quality of life are exceptional in return. For rent, a one-bedroom apartment in a central neighborhood like Grossbasel or near the Rhine runs around $2,170-2,470 per month. Move out to areas like Gundeldingen or St. Johann and you can bring that down to $1,480-1,730. Short-term furnished rentals through platforms like Airbnb push those numbers significantly higher, so finding a monthly sublet or a coliving arrangement is worth the effort if you plan to stay more than a few weeks. Monthly grocery costs for one person run $495-740, depending on whether you shop at Coop, Migros, or premium supermarkets. A sit-down meal at an inexpensive restaurant costs around $30, and a two-course dinner for two at a mid-range spot runs about $125-150. If you cross into Germany or France, you can cut food costs noticeably, and many Basel residents make regular shopping trips across the border. Coworking hot-desk memberships start around $310-370 per month at budget-friendly spaces and climb to $595-655 at more premium spots. A monthly local transport pass (trams, buses within Basel) costs $110. Internet in an apartment runs about $62-68 per month. Realistic monthly total (excluding rent): $1,730-2,230. Add rent and you are looking at $3,220-4,700 per month depending on how centrally you live and how much you eat out.
basel.whereToWork: Basel has a solid coworking scene for a city of roughly 180,000 people. Westhive Basel Rosental (Sandgrubenstrasse 44, Rosental quarter) is the most polished option, a 2,600 sqm space with an on-site restaurant, gym, terrace, and day passes for $48. RHIZOM (Steinentorstrasse 19, central) is a boutique independent space in a former factory hall with high ceilings, good natural light, and day passes at $37. Unternehmen Mitte (Gerbergasse 30, city center) is Basel's famous coffeehouse in an old bank hall, with a free-to-sit-in ground floor cafe and a proper coworking space upstairs for $435 per month. kHaus near the Kaserne area in Kleinbasel operates as a community-oriented space for around $310 per month. Cafe working culture in Basel is moderate, not outstanding. Many cafes are happy for you to sit for a couple of hours with a laptop, but dedicated laptop-friendly spots with reliable power outlets and fast WiFi are rarer than in Berlin or Lisbon. Budget $12-19 per session for drinks. Public WiFi across the city is available but inconsistent in quality, so a local SIM or mobile data plan is worth having. Fiber speeds in apartments and coworking spaces are fast (60 Mbps and above is typical).
basel.gettingAround:
Basel is compact and highly walkable. The old town and both main riverbanks are easy to cover on foot, and the tram network is excellent, covering the wider city reliably. Most errands and work commutes within the city are handled on trams or on foot. Cycling is popular and bike lanes are reasonably well laid out, though the terrain is mostly flat, making it comfortable.

Basel has three countries within a short distance: the German city of Freiburg is about 45 minutes by train, and Mulhouse in France is under 30 minutes. This cross-border access is genuinely useful for cheaper groceries, restaurants, and day trips.

The airport (EuroAirport Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg) sits technically in France, about 9 km from the city center. Bus 50 runs directly from Basel SBB train station to the airport in around 20 minutes for $5.50. There are no trains to the airport itself from Basel city, so the bus or a taxi are your options. Connections are good, with direct flights to many European hubs and a handful of long-haul destinations.
basel.visas: Switzerland is part of the Schengen Area. If you hold a US, Canadian, Australian, UK, or most other Western passport, you can enter visa-free and stay up to 90 days within any 180-day rolling period. This is the standard Schengen rule: 90 days in, 90 days out, across all Schengen countries combined. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa for Switzerland as of mid-2026. Your realistic long-stay options are limited: you can apply for a self-employed or entrepreneur permit if you have a genuine business plan and proof of financial self-sufficiency, or explore a lump-sum taxation arrangement if you are wealthy enough to qualify for the cantonal scheme. For most nomads, the 90-day window is the practical limit before you need to leave Schengen and reset. From October 2025, Switzerland implemented the EU Entry/Exit System (EES), which collects biometric data (face scan and fingerprints) on your first entry. This does not change the 90/180 rule, but border crossings now take slightly longer. Always verify current entry and visa requirements directly with the Swiss State Secretariat for Migration (sem.admin.ch) before traveling.
basel.bestTime: The most comfortable window for a working stay is May through mid-October. Late spring (May to June) is the sweet spot: mild temperatures of 18-22C (64-72F), long daylight hours, the Rhine promenade is lively, and accommodation prices have not yet peaked. Summer (July and August) is warm and vibrant but busy with tourists and the Art Basel crowd (Art Basel runs in June), which pushes hotel prices sharply upward. If you want energy and street life, summer delivers it. September and early October are excellent for focus work: the tourist rush fades, the weather stays pleasant (16-20C), and the city settles into a productive autumn rhythm. Winters are cold and grey, with temperatures sitting between 0-7C (32-45F), occasional fog, and little snow. The Christmas markets in December are charming and Basel has a genuine local feel in winter, but if you rely on outdoor time for your routine, January and February are tough.
basel.whoFor:
Basel works best for nomads who have the budget to absorb Swiss prices and want maximum stability: fast internet, zero friction with logistics, physical safety, and a beautifully organized city. If you are a senior professional, consultant, or founder with clients in European time zones, Basel's combination of infrastructure and cultural reputation makes it an easy base for short productive sprints.

It also suits people who genuinely value museums, architecture, and access to the Rhine, the Black Forest, and Alsace. If your idea of a good remote work stretch includes a Saturday at the Kunstmuseum and a Sunday bike ride into France, Basel delivers that without effort.

Skip Basel if you are budget-conscious, need more than 90 days in Schengen, or are looking for a buzzing nomad community with regular meetups and co-living energy. It is not a digital nomad hub in the way Lisbon or Chiang Mai are. It is a serious, refined city that rewards those who can afford to be there and appreciate what it offers.

bath.costOfLiving: Bath sits firmly in the expensive tier of UK cities. You will not find the bargain lifestyle you might get in Eastern Europe or Southeast Asia, but you get a compact, walkable Georgian city with genuinely fast broadband and a high standard of services in return. Rent is the biggest line item. A one-bedroom flat in the city centre typically runs $1,600 to $1,950 per month. Head to Oldfield Park or Twerton, about a 20-minute walk southwest, and you can find the same space for $1,150 to $1,450 per month. Groceries for one person buying sensibly at a Sainsbury's or Aldi cost around $230 to $270 per month. A sit-down meal at a casual restaurant runs $16 to $24 per person; a good mid-range dinner for two lands around $80 to $110. A coworking hot desk runs $100 to $210 per month depending on the space. A local bus pass costs $120 per month. Home broadband is around $43 per month. Total realistic monthly range: $2,250 to $3,050, covering rent in a cheaper area, food, coworking, transport, and incidentals. City-centre rent pushes that to $2,650 to $3,750.
bath.whereToWork: Bath has a small but solid coworking scene for a city its size. Runway East Bath at Kings Court, Parsonage Lane is the most professional option, close to Bath Spa station with meeting rooms and reliable gigabit-class connectivity. Rengen House on Argyle Street suits freelancers and creatives: community-oriented, wheelchair accessible, and priced from $330 to $470 per month for a dedicated desk. Gather Round at Trinity Church near Queen's Square is a striking French Gothic conversion housing over 120 creatives; hot desks start from $210 per month. Spaces Northgate House on Upper Borough Walls offers day passes from $60 and monthly flex memberships from $330 if you need a corporate-grade environment without a long commitment. Cafe work is genuinely viable in Bath. Society Cafe has two city-centre locations (5 Kingsmead Square and 19 High Street) with fast free WiFi, plentiful power sockets, and enough table space to feel settled rather than squeezed. The atmosphere on Kingsmead Square, with outdoor seating on the square itself, is hard to beat on a good day. Landrace Bakery on Walcot Street is quieter and has a loyal local crowd; it suits focused morning sessions before it fills up. The general WiFi situation in Bath is good: most independent cafes offer reliable connections, and the city's compact footprint means you are rarely far from an option.
bath.gettingAround:
Bath is one of the most walkable cities in England. The historic core is about a mile across, and you can get between most points of interest on foot in under 20 minutes. The Roman Baths, train station, main shopping streets, and most coworking spaces are all within comfortable walking distance of each other.

For longer trips within the city, First Bus runs a fairly reliable network. A single fare costs $3.50; a monthly pass is $120. Cycling is possible on some routes but the hills around the city and the narrow Georgian streets can make it challenging. Bath does not have a tram or underground system.

Getting out of Bath is easy by rail. Bath Spa station sits in the city centre and has frequent Great Western Railway services to London Paddington (roughly 90 minutes) and to Bristol Temple Meads (12 minutes). The nearest international airport is Bristol Airport, about 25 kilometres southwest. The A4 bus service connects the airport to Bath, and the journey takes roughly 45 to 60 minutes and costs around $12 to $19 single. You can also take a bus to Bristol Temple Meads and pick up an airport bus from there. Taxis to Bristol Airport from Bath city centre run approximately $53 to $73.
bath.visas: Most Western passport holders, including Americans, Canadians, Australians, and EU citizens, can enter the UK visa-free as a standard visitor for up to six months. The UK does not currently offer a dedicated digital nomad visa. You are permitted to work remotely for a foreign employer while in the UK on a standard visitor entry, as long as you are not working for a UK-based employer or offering services to UK clients. The Home Office scrutinises stays longer than 90 days more carefully; if you plan to stay close to the six-month limit, keep clear records showing your income source is abroad. There is no straightforward way to extend a visitor stay beyond six months; you would need to leave and re-enter or qualify for a different visa category such as the Global Talent Visa if eligible. Always verify current rules with the UK Visas and Immigration website (gov.uk/browse/visas-immigration) before you travel, as rules can change.
bath.bestTime:
Bath has a temperate maritime climate: mild, damp, and rarely extreme in either direction. Summer (June to August) offers the warmest temperatures, typically 18 to 22 degrees Celsius, and the most daylight. It is also when tourists arrive in force. The Roman Baths and Pulteney Bridge areas become crowded on summer weekends, and accommodation prices rise. If you are primarily here to work, heavy foot traffic on narrow streets is a minor irritant rather than a deal-breaker.

The best window for remote workers balancing good weather with a quieter city is May to early June or September to October. Temperatures are comfortable, days are long enough, and the tourist pressure eases noticeably. Winter (December to February) is grey, damp, and cool with average highs around 8 degrees Celsius. It is the cheapest time to rent and the city has a quieter, more local feel, which suits some people well. Rainfall is spread across the year; there is no reliably dry season, but September tends to be one of the drier months.
bath.whoFor:
Bath suits nomads who want a base in England that offers genuine character rather than the anonymity of a large city. If you have existing connections to the UK, need easy access to London, and value beauty, safety, and a high standard of daily life, Bath delivers. It works well for people who prefer a slower pace and do not need a buzzing nomad meetup scene to feel at home. Writers, designers, and solo workers who thrive in a quieter, aesthetically rich environment often find Bath disproportionately inspiring for its size.

It is a harder sell if you are on a tight budget, need a large coworking community, or are chasing good weather for months at a stretch. Digital nomads used to the cost efficiency of Lisbon, Tbilisi, or Chiang Mai will find Bath a significant adjustment upward in price for a city that does not offer much in the way of a nomad infrastructure in return. Bristol, 20 minutes by train, offers a larger scene and lower rents if community and variety matter more to you than beauty and calm.

belgrade.costOfLiving:
Belgrade is one of the most affordable European capitals for digital nomads. Your biggest variable is rent. In central neighborhoods like Stari Grad and Vracar, expect to pay $590-785 per month for a one-bedroom apartment. In slightly further areas like Dorcol or Zemun you can find similar quality for $390-590. Utilities add roughly $98-155 on top.

Groceries for one person run about $245-295 per month shopping at local markets and supermarkets. Eating out is genuinely cheap: a full meal at a local kafana costs $12-20 including drinks. A coworking hot desk runs $98-195 monthly at most spaces. Public transport in Belgrade became free for all passengers in January 2025, covering all buses, trams, and trolleybuses. Mobile data plans start around $12 for 10GB.

A realistic total monthly budget for comfortable solo nomad life: $1,270-1,710. You can stretch it down to $900 with discipline or up to $2,000+ if you eat out often and want a premium central apartment.
belgrade.whereToWork: Belgrade has a solid and growing coworking infrastructure. Nova Iskra Workspace operates locations in Savamala (the creative neighborhood hub) and Dorcol, with fiber-optic WiFi and a strong community of freelancers and startup founders. ICT Hub at Kralja Milana 10 offers 24/7 access and a 1 Gbps connection, making it the top pick if speed is your priority. Anticafe Black Cat (Brace Baruh 6) runs a pay-per-hour model with free coffee and snacks, ideal for short or irregular work sessions. Cafe-working culture is well-established. Kafeterija Magazin 1907 (Kralja Petra 16, Stari Grad) is housed in a stunning 1907 Art Nouveau building with multiple floors, ample power sockets, and good WiFi. It is explicitly laptop-friendly and heavily used by remote workers. Coffee, Tea and Sympathy in Dorcol and Red Bread in the center are both comfortable, smoke-free, and work-tolerant. WiFi in coworking spaces is reliably fast. Cafe WiFi is generally usable for calls and regular tasks, though speeds vary. If you are staying in an apartment, confirm WiFi quality before booking as some older buildings still have slow connections. A local SIM from Telenor or SBB with a data plan is a sensible backup.
belgrade.gettingAround:
Belgrade has no metro. The network of buses, trams, and trolleybuses covers the city thoroughly, and since January 2025 all of it is completely free for everyone, including tourists. You simply board and ride. Google Maps handles Belgrade routing reliably.

The city is walkable in the central districts. Stari Grad, Vracar, and Dorcol are all comfortable to cover on foot, and the riverfront Savamala area is easy to walk. Taxis and Bolt (the dominant rideshare app) are inexpensive for longer trips or late nights.

Getting to and from Nikola Tesla Airport: the A1 minibus from Slavija Square costs $4 (under $4) and takes about 30 minutes, running every 15 minutes during the day. Bus 72 is a free option, running to Zeleni Venac in about 45 minutes depending on traffic. A taxi or Bolt to the center costs roughly $24-34.
belgrade.visas:
Serbia is not in the EU and has generous visa-free entry for most Western passport holders. Citizens of the US, UK, EU countries, Canada, and Australia can enter without a visa and stay for up to 90 days within a 180-day period. Some nationalities, including the US, are technically limited to 30 or 60 days on certain interpretations; in practice most travelers stay up to 90 days without issue, but check the official Serbian Ministry of Foreign Affairs website for the current rule for your specific passport before you travel.

Serbia does not have a designated digital nomad visa as of mid-2026. The formal long-stay option is a Temporary Residence Permit based on self-employment or company formation, which can be granted for up to three years and requires a minimum confirmed income of around $4,030 per month, proof of accommodation, medical insurance, and registration at the local police station within 24 hours of arrival. Processing takes roughly 30 days. If you stay 183 or more days in a calendar year, Serbian tax residency rules apply. Confirm all current requirements with official sources before applying.
belgrade.bestTime: Belgrade has a proper continental climate with hot summers and cold, damp winters. The sweet spots for remote work are April to early June and September to October. Temperatures sit in the 18-26C (65-79F) range, there is less rain than spring, and the city has an outdoor energy that makes it genuinely pleasant to be in. July and August get intense, regularly hitting 32-35C (90-95F) with high humidity. Air conditioning is common in newer apartments but not universal in older buildings. Winter (December to February) is cold and grey, and Belgrade's air quality deteriorates significantly due to coal heating, wood burning, and traffic, with PM2.5 concentrations often well above WHO guidelines. If air quality matters to you, avoid November through February. For the most balanced combination of good weather, manageable crowds, reasonable flight prices, and a lively local scene, late September and early October stand out as the best single window.
belgrade.whoFor:
Belgrade suits nomads who want a European city experience at a budget that actually makes sense. If you are coming from Western Europe or North America and find Lisbon or Barcelona too expensive for long stays, Belgrade delivers comparable energy at roughly half the cost. The city rewards people who lean into the local scene: kafanas, river clubs, Skadarlija, and the genuine bohemian feel of the older neighborhoods are part of the appeal.

It is a particularly good fit for freelancers in tech, design, or creative fields who will benefit from the growing startup community and coworking culture. The nightlife is genuinely world-class if that matters to you.

Skip Belgrade if air quality is a health concern for you, especially for winter stays. It is also a harder sell if you need seamless bureaucratic support for long-term residency, since the permit process requires legal help and meeting relatively high income thresholds. Travelers who prioritize outdoor nature activities year-round will also find the city limiting compared to coastal or mountain alternatives in the region.

bergen.costOfLiving:
Bergen is one of the most expensive cities in Scandinavia, and you should budget accordingly. Rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the city centre runs $1,260-1,580 per month. Step 20 minutes out to areas like Landas or Laksevag and you can find the same footprint for $735-1,050. Groceries are costly: expect to spend $420-580 per month if you cook most meals. A single sit-down meal at an inexpensive restaurant costs around $26; a mid-range dinner for two runs $125-160.

A hot-desk at a coworking space such as Impact Hub Bergen or Bergen.Works typically costs $210-420 per month. The monthly public transport pass is $87. Add utilities of around $84-125 and your all-in monthly total lands somewhere between $2,950 and $4,420 depending on your lifestyle and how centrally you live.
bergen.whereToWork: Bergen has a handful of solid coworking options for the size of the city. Impact Hub Bergen, Norway's first coworking space, occupies a historic warehouse near Bryggen and draws a community of social entrepreneurs and freelancers. Bergen.Works in Skostredet is central, has fast fibre internet, and offers both hot desks and private offices with 24-hour access. BKOLON on Nygardsgaten caters to creative and tech workers and has a strong community feel. Cafe work culture exists but is more limited than in Southern Europe. Norwegians tend to linger over coffee, but many cafes are small and get busy quickly. Kaffemisjonen near Torgalmenningen is a specialty coffee standout and tolerates remote workers during off-peak hours. Godt Brod has multiple locations with seating, though tables fill fast at lunch. Bergen Public Library in the city centre is a genuinely good free option: comfortable seating, free fast WiFi, and a cafe on site. WiFi is reliable across the city. Norway's fixed broadband averages download speeds above 100 Mbps and public WiFi in cafes and coworking spaces routinely delivers 40-80 Mbps. You will not struggle with connectivity for video calls or large file uploads.
bergen.gettingAround:
The city centre is compact and very walkable. Most of what you need as a remote worker, including coworking spaces, cafes, supermarkets, and restaurants, sits within a 15-minute walk of Torgalmenningen. You can cover the main districts on foot without needing public transport day to day.

For longer trips, the Bybanen light rail and Skyss buses cover the city well. A single ride costs $5 and the monthly pass at $87 pays for itself quickly. The light rail Line 1 connects the city centre directly to Bergen Airport Flesland in about 45 minutes for a standard fare of $5.50. The express airport bus, Flybussen, takes around 30 minutes but costs $16 each way. Taxis are available but notoriously expensive: Bergen holds one of the highest taxi start fares in the world.

Cycling is possible but Bergen's hilly terrain and frequent rain make it an option rather than an obvious default. Most residents walk or use the light rail for daily errands.
bergen.visas:
Norway is part of the Schengen Area, which means the standard 90-day-in-any-180-day rule applies for citizens of the US, Canada, Australia, the UK, and most other non-EU countries. You can enter without a visa for short stays, but you cannot work remotely for longer than 90 days under a tourist entry.

Norway does not offer a dedicated digital nomad visa. The closest option is a self-employment permit, but it requires a contract with a Norwegian client and a demonstrated income of at least $37,920 per year. EU and EEA citizens can live and work in Norway without restriction under freedom of movement. If you want to stay longer as a non-EU remote worker, your realistic options are either using the 90-day allowance, leaving and re-entering after the 90-day period resets, or exploring a longer-term residency route if you have Norwegian connections or employment. Always confirm current entry requirements with the official Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) at udi.no before you travel.
bergen.bestTime: Bergen is the rainiest city in Western Europe, receiving around 2,500 mm of precipitation annually. Rain is spread throughout the year, with November through January being the worst months for both darkness and rain. If you are coming primarily to work remotely and want the best conditions, May, June, and early July offer the most daylight (up to 19 hours in midsummer), the driest spells, temperatures between 14-20 degrees Celsius, and an energetic city atmosphere. Late July and August bring the main tourist season, which means crowds at cafes and a tighter rental market for short-term lets. September is a reasonable shoulder choice: fewer tourists, still decent light, and the fjords and surrounding trails are at their most dramatic in autumn colours. Avoid October through March unless you are specifically drawn to the moody Atlantic atmosphere and low-season quiet; the short days and persistent rain are a genuine productivity drag for many people.
bergen.whoFor:
Bergen rewards remote workers who earn in stronger currencies and value natural beauty, outdoor activities, and a high quality of life over budget friendliness. If you want to combine productive work weeks with weekend hikes through the Fjaerland fjords, day trips to Sognefjord, or kayaking in the archipelago, Bergen delivers this within arm's reach of a city with real infrastructure.

You will get the most from Bergen if you come during May to July, have an income comfortable for Scandinavian costs (think at least USD 4,000 per month after accommodation), and are the kind of person who enjoys a smaller, quieter city rather than a loud nomad social scene.

Bergen is not a great fit if you are budget-conscious, need a large English-speaking nomad community, want longer-term residency options, or struggle with grey weather and limited daylight. Those prioritising warm weather, low costs, or a well-established nomad network will find better options elsewhere in Europe.

bogota.costOfLiving: Bogotá is affordable by Western standards but not as cheap as smaller Colombian cities. Budget $1,560-2,810 per month for a comfortable remote-work lifestyle. Rent: A furnished one-bedroom in Chapinero or Zona Rosa runs $780-1,250 per month. In more residential areas like Engativá or Fontibón you can find similar-sized apartments from $375-560, though these areas are farther from coworking clusters. Groceries: A week of groceries from a supermarket like Éxito or Carulla costs $47-78. Fresh produce at local markets (plazas de mercado) is significantly cheaper. Eating out: A set lunch (almuerzo ejecutivo) at a local spot runs $3-5.50 and is usually a full meal. Sitting down in a mid-range Chapinero restaurant costs $12-25 per person. International food and Zona Rosa restaurants push higher. Coworking hot-desk: A monthly hot-desk pass at a quality space costs $110-225. Day passes run $8-19. Local transport: A TransMilenio ride costs $1 (under $1). Most nomads budget $25-47 per month on transit plus occasional Uber rides. Monthly total range: Budget nomad $1,090 living simply; comfortable mid-range $1,720-2,500; with private apartment and eating out regularly, $2,190-3,120.
bogota.whereToWork: Bogotá has a mature coworking scene. Tinkko Ecotek (Calle 99, near Parque 93) is one of the best-regarded options, with 6,000 square meters of flexible space and reliable fast internet. Impact Hub Bogotá (Zona G, Calle 70) is popular with social-enterprise types and freelancers, with event programming and a strong community. HubBOG (Calle 98) caters to startups and has a consistent reputation for fast WiFi and professional atmosphere. WeWork operates multiple Bogotá locations including Chico Norte, suited for those who want a polished, predictable experience. Cafe-working is very viable. Amor Perfecto (Chapinero Alto) is the go-to specialty coffee spot for remote workers: good WiFi, plenty of seating, and excellent coffee. Azahar Coffee (Parque 93) is consistently praised for its reliable WiFi and all-day hours. Note that many neighborhood cafes do not have WiFi or have unreliable connections; stick to spots known for laptop work. Home internet in residential areas is generally good, with fiber packages delivering 100-300 Mbps for $16-31 per month. Coworking spaces and the top cafes offer genuinely fast, stable connections. Public WiFi on TransMilenio (called Bus-fi) exists but is too slow for real work. Expect some variation: a few spots overstate their speed, so test before committing to a monthly pass.
bogota.gettingAround: TransMilenio, the bus rapid transit system, is Bogotá's main public transport backbone. It covers most of the city and is cheap at $1 per ride, but it gets very crowded during rush hours and can be slow in traffic. The newer Metro line (Line 1) is under construction and not yet open as of mid-2026. Uber and InDriver work reliably in Bogotá and are the preferred way to move after dark or when carrying equipment. Taxis are available but always insist on the meter or agree on a price first. Cycling has improved significantly: Bogotá has an extensive ciclovía network and a Sunday car-free program where major roads open to cyclists and pedestrians. Walkability is high in Chapinero, Usaquén, and Zona Rosa. La Candelaria is walkable within itself but less connected to the northern expat belt. Airport: El Dorado International Airport (BOG) is about 15 km from the city center. By taxi or Uber the trip takes 25-40 minutes (longer in traffic) and costs roughly USD 10-18. There is a TransMilenio feeder route to the airport (very cheap) but it is slow and not practical with luggage.
bogota.visas: Citizens of the US, Canada, UK, EU member states, Australia, and most Latin American countries do not need a visa in advance. You receive a tourist entry stamp at the border for up to 90 days, extendable once for a further 90 days (total of 180 days per calendar year). Colombia launched a Digital Nomad Visa in late 2022. It allows a stay of up to two years. Requirements include a valid passport, proof of income from foreign sources equivalent to at least three times Colombia's monthly minimum wage (roughly $1,340 or about $1,100 per month as of 2025), and valid private health insurance covering Colombia. The visa also grants a foreigner ID card (cédula de extranjería), which makes renting apartments and opening bank accounts simpler. Confirm current entry conditions and visa requirements with Colombia's official Cancillería website (cancilleria.gov.co) before you travel, as rules can change.
bogota.bestTime: Bogotá sits at 2,600 meters above sea level and has a stable, cool climate year-round, averaging 13-18°C (55-64°F). There are no proper summer and winter seasons; instead, you get two dry periods and two wetter periods each year. Dry seasons (best for remote work): December through February and July through August. These months bring the most reliable weather, clearer skies, and less likelihood of afternoon rain disrupting your plans. Wetter seasons: April to May and October to November. Rain tends to fall in afternoon downpours rather than all-day drizzle, so mornings are usually workable. These months are not a reason to avoid Bogotá, but pack a rain jacket regardless. For a first visit focused on settling in and working, December through February is the most comfortable window. July through August is also excellent and coincides with international travel off-season, so accommodation prices tend to be more reasonable.
bogota.whoFor:
Bogotá suits nomads who want a real city experience at a significantly lower cost than equivalent European or North American capitals. If you value a dense cultural scene, good coffee, a growing startup community, and don't mind learning at least basic Spanish, Bogotá rewards the effort. It works especially well for those on a budget of USD 1,500 or above per month who want to live comfortably, not just survive.

It is a strong fit for people who have done Latin America before and know how to navigate urban environments with appropriate caution. The Digital Nomad Visa makes it attractive for anyone wanting a stable legal base for six months or more.

Skip Bogotá if you are sensitive to altitude or air pollution, strongly prefer warm sunny weather, need most people around you to speak English, or are looking for a beach-and-relaxation base. Those priorities are better served by Medellín, Santa Marta, or Cartagena.

boston.costOfLiving: Boston is one of the most expensive cities in the United States, and you should plan accordingly. Rent is the biggest line item. A studio or one-bedroom in central neighborhoods like Back Bay, Beacon Hill, or the South End typically runs $2,800-3,800/month (USD). Move out to Allston, Brighton, Jamaica Plain, or Somerville and you can find studios for $1,800-2,400/month, though nothing is truly cheap here. Groceries for one person cooking at home cost around $350-500/month at a typical supermarket. Eating out is pricey: a casual lunch runs $15-20, dinner at a mid-range restaurant $35-60 per person with a drink. Budget-conscious nomads can keep food costs near $500-700/month by cooking most meals. A hot-desk coworking pass at places like Workbar or Industrious runs $29-50/day or roughly $200-400/month for a monthly plan. The MBTA subway (the "T") costs $2.40/ride with a CharlieCard, and a monthly pass is around $90. All figures are in USD. Realistic monthly total range: $3,500-5,500/month depending on your rent situation, how often you eat out, and whether you use a coworking space daily. Boston is not a budget destination; it rewards you with world-class universities, healthcare, and culture in exchange.
boston.whereToWork:
Boston has a strong coworking market, particularly in Downtown, Back Bay, and the Seaport District. Workbar is the city's homegrown network with locations in Downtown (24 School Street) and Back Bay (399 Boylston Street), offering quiet zones, open areas, and flexible day passes from $29. Industrious has a well-regarded Seaport location at 22 Boston Wharf Road with high-end amenities and included breakfast, plus a Back Bay outpost at 855 Boylston Street with river views. WeWork South Station at 745 Atlantic Avenue is a solid choice, sitting above one of the two main rail terminals with the Red Line underneath it and the commuter network beside it.

Cafe work culture is genuinely strong here. George Howell Coffee (505 Washington Street, Downtown) offers abundant seating, fast WiFi, and a professional crowd. Thinking Cup on Tremont Street and Newbury Street has multiple locations with good WiFi and plenty of solo seating, though WiFi can be inconsistent at peak times. Broadsheet Coffee Roasters in Cambridge draws academics and tech workers but restricts laptops during brunch hours.

WiFi reliability is generally good across Boston coworking spaces. Public libraries, especially the Boston Public Library in Copley Square, are free alternatives with solid connectivity. Coffee shops near universities (especially around Kenmore, Cambridge, and Fenway) are used to laptop workers and rarely push you out.
boston.gettingAround: Boston is one of the most walkable cities in the United States. The compact downtown core, Beacon Hill, North End, and Back Bay are all easily navigated on foot. Many nomads go entire weeks without needing a vehicle. The MBTA (the "T") covers most key areas with four subway lines, Silver Line buses, and commuter rail. A single fare is $2.40 with a CharlieCard. The system is functional but aging, with occasional delays and weekend service gaps. It connects well enough for most daily needs. Getting to Logan International Airport is easy and inexpensive. The Silver Line 1 (SL1) bus runs directly from South Station to all terminals and is free from the airport to downtown. The Blue Line subway also connects to Airport Station with a free shuttle to terminals. Budget $2.40-3 inbound. A taxi or rideshare runs $25-45 depending on traffic and tip. Cycling is viable with the Bluebikes bike-share network, though winters make it impractical from December through March. Car ownership in the city center is expensive and largely unnecessary.
boston.visas: The United States does not offer a dedicated digital nomad visa. Your options depend on your passport. Visa Waiver Program (VWP/ESTA): Citizens of around 42 countries (including most of the EU, UK, Australia, Japan, South Korea, and others) can enter for up to 90 days per visit without a visa via ESTA approval, obtained online before travel. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on ESTA is a legal gray area; the US does not have clear rules permitting it. B-2 Tourist Visa: Nationals of countries not in the VWP must apply for a B-2 visa. It can allow stays of up to six months as determined by a customs officer at entry, with multi-entry validity up to 10 years. As of 2026, a new $250 Visa Integrity Fee has increased the total application cost to roughly $435. There is no US nomad visa, no straightforward extension pathway for tourists, and overstaying has serious long-term consequences for future US entry. Always confirm current rules with official US government sources (travel.state.gov) before booking.
boston.bestTime: The best windows for remote work in Boston are late May through mid-June and September through mid-October. Temperatures sit in the 18-25C (65-77F) range, humidity is manageable, and the city is energized without the peak summer crowds. Fall foliage in early October is genuinely spectacular and transforms the city. Summer (July-August) is peak tourist season: crowded, expensive, and humid, though still workable. Spring (March-April) is unreliable with cold snaps and occasional late snowstorms. Winter (December-February) brings genuine cold, frequent snowstorms, and temperatures that can drop below -15C. Productivity can suffer if a blizzard disrupts transit and you need to be anywhere. It does offer the lowest accommodation rates if you are flexible and well-prepared.
boston.whoFor:
Boston suits nomads who earn in USD or another strong currency and are not compromising on quality of life. If you work in tech, biotech, finance, academia, or law, the professional ecosystem here is unmatched in the Northeast. It is a particularly good base for Americans who want an urban hub with excellent infrastructure, no language friction, and strong networking opportunities. The city also works well for anyone on a longer-term US stay on a B-2 visa who wants a stimulating, walkable city with access to serious professional communities.

Skip Boston if you are on a tight budget, rely on visa-free stays that expire at 90 days and cannot easily return, or simply want warmth and low cost of living. Southeast Asia, Latin America, or Southern Europe will stretch the same income three to five times further. Boston is also a tough fit if you dislike cold winters and need outdoor weather year-round.

bristol.costOfLiving: Bristol sits in a middle tier for UK cities: noticeably cheaper than London, but not cheap by European standards. Rent is the biggest variable.
