On arrival you receive a Forma Migratoria Multiple (FMM) tourist card. The legal maximum stay is 180 days, but immigration officers now often grant fewer days based on your stated travel plans. If you receive less than 180 days you can request a single extension at an immigration office inside Mexico. There is no official digital nomad visa for Mexico as of mid-2026, so most remote workers cycle in and out on tourist entries. Technically you are not permitted to perform paid work on a tourist entry, though this is rarely enforced for remote workers employed abroad. Confirm current entry rules with the official INM website (gob.mx) or your nearest Mexican consulate before you travel.
sayulita.bestTime: The dry season from November through April is the most pleasant window for remote work. Temperatures sit at 24-29C (75-84F), humidity is manageable, and days are reliably sunny. December through March is peak tourist season, which means higher prices, busier coworking spaces, and accommodation booked months in advance. The shoulder months of October and early November are arguably the sweet spot: the rain eases off, fewer tourists have arrived, and prices are softer. Some restaurants and venues that close in low season begin reopening in late October. May through October is the rainy season. Humidity climbs above 80%, heat indexes regularly exceed 34C (93F), and afternoon downpours are common. Hurricane activity is possible from August through October. A meaningful number of businesses close or reduce hours during this period. If you can tolerate heat and humidity and want lower rents and a quieter town, it is workable, but it is not a comfortable environment for sustained focus.
sayulita.whoFor: Sayulita works well for surfers and ocean-oriented workers who want to build a life around early morning waves and afternoon focus sessions. It suits people with flexible schedules who can handle connectivity that occasionally forces you to adjust plans. Creative workers, freelancers, and those on async-heavy teams tend to thrive here. If you want a mellow, small-town beach vibe with a ready-made social scene and good food, Sayulita delivers. It is less suited to workers with strict daily video call schedules who need fast, consistent internet at all hours. People on tight budgets will find better value elsewhere in Mexico: Oaxaca, Merida, or Mexico City all offer faster internet and lower costs. Those who need urban stimulation, variety, or big-city infrastructure will feel the walls closing in after a few weeks. And if you visit in high summer expecting the same laid-back surf town, the heat and humidity will be a rude surprise.

seattle.costOfLiving: Seattle is one of the more expensive cities in the United States, but costs vary significantly depending on where you choose to live and how you spend. All figures are in USD. Rent is the biggest line item. A furnished studio or one-bedroom in central neighborhoods like Capitol Hill, Belltown, or South Lake Union runs $2,000-2,600 per month. Move out to Ballard, Fremont, or Beacon Hill and you can find comparable space for $1,700-2,200. Groceries at a standard supermarket cost around $300-450 per month for one person. Eating out ranges from $18-25 for a casual meal to $90-130 for dinner for two at a mid-range place. A coworking hot desk runs roughly $40-65 per day or $300-550 per month on a membership. Local transport is a flat $3 per ride on buses and light rail, or $108/month for a pass. A realistic monthly total for a solo nomad is $3,500-5,500, depending on your accommodation, how often you cook, and whether you use coworking daily.
seattle.whereToWork: Seattle has a solid coworking scene anchored by established operators and a genuinely laptop-friendly cafe culture. The city's tech roots mean most venues take reliable connectivity seriously. Coworking spaces include WeWork at 1448 NW Market Street in Ballard, Industrious at 2033 6th Avenue in Belltown, and Pioneer Collective with locations in Ballard and Capitol Hill. Industrious day passes start around $50-63. WeWork and Pioneer Collective offer similar flexibility. All three have fast, consistent internet suited to video calls. Laptop-friendly cafes are plentiful. Zoka Coffee in the University District, Ballard Coffee Works on Market Street, and Caffe Vita's Capitol Hill flagship are all well known among remote workers. Most offer reliable WiFi and enough seating to make a half-day session practical. Expect to spend $5-8 on drinks to justify a long stay. In terms of the real WiFi situation: speeds at coworking spaces are consistently strong. Cafe WiFi is generally good enough for calls and video conferencing at the places listed above, though crowded chains can be inconsistent. If you need guaranteed uptime, a coworking day pass is worth it.
seattle.gettingAround: Seattle's public transport is anchored by the Link Light Rail, which connects Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to downtown in around 38 minutes for a flat $3 fare. The 1 Line runs through Capitol Hill, downtown, and continues south toward Federal Way. Bus service fills in most other areas, but coverage is uneven: neighborhoods like Ballard, Fremont, and West Seattle have no light rail and rely entirely on buses. Walkability is neighborhood-dependent. Capitol Hill, Belltown, and South Lake Union are genuinely walkable with dense amenities. Ballard is walkable within its core. The further you get from central neighborhoods, the more you need a bus, bike, or rideshare. Seattle has a growing network of protected bike lanes, and e-bike and scooter rentals are available citywide. Rideshare (Uber and Lyft) is widely available. Driving is possible but parking downtown is expensive and traffic is notoriously congested during peak hours. Most nomads find they do not need a car if they base themselves in Capitol Hill or downtown. The airport is well connected by light rail with no need to book a transfer in advance. Just follow signs to the station from the 4th floor of the parking garage via Skybridge Six.
seattle.visas: The United States does not offer a dedicated digital nomad visa. Your options depend on your passport. Citizens of Visa Waiver Program (VWP) countries (including most of the EU, UK, Australia, Japan, and many others) can enter without a visa and stay for up to 90 days, authorized through ESTA. Citizens of countries not on the VWP list need a B-2 tourist visa, which can grant up to 6 months per entry at the discretion of the border officer. There is no official extension path for tourist or visa-waiver stays beyond the initial period without leaving the country. You can legally work remotely for non-US clients or employers while on tourist entry, but you cannot be employed by or receive US-source income from a US company. There is no nomad visa category for the US as of 2026. Always confirm entry rules with your country's US embassy or the official USCIS website before travel, as policies can change.
seattle.bestTime: Seattle has a temperate marine climate: mild, wet winters and dry, warm summers. The pattern is predictable enough to plan around. July through September is the clear sweet spot. Temperatures reach the mid-70s Fahrenheit (around 23-24C), skies are mostly clear, and the city comes alive. Long daylight hours and easy access to outdoor activities make productivity feel easier. August in particular is reliably sunny with very few rain days. October through April brings persistent overcast skies and frequent light rain. It is rarely cold enough for snow in the city, but grey days are relentless from November through March. This can affect mood and motivation for longer stays. Accommodation is cheaper in winter, and coworking spaces are less crowded, which some nomads prefer. April through June is a reasonable shoulder option: temperatures rise steadily, rain becomes less constant from May onward, and summer crowds have not yet arrived. It is a decent compromise if July and August are not possible. For a short remote-work trip, July to early October is hard to beat. For a longer stay of several months, timing your arrival before the grey season sets in matters.
seattle.whoFor:
Seattle works well for nomads who already earn in USD or have a budget that comfortably covers $4,000-5,000 per month. Tech workers, designers, and anyone with US-based clients will feel at home: the city's professional culture and infrastructure are calibrated to remote work in a way that few US cities match. Nature lovers who want to combine serious outdoor access (hiking, skiing, kayaking, whale watching) with a full urban experience will find the combination here is genuine, not just marketing copy. The coffee culture is real and among the best in North America.

Seattle is less suited to budget-conscious nomads or those relying on cheap extended stays. The 90-day visa limit makes it impractical as a long-term base for international nomads without additional planning. Anyone who needs consistent sunshine for their mental health should treat Seattle as a summer destination only and plan to leave before October.

semarang.costOfLiving:
Semarang is one of the cheapest provincial capitals in Java for remote workers. Your biggest variable is rent. A furnished one-bedroom apartment in the central Simpang Lima or Candisari district runs roughly $140-250 per month. Move out to residential suburbs like Banyumanik or Tembalang and you can find comfortable rooms for $83-140.

Eating out is very affordable. A full meal at a local warung costs $1-1.50 (under $2), while a sit-down meal for two at a mid-range restaurant runs $8.50-14. Groceries from a traditional pasar market are cheaper still; a week of basics costs around $11-17.

A hot-desk at a dedicated coworking space costs $55-89 per month, with drop-in day rates available from $2-3.50. Local transport is extremely cheap: a Trans Semarang BRT ride is $0 (under $0.25), and a typical Grab/Gojek motorcycle taxi trip across town runs $0.50-1.
semarang.whereToWork: Semarang has a small but functional coworking scene. Collabox Creative Hub in Semarang Tengah is the most established option, offering daily and monthly memberships, fast Wi-Fi, meeting rooms, and a pet-friendly lounge. Hetero Space in Banyumanik caters to freelancers and small teams with flexible desk rentals. DS CoWork near Jenderal Sudirman runs 24 hours, which is useful if your timezone requires odd hours. Cafe-working is very popular locally. Makabana Space on Jl. Diponegoro doubles as a specialty coffee shop and coworking space with dedicated desks, power outlets at every seat, and refill water. The atmosphere is relaxed and staff are used to remote workers spending hours at a stretch. Dozens of independent coffee shops in the Simpang Lima and Kota Lama areas are similarly laptop-friendly. The honest Wi-Fi picture is mixed. Average fixed-line speeds sit around 10-20 Mbps, which is adequate for video calls and most remote work but below what you find in Bali or Jakarta. Cellular data from Telkomsel or XL on a local SIM is often faster and more reliable than cafe Wi-Fi. Budget $3-5.50 per month for a solid mobile data package as a backup.
semarang.gettingAround: Semarang is not a walkable city. The urban area is spread out, heat and humidity make long walks uncomfortable, and footpaths are inconsistent. For day-to-day movement you will rely on Grab or Gojek (app-based motorcycle or car), which are cheap and widely available. A typical cross-city car trip costs $1.50-3. The Trans Semarang BRT network covers most major corridors with 18 routes at a flat $0 per journey including transfers. It is reliable but slow in traffic and not designed for the last mile. Jenderal Ahmad Yani International Airport (SRG) sits about 5 km from the city center. The Trans Semarang Airport Corridor connects the terminal to Simpang Lima for $0, though you need to walk about 100 m to the bus shelter from the arrivals gate. A Grab car to the center takes 15-20 minutes and costs around $2-3.50. Direct flights connect Semarang to most major Indonesian cities; international connections go through Kuala Lumpur, Singapore, or Jakarta.
semarang.visas: Citizens of most Western countries (US, EU, UK, Australia, Canada) receive a 30-day visa-free entry to Indonesia, which cannot be extended or converted inside the country. If you leave and re-enter, you get another 30 days, but immigration officers can and do refuse repeat visa runs. The more practical option for longer stays is the Visa on Arrival (VoA), available to roughly 90 nationalities, which costs USD 35 and is valid for 30 days with one 30-day extension, giving you up to 60 days total. For remote workers planning to stay longer, Indonesia launched the E33G Remote Worker Visa (also called the digital nomad visa) in 2024. It is valid for one year and allows you to live anywhere in Indonesia. Requirements include proof of foreign employment, an annual income of at least $60,000, and minimum savings of $2,000. The official fee is $390, with total first-year costs including KITAS processing often reaching $600-1,000. Always confirm current requirements and fees directly with the Indonesian Directorate General of Immigration (imigrasi.go.id) before applying.
semarang.bestTime: Semarang has a tropical climate with two seasons. Temperatures stay consistently around 30-33 degrees Celsius (86-91 F) year-round, so heat is always a factor. The main variable is rain. The dry season runs from May through September, with July and August being the driest months. This is the best window for visiting: lower humidity, fewer power outages during storms, and more reliable transport around the city. Air quality also tends to improve in the dry season. The wet season (October through April) brings heavy afternoon downpours, occasional flooding in low-lying parts of the city (Semarang has a longstanding flood management problem in its northern coastal areas), and higher humidity. December is the wettest month. Remote work is still perfectly possible in the wet season, but flooding disruptions and poor road conditions are real inconveniences. If you have flexibility, aim for June through September for the most comfortable experience.
semarang.whoFor:
Semarang suits remote workers who want a genuinely local Indonesian experience at a fraction of Bali's price. If you are comfortable navigating without much English infrastructure, enjoy exploring history and street food over beach clubs and yoga studios, and can handle a city that was not designed with nomads in mind, you will find Semarang rewarding and extremely affordable.

It works particularly well for people on extended Indonesia stays who want to experience Java beyond Yogyakarta, solo workers who do not depend on a large nomad community, and anyone doing a slow-travel loop through Indonesian cities.

Skip Semarang if you need fast and reliable coworking infrastructure as a baseline, if a thriving English-speaking social scene is important to you, or if you are looking for the kind of outdoor recreation and beach access that draws people to Bali or Lombok.

sofia.costOfLiving:
Sofia is one of the most affordable capitals in Europe, and that gap remains wide compared to Western cities. Expect to spend roughly $940-2,060 per month depending on how you live.

Rent is the biggest variable. A one-bedroom apartment in central neighborhoods like Lozenets or Oborishte runs $705-885 per month. Move out to areas like Studentski Grad or Mladost and you can pay $410-590 for something comparable in size. Groceries from a supermarket cost roughly $235-355 per month if you cook regularly. A sit-down lunch at a local restaurant is typically $9-13; dinner for two at a mid-range spot comes to around $47-59. A coworking hot-desk pass runs $29-59 per day, or $145-295 per month. A monthly public transport card costs around $32. Add utilities and internet (around $88-100 total) and a realistic comfortable budget lands at $1,060-1,770 per month. Budget-conscious nomads can get by on less; those renting centrally and eating out often will land near the top.
sofia.whereToWork: Sofia has a genuinely strong coworking scene for a city its size. Betahaus (Shipka Street and Slaveykov Square) is the most established, with a community-focused atmosphere and regular events. SOHO (4 Iskar Street, near Serdika metro) blends creative professionals and has flexible memberships starting around $18 per day. Cosmos Coworking Camp (Angel Kanchev 3) is centrally located, open 24/7 for members, and has a good cafe downstairs. Monthly hot-desk rates at these spaces typically run $145-295. Cafe culture in Sofia is well-suited to laptop work. Photosynthesis (Vasil Levski 57) is a photography shop and art gallery with a second-floor cafe, generous power outlets, and excellent natural light. Social Cafe Bar and Kitchen on Vitosha Boulevard offers quieter interior seating despite its busy street. Coffee Fellows (Vitosha 52) has a large front window and plug access along seating rows. Internet is genuinely fast. Bulgaria ranks among Europe's top countries for broadband speed, and most cafes and coworking spaces deliver reliable connections. A home broadband plan runs $12-15 per month. You will rarely struggle with connectivity.
sofia.gettingAround:
Sofia has a metro, extensive bus and tram network, and is walkable in the center. A single ticket costs $1; tap a contactless card and after three rides in a day you automatically hit the daily cap. The historic center, Vitosha Boulevard, and most neighborhoods nomads care about sit within 20-30 minutes on foot of each other.

The airport is 10 km east of downtown. Metro line M4 (yellow) connects Terminal 2 directly to Serdika Station in about 30 minutes for $1. A taxi costs $9-15 depending on traffic and whether you use the official taxi companies or an app like Yandex or Bolt.

Cycling infrastructure is limited and roads can be rough in places. Ride-hailing is cheap and widely available as a practical alternative.
sofia.visas:
Citizens of the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and most Western countries enter visa-free for up to 90 days within any 180-day period. Bulgaria is an EU member but not yet in the Schengen zone (as of 2025 it has partial accession), so those 90 days are counted separately from the Schengen area, giving you additional time in Europe before border rules kick in.

Bulgaria launched a formal digital nomad visa in December 2025. It is open to non-EU/EEA citizens who work remotely for clients or employers outside Bulgaria. Requirements include proof of at least $35,690 annual income (roughly $2,970 per month), a clean criminal record, and proof of Bulgarian accommodation. The visa lasts one year and is renewable for a second year. You apply first for a Type D long-stay visa at a Bulgarian consulate, then for a residence permit within 14 days of arriving. Processing typically takes four to eight weeks. Always confirm current requirements with the official Bulgarian Ministry of Interior website or a licensed immigration attorney before applying.
sofia.bestTime:
Spring (April to June) and early autumn (September to October) are the most comfortable windows. Temperatures sit between 15-25 C, skies are mostly clear, outdoor seating opens up, and the city is at its liveliest without summer heat. These months are the sweet spot for productivity and exploring.

July and August are warm to hot (28-34 C), and the city quiets down as residents leave for the coast. It is workable, especially in air-conditioned coworking spaces, but not peak conditions.

Winter (December to February) is cold, sometimes snowy, and comes with a real air quality problem. Sofia sits in a valley and temperature inversions trap pollution from wood and coal heating. PM2.5 levels in winter are significantly above WHO guidelines. If you have respiratory sensitivities, winter is the season to skip.
sofia.whoFor:
Sofia works best for nomads who want to stretch their budget without leaving Europe. If you are on a monthly income of 2,000-4,000 USD and want to save more while living comfortably, Sofia delivers that. It suits people who appreciate authentic, unhurried city life over trendy expat hubs, and those interested in Bulgarian food, Orthodox architecture, and accessible mountains for weekend hiking.

It is also well-suited for people who want the EU legal framework (easy banking, clear residency rules, safety) without the Western Europe price tag. The digital nomad visa makes longer stays genuinely viable if you meet the income requirement.

Skip Sofia if you want a warm, sunny climate year-round, a large English-speaking social scene, or a city with immediate, obvious charm at street level. Sofia rewards patience and curiosity; it does not sell itself loudly. If you need reliable coworking, low costs, and a solid base with good flight connections across Europe, Sofia is a strong choice. If you are chasing beach weather, nightlife variety, or a curated nomad hub with hundreds of co-located remote workers, look elsewhere.

taghazout.costOfLiving: Taghazout is affordable by European standards, though it is not as cheap as many nomads expect before arriving. Your biggest variable is housing.
taghazout.whereToWork: Taghazout has a surprisingly solid coworking infrastructure for a village of its size, largely because it has been a nomad destination for over a decade. SunDesk is the most established option, with 200 Mbps fiber, ergonomic desks, indoor and outdoor areas, a rooftop with power outlets, and private call booths. It is genuinely well-run, and the crowd it draws is the closest this coast has to a year-round community. Coworksurf (also listed as Adventurekeys) occupies a full floor near the main street with ocean views, 200 Mbps fiber, and up to 30 desks. Atlas Wonders offers a mix of outdoor ocean-view desks and indoor focus space and is popular with surfer-nomads. Cafe work culture is limited compared to a city like Lisbon or Chiang Mai. The Teapot Cafe has a small upstairs coworking area free with a minimum $5.50 spend. Most other cafes tolerate laptops but are not set up for full workdays. WiFi reliability is the honest caveat here. Fixed broadband in the village can drop during busy periods. The coworking spaces with dedicated fiber are consistently reliable, but cafe or Airbnb WiFi is hit or miss. Picking up a local SIM from Maroc Telecom, Inwi, or Orange and using mobile data as a backup is strongly recommended. Maroc Telecom has the strongest 4G coverage in this region.
taghazout.gettingAround: Taghazout village is small and entirely walkable. The main strip runs along one road, and you can cover the whole center on foot in under 15 minutes. Alleys and staircases connect the upper and lower parts of the village, and the beach is always close. For getting to Agadir (the nearest city, about 20 km south), local bus lines 32 and 33 run regularly from early morning until around 9-10 PM, costing $0.50-1 per trip. Shared grand taxis run the same route for $2-3 per person. Both options drop you in Agadir center in 30-40 minutes depending on traffic. Getting to/from Agadir Al Massira Airport (AGA): The airport is roughly 45 km from Taghazout. A private taxi costs around $32 for the whole car. The Souk to Surf shuttle runs once daily for around $11 but only operates daytime hours. For flexibility, a private transfer booked in advance is the most reliable option. There is no need to rent a car to live in the village itself, but having one opens up day trips to Agadir, the Paradise Valley gorge, and other Atlantic surf spots further north.
taghazout.visas: Morocco is visa-free for passport holders from the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Australia, New Zealand, and approximately 70 other countries. On arrival you receive a 90-day tourist stamp. If you want to extend, you can apply at the nearest police station before your 90 days expire for an additional 90 days, though the process is informal and not guaranteed. Morocco does not currently offer a formal digital nomad visa. Most long-stay nomads do border runs to the Canary Islands or mainland Europe and re-enter. There is no formal "exit stamp" requirement, so many people simply overstay and pay a small fine on departure, though this is not officially condoned. Always confirm current entry rules with your country's official travel advisory and the Moroccan embassy before traveling.
taghazout.bestTime: Taghazout has a mild Atlantic climate year-round, with around 300 sunny days per year and modest rainfall mostly in brief winter showers. October to March is the sweet spot for most nomads. Daytime temperatures sit between 18-25°C (64-77°F), the surf is at its most consistent and powerful, and the nomad community is at its largest. November through February brings the best waves but also the most rain, which is still quite limited. April and May offer a quieter village, pleasant warmth, and good weather without peak-season crowds. Good for focused work with fewer distractions. June to September is summer: temperatures reach 28-30°C (82-86°F), the sea is calmer, and the village gets busy with European package tourists. Surf conditions are less reliable in summer, and the village can feel crowded around the main beach. If you want pure sun and beach time alongside work, it is fine, but it is a different atmosphere. For the best combination of good surf culture, a strong nomad community, manageable crowds, and comfortable working weather, October through April is the recommended window.
taghazout.whoFor:
Taghazout is an excellent fit for nomads who want to combine a productive work base with an active outdoor lifestyle. If you surf, or want to learn, it is one of the best places in the world to do both at once. The village suits people who thrive in small, community-oriented settings where you will see the same faces at the coworking space, the cafe, and the beach within the same day.

It also works well for nomads wanting a warm, affordable Atlantic escape from November through April, especially those coming from Europe looking for a short flight and no culture shock on the cost side.

You should probably skip Taghazout if you need fast-paced urban energy, a wide restaurant and nightlife scene, or if reliable home WiFi is non-negotiable for your work. It is also not ideal if you are sensitive to being a visible outsider in a conservative Moroccan coastal community. Those who want the Moroccan city experience are better served by Marrakech or Casablanca.

tainan.costOfLiving:
Tainan is one of the cheapest cities in Taiwan, noticeably lower than Taipei and a bit under Kaohsiung. Your rent will do most of the work. A studio or one-bedroom apartment in a central district like West Central or North runs roughly $310 to $560 a month, while the same thing a short scooter ride out, in Yongkang or the eastern suburbs, drops to $190 to $370. Short lets and furnished monthly rentals cost more, so expect to pay a premium if you are not signing a year.

Food is where Tainan earns its reputation and its low bills. The city is Taiwan's street-food capital, and a bowl of beef soup, danzai noodles, or a plate of rice with braised pork costs $2 to $3.50. A sit-down meal for two at a mid-range spot lands around $22 to $25. Cooking at home is cheap too, with a week of groceries for one person around $37 to $56, though imported Western items cost more.

A coworking hot desk runs roughly $9.50 to $15 a day or $120 to $220 for a monthly pass. Local transport is minor: a scooter rental or fuel plus the odd bus and YouBike ride comes to well under $62 a month. Add utilities, a SIM, and the occasional bar or coffee, and a comfortable single-person total sits around $870 to $1,400 a month. Live frugally and you can go lower.
tainan.whereToWork: Tainan has a small but real coworking scene. Spaceout is the best-known option aimed at remote workers and international nomads, with quiet desks, fast WiFi, free coffee and water, and staff who speak English, which matters here. Other spaces include Planett, Big O, and Hour Jungle, though hours, English support, and desk availability vary, so check current listings before you commit to a monthly plan. Cafe-work culture exists but is more casual than in Taipei. Independent coffee shops in the West Central District are laptop-friendly, and you will find people working over pour-overs, though some smaller places prefer you not camp for hours. Chain cafes and the ubiquitous convenience stores give you reliable backup power and seats. WiFi is generally solid across the city, and home fiber is fast and cheap, but if your income depends on stable video calls, do not rely only on cafe connections. A local SIM with a generous data plan is a smart backup, and coverage in the city is good.
tainan.gettingAround: Tainan is built around the scooter. Locals ride everywhere, and if you can legally rent one and are comfortable in dense traffic, it is by far the most practical way to get around a city that sprawls beyond its walkable historic core. Rentals are cheap and widely available. If you would rather not ride, plan carefully, because public transit is the city's real weakness. City buses cover the main corridors but run infrequently on quieter routes, so journeys can involve waiting. YouBike public bicycles are dotted around the center and are great for short daytime hops between temples, markets, and cafes. The TPASS 799 monthly pass bundles unlimited local buses, regional TRA trains, and free 30-minute YouBike rides for $25, which is excellent value if you stay a while. For other cities, the conventional TRA railway stops at central Tainan Station, while the High Speed Rail (HSR) station sits on the edge of town at Shalun; a short TRA branch-line shuttle connects the two. HSR reaches Taipei in around 1 hour 45 minutes and Kaohsiung in about 15. For flights, tiny Tainan Airport (TNN) handles limited domestic and a few regional routes, so most international travel goes through Kaohsiung International Airport (KHH), roughly an hour away by shuttle bus (Route 111) or by train via Zuoying.
tainan.visas: Most Western passport holders, including citizens of the US, UK, EU countries, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, get 90 days visa-free on arrival. UK and Canadian passport holders can extend that initial stay to 180 days without leaving. Otherwise, the standard 90 days is not extendable for tourism, so longer stays mean a border run or a proper visa. For staying put, the Taiwan Employment Gold Card is the standout: a combined open work permit, resident visa, and residence certificate valid for one to three years, aimed at professionals in fields like tech, finance, science, and the arts, typically requiring a recent monthly income near $5,700 or equivalent qualifications. It also opens the door to National Health Insurance. Taiwan additionally launched a Digital Nomad Visa in 2025 for remote workers from visa-exempt countries, allowing up to six months but with income and savings thresholds and no health insurance included. Rules and figures change, so confirm the latest requirements with official sources (the Bureau of Consular Affairs and the Taiwan Gold Card site) before you plan.
tainan.bestTime:
Tainan is hot, humid, and subtropical. Summers, roughly May through September, are genuinely brutal: high heat, heavy humidity, afternoon downpours, and typhoon risk. If you work indoors with air conditioning you will cope, but sightseeing and scooter rides in July feel like effort. Winters, from about November to February, are the payoff: mild, mostly dry, and pleasant, with comfortable days and cool evenings. Tainan gets more sunshine and less winter drizzle than the north, which is a real advantage over Taipei.

The best window for remote work is late autumn through early spring, roughly November to March, when the weather is easy and outdoor life is genuinely enjoyable. Book earlier around Lunar New Year, when prices rise and the city fills up.
tainan.whoFor:
Tainan suits self-directed remote workers who value low costs, great food, and a slower pace over nightlife and a big expat crowd. If you are comfortable riding a scooter, happy to pick up a little Mandarin, and want a genuinely affordable base with strong culture and easy weekend trips by rail, it is a rewarding place to settle for a season, especially in winter.

Skip Tainan if you refuse to ride a scooter and need frequent public transit, if you want a large ready-made nomad social scene, or if you cannot tolerate intense summer heat and humidity. In those cases Taipei, with its metro and bigger community, or Kaohsiung, with its own MRT and international airport, will serve you better while keeping you close enough to visit Tainan for the food.

trujillo.costOfLiving:
Trujillo is one of Peru's most affordable mid-sized cities. A one-bedroom apartment in the central districts of El Golf or Primavera runs roughly $240-350 per month. Step further out toward California or San Andres and you can find decent one-bedrooms for $180-260. Groceries from local markets run about $120-180 monthly if you cook most meals. Eating out is cheap: a solid lunch menu at a local cevicheria or menu del dia costs $3.50-6, and even a sit-down dinner at a nicer restaurant rarely tops $18 per person with drinks.

A hot-desk day pass at Estacion Coworking or Centrika typically runs $9-15; monthly memberships range from $88-160. Getting around by combi or micro bus costs $0.29-0.59 per ride. Uber and InDriver rides across the city average $2.50-4.50. All in, a comfortable nomad budget for Trujillo lands around $1,000-1,400 per month, making it one of the cheaper cities in South America for remote workers.
trujillo.whereToWork: Trujillo has a small but functional coworking scene. Estacion Coworking in San Andres is the main hub, offering fast fiber internet, a cafe, printer access, and a startup-leaning community. It hosts occasional events and is the closest thing the city has to a nomad focal point. Centrika Coworking on Jiron Ayacucho in the historic center rents offices and flexible desks and caters more to local professionals than nomads, but it is a solid backup option. Cafe-working culture is emerging but not yet as established as in Lima or Medellin. Specialty cafes like Moche Cafes Especiales in the historic center and Elevaria Cafe near Av. Fatima welcome laptop workers and serve excellent Peruvian specialty coffee. Home internet via Claro or Movistar fiber delivers 50-100 Mbps at $24-35 per month and is generally reliable in El Golf and Primavera. Power cuts are rare in the modern residential areas. Budget for a local SIM as a backup hotspot; both Claro and Entel offer 4G LTE with good coverage in the city.
trujillo.gettingAround:
The historic center is walkable and compact. Most attractions, cafes, and restaurants in the centro are reachable on foot within 20 minutes. Beyond the center, you will need wheels. Combis and micros cover the whole city for $0.29-0.59 per trip and run from early morning until about 9 PM, though routes can be confusing at first. Uber and InDriver are both active in Trujillo and are the recommended options for evening travel or any time you are carrying a laptop bag, given occasional petty theft on public buses.

Taxis exist but always agree on a price before you get in; a cross-city ride should be $2.50-4.50. The beach suburb of Huanchaco is a popular side base for nomads; colectivos run there for $0.88-1, or a taxi costs around $4.50-6. Trujillo's airport (TRU, Capitan FAP Carlos Martinez de Pinillos) is about 10 km from the center. A taxi to downtown costs roughly $6-7.50. There are no direct bus routes that serve the airport entrance conveniently, so a taxi or ride-share is the practical choice with luggage.
trujillo.visas: Citizens of the United States, Canada, the EU, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, and most of South America enter Peru visa-free and receive a tourist permit of up to 90 days on arrival. Your passport should have at least 6 months of validity remaining. You can extend your stay by 30 days by visiting the Direccion General de Migraciones; the process requires a return ticket and a small fee. Peru passed legislation in late 2023 creating a dedicated digital nomad visa with a 365-day stay, but as of mid-2026 that visa has not been implemented by immigration authorities and was not included in updated TUPA publications. There is no workaround other than the standard tourist permit or exiting and re-entering the country. Always confirm current rules with the official Migraciones website (migraciones.gob.pe) before your trip, as regulations can change.
trujillo.bestTime: Trujillo is a genuine year-round destination. The coast here is arid desert, so rain is almost never a factor. Temperatures stay between 16-29 degrees C (61-84 F) throughout the year. The warmest months run January through March, with afternoon highs touching 28-29 C (82-84 F) and occasional coastal humidity. June through October is drier and slightly cooler, averaging 20-24 C (68-75 F) during the day with fresh breezes off the Pacific. For remote work, the sweet spot is April through November. Temperatures are comfortable, humidity is low, and the city runs at a calm pace outside of major festivals. If you visit in late January or early February, you will catch the Festival Internacional de la Primavera (Spring Festival) and the Marinera dance competition, which are culturally unmissable but also mean busier streets and higher short-term rental prices. The December-to-March window is perfectly fine to visit, just warmer and more festive.
trujillo.whoFor:
Trujillo suits nomads who want a genuinely affordable South American base without the chaos of Lima or the tourist-trap pricing of Cusco. If you can work independently from a home office or are comfortable with a small coworking ecosystem, and you already speak basic Spanish, you will find the low costs, good food, and stable year-round climate rewarding. It is particularly good for people interested in pre-Columbian history, surf day trips to Huanchaco, or those doing longer slow-travel stays in Peru outside the beaten Gringo Trail.

Skip Trujillo if you need a large nomad community, frequent English-language networking, or a mature coworking infrastructure. It is also a poor fit if you are unwilling to take basic urban safety precautions, especially at night. Travelers who want consistent sun, low prices, and an authentic Peruvian city that has not been packaged for foreign visitors will feel right at home here.

utrecht.costOfLiving: Utrecht is noticeably cheaper than Amsterdam, but it is still one of the more expensive cities in the Netherlands. Expect to spend in the range of $2,500 to $3,650 per month depending on your lifestyle and where you choose to live. Rent: A one-bedroom apartment in the city center (Binnenstad, Neude, Oudegracht area) costs roughly $1,500 to $1,800 per month. In more residential areas like Zuilen, Overvecht, or Leidsche Rijn, you can find similar apartments for $1,150 to $1,500. The housing market is tight and competitive, so budget extra time to find a good place. Groceries: Expect to spend $230 to $340 per month (~$220 to $330) shopping at Albert Heijn, Jumbo, or Lidl. Cooking at home regularly keeps this manageable. Eating out: A casual lunch or dinner runs $14 to $23 per person (~$13 to $22). Sit-down dinners at mid-range restaurants cost $28 to $51 per person (~$28 to $50). Coworking hot desk: A flexible hot desk at spaces like WERF5, Mindspace, or Spaces Utrecht runs $74 to $340 per month (~$72 to $335), depending on the space and access tier. Local transport: A monthly public transport pass costs around $110 (~$106). In practice, most people use a bicycle and rarely need transit. A decent second-hand bike costs $110 to $230 upfront. Total monthly range: A frugal nomad can live on $2,050 to $2,500 (~$2,000 to $2,450). A comfortable mid-range budget sits around $2,850 to $3,650 (~$2,780 to $3,560).
utrecht.whereToWork: Utrecht has a solid mix of formal coworking spaces and relaxed cafes. Coworking is well-developed here. WERF5 on the Oudegracht canal is a community favorite with a very approachable price point (from $74/month) and a genuine community feel. Mindspace Utrecht near Central Station is more upscale, with a polished setup and 24/7 access. The Forty Hub on Maliebaan occupies a beautiful historical building with a rooftop terrace and a quieter, focus-oriented atmosphere. Spaces Utrecht offers two locations with professional amenities and meeting rooms starting at $100/month for part-time access. For cafe working, Utrecht is genuinely welcoming. Coffeecompany at Vismarkt has reliable fast WiFi, plenty of power outlets, and a good tolerance for laptop workers. The 5th on Neude is a popular choice, with comfortable seating, sockets throughout, and a central location next to the public library. DUBBEL/DWARS near Weerdsingel has dedicated laptop-friendly seating with charging ports built into the tables. Most cafe-work spots expect you to order periodically, but nobody will rush you out. The WiFi situation is strong by European standards. Fiber is the norm in most buildings, and speeds of 200 to 300 Mbps are typical at home and at coworking spaces. Public cafe WiFi is generally reliable enough for video calls.
utrecht.gettingAround: Utrecht is one of the best cycling cities in the world. The city center is compact and almost entirely navigable by bike. Once you have a bicycle, you will rarely need anything else for day-to-day movement. The bike parking under Utrecht Centraal station holds over 12,000 bikes, which tells you everything about cycling culture here. The bus and tram network (operated by Connexxion and U-OV) covers areas outside the center well. Trains from Utrecht Centraal connect to Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Den Haag, and Eindhoven in under an hour, with trains running every 10 to 15 minutes during the day. Getting to the airport: Utrecht Centraal to Amsterdam Schiphol Airport (AMS) by direct train takes around 30 to 35 minutes, with trains running roughly every 15 minutes. This is one of Utrecht's biggest practical advantages over other Dutch cities.
utrecht.visas:
The Netherlands is part of the Schengen Area. Most Western passport holders (US, UK, Canada, Australia, and others) can enter visa-free and stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen zone. EU and EEA citizens have full freedom of movement and can stay and work indefinitely after registering with the municipality.

The Netherlands does not currently offer a dedicated digital nomad visa for remote workers employed abroad. The closest option for freelancers or entrepreneurs is the Self-Employed Residence Permit (Zelfstandig Ondernemer), which requires demonstrating a business plan with proven economic value to the Netherlands. It is a more involved process than a simple nomad visa.

For most nomads, the practical approach is staying within the 90-day Schengen limit and rotating out to non-Schengen countries between visits. Always confirm current visa rules with the IND (Dutch Immigration and Naturalisation Service) at ind.nl before booking.
utrecht.bestTime: Utrecht has a temperate maritime climate with mild, damp winters and cool summers. Average highs in summer reach around 22°C (72°F), while winters rarely drop below freezing but are grey and wet for long stretches. The best months for a working visit are May, June, and September. Spring brings longer daylight hours, blooming canals, and outdoor cafe season. Early September offers similar weather with thinner tourist crowds. July and August are pleasant but busier and slightly more expensive. Avoid November through February unless you are comfortable with short, overcast days and frequent rain. Winter has its own charm, particularly around the December holiday markets along the canals, but it is not ideal for the kind of outdoor exploration that makes Utrecht enjoyable day-to-day.
utrecht.whoFor:
Utrecht works well for nomads who want a genuinely livable European base rather than a tourist destination. If you value a walkable canal city with excellent infrastructure, fast internet, and easy access to the rest of Europe, it rewards longer stays. It suits people who are comfortable with higher costs, can work within the Schengen 90-day window, and want a city that feels real rather than overrun. It is a strong choice for freelancers in design, tech, or writing who value focus and quality of life over hustle and nightlife.

Skip Utrecht if you are on a tight budget (Southeast Asia or Eastern Europe will stretch your money far further), if you need a nomad visa pathway, or if you want a warmer climate for most of the year. It is also a poor fit if a buzzing nightlife scene is a priority. Amsterdam is just 25 minutes away by train, but Utrecht itself is not a party city.

warsaw.costOfLiving: Warsaw is one of Europe's more affordable capitals, but it has risen in cost over recent years and no longer qualifies as a budget destination. Expect a wide range depending on how centrally you want to live and how often you eat out. Rent: A one-bedroom apartment in the city center (Srodmiescie, Zoliborz, Mokotow) runs roughly $935-1,340/month. In cheaper outer areas like Praga or Bemowo, the same apartment costs $535-800/month. Groceries: A reasonable weekly shop at a Biedronka or Lidl comes to about $67-94/month, so roughly $265-375/month for one person cooking regularly at home. Eating out: A sit-down lunch at a mid-range restaurant costs $8-16. A traditional milk bar (bar mleczny) meal is under $5.50. Dinner with drinks at a decent spot runs $21-40. Coworking hot desk: Expect $135-240/month for a dedicated hot desk at spaces like Brain Embassy or WeWork. Day passes run $21-35. Local transport: A monthly ZTM pass covering all trams, buses, and both metro lines costs $29. This covers the whole city reliably. Total monthly range: A solo nomad living centrally with coworking, eating out a few times a week, and a mid-range apartment should plan for $1,740-2,410/month. Living further out and cooking more often brings it to $1,200-1,600/month.
warsaw.whereToWork:
Warsaw has a mature coworking market. Brain Embassy operates several well-designed locations across the city including Czackiego in the center, with 24/7 access and consistent fast internet. Mindspace has two flagship locations, including one in the Skyliner tower near Rondo Daszynskiego metro station, with a premium feel and strong community events. WeWork runs five locations across Warsaw for those who want a more corporate setup or flexible day passes.

Cafe culture for working is well established. CoffeeDesk operates multiple Warsaw branches as hybrid cafe-coworking spaces with dedicated power sockets, strong WiFi, and extended hours. Green Caffe Nero has locations across the city, most open until 11 PM, with reliable internet and spacious seating that tolerates long laptop sessions without pressure to leave. You will generally find WiFi usable and widespread in cafes.

The real WiFi situation: connectivity is strong in dedicated coworking spaces and decent in most cafes. Mobile data on Polish SIMs (Play, Orange, T-Mobile) is fast and cheap, making a SIM-based hotspot a reliable backup. You will rarely struggle to find a connection in the center.
warsaw.gettingAround:
Warsaw's public transport network is genuinely good for a city its size. Two metro lines (M1 running north-south, M2 running east-west) cover the key areas and intersect at Swietokrzyska. Trams and buses fill in the gaps. A monthly ZTM pass at $29 gives unlimited access to the whole network and is the obvious choice for any stay longer than two weeks.

Walkability is high in the central districts. Srodmiescie, the Old Town, and Powisl are pleasant on foot, and the city has invested in cycling infrastructure, making renting a Veturilo city bike practical for short trips in good weather.

Getting to/from the airport: Warsaw Chopin Airport (WAW) is about 7 km southwest of the center. The SKM commuter rail line (train 69) runs between the airport and Warsaw Central station in about 20 minutes for $1. A taxi or Uber costs $11-19 depending on traffic and time of day. There is no reason to take an expensive transfer service.
warsaw.visas: Poland is part of the Schengen Area. Citizens of the US, Canada, Australia, UK, and roughly 60 other countries can enter visa-free for up to 90 days within any 180-day rolling period. This covers a standard short stay comfortably. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa for Poland as of mid-2026. For longer stays, the main option is a Type D national visa, which can be issued for up to one year and, in some cases, allows renewal. A freelance pathway exists under Type D but requires registering as a sole proprietor in Poland and engaging with the Polish tax system. This is a meaningful administrative commitment and works best for those planning a multi-year base rather than a temporary stint. Always verify current requirements with the official Polish consulate or government immigration portal before making plans.
warsaw.bestTime:
Warsaw's climate is continental: cold winters (January averages around -1.5C/29F, with grey skies and occasional snow), warm summers (July peaks at about 26C/79F), and genuinely pleasant spring and autumn months.

For remote work, the best window is May through June and September through October. Temperatures are comfortable, the city is lively without peak-tourist crowds, and daylight hours are long in late spring. July and August are warm and sunny but bring the most tourists, higher short-term rental prices, and occasional city-center congestion. Winter (December through February) can be grey and cold, which some people find productive and others find draining. November is probably the least appealing month, combining short days with damp cold and limited daylight.
warsaw.whoFor:
Warsaw suits nomads who want a serious European city with real infrastructure: fast internet, proper coworking, good food, and a functioning metro. It works especially well for people in tech, finance, or creative industries who benefit from being in a city with a growing startup ecosystem and a large professional expat community. Those who appreciate history, modern architecture, and a city that is actively rebuilding its identity will find Warsaw genuinely interesting rather than just functional.

It is also a strong choice for people on a US or UK salary who want to spend time in Europe without paying Paris or Amsterdam prices. Budget-conscious nomads who cook at home and use public transport can live comfortably for under $1,500 a month.

Warsaw is less suited to nomads who prioritize warm weather year-round, beach access, or a strong outdoor lifestyle. Those sensitive to urban air pollution may find the city uncomfortable, particularly in winter and spring. If you need to stay longer than 90 days without engaging with visa paperwork and local registration, Warsaw is also not the easiest base to sustain legally.

yerevan.costOfLiving: Yerevan sits at the affordable end of the European nomad circuit. Expect to spend between $900 and $1,600 per month depending on how central you live and how often you eat out.
yerevan.whereToWork: Yerevan has a genuine and growing coworking scene, driven partly by an influx of remote workers since 2022. The main options are well-equipped and affordable by any standard. Impact Hub Armenia on Tigran Mets Avenue is the most established space: high-speed fiber, meeting rooms, a social enterprise community, and reasonable day and monthly rates. LOFT Yerevan on Moskovyan Street is 24-hour, centrally located near a metro stop, and popular with freelancers who keep irregular hours. It offers Skype booths, lockers, and a quiet zone. EVN Coworking on Mashtots Avenue is a newer, well-reviewed option if you prefer a less community-heavy setup. Cafe work is widely accepted. Achajour Parpetsi near the Opera Theatre is the go-to for serious laptop sessions: reliable WiFi, plenty of seats, and no pressure to leave. Saryan Street has a concentration of cafes with outdoor terraces that work well in spring and autumn. WiFi throughout the city is solid. Average fixed broadband speeds are around 80-100 Mbps download, with the fastest ISP (Ucom) reaching over 100 Mbps. Mobile 4G LTE is stable across central districts, and 5G is rolling out in Kentron. Power cuts, once common, are now rare in central Yerevan. You will occasionally encounter slower connections at smaller cafes, but this is the exception rather than the rule.
yerevan.gettingAround: The city centre is genuinely walkable. Kentron, where most nomads stay, is compact enough that you can cover most of it on foot. Northern Avenue, Republic Square, the Cascade complex, and Abovyan Street are all within a 15-20 minute walk of each other. Public transport is cheap and functional. Buses and minibuses (marshrutkas) cover most of the city and cost $0.50 per ride, with electronic payment cards introduced in 2025. The metro has a single line running roughly north-south through the centre and operates until midnight. Trolleybuses are slower but useful for east-west routes. Yandex Taxi and Bolt are the standard for on-demand rides: cheap, metered by app, and consistently faster than hailing a street cab. Airport: Zvartnots International Airport is about 12 km southwest of the city centre. Bus route 100 runs 24 hours and costs around $1. A Yandex Taxi or Bolt ride takes 20-30 minutes and costs roughly $7-11. Avoid the unofficial taxi touts inside the arrivals hall; prices are 3-4x higher than app-booked rides.
yerevan.visas: Armenia is unusually open for long stays. Citizens of most Western countries including the US, EU member states, UK, Canada, and Australia receive visa-free entry for up to 180 days within any 12-month period. There is no stamp in your passport that resets at the border: the 180 days are tracked cumulatively per calendar year. Armenia does not currently offer a dedicated digital nomad visa. For stays beyond 180 days, you need to apply for a residency permit through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or depart and re-enter at the start of a new annual period. Many long-term nomads simply leave briefly to Georgia (a short flight or bus to Tbilisi) and return. If your country is not on the visa-free list, an e-visa is available online for stays up to 21 or 120 days. Always verify current entry requirements through your country's official foreign ministry before travel, as rules can change.
yerevan.bestTime: Yerevan has a dry continental climate: summers are genuinely hot (July and August regularly hit 35-40C), winters are cold (lows of -6 to -10C) with occasional snow, and spring can be rainy and windy. For remote work, the two sweet spots are late April through June and September through early October. These windows give you 18-25C temperatures, long daylight hours, clear skies, and the city at its most social. Outdoor cafe terraces are open, the parks are pleasant, and you can take weekend day trips to Garni, Geghard, or Lake Sevan without battling heat or ice. Summer (July and August) is doable if you have air conditioning in your apartment, but working in a hot coworking space or cafe without strong AC gets uncomfortable. Winter is quiet, affordable, and Yerevan still functions normally, but it is not the most inspiring time to arrive for the first time.
yerevan.whoFor:
Yerevan is a strong fit for nomads who want a European-adjacent base that is genuinely affordable without feeling like a compromise. If you are from a country with visa-free access and you want 3-6 months somewhere with good internet, real food culture, a walkable city, and low costs, Yerevan delivers consistently. It also suits people with an interest in history and ancient culture: the Armenian highlands, monasteries, and the Ararat valley are on your doorstep.

It works especially well as a long-stay base rather than a brief stopover. A week here barely scratches the surface; two to four months is where it makes sense both logistically and financially.

It is probably not the right fit if you need a large English-only community, direct flights to multiple continents, or beach access. It also requires a higher tolerance for urban grit: pavement quality outside the centre is uneven, traffic is noisy, and summer heat can limit how much you enjoy the city outdoors. Those who come for the culture, the affordability, and a slower pace tend to stay far longer than planned.

zaragoza.costOfLiving: Zaragoza is one of Spain's most affordable large cities, with monthly costs well below what you'd pay in Madrid or Barcelona. Rent is the biggest variable: a one-bedroom apartment in the center (Casco Antiguo, El Rabal) runs roughly $805-980 per month, while apartments a bit further out in districts like Delicias or Torrero drop to $520-690. Groceries at a local supermarket cost around $230-290 per month if you cook regularly. Eating out is a pleasure here: a pintxos crawl in El Tubo rarely breaks $17, and a solid sit-down lunch menu is typically $14-17. For remote work infrastructure, a hot-desk at one of Zaragoza's coworking spaces runs $115-175 per month, which is very reasonable by European standards. A monthly public transport pass costs around $23-35, and the city's bike-share scheme runs just $40 per year. Utilities average $115-150 per month for a one-bedroom flat.
zaragoza.whereToWork: Zaragoza has a small but real coworking scene. TheHackership on Via de la Hispanidad is a tech-focused space with 300 Mbps internet, 24-hour access, free coffee, and a recording studio, at $115 per month. Coworking ConJota near Parque del Buen Humor offers a bright, community-driven environment with an outdoor terrace for $175 per month. Regus Torre Aragonia on Avenida Juan Pablo II is the largest flexible workspace in the city (900+ sqm), housed in a landmark Rafael Moneo building, and suits those who prefer a corporate-grade setup. CIEM Zaragoza on Avenida de la Autonomia is a business incubator with coworking access, strong for networking with local startups. Studio 9 Space on Calle del Rio Huerva caters to creatives. Cafe-working culture in Zaragoza is more limited than in cities like Barcelona. Spanish cafe culture prizes quick coffee over lingering with a laptop, so you'll get mixed results in traditional bars. That said, several cafes actively cater to remote workers: Cafe Nolasco (Calle San Jorge) has high chairs and laptop-friendly tables; La Clandestina Bistro (Calle San Andres) in the historic center offers WiFi and specialty coffee; Didola (Calle Don Jaime I) is a converted-library cafe with large tables and free WiFi. Veintiuno Coffee roasts its own beans and has multiple locations with WiFi. The city's average internet speed is around 262 Mbps, and fiber coverage is excellent. You should not have connectivity problems at any coworking space or modern apartment.
zaragoza.gettingAround:
Zaragoza is a compact city of around 700,000 people and very walkable in the center. The Casco Antiguo, El Tubo, and the area around the Basilica del Pilar are all easily covered on foot. For longer distances, the city runs a single tram line crossing north to south with 25 stops, plus over 30 day bus lines and 7 night lines. A single ticket costs $1.50; a monthly pass is around $23-35. The tram is the fastest way to get across the city and runs until midnight on weekdays.

The city also has a bike-share scheme (Bizi Zaragoza) at $40 per year, and the flat terrain makes cycling practical for most of the urban area. Taxis are available throughout the city and easy to hail or app-book.

Zaragoza Airport (ZAZ) sits about 10 km west of the center. Bus Line 501 connects the airport to the main bus station and Delicias railway station in 20-30 minutes for $4.50. A taxi runs $23-29. The city also has a major AVE high-speed rail station (Delicias), putting Madrid 1h20m away and Barcelona under 2 hours, which is a genuine advantage for anyone who travels frequently for work.
zaragoza.visas: Citizens of the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and most other non-EU countries can enter Spain visa-free for up to 90 days within any 180-day period under Schengen rules. This 90-day counter applies across the entire Schengen Area, not just Spain, so days spent in France or Germany count against your allowance. If you want to stay longer, Spain offers a Digital Nomad Visa (formally the ARTIN, Autorizacion de Residencia para Teletrabajo de Caracter Internacional). As of 2026, the income requirement is approximately $3,280 per month for a single applicant. You must work remotely for a company or clients outside Spain, and no more than 20% of your income can come from Spanish sources. The initial authorization is valid for 3 years and renewable for a further 2. EU and EEA citizens can live and work in Spain without any visa. Always verify current requirements with Spain's official consulate or immigration authority before making plans.
zaragoza.bestTime: Zaragoza sits in the Ebro valley with a continental Mediterranean climate: little rain, low humidity, and strong temperature swings between summer and winter. The city is also notorious for the Cierzo, a cold dry wind that blows from the northwest, which can make winter days feel harsher than the temperature suggests. Spring (April and May) is the best window for remote work. Temperatures are mild (15-22 C / 59-72 F), the city is lively without being overwhelmed by visitors, and outdoor work or evening exploring is genuinely pleasant. September and October are a close second, with summer heat fading, excellent produce in the markets, and the city returning to its local rhythm after August holidays. Avoid July and August if you can. Temperatures regularly hit 35-40 C (95-104 F), many local businesses close for extended periods in August, and the heat makes midday work uncomfortable unless you have strong air conditioning. Winter (December to February) is cool and manageable at 7-11 C (45-52 F) but the Cierzo wind can be unpleasant, and the city is quieter.
zaragoza.whoFor:
Zaragoza suits remote workers who want the infrastructure and culture of a mid-size Spanish city without paying Madrid or Barcelona prices. You will do well here if you value affordability, good food, a walkable center, and easy rail access to Spain's major hubs. It's a strong pick for anyone on a tighter budget who still wants a real city experience, or for those spending several months in Spain who want somewhere quieter and more genuinely local than the well-worn nomad trail.

It is less well suited to people who rely on a large English-speaking community, want a lively digital nomad social scene, or need regular direct international flights. Those who want beach access or warmer winters will also find better options along Spain's Mediterranean coast.
